items.title: “Tip Toe” Rails Against the Rolling Back of Progress
items.description: Early in the new miniseries “Tip Toe,” two older gay men debate how worried they should be as homophobia surges in the U.K. Leo Struthers (Alan Cumming), the owner of a bar in Manchester’s storied queer quarter, asks his longtime friend Melba (Paul Rhys) wheth
items.author: Inkoo Kang
paragraphs: Early in the new miniseries “Tip Toe,” two older gay men debate how worried they should be as homophobia surges in the U.K. Leo Struthers (Alan Cumming), the owner of a bar in Manchester’s storied queer quarter, asks his longtime friend Melba (Paul Rhys) whether the vintage intolerance of the nineteen-nineties seems to be coming around again. “It’s back, you fucking idiot,” Melba responds. “We’re in the middle of it right now.” Online hate for Leo’s business, his friend notes, is as “regular as the morning shit.” Melba’s the sort of scenester who’s hard to miss—statuesque, with a signature look of dark lipstick and Robert Smith-style eyeliner—but he confesses to toning himself down lately. In the current climate, he says, “Now I tiptoe, just in case.”

The social revanchism of the twenty-twenties has largely shown up in pop culture as triumphalism on the right and silence on the left; on television, the neo-Western TV mogul Taylor Sheridan blankets the proverbial airwaves with trucks, horses, and anti-California jabs, while programs centered on queer characters and protagonists of color continue to dwindle. “Tip Toe,” from the television auteur Russell T Davies, is a rare outcry from the side of the progressives, who are seeing their political and cultural gains rapidly erode. In 1999, Davies created the original “Queer as Folk,” a groundbreaking show about ordinary gay Mancunians who spend their nights at the club, where they find almost everything they want: sex, drugs, family, friendship, freedom. A quarter century later, Leo’s bar is less a temple to liberation than a fortress under sporadic siege, where drag performers have protocols for emergency exits and bartenders, between pours, watch the door for troublemakers.

What if such measures aren’t enough? What if the atavism under way isn’t just a miasma of unpleasantness but a buildup of gas waiting to combust? That panic fuels “Tip Toe,” a siren of a series that confirms Davies’s standing as one of the medium’s essential creators. The five-episode drama—which aired this summer in Britain, on Channel 4, and wraps up its American run this week, on Starz—is a minor work with ample speechifying and visible budget constraints, and yet it offers more thoughtfulness and ingenuity than most of the year’s prestige programming.

It’s also a bit of a tough watch, opening with a flash-forward in which Leo is found hanged from a lamppost outside his home. His presumed killer is his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), a fitfully employed electrician with an unshakable suspicion that Leo has designs on his sons, twenty-five-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans) and sixteen-year-old George (Jackson Connor). The time line then jumps back ten days, when, after more than a decade of wordless coexistence on opposite sides of a shared wall, Leo locks himself out of his house and asks to borrow Clive’s phone to call a friend with a spare key. Suddenly, the two men become enmeshed in each other’s lives, with Clive on the attack despite practically begging Leo for odd jobs, and Leo on a mission to soften Clive’s bigotry, tragically mistaken about his ability to win over a man who can no longer hear reason.

That naïveté is a surprising blind spot for the fifty-nine-year-old Leo, a man steeped in experience. “Tip Toe” is one of a vanishingly few series centered on gay men in late middle age, and Leo’s well-roundedness hints at all we miss out on in the absence of perspectives like his. An elfin force of nature with the natural showmanship of someone who takes hospitality seriously, Leo has the charisma to command the loyalty of his fresh-faced staff—and the pragmatism to resent the Labour Party’s business reforms. Having seen too many gay kids sink into hopelessness, he treats the bar like an unofficial employment-training center for L.G.B.T.Q. youth, though he’s not above grousing at a trans bartender (Iz Hesketh) about the transgender movement’s emphasis on pronouns—a carp he quickly takes back. But Cumming gets to show here the vulnerability so frequently lacking in his waspish supporting roles or in his hosting gig on the reality-competition series “The Traitors,” where he’s a master of self-aware camp. Leo is still smarting from his ex-husband’s decision two years prior to leave him for a woman. And he hates that, in his escalating spats with Clive, he’s the first to apologize or to compromise. Cumming has seldom laid himself so bare as he he does late in the show, when Leo gulps down the self-loathing that rises in his throat as he finally explodes at Clive, lamenting that he’s spent a lifetime making himself palatable, even pitiful, to shield himself from a hostile heterosexual world.

“Tip Toe” is at its best when it captures what it feels like to live through the present-day backlash. Davies has a keen eye for how societal tensions trickle down into interpersonal dynamics; the characters’ habit of lodging accusations against “you lot”—not only across tribal lines but between assumed allies, as with the questionable gripes from Leo’s social-worker best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington), about how the practice of queer self-identification endangers her female charges—reflects the fractured nature of life today, where every systemic problem comes with an automatic scapegoat. Davies also effectively depicts technology’s destabilizing influence—a theme that animated his 2019 dystopian HBO drama, “Years and Years,” which followed the gradual dissolution of an English family in an age of online alienation and populist politics. At the Goss residence, no one seems aware that Clive has disappeared down some gnarly internet rabbit holes, spending his nights on the couch, estranged from his wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), watching bombings and car crashes. The serendipity of the internet means that Leo and George, a closeted high-schooler, can end up chatting on a hookup app; in classic teen-age form, George is sexually active (with a boy his age) but squeamish when Leo brings up protection. The speed and unpredictability of information online likewise mean that everything becomes easier: outings, misunderstandings, hate crimes.

“Tip Toe” also compellingly dramatizes the widespread, but not always convincing, axiom that bias is hardened by economic uncertainty. The show’s longitudinal view becomes an asset again; what appears to unsettle Clive and Marie, who came of age when queer Britons had been forced into the margins, isn’t so much that Leo is gay as that he’s thriving. When Clive asks Leo for work, he frames each request as a play for dominance. (Given Leo’s fate, I could feel my cortisol spike whenever Leo indulged a streak of impertinence by pausing to put Clive in his place.) Clive’s homophobia, which draws on the myth that gay men are prone to pedophilia, seems less rooted in concern for his sons than in a fear that Leo will take or alter something that Clive claims as his own.

But Davies is unable to make the humorless Clive—a man not of retrograde values but of no core principles—an engaging figure. It’s not difficult to believe that people like Clive exist: compulsive scrollers driven by reaction and disillusionment, who know and care so little of the lives of others they could believe H.I.V. and dyslexia to be mass hoaxes. When Clive tries to let Leo in on his world view, he raves incoherently about immigrants, Elon Musk, and outlet voltages. Even if there’s something infuriatingly familiar about Leo’s difficulties in making logical inroads with Clive—a task he mostly takes on to insure a safe coming-out for George—there’s no satisfaction to be had in arguing against a jumble. Morrissey is able to physically convey Clive’s existential discomfort; despite his conventional handsomeness, the character often looks like he’s dying to inhabit a completely new skin. Still, any empathy that the series looks to drum up for him is limited by the fact that the character takes equality as an affront—Clive can’t feel tall without someone to stand over.

The dread-filled lead-up to Leo’s murder, in which he and Clive quickly amass a ledger of mutual grievances, proves more gripping than the forced dénouement. Eventually, allegory overwhelms dramaturgy, with a group of soccer hooligans—emblems of the volatility of men under threat—playing a pivotal role in Leo’s end. More haunting are the reverberations of his death, told in an extensive coda, which allude to the role that gay elders have often played in maintaining safe spaces for the next generation—and how quickly those places can disappear without the old guard’s dedication and logistical know-how. The warning from Leo’s cohort that a “new Dark Age” is on the horizon may register as alarmist, but “Tip Toe” makes a persuasive case that it may be the only clear-eyed response. ♦

items.title: Roy Lichtenstein’s Witty Critiques of Masculinity
items.description: “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and
items.author: Hilton Als
paragraphs: “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and the curator Meg Onli, it’s the first retrospective of Lichtenstein’s work in New York since his splash at the Guggenheim in 1993. The show takes up the museum’s entire fifth floor and ends as it begins: with the artist’s signature brightly colored brushstrokes, lines, and Benday dots causing pleasurable kinetic movements in the mind. Lichtenstein’s dynamic style is ubiquitous by now—as are his professional sheen and finish—but that doesn’t cancel out his winning charm, which, like most charm, can warm you up or wear you out. At “Like New,” you may experience both feelings. It’s a show that aims to keep the real world, our gothic political climate included, at bay, while also distracting us from what one might call the grief porn of contemporary art and its constant reminders of our failures as humans.

For years now, the Whitney has foregrounded race- and gender-based political art, and it’s a little trippy to walk around this show’s pearl-gray-painted rooms, looking at Lichtenstein’s Fantastik-clean white world of orderly studios, shiny blondes, and square-jawed men, in a place where white male power has been repeatedly denounced and the sins of past neglect redressed. No one can make up for the past—certainly not by demanding that it be corrected in the present—and it was perhaps inevitable that the Whitney would have to turn, or return, to white men with name recognition to get people back into its galleries post-COVID. Exhibitions devoted to Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol helped, and still fit the Whitney framework: both artists were queer. And although Lichtenstein wasn’t gay, there’s enough irony about gender in his early work to qualify him as being interestingly gay-adjacent.

Still, it’s difficult to entirely undo the way we’ve been viewing art for a while now, and, after having a great time at “Like New,” you may find yourself feeling slightly guilty about it. But one of the more poignant subtexts of the show is that it’s a reminder of the New York avant-garde in the sixties, and of what a beautiful, forceful energy there was to its various voices, with Lichtenstein the least dirty and anarchic of them all. There’s a sweetness in that, and a sadness, too.

I first spent time with Lichtenstein’s work in the early eighties, when I took a class at Columbia on the art of the nineteen-sixties. The professor led us from the glory days of Abstract Expressionism in the fifties, through the emergence of Robert Rauschenberg and Johns by the end of that decade, to this new era in American art. Inspired by Marcel Duchamp and his poetry of the everyday, Rauschenberg and Johns used commonplace objects—a flashlight, a bedspread—in their creations. But artists working under the Pop-art banner in the sixties, including Lichtenstein, Claes Oldenburg, James Rosenquist, Tom Wesselmann, Marisol, and Warhol, picked at the surface of the world that had made them, in order to show us how much it could reveal about what lay beneath it. You can still feel, in the memorable work produced during that period, the critical embrace of all those dance-lesson diagrams, Campbell’s soup cans, ice-cream cones, and Coca-Cola bottles, alongside images of electric chairs, car crashes, and atomic-bomb detonations.

In the Cold War universe, where everyone was isolated and class was defined by the power to acquire (and to oppress), Pop artists painted or sculpted what they saw and heard. The artist’s “aura” had no place in those works; instead, Pop art was a kind of supersonic whistle heralding the disasters to come, that had already come. But unlike, for instance, Rosenquist, in such charged political pieces as “F-111” (1964-65), which juxtaposes consumer objects with missiles, Lichtenstein made work that was less about conscience than about control, and the eradication of mess, of feeling.

Lichtenstein became Lichtenstein in 1961, when he made “Look Mickey.” He had flirted with cartoon characters before then, but “Look Mickey” took things further. Four feet by nearly six, the painting features the brightest of reds, blues, and yellows. In it, Mickey Mouse and the bombastic Donald Duck are standing on a dock, fishing. Mickey covers his laughing mouth because Donald thinks he’s hooked a fish, but the hook is caught on his own coat. The delight of the painting is the pleasure that Lichtenstein took in the joke—and in this new way of making work that was both free and not free of the artist’s hand. (In the age of Pop, achieving an automated look was part of the process.)

Decades before Richard Prince made his fantastic and forlorn cartoon paintings, Lichtenstein was already exploring the idea of entertainment and raising questions: If cartoons were a form of entertainment, was painting a cartoon a form of entertainment, too? Was modern art a put-on? Or something that could be put on? One question that the Whitney show didn’t answer for me was how Lichtenstein got to cartoons, and then to his comic-strip paintings, with their speech balloons, women in distress, and silent men—whose reserve makes us wonder if their creator was a silent man, too.

Born in 1923, into an upper-middle-class German Jewish family in New York, Lichtenstein grew up on the Upper West Side, with easy access to museums and other cultural institutions. He loved music and art, and in 1940 he enrolled at Ohio State University, where he studied life drawing, painting, and the work of the masters, including Picasso. If he insisted on pursuing art, his parents felt, it would be good for him to get a degree, in case he had to teach to get by.

The Whitney retrospective includes “Drawing by Seeing,” a short film about Lichtenstein’s artistic education, made by Da Corte, whose own work includes video, performance, and installations, driven by the kind of avant-gardism that Lichtenstein espoused for a time. The film is shot in color, but with the performers and their costumes colored a “Twilight Zone” gray. It features a voice-over drawn from a text by Hoyt L. Sherman, Lichtenstein’s teacher and mentor at Ohio State. Sherman’s work centered on perception; he’d flash an image on a screen and then have his students draw what they had seen. Or hadn’t. Da Corte’s film also animates some of Lichtenstein’s early works, including “Step-on Can with Leg” (1961), a two-panel painting that shows a woman’s high-heeled foot stepping on the pedal of a closed garbage can, and then the same image with the lid open. Like Warhol, in “Before and After,” a study of a nose job, also from 1961, Lichtenstein was interested in how time can be represented in a static medium, thus changing how we see a thing, or making us realize that we weren’t really looking.

Lichtenstein’s studies were interrupted when he was drafted, in 1943, but he returned in 1946 to finish his degree on the G.I. Bill. By 1949, he was married to the artist Isabel Wilson Sarisky, with whom he had two sons. (Divorced in 1965, he married Dorothy Herzka, a philanthropist, in 1968.) Lichtenstein, shy and reclusive, was a responsible fellow; he supported his family by teaching, while making art that was at first representational, then a little abstract, not terribly distinguished. The breakthrough came in 1960, when he was teaching at Douglass College (which later became part of Rutgers), where he met the performance artist Allan Kaprow, who introduced him to Claes Oldenburg and George Segal, artists who were as taken with the look and signs of masculinity as Lichtenstein was. (Oldenburg’s 1959 work “ ‘Empire’ (‘Papa’) Ray Gun,” for instance, plays on the phallic shape of a firearm.) Surely the freedom that Lichtenstein saw in those sculptors’ work and at Kaprow’s “happenings” helped to release him and open him up to his strongest qualities as an artist: his interest in gender and his amused wit.

Lichtenstein’s wonderful early work “Masterpiece” (1962) still makes me laugh. In it, a couple are looking at a canvas. The woman, a blonde, has a speech balloon issuing from her red lips: “Why, Brad darling, this painting is a masterpiece! My, soon you’ll have all of New York clamoring for your work!” The man is silent, only partially visible, in profile; the woman is our focus. She may be the kind of woman who needs her man to be a success, in order to validate her power as a woman, one who, unlike Donald Duck, has caught a big one. It’s a joke on the bright and shiny, profit-driven art world, where nothing resonates like success. Among other great early works, there’s the funny, ’tude-filled “Ohhh . . . Alright . . .” (1964)—a closeup of a red-haired woman on the phone, looking slightly annoyed as she speaks the title—and “Drowning Girl” (1963), in which a blue-haired woman with tears falling from her closed eyes drowns as much in misbegotten love as in a swirl of black-and-white waves. A thought bubble reads, “I don’t care! I’d rather sink—than call Brad for help!”

These are not really paintings about distress or isolation. They’re about fake feelings in a manufactured world. What was real in Pop? What wasn’t? I liked these works so much when I was younger, and still do, because, for me, Lichtenstein was at his strongest when he wasn’t just a straight man but, rather, a Warhol-adjacent straight man who could critique both masculinity and the self-consciously feminine. The truth is that when Lichtenstein stopped painting “gay,” I stopped looking. From the seventies on, in work that seemed influenced by Léger, Matisse, Picasso, and others, he appeared to be more at play with the straight boys than questioning their performative creativity. (The Whitney curators have put some of the gay back into his work by treating it as a kind of exquisite California-modern decoration; all that’s missing are gray throw pillows.) Still, at the end of the show, I stood by Da Corte’s replica of Lichtenstein’s enormous 1967 work “Super Sunset Billboard,” which shows a horizon and, above it, white streams of light shooting up and out, like klieg lights announcing a show. The painting is the show. Da Corte and Onli have placed the piece in front of a wall of windows overlooking the Hudson; it’s a calming, lovely thing to see a “real” sky echoing Lichtenstein’s. It’s also a thrilling and moving coda to his work—so much so that I got goosebumps. It was the first time I’d ever thought of goosebumps as Benday dots. ♦

items.title: A Song of Grief and Union in “Lincoln in the Bardo”
items.description: A measure of vitality in opera—or any creative form—is the number of interesting artists it carries into the open space of mid-career. The innovations of early work are frequently flukes. The middle years bring longer strides and deepening ambitions. The sixth
items.author: Nathan Heller
paragraphs: A measure of vitality in opera—or any creative form—is the number of interesting artists it carries into the open space of mid-career. The innovations of early work are frequently flukes. The middle years bring longer strides and deepening ambitions. The sixth opera by the forty-six-year-old American composer Missy Mazzoli premièred, last month, at the Metropolitan Opera, with an air of arrival that seemed leavened by relief. Mazzoli, once best known for her indie-electro band, Victoire, has emerged as one of our leading dramatic composers, and the opera, “Lincoln in the Bardo,” written with her longtime librettist, Royce Vavrek, is both her first Met commission and the company’s first première by a woman. An occasion like that deserves a charismatic, openhearted work, and Mazzoli and Vavrek deliver one in the form of a comedy with a melancholy guise. Based on the novel by George Saunders and set a year into the Civil War, the opera follows Abraham Lincoln as he visits his deceased eleven-year-old, Willie, in the cemetery where the boy lies amid restless ghosts. The President has not resigned himself to the death, and neither has his son.

“Bardo” is a Tibetan term, referring to an intermediate state following death, but its assonance with the English “bard”—one who recites, or sings, tales of lives and deeds—can’t have been lost on Saunders. The residents of the graveyard rehash their pasts obsessively, ritualistically, and all the time. In a basic sense, they can’t let go; they linger, fretting about experiences never tasted, errors left unremedied, vindications not received. Their self-absorption is so great that they do not realize they are dead. (They think they’re convalescing.) They refer to their coffins as “sick-boxes” and complain, like captious hostel guests, about the lack of blankets.

Opera is a hybrid form, allowing for storytelling approaches not available to the novel. In the early scenes, Mazzoli and Vavrek weave two supporting characters, Vollman and Bevins, into a single aria of aggrievement. Vollman, a homely middle-aged printer (sung by the baritone Ryan McKinny), was on the verge of consummating his marriage when a falling beam killed him. Now he rests in a purgatorial state of sexual excitement, fitted onstage with a buffa penis that disturbingly resembles a piñata. (The appendage, lofted by a valiant puppeteer, is briefly played for laughs and never seen again.) Bevins, sung by the tenor Jonah Hoskins, is a young gay man who slit his wrists after being jilted by a lover. His song is an overwrought lament of curlicues and tortured intervals dancing around Vollman’s squarer line, for an effect both dreamlike and uncanny. Their two complaints—love without sex and sex without love—mark a barycenter of human loss, the stuff of operatic duets.

Elsewhere in the Bardo we find three Black people who had lived through slavery and were buried in coffinless graves, and a ghoulish pair of boozy sadists, Mr. and Mrs. Baron, imagined somewhere between the Dickensian and the Dahlian as they teeter in a sick, odd-meter duet. But the heart of this production is the dramatic soprano Christine Goerke, who plays a deceased clergyman known as the Reverend. Goerke is a wonderful actress, funny and free, who can project irony while projecting her voice. The bravura aria that Mazzoli gives her at the start of the second act—soaring and droll, and slowly intensifying—is a musical delight. In another gender-swapped role, the celebrated countertenor Anthony Roth Costanzo plays Miss Elise Traynor, a fourteen-year-old trapped in the Bardo. Her lilting, clucking vocal line may not contribute much to Costanzo’s musical reputation, but the part adds mightily to his repertoire of outré costuming, which includes singing Philip Glass’s “Akhnaten” nude. Miss Traynor—a kind of nightmare version of the Queen of the Night—appears swathed in an enormous, mildewing white dress, its hems nibbled by rubber pig heads. She’s a cautionary tale of what awaits children who “tarry” in this world of irresolution, and the dramatic arc of the opera follows Bevins, Vollman, and the Reverend’s scheme to compel the President and his son to move on.

To Lincoln, Willie’s death is weighted with the Civil War. “I have exported this grief / three thousand times,” he laments. When he enters the crypt and embraces his son’s corpse, his shirtfront glows and throbs like a linked Bluetooth device—the way the production, directed with a marvellous contemporary edge by Lileana Blain-Cruz, signals Saunders’s concept of “occupation,” in which ghosts enter living people and their thoughts. The Swedish baritone Peter Mattei, who sings Lincoln, is tall and rightly renowned for his rich, unmuddy voice, here channelled into plausible Midwestern vowels. Yet his aspect onstage, vexed and exercised and diligently in tempo, is nearer in spirit to the Wagnerian mountaintops than to the lonely terrors of a plainsman, and the dazzling performance he delivers ends up seeming less specific than so singular an opera might call for.

Mazzoli, who has trained as a death doula, is known for burrowing deep into specific worlds. (For the reputation-making “Breaking the Waves,” based on the Lars von Trier movie, she and Vavrek studied the language and the music of the Scottish Highlands.) In “Lincoln in the Bardo,” she has produced a rich twenty-first-century score with musical shadows of both the Civil War era and the Halloween graveyard, opening with a spooky stacked minor tone cluster (made spookier by knitting needles rattling the percussion) and extending to gorgeous snatches of chocolatey writing in the low brass, befitting a bereaved President. The orchestra, under the direction of Yannick Nézet-Séguin, comes at this music with terrific confidence, delivering the sort of fully conceived performance that rarely awaits brand-new work (and only occasionally overpowering the singers). Mazzoli’s setting of text can be a mixed bag; her melodies now and then seem to take a purgatorial path themselves, patiently cycling among set intervals when the ear, and the libretto, might wish them to move. But the intelligence of her dramatic writing haunts the score. She makes much of big glissandos, in which the men and women of the chorus slide together through a scale, like a winding siren. Heading upward, these slides impart moments of ecstatic, unworldly levitation. Sent downward, they plummet us into the earth.

Saunders’s novel mixes his characters’ epitaph-like accounts of their lives and other dialogue with real text from the historical record, blurring the boundary between speech, which rises in living time, and writing, which exists outside it. The page, we are meant to see, is an inherently ghostly place, at once a paltry shadow of the world it describes and a realm of empathetic reach. The written word, like the Bardo, carries both life, in all its specificity and imperfection, and abstractions of the sort that might define a nation, affording people trapped within themselves a chance to step into other points of view. In a climactic effort to enjoin Willie and the President to go on without each other, the spirits—not least Thomas Havens, a Black freedman, movingly sung by the young tenor Joshua Blue—gather in an effort to occupy Lincoln together. Union is the governing metaphor, and, in the book, it’s a union carried by the intermingling of voice and text, of varied experience and inky phrase. “Lincoln in the Bardo,” published in the first weeks of the first Trump Administration, today reads distinctly as a novel of the Obama years.

Despite an occasional groan of narrative machinery, Vavrek ably repaces Saunders’s story line and carries its texty voices into song. Gnarled, consonant-laden phrases such as “conjoined, mass-minded, positive intention” and “two passing temporarinesses” are hard to say, let alone sing. They are retained here as if to underscore the messy peculiarity of the world left behind. The language of the afterlife, by contrast, seems flat and stutteringly insistent: “Lingering lingering lingering,” the dead intone. “Worthy worthy worthy.” In one of the opera’s lovelier ensemble arias, the ghosts praise “the things of the world,” enumerating the small, sticky details that they miss from human existence: “beerfroth,” “toweling off one’s clinging shirt post June rain.” Language, like irresolution, is a thing that belongs to the living world. ♦

items.title: A Visual Tour of the Place de la République, a Site of Protests in Paris
items.description: At the height of the Dreyfus Affair, as false accusations of treason against a Jewish military officer ignited antisemitic riots across France, a rally was held on the square in support of Max Régis, a vehement antisemite and a polarizing figure of the far rig
items.author: Maurice Samuels
paragraphs: At the height of the Dreyfus Affair, as false accusations of treason against a Jewish military officer ignited antisemitic riots across France, a rally was held on the square in support of Max Régis, a vehement antisemite and a polarizing figure of the far right who was running to become mayor of Algiers.

In the years leading up to the Second World War, the Place de la République, pictured on a quiet day here, became an important setting for leftist groups. A 1934 rally led to the creation of the Popular Front. As Hitler consolidated power in Germany and home-grown fascist groups threatened the French Republic, there were annual demonstrations on the square to commemorate working-class resistance to fascism.

In one of the final battles before the liberation of Paris, French Resistance forces fought more than a thousand Nazi troops at the Place de la République. General de Gaulle made his triumphant entry into the city later that afternoon, and, the next day, hold-out snipers forced celebrating citizens to take cover behind the statue of Marianne.

When France’s ill-fated war to retain control of its Algerian colony threatened to bring down the government, de Gaulle came out of retirement to steer the nation through the crisis. Standing at a giant podium before the Marianne statue, whose base had been covered with ceremonial banners, he made his case for a new constitution, which would become the foundation of France’s current Fifth Republic.

The legendary protests of May, 1968, began as a student revolt against the bureaucracy of the French university system, and brought France to the verge of revolution yet again. Hundreds of thousands of striking workers and countercultural militants joined the demonstrations, which were concentrated on the Left Bank but spread across Paris, including to the Place de la République.

The day before International Women’s Day, in 1982, twenty thousand women marched on the square, calling for practical reforms, such as workplace equality and free day care, along with an end to patriarchal oppression. A sign draped over Marianne proclaimed, “A la conquête de nos droits”—“Fighting for our rights.”

In a year marked by celebrations of the two-hundredth anniversary of the French Revolution, around fifteen hundred Muslims knelt in prayer on the Place de la République as part of a protest against Salman Rushdie’s 1988 novel, “The Satanic Verses.” The author had been accused of blasphemy for his depiction of the Prophet Muhammad.

On World AIDS Day, demonstrators from ACT UP Paris congregated on the square to protest the government’s treatment of H.I.V.-positive people. Along with the iconic “Silence = Death” sign, banners proclaimed “SIDA, honte à la France” (“AIDS, shame on France”) and “Lesbiennes, La France vous préfère mortes” (“Lesbians, France prefers you dead”).

Several thousand people gathered on the square to protest Israel’s actions during the 2014 Gaza war, despite the fact that French officials had banned the event after Jewish shops and synagogues in Paris were attacked in the preceding weeks. A heavy police presence led to altercations with protesters and approximately fifty arrests.

On the day that gunmen allied with Al Qaeda attacked the editorial offices of the satirical journal Charlie Hebdo, killing twelve people, a crowd of thirty-five thousand assembled for a spontaneous vigil on the square, holding signs that read “Je suis Charlie”—“I am Charlie.” Later that week, 1.3 million demonstrated in solidarity with the victims. In the era of smartphones, images of these events proliferated on social media.

In the spring of 2016, the Nuit Debout (sometimes translated as “Standing Up at Night”) protests against the government’s proposed labor reforms drew up to thousands of visitors nightly to makeshift encampments on the square; French police eventually evacuated the area. The reforms went into effect despite the protests, which were often compared to the Occupy Wall Street movement.

After Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party gained the most votes in the first round of legislative elections in June, 2024, thousands of protesters assembled in the Place de la République to call for a New Popular Front of left-leaning parties, with the hope of preventing the far right from gaining a majority in the legislature.

Students raised signs on a warm fall day, at the first large-scale demonstration protesting conditions in French schools. By then, a hundred and ninety students had already been injured as police cracked down on individual blockades at schools. One fifteen-year-old boy had his hand blown off by a police grenade.

A week and a half into the October protests, students were joined by demonstrators angered by the government’s economic policies. A yellow vest proclaiming “2026, La Police Mutile Les Lyceen-nes” (“2026, The Police Mutilate High-Schoolers”) adorned the statue of Marianne. French authorities blamed ultra-left groups and criminal bands for the violence and looting, while far-left figures castigated the government for its inept response.

Today, the Place de la République remains a destination for protesters from around the world. The documentarians Snapp and Gogineni point out that, on any given day, French yellow-vest protesters might occupy one area of the Place and Sudanese refugees another. “It’s serving now as this kind of portal for all these different movements,” Snapp said.

items.title: “Chronovisor” Captures the Terror of Thinking
items.description: In my former life as a Ph.D. candidate in philosophy, I spent a lot of time doing what looked like a lot of nothing. I read; I ruminated; I sat in apparent idleness, unknotting skeins of arguments in my head. At my most gregarious, I talked with other graduate
items.author: Becca Rothfeld
paragraphs: In my former life as a Ph.D. candidate in philosophy, I spent a lot of time doing what looked like a lot of nothing. I read; I ruminated; I sat in apparent idleness, unknotting skeins of arguments in my head. At my most gregarious, I talked with other graduate students; we had a habit of contorting our fingers into what those in the business call “philosophy hands,” which at least looked like something, if not exactly like most people’s idea of a meaningful contribution to society. Physicists and chemists could produce pictures of themselves manifestly Doing Science, wearing white coats and wielding pipettes. What did we have to show for ourselves? What did thinking look like, which is another way of wondering, What is thinking, anyway? Is it a substance? A spirit? A shiver?

Whatever it is, it is maddeningly spectral, which is why it was so hard for me to convince anyone (not least my parents and the administrators of my erstwhile university, who refused to provide dental insurance for graduate students until we went on strike) that what I was doing when I was sitting in silence was work, labor in want of compensation or at least dental insurance, alchemy that had the potential to alter the world, however impalpably. The philosopher and critic Elaine Scarry once wrote that “to have great pain is to have certainty; to hear that another person has pain is to have doubt.” We could say almost the same of thinking: from the inside, there is nothing more undeniable (though the thinker may come to doubt her conviction in the face of so much skepticism); from the outside, it is wispier than vapor.

But the difficulty of visualizing thinking hasn’t dissuaded filmmakers from attempting to stage thought’s convolutions onscreen. Cue montages of cryptographers staring at strings of numbers that light up suggestively (the film “A Beautiful Mind”), detectives taking stock of the corpses of murder victims as the camera zooms into the details that strike them as salient (the series “Sherlock”), chess prodigies hallucinating games on the ceiling (the series “The Queen’s Gambit”), and policemen affixing bits of yarn to bulletin boards with thumbtacks (innumerable crime procedurals). In movies and television shows, tortured geniuses think for brief, febrile stretches; then their paroxysms end, and the product of their toil (a cracked code, a jailed murderer, an especially clever checkmate) sets a more readily legible plot into motion. Thought is invariably the handmaiden of action, and the experimental contrivances that dramatize mental exertion—the closeups, the animations, the glowing numbers—are impatiently retired in favor of more standard fare.

“Chronovisor” is one of the few movies about thinking to deviate from this formula. In Jack Auen and Kevin Walker’s mesmerizing directorial début, mental foment is not a prelude to car chases or crime-fighting but an event in its own right. The film has just one character: Béatrice Courte (played by the real-life academic Anne-Laure Sellier), a philosophy professor at Columbia who is hard at work on a monograph about memory. In the opening scene, she describes her project to her peers over drinks in a dark, loud restaurant. She tells them that she is interested in ancient theories of the mind, which hold that different regions of the brain give rise to distinct mental functions—but above all, she continues, she is fascinated by memory palaces. According to the Roman rhetorician Quintilian, Béatrice explains, “an orator wishing to fixate an oration in memory should plan an itinerary through a large imaginary building, all of whose rooms and galleries, courtyards and corridors, statuary and adornments, are as clearly lined out as possible.” Thus a speaker’s roving thoughts are fixed, outfitted with an architecture. But Béatrice’s peers are not interested in memory palaces, and they are not impressed by her fervent monologue: they make their excuses and beg off, leaving her to return home to her desk.

Soon, however, she happens upon an even more ambitious effort to instantiate the insubstantial, to endow memory with form: the chronovisor, a real device that the Benedictine monk Pellegrino Ernetti claimed, in 1972, to have invented. Ernetti hypothesized that events emit electromagnetic waves that linger in the ether, and the chronovisor is intended to record these traces and reconstruct them, creating audiovisual documentation of history, much like a camera shooting a film. “Each one of us gradually leaves behind what happens in a span of seconds, hours, days, months and years, as a visual-acoustic double track,” Ernetti is quoted as saying in one of the sources that Béatrice consults in the course of her manic research. Exploiting this “visual-acoustic double track,” both the real and the filmic Ernetti took what he insisted was a kind of “photograph” of Jesus.

In reality, Ernetti was outed as a fake—the image was revealed to be a doctored reproduction of a sculpture by the Spanish artist Lorenzo Coullaut Valera—but in “Chronovisor” this verdict comes to seem wavering and indeterminate, at least as elusive as the residue of history that he purported to synthesize into images. As Béatrice combs through the archives, always alone, always in the dead of night, always in libraries dense with darkness, she becomes skeptical of the many attempts to discredit the monk and his discovery. “Chronovisor” accelerates and syncopates as she reads on and on—at an ever faster and more scrabbling clip, in increasing desperation—about the Vatican’s determination to silence him and suppress his findings, about threats and subterfuges, about the makings of a great conspiracy. The chronovisor, Ernetti and his supporters claim, was capable of recording not just history but also memories and fantasies, affording whoever controlled it the ultimate means of surveillance. “If I could reach into my heart, take hold of my thoughts, and with my bare hands lay them without further embellishment in your own, then, I confess, the innermost desire of my soul would be fulfilled,” the German Romantic novelist and playwright Heinrich von Kleist wrote, in 1811. Ernetti’s device intrigues and appalls us because it seems to be a means of both satisfying this desire and realizing the fears that it raises: the machine promises, horribly and redemptively, to transmute our inner intangibilities into something that others might see and touch.

Perhaps “Chronovisor” is one of its emanations. The film has the soft, blurred texture of a dream, and it teems not with things themselves but with their echoes. Shadows flit over a curtain in Béatrice’s apartment, and beams cast by a pair of headlights extend into the offing of a road while the car from which they emanate remains out of sight. In place of people’s bodies or faces, we see photographs from the archive and hear voices issuing from offscreen. When Béatrice meets her colleagues at the restaurant, they are positioned behind the camera; in another scene, she delivers a lecture, but the shot conceals her audience, which declines to ask her any questions during the period designated for Q. & A.

What “Chronovisor” captures is not quite the past so much as an oneiric alternative to the present—a place where time detaches from linearity and twines into unrecognizable loops, doubling back on itself. Béatrice is curiously out of synch with the world around her. Night after night, she sits and works. Her life consists of compulsive repetition, of what might even be regarded as a single event: she reads and reads. Her frenzied reading is set outside of time, in an epoch eerily adjacent to our own. Instead of a laptop, she takes notes with a typewriter; instead of searching for references in a digital database, she consults a librarian. All of her sources—books, photographs, magazine articles—are physical, many of them faded with evident age. She uses an iPhone, but only to make calls, never to send texts or summon Ubers or look up directions. She is as much at odds with the norms of her era as she is with the daily rhythms of the city. “Chronovisor” is set almost exclusively at night, when Béatrice sits in gloomy libraries that are otherwise empty, or works in the smudged chiaroscuro solitude of her apartment.

There are many reasons that this ruminative film surpasses previous efforts to portray the vellications of thinking. For one thing, contemplation—not the sheer fact of it but its content—drives the plot. “Chronovisor” makes no capitulations to conventional action; the only drama is the drama of research. (“We view the act of research and scholarship itself as high adventure in its own right,” Auen told an interviewer.) As Béatrice reads, racing toward discovery, we are obliged to read along with her. Passages are limned in white as her gaze passes over them. Sometimes the surrounding text fades away as she homes in on a sentence or phrase. She reads in French, German, and Italian, and the film translates for us in real time, overlaying the words with their English renderings until the pages on the screen become palimpsests. Our eyes move as Béatrice’s do: as she grows hysterical, an enigmatic snippet that she encountered in a book apparently unrelated to Ernetti at the beginning of the film fragments into its rudiments. At first, she reads,

Later, each word is isolated in its own shot: “I,” “carefully,” “collected,” “information,” and so on and on. The words flash onto the screen slowly, then accelerate frenetically. “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” repeats faster and faster. As Béatrice sits at her desk, phantasmagoric music—selections from Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite “The Planets” and the Gregorian chants that Ernetti studied when he was not too busy inventing occult machines to devote himself to his other interest, musicology—swells and surges. “Chronovisor” is both a patient movie—a steady accretion of atmosphere—and a feverish one. It has the cadence of a burgeoning obsession.

But, above all, it succeeds because Auen and Walker have finally hit on the ideal genre in which to depict the pangs of thinking: horror. At one point, Béatrice listens intently to a 1977 interview with the philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine. The interviewer asks the eminence what he thinks of dualism—the view, hegemonic for much of the history of Western thought, that “there were bodies and there were minds, and that these were two fundamentally different kinds of thing.” Quine rejects dualism on the ground that it cannot explain the mind’s influence on the body, and opts instead for a thoroughgoing physicalism. But Béatrice takes the opposite tack: for her, thought and memory wreak havoc on dualism’s neat dichotomies—and thereby suggest that there is some interstitial entity quivering at the junction of the corporeal and the incorporeal. What is so chilling about this entity is that it always tempts us to suspect that it may not actually exist.

“Chronovisor” is, after all, a chronicle of bruising failures of acknowledgment. Béatrice gives a lecture, and no one asks her any questions; she explains her research to her colleagues, and they leave the restaurant as fast as possible. The academic speaks—and is so resoundingly ignored that she is justified in wondering if she has only imagined it. Most of what happens in “Chronovisor,” like most of what happens when Béatrice is entombed in the library, may or may not have really happened at all, which is another way of saying that “Chronovisor” is a ghost movie, which is another way of saying that it is a film about scholarship. Horror is the ideal genre in which to represent thinking because the true terror of the life of the mind, like the true terror of a haunting, is the sneaking suspicion that nothing is there, that all the agonies of rumination are mere phantoms. Contra Descartes’s famous dictum, to think is to inherit a sliver of the anti-intellectual’s uncertainty—to wonder helplessly if one has in fact accomplished anything at all. I think, therefore I worry that thinking is illusory.

In “Chronovisor,” we eventually come to see some of the images that the device has supposedly recorded—and then we wonder if we are watching a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations, and then we wonder if the existence of a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations proves that the chronovisor is real enough to have recorded them. The film is ingeniously ambiguous between these possibilities. But, whether Ernetti’s opus is a momentous innovation or a cheap hoax, whether Béatrice devolves into delusion or comes to see the truth, “Chronovisor” provides what the machine promises, what would be in equal measure harrowing and consoling, what will in any case remain elusive once we leave the cinema and return to the library: proof, for once, that the ghosts are real. ♦

items.title: Charles Porch Is OpenAI’s Hollywood Whisperer
items.description: In August, news leaked that Gwyneth Paltrow was set to host “a private, off-the-record, alfresco dinner” at her Amagansett home in honor of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “I guess summers in the Hamptons just aren’t complete these days without sucking up to our new AI
items.author: Charlotte Klein
paragraphs: In August, news leaked that Gwyneth Paltrow was set to host “a private, off-the-record, alfresco dinner” at her Amagansett home in honor of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “I guess summers in the Hamptons just aren’t complete these days without sucking up to our new AI overlords,” Puck’s Matt Belloni, who broke the news, wrote. “Luckily, Gwyneth Paltrow has you covered.” The backlash was vicious — “tone-deaf dumbass,” one X user wrote — and the dinner was postponed.

“God, the internet made it such a bigger thing than it was,” says Charles Porch, who brokered the dinner with Paltrow’s team, as he sips an Arnold Palmer on a crisp afternoon in October outside Sant Ambroeus in Soho. “Gwyneth invests in the space. She does these investor dinners all the time. Sam was coming through town and I was like, ‘Let’s just do this.’”

Altman had hired Porch in 2025 to do for OpenAI what he had done so successfully for Instagram for more than a decade: persuade famous people in Hollywood and beyond to use and partner with the platform and help the tech company be culturally relevant. The freak-out over Paltrow’s dinner reflected how much public sentiment toward big tech had shifted since Porch’s Instagram days, when Anna Wintour hosted the same kind of event for its CEO at the time, Kevin Systrom. I ask him if it made him rethink the playbook. “It makes it look like that’s the strategy, and it’s not the strategy. That was, like, a dinner,” Porch says. “But I know those dinners are effective because I see it. We did the dinner eventually, and it was great.” It took place at the apartment of an AI enthusiast at the end of September in New York.

Everyone above a certain income bracket seems to know Charles Porch, but few can tell you what exactly he does. He showed up in Los Angeles in his grandmother’s Honda Accord wagon when he was 20 and spent the next two decades cultivating a formidable network of celebrities and influencers. “He took one step at a time very carefully, never burned a single bridge, never spoke out of turn, never took advantage of an opportunity in the wrong way,” says Erin Foster, the well-connected daughter of music producer David Foster, who met Porch when they were both underlings at Warner Bros. Records.

“I’m not a business-development guy or the brand guy. I’m the relationships person that’s bringing everyone along on new tech,” says Porch, 45, a self-described “tech optimist” who has long been comfortable in the gray area between the personal and the professional. “There’s a strategy around making friends.”

When he arrived in New York just before the pandemic, few seemed to notice. For those who either didn’t know or didn’t care about what was going on in Menlo Park in the early 2010s, the first time they heard of Porch was likely after his wedding to the billionaire’s scion Robert Denning in 2025, three days of Parisian opulence shared with Jerry and Jessica Seinfeld, Mariska Hargitay, Antony Blinken, Harry Styles (with whom he shares a godchild), Nicky Hilton Rothschild, Darren Walker, Jenna Lyons, and various European aristocrats. After that of Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos, it turned out to be the ritziest wedding of the summer. Suddenly, he and Denning were everywhere, a power-gay couple imbuing the fabric of New York society, at every gala and fundraiser and opening. The swirl of Porch’s life plays out on his Instagram Stories: courtside at the Knicks’ season opener, Hawaii for Jen Meyer’s star-studded wedding, Paris to see Céline Dion with Reese Witherspoon and Karlie Kloss.

In the process of connecting entertainment and tech, he has found himself at the center of several overlapping circles of power — and become a character in his own right. “I know, scary,” he says when I point this out. “He is really good at putting a room together, and now he is of the room,” says someone who worked with him. “He was someone who understood the room before he was part of the Establishment.”

It’s not hard to see why OpenAI would want Porch on its side. “It’s funny: I think everyone wants to hate Open AI and everyone wants to love Charles Porch,” says podcaster Nayeema Raza. “That’s probably the value for Sam.”

Porch’s job was never going to be easy. Why would artists and other creative types want to plug something that threatens to replace them? “The full-throated endorsement of AI is probably the biggest third-rail issue in Hollywood right now. And people are terrified,” says a media executive. Headlines about AI in recent months have generated panic about not just job displacement and copyright infringement but also OpenAI agents going rogue and threatening to take down the entire internet. The evil of the tech industry is the subject of several of the year’s biggest films — made by precisely the industry Porch is trying to court. “Charles can get them to sit down and listen to Sam Altman lay out his vision. But if the vision is ‘I’m going to destroy your industry,’ it doesn’t really matter,” says one of Porch’s former colleagues.

“I’m trying to pinpoint ways and moments where AI can show up in culture in a good way,” says Porch, who, with his wide ice-blue eyes, perfectly smooth head, and perma-smile, looks a bit like how AI would render a human. “What I see every day is that people are externally anti-AI but completely in the closet on how they’re using it. It’s almost like they’re at an AI protest in the morning and then a meeting with me in the afternoon. You know what it reminds me of? The early days of GLP-1’s, when it was like, This is kind of shameful; you’re cheating. But then everyone’s like, Wait, this thing’s incredible.”

Porch grew up in Charleston, South Carolina. He had a French mother and an Alabamian father and a severely disabled sister. “I was always kind of behind the scenes, taking care of my sister and making sure everyone was comfortable,” he says. “Because my sister couldn’t speak, people would be strange around her. And I wanted everyone to feel good, so I was all about setting the temperature. This caretaker thing is just innate in me.” He spent middle school at a boys’-choir boarding school in Princeton, New Jersey. “We’d have school on the bus, and we’d tour the world and sing religious music,” says Porch, noting he performed at Carnegie Hall several times as a child. He finished high school in Monterey, California, and after graduating from McGill University in 2002, he drove to Los Angeles.

In some ways, Porch has Craigslist to thank for his good fortune, because the landlady of the apartment he found on the site got him an internship in the marketing department of Warner Bros. Records, where he met Foster. “And then, all of a sudden, I was at Kate Hudson’s Halloween party.”

“When I was bringing him into my world, which was more industry forward and had sort of celebrity access points, I found that people were always drawn to Charles,” says Foster, “because he didn’t want anything from anyone” and he “didn’t seem like he himself was trying to be the talent.” Porch “became a person people felt safe having around, whether that be in their work life or in a friend group,” adds Foster. “He never came across as someone who was a user or someone who was going to speak out of turn or share private information.”

Four years later, in 2008, Porch left to run strategic relationships at Ning, the now-defunct social-networking start-up co-founded by Marc Andreessen. Through that job, he met Randi Zuckerberg, Mark’s sister. Says Porch, “She called me in 2010 and said, ‘Can you move to Palo Alto in a week? I need help talking to L.A. and translating.’” At Facebook, Porch’s job was convincing people to use Facebook Pages, which were good for brands and businesses but less useful to celebrities. “They weren’t going to buy ads. They didn’t have those needs,” he says. Meanwhile, celebrities were starting to join Twitter: “Then I woke up to the fact that we bought Instagram and I was like, Aha! I cornered Kevin Systrom in a kitchen at work and said, ‘I think we can move pop culture from Twitter to Instagram.’ And he said, ‘Who are you?’ I was like, ‘My name is Charles. This is what I do. I’m going to set up a desk in the Instagram area and do this pro bono. If you hate what I’m doing, I will scurry off to Facebook.’”

Porch’s mission was to teach celebrities that the app was not just a place to post your grainy breakfast photos but a marketing platform that offered direct fan connection and full message control. “My thing was ‘Why does this movie studio or record label own your entire fan base? You should own it and take it with you wherever you want and build whatever business you want on top of it,’” he says. Meanwhile, digital natives like fashion bloggers were moving to the app. “That’s really where the influencer started to come from,” he adds.

At the end of 2013, Beyoncé’s team approached Porch about a surprise album release. “She doesn’t want to do press; she doesn’t want to tell anyone that it’s coming. She just wants to come off the mountain and deliver an album,” Porch recalls her team saying. “I don’t even think Sony, her label, knew how she was going to launch it.” She did so on Instagram, writing “Surprise!” to her more than 8 million followers as the full album appeared on iTunes. The successful rollout was proof that artists could sidestep the traditional press apparatus and other industry conventions if they had a strong enough connection with their fans. It was a flex of social media’s power.

In the fall of 2014, the cover of Vogue’s September issue featured the nine hottest models of the moment, all of whom had gained large followings on social media. “Instagirls!” the cover line read. That was “the moment I really knew we’d tipped something in culture,” says Porch.

“He came into tech at a time when they recognized they could become a supplemental engine to power in culture,” says a tech adviser. “He, as a result, controlled massive marketing budgets to deploy that, and what that looked like was partnerships — funding parties, events.” Porch came to serve as a kind of social fixer for Instagram co-founders Systrom and Mike Krieger. “I’m like, ‘Great, you’re gonna come to L.A.? I’m going to have Guy Oseary throw a cocktail party for you where you’re gonna tell Ariana Grande about Instagram and why it’s valuable,’” Porch recalls. “We’re this new service. We’re trying to convince people to use it. I want them to be able to picture the people that are leading it because otherwise they think it’s going to be a bunch of robots that are controlling things behind the scenes.”

When Adam Mosseri became head of Instagram a few years later, Porch ran the playbook back, getting his friend Jen Meyer, the jewelry designer who was then married to Tobey Maguire, to host a cocktail party for him at her house. Some of the Kardashians came. Porch became a trusted source for Mosseri on all things related to public figures and influencers and showed him the value of, say, Instagram sponsoring the Met Gala. “Charles is a generational talent at managing up,” a former colleague of his at Facebook says. There are lots of people today who play this liaison role at tech companies, but Porch was a pioneer in the field, helping craft a template that Meta still follows. In 2015, he recruited Eva Chen, who, two years earlier, had been handpicked by Wintour to lead Lucky magazine; after a stint as director of Instagram’s fashion partnerships, one of several industry-focused subsections Porch created, she is now the vice-president of fashion at Meta. “These are not socially gifted people, so if you have any social skills, you’re ahead,” says a former colleague of Porch’s at Meta. “Technical engineers building products and Hollywood actors speak completely different languages. So for Charles to be able to explain them to each other in plain terms and not make either one feel stupid — he’s very graceful in his diplomacy.”

There was, of course, mutual benefit to these relationships. Porch’s greatest skill, perhaps, is the fact that many around him tend to think otherwise. “You don’t even know you’re talking about work until it’s over. It’s almost like you leave the table and you’re like, Oh,” says actress and influencer Dylan Mulvaney. “I think he’s kind of a seed planter. The rest of his team are the ones executing in inbox and doing some of the heavier lifting, but he is so good at making you feel like you want to be a part of something.” And, Mulvaney adds, “he’s fun. That’s the other thing. He’s kind of the — I don’t want to say ‘life of the party.’ I want to say ‘a really good addition to the party.’”

When Porch moved to New York in 2019, he was approaching 40 and ready for a fresh start. Nine years in San Francisco and the city had never quite become home, in part because Porch traveled every weekend, most often to L.A., where he would crash at Foster’s. He wanted more of a community and, after years of singledom, a partner. Also, Wintour told him to. “We were both at a wedding, and I get on the flight back — it was somewhere in the Caribbean — and my seatmate is Anna Wintour,” Porch recalls. They knew each other only distantly through Instagram, but they talked the whole way home. “She’s like, ‘Charles, if you want to do culture, you need to move to New York.’ And I was like, ‘Well, if you say so.’” He bought a palatial apartment in an old townhouse in the West Village and began a yearslong renovation, documenting it every step of the way on Instagram, though he would end up living in the completed project for a mere six weeks. Because by then, he’d met Robert Denning.

Porch has seemingly always enjoyed proximity to power, not the public display of it. Denning, a philanthropist whose late father was one of the founding members of the private-equity firm General Atlantic, enjoys both. His Instagram is a catalogue of famous people he has met and events he has attended. But he is also an entertainer, enrapturing dinner tables with his eclectic interests (aviation, for one) and hot takes. “Charles is such a professional, buttoned-up guy. He’s very loyal, he’s very thoughtful, but he’s not, like, Let loose and party. He’s almost got a work vibe, even socially,” says a close friend of Porch’s. “When we all met Robert, we thought, This is amazing, because Robert is not a filtered, edited guy. We were all just so happy for Charles that he could have that joy of life and the extravagance.”

Denning first heard of Porch on a group chat with a bunch of gay men from Stanford business school. “I’m a reject of one of his friends,” Porch tells me. One person in the chat wrote that he’d been told to go on a date with Porch — and he followed this announcement with multiple vomit emoji. Denning looked up Porch to find him chatting with Gayle King on CBS This Morning about onboarding the pope to Instagram. Says Porch, “He’s like, ‘I think he’s cute. Can I go out with him?’ The friend says ‘no.’ So then Robert’s like, ‘Now I have to go on this date.’”

Denning went on Instagram and found a mutual follower he knew from business school and Porch knew through Randi Zuckerberg. “And he DMs his friend and says, ‘Becca, I’m sorry for not RSVP-ing to your wedding ten years ago or acknowledging your two children, but I need you to do something for me,’” Porch says. “And she writes back right away and she’s like, ‘I don’t know him that well, but I’ll try.’” The next day, Denning and Porch got drinks at Temple Bar. “Becca had a place of honor at our wedding, but we both barely know her,” says Porch.

Denning had just moved to New York. He was recently sober and, following the fire sale of his luxury-eyewear start-up, trying to figure out what to do next. His father, Steve Denning, sat on several boards; as Steve’s health declined, Robert started filling in for him, and his philanthropic career took off from there. In 2024, Denning became the then-youngest member of the board of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. “He’s great on a board,” Porch says.

By December 2022, they had made the relationship Instagram official, hard-launching with a photo in front of Joe Biden’s White House (Denning is a big Democratic donor). And the following October, they were engaged. Denning thought they were going to a dinner at the Met in honor of an exhibit opening, but really they had the entire museum to themselves. Porch got down on one knee in the Greek and Roman wing.

In the spring of 2025, Amy Griffin, Foster and her two sisters, Naomi Gleit, and Meyer threw Porch a Charlie’s Angels–themed bachelor party at the ultraluxury Amangiri resort, all of which was documented on Instagram. For the wedding, Porch and Denning hosted roughly 400 guests at Le Bristol, renting out the luxury hotel for the first time in its 100-year history. They paid for everyone’s room as well as their room service. Night one was a party in the hotel courtyard; night two was the ceremony, held in the sculpture garden of the Rodin Museum. Ten minutes before the ceremony was to begin, the sky opened to a downpour, only to clear suddenly to an amber light. First came the bridal party, a group of six children — godchildren and spawn of close friends — outfitted by Thom Browne in seersucker suits, ties, and knee socks (Porch’s idea). Then came the grooms, who walked down the aisle to the Jurassic Park theme (Denning’s idea). Foster officiated. Barbara Bush gave the first reading, Griffin the last. The couple encouraged women to repurpose their old wedding dresses for the event; seemingly the only one who did was Real Housewife Carole Radziwill.

Then it was off to the Hôtel de la Marine for a reception and dinner. Before the guests sat down, Denning gave a vaguely political speech calling attention to the fact that this was a gay wedding and urging the roomful of people with lots of resources and power to take care of those whose rights they were celebrating. At the after-party, French drag queen Nicky Doll performed. The fairy-tale weekend ended with a black-tie affair at Château de Villette on the last Saturday of summer with the couple in custom midnight-blue Hermès tuxedos.

The pair have been well received in New York in part because they’re so happy to be here. “Anna loved him because she could invite him to any dinner party and sit him next to any annoying or difficult person and he knew how to show up, lift the conversation, and never complain,” one fashion editor recalls of Porch. “He’s just very kind and normal and unassuming,” says Wes Gordon, the creative director of Carolina Herrera and a friend of Porch’s. “It’s easy to forget he was a very senior person at Meta and now OpenAI.”

Porch and Denning are tight with theater producers, fashion designers, art curators, and socialites such as Lauren Santo Domingo, Jenna Lyons, and Derek Blasberg. “They were two separately quiet people in different realms and then when they came together, they started making a splash,” says one journalist. “A lot of people will make names for themselves in San Francisco and L.A. and then they come to New York and it’s like being shot out of a cannon into other worlds.”

A couple of months after the wedding, Porch was at Instagram HQ in Menlo Park when Altman’s call came through. They discussed how “everyone’s talking about AI and productivity and that’s great, but no one’s talking about AI and culture,” Porch recalls. “And those two things are going to come together, and culture is run by all these creative industries, and question mark on what that’s going to look like.”

There were more conversations, with Altman and Fidji Simo, Altman’s then-No. 2, with whom Porch worked for more than a decade at Meta. “I think what Fidji really realized is there was an enterprise-and-sales arm that was being built for it, but there wasn’t anyone to work on the talent side,” Porch tells me. “That is where there was an obvious opening for me to come in.” Still, he had just gotten married, and he politely declined. When Simo came calling again in January, Porch was more receptive. “It was like, ‘New Year, new me.’ Time to jump to the next frontier,” he says. “Sam, I feel, is the same person I met socially years ago in San Francisco. And it’s kind of fun to work for a gay guy.”

He started in March, spending his first few months on a listening tour, mostly in New York and L.A., meeting with everyone from the Council of Fashion Designers of America to HBO showrunners. “I ran around and went to a bunch of people I knew would have strong opinions on it, good or bad,” says Porch. He went to the Cannes Film Festival, meeting with directors and hearing their feedback on the technology. “There was way more openness because directors have been using AI forever,” says Porch. He also went to San Francisco — “a lot,” he says, stressing the t — “to bond with the product folks and the researchers and try to get a sense of what they’re really interested in. I don’t have that many mathematicians on speed dial.”

Then he brought people together for intimate events — “just a lot of relationship building for the company,” says Porch. At Paris Fashion Week, he hosted a dinner at Sushi Park with Joopiter, Pharrell Williams’s digital-first auction house, for various French creators. “It wasn’t heavy programming, and it wasn’t branded,” Porch says. “It was just a collab with Joopiter to get people talking.” He has also hosted dinners for TBPN, the daily tech-industry podcast OpenAI acquired in April to help bolster positive conversation around AI. The first TBPN dinner was held in L.A. and attended by the Foster sisters, Monica Lewinsky, Crazy Rich Asians director John Chu, and manager turned tech-investor Guy Oseary. They replicated it in New York a few months later at the downtown restaurant Kiko, where TBPN president Dylan Abruscato was seated next to SNL’s Chloe Fineman and Kareem Rahma of “Subway Takes.” Vogue head of editorial content Chloe Malle and Vanity Fair editorial director Mark Guiducci were also in attendance. “He has been very instrumental in helping TBPN deepen our relationships with Condé Nast,” says Abruscato.

A few days before our interview, I attended one such event, a dinner Porch co-hosted at the subterranean members’ club Chez Margaux. In celebration of influencer Serena Kerrigan’s new book, the gathering was attended by a mix of podcasters, creators, and Real Housewives, but, I noted to Porch, I didn’t hear any discussion about AI. “That was a personal dinner, just so you understand. My personal and professional kind of blend,” he says. “But what’ll happen from that dinner is Serena’s probably going to call me in two months and be like, ‘Wait, I have this idea. I love Chat for this. Do you wanna do this thing with me?’ So there’s a nice cadence of how that happens. But also, you know, there were three Real Housewives there. If an AI model comes up on the show, it might be Chat because we have this nice drumbeat. This is what I’ve been trying to explain to folks: It’s not about deals; it’s about relationships.”

Still, it’s hard to say what exactly is supposed to result from this strategy. The idea appears to be that all this social lubrication will pay off and that Altman and his ilk will one day be seen less as freakish world destroyers than as parts of a broader mosaic of American celebrity. Familiarity, even at an elite level, tends to trickle down.

So far, though, things look decisively less glamorous than they did at Instagram. Aside from Lionel Messi’s ChatGPT World Cup partnership, the most prominent celebrities working with the company have been rookie NFL quarterback Fernando Mendoza, who recently spoke to GQ about using ChatGPT for meal planning and nutrition, and designer Francesco Risso, who discussed the role of Astra in his creative process in an OpenAI-sponsored video on Vogue’s YouTube channel. “There might come a day when I get a call from Charles about doing something, and I’ll navigate that in real time, but I recognize this brand has very bad PR right now,” says one creative professional. They add, “If you’re someone who doesn’t like where things are headed, anyone affiliated with this world is going to be seen as part of the problem.”

“When Kevin Systrom or Adam Mosseri were having events with celebrities, people wanted their leverage to help them grow their account, grow their influence,” says one media executive. Instagram is inherently about marketing yourself; OpenAI’s main product isn’t yet public facing. “Aligning yourself with OpenAI, every star has to ask, ‘What’s in it for me?’ — except for potentially a big check and a lot of blowback,” says the media executive. Skepticism around technology has only grown since Hollywood cashed in on the NFT and crypto crazes, resulting in embarrassing commercials and promotions that blew up in many high-profile faces. And the threat AI poses to cultural fields also seems to be putting a higher premium on good old-fashioned human creativity and originality. “I don’t care how cute you make Waymo look: This autonomous-AI-powered life is not warm and cuddly,” says the media executive. “There’s not a cool factor.”

At the same time, many in the entertainment industry are desperate. “Right now in Hollywood, only the top people are working,” the executive says. “It’s why Robert Pattinson is in every project or why Nicole Kidman is literally in everything you watch on TV. The next tier down is not getting jobs.” According to Porch, when he joined OpenAI, there was a backlog of inquiries from various celebrities looking for an endorsement deal, production studios wanting to become more AI focused, fashion houses trying to figure out e-commerce, and sports teams and leagues looking to integrate more AI. It’s possible that we will look back at this moment as we do at musicians who wouldn’t give their songs to iTunes. “Now, it’s like, ‘I can’t believe you would have turned down the check,’” one journalist says.

Some people roll their eyes at Porch, dismissing him as someone whose job is to be friends with famous people and questioning whether he has any expertise at all. “He’s a super-wily leverager of social relationships, but it helps when you have multimillion-dollar marketing budgets to get people what they want,” says a tech adviser. Another media executive sees what Porch has done as a kind of surfing: You choose your wave, start paddling at the right time, and rise at the perfect moment. It’d be fair to say Porch is a good surfer, they note. And now people are watching to see if he can stay up. “He sits in the middle of the convergence of media, culture, and tech, but he’s also right at the changing of the tide,” says the tech adviser, noting that Porch embodies a certain older-millennial brand that may be going out of fashion. “How much longer does someone like him maintain clout when it may be based on an outdated model of how those worlds interact?”

Porch insists he’s not worried. “What I keep coming back to is, I think, the usefulness of AI,” he says. “What it’s transforming for people is undeniable. And the more conversations I have, I just — I feel it coming, people being able to talk about it more.” He adds, “Everything moves faster in AI.”
*A previous version of this story misstated Eva Chen’s role at Meta.

items.title: The Future of AI Will Be Shaped by an Astonishingly Small Number of People
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: The Editors
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

AI has minted a new power structure. A handful of private companies command the might and wealth of small nation-states and are mostly left to self-govern. A few dozen employees are on the brink of becoming centimillionaires and considering which causes and presidential candidates they will funnel their vast resources toward. The industry is perpetually one breakthrough away from a step change in capability or public adoption, the question of who gets there first dependent on the specific expertise and visions of a handful of engineers.

One way to tell the story of how AI is changing our world is through some newly familiar names. Sam Altman and Dario Amodei are locked in a race to build AGI and persuade President Donald Trump to regulate the technology to their liking. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and venture capitalist David Sacks are advocating for the president to take a light touch, concerned about how regulation might jeopardize America’s dominance. As these figures have scaled their public influence, their surrogates and spokespeople (OpenAI president Greg Brockman, top OpenAI lobbyist Chris Lehane, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark) have populated news stories, too.

But an astonishing amount of power rests in the hands of a few dozen other people, none particularly well known, some virtually anonymous. So New York Magazine has dedicated this year’s annual “Power” issue to surfacing 26 people whose influence on the AI landscape far outstrips their fame. To assemble the list, we partnered with Transformer, a small but impressive publication with a command of the politics within transformative AI. The Transformer team drew on its years of reporting, as well as new interviews with more than 50 high-ranking industry leaders, to help articulate what makes these people powerful. We then commissioned multi-media artist Simon Denny to create images of each.

Despite the hundreds of billions in capex and upcoming IPOs, many parts of the field are immature, which means those who decide how AI is built, adopted, and controlled can quickly become among the most influential people in the world. A few on this list, for example, are tasked with shaping how the public, or a company, thinks about the technology — a high-leverage role for a field where everyone’s views are still being formed. (This is, in part, why AI has such an “essay”-driven culture — a blog post really can cause a seismic change.) Some will invent entirely new product categories, reimagining how we interact with AI, while others can spin up new industries or advocacy groups with a single check. Who is ahead and who is behind can change almost overnight (just look at Microsoft), which helps explain why a legacy tech CEO could have less sway over what Altman thinks than a 26-year-old with a podcast and why an engineer who runs a new critical function may appear on this list instead of a colleague who sits several rungs higher in their org chart. (Relatedly, the list’s average age is 36. It is also overwhelmingly male.)

The AI scene is still small. The 26 individuals on our “Power List” are remarkably intertwined, some even sharing offices, homes, or funding. (Transformer receives funding from an organization run by Alexander Berger, who appears on this list — and he in turn has ties to many of the other people cited.) The widespread societal impact of AI led us to include names from both private and public sectors, so you’ll find founders and engineers as well as lawmakers and regulators. Most important, they still have everything to play for. The new power brokers will decide how it all shakes out, refashioning the world for the rest of us in the process.
Logan Graham Stands Between Us and the Next Rogue AI Model
