Head of the Frontier Red Team at Anthropic | Age: 32

As the leader of Anthropic’s frontier “red teaming” efforts — a Cold War–inspired practice of playing the villain to find holes in your own defenses — Logan Graham has the job of pushing AI models to do terrifying things. This may mean persuading models to run cyberattacks or explain how to build a bioweapon. If the model then behaves dangerously, Graham’s Frontier Red Team is in charge of warning both company leadership and the public. So far, that’s happened at least twice, and each time Anthropic has pointed to Graham’s work as evidence. On April 7, the Frontier Red Team announced that Claude Mythos Preview had surpassed the usual cybersecurity benchmarks — tests designed to measure how good models are at hacking — and had to be tested on real-world security tasks instead. It found that the model could locate and exploit security bugs in every major operating system and web browser, potentially empowering nonexperts to run major cyberattacks. The company withheld Mythos from the public but granted limited access to a few dozen big-tech companies, including Amazon Web Services, JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft, and Google. Graham became the public face of this decision, which critics called a marketing strategy or elitist with Anthropic unilaterally determining whose cyberinfrastructure was worth defending first.

Graham joined Anthropic part time in 2022. That November, Graham “started red teaming LLMs for biorisks/weapons risks in my bedroom,” according to his subsequent tweet. Back then, frontier models couldn’t reliably do math or count the number of r’s in strawberry, but Graham still persuaded his bosses to dedicate resources to figuring out what AI could do at its worst. The Frontier Red Team he built would be one of the first in-house research groups of its kind.

“Some people’s intuition from growing up in a peaceful world is that somewhere there’s a room full of adults who know how to fix it,” Graham told Time earlier this year. “There are no groups of adults. There is no room in the first place … You are responsible.” Despite the nature of his work, a colleague described Graham as “very chipper.” Once, when asked what quality he most sought in red teamers, he responded “craftiness.”
Paul Christiano Is One of the Few People Who Can Slow Down OpenAI From the Inside
Founder of Alignment Research Center | Age: 37

Over the past 15 years, Paul Christiano has helped pioneer the AI-safety movement, converting the mostly theoretical concerns of figures like Eliezer Yudkowsky into hands-on research and seeding the ideas and frameworks — documented in papers, blog posts, and comment threads — that have become the air the whole field breathes. But as an early researcher at OpenAI, he was integral to inventing the technique that helped make the company’s products commercially viable, kicking off the AI arms race.

As an undergraduate at MIT, Christiano read LessWrong, the online forum co-founded by Yudkowsky that helped birth today’s AI-safety world. Christiano was studying math and quantum computing but gradually turned his attention to alignment, the challenge of creating AI systems that do what human users want them to do. A blog post of his, titled “What Failure Looks Like,” laid out what have become the two dominant visions of AI’s worst-case scenarios: one, which Christiano calls “going out with a whimper,” where humans gradually render themselves irrelevant; another, “going out with a bang,” where AI-controlled critical infrastructure breaks down, leading to societal collapse. When doomers talk about “doom,” they’re often picturing Christiano’s nightmare.

In 2017, Christiano joined OpenAI, where he led the development of reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, a method that turns raw language models into helpful, instruction-following assistants. RLHF is one of the biggest differences between Sydney — an unhinged Microsoft chatbot rumored to be an early version of OpenAI’s GPT-4 — and today’s polite, helpful chatbots. It’s now a crucial part of all frontier AI-training pipelines and may have done more to unlock the technology’s mass-commercialization potential than almost anything else.

Around the time Dario Amodei, Christiano’s co-author of the paper that helped introduce RLHF, exited OpenAI, Christiano left, too, founding a research nonprofit called the Alignment Research Center. In the spring of 2024, the Biden administration brought him on as the AI Safety Institute’s head of AI safety, where he would be in charge of testing frontier AI models. Government staffers threatened to quit over his ties to effective altruism before his first day on the job. But through widespread DOGE-era cuts and institutional overhauls, Christiano somehow stayed put — he still works part time as a special government employee. In September, the day after Jacob Coxon’s viral Anthropic resignation tweet, Christiano announced that he was joining OpenAI’s nonprofit board to serve on its Safety and Security Committee. The five-person committee, at least on paper, has the power to delay OpenAI’s model releases, giving Christiano the chance to wrangle his former employer into controlling its AI risks before it’s too late.
Dylan Patel’s Analyses Can Spook Even Nvidia’s CEO
Founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis | Age: 30

Jensen Huang runs the world’s most valuable company. Even he cares what Dylan Patel, founder of the research-and-consulting firm SemiAnalysis, thinks: At the company’s conference this year, Huang took a moment to say that Nvidia’s chips are good because SemiAnalysis says they are. Since Patel launched it six years ago as an anonymous blog about semiconductors and hardware, SemiAnalysis has quickly become one of the industry’s leading sources of research and analysis of the chips, data centers, and power that AI runs on. When SemiAnalysis said AMD’s chips were being held back by poor software, CEO Lisa Su met with Patel the next day. The company publicly acknowledged the critique and set up a developer-relations team seemingly as a result.

Patel has been obsessed with the technical nuances of silicon since he was a teen lurking on chip sub-Reddits and has a talent for networking that feeds him a steady stream of gossip. In 2023, when everyone was reporting that TSMC’s limited chip-packaging capacity was curtailing the supply of Nvidia chips, SemiAnalysis mapped the upstream suppliers, showing how long the bottleneck would last and who would profit. “There were a bunch of people doing technical research” when SemiAnalysis launched, according to Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, “but no one that could combine the technical breakthroughs with the business impact.” (Sequoia has invested in SemiAnalysis.) When the AI boom started, Patel and his team “were the first to really understand the whole systems math,” says Maguire, building complex models that linked the cost of chips to AI companies’ margins — and selling them to hedge funds, AI companies, and semiconductor giants.

SemiAnalysis reportedly expects $100 million in revenue this year. It recently acquired Citrini Research and raised $500 million for a fund investing in AI infrastructure and chip companies. Critics note that could create serious conflicts of interest — something Patel has brushed off.
Every Silicon Valley CEO Is Listening to Dwarkesh Patel
Host of ‘Dwarkesh Podcast’ | Age: 26

Top episodes of Dwarkesh Podcast, where guests talk unabashedly about “the parallelization penalty” and “the Schwarzschild metric,” often for well over 90 minutes, can attract some 2 million views. But the scale of the audience matters less than its composition: It has become required listening for Silicon Valley’s top AI researchers and executives. Big industry names like Jane Street and SpaceXAI’s Grok Bot have sponsored the show, knowing they’ll get in front of nearly every AI executive in the Bay Area. And while many of the guests — which include Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk — might be unavailable to most reporters, they’ll agree to be interviewed by Patel. One top tech PR representative told us that clients would rather be on his podcast than 60 Minutes.

Patel’s show sets the agenda for what the industry thinks about. Take his November 2025 interview with Ilya Sutskever, the tight-lipped co-founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc. Sutskever — who, while working at OpenAI, correctly foresaw that training bigger AI models on more data with more computing power would reliably make them smarter — told Patel, “Now that compute is big, we are back to the age of research.” Sutskever was predicting that we’d hit the limits of what increased computing power alone could do and sparked fierce debate about whether AI progress was about to hit a wall. Through essays and interviews, Patel also seeds his own point of view — that AI will be a big deal, but truly transformative models will come slower than companies have promised because they haven’t yet achieved continual learning, or the ability to learn independently in real time. While “people were aware of it as a problem,” Anthropic’s Sholto Douglas said in an interview earlier this year, “a lot of the AI labs started talking about it publicly after Dwarkesh raised its public prominence.”

Patel isn’t exactly a journalist, and what might qualify as egregious conflicts of interest in legacy media give him a leg up in tech podcasting, where busy researchers tend to distrust reporters and lack the patience for surface-level conversations. His interview with Mechanize founders Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu, whose stated mission is the “full automation of the economy,” dropped the day the company launched; Patel disclosed himself as an angel investor in Mechanize as well as several other companies whose founders he’s interviewed. A friend of Patel’s says they “would go as far as saying that if he wasn’t an insider, the researchers wouldn’t trust him.”
Thibault Sottiaux Is Deciding How You, Your Boss, and Your Employee Use AI at Work
Head of core products at OpenAI | Age: 34

In the two years since he joined OpenAI, Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux has become one of its top executives, overseeing ChatGPT, Codex, and the company’s API platform. His decisions affect all 1.2 billion weekly users of ChatGPT and the future of work as we know it.

Anthropic originally had the advantage in the coding market with a cultlike following among developers for Claude Code. OpenAI’s competing product, Codex, was faltering. That changed once Sottiaux took over the team last year. At the time, coding agents were mostly used via developers’ “terminal” apps — a clunky, text-only command-line interface that scared off the average user. Sottiaux, who has a background building internal tools for researchers, realized that this wouldn’t work, especially once users’ interactions with agents became more complex and they began to run multiple agents simultaneously and work on longer tasks. So he pivoted the team to building a native desktop app, a simple interface that would let nontechnical people direct AI agents for office work (sifting through emails, handling spreadsheets, writing memos). It was a “contrarian bet,” says Dan Shipper, a founder and AI commentator who recently wrote a lengthy history of Codex. But the team yielded to Sottiaux’s “sense of focus,” an OpenAI colleague says.

The Codex app was released in February, and Codex had 2 million weekly users by March 19. In May, Sottiaux was promoted to head of core products, reporting directly to president of OpenAI Greg Brockman. Two months later, ChatGPT’s desktop app was rebuilt around Codex. Sottiaux’s “little backwater … became the foundation of ChatGPT, and their leaders became the people who run the whole of the ChatGPT org,” Shipper says. It helped that Sottiaux had become something of a personality among the AI crowd, thanks to his remarkably accessible X presence and his habit of frequently and publicly resetting people’s usage limits, handing out tokens as freely as Oprah once did cars.

Sottiaux, who deploys Codex as a “little chief of staff,” now has his sights set on something bigger. In a recent podcast interview, he described wanting to build a “permanent active intelligence that knows everything it needs to do and is available through any client, any screen”: something similar to the omnipresent AIs of Star Trek. Dots, a personal assistant slowly rolling out to ChatGPT’s billion-plus users, is a step in that direction.
Nat Friedman Put Back in the AI Race
Head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs | Age: 49

In the spring and summer of 2025, Meta’s AI strategy looked desperate and lost. The latest version of its open-weight Llama model had been a bit of a bust, so Mark Zuckerberg went on a spending spree to lure the world’s best AI researchers and executives. Two of the pickups were Scale AI co-founder Alexandr Wang and former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman.

Things were tumultuous for a bit. Legacy AI talent headed out, Meta cut about 600 jobs in its AI division, and some new hires left, some almost immediately. This past June, when Meta delayed its new AI model Muse Spark, the division looked dead on arrival.

In September, the company released Muse, an agentic AI assistant that can book flights, organize your inbox, and discover money that you may be owed. Although it arrived amid a wave of agents released by tech companies — SpaceXAI, OpenAI, and Instinct — Muse, powered by Spark, rose to the top of the app charts. Wang has been the face of Muse, appearing onstage at the annual Meta developer conference and turning his X account into a flow of memes featuring the app’s fuzzy mascot. But sources close to Meta’s AI team say the credit for the app’s success belongs to Friedman. While Wang is head of Superintelligence Labs, the AI division responsible for developing the models, Friedman is tasked with Muse’s product development. He technically reports to Wang, but sources say they’re valued equally in Zuck’s eyes. It’s still unclear how big AI agents will get, but Muse is best positioned to market itself on the back of Meta’s billion-plus-user platforms.

Friedman has made a career of taking open-source software that only programmers could love and making it publicly accessible. He co-founded a company in the late 1990s that tried to make the free Linux operating system friendly for ordinary computer users. He later went on to run GitHub, the Microsoft-owned site where millions of software developers store and share their code. On his watch, GitHub released Copilot, the first AI coding assistant to really catch on. Likewise, Friedman said Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, a free AI assistant that went viral with programmers earlier this year but was too technical for the average person to use.
Sarah Guo Might Pick the Next Baby Billionaire
Founder and partner of Conviction | Age: 37

In June, the venture capitalist Sarah Guo published a blog post about an “AI psychosis” that had consumed her fellow investors across the Valley. It was characterized, she wrote, by “a despair that nothing is investible, that we should put all our money into Anthropic and Nvidia and go home.” But that “psychosis,” she says, didn’t reach her. “I have never felt it,” Guo wrote.

Guo is the founder of Conviction, one of the biggest AI-native VC funds to emerge from the post-generative AI era. She started it in 2022 after leaving Greylock, where she’d become its youngest partner at 28. Her thesis: Capital won’t just flow to a small number of vertically integrated frontier labs but to a whole ecosystem of AI: AI-native software companies, data-serving providers, chip manufacturers, and scientific researchers. Her first investment, the then-little-known legal start-up Harvey, is now valued at $15.5 billion. She followed with early-stage investments in European lab Mistral, AI-assisted medical-search engine OpenEvidence, and coding tool Cognition. OpenEvidence, or “ChatGPT for doctors,” has become so popular OpenAI is competing with its own copycat product, while Cognition has started to raise at the dollar amounts of frontier AI companies (it is reportedly pursuing a $1 billion raise).

On the podcast she co-hosts, Guo has interviewed industry veterans like Jensen Huang as well as founders she’s invested in, building hype for follow-on funding rounds and attracting customers. Critics may say she is too gauche, too flashy — the type of investor who makes a celebrity of themself with vinyl outfits and a podcast. But a peer investor says Guo has a knack for making the founders best suited to build ecosystem projects eager for her coaching. The child of two engineers, Guo tends to zero in on technical people, whom she invests in at the Series A or seed stage, or even earlier, incubating start-ups in their infancy. Her investments sometimes act as a signal to other venture capitalists as to where to invest and trigger trends in and of themselves. “I love killer nerds,” she says.
Karol Hausman and His Team Could Break AI’s Physical-World
CEO of Physical Intelligence | Age: 38

AI may be on its way to automating knowledge work, but it still can’t interact with the real world, leaving large swaths of the economy mostly off-limits. Many companies are squaring up to the challenge of building AI for robotics, but Physical Intelligence, a start-up led by former Google researcher Karol Hausman, has set itself apart by trying to solve one very fundamental part of the problem: It is trying to design AI models to build a universal robot brain.

In November 2024, Physical Intelligence, also known as Pi, announced it had received $400 million in funding from the likes of Jeff Bezos, OpenAI, and Thrive Capital. Another $600 million followed in November 2025, and a further $1 billion earlier this year — all for a company with no commercial product and no revenue. The start-up reportedly held discussions with Anthropic about a potential acquisition, too. (A representative for Pi declined to comment.) Making its financials more mind-boggling is that the company has made no promise to investors about selling products.

Hausman left his role leading research into robot manipulation at Google to start the company. Also on the founding team: Sergey Levine, who is a professor at UC Berkeley and, by some metrics, the most-cited researcher in robotics; Chelsea Finn, whose Ph.D. was co-advised by Levine and whom former colleagues call a “robot whisperer” and who is a professor at Stanford, where her lab masterminded the low-cost two-armed-robot setups that many serious robotics labs now use. Together, the three helped lead a project at Google that’s broadly thought to have parlayed the transformer architecture of LLMs into robotics by adding images and motion to the training data to create vision-language-action models, or VLAs. Two of the other co-founders, Brian Ichter and Quan Vuong, also worked on that project. Adnan Esmail, another technical co-founder, was previously SVP of engineering at Anduril Industries. On the business side is Lachy Groom, an early employee at Stripe, when he was just 18, and a solo VC who invested in Figma, Notion Labs, and Ramp.

Already, Pi has managed to show progress on the fundamental problems that still puzzle flashier companies. Most humanoid robots have yet to live up to the hype of their developers. Tesla’s Optimus has faced criticism for reliance on remote controls during presentations; the AI robotics company Figure has reportedly exaggerated the scope and scale of its deployments; the home helper of rival company 1X requires a remote operator to do anything that could count as useful. But Physical Intelligence’s latest model, π0.7, eventually worked out how to cook a sweet potato in an air fryer it had barely seen in training. Critics contend, with no agreed benchmarks in robotics, it’s hard to say if the progress it has made is particularly meaningful. Proponents argue that it’s a glimmer of what researchers call compositional generalization, the ability of a model to stitch together snippets of what it knows into a bigger, more complex task.
Beth Could Force the Industry’s Secrets Into the Open
Founder and CEO of METR | Age: 29

On September 16, in the middle of apocalyptic statements from industry defectors and polarized calls for regulation, the New York Post published a cover story: “The Woke Wizards of A.I.” Its subject was METR, a nonprofit that tests AI models before they’re released. The previous week, Dario Amodei had named METR a potential “embedded third-party evaluator” meant to monitor his and other labs. Now the Post was painting Beth Barnes as the leader of a band of “globalists” who believe in “genderless pronoun[s]” and the impending AI apocalypse.

Barnes spent three years at OpenAI researching how to stop AI models from going rogue or otherwise acting against human intentions but lost confidence in anyone’s ability to change the industry from the inside. (“I think I am a very open and honest person,” she told Time in 2024. “I am not very good at navigating political things and not making disagreements pretty obvious.”) Founded in 2022, METR has positioned itself as a small team of trusted technical experts, more resourced and bullish on AGI than existing academic labs. The first of its kind, it used its ties with industry researchers to gain early access to OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Anthropic’s Claude, pioneering the practice of third-party model evaluations in the world of AI safety. It would be another year until peer-auditing organizations like Apollo Research and the U.K.’s AI Security Institute came along. METR’s “time horizon” chart — a curve illustrating the exponential growth in the difficulty of tasks models are capable of — has become one of the most-cited charts in AI. It’s what people point to as a sign the singularity is coming.

Barnes, a scrupulous technical researcher, has managed to earn the trust of nearly everyone in and around major AI companies. Today, METR shares a building with a number of AI-safety nonprofits, funders, and industry research fellows, providing “lots of opportunities to interact directly with people at the AI companies,” said David Krueger, former research director at the U.K.’s AI Security Institute. That, on top of Barnes’s long-standing connections to OpenAI, gives METR rare access into otherwise-impenetrable companies. And while METR doesn’t take money from AI companies or individuals working at them, it uses their free tokens and relies on the continued goodwill of industry researchers, who can revoke METR’s access anytime they’d like. Anthropic recently gave six METR staffers “employee-like access” to its office, including hardware and tools normally hidden far from outsiders.
Brendan Foody Might Be the Reason Your Job Gets Automated
Co-founder of Mercor | Age: 23

If AI comes for your job, there’s a good chance it’ll be because of Mercor. The early years of hiring thousands of people to prod, test, and train AI models mostly focused on cheaper labor, but Mercor, founded in 2023 by Brendan Foody and his high-school debate friends Adarsh Hiremath and Surya Midha, recruits doctors, bankers, academics, and even poets.

These highly skilled employees are paid to help train AI models to do their jobs. They evaluate how good models are already, develop rubrics to measure what “good” looks like, and rate models’ outputs to help train them. Mercor’s AI Productivity Index (APEX) has become a core standard against which models are judged, feeding into predictions about how much of the knowledge economy AI will eat and letting companies know where they are falling short. “When a gap shows up in APEX, it tends to become what the whole industry works to hill-climb next,” says Foody. But the longer-term goal is to use that data to make those workers replaceable by turning their knowledge of their own jobs into training environments for AI. (A spokesperson for Mercor says the goal is for AI to take on “more of the routine tasks, and professionals move up the value chain to focus on higher-order work.”) As Foody told economist Tyler Cowen last year, “We’ll move toward these fixed-cost investments of teaching an agent how to do something … then being able to use agents as many times as we want.”

The focus on the premium end of the economy has already borne fruit, making the founders, all college dropouts, the world’s youngest self-made billionaires. As of last October, Mercor was valued at $10 billion and was reportedly in talks over a $20 billion valuation in July 2026. It sells its data and training environments to all the leading AI companies, and the valuations reflect how central Mercor’s approach may be to breaking down the barriers currently stopping AI models from becoming workers.

Mercor’s next step is to become indispensable to everyday businesses running AI agents and getting employees to improve their own employer’s AIs. “Companies are deploying agents without knowing whether they work,” says Foody. “The people who know what good work looks like are their own employees. In five years, Mercor will be the infrastructure every company and every lab uses to measure and improve how AI performs on real work.”
Dean Ball Is Nudging OpenAI to Embrace Regulation
Head of strategic futures at OpenAI | Age: 34

Earlier this year, OpenAI employees became increasingly upset with the company’s global-affairs team. Under Chris Lehane, OpenAI had taken a more reserved approach to AI regulation — one at odds with its engineers, many of whom had AI-safety concerns. The problem, some thought, was that the lobbyists thought of AI as a normal technology (Lehane had a background at Airbnb and in crypto) rather than the world-changing, godlike technology its staff were trying to build. The employee uproar seems to have worked: OpenAI’s policy stances have grown more pro-regulation in recent months. Perhaps more importantly, it hired Dean Ball.
Ball reports to chief strategy officer

items.title: Trump’s Closing Argument: Get a Load of the Reflecting Pool!
items.description: President Trump’s deep unpopularity is dragging down Republicans around the country. His personal intervention in Texas’s primary has made the GOP’s Senate majority significantly more difficult to defend. Some wonder if he even cares about Republicans winning
items.author: Benjamin Hart
paragraphs: President Trump’s deep unpopularity is dragging down Republicans around the country. His personal intervention in Texas’s primary has made the GOP’s Senate majority significantly more difficult to defend. Some wonder if he even cares about Republicans winning the midterm elections at all.

The president didn’t exactly allay those concerns on Monday, a day before polls close. As his X account rolled out pro forma endorsements of various Republicans, the real Trump was laser-focused on the one thing that really animates him right now: Washington renovations. During a roughly 20-minute address in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump took a rhetorical victory lap for restoring the beleaguered body of water, even though his administration first bungled the job in extremely high-profile fashion over the last few months. Holding up oversize posters and backed by visual aids, the president went into granular detail about the landmark, which is no longer glaringly empty.
He marveled at the new water’s hue:
He uttered the word “recaulked.”
And of course, he mulled adding his name to the finished product:
The New York Times’ Shawn McCreesh compiled a list of some of the topics Trump touched on:

Though deadlines prevent a full fact-check, it seems unlikely that any of these place highly on lists of Americans’ leading concerns at the moment. Nor do Trump’s other projects around town, like the gigantic White House ballroom or the club-ified Rose Garden. Still, Trump was intent on keeping the focus local. “We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that, you don’t have enough time,” Trump said, according to the Associated Press.

To be fair, Trump did touch on weightier topics like the Iran war he started (not actually a war, per Trump). But the star of his “weave” was the pool, which since the beginning of Trump’s second term has starred in a very Trumpian saga featuring cut-rate contractors and the unjust prosecution of a blameless ex-Olympian.

Oh, right, there’s an election coming up! Trump did get into all that, more than 20 minutes into his appearance. He went typically dark, remarking that “the Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history.” He called the election the “the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime.” But strangely, he also struck a tone of resignation.

The desultory nature of Trump’s comments was no surprise, and neither was his lack of enthusiasm for an election that polls project will be a drubbing. Trump has been holding rallies around the country, though at a lower rate than he has in the past. (He was scheduled for nine telerallies on Monday, but zero in-person events.) And while he has extolled the virtues of Republican lawmakers, and the ass of one in particular, he has mostly framed the proceedings around himself, urging Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot. Given his current poll numbers, Republicans would probably rather they not.
Still, the GOP can take comfort that by putting water back in the reflecting pool, Trump may have at least pleased some middle-schoolers on field trips, a key demographic for the midterms (of 2034).

items.title: The Wildest Details From the Haley Stevens Train Wreck
items.description: On Sunday morning, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens shocked her party by endorsing Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s hotly contested Senate race over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — just hours after telling colleagues she would not do such a th
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: On Sunday morning, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens shocked her party by endorsing Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s hotly contested Senate race over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — just hours after telling colleagues she would not do such a thing. Maryland representative Jaime Raskin, for one, said he was “dumbfounded” Sunday morning by the news after speaking with Stevens the previous night. Fellow Michigan representative Debbie Dingell said Stevens told her around midnight Saturday that rumors of switching sides were not true and had even texted her on Sunday morning: “Watching you on MS NOW, heart, heart.”

Unsurprisingly, the fallout has been swift. More than half of Stevens’s Congressional staff resigned, and words like “despicable betrayal,” “self-immolation over hurt feelings,” and “saddest sore loser in politics since Trump 2020” have been used to describe her about-face. But how, exactly did it all go down? Did she endorse Rogers on Sunday because El-Sayed disinvited her the day before to a church service? Did her fiancé, who bizarrely conducted his own series of interviews, pressure her into it? Does she think she still has a future in the Democratic Party?
Here’s what we’ve learned so far.
Stevens hasn’t come up with a great explanation for the 11th-hour Rogers endorsement

During an interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper that has been described as “one of the worst political interviews in modern history,” Stevens claimed she “absolutely” wants Democrats to win control of the Senate, despite publicly endorsing a Republican for the open seat in Michigan.

Asked what changed in the hours between Stevens telling various elected officials that she wouldn’t be endorsing Rogers and then going ahead and endorsing him, she replied, “This is a broader point about what’s going on in our own party.” Told “it’s actually not,” she then appeared to weirdly suggest maybe she’d vote for El-Sayed after all, saying, “I haven’t cast my vote yet.” But when asked by Cooper if she “might change her mind again,” Stevens told him, “Anderson, my mind is made up, I’m rock solid, I’m an independent woman, I’ve made my decision.”

When Cooper pointed out that in August, Stevens wrote on social media, “Mike Rogers will be another rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s dangerous agenda, we can’t afford to give MAGA another senate seat in November,” and asked the congresswoman, “Why is it okay now?” she dodged the question. “Why is it okay to have the Democratic Party and a top nominee injecting this type of anger and lack of kindness?” Stevens asked.

Stevens suggested in Sunday’s video announcement that El-Sayed was snubbing her drove her to endorse Rogers. “Our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” she said. “He’s right, and that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate.” She has mentioned other gripes with El-Sayed over the past day, including his ties to Twitch streamer and supporter Hasan Piker and a third-party ad that suggested higher grocery prices stemmed from U.S. aid to Israel — a spot that never aired in Michigan, which El-Sayed said he didn’t agree with, and which his campaign wasn’t affiliated with.

On Monday, conservative host Scott Jennings asked Stevens on his radio show why she made her decision, to which she responded: “Let’s go through the sequence of events, Scott. Immediately after the primary, I tried to do everything right. I did it right. I put party first. I endorsed him to which the response was — ignored. And cut off! I said, I get that, I’ll just go back to my regular life. Tuck this away. And then the ads came out, ads blaming Jews for everything!”
She’s saying things like how Mike Rogers could be the next John McCain

In an interview Sunday night with the Free Press — conducted on her fiancé’s couch while wearing “pink fuzzy slippers” and eating popcorn — Stevens said she endorsed Rogers because “I think he loves the country,” adding, “Maybe he can be a [John] McCain–type person or a Lisa Murkowski,” a reference to the moderate Republican senator from Alaska. She did not discuss the many, many substantive issues she disagrees with Rogers on — including abortion rights, health care, unions, and 2020-election denial — or that she has said Rogers is “just the latest MAGA grifter in politics for a paycheck.”
People close to Stevens think her fiancé may be to blame

In an interview with Gongwer News Service on Sunday, former Michigan governor James Blanchard said that during a dinner on Friday with Stevens; her fiancé, Jason Turkish; Blanchard’s wife; and another couple, Turkish criticized Stevens for endorsing El-Sayed. (Turkish, a Democratic attorney, publicly endorsed Rogers last week.)

“He was working her over,” Blanchard said of Turkish. “The way he was saying it was ‘Everyone is disappointed in you, they did everything they could to help you and then immediately after you lose the primary, you endorsed him.’” Blanchard told the outlet he pushed back in defense of Stevens, saying he told Turkish, “Yeah, because she’s a team player. You have to be gracious. Come on.” Turkish reportedly responded, “I know, but they’re really disappointed in her.” Blanchard, who was set to attend the church event with Stevens and El-Sayed on Sunday, believes “something snapped in her. And it snapped in 24 hours.” He added that Turkish has “terrible political judgment.”

On X, University of Michigan regent Jordan Acker wrote, “As Haley’s friend, I can’t be silent … I’ve known her fiancé, Jason Turkish, for years. I respect him as a brilliant lawyer and advocate for disabled Americans. But I have become deeply troubled by his behavior. I’ve heard serious concerns about his treatment of Haley’s staff, friends, and allies. My own experiences have only deepened those concerns. It is painful to watch someone you care about go through something like this.”

Acker also wrote on X that Turkish “took her phone away,” prompting a response from the fiancé: “Haley turned off her phone because of the amount of incoming calls. You are welcome to come over whenever you want. No need to make things up.”

On MS Now, Dingell said she’s “upset” and “very concerned” about what is going on with Stevens. Representative Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Michigan primary in July, said that if her husband “ever tried to speak for me the way” Turkish has for Stevens, she would divorce him.

Turkish attended an event for Rogers last week, where he called El-Sayed an antisemite. On Friday, he told TMZ of his fiancée, “I don’t think she’s going to be supporting Abdul El-Sayed very much longer.” As the New York Times notes, Turkish’s political commentary and public endorsement of Rogers seemingly came out of nowhere, and “though he is a veteran fund-raiser and an accomplished lawyer,” he “had not been a sought-after political surrogate.”
Stevens apparently found time Monday to send out save-the-date invitations:
Stevens still identifies as a Democrat
Asked if she will leave the party, the Congresswoman told Politico, “I am still very much a Democrat,” and said she will vote for Democrats for other races.
Stevens told the Free Press she is “at peace with this,” adding, “I’m not wrestling with this.”

items.title: Caviar and Caged Zebra: Inside Trump’s Halloween Bash For ‘Rich Friends’
items.description: Donald Trump has never been shy about showing off his wealth, even when it’s not politically prudent. During the 2025 government shutdown, he threw a Great Gatsby–themed Halloween party, mingling with Mar-a-Lago members dressed in glittering 1920s getups hours
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump has never been shy about showing off his wealth, even when it’s not politically prudent. During the 2025 government shutdown, he threw a Great Gatsby–themed Halloween party, mingling with Mar-a-Lago members dressed in glittering 1920s getups hours before SNAP funding lapsed. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump has repeatedly called Americans’ affordability concerns a “hoax” and made no secret of his focus on building himself a ballroom and gilding every available surface of the White House.

Still, Trump’s decision to host another ostentatious Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago just days before an election focused on voters’ economic concerns was really something. Here are some of the wildest details from Trump’s 2026 Halloween bacchanal.
Trump kept talking about his “rich friends.”

The president did not wear a Halloween costume; he showed up to the party in his usual red tie and navy suit. He noted that a lot of the “rich people” in attendance had spent far more time and money on their look.
“I came as Donald Trump,” he said. “I didn’t have time to get — people spent a lot of time and money. Rich people. They spent nine hours getting ready. I had ten minutes, so I came as Donald Trump.”

Membership to Mar-a-Lago is believe to be at least $200,000 a year, and at the party, Trump kept pointing out that his pals are quite wealthy. According to the New York Times, he repeatedly referred to attendees as his “rich friends.”
“Look at all my rich members,” Trump said. “They spent all day getting ready. Look at these guys.” He added, “These are the biggest guys on Wall Street.”

While most Americans served pizza and bowls of “fun size” candy at their Halloween parties, Trump’s bash featured Alaskan king crab and a caviar bar. The Daily Beast noted that Golden Goat Caviar tagged Mar-a-Lago in an Instagram story showing its products, and one partygoer posted this photo of the spread:

Diverging again from the typical October 31 bash, the theme of the party wasn’t simply “Halloween.” The Mar-a-Lago ballroom was transformed with green lighting, elaborate centerpieces, and a leafy archway with a sign that read “Jungle Cirque Adventure.” The Times noted:
There were cheetah and zebra stripes on the walls and tables. Women wore sequined leotards and elaborate headdresses, and one couple flocked around in bright-feathered costumes of jungle birds.

Many of the partygoers wore elaborate, skin-tight costumes and body paint that appeared to be custom-made for the event. Aside from the one guy in a rubber Joe Biden mask, no one was wearing some old costume they pulled out of the back of their closet:
A live zebra and a miniature pony were used as décor.

If you scrolled through those last few Instagram posts and thought, “Wait … is that a real zebra?” your eyes were not deceiving you. Multiple party photos posted to Instagram show people posing in front of a caged zebra. According to the Times there was also a miniature pony, but it seems he managed to avoid the shame of being caught at this tacky soirée:
Trump invited Speaker Mike Johnson.
And surprisingly, the Speaker didn’t think attending this ostentatious party just days before the midterms might be a bad idea. The Times spotted Johnson in an extremely sad VIP section:
There was Speaker Mike Johnson and Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India, in the cordoned-off section of the ballroom.
MAGA influencer Michael Solakiewicz also posted footage of Johnson mingling with Trump as a very on-the-nose remix of “Everybody Wants to Rule the World” plays in the background:
The Times noted Attorney General Todd Blanche was also supposed to attend the party, but it seems he thought better of it:

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who traveled with Mr. Trump on Air Force One on Friday, told reporters that he planned to wear an astronaut suit to the party. (On Sunday, a spokeswoman for Mr. Blanche said he neither attended the party nor intended to.)
Trump also invited the press.

How do we know exactly what went down at this party for extremely wealthy Trump fanatics? It’s not because some clever journalist snuck in disguised as the miniature horse. The president invited a gaggle of reporters into the event, and he spent about ten minutes gabbing with them on the dance floor as Secret Service agents kept people in parrot and safari costumes at bay. Trump answered questions on a variety of topics, from terrorism to the Iran war to why he doesn’t want his former lawyer Alina Habba Mildon to be paid $50 million for helping someone seek a pardon (unless she gives him a cut):

So there’s Trump’s closing midterms message: I’m eating caviar with my rich friends at a tacky Halloween party rather than doing anything to help everyday Americans — but at least I’m transparent about it!
It’s not great, but it does beat Damn, Jon Husted’s got a beautiful ass!

items.title: Our ‘Design Directory’ 2026: The architects, studios and designers to know around the world
items.description: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the coun
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the countries where they work to produce objects and buildings that enhance our lives.

Europe’s architectural and design landscape has a rich history, from ancient castles and cathedrals to modernist masterpieces. Contemporary designers are using this as a foundation for cutting-edge adaptive reuse and the establishment of circular economies, setting global industry standards.
The country’s contemporary designers build on a foundation of secessionist art and early modernist rigour.
This Vorarlberg-based studio’s practice draws on the region’s timber-building traditions and exacting craftsmanship.
+43 5574 44440, bernardobader.com
Innsbruck architect behind light-filled houses, schools and rooftop extensions, with a gift for breathing new life into existing buildings.
Höttinger Auffahrt 11, Innsbruck
+43 5122 38601, fuegenschuh.at
Architecture studio known for designing markets, civic buildings and public spaces. Most recently, it completed Vienna’s Naschmarkt, a hybrid timber market hall and public green space.
Schottenfeldgasse 62/2/22, Vienna
+43 1 890 8921, mostlikely.at
Tapping into a storied heritage of art nouveau and Flemish urbanism, modern Belgian design is a leader in minimalist creativity.
Landscape architect who designs with the climate and microclimates in mind, working with prevailing conditions to create welcoming, self-sustaining environments.
Place Eugène Flagey 7, Brussels
+32 2 219 75 21, bassmets.be
Architecture and urbanism practice designing housing and mixed-use city blocks, including in the canalside City Dox district.
Square Eugène Plasky 92-94, Brussels
Architect and designer (and Molteni creative director) renowned for creating pared-back, material-rich homes and furniture.
+32 3 205 91 90, vincentvanduysen.com
Studio that fuses branding and identity work to create engaging, narrative-driven spaces.
Hessenstraatje 1G, Antwerp
+32 3 290 62 73, wewantmore.studio
From gothic towers to brutalist works, Czech architecture offers a wide range of styles. Today the nation is a pioneer in adaptive reuse.
Renowned for its thoughtful, community-minded approach to schools and civic infrastructure, including an extension to Prague’s Deutsche Schule.
Vaclavske namesti 828/23, Prague
Adept at marrying old and new, this studio has worked on heritage sites, transformed historic city gates and made gentle additions to civic spaces.
Hollarovo namesti 2275/2, Prague
Architecture studio that turns neglected urban spaces such as underpasses into sculptural skateparks and lively public areas.
+420 724 819 859, uustudio.cz
A new generation of designers is now standing on the shoulders of the country’s mid-century masters, ensuring that Denmark remains a leader in functional minimalism.
Cassandra Bradfield and Sofia Olsson’s studio for material-focused interiors and objects, spanning hospitality, retail and homes.
Sturlasgade 14, Copenhagen
Copenhagen studio that designs galleries, boutiques and furniture with crisp geometry and warm materials.
+45 22 25 65 47, atelier-axo.com
Designer making elegant utilitarian objects, from chairs and speakers to lamps and textiles.
+45 26 25 10 34, ceciliemanz.com

Vermundsgade 40B, Copenhagen
+45 51 90 01 17, gamfratesi.com
Founded in 1959, Henning Larsen is celebrated for light-filled civic buildings such as Reykjavik’s glittering Harpa concert hall.
Vesterbrogade 76, Copenhagen
Furniture designer winning awards for her sculptural contemporary updates to Denmark’s traditional design heritage.
+45 51 29 78 20, mariabruun.com
Danish practice with Japanese sensibilities creating pared-back furniture and restaurant, retail and hotel interiors.
Forbindelsesvej 12, Copenhagen
Nature-based studio of landscape architects and biologists creating biodiverse parks and urban spaces.
Njalsgade 17B, Pakhus 2, Copenhagen
Cross-disciplinary studio that specialises in world-building, combining architecture, scenography and furniture design.
The home of organic modernism, Finland has a contemporary scene that celebrates natural materials and human-centred design, while making room for new ideas and technological innovations too.
Helsinki practice that champions traditional construction materials and methods, such as the use of solid brick and natural ventilation.
Punavuorenkatu 1, Helsinki
Storied interiors firm that has completed more than 1,600 workplaces, schools and public spaces since its foundation in 1972.
Established by the late Yrjö Kukkapuro and run by his daughter, this Kauniainen-based museum continues to release colourful, playful archival designs.
+358 9 505 1080, studiokukkapuro.com
French design expands on centuries of haute-couture craftsmanship, pairing new technologies with exceptional handicrafts.
Design practice that plays with form and materiality to create sculptural, geometric architecture, interiors and furniture.
+33 1 71 20 31 01, corpus.studio
Dorothée Meilichzon’s studio weaves local history into cinematic hotels, bars, restaurants and lounges.
54 Rue Greneta, Paris, chzon.com
École Camondo-trained duo making lights and furniture in alabaster, plaster and cast glass in partnership with French ateliers.
22 Rue de l’Echiquier, Paris
+33 6 73 51 76 18, garnieretlinker.com
Young collective taking inspiration from Bauhaus design, the African and Arabic diasporas, and street culture to create bold furniture and scenography.
Paris-based practice creating climate-sensitive architecture through adaptive reuse, renovation and low-carbon architectural interventions.

6 Bis Rue Gabriel Laumain, Paris
+33 1 42 71 13 92, studioko.fr

Practice known for building tall towers with a sensitivity to place and human scale – showing that bigger can also be better.
Gubener Strasse 47 (Fabrik), Berlin
Pritzker Architecture Prize winner Francis Kéré’s Berlin studio has a focus on using regional materials and building capacity in communities.
+49 30 78952391, kerearchitecture.com
Industrial designer bringing raw materials and craft to contemporary industrial-production methods.
Ludwigstrasse 4, Offenbach am Main
+49 69 82368081, sebastianherkner.com
Classical antiquity and modern regionalism combine to define the contemporary Greek design scene.
Architecture studio known for making hotels, housing developments and cultural venues at scale.
Architecture practice focused on reworking historic buildings with Greek materials and a minimalist aesthetic, while displaying a sensitivity to context.
Objects of Common Interest
Split between Athens and New York, this studio is turning heads for its colour-shifting objects, furniture and installations that sit at the intersection of art and design.
+30 210 331 2860, objectsofcommoninterest.com
A studio creating sunny, contemporary residences with bright colours and raw materials.
Renaissance roots and postwar radical design continue to have an influence on contemporary Italian design, which now strikes a balance between industrial efficiency and elegant opulence.
Acclaimed architect Michele de Lucchi’s studio works at all scales, from well-designed desk chairs to community master plans.
+39 02 637 8681, amdlcircle.com
Furniture and interiors studio pairing Brianza craftsmanship with a commitment to promoting wellbeing, exploring the link between the mind, the body and the spaces that we inhabit.
Industrial-design studio that is a pioneer of modular and repairable furniture, as well as lighting for circular economies.

Interiors and furniture studio creating moody, nostalgic works that mix mid-century traditions with contemporary influences.

Industrial designer making clean-lined, organically curving furniture and objects for major design labels.
Via Privata Giovanni Ventura 5, Milan

Milan studio that has a well-earned reputation for its warm, minimalist interiors and solid-wood furniture.
+39 02 3293 2044, studioutte.com

Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara’s Pritzker Architecture Prize-winning practice reshapes communities for the better with its cultural, civic and housing projects.

+353 1 671 3365, graftonarchitects.ie

items.title: The best new homewares, books and accessories for design lovers
items.description: Vite Espresso Coffee Maker
items.author: Nic Monisse; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Vite Espresso Coffee Maker
Alessi is expanding its celebrated kitchen range with this screw-themed moka pot, which takes inspiration from machinery in the company’s factory.

London-based designer Philippe Malouin worked with Italian brand Alessi to create this take on the stovetop moka pot. The piece draws inspiration from the threads of screws, with its spiral ridges and grooves referencing the twisting motion used to assemble the pot – making aesthetics part of the pot’s intuitive use. Its lower chamber is made from die-cast aluminium and its upper section features a heat-resistant thermoplastic-resin handle. Its colours are taken from the surfaces of machinery inside the Alessi factory. Adding to its appeal is the fact that it features a magnetic steel base that works on induction, gas and electric stoves.
Rediscover the joy of traditional film photography with this revamped camera design.

Kodak has provided an upgrade to the traditional plastic disposable camera with its new 35mm film model, the Snapic A1. It features a sharp three-element glass lens for crisp images, a two-zone focus (which allows you to switch quickly between close-up portraits and wide landscape shots) and a built-in flash. It also has a wide focal length that keeps scenes sharp: perfect for everything from travel and street photography to casual indoor shoots. The main appeal, though, is in its simplicity.
Free from distractions such as digital screens or phone apps, the Snapic A1’s pared-back design keeps its user in the moment and on the task.
Fiio CP13 Portable Cassette Player
Chinese brand Fiio plugs into the trend for retro audio players with this superior throwback.

Though China has long been disparaged as the home of cheaply made electronics, its new domestic makers are proving that the country has the manufacturing chops for quality audio. Analogue tapes are enjoying a resurgence in popularity (fans point to the allure of being able to “own” music) and Guangzhou-based Fiio’s CP13 Portable Cassette Player has found its way into New York’s Museum of Modern Art shop. It features old-school physical buttons, while its modern touches include USB-C charging and a 13-hour battery life.
The CP13’s 13 hours of continuous playback marks a significant improvement on the classic Sony Walkman.
Hay Outdoor Market Fire Pit
Light up your garden party or campsite with this versatile portable fireplace and cooker.

Designed in collaboration with Jasper Morrison, this fire pit brings to life the London-based product designer’s “super normal” ethos – an approach that aims to make everyday objects feel essential. Made by Danish brand Hay, its stainless-steel construction is portable, making it equally at home on a terrace or a trail. More than just an outdoor fireplace, it doubles as a cooker, thanks to its removable grill and charcoal basket.
There’s something about a fire pit that lights up our brains. Humans have evolved to associate flames with warmth, nourishment, safety and connection.
Looking for guides to visionary contemporary architects and era-defining design movements? Here’s our pick of five books to add to your shelf.
Published by oro Editions, Chairman is a new monograph documenting chair designs by London-based Yinka Ilori.
Oríkì: Material Affirmations in Three Acts from Apartamento Publishing is the debut work of Nigerian designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello, telling the story of a three-part sculptural series.

The Albanian Files: Freedom and Architecture, published by Lars Müller, chronicles two decades of urban change in the Balkan country. Tadao Ando has released Towards Light, which outlines his philosophies on life and architecture.
Riverside Modern explores the homes of Melbourne’s Studley Park, with photography by Jack Lovel.

The challenge for any specialist design publisher is to blend the academic with the entertaining. A good architectural book should translate complex information into inspiring, visually engaging content that also pushes readers to build better.

items.title: From historic emporiums to literary cafés: Our favourite bookshops in Barcelona
items.description: In a city where tourism is increasingly seen as a threat to local culture, Barcelona’s independent bookshops are thriving. Even as cinemas close and small music venues disappear, the city’s number of bookshops has climbed to 140, a 30 per cent increase since 2
items.author: Julia Webster Ayuso; Tabitha Sipp
paragraphs: In a city where tourism is increasingly seen as a threat to local culture, Barcelona’s independent bookshops are thriving. Even as cinemas close and small music venues disappear, the city’s number of bookshops has climbed to 140, a 30 per cent increase since 2008. According to the Catalan Guild of Booksellers, new openings have far surpassed closures in recent years, though some have struggled to keep their doors open.

In 2024, the threatened closure of the historic Llibreria Sant Jordi triggered weeks of public mobilisation. While it ultimately shut, it reopened a year later with a gastronomic offering. The episode underscored deeper anxieties over skyrocketing rents, the declining use of Catalan and the strain that a tourism-driven economy places on local life. And yet, while more retailers stock titles in English and other languages, Catalan-language publishing is growing too. Barcelona’s new wave of bookshops has become a valuable refuge for locals and foreigners alike.

Since launching as a small shop in Gràcia in 1962, Ona slowly built a reputation for its selection of Catalan literature. A few years ago, second-generation owner Montse Úbeda teamed up with entrepreneur Tatxo Benet to expand the business and, upon opening a 900 sq m space on Carrer Pau Claris in 2020, Ona became the world’s largest bookshop dedicated to Catalan-language books.

The boutique also stocks a selection of Catalan literature translated into 15 languages, from English to Mandarin. “We stock 1,500 references by authors who write in Catalan that have been translated into other languages,” says Ona’s director, Iolanda Batallé. “It’s painstaking work because we have to go publisher to publisher but we’re very proud of it.”

Ona has grown fivefold over the past six years, hosting book clubs, talks and live music in its café space, as well as a busy schedule of events in its vast children’s section. “Most bookshops have only about 30 per cent of books in Catalan because Spanish takes over,” says Batallé. “Shops like Ona are very important for the growth of the Catalan publishing industry.”
- Recommended novel: Ona director Iolanda Batallé is the author of I’ll Do Anything You Want, published in 2013
- Current bestsellers: Death in Spring and In Diamond Square by Mercè Rodoreda

When the longtime owner of Llibreria Sant Jordi, Josep Morales, passed away in 2024, the historic bookshop in Barcelona’s Gothic Quarter announced that it would be closing its doors. After an appeal urging book lovers to buy its remaining stock, hundreds of people turned up to purchase discounted books on art, photography, design and illustration. The event morphed into a spontaneous tribute to a local business which – with its listed 19th-century wooden shopfront – had been a fixture of the street since the early 1980s.

“The neighbours made it clear that they didn’t want yet another shop to close,” says Alba Biliotti, who now helps run the business under a new model. To the delight of locals, Llibreria Sant Jordi reopened its doors in December 2025 with most of its interiors unchanged. In the evenings after shoppers have left, the space transforms into a restaurant that hosts book clubs, literary discussions and dinners with authors. “Most people still come because it’s their local bookshop,” says Billiotti. “But now it has two different atmospheres. Some people come for dinner and walk out with a book, while others come to buy a book and end up staying for a drink.”
- On the menu: Piquillo peppers stuffed with cod brandade and caramelised foie with Kalamata olives and fig jam
- Current bestseller: The Little Frog’s Guide to Self-Care by Maybell Eequay

In 1980, four young women opened the doors of Laie on Barcelona’s Carrer de Pau Claris without much fanfare. “Back then it wasn’t customary to announce the opening of a bookshop; it wasn’t considered particularly newsworthy,” co-founder Conxita Guixà wrote for the shop’s 40th anniversary in 2020. “Perhaps three or four people came in during the first few hours.” Four decades later, Laie runs 35 outposts all over Spain, from Santiago de Compostela to Palma de Mallorca.

Fresh out of university, co-founders Conxita Guixà and Montse Moragas wanted to create a space dedicated to the humanities and critical thinking. It quickly became a meeting point for the city’s intellectuals, who would hide their favourite books in the wrong sections so that they could purchase them later. In the 1990s, a café and restaurant opened on the first floor. On any given day, you can still spot journalists, authors, playwrights and politicians conducting interviews or discussing book deals over a plate of ham croquetas or fish soup. “Gustavo Petro, the president of Colombia, walked in the other day and I had to act normal,” says literary director Damià Gallardo. “Laie has become a nerve centre of Barcelona’s culture; people have made it their own.”
- First book ever sold: An anthology by the Greek poet Giorgos Seferis
- Current bestseller: La Bola by Daniel Verdú, which was recently presented at the bookshop
- Recommended novel by Damià Gallardo: What I Loved by Siri Hustvedt

Huygens, a publisher dedicated to academic and educational titles, was planning to open its first bookshop in April 2020 when the coronavirus pandemic hit. When it finally opened months later, it was welcomed by locals who had rediscovered the pleasure of reading during Spain’s strict lockdowns. Founded by editor Mariana Sarrias and law professor Víctor M. Sánchez, Llibreria Byron – named after the British poet – opened with a café, quiet reading nooks and a space for events, designed with the ambition of giving neighbourhood residents a place to reconnect. “We decided to call it a bookshop but right from the start, we wanted it to be more than that: a place where culture is brought to life, not just sold in the form of books,” says Sarrias.

Byron has a large children’s and young-adult section, and a packed calendar of community events. Every Friday a group of neighbours from El Raval gathers for a philosophical coffee hour to debate a variety of questions from the dangers of consumerism to the role of uncertainty in daily life. These discussions often take place around a walnut-panelled fireplace that Sarrias found in an antiques shop and had restored before placing it at the heart of the shop. Though it’s powered by electricity, it still fulfils its intended purpose: to create a cosy, welcoming atmosphere for people to get lost in a book. In the evenings, Byron makes space for music too. The café’s grand piano is used for everything from jazz performances to renditions of Puccini’s Madama Butterfly.
- Recommended book: A Man Asleep by Georges Perec
- Poetry book-club pick: Hardly Creatures: Poems by Rob Colgate
- Bestselling Spanish-language book: Insular by Franco Chiaravalloti

Llibreria Finestres (Catalan for “windows”) opened in 2021 inside a modernist building by architect Enric Sagnier. Just a few steps from Passeig de Gràcia, the shop was designed by Quintana Partners and is furnished with carpets, sofas, well-lit reading nooks and a fireplace. The retailer describes itself as “a bookshop for reading”, where patrons are invited to curl up with a book inside or linger on the terrace with a glass of vermut.

A second location opened shortly after the first, dedicating its venue to comic books as well as publications on illustration and art. Thanks to its success, the business’s expansion has continued: another outpost arrived in the coastal town of Palamós last summer and in May, Finestres Palestina, an outlet devoted to Palestinian culture and literature, opened in the Gràcia neighbourhood. Designed by Valencia-based Palestinian architect Malek Murad Mateu, the latest addition features bright green sculptural bookshelves, hand-woven rugs and an indoor fountain inlaid with a mosaic map of Palestine.

Run by the Finestres Foundation, the bookshop is also behind several literary awards and writers’ residencies. Its impressively multilingual selection includes titles in English, French, Italian, German, Portuguese, Galician and Basque, alongside Spanish and Catalan.
- Phones off: The poor signal inside the shop serves as an unexpected advantage, stopping notifications and incoming calls from interrupting your browsing session
- A line from its foundational manifesto: “We know that there are a lot of bookshops in the city. We also noticed that there are even more readers than bookshops.”

After several bookshops in Catalonia closed following the 2008 financial crisis, journalist and writer Isabel Sucunza and historian Abel Cutillas teamed up in 2014 to open a space to showcase the work of new small publishing houses. Named after Catalan writer Pere Calders, who lived in the Sant Antoni neighbourhood in his later years, Llibreria Calders occupies a former button factory in a small alley. It has gathered a loyal following for prioritising local authors over bestsellers. “At the time there were very few independent bookshops in Barcelona,” says Sucunza. “There also wasn’t a single one named after an author.”

The space resembles a vast wine cellar, with dark bookcases set against bare stone walls. Customers seek it out for its well-stocked poetry section, as well as its selection of titles on theatre and dramatic theory. “Poetry wasn’t so central to the bookshop at first but as soon as we started hosting recitals, we noticed that there was a huge demand for it,” says Sucunza. Readers can continue to pay homage to one of Catalonia’s most famed writers at the nearby bar, Calders, which serves “dishes of exile” inspired by the author’s banishment to Mexico after the Spanish Civil War.
- Books recently presented at the bookshop: A new Catalan translation of Homer’s Odyssey by Pau Sabaté
- All-time favourite book: The Day of the Watusi by Francisco Casavella, a coming-of-age novel about Barcelona from the Spanish Transition to the eve of the 1992 Olympic Games
- Number of titles in stock: Between 10,000 and 12,000

A bookshop that specialises in art publications occupies a former shoe boutique on the corner of a 19th-century building in Sant Antoni. When the space became available in 2020, it caught the eye of Lucía Bonet and Luis Cerveró, who had long dreamt of opening a dedicated outpost of their publishing house, Terranova.

With the help of furniture design studio Owl, the pair restored the modernist listed building’s original features, including its tall ceilings and white wooden floorboards. The original bookshelves, which once stored shoe boxes, returned to their olive-green colour, while a custom-made central island that sits in the centre of the space was painted the same bright red as the Vico Magistretti Carimate chairs scattered throughout.

The shop features Terranova’s design-focused publications, alongside a broader selection of titles on art, fashion and design. Highlights include Servilletas, a book by photographer Felipe Hernández on napkins gathered from bars across Spain, and Sofia Coppola’s visual history of Chanel’s haute-couture designs.

Rather than sorting books by category, the duo has decided to arrange them randomly for customers to stumble upon as they browse. The shop hosts monthly exhibitions and houses a collection of rare books, which are available to view by appointment.
- Recent exhibitions: Madrid-based photographer Jesús Umbría Brito’s Familia Real, a series focusing on Spanish youth and counterculture
- Period covered by its rare-book collection: More than seven decades, from the 1950s to the present
- Year that publishing house Terranova was founded: 2014

With so many visitors regularly passing through the city, it’s perhaps not surprising that Barcelona is home to Europe’s biggest travel specialist bookshops. In 1979, Pep Bernadas founded Altaïr – named after one of the brightest stars in the night sky – in a small space in Barcelona’s El Raval neighbourhood, where he began to collect guidebooks. It quickly outgrew that first venue and, for the past 20 years, has occupied a vast space spanning three floors in the Eixample, where globetrotters can peruse an unparalleled selection of maps, travel guides and titles that cover every corner of the world. “The only country that we haven’t been able to get any books on is San Marino,” says Altaïr’s director, Helena Bernadas.

Books are organised by country in order of their proximity to Spain, from an extensive selection of publications on Barcelona all the way to a section on Oceania downstairs. Since 1992 the business has also housed a travel agency and an online magazine of the same name, both of which are centred on a “more anthropological than touristic” approach to travel. It is the bookshop, however, that plays the most important role in preparing for any trip. “We like to put together a curated reading list for our customers that includes guides but also fiction or poetry,” says Bernadas. “There are a million different ways to engage with Japanese culture, for example, so we try to find the titles that best reflect our customers’ specific interests.”
- Recommended book: The Innocent Anthropologist by Nigel Barley
- Number of maps in stock: 11,000
- Number of guidebooks in stock: 16,000

During his teenage years, Carles Armengol helped his parents’ business by serving tables at their restaurant in L’Hospitalet de Llobregat. When the establishment eventually closed in 2012 after 80 years in the family, Armengol began to write. His debut book, Collado: La maldición de una casa de comidas (Collado: The Curse of a Diner), was published in 2022 and explores his complicated feelings about the restaurant industry.

Today Armengol has brought his two passions – food and literature – into a single space. After he presented his novel at +Bernat, the bookshop’s owner, Montse Serrano, offered him the opportunity to open a café inside the shop. Today +Bernat describes itself as a place where “literature feeds you”. Walls lined with the latest releases surround tables where Armengol serves a simple lunch menu of classic Catalan dishes, such as fideu casserole or chickpea stew with calamari. He spends the rest of the day assembling sandwiches named after classics made with local produce, from Crime and Punishment (sobressada and Minorcan cheese, roast aubergine and honey) to Il Gattopardo (mortadella from Bologna with cashew pesto, scamorza and spinach). “A café and a bookshop are destined to work well together,” says Fernando Pelayo, who runs the bookshop while Armengol tends the bar. “They make each other stand out.”
- Recommended book: Beginning, Middle, End by Valeria Luiselli
- Bestselling sandwich: The Bikini (Barcelona’s iconic grilled ham-and-cheese sandwich). At +Bernat it is named Collado, after Armengol’s book
- Year that the bookshop first opened: 1978

items.title: Issue 61 - Kinfolk
items.description: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute
paragraphs: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute for Play, explains to us on page 154. Throughout the issue, we explore pathways to play, including expert advice on rediscovering your own play type as a busy adult and, failing that, five games devised and demonstrated by artist Carsten Höller for those who don’t know where to begin.

In a study of architects, psychologist Donald MacKinnon found that those considered most creative by their peers were often those who knew how to play; this is certainly true of John Outram, whose over-the-top masterpiece, Sphinx Hill, we visit on page 70. Painters play with color and line—a type of immersive flow state our fashion editorial explores on page 60. And musicians improvise and experiment, a process familiar to the band Balming Tiger (interviewed on page 78), whose alternative approach to K-pop subverts the genre’s perfectly synchronized image.
