items.title: Balming Tiger - Kinfolk
items.description: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
paragraphs: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
- Hair & Makeup Mahito Ohtani

My Zoom interview with Balming Tiger is chaotic. Five of the eleven members are on the call, each in a different location in Seoul. Omega Sapien is at a salon, dyeing his hair green for a music video. Leesuho is munching on a snack with a soda. Unsinkable is strumming a guitar, on mute. bj wnjn is lying in bed in sweatpants. Mudd the Student sits calmly, his long wavy hair dyed like a lion’s mane. There are multiple conversations all happening at once as we wait for the other members, some of whom never show up.

When the interview starts, however, the group is focused and attentive. A self-described “alternative K-pop group” from South Korea, Balming Tiger is composed of two women and nine men. They’ve been described by critics and fans as pioneering, experimental, an artist collective beyond music and, last but not least, “a group of hairstyles that elderly Koreans would definitely hate,” a running joke among fans online. In their two studio albums and a debut mixtape, released in 2018, they sing about alienation, absurdist humor, friendship and love, pigeons and frogs.
“We want Balming Tiger to be its own genre,” says Omega Sapien, a rapper and singer-songwriter, holding up the phone as his hair, now fluorescent green, is being rinsed out in the sink.

Ironically, Balming Tiger’s alternative identity depends on its proximity to South Korea’s best-known cultural export. K-pop, literally Korean popular music, is itself less of a distinctive genre than a cultural phenomenon. Within South Korea, it can refer to a wide variety of styles including ballads, EDM and hip-hop. Abroad, K-pop most often means idols: entertainers whose music and image are strictly produced by massive entertainment conglomerates, such as mega-groups like BTS and Blackpink, or soloists such as Somi and G-Dragon. However you define it, K-pop is a glittering symbol of Korean soft power. The stratospheric success of different Korean musicians in the past decade—especially BTS on the US charts—has catapulted K-pop into a household name everywhere.
“Honestly, we don’t really think about what genre we are, other than during interviews,” says Leesuho, one of Balming Tiger’s producers and video directors.

True as that may be, the label they have chosen—alternative K-pop—is a strategic choice, devised by the group’s founder and creative director, San Yawn. With K-pop’s international popularity, Balming Tiger has smartly positioned themselves as adjacent to something familiar to the global audience—giving themselves a wide playground to try anything and everything.

“It’s always more fun when the possibilities are open,” San Yawn later explains over email. “Whatever we are now won’t be ‘the final version’ of us. We have no idea what we’ll be in the future, but we want to continue to express the little joys of the world in our own language.”

It’s true that the structure of Balming Tiger is wildly different from a conventional K-pop idol act. Idols are usually conceptually defined by an agency, with clear roles differentiating members, for example “lead vocalist” or “lead dancer.” Idol wannabes train, sometimes for years, to audition for a role. Once the group is formed, the performers are the faces of a much larger and more intricate corporate structure.

There were no trainees in Balming Tiger. And no auditions—think more “Wanna join?” conversations at waffle houses and barbecue joints. Nor are all of Balming Tiger’s members performers—their 11 members include producers, photographers, music video directors, A&R managers and DJs. Some faces are more familiar, like those who sing, rap and dance in the music videos (usually Omega Sapien, bj wnjn, Mudd the Student and Sogumm, with cameos by others), but behind the scenes, everything is more collaborative and collective.

Balming Tiger can be seen as less a band with a signature sound than a creative universe, a rainforest of different species colliding and coexisting with each other. From their critically acclaimed debut mixtape, Homie304, to their first studio album in 2023, January Never Dies, to the 2026 album, Gongbu, Balming Tiger’s music defies classification—as does their creative direction. Their videos embrace Hong Kong noir (“SOS”), a ’90s boy band parody (“Big Butt”), and the industrial-era alleyways of the Euljiro neighborhood in Seoul (“Sexy Nukim,” featuring BTS member RM). Their sounds traverse old Korean pop, EDM, psychedelic rock and—of course—hip-hop, many of the members’ first love and forays into music.
“We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

The origins of Balming Tiger can be traced to Itaewon, one of the most culturally diverse neighborhoods in Seoul. It’s a place where the city’s only mosque towers over a hill, next to mom-and-pop stores and cockroach-filled villas, the US military base and ritzy alleyways that are home to the Samsung family and BTS members.

“Balming Tiger is basically a meeting of people that are full of holes,” San Yawn once said on the Korean talk show Moneygraphy. These “holes”—loneliness, for instance, and the desire to fill them through music and art—were what brought together this cacophonous collective through a random series of events starting in 2017, when San Yawn began looking for a crew.

They met at San Yawn’s home in Itaewon and spent much of their time together at Trans 201, on the second floor of a run-down villa in an area popularly known as Transgender Hill. The members started connecting in various ways: through friends of friends, an Instagram message, a chance listening to a future member’s SoundCloud account. “Trans 201 was Omega Sapien and bj wnjn’s house,” recalls Mudd the Student. “The space was very damp and full of dark energy.”

“After a heavy rain, the ceiling in my room was bulging with water, like a giant pimple,” Omega Sapien adds. “We had horrible mold problems. bj wnjn and I split the rent, which was like 600,000 won [approximately $400], and I didn’t even have that money, so my older sister helped pay half of my 300,000. It really was an awful time.”

“Not for me,” says bj wnjn, a vocalist, singer-songwriter and producer. “That space is one of the most memorable moments of my youth. Even with the cockroaches and all that noise from the clubs outside, there was a joy particular to that time.”

Memories like this are specific to Balming Tiger, to Seoul, and permeate their art in ways that can’t be manufactured. The evolving members remain consistently curious about their own experiences and the world around them. There have been some member changes over the years, including the exit of Byung Un, a beloved front man in the early years. But the joy—and the DNA—from that early, formative period is still alive, holding everyone together 10 years later. “There’s a childlike attitude that we never lost as a group,” Sogumm, a singer-songwriter and vocalist, says in an email. “A simplicity that feels honest.”

Often, Balming Tiger’s childlike experiments feel much deeper than mere fun and play, resonating like a sharp resistance against the norms imposed by others. Sometimes this critique feels particularly Korean—like in the 2023 music video of “Kamehameha,” where exhausted office workers are forced to drink with their superiors at a hoesik, an after-work company gathering notorious for heavy alcohol consumption. And at other times it feels fantastically delocalized, like in “UP!” where a cashier at a mega supermarket climbs up the mountain of objects he must clear, reaching for the sky.

“It’s different for me,” says Omega Sapien, who grew up in Korea, China, Japan and the US. “I’m not trying to be rebellious. But I do like provoking a sense of discomfort in others. I like creating differences of opinion through what we do.”

“I’m less interested in making others uncomfortable than in creating a sense of wonder,” says Mudd the Student, who is from Busan, down south. “I love art that makes me feel things for the first time. I suppose that can sometimes make people uncomfortable.”

Despite their almost tongue-in-cheek label as alternative K-pop, Balming Tiger is grateful to the K-pop industry for opening doors for other Korean musicians. The group has performed at major music festivals including SXSW in the US, Primavera Sound in Spain and Fuji Rock Festival in Japan. Their creative orbit is similarly wide-ranging: they’ve collaborated with artists including Japanese girl group ATARASHII GAKKO! and RM of BTS, while independently creating content celebrating figures they admire, such as Korean artist Lee Bul and Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Their music video with RM, “Sexy Nukim,” remains Balming Tiger’s most viewed, with 20 million views.

“People often think of idols as these puppets, who only do what they’re told,” says Omega Sapien. “But creative languages within the idol industry are changing too. I really love groups like CORTIS. I think their work is raw and fantastic.”

“I’m really interested in girl groups,” says Unsinkable, a producer and DJ. “These days we see groups that are more like crews, with more creative independence from their company. I sometimes wonder if new idol acts are inspired by what we do.”

In Gongbu, Balming Tiger explores themes of Korean and Asian identity. The single “Home” is absurdist and nostalgic, evoking Korean folk music while mixing synthesizers, rap and ritualistic chants. The music video is black and white, reminiscent of a Park Chan-wook film or a Lee Gap-chul photo. It’s inspired by the architecture of Kim Chung-up and the traditional marriage ritual hamjinabi.

“What does it mean to be Korean? To be Asian? When we were younger, we looked up to American hip-hop,” says Omega Sapien. “I wanted to be like J. Cole. But now I see that that’s his thing. We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

items.title: Taking Play Seriously - Kinfolk
items.description: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
paragraphs: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
A conversation with the National Institute for Play.

In 1966, psychiatrist Dr. Stuart Brown was appointed by the governor of Texas to investigate a mass shooting at the state university—at the time the deadliest in American history. Brown realized there could be a connection between the gunman’s actions and his oppressive childhood, which had been dominated by his controlling father. He would go on to spend the following decades showing that the need for play is biologically hardwired into the brain stem—the part of the nervous system that governs our essential functions like breathing and heart rate.

“When we’re deprived of play, it can be similar to being deprived of sleep and nutrition and connection—the things that fundamentally make us human,” explains Mia Sundstrom, Dr. Brown’s granddaughter and the CEO of the National Institute for Play—a nonprofit organization Brown established in 1994 to champion play as a public health necessity. “I grew up through play,” she says, “and have firsthand seen the benefits of it.”
Appointed to her role earlier this year, her mission at the institute is to show “how people can incorporate play into their lives to promote cognitive, social, emotional and physical health.”
Ellen Peirson-Hagger: Why is play important?

Mia Sundstrom: Here’s the paradox—and it’s why it’s so difficult to convince people that play matters: One of the core definitions of play is that it’s purposeless, that it’s not done for any specific outcome. Yet there’s a ton of purpose in the outcomes we get. We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.
EPH: What are the benefits of play?

MS: When we are in a state of play, it boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is the neuroplasticity protein that helps to create new neural connections and strengthen existing pathways. Play also calms down our amygdala—our emotional processing center—meaning it takes us out of a stress response, which is great for emotional regulation. And in the case of social play, our mirror neurons—which light up when we observe the motor activity of someone else—allow us to develop the basic foundation of attunement, which is the first seedling of connection with another human being, and which in time leads to trust, to community, to belonging. So on a neurobiological level, play promotes our cognitive health, our emotional resilience and our social competence.

Physical play is obviously good for us: Exercise is healthy, whether we enjoy it or not. But we’re a lot more likely to sustain it when it’s something we enjoy, so we might as well try and find a form of physical exercise that feels like play.
EPH: If we don’t play, are those things lost?

MS: When we’re play-deprived, there can be really severe consequences. It can lead to cognitive rigidity, which is when you can’t think outside the box and solve problems creatively. We have seen that a lack of play can lead to susceptibility for anxiety and depression, and toward addictive behaviors, because we try to find those things that we need from play in other forms—alcohol, drugs, social media, sugar—all these things that offer short-term relief rather than long-term benefit.

And then there’s social incompetence: As my grandpa’s research showed, when we don’t play it’s hard to build tolerance and empathy for each other because we miss that fundamental level of attunement. This leads to diminished well-being.
EPH: How does our need for play change as we become adults?

MS: There’s a misconception that it has to change like crazy, that what you do as a kid is not what you should do as an adult. But we don’t ever lose the desire to play, we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways. For example, as you go through grade school, the playgrounds change—there is no longer the opportunity to go down a slide at recess—and then all of a sudden you forget that you love to do that, and you might never do it again.

I don’t think adults should stop swinging, or playing at parks, or jumping on a trampoline in the backyard. We often think that we outgrow these things, but we really shouldn’t. Lego is a breaker of this rule: Lego adult sets are selling so well right now because of their connection to nostalgia and childhood. And what’s great about moving from childhood to adulthood is that the possibilities to play open up significantly: Instead of exploring your backyard with a stick and turning your cardboard box into a rocket ship, you have access to a car and a plane.
EPH: Is play different to different people?

MS: Everyone is born with a deep natural predilection for play, but that looks different for each of us. There are people who love to make things—art, music, building, tinkering with objects. There are people who love to dream or get lost in a book or movie and create imaginary worlds in their mind. There are people who love to compete, who play through mastering. There are people who love to organize—collecting new things, arranging social gatherings, even cleaning out a junk drawer. These are all different play styles, and one of the greatest gifts you can give a child is to notice what those natural tendencies are and help nourish them.
EPH: Do you think we need to take a broader view of what play is or can be?

MS: Yes! Most of the time, when I ask people “What is play to you?” they say “a board game” or “my kid’s sport.” We have confined play to this really narrow scope, when actually play is any activity that brings us into the play state, which is an altered state of being, almost dreamlike, that takes us out of the usual experience of time and space and evokes positive emotions like joy and awe. It is intrinsically motivated, not coerced, so it’s done for its own sake, and it’s self-reinforcing, so the benefits of a play state last beyond the time we’re playing.

Any activity that meets that criteria can be play—that could mean coding for someone who loves to code, or cooking for someone who loves to cook. Heck, that could even be cleaning if you put on a great song and you turn your broom into a microphone.
EPH: Why is society so resistant to play?

MS: Well, the psychologist and play researcher Peter Gray would answer by taking us back to the 16th century, when the Protestant Reformation taught us to believe in the moral virtue of work and that play, by contrast, is the breeding ground of sin. And then you throw capitalism into the mix which calls for more production, more consumption: that’s what defines success in the capitalist dream, right? Then you add in the compounding effects of automation and AI. Of course play isn’t celebrated in a world that prioritizes those things.
EPH: Has digitization played a role?

MS: We can’t prove causation, but our screens do seem to be factor in why we’re not playing. Scrolling on your screen disguises itself as play because you lose track of time, and it feels fun in the moment. But it has long-term detriments in terms of our attention span and our loneliness. If we’re scrolling, we’re not connecting with each other on a human level.
EPH: What kind of society would we have if we all played more?

MS: Play dissolves our differences and reminds us of what we have in common. Our world is so polarized, but play brings us together and is one of the most powerful ways to create a better society. Play lowers our inhibitions—I want to shout that from the rooftops. If you disagree with someone and go play with them, you’ll see the humanity in one other. It can also help combat the trends that we’re talking so much about right now—loneliness, disengagement, burnout—because play brings us back to that deep intrinsic drive to do something for a sustained period of time that makes the time pass more quickly.
EPH: What should adults do to help recover their love of play?

MS: We help adults rediscover their natural spark—their thing that makes them most curious and fully alive—and then think about small ways to reintegrate that into their life. The first step is to think back to your earliest memory of play: What was that thing you loved to do before the world told you who to be? Second, based on that, what do you love to do now—is there something that you’ve forgotten about and haven’t done for ages? Third, nothing ever works when we try to create massive changes all at once. So we say that 30 seconds is enough. See if you can add a burst of play into your morning or evening routine, based on those two things you reflected on. What’s great about play is that it’s self-reinforcing, so as soon as you give yourself that permission, it will keep you coming back for more.
“We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.”

items.title: Kyle Kuzma - Kinfolk
items.description: The NBA forward is playing the long game.
paragraphs: The NBA forward is playing the long game.

Kyle Kuzma is enjoying himself. He’s about to catch a flight for the south of France, where he’ll be attending the Cannes Film Festival, and is midway through the long, complex and, for him, extremely pleasurable process, of picking out what to wear. “If I’m going somewhere in three days, I may already be in my closet, just trying on clothes, seeing what I want to wear, thinking about what type of events I’m going to,” he says over a video call from his home in Miami. He’s planning ahead for the films, parties and red carpet events.

If a lot of this sounds like fun, Kuzma thinks so too. “Everything is play—unless, you know, it’s your profession,” he says. This is the challenge because Kuzma’s job is, after all, a form of play. He is in his 10th year in the NBA. A first-round draft pick in 2017, he’s currently a power forward for the Milwaukee Bucks; in 2020 he won the NBA national championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in only his third year in the league.

items.title: TEEKS Is Done Being a Sad Boy
items.description: photography HOLLY SARAH BURGESS
items.author: Alex Kessler
paragraphs: photography HOLLY SARAH BURGESS

With a baritone that could make just about anyone weak at the knees, TEEKS has spent much of his career singing about love, usually the painful kind. But five years after releasing his platinum-selling debut album, Something To Feel, the New Zealand singer has made peace with heartbreak and is ready to have some fun. “I decided going into this project that I wasn’t going to write sad songs,” he says. “By that point I just wanted to enjoy life and have fun.”
On Lovers Comet, his new album, the Māori musician is feeling himself: “Leaning into my sexuality and drawing from it as a source of power,” he says.

But there’s more to it than sex. The album finds TEEKS reconsidering masculinity, embracing his queer identity, and figuring out what he actually wants from love. Not that he’s got it all worked out. He admits to once flying halfway across the world on Valentine’s Day to win someone back. “Is it poetic or pathetic? I’m not sure.”
Below, TEEKS talks romantic red flags, what makes him feel sexy, and the art of flirting through intense eye contact.
ALEX KESSLER: What’s changed most about you since your debut album?

TEEKS: I’ve done a lot of living and learning within these five years. I’ve experienced some pain and discomfort, but those hardships have been a catalyst for growth. I’ve also had the time and opportunity for self-discovery. I’m at a point now where I feel more sure of myself than ever before.
Tell me about Lovers Comet. Where did it all begin?

To me,Lovers Comet is a meditation on desire. It explores love not as fantasy but as a cosmic phenomenon. The beauty and the destruction. The purity and the shadow. It actually began with a poem I wrote about someone, using the comet as a metaphor to describe the impact they had on me.
What’s the story behind “My Boy”?

I wrote “My Boy” after doing back-to-back writing sessions, meeting and working with new people every day. I was frustrated with myself because people would assume my sexuality, and I never corrected them. I came home and did a session with good friends and longtime collaborators Josh Fountain and M Basa. I felt empowered to write something more direct that left no unanswered questions.
Were you nervous about being so open on this album?

My writing up to this point had always had a level of mystery and obscurity, so there were some nerves around how honest and audacious I was being. But I’m at a point in my life where I couldn’t care less about other people’s opinions, in the best possible way.
How has your relationship with masculinity evolved?

My belief is that masculinity and femininity are two sides of the same coin. Healthy masculinity, in my opinion, is embracing the feminine and vice versa. It’s required a lot of unlearning, but also a reclamation of culture and tradition. Being a man can look and feel like so many different things.
How has your Māori heritage shaped your music?

My people are orators and storytellers, and music and dance play an integral role in the retention and transfer of knowledge. Because of my relationship with music in a cultural context, I’m able to approach my work with a sense of spirituality, tradition, and ceremony.
Who are your musical heroes?

Bob Marley was a constant in my household growing up. My father indoctrinated his children. Lauryn Hill and Stevie Wonder also come to mind. Eventually, I discovered D’Angelo and Frank Ocean, who altered my brain chemistry. Sade is and always will be my northern star.
What makes you feel your sexiest?
I feel my hottest when I’ve been consistent enough at the gym and you can see the pump through the clothes.
Are you a hopeless romantic or a heartbreaker?
It depends on the situation, but I’d say hopeless romantic for sure.
What’s your biggest red flag?
I have an addictive personality.
How do you approach… flirting?
Maybe roasting the person and cracking jokes mixed in with some intense eye contact.

items.title: i-D X New Balance, Straight-Up!
items.description: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheeseca
items.author: Tiffany Lai
paragraphs: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheesecake before the party continued downstairs at the Knave of Clubs for pub drinks and a boogie.

At 8 p.m., a new billboard was unveiled outside the pub, celebrating version 7 of New Balance’s iconic 990 silhouette, set to release globally on November 6. Made in the USA, the 990 has been a proud “dad shoe” since 1982, so naturally, we had to ask our guests: who is your favorite American? And which celebrity dad has the best style?

Who is your favorite American? Kim Kardashian or Adam Sandler. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Rey Mysterio from WWE. What’s an album that’s on repeat right now? The new Worldpeace DMT album. What are you doing this weekend? Spreading optimism and premature Christmas cheer!

What do you do? I’m a stylist. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Ford Bronco cars. What are you wearing today? Mules, which aren’t very practical for walking in the rain, an old pair of Our Legacy jeans, a cashmere jumper to keep me warm, and a vintage bomber. My hat is made by my friend Biddyish. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Brad Pitt.

What’s an item of clothing you’d never part with? My 1960s vintage McGregor jacket that I picked up in Paris a few years ago. What are you drinking tonight? Guinness. Who’s your favorite American? Jim Carrey. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My granddad, actually. What’s your favorite form of exercise? Running, because of the mental clarity and the long and steady journey I’ve had with New Balance.

What do you do? I’m a photographer, director, and DJ. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? A secondhand leather jacket from a market in Paris. What album is on repeat right now? Choke Enough by Oklou. What’s a color that you’d love to wear more of? Green.

items.title: Instagram Rings’ 2026 Picks Are Pure Gold
items.description: If you’ve woken up this morning to a shiny, gold ring around your Instagram profile picture: congratulations! And if you haven’t, don’t worry, there’s always next year! Today, IG announced the 2026 winners of Instagram Rings, its annual awards celebrating the
items.author: I-D Staff
paragraphs: If you’ve woken up this morning to a shiny, gold ring around your Instagram profile picture: congratulations! And if you haven’t, don’t worry, there’s always next year! Today, IG announced the 2026 winners of Instagram Rings, its annual awards celebrating the courageous creatives that use the platform, and awarding them with both a virtual gold halo and a real ring, designed by slow-fashion maverick Emily Adams Bode Auijla. So who bagged one, then?

This year’s Rings luminaries span every corner of creativity. The beauty scene got its flowers: Demna’s ride-or-die Sam Visser, viral blush pioneer Ngozi Edeme, LISA’s nail artist Juan Alvear and “wavy brow” aesthete Me Love Me A Lot have all been recognised.

Across fashion, there’s groundbreaking Chanel muse Bhavitha Mandava, “Portuguese girl aesthetic” neologiser Vic Montanari, Brooklyn-based it-girl Skylar Marshai, buzzy sneaker designer Salehe Bembury, and LaWatch Party thrower Lyas.

But that’s not even half of it. Behind the lens, lo-fi music video director Medet Shayakhmetov, ICE magazine founder Renell Medrano and otherworldly style photographer Szilveszter Makó all got kudos. Move-makers Damien Jalet—the choreographer who worked with Yung Lean on that video—and Sabrina Carpenter’s right-hand-woman, Jasmine Badie, also feature. And in the world of music, wrap your ears around Mexican trio LATINMAFIA, rapper-actor Little Simz, and Latin Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter Joyce Alane.

Comedy’s hot right now on Instagram, so it’s great to see Club Kid writer and director Jordan Firstman, Brooklyn Coffee Shop skit creator Pooja Tripathi, and Subway Takes Kareem Rahma all get a showing. For foodies, Alexis Nikole Nelson AKA Black Forager and culinary creator Steven Moto both got nods. And for bookworms, the Under The Cover book series. Completing the dream guestlist, two ballers: freestyler Muhammed Riswan and the raccoon-toting, goal-scoring GOAT himself: Erling Haaland.
Rings winners don’t just get an accolade—they’re also being co-signed by a panel of genuine icons.

This year’s judges included the no-introduction-needed Chloé Zhao, Isamaya Ffrench Donatella Versace, who i-D readers recently got the chance to DM. Joining them were hitmakerFINNEAS, street artists OSGEMEOS, alpine skier Mikaela Shiffrin, Emmy-winning choreographer Charm La’Donna, editor Will Welch, rapper A$AP Rocky, Indian celebrity chef Vikas Khanna and resident internet librarian Jack Edwards.
The lineup was finished with Instagram’s CEO Adam Mosseri and head of fashion partnerships Eva Chen, plus this year’s Rings designer Emily Adams Bode Auijla.

What were the judges looking for? (This is where you take notes for next year.) “I’m always looking for people with a unique voice and a point of view that is distinct and instantly recognizable as their own. Especially if they are able to build a whole cinematic universe,” Welch tellsi-D. He gravitated to the people whose Stories and Reels he never misses, the accounts he’s always keen to see more of. “If I already follow you and I think of your account as appointment viewing, I nominated you.”

When voting on other judges’ nominations, it was about instant originality. “If I landed on a profile and immediately felt vision and work that just kind of radiates electric newness, I cast a vote.” Instagram, he says, is a portal to experience this next gen of visionaries. “Radical newness comes from subcultures, and through Instagram we get instant access to all these niche areas of global interest and expression.”

In the words of Subway Takes’ Kareem: “100% agree.” Rings’s Class of 2026 provides the ideal inspo for zhuzhing-up your Instagram presence. These gold-gilded profiles are the circles you want to be moving in—so start sending those DMs, you never know. But remember, it’s about creativity, not clout.

As FINNEAS puts it, “My advice is not to wait, to keep writing, working, creating, sharing and putting your art out there. You might just reach someone and change their life, it could even change your life. You just never know what might happen and who you might reach.”

Case in point—when he sent a message to Lizzy McAlpine, resulting in a collab. Don’t be afraid of shooting your shot. “I’m usually the one asking creators I admire to collaborate on a project. When they say yes, it’s a good day.”

items.title: RIO's New Era Proves Fashion Is Cyclical: And the Future Is Latino
items.description: There are moments in fashion that remind us why this industry matters beyond the clothes. The new era of RIO is one of those moments.
items.author: Ricardo Diaz
paragraphs: There are moments in fashion that remind us why this industry matters beyond the clothes. The new era of RIO is one of those moments.

What Rio Uribe has built over the years—from the groundbreaking days of Gypsy Sport to the evolution of his namesake label, RIO—has been nothing short of remarkable. At a time when conversations around inclusion, diversity, and representation often feel performative, Rio has consistently demonstrated what authentic community-building looks like. For many Latinos working in fashion, his journey has been proof that anything is possible.

I still remember attending the Gypsy Sport shows years ago. The energy was electric. Those presentations weren't simply runway shows; they were celebrations of creativity, individuality, and belonging. They were among the experiences that made me fall in love with fashion in the first place. Today, seeing Rio not only as a creative force but also as one of my closest friends has made witnessing this evolution even more meaningful.

Working alongside a Latino-led team that continues to push fashion forward has been an incredible experience. As Fashion Director, one of the most exciting parts of the process is hearing what Rio is dreaming up next—how we can engage with current trends while simultaneously developing our own visual language and creating statements that feel entirely original.
That spirit is captured perfectly in RIO's first campaign since the brand's transformation from Gypsy Sport in 2025.

Unveiled on June 15 in New York City, the campaign marks a defining new chapter for both the designer and the label. Photographed by Harry Eelman, the imagery captures a pivotal moment in RIO's ongoing evolution. Balancing rebellion with refinement, the campaign reflects a collection rooted in fearless self-expression while embracing a newfound creative maturity. You only need to take a look at the incredible hair and makeup to understand that the team truly understood the assignment and delivered. We are incredibly grateful to have the support of Oribe as a partner, as well as the exceptional work of Kien Hoang and David Velasquez. A quick visit to their Instagram accounts is enough to understand the caliber of artists we are talking about.

Of course, RIO's story didn't begin with this campaign. Long before the rebrand, Gypsy Sport was already creating defining moments that shifted the conversation around fashion and culture. Let's not forget the milestones: bringing a then-rising Cardi B to the runway before she became a global phenomenon, or having Rico Nasty close the Fall/Winter 2019 show with the kind of energy only Rio's universe could attract. These weren't simply celebrity cameos—they were cultural statements. They reflected a brand that has always had its finger on the pulse of what comes next.

The achievements and experiences built through Gypsy Sport have now evolved into something even greater with the arrival of this new campaign. At a moment when Latino culture is increasingly shaping every corner of the global creative landscape—just look at our model Kandrex’s appearance during Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime performance—RIO offers something refreshingly nuanced. The imagery feels like a breath of fresh air, presenting a different perspective on what it means to be Latine today.

Ten years later, a different generation has found its way to RIO. This audience is politically engaged, environmentally conscious, and deeply invested in conversations around sustainability, identity, and community. They care about the future of the planet just as much as they care about personal style. In Rio's world, those values aren't contradictory. The RIO generation understands that you can advocate for change, challenge the status quo, and still look incredibly hot while doing it.

The images feel both intimate and aspirational—grounded in authenticity while reaching toward something larger. They serve as a powerful introduction to RIO's next chapter, one that remains deeply connected to its roots while making subtle winks to iconic cultural moments many of us grew up with, from Jenny From the Block to the broader visual language of Latino pop culture. At the same time, the campaign confidently steps into a broader contemporary conversation.
More than a campaign, this moment establishes the foundation for the brand's future as RIO expands its design universe and builds momentum toward its highly anticipated September runway show.

Fashion has always been cyclical. Trends return, references are revisited, and aesthetics are constantly reinterpreted. But what makes RIO's current moment so significant isn't nostalgia—it's evolution. It's proof that a brand can grow without losing its identity, that representation can be both meaningful and aspirational, and that Latino voices continue to shape the future of fashion on a global scale.
Creative Direction: Rio Uribe
Hair: Oribe por Kien Hoang

items.title: Prosecutors Intend to Retry Lindsay Clancy for Deaths of Her Three Children
items.description: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three children to death in 2023 whose trial ended in a hung jury on Sept. 4, will likely be retried, prosecutors said on Monday.
items.author: Althea Legaspi
paragraphs: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three children to death in 2023 whose trial ended in a hung jury on Sept. 4, will likely be retried, prosecutors said on Monday.
During a hearing on Monday, Clancy returned to court for a motion to dismiss the charges that she murdered her children. It was the second time she’s headed to court following her first trial.

On Monday, the defense argued to dismiss the charges citing double jeopardy, a legal rule that protects an accused person against being prosecuted by the state twice for the same crime. Prosecutors argued that double jeopardy “does not bar the Commonwealth from seeking justice on behalf of the three victims.”

According to Associated Press, Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington asked the judge to investigate the sole holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil, bringing into question the juror’s use of a cell phone while the jury deliberated, alleging the juror researched terms related to the case. He also questioned if the juror had been telling the truth during jury selection in terms of disclosing previous criminal history that may have affected whether he would be selected, which if true would be a “fatal infection of the independence, the honesty and the integrity of this juror.”

Heather O’Connor, an attorney for Desronvil, said the defense were able to question the juror prior to the trial, accepted him, and only began to challenge his credibility once he became a holdout. She also disputed the cellphone allegation.

Things became heated between Judge William Sullivan and Reddington after Reddington publicly identified the holdout juror, with Sullivan alleging this was potentially confidential information. Reddington claimed the name was already “all over the internet,” but then acquiesced and stopped using the name.
Sullivan also heard arguments from the prosecution’s request for a gag order to restrict public statements from the attorneys involved, which could affect future court proceedings.

Clancy’s triple-murder trial ended in a mistrial after jurors said they were deadlocked and a higher court rejected the defense’s bid to intervene in the deliberations. The jury could not reach a unanimous verdict with the vote remaining 11-1 for at least two days.

Clancy had admitted to strangling her three children to death in January 2023, with her defense lawyers arguing she was in the throes of psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. Meanwhile, prosecutors argued that while Clancy was deeply troubled, she understood that what she was doing was wrong. They asked the jurors to convict her of three counts of first-degree murder.

At the hearing on Monday, Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. Prosecutors said they plan to retry Clancy if the case proceeds, but they have not identified if they would pursue the same charges. The next hearing is scheduled for Nov. 16, and if there is a retrial it could begin in March.

items.title: Timbaland Sues Ex-Managers for $15 Million, Fires Back at Claim He Blew Fortune
items.description: Timbaland, the Grammy-winning producer known for smash hits including Justin Timberlake’s “Sexy Back” and Missy Elliott’s “Get Ur Freak On,” is suing his ex-managers for $15 million and blasting claims by one of the managers, Gary Marella, that the hitmaker is
items.author: Nancy Dillon
paragraphs: Timbaland, the Grammy-winning producer known for smash hits including Justin Timberlake’s “Sexy Back” and Missy Elliott’s “Get Ur Freak On,” is suing his ex-managers for $15 million and blasting claims by one of the managers, Gary Marella, that the hitmaker is trying “to shift responsibility for his own overspending.”

“Mr. Marella is the one attempting to shift responsibility here,” the producer’s lawyer, Tynia Coats, says in a new statement sent to Rolling Stone on Monday. “Timbaland hired him to manage his business affairs and protect his interests. Holding someone accountable for the responsibilities they were hired and paid to perform is not shifting blame.”

Timbaland, whose legal name is Timothy Mosley, filed his lawsuit Friday in Los Angeles County Superior Court. It alleges Marella, along with Mosley’s business manager, Bruce Seckendorf, took over his finances in 2016 after the musician uncovered alleged misconduct by a prior management team. Rather than look after his interests, the lawsuit claims, the new managers used “their entrusted authority to enrich themselves and others, conceal financial misconduct, and deplete Timbaland’s valuable assets.”

According to the new lawsuit, obtained by Rolling Stone, Marella took at least $2.5 million in “excessive or unauthorized” commissions and saddled Mosley with fees, reimbursements, and “undisclosed American Express cards” that Marella allegedly used for groceries, cosmetic medical procedures, family vacations, and other personal expenses.

Mosley alleges that when he received two $5 million payments in 2021 from the Verzuz platform he created with Swizz Beatz, Marella was entitled to $1 million in commissions but took two payments of $750,000. He claims Marella and his company also “took $775,000 more than their authorized 10 percent commission” from his 2019 Hipgnosis catalog sale and that Marella “grossly mismanaged” their Beatclub venture, treating it like “a piggy bank to repair the problems he created.”

Mosley accused Seckendorf of facilitating the unauthorized payments, failing to disclose irregularities, failing to pay his taxes and mortgage, and taking a cut of sale proceeds without transparent accounting. He says the “scheme began to unravel in March 2025,” when a foreclosure notice arrived at his home.
In a statement sent to The Hollywood Reporter, Marella said Mosley was to blame for his financial issues.

“Unfortunately, Tim is attempting to shift responsibility for his own overspending and financial decisions onto someone else (again) as he did before we managed him,” Marella told the outlet, which first reported the new lawsuit. He claimed Mosley “had spent all of his money and was living in a rental,” and that over nine years, they generated about $75 million in business together. “Despite that, Tim continued spending beyond his means, ultimately having to sell his home last year due to his actions and move into a rental in Coral Gables. Those were the consequences of his own financial decisions, no one else.”
On Monday, Mosley and his lawyer said the issue isn’t “a problem with the artist’s spending.” They said they would “welcome a full accounting” showing how Mosley allegedly spent the $75 million.

In their response, Mosley and Coats alleged that beyond missing money, they have evidence that financial records were falsified to show that a third-party consultant was paid $16,000 when he actually received $165,000. They further claimed emails were altered to make it appear that Mosley approved paying an attorney $250,000 instead of $100,000.

Seckendorf did not immediately respond to requests for comment, but Marella sent an email statement to Rolling Stone claiming Mosley “was already in a bad financial place” when they started working together.

“The allegation that I paid myself without his knowledge is not possible. His business manager handled his finances and paid management commissions along with every other payment on Tim’s behalf, which Tim was aware of,” he said. Regarding Beatclub, he said, “Tim and I come from the music business, not the technology area.” He blamed Beatclub’s problems on an employee who allegedly “failed to build the platform properly.” Marella also claimed he and Mosley took out a joint $1 million loan and used $980,000 to cover outstanding company obligations.

Mosley’s new 75-page lawsuit includes claims for breach of fiduciary duty, fraudulent concealment, breach of contract, and civil theft. It alleges Mosley suffered damages estimated to exceed $15 million and asks for a jury trial.

items.title: Thom Yorke and Harry Styles Come Together in Epic Conversation
items.description: T wo years ago, in the summer of 2024, Harry Styles was strolling down a small cobblestone side street in Rome, when he suddenly noticed a face he recognized. It was Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, one of his biggest musical heroes. He introduced himself — just two st
items.author: Rob Sheffield
paragraphs: T wo years ago, in the summer of 2024, Harry Styles was strolling down a small cobblestone side street in Rome, when he suddenly noticed a face he recognized. It was Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, one of his biggest musical heroes. He introduced himself — just two stars walking the streets incognito, with no entourage. As Styles confesses to Yorke now, with a shy grin, “You, to me, had always been that person that I was scared of meeting.”

Yorke and Styles might seem like they’re from two different worlds — the planet’s most dazzling glam-pop prince versus the high priest of art-rock angst. But today, they’re busy making each other laugh on a sunny July afternoon in London, at a studio near Camden Town. Yorke has been known to be a thorny interview subject, ever since the early days of Radiohead. Yet today he lets down his guard, as he basks in the presence of the equally notorious charm of Harry Edward Styles. They crack each other up like mischievous schoolboys.

In May of this year, Yorke was honored at the U.K.’s prestigious Ivor Novello Awards, where Styles gave a heartfelt tribute, saying, “Radiohead is my favorite band.” He also made a surprise admission about one of the band’s B sides.
“I lost my virginity to ‘Talk Show Host,’” he declared, then corrected himself. “I lost my virginity to the intro of ‘Talk Show Host.’”

Radiohead released their first album in 1993 — the year before Styles was born. But both have built their careers around defying expectations and refusing to repeat their successes. Styles could be said to be going through his own Kid A moment right now, with the experimental electro-pop of Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally. This summer, when he did a record-breaking 12-night residency at London’s Wembley Stadium, Yorke came the very first night — he was up and dancing right from the opening song.

Yorke has been on a creative roll lately. In his conversation with Styles, he reveals that he’s working on an upcoming solo album, although it hasn’t been officially announced. He dropped two acclaimed 2024 albums with the Smile, his band with Radiohead guitarist Jonny Greenwood. Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a production of the Shakespeare play featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album, runs at the Barbican Theatre in London from Oct. 31 to Jan. 23. And Radiohead recently answered the world’s prayers with their first live shows in seven years. They return in mid-2027 for residencies in Australia and Japan.

Styles and Yorke are both famously magnetic performers, but famously private offstage — shy of giving anything away, wary of outsiders. Yet face-to-face for their Musicians on Musicians cover story today, they bring out different sides of each other that the world doesn’t always get to see. In this wide-ranging two-hour conversation, they go deep on fame, fandom, songwriting, suffering from impostor syndrome, the inspirational power of walking, and the emotional intensity of weeping onstage.
Watch the video interview below
Styles: We met for the first time in Rome, on a small street. You were playing in Rome that week with the Smile. I was going to that show.
Yorke: Was it before the show?

Styles: It was before the show, yeah. A friend of mine had asked me if we’d ever met, and I had said that we hadn’t. So I was walking down the street, and I noticed you because you were wearing a hat that said “Acid” on it. I thought, “Oh, that’s a cool hat.” And then I was like, “Oh, it’s you.” I had A Moon Shaped Pool [the 2016 Radiohead album] playing in my headphones, and I stopped it. “Oh, hello—”
Styles: “Mr. Yorke, hello.” You said, “Oh, hi.”
Yorke: No, I said, “What the fuck [laughs] are you doing standing in the street?”
Styles: Then I came to the show, and we met properly.
Yorke: I didn’t know you were living in Rome a lot. I had no idea. So I was doubly confused.
Styles: You, to me, had always been that person that I was scared of meeting.
Yorke: Oh, yeah. I’ve got a whole list.
Styles: Yeah, totally. And I remember feeling so light afterwards. “Oh, people are kind, and they’re nice.”
Yorke: I was also impressed that you were just walking down the street. I was like, “Where’s his security?” Because I mean, I know I can do it, but I didn’t know you could do it. Is that a choice?

Styles: I think in the early days, when I was in the band [One Direction], so much of the hotel experience felt very locked-in. When I’d be home, it felt like, “Oh, it’s not safe for me to be out.” Then I had a girlfriend who was very outgoing, and she was coming to London and I was like, “Oh, if we just sit in my house for three days, she’s gonna think I’m nuts.” So we walked everywhere, and it was this realization for me: “Oh, it’s fine to be outside.” It kind of broke that thing. Now, it’s changed my life in such a big way, because it’s how you stay connected to the world.
Styles: I read something about walking being the artist’s kind of perspective, because you’re at ground level and you see things that you just don’t see if you’re driving everywhere.

Yorke: It’s also a good way to write. I wrote “A Wolf at the Door” — I was going through a really bad moment and I walked for like two-and-a-half days, rain, didn’t matter. A notebook in my hand, and just wrote it all. I felt so much better at the end of it.

But also it’s not just the walking — it’s the walking past people. The simple thing of people-watching, playing that game of imagining as someone walks by — where they’re going, what they’re doing, all that stuff. It brings you out of yourself, brings you out of your troubles. I mean, without it, see, it’s really easy to get lost.

I remember when we were on tour with R.E.M. [in 1995] and Michael Stipe figuring out that I would just hide in the dressing room, and never went out anywhere. So he started dragging me out, and he gave me this trick. He said, “If you don’t care, they don’t care. If you’re not looking, they’re not looking.” And it works. I remember being in Stockholm going to some really busy club, and he said, “Try it.” And it worked. Nobody bothered us.

There are moments when you will feel vulnerable. There are moments when shit will happen, or The Sun will be printing your picture one too many times. I’ve had that. So it’s not easy. It’s not an easy decision to make, but it’s better than the alternative. I know people who got death threats, and then wouldn’t leave the house and had security patrolling their house. You don’t want that.
“If you write ‘Everything in Its Right Place,’ do you think, ‘Yeah, I’ll write another one’? You can’t. I’ve tried.”

RS: You both have a history of leaving your comfort zones behind. That’s a pattern for you as artists — after you do something hugely successful, you say, “OK, I did that already. I’m not doing that again.” How do you avoid repeating yourself?

Yorke: I can’t, even if I wanted to. I couldn’t do it again. If you write “Everything in Its Right Place,” do you think, “Yeah, I’ll write another one of them”? It doesn’t make sense. You can’t. I’ve tried.

I think if you have something that’s very successful, there’s a lot of pressure to repeat that, which I’m sure you’ll probably feel, or you do feel sometimes. Or you will feel. It doesn’t go anywhere, because that’s like working to commission.
Styles: “Paint that again.”
Yorke: Yeah. It’s a commercial art form, so you’re always going to get people asking you to do that.

Styles: It’s an interesting cycle, I think. You make something that connects with people, because you’ve captured something about the human experience, whether it’s a vulnerability or a sensitivity that comes with being human. And then any kind of success around that thing makes it take on this life of its own. Then everything around you makes your experience incredibly not human.

Styles. Yeah. The goal is how you shut that out when you’re making stuff, so you can still be making music about the human experience. I’ve always thought if I was to make music about being in a studio, and touring, and all of the shiny things that come with that—
Yorke: Shiny for you, mate. It’s not shiny for everyone.
Styles: That’s definitely not interesting to me, so it can’t possibly be interesting to anyone else.

What I love about your work, for example, so many people look at you in this kind of godlike status — to still be someone who looks at it like, “This is the gritty part of life.” I think that’s what’s so impressive about your work — for people to revere you and to still be looking at what’s under the fingernails.

Yorke: I think the reason for that was having to learn quite a difficult lesson. Around Kid A, Amnesiac, before that, I really struggled every time I had to try to do something new. I was explaining it to myself while I was doing it, literally. It’s like a form of madness, and I couldn’t get out of it. I felt I needed to justify it somehow — not apologize, but justify it in an intellectual way.

The reason for that was I needed to get out of it. I needed to just get out of the studio, and I needed to just walk. I used to just walk on the cliffs in Cornwall, for example. And a lot of that was down to the fact that nobody cares, man. Nobody cares that it’s difficult. If you’re bummed out that it’s difficult, fucking stop. Go and do something else — go dancing. Also, later on, as you have kids, the choice to carry on doing this kind of work, you have to enjoy it. And the enjoyment comes from having to start again from scratch every time. Whatever you learn, you’ve got to unlearn.

Also, songwriting is very odd. Going to the Ivor Novello thing — I don’t hang out with songwriters, but apparently I am one. And you realize that songwriting is quite a naive thing. You can’t be savvy about it. You can work really hard on it — but the good stuff just happens, and you don’t know why. And you’ve got to be honest with yourself that you don’t know why. When stuff forms that you like, you just grab onto it and you don’t let go. “Pyramid Song” — I mean, it’s three chords over and over again, and the same lyric. How does that make sense? But you like it, and you’re not bothered about if anyone else likes it.
“The thing that excites me the most is when I start a record, I have no idea how it’s going to end up sounding.”
Styles: I’ve always wondered if that’s part of why the impostor syndrome that can come with that commercial success exists.

Styles: If you write in that way, it almost feels like you’re not responsible for it. So then if people are like, “Oh, you’ve made this thing and that means that you’re this,” there’s something in there that feels like, “Oh, I can’t take credit for it. It just happened to me.” Like you were saying, the best things tend to just happen. I’ve always found the things that I end up liking the most, or have been the most special things to me, are the ones where you write it, and then as you’re listening back, you’re learning something about yourself. You’re realizing that you’ve said something, rather than, “I’m going to sit down — I’m going to say this.”
Yorke. Yeah, and you might not realize. You might record it and track it and everything, and not realize until you’ve mastered it — and then you suddenly hear, “Oh, shit, that’s what I meant.”

But it’s not divine intervention or anything like that. You’ve got to show up. You have to learn to accept the months of impostor syndrome, where you’re like, “I don’t have anything to justify all this amazing equipment in my studio.” And then you’ll pick up your notebook, and there’ll be one line in it that sets you off. But the point is, you showed up. Because it’s really easy not to show up.

Styles: Someone once described it to me as like surfing, where you can practice getting up on the board. Sometimes there’s no waves. If a wave comes but you haven’t practiced enough, you’re not going to be able to surf it. When they happen, it’s the combination that you’ve practiced being able to capture it, and something is happening at the right time.
Yorke: Yeah, you’re ready enough. Or if I’m surfing, you’re not ready, ever. You’re on the rock going, “Fuck!”
Styles: I’ve had a big shift — I used to feel labor-focused about art in general. I felt like to justify it, I had to be in the studio months at a time.

Yorke: That’s your impostor syndrome speaking. I’m the same — sometimes it’s fun, but sometimes you’re doing it because you feel you should do it, because you need to stay ahead of the game. Or you need to keep proving that you are who you say you are, or other people say you are.

Styles: I feel like it’s a real line to ride with that. Because I still feel like I get it onstage sometimes. The sweet spot is where you’re relaxed, in that flow state where it feels like, “Oh, this feels really easy. It feels like it’s just happening, and this is great.” And then I click over to “Oh, it feels too easy. Am I not working hard enough?” When it feels most natural is when I think the show is at its best, but then I have this voice of “It shouldn’t be this easy.”

Yorke: That’s completely normal. The joke with Radiohead is always, like, we’ll have moments in the show like, “Oh, my God, we’re so great!” And exactly that moment, someone fucks up. Every time, without fail.
“I’m jealous of people who can just free flow onto a mic and put it out. All my hip-hop heroes freestyling.”

Styles: How different is it for you in terms of how much you enjoy making music with the band, versus making stuff by yourself? Do you like what the friction can make in that scenario? Or do you tend to enjoy, like, “Oh, I’m going to have this idea, and I’m going to just see this all the way through.” Because it’s both, I’m sure.

Yorke: It’s both. There’s a kind of mad history to that. It wasn’t until after Kid A that I remember quietly saying to Nigel [Godrich], “I’ve got all these things. I just want to do them on my own with you, because it doesn’t make sense to try and include anybody else.” Up until that point, it was a really alien concept.

We’ve known each other a mind-boggling number of years now. [Radiohead met in 1985.] We all know each other’s musical strengths and musical weaknesses. So you’re spending a lot of the time working around that. I mean, we haven’t worked. We haven’t been in the studio together for a long time, so I don’t know how it would actually feel now.

With the Smile, it’s totally different because Jonny [Greenwood] just generates ideas all the time. [Drummer Tom] Skinner works faster than any human being I’ve ever met and can respond to literally, as you probably know, anything you throw at him. I’m in the middle going, “All right, why don’t you guys record this, because I don’t understand what’s going on?” My favorite experiences in the studio are something that’s good, and I don’t understand why it’s good, but I pick up a mic and respond to it. I will listen back to it like, “I have no idea who that was. Is that us?” Yeah, that’s us. And you only get that when you have other people.
Styles: Do you find it more vulnerable to be putting out your own stuff?

Yorke: It’s all vulnerable. But at the same time, I don’t know about you, but if I’m finishing a record, if I can’t sit down and listen to it and be comfortable with it and happy with it, it’s not going out. So the vulnerable bit happens …
Styles: When you’re writing it?
Yorke: Yeah. When you’re trying to finish the fucking lyrics. That’s when it’s the worst. Words, right? How do you do words?

Styles: I think what I’ve always found so exciting is that I’ve never found the one method. It’s never been like, “I’ll write a poem, and then I put it to music.” The good stuff tends to come from a few weeks or a couple months of “Oh, I’ve got nothing. I don’t have anything. It’s all gone.” Then all of a sudden you write something and you’re like, “I really like this. I don’t know why.” And that comes in lots of different ways — I have a line, or I have a piano thing, or a melody that’s mumbled. I’m building a song around these three words that sound great over this thing.

Yorke: That is the correct process, in my opinion. If you’ve got a few words that you hang everything off, and you don’t understand why, then that’s the most exciting. Even though it’s painful, because then you have to spend weeks trying to fill in the blanks.

Styles: Sometimes, with some of the best stuff, I think it’s more difficult to be concise. I know I like a melody when I overwrite the song — I’ll write a bunch of verses, a bunch of lyrics. Then I think, “Oh, you take these three verses, take these lines, and make them one verse — it’s actually much more powerful in what it’s saying.” It’s better than explaining everything.
Yorke: Honestly, the thing I’m most jealous of will always be people who can just free flow onto a mic, and put it out. All my hip-hop heroes freestyling. I wish I had that brain.

Styles: I listened to a podcast you were on. You said you think of your vocal as one of the instruments in the song, and that’s how you tend to approach composition now. Is that something you noticed, when that changed for you? Because you say you don’t so much sit and write a song, like, “I’m going to sit here, and this is a song and this is how it goes” — you think of how it sits in the production. But obviously, if you go back to The Bends, for example, like “High and Dry,” that is a song.
Yorke: Yeah, a guy with an acoustic guitar. Singing his song. That particular one I wish I hadn’t [winces in pain], but there’s nothing wrong with that.

I don’t listen to a lot of singer-songwriters. I listen to a lot of mad old folk music, or I listen to film music, or I listen to electronic music. The banging away on the guitar thing is sometimes when it really speaks to me, but not a lot. I’m not quite sure why that is — probably because we grew up when there was a real renaissance of that, and The Bends was that.

But by the time we got to Kid A, I was excited about what else you could do with your voice, really. Jonny and Nigel set up this thing where Jonny’s playing the Martenot [a vintage electronic keyboard] and I’m just picking out random lines from my top hat. And that became the vocal. I’m not singing that at all — I’m literally speaking it.
“I remember watching the ‘Karma Police’ video thinking, ‘This is so brilliant.’ So much of your music has that weight.”

One of my favorite singers ever is Michael Stipe, who for the first two or three [R.E.M.] records didn’t even bother writing the lyrics. Or if he did, it was stream of consciousness. “I’m not going to make this explicit. I’m just the human sound in the middle of all these amazing jangling guitars.” Sometimes I don’t like the lyrics being the point. Sometimes it’s really exciting that there’s just this sound. [Yorke pulls out a notebook full of his questions.] I’ve got notes.
Styles: [In mock horror.] Homework!
Yorke: Do you travel with a laptop?
Styles: My laptop has been dead for about six years [laughs]. I don’t know where the charger is.
Yorke: We can help you with that. Where are your ideas? In your pocket?
Yorke: On your phone. You know your phone is basically a computer?
Styles: But just a phone. I use GarageBand a lot, and voice notes.
Yorke: Really? Wow. Fuck a duck.
Yorke: No, I mean in a way that’s good. I remember my MiniDisc. That was my best friend.
Styles: Yes, I remember being in primary school. [Both are laughing too hard to continue.]
Yorke: OK, let’s try it again.
Styles: The voice-note thing, I like something about it being its blankest version.
Yorke: Yeah. It’s the pencil drawing.
Styles: I think I like that. The thing that excites me the most is when I start a record, or before I’ve started something, and I have no idea how this is going to end up sounding.
Yorke: I’m surprised, because the last album [Kiss All the Time] very much sounds like it was developed in the studio. It doesn’t sound like it comes from voice notes.

Styles: That one was less from voice notes. There were a few moments — the orchestral thing [“Coming Up Roses”], or the piano songs. There’s a couple of much more straightforward songs. There’s probably three or four moments that are the most down the middle like that.
Yorke: So the rest are worked up in the studio?

Styles: A lot of it, yeah. Probably two-thirds of this one. I think it was just where I felt like I was at in my life, and the music that I was experiencing. I wanted to meld the parts of my life together. I’d started going out dancing a lot more. I really didn’t want it to be like, “Oh, I’m listening to this music — this is where I’m at,” but then I go in the studio and say, “Well, I have to make this sort of music instead.”
“Being open and exposed to people doesn’t bother me now. It used to.”
Yorke: I know that feeling. I know that feeling very well.
Styles: It was really like, “I’ve just come from this place. I want that beat to keep going. I want to be onstage feeling in the middle of it.” That was the kind of thing that informed the record.

Yorke: I think you did that. That’s my favorite part of the show, where you literally do that. There was a generosity to that, where I thought, “Yeah, that’s really cool. That is clearly someone who’s discovering this thing and wants to share it.” The honesty of it was very cool. I was really into that. I mean, it’s very difficult to take that kind of music into those places. It’s much easier to just make yourself totally deaf DJ’ing in a club in Berlin.
I was going to ask you: Where’s home? Because you have more than one.
Styles: I think when I’m in London, it feels the most like home. And I’m not from here.
Yorke: Where’s your stuff? Your important stuff?

Styles: London. Because I’ve lived in my house for 12 years or something. That’s the place where I feel like I’ve been through so many versions of myself, even in the same space. I feel like I really grew up in this house, in a big way. I remember moving in — right after my 19th birthday. It’s been through a lot of changes, but in there, in my kitchen, is the most like “This is where I live.”
Yorke: You’re probably pretty good, aren’t you?
Yorke: I’m fucking terrible.

Styles: To stay on you for a second, if I may. [Yorke snaps his fingers in disappointment.] I was curious about doing this interview, for example, or the Ivors thing — I think everyone communicated a surprise that you were willing to be celebrated. I’m curious about how your relationship with that has changed over time. In terms of someone who’s so innovative, how much of it has always been a need to reject any sort of nostalgia, to assure yourself that you’re moving forward?

To me, it feels like maybe just being in a happier place, to realize that you can do both: You can still innovate, and also allow people to celebrate things you’ve done, whether it be the Ivors, or touring and playing a deep selection from your catalog. To be able to play those songs and not feel “We’re living in the past right now,” but just be like, “We made something really beautiful. I’m going to play it, and that’s beautiful. And I can now also still be moving forward.”

Yorke: You’re answering this better than I can do. You’re right, that I’m in a slightly better place nowadays, but I’d be lying if I didn’t say that something like getting an Ivor Novello fellowship was not deeply confusing for me. I admire a lot of the people that they’ve given those awards to. Some of these people are my heroes. But I have a very, very strange relationship to … God, this is really hard to explain. I have a very strange relationship to that element of my work.
“Playing live is where you embrace that your music has connected with People”
Yorke: I find it hard to believe in it. The moving-forward thing, that’s what I believe in. That’s easy to believe in, because it’s new. I don’t have to explain it, so I’m happy.

After the [2025 reunion] Radiohead tour — even though in the middle of it, it was really fun — my response to it afterwards was to crash, like massively crash, in terms of self-confidence. It took me months.… It took me starting on my own record again two months later to go, “Oh, OK. I’m good now. I’m fine.” I just have a really odd relationship with it. And I’ve just grown used to that.

The Ivors, to be honest, your speech was great, because it was really honest and personal, and I could relate to it. Whereas when it feels like a business, and you’re part of a business, and the cameras are running … I don’t know, man. I got this legacy feeling about all of it.
Styles: Something I’m curious about: I wonder if it’s something that maybe happens when you have children, then keep creating.

Yorke: It’s really important they all integrate, and keep informing who you are. You probably saw Agnes and Noah at the Ivors. They were very emotional about it, and Dajana, my wife, was as well. I do it for them, because if they’re emotional about it, OK, that’s why I’m here. Because for me, I feel quite numb about it.

One of the things I’m most proud of is, some of the attitude that I have has rubbed off on [Agnes and Noah] as they grow up. I can see they have that kind of attitude in what they’re doing. Quite fearless about being creative, and quite open. Not embarrassed. Because I mean, obviously, when your kid’s a teenager, they’re like, “Oh, God, my father’s blah, blah, blah.” But now it’s really nice. It’s a good thing. I feel super lucky about that, because it wasn’t easy, for a long time.

Styles: The “Karma Police” video — I remember watching that and thinking, “Oh, this is so brilliant.” I feel like so much of your music has that weight where you just remember hearing it. It’s so inspiring just to see someone be so consistently great, in so many different ways. I’ve always really been drawn to stuff like “Codex” or “True Love Waits.” “Everything in Its Right Place” is it for me.

Yorke: “Everything in Its Right Place” was my response to not being able to write. We had an empty house. We had a grand piano, and we had a mattress. And that’s the first thing I did when we moved into this house. I’d felt lost since the OK Computer thing. It was like a mantra. I wasn’t thinking, “Oh, I’m writing a song.” I was really enjoying playing piano in this empty house; I just had one CD, [minimalist composer] Arvo Pärt, and that’s it. It was during the winter, there were storms all the time, and it was so great — playing this riff over and over and over again to make myself feel better.
RS: Harry, you just finished your massive run at Wembley Stadium, and on the final night, people were so moved to see you in tears. For both of you, what’s it like to get emotional onstage?

Styles: For me, so much of the studio experience of making something is almost trying to block out the fact anyone’s going to listen to it. You have to be “What do I want to listen to at this time in my life? What is it that I feel like I want to do, say, make?” The fact people are going to hear it — that realization happens later. Playing live is the part where you’re embracing that people listen to it, that it’s connected with people.

The kind of emotion that happened at the end of the London shows — I think it was a realization that these shows felt like a culmination of so many people’s support. I felt supported, in a way that’s more than like, “We’re here because we want to hear this song that you’ve done.” It just felt like, “We’re here because we believe in what you’re doing.” That’s why I found it so emotional.

Yorke: Also, you have to give a lot of yourself, and that makes you very … what’s the word? Open. You’re exposed to all these people. It doesn’t bother me now. It did, it used to — it doesn’t bother me any more. But it makes you very open.

Styles: A lot of the time, when you’re making stuff, you’re trying to reject what’s coming back at you, to remain in a beginner’s mind. You’re always trying to get back to a sense of starting again. Those moments where you let go and open up and allow it all to come in, and you get to feel that — it’s a wave of something that you don’t live with every day.

Yorke: When we did the first Radiohead show, in Madrid last year, we did this thing where we had to walk through the audience. Never done that before. Then we had to stand on the stage getting prepped before we went up. It was the first time we did that [going onstage together], after I don’t know how many years. All of us, the whole band, were like, “OK, keep it together. Keep it together.” Because I wanted to burst into tears, and we hadn’t even played a note. I hadn’t been exposed to whatever that was for so long, and to walk through the middle of it … I mean, all of us, we were like, “Holy shit. Holy shit.”
Styles: Which brings us back to walking — the artist’s perspective, where we began. There’s the bow. There’s the seal.

Styling by HARRY LAMBERT at BRYANT ARTISTS. Hair by MALCOLM EDWARDS at LGA MANAGEMENT. Makeup by NIAMH QUINN at LGA MANAGEMENT. Set Design by PATIENCE HARDING. Production by FARAGO PROJECTS. Lighting Director: KAI NARINS. Photo Assistance: GEORGE HUTTON and BENEDICT MOORE. Digital Technician: GILES SMITH. Styling Assistance: NAOMI PHILLIPS and ELLA BACON.  Set Design Assistance: MIRANDA LATIMER, EDDIE AMOS, and JACK SHORT. Video Interview Director of Photography: NICK CARTER. Video Interview Camera Operators: STEPHAN KNIGHT and ISSEY RIDER. Video Interview Gaffer: JACK GOULD. Video Interview Camera and Lighting Assistant: TOM WOOD. Video Interview Sound Operator: JAVIER CARLES. Video Interview Production Assistant: ALCIA WOODS. Photographed and filmed at BIG SKY.

YORKE: Artist’s own clothing.

items.title: The 76 Best Albums of 1976
items.description: The year was 1976. Everything was weird — but especially the music. Everyone walked around saying, “Dy-no-mite!” or “Up your nose with a rubber hose.” Jimmy Carter became the first president to hang out with the Allman Brothers. The Apple computer and VHS play
items.author: Jon Dolan; Angie Martoccio; Rob Sheffield
paragraphs: The year was 1976. Everything was weird — but especially the music. Everyone walked around saying, “Dy-no-mite!” or “Up your nose with a rubber hose.” Jimmy Carter became the first president to hang out with the Allman Brothers. The Apple computer and VHS player were invented. So was The Muppet Show. The Farrah Fawcett poster was everywhere. The radio was full of Stevie Wonder and Kiss. On Saturday Night Live, Lorne Michaels offered the Beatles $3,000 to reunite. A few months later, George Harrison showed up to collect. It was that kind of year.

You could go to the movies and see Sly Stallone in Rocky, Robert De Niro in Taxi Driver, and Sissy Spacek in Carrie. (Blood had a big year.) Or you could sit around the house, get high, and watch the tube for The Jeffersons, Charlie’s Angels, What’s Happening!!, Family Feud, Good Times, or Welcome Back, Kotter. It was a great baseball summer, thanks to The Bad News Bears and Rolling Stone cover star Mark “The Bird” Fidrych. Richard Pryor was dating Pam Grier. Everyone was workin’ on their night moves.

But nothing was weirder — or cooler — than the music. So let’s break it down, with our celebration of the 76 best albums of 1976. Wonder made everybody’s fave with Songs in the Key of Life. New sounds were rising up, from Jamaican dub to CBGB punk, from outlaw country to stoner rock. The Band played their farewell Last Waltz show on Thanksgiving. Frampton came alive. P-Funk met Dr. Funkenstein. It was the Bicentennial summer immortalized in Dazed and Confused. Rush traveled to 2112. The Eagles checked into the Hotel California, and last we heard, they’re still arguing with the front desk.

It was a glorious year for one-hit wonders on the radio — Number One hits included “Disco Duck” (feathers in the club), “Play That Funky Music” (“white booooy”), “A Fifth of Beethoven” (classical disco), “Convoy” (truckers on CB radio), or “Afternoon Delight” (don’t aaaask). But it’s the classic albums we’re toasting right now. Our list has disco, prog, soul, folk, metal, Chicago blues, Brazilian samba, New Orleans funk. We’ve got classic debuts from the Ramones, Boston, Blondie, and the Runaways. We’ve got singer-songwriter gems from Joni Mitchell, Jackson Browne, Bob Dylan, Al Green, and Warren Zevon.
But the one thing all these albums have in common? They still sound dy-no-mite 50 years after they came out. So here’s to the Spirit of ’76. Don’t fear the reaper, people, and have a nice day.

- Hall & Oates, ‘Bigger Than Both of Us’ Welcome to 1976, the kind of year where the hottest boy-boy duo in pop history could introduce themselves with the question “Do you believe in hot cars, leather bars, and movie stars?” Philly dogs Daryl Hall and John Oates hit the spotlight with their breakthrough album, Bigger Than Both of Us, and their first Number One smash, “Rich Girl.” It also has the awesome Me Decade pep talk “Do What You Want, Be What You Are,” where Daryl sings the wise words, “The strong give up and move on/While the weak give up and stay.” “John and I have never been lovers,” Daryl confided to Rolling Stone. “He’s not my type. Too dark and short.” But 50 years later, they’re still on top of … [touches earpiece] Wait, seriously? They broke up? Why? Get it together, you two! But Bigger is an archetypal 1976 pop classic — and the perfect place to start this party. —Rob Sheffield

- James Brown, ‘Get Up Offa That Thing’ In 1976, the Godfather of Soul was starting to key into the disco sounds of acts like Earth, Wind & Fire and the Ohio Players. But he wasn’t interested in their lavish productions, and his sound stayed as raw as ever. His second LP of three he’d released in 1976 opens with the in-the-red shriek that kicks off its title track, a nine-minute jam inspired by a audience members at a show in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, that stayed seated during Brown’s set. Their lameness is our lucky break — the song is one of his last true classics. Get Up Offa That Thing also has “I Refuse to Lose,” an empowerment anthem for the doldrums of the stagflation-plagued Seventies, and the good-footin’ workouts “Can’t Take It With You” and “This Feeling.” —Jon Dolan

- Al Stewart, ‘Year of the Cat’ Scottish singer-songwriter Al Stewart started out on the London folk scene of the mid-Sixties, briefly sharing a flat with another unknown guy on the scene named Paul Simon.
