By the mid-1970s, he was riding the soft-rock wave, with a yen for literary lyrics, meticulous arrangements, and lithe, airy guitar work. Stewart had his biggest success with his seventh album, Year of the Cat. “On the Border” floats an evocation of anti-colonial struggle in on a sea-breeze melody; on “Flying Sorcery,” planes in a fog are a metaphor for doomed lovers; “Broadway Hotel” is about a lonely woman having an affair with a hotel-room service attendant. It all flows into the hit title track, a Casablanca-inspired intrigue about a man on an exotic vacation who falls for a mysterious patchouli-scented woman and gets his travel itinerary upended and his life turned upside down. —J.D.

- Loretta Lynn, ‘When the Tingle Becomes a Chill’ By the time Loretta Lynn’s 27th solo album hit shelves, she’d already spent the past few years releasing songs that redefined how a woman in country music was able to sing about sexuality and desire (“The Pill,” “Rated X”). Made at producer Owen Bradley’s barn in Mount Juliet, Tennessee, When the Tingle Becomes a Chill boasted a title track, written by Lola Jean Dillon, that charted what happens when the spark leaves a relationship and the bedroom. (“The body performs, but the soul has no will.” Ouch.) Lynn also offered a gloriously glossy version of Glen Campbell’s hit “Rhinestone Cowboy,” the moody misdirection of “Red, White and Blue,” and “All I Want From You (Is Away),” which showcased her snappy sonic sense of humor. —Marissa R. Moss
- Kiss, ‘Rock and Roll Over’

Following the conceptual stretch of their other 1976 album, Destroyer (see Number 25), Kiss got back to straight-ahead hard rock on their fifth studio LP, hailed by some fans as their finest release. It was their first time in the studio with super-reliable producer Eddie Kramer, who’d mixed their breakthrough 1975 live album Alive!, and the sound is much punchier than their sometimes murky-sounding earlier records. “I Want You” starts off as sensitive acoustic schlock but quickly turns into irresistibly swaggering pop metal, and the solid songs keep on coming, from “Take Me” to “Calling Dr. Love” to “Hard Luck Women,” originally written for Rod Stewart and containing a spot-on Rod impression on vocals from drummer Peter Criss. —J.D.

- Burning Spear, ‘Garvey’s Ghost’ Garvey’s Ghost was the pioneering dub version of Burning Spear’s radical reggae statement, Marcus Garvey. Winston Rodney was on a tear in 1976 — he also released Man in the Hills. Garvey’s Ghost was mixed in London, but the goal was taking dub somewhere new sonically. “Now you get lots of artificial dub effects in Jamaica,” producer Jack Ruby explained in Sounds, “but I used none with this record, not to get in the way of the music.” The spectral grooves cast a spell by zoning in on individual instruments, especially Leroy “Horsemouth” Wallace’s drums, for an eerie sense of dread. “Jamaican surf music,” Greil Marcus called it. “Which is to say that slave ships are visible on the horizon.” —R.S.

- KC and the Sunshine Band, ‘Part 3’ A disco celebration, with a great big rainbow on the cover. On Part 3, KC and the Sunshine Band offer a tripartite plan for spiritual unity: (1) Shake shake shake, (2) Shake shake shake, (3) Shake your booty. Then start back at the top. The Miami funkateers, led by Harry Wayne Casey and Richard Finch, felt like strutting their stuff after their 1975 self-titled smash. So they upped the ante, refining disco bliss into pure tantric repetition: “Shake Shake Shake (Shake Your Booty),” “I’m Your Boogie Man,” “I Like to Do It,” and, best of all, “Keep It Coming Love.” KC and the Sunshine Band appeared on Dolly Parton’s variety show in December 1976: You haven’t lived till you’ve seen Dolly jam with them on “That’s the Way I Like It.” —R.S.

- Merle Haggard, ‘My Love Affair With Trains’ On Merle Haggard’s 20th album, My Love Affair With Trains, the slow death of the black iron horse is a metaphor for the loss of a way of life and a vision of America itself. On the Dolly Parton penned title track, Merle plays a settled down family man whose hobo blood boils every time he hears that lonesome whistle blow. “Here Comes the Freedom Train” chugs through our nation’s history with democratic progress pumping the engine and heroes from Washington to Lincoln to MLK as conductors. The heart of the album is in the nostalgia of “Where Have All the Hobos Gone” and “No More Trains to Ride,” songs that, in Hag’s words, “may make you a little bit sad when you realize what we’re leaving behind.” —J.D.

It was a golden age for funk upstarts, and Foxy were quintessential class-of-’76 disco weirdos. After KC and the Sunshine Band became stars, Foxy took over as the new house band at the crucial Miami indie-dance label T.K. Records, with Cuban-born bandleader Ish Ledesma. Their 1976 debut is an underground funk cult item, trashy and proud, with club hits like “Get Off Your Aahh and Dance,” an orgiastic conga groove where even the flutes sound like they’re panting lasciviously. Foxy went Top 40 with their 1978 hit “Get Off,” a perv-disco banger that spawned sequels like “RRRRRock.” (Take that, Charli XCX.) Ledesma moved on to a strange career writing and producing for one-hit wonders, like Oxo’s 1983 pop hit “Whirly Girl” and Company B’s 1987 freestyle classic “Fascinated.” —R.S.

- Genesis, ‘Wind & Wuthering’ Genesis kick-started 1976 by dropping their first post-Peter Gabriel LP, A Trick of the Tail (See Number 36), toured North America and Europe, and then headed right back into the studio to craft a follow-up, which they got into stores just a couple of weeks before 1977. Phil Collins was the face and voice of the band at this point, and still had his old job as drummer, but he hadn’t come into his own yet as a songwriter. This created space for guitarist-bassist Mike Rutherford to write the ballad “Your Own Special Way,” keyboardist Tony Banks to compose the 10-minute prog epic “One for the Vine,” and for everyone to come together on the soaring instrumental suite “Unquiet Slumbers for the Sleepers/In That Quiet Earth.” Guitarist Steve Hackett’s departure after this album solidified the three-man lineup that would go on to very big things in the Eighties. —Andy Greene

- George Harrison, ‘Thirty Three & 1/3’ The Beatles were riding a massive resurgence in 1976, years after they broke up — they shocked the industry with the blockbuster hit anthology Rock & Roll Music, while “Got to Get You Into My Life” became a Top 10 smash a decade after it was released. But George Harrison was coming out of a few hard years, with his voice, health, and career in rough shape. Fortunately, the Quiet One came back strong on Thirty Three & 1/3, revitalized by his new love Olivia Arias Harrison, with his tributes “Beautiful Girl” and “Learning How to Love You.” It also has one of his most soulful love songs ever: “Pure Smokey,” where he thanks the Lord for giving the world the genius of Smokey Robinson, always one of the Fabs’ biggest heroes. “Pure Smokey” was never a hit, but it’s Harrison at his most humane and lovable. —R.S.

- Bob Seger, ‘Live Bullet’ Much like it did with Cheap Trick, Kiss, and Peter Frampton, it took a live album to break Bob Seger. In his case, it followed a decade of grueling roadwork, and an astounding eight flop albums. But these lean years turned Seger & the Silver Bullet Band into a ferocious live band, and gave them a repertoire of songs like “Turn the Page,” “Travelin’ Man,” “Beautiful Loser,” “Heavy Music,” and “Katmandu” that crushed every time they went onstage. And once the public finally heard this live album taped across two nights at Detroit’s Cobo Hall in September 1976, Seger finally found the audience he long deserved. Many studio albums followed, and a handful of live ones, but none of them quite captured the magic of this one. It’s an artist right on the cusp of superstardom with a lot to prove. There’s simply no way to recreate that. —A.G.
- Rod Stewart, ‘A Night on the Town’

The cover of Rod Stewart’s seventh album, based on Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s painting Bal du moulin de la Galette, gives you a clue to its grand ambition. “Tonight’s the Night” pushed the envelope for suggestive radio ballads with the line “Spread your wings and let me come inside.” He closes Side One with the Dylanesque story song “The Killing of Georgie (Part I and II),” about a gay friend who gets killed by a street gang in New York. The album’s choice of covers is exquisite — a rollicking version of Hank Thompson’s honky-tonk classic “The Wild Side of Life,” a bar-band rip through Manfred Mann’s Sixties sunshine-pop tune “Pretty Flamingo,” and sensitive readings of Cat Stevens’ “The First Cut Is the Deepest” and “Trade Winds,” a politically minded ballad originally recorded by Roberta Flack for her landmark debut, First Take. —J.D.

- George Jones, ‘Alone Again’ A year after his divorce from Tammy Wynette, which she credited to “his nippin’,” the country icon opened Alone Again with “A Drunk Can’t Be a Man,” a devastating portrayal of alcoholic paralysis. The existential gut punches continue with “Ain’t Nobody Gonna Miss Me” and “Stand on My Own Two Knees.” Alone Again is one of the best albums Jones made during his historic run with producer Billy Sherrill, all heartbreaking ballads full of sad newly-single-guy angst and longing for anyone to take the pain away. The scorched-earth mood is interrupted by one upbeat novelty tune, “Her Name Is,” where Jones imagines the woman of his future with an electric clavinet chiming in every time he wants to say her name because he hasn’t found her yet and it doesn’t sound like she’s going to show up any time soon. —J.D.

- Bryan Ferry, ‘Let’s Stick Together’ Bryan Ferry, a man of wealth and taste, was also a man without a band on Let’s Stick Together. Roxy Music split up after their 1975 gem Siren and would take a few years to reunite, though almost everyone in Roxy played on Ferry’s next solo album. Let’s Stick Together is a strange but seductive collage, with the Divine Bryan embracing his new vocation as the ultimate art-rock lounge crooner. He interprets blues standards and pop ballads from the past, but also a batch of Roxy Music songs, giving them a jazzy new groove. Roxy played “Casanova” as a guitar screamer, but here it’s a smoldering torch song, as Ferry dismantles his own Don Juan image. The swinging title tune’s video stars a temptress in a tiger-stripe dress — played by Ferry’s paramour Jerry Hall. Bonus points for his brief fling with facial hair — nobody rocks a louche Seventies mustache like Bryan. —R.S.

- Lynyrd Skynyrd, ‘One More From the Road’ Lynyrd Skynyrd were one of the era’s great road bands, so thank the rock gods these Southern boys got to leave a definitive live testament, just a year before the fatal plane crash. One More From the Road is a blowout from the Fox Theatre in Hot’lanta. Ronnie Van Zandt sang barefoot — as he says in Cameron Crowe’s famous liner notes, “I love to feel that stage burn.” But the grease hits the skillet at the end of the night, when Ronnie asks the crowd one final question: “What song is it you wanna hear?” Shockingly, everyone in the 404 area code screams, “Freeee Birrrrrrd!” This album is why annoying people still yell “Free Bird,” a gag that started as soon as the album dropped. As Rolling Stone’s Greil Marcus noted in his review of the Band’s Last Waltz concert that Thanksgiving, “Damned if somebody didn’t yell for ‘Free Bird.’” —R.S.
- Queen, ‘A Day at the Races’

As its title suggests, A Day at the Races is a kind of sequel to Queen’s 1975 breakthrough, A Night at the Opera. Songs like “The Millionaire Waltz” and “Teo Torriatte (Let Us Cling Together)” reach for the Galileo grandeur of “Bohemian Rhapsody” without the same magnifico results, and there isn’t a standout pop hit like “Your My Best Friend.” Still, there are great moments here: “Tie Your Mother Down,” written by guitarist Brian May back in the band’s pre-Queen days, is pop-metal thunder. May sings lead on “Long Away,” a lovely light-touch moment of Beatles/Beach Boys prettiness. The peak is “Somebody to Love,” with one of Freddie Mercury’s toughest, realest heart-hungry vocals, an Olympian solo from May, and a mountainous build-up toward a grand finale — killer Queen indeed. —J.D.

- Son Seals, ‘Midnight Son’ A native of Osceola, Arkansas, where he grew up playing in his father’s juke joint, blues-guitar great Son Seals moved to Chicago and broke out with his excellent second album, Midnight Son, widely regarded as one of the 1970s best blues LPs. Unlike most upstart bluesman, he didn’t fill out his records with covers, giving Midnight Son a potent coherence. Backed by a sharp horn section, Seals’ playing on songs like “I Believe,” “Telephone Angel,” and the searing seven-minute closing track, “Going Back Home,” is explosive and precise, gritty and piercing, fitting the raw intensity of his singing, whether he’s lamenting the crummy Windy City job market or threatening to get his rod to settle a romantic situation. —J.D.

- Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, ‘Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers’ Don’t let the leather jacket and bullets on the album cover fool you: Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers were not a punk band. “Call me a punk and I’ll cut you,” he kindly told the press. And while it was their debut, they were hardly a new band, having spent years on the road as Mudcrutch to little commercial success. The record showcased not just how seasoned they were as a band, but how much potential they had. Of the 10 tracks, two would become future hits: “Breakdown” and “American Girl,” the latter the best song of their career, fittingly recorded on the Fourth of July. How’s that for a little punk? —Angie Martoccio

- Wings, ’At the Speed of Sound’ Paul McCartney and Wings spent the summer at Number One with At the Speed of Sound, a concept album about filling the world with silly love songs. (And what’s wrong with that? We’d like to know.) The band at Number Two? The Beatles, with their surprise posthumous hit Rock & Roll Music. Speed of Sound has awesome lonely-yachts-club grooves like “She’s My Baby,” plus Linda McCartney’s first (and last) lead vocal, “Cook of the House.” Then there’s “Let ’Em In,” one of the most stoned-sounding Top 10 hits in history, about being too catatonically zonked in your bean-bag chair to get up and answer the damn door. That trombone solo alone was enough to get 1970s hippies reaching for the Visine. Speed of Sound remains influential — you can hear it all over Harry’s House, from Wings superfan Harry Styles. (The fact that Paul immediately added “Let ‘Em In” to his set list proved he’s a “Grapejuice” girlie.) —R.S.

- Dr. Buzzard’s Original Savannah Band, ‘Dr. Buzzard’s Original Savannah Band’ One of the most out-there and inventive products of the disco era, Dr. Buzzard’s Original Savannah Band was the vision of Stony Browder Jr. and his brother Thomas Browder (who adopted the stage name August Darnell), a band of Black and Latino musicians coming out of the Bronx who dressed like 1940s hepcats, sang in four languages, and reimagined the Big Band refinement of Cab Calloway for the anything-goes Seventies club scene. Highlighted by the hit “Cherchez La Femme” (a plush showcase for singer Cory Daye), the kids-choir urban pastoral “Sunflower,” and the swing banger “I’ll Play the Fool,” this joyously sophisticated album plays like the soundtrack to a night out in heaven. —J.D.

- The J. Geils Band, ‘Blow Your Face Out’ You were nobody in the 1970s rock hustle until you made a live album — but it was real boss behavior to crank out two of them. The J. Geils Band’s Blow Your Face Out was a frenzy of double-live gonzo, just three years after Live Full House, yet a whole different kind of fire-breathing blues-rock house party. The Geils gang raise hell onstage in Detroit and Boston, two quintessential live-album towns, with a gloriously scruffy desecration of the Motown classic “Where Did Our Love Go,” as Magic Dick honks his Hohner. But the peak is “Musta Got Lost,” with Peter Wolf’s epic intro monologue, a madman preacher testifying, “This is a song about L-O-V-E!” He riffs on fairy tales (“What’s the name of that chick with the long hair?” “Rapunzel!”) and proclaims himself the “Woofa Goofa with the green teeth.” —R.S.
- Bunny Wailer, ‘Blackheart Man’

Bunny Livingston co-founded the Wailers alongside Bob Marley and Peter Tosh, and contributed  spiritual stunners “Pass It On” and “Hellujuah Time” to 1974’s Burnin’, his last album with the group. His debut is a musically multifaceted statement of his Rastafarian ideals. Rather than sweeping Marley-size  anthems, he goes for the subtlety of his down-to-earth singing, sticky grooves and melodies, and ingenious musical flourishes, such as the Jew’s harp on the incredible title track, the laid-back sax on “Bide Up,” and the utopian synth on “Dream Land.” Bunny balances urgent political messages and playful escapism (see “Fig Tree,” about sitting in one), and he can sound equally deep whether he’s stoking revolution, prophesying armageddon, or simply advising “drink water children.” —J.D.
- Boz Scaggs, ‘Silk Degrees’

John Travolta said that when he was working on his moves for Saturday Night Fever he was “dancing to Stevie Wonder and Boz Scaggs.” Everybody in America was in 1976. Boz Scaggs’ multiplatinum hit Silk Degrees had the perfect mix of Southern rock, soul, and disco, sculpted with A-list L.A. session guys like keyboard player David Paich and drummer Jeff Porcaro. Ohio-born, Texas-raised Scaggs was a veteran with a long track record, and he lent a subtle old-soul warmth to the sublime slickness of “Lido Shuffle” and “Lowdown,” as well as the Mott the Hoople swagger of “Jump Street,” the reggae-tinged “Love Me Tomorrow,” and the New Orleans R&B bounce of “What Do You Want the Girl to Do.” —J.D.

- Blue Öyster Cult, ‘Agents of Fortune’ In the summer of 1976, Patti Smith spoke about why she thought Blue Öyster Cult’s new album was gaining traction. “After six years together, they finally decided to let each guy emerge personally,” she said. “They wanted to gamble, like the cover shot, to take risks, shoot for the stars.” Agents of Fortune did exactly that, making it the first — and only — Cult album to feature each member on lead vocals. Smith, who was dating guitarist-keyboardist Allen Lanier, also took the reins on the gloomy rocker “The Revenge of Vera Gemini.” And, oh yeah, the record also contains their biggest hit, “(Don’t Fear) the Reaper,” Buck Dharma’s haunting rock & roll odyssey about eternal love, the inevitability of death, and the importance of using the cowbell. “Reaper,” Laurie Strode’s toking song of choice, inspired Stephen King to write The Stand and one of the best SNL sketches in history. Shooting for the stars, indeed. —A.M.

- Marvin Gaye, ‘I Want You’ Three years after Let’s Get It On, Gaye linked up with co-writer and producer Leon Ware for his most sensual album yet, inspired by his second wife, Janis Hunter. “The time when we did I Want You had to be the most happy time in Marvin’s life,” Ware recalled. “Because he was freshly in love, and the album exhibits that atmosphere.” Come for the sugary funk of “Come Live With Me Angel,” stay for the sexy conga-filled “Soon I’ll Be Loving You Again” and various “I Want You” jams. “When I’m told by different people all over the world how many babies that album has made,” Ware said, “the record stands so high in my life.” —A.M.

- Led Zeppelin, ‘Presence’ For Robert Plant, Led Zeppelin’s seventh album was about pure survival. “There won’t be another album like it, put it like that,” he told us. “It was a cry from the depths, the only thing that we could do.” Led Zeppelin were hardly in a good place when they recorded Presence. Following their 1975 masterpiece Physical Graffiti, a frightening car crash on the Greek island of Rhodes left Plant unable to walk. Shows were canceled, and they headed into the studio to record new material. Besides the opening 10-minute epic “Achilles Last Stand,” several of the tracks remain underappreciated, like the jaunty “Hots on for Nowhere” and the searing “Tea for One,” both of which the band never performed live. “Presence was pure anxiety and emotion,” Jimmy Page said. “We didn’t know if we’d ever be able to play in the same way again. It might have been a very dramatic change, if the worst had happened to Robert. Presence is our best in terms of uninterrupted emotion.” —A.M.

- Max Romeo & the Upsetters, ‘War Ina Babylon’ The first salvo in Lee “Scratch” Perry’s “holy trinity” of dub records birthed at his mythical Black Ark studio, War ina Babylon found the producer merging Max Romeo’s commercially viable roots-reggae stylings with the dark, dense grooves of the Upsetters. Romeo, who previously sang one of reggae’s earliest international hits with 1968’s “Wet Dream,” instead focused on his burgeoning political consciousness at the time on the title track and opener, “One Step Forward.” War Ina Babylon also boasts what remains Romeo’s signature song, “Chase the Devil,” a track that Romeo himself tried to cut from the album before Perry intervened. —Daniel Kreps

- Michael Hurley, the Unholy Modal Rounders, Jeffrey Fredericks & the Clamtones, ‘Have Moicy!’ Few albums have aged as well as Have Moicy!, the ragtag folk-supergroup opus from a collection of musicians (Peter Stampfel, Michal Hurley, Jeffrey Frederick, and Paul Presti, to name just a few). The album, per the critic Robert Christgau, “renewe[ed] the concept of American folk music as a bizarre apotheosis of the post-hippie estate.” To say it’s become an influential cult classic is an understatement: The album has gone on to spin its tendrils into just about every corner of anything on the anti/freak-folk-outsider roots-indie-singer-songwriter spectrum in the 50 years since its release, resulting in covers by everyone from Yo La Tengo to Cass McCombs to JP Harris. —Jonathan Bernstein

- The Runaways, ‘The Runaways’ The Runaways were put together by sleazy L.A. rock mogul Kim Fowley as a teenage all-girl novelty band, but they broke through that cliché and immediately had their own identity and sound — “the Queens of Noise, the answer to your dreams.” The Runaways become pathfinding feminist heroes, playing hard rock with punk’s spirit and energy on fantastic songs like “American Nights,” “Thunder,” a hot-wired version of Lou Reed’s “Rock N Roll,” and the iconic album opener “Cherry Bomb,” later covered by 1990s riot grrrls Bratmobile. Along with putting out this killer debut, the Runaways were the launching pad for the legendary careers of guitarists Joan Jett and Lita Ford. —J.D.
- Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Jessi Colter, and Tompall Glaser, ‘Wanted! The Outlaws’

The first country-music album to ever be certified platinum was more of a compilation package meant to exploit the popularity of the outlaw-country trend than a proper album. Even so, the collection of songs, many of them previously released, by Willie Nelson, Waylon Jennings, Jessi Colter, and Tompall Glaser remains a touchstone within the genre. The Willie and Waylon entries — Jennings’ “Honky Tonk Heroes,” Nelson’s “Me and Paul,” and their duet “Good Hearted Woman” — are the most widely known, but some of Wanted!’s best and most lasting moments come from the voice of Colter, whom Jennings married in 1969. Her “I’m Looking for Blue Eyes,” one of the LP’s “new” songs, is a stunner. —Joseph Hudak

- Rose Royce, ‘Car Wash’ Rose Royce were R&B funk legends from L.A., led by the heavenly voice of Gwen Dickey. Car Wash was officially the soundtrack to the funky comedy flick, one of the best movies either Richard Pryor or George Carlin ever acted in. Director Michael Schultz had the soundtrack recorded before filming started, so the actors at the car wash would hear the same music as the audience. Motown legend Norman Whitfield produced and wrote, with the social-realist disco classic “Car Wash” (“This ain’t no place to be if you planned on being a star”) and the anti-capitalist funk chant “Put Your Money Where Your Mouth Is.” But Dickey’s voice makes the ballads irresistible — “I’m Going Down” and “I Wanna Get Next to You” have been classics ever since. —R.S.
- The Stills-Young Band, ‘Long May You Run’

“I don’t think there’s anybody who writes like Neil,” Emmylou Harris once said. “His songs are an odd combination of being straightforward and elusive at the same time.” It’s an astute description for a song like “Long May You Run,” the most romantic song anyone has ever written about a hearse. Nostalgic for their Buffalo Springfield days, Young linked up with Stephen Stills for a joint album down in Miami, yielding underrated Young gems like “Midnight on the Bay” and “Fontainebleau” (after the luxury hotel on Miami Beach). That unique combo of straightforwardness and elusiveness leaked outside of the music, as well. Graham Nash and David Crosby recorded backing vocals on the tracks, but Young ended up removing them. Then he briefly toured with Stills, only to abandon ship and leave a note. “Dear Stephen, funny how some things that start spontaneously end that way,” it read. “Eat a peach, Neil.” As Harris said, nobody writes quite like him. —A.M.
- Bob Marley, ‘Rastaman Vibration’

Marley’s gift at smuggling radical politics in a smooth package was on prime display on his eight album, his first to make the Top 10 in America. He kicks it off with two statements of optimism, “Positive Vibration” and “Roots, Rock, Reggae,” setti

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: The Homecoming Committee
items.description: You know that thing where you go off to war where there’s a high likelihood you’re going to die, and then your own father betrays you to join the enemy, and then you have to infiltrate an English prison, kill multiple people, save your friend from drowning whi
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: You know that thing where you go off to war where there’s a high likelihood you’re going to die, and then your own father betrays you to join the enemy, and then you have to infiltrate an English prison, kill multiple people, save your friend from drowning while watching another guy drown in front of you, and then you return to safety just to be informed of the worst news of your life? Yeah, that’s what happened to Brian Fraser. My greatest wish for this man is that he finds two hours to go stare at a wall in a dark room and dissociate for a while. He’s earned it.

But Brian does not get to dissociate! The man doesn’t even get to bathe, and you know he smells awful. He and Murtagh deliver Dougal back to Castle Leoch, and as a thank-you for saving their brother and the War Chieftain’s life, all Brian wants is to go see Ellen. Of course, when he does find Ellen, she’s in bed crying and still in pain. This whole scene is heartbreaking. From Ellen telling Brian that she hoped for a girl and prays she is with Janet now, to her breaking the news that it was Brian’s father who did this to her and the doctor doesn’t think she’ll ever be able to have children, to her assuming if she can’t have kids, Brian won’t want to be with her anymore. The depths of despair on this show know no bounds.

And while I get Ellen’s insecurity about her (possible) infertility — I mean, her brother is in the next room freely uttering phrases like “a woman with no womb is worth nothing at all,” fucking Colum — we (and Ellen) also know that Brian and Arch Bug are constantly duking it out for biggest wife guy on Blood of My Blood. He would never leave her. Well, emotionally speaking. Literally speaking, he does immediately tell her that he loves her always and then walks out the door. But guys, don’t worry, he’s just running off to kill his dad. Oh, wait, on second thought, maybe do worry a little bit.

Brian, understandably, wants Lovat to die. In a truly boss move, he walks into Castle Leathers, slams Balloch’s face into a table, and asks, “Do I have your attention, Father?” I wish Ellen was there to see it because it is honestly very hot. Lovat doesn’t try to deny anything and instead tells his son quite forthrightly that he did it because of the prophecy. He wants that baby to be king, so he had to make him the last of his bloodline. Brian’s disgusted by that, but it’s not until Lovat calls Ellen a “barren MacKenzie whore” that he takes his father by the throat and slams him against a wall. He thinks about cutting off Lovat’s dick, which would do a lot of people a favor, but then Julia and Davina arrive to beg Brian not to kill Lovat. If he does, he’ll be hanged. Think of Ellen, they tell him. And so he does. Instead of revenge, Brian demands a piece of land and the promise that Lovat will never set foot on it. If Lovat ever touches Ellen again, Brian will not hesitate to kill him. And then he’s gone.

Brian returns to Ellen safe and sound, and he hands her a rock from the bridge where they had their first meeting — “Our bridge,” he says — and tells her that this stone will be the hearthstone that he builds their home around. My heart wishes them peace and joy in this new home even though my head knows it is impossible on a show like Blood of My Blood.

If that was Brian’s welcome home from Sheriffmuir, you should hear about Dougal’s. Holy hell, could Colum be any angrier with his brother? I get Colum has had to bury so many MacKenzie men, and it was Dougal who pushed their clan to the Jacobite side, but you’re not even a little relieved to see your brother still alive? Colum is falling deeper and deeper into the clan above all else, and it’s frustrating to watch. He berates Dougal in front of their sisters and Maura and lays the blame for every single MacKenzie death at Dougal’s feet. He also calls him a “selfish cunt,” so you know he’s big mad. Since Dougal just escaped from prison, the English will surely be coming after him, so Colum banishes him to a cottage away from Castle Leoch.

Dougal, by the way, has barely said three words. He looks haunted by everything he’s endured. Colum didn’t even need to blame Dougal for all the men who died; Dougal is already walking around with that guilt. It’s wild to see him so still. He doesn’t fight back.

Before he leaves Leoch, Colum allows him time with his wife, which he accepts because come on, Dougal’s always gonna Dougal. And yet … he can’t really, um, Dougal? We find him and Maura in bed, and the sex looks terrible? No one is enjoying it, and Dougal can’t even look at Maura. He stops and sits on the side of the bed. She sits next to him. He still can’t even speak about how he’s feeling, so she takes his face in her hands, kisses him, and whispers, “Be with me.” She wants him to focus on her; she wants to give him a reprieve from how he’s feeling. And he kisses her back. It is, maybe, the first actual kiss they’ve shared? He takes her onto the bed, and this time they can’t look away from one another. Is it possible this husband and wife have — gasp — fallen in love with each other? It remains astounding that somehow it’s these two who are giving us the most achingly romantic moments in this entire series.

Sure, Henry and Julia can be romantic, too; it’s just that their story is getting a little ridiculous and drawn out at the moment. Right now, they’re writing letters, and Henry’s trying to procure three gemstones so they can time travel again, and the plan is to … rappel down a gorge and chisel three pieces of amethyst from a rock formation? He can’t just nick some jewelry from the affluent Grants, who he lives with, and make a run for it? At the very least, after almost dying while getting into that gorge, he only takes three tiny pieces of amethyst? No backups? Some to sell in case he or Julia needs money? This is why Julia should be head of all time-travel operations from here on out.

But Henry and Arch Bug — at the insistence of Murdina, who believes if Arch brings some amethyst, which is tied to stories of the Fair Folk, back, maybe the faeries will grant them another child — do go to that gorge, and Henry does come out of it with three pieces of stone. Henry brings those gemstones to Julia, and they decide they will make their escape in a few days’ time when all of the lairds of Loyalist clans, including Lovat and Uncle Grant, will be convening at the Duke of Sandringham’s for investitures by invitation from the king. Both Julia and Henry will be there, and they’ll be able to slip away while everyone is distracted. A solid plan!

There is one tiny problem. After blissfully leaving Henry at the wall, knowing that soon they’ll be together and they’ll get to the stones and back to Claire in just a few days, Julia finds that Maisri has returned to Leathers. When Julia asks if she’ll ever see Claire again, Maisri dumps some news on her that we’ve all pretty much known was coming since the season-two premiere: Julia can’t time travel, and the only reason she traveled the first time was that she was pregnant with William, who does have that ability. Julia is stuck 200 years in the past forever. Yeah, they’re going to need a new plan.

• In one happy bit of news: Murtagh and Grace tell each other how they feel, and then they have sex in a barn, and it is sweet, if a bit awkward. But I still fear for Grace’s life. Perhaps now more than ever!

• Is Murtagh actually the most romantic character in all of the Outlander-verse? When Grace stops herself from kissing Murtagh because she fears “wanting too much,” he replies with “Too much? How will it ever be enough?” before kissing her.

• Arch tearfully opens up to Henry about him and his wife losing their baby. Their son died before they could give him a name, but Arch called him “Wee Bug.” He and Murdina love each other so much. I think I like them now? Don’t tell Jamie, Claire, or Young Ian, okay?

• We get a flashback, er, forward maybe, that shows us Henry and Julia out on a date after getting married and running into Henry’s terribly snobbish ex. It’s both a way to explain how Henry knew about the amethyst (Julia talked about the supply in the Highlands because her wedding band has an amethyst in it) and to remind us how much they loved each other from day one.

• When Colum learns that Brian didn’t kill Lovat and there’s no real recourse for what Lovat did to Ellen, he seems angry that he’s taking yet another loss as laird so soon after the Sheriffmuir disaster. I’m worried he’s going to go all unhinged on us soon. Is Colum going to do something reckless?

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: What I Like About Choux
items.description: I hate to come right out of the gate with the obvious baking pun, but didn’t Pastry Week fall a little flat? I feel like I had a bit more fun watching Léa Seydoux refuse to eat various croissants than watching this episode. The bakers have many triumphs, which
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I hate to come right out of the gate with the obvious baking pun, but didn’t Pastry Week fall a little flat? I feel like I had a bit more fun watching Léa Seydoux refuse to eat various croissants than watching this episode. The bakers have many triumphs, which I think is usually a hallmark of a great episode, but from the on set, the editors are clearly telegraphing who is going home and who is going to be Star Baker yet again. Everyone is having fun and (nearly) everyone is triumphant, but the episode is lacking the suspense we usually get from a good reality-television program.

The first challenge is for the bakers to make eight handheld pies, which are ubiquitous in English bakeries. (I know Gail’s is basic, but its chicken, ham, and tarragon hand pie is basically delicious.) Many of the bakers are making a version of the pasty (with a short A so it rhymes with nasty, which they decidedly are not). Also known as the Cornish pasty, they come from Cornwall, the temperate and beachy region in England’s extreme southwest. They’re sort of like giant empanadas, but the crust is pinched together on one edge and crimped or braided into a thick closure that functions something like a handle. The idea was that farmers and miners — anyone who has watched Poldark knows Cornwall was famous for its mines — could hold the braid with their hands and eat their lunches without utensils since they were leagues underground trying not to die extracting undersea copper. Also, because their hands were filthy, they could throw the remainder of the crust to the crows. (While we’re on the subject of the Cornish, do not ask them about Cornish game hens. They are an American invention, and locals will laugh at you if you bring them up. Not that I know this from experience or anything.)

In the judging, we are close to two handshakes. Connie’s pasties, inspired by Jamaican patties and filled with jerk chicken, get praised by Paul, Nigella, and Alison, who seems to be angling to take over Paul’s job when he quits in a huff because people like Nigella more. Tom makes pasties inspired by banh mi, the delicious Vietnamese sandwich. Paul has never had a banh mi, and when he admits that, Tom says it’s a bit embarrassing, and he has never been more right about a single thing in his life. When Paul tries his first one, he says the spice is fantastic, and Nigella can’t get enough. Moyin’s Nigerian meat pie is so good that Alison also has to get a taste in, and you can almost see Paul swat her hand away with his eyes.

The one who struggles most is Clara, who makes venison pies that look like deer. As the judges explain to her how badly they could go, you know those antlers are going to be a failure. Because of their fiddly shape, they are about as full as a vegan at an all-you-can-eat barbecue buffet. Mo’s take on a samosa looks bright green, which is never a good idea for food unless it is a Jolly Rancher. (The thought of a Jolly Rancher handpie makes me think of that kombucha meme? Gross. But maybe! No.) Nigella tells him it’s too “gungy,” which is an English word for slime and also a uniquely British kink.

The judges don’t love Gabe’s bostin Brummie balti pie, and American viewers probably have no idea what any of those words are other than pie. “Bostin” is West Midlands slang for something that is great, like how people in Boston (no relation) say “wicked.” “Brummie” is what you call someone or something from Birmingham, England’s second-largest city, which is in the West Midlands and where Gabe lives and Alison is from. A “balti pie” is a Birmingham staple that takes a usual English meat pie and adds a filling typical of a curry, which is why Gabe’s are made with lamb, spices, mango chutney, and colonialism. I have never had one because they’re often served at football — sorry, soccer — games, and I do not go to those. Also, every person I’ve ever met from Birmingham says, “Don’t go, it’s terrible.” Not even for the bostin Brummie balti pies? (Don’t you feel smart now that you get that?)

The bakers all do similarly well at the technical challenge, which is solid but uninspired. Nigella tasks them with making a karpatka, a Polish dessert no one has ever heard of. But Nigella is right in her introduction. While it is unfamiliar, they should all be familiar with the components: two big slaps of choux pastry with vanilla custard in the middle. If these bakers haven’t made choux and custard, how did they get an invitation to the tente? While everyone seems confident in what they’re doing, Clara’s karpatka ends up not rising. Her choux is flat. (Oh, and you thought you would escape without one terrible shoe pun. Actually, that was two-thirds of a pun. P. U.)

After the technical, it’s clear Tom or Connie is going to be the winner and Clara or Mo is going home, unless something miraculous or disastrous occurs. I’m suitably impressed by Connie and Gary in this year’s competition. They both fulfill the archetype of an older baker who hews a little too closely to the classics and might not be as tidy as some of the other bakers. However, they’ve defied that, turning their knowledge bases and tidiness into strengths and lasting far longer in the competition than their archetype usually does.

The showstopper is to make a free-standing pie without using any pans, which is such a simple but, er, challenging challenge that I am impressed with the assignment for the third time in one episode. The result is seven amazing-looking P to the I to the E, pies! (It’s still stuck in my head.) Even Clara’s, which is cracked, looks great. Nigella says up close, it’s not that great, since she topped it with edible glitter, which settled into the cracks. Nigella, as relatable as ever, says that is what happens as you age and apply powder to your face. All the women (plus Tom and Gabe) nod in agreement. There is a groundswell of love and support even as Clara’s sun- and moon-shaped apple pie really dissatisfies the judges, and we all know the inevitable has come true: Clara, one of the front-runners, is going home.

The judges are also unimpressed with Moyin’s Nigerian mask–inspired apple pie, tanking what was otherwise a good week for him. Even still, all the pies look as beautiful as Nigella, powder in the cracks or no. Mo’s multicolored butterfly is like a stunning bit of stained glass, even though it was overbaked and underfilled. Gabe’s is shaped like his napping dog and looks spot on, but Paul says it’s too dry, even if Nigella disagrees. Connie’s sweet-potato-curry pie is inspired by a pet snake named Dave and looks like a delicious little cartoon. Gary makes a fish pie that looks like a fish because he is the most creative person in the tent. Still, it is prettier than Brad Pitt fishing in A River Runs Through It. Tom is similarly inspired making a Mexican chicken pie shaped like one of the chickens from the movie Chicken Run, even though he isn’t allowed to say the title, just like we’re not allowed to call it Bake Off.

It comes out of the oven like a little bit of ingenuity and looks exactly like the cartoon but also shockingly appetizing. He presents it to the judges, and they have their first bite. Nigella lavishes this chicken with praise, and Paul experiences the pressure. He feels the love she’s getting, the uneasy pang of people disagreeing with him, the camaraderie of talking about the difficulties of aging as a woman in society. He feels it all slipping away from him — the power, the control, the show — and he does the only thing he can: He approaches Tom, naturally Star Baker for the third time, with his hand extended, not in congratulations but to pull it all back toward him.

items.title: Dark Matter Season-Finale Recap: Into the Great Unknown
items.description: At the end of Dark Matter’s first season, the many Jasons of the Jason-pocalyse were still stuck somewhere between the anger and bargaining phase of the five stages of grief, having blown past denial yet still too engaged in reconnecting with Daniela and Charl
items.author: Scott Tobias
paragraphs: At the end of Dark Matter’s first season, the many Jasons of the Jason-pocalyse were still stuck somewhere between the anger and bargaining phase of the five stages of grief, having blown past denial yet still too engaged in reconnecting with Daniela and Charlie to move forward. The standalone fifth episode of this season, “Love and Be Loved,” marked a pivotal shift through depression and acceptance, as one such Jason contemplated suicide before opting to get a fresh start in a world where Jason Dessen had died as a child, and his mother was still alive to welcome his miraculous return. Even then, it took more than a few dark nights of the soul for this Jason to work his way through the fog, surrender his ties to the recent past, and build a new life with someone else. When he meets the Daniela of that world and is able to exchange pleasantries with her before heading home to his new partner, acceptance has been achieved.

And so now, in the final episode of the second season, one such Jason is able to have a conversation with Daniela as if they’ve gone through an amicable divorce years earlier and can reminisce about their history without falling into despair. This Jason is essentially escorting his wife through the box to find their son, but he’s resigned to the fact that there’s no getting either of them back. They laugh over a memory involving the twins when they were young, but Jason cuts the conversation short by opening the door to the world where he believes Charlie has landed. He rejects the idea of stepping through to see Charlie himself, because it’s not his role to play anymore. “It’s not fair to any of us, but we keep going,” he tells Daniela. “Thank you for a really great life.”

The tone of these sorts of interactions has changed over the course of this season, as different people from different worlds have collided and been able to get past the impossibility of it. When Charlie No. 1 proved to Max that he was a multidimensional traveler and not his twin brother coming home early from college, what choice did Max have but believe him? And when Daniela No. 1 goes looking for her son and gets caught in the house by this world’s Daniela, the show doesn’t pause long to register this shocking revelation before it turns into a metaphysical therapy session. Daniela gets to tell some version of herself how she feels about her marital problems and her lingering guilt over having to kill one of the Jasons to protect her family. Often in life you need to be able to forgive yourself, but Daniela gets the rare opportunity to make that idea as literal as possible. It’s the sci-fi version of Stuart Smalley looking into the mirror and doing his daily affirmations.

Though this season two finale is appropriately scaled up and exciting, with a lot of frantic action across multiple realities, the progression that Dark Matter has made to get to the acceptance phase of its premise raises an obvious question: Where could it go from here? There are some plot-related questions that will need to be answered next season — we’ll get to those in a bit — but there are signs in this last hour that Dark Matter has reached a potential dead end on an emotional and philosophical front. The impact of the two scenes with Daniela described above should be seismic given how much box-related upheaval she’s had to face since Jason No. 2 invaded her life. But this season, the show has reckoned so much with this type of emotional fallout that the scenes are feeling a little redundant and drippy. There’s no physical (or metaphysical) limit to where the series might go from here — the box does, after all, open up into infinite possible realities — but the door might have closed on a “Love and Be Loved”-type tearjerker again.

On the other hand, perhaps the dramatic realignment of the major characters in the finale will open up other avenues. Heading toward season’s end, there appeared to be two camps working at cross purposes: Jason No. 1, Amanda No. 2, Ryan No. 1, and Blair No. 2 have been fussing over the science and logistics of destroying the box, starting from the original sources in World No. 2, because the boxes everywhere else would just respawn. Meanwhile, Leighton No. 2 and Jason No. 2 have been looking to refine their project through the Pyramid and perhaps return to the idealistic vision of addressing big problems with multi-dimensional solutions. But in an abrupt turn of events, Leighton No. 2 and Jason No. 2 start to regret this monstrous invention they’ve unleashed on humanity. Leighton talks about a world where Mt. Rainier had blown, leading to massive crop death and starvation, but the ecological solution he offered wound up deepening the crisis, starting with developing countries before spreading to the rest of the world.

“We fucked up,” laments Leighton in a truly massive understatement. And in an even more surprising moment of self-awareness, he expresses regret over “letting millions of people die for money” and “walking around in awe of my own fucking greatness.” Jason No. 2 tries to ease the guilt that’s suddenly stabbing away at Leighton’s conscience by suggesting that the implications of the box were not knowable and “this thing has brought out the most terrifying aspects of who we are.” While it does seem a bit surprising that the Velocity braintrust didn’t think through the massive potential for disruption that the box would cause, it does track historically that scientists often think about what’s possible more than about where great advancements might lead humankind (see also: Oppenheimer). Still, it’s a startling gearshift for all parties to come around on the idea that the box (and the Pyramid) might be worth shutting down.

All parties, that is, except for Oluko, who has emerged as a late-breaking villain and ghost in the machine. Amanda No. 2 and Ryan No. 1 meet him at the Velocity building in Analog World with the intent of securing vaccines and medications to fight a plague in another dimension. But their true goal is to access the Analog World box in order to work back to the original box with the technology needed to “decohere” and destroy the entire system. Blair warns them that Oluko gave her “major creep vibes,” and indeed he sniffs out their intention and sends a security agent after them, leading to a splashy action sequence in which they’re being chased through multiple worlds, including one where Chicago has become a war zone. That sequence alone makes it seem like the show’s producers were saving the budgetary fireworks for the grand finale, just as last season ended with a rush of Jason-on-Jason violence.

But once the dust has settled, Dark Matter lands in a tricky spot for next season. As hard as it was to get back to the original box in World No. 2, it appears that Blair No. 2 and Jason No. 1 succeeded in their de-coherence plan, but as with all box-related issues, the result is messier than anticipated. Oluko winds up escaping to some unknown world, leaving him as a looming threat, and more crucially, time runs out before Daniela and Charlie can make it back to Analog World for a family reunion. They open a door into an unknown future, but it’s obvious that they’ll need these dimensional portals to be opened up once again. The second season of Dark Matter has been a significant improvement on the first, but if the show gets a third — news on a renewal has yet to be announced — it will need to open that portal door, too, and find new possibilities.

• Blair offers some wonderful sci-fi nonsense in explaining how her gizmo will kill the box: “Basically it’ll attack not just the local qubits but all programming for the adaptive shielding, slowly corrupting the error-correcting protocols.” Adaptive shielding, error-correcting protocols. Got it.

• Though the heart-tugging moments are not as potent in this episode as they were in earlier parts of the season, Daniela’s farewell to the grown-up version of Max she never knew is a killer. “It’s really nice to meet you” is a lovely bit of understatement.
• Good on Charlie for going record shopping in Max’s world. Nirvana’s Bleach is a solid choice.
• Oluko’s rise brings the first major character death in his doppelgänger, Leighton No. 2, whose murder ends up serving as a gruesome narrative sacrifice for his sins in exploiting the box.

items.title: Cupertino Recap: The Split
items.description: There’s one particular shot I love in this week’s Cupertino. The camera is fixed at a corner that connects two hallways in the labyrinthine San Mateo Hall of Justice. Michael and Olivia have been defending two tech bros, A.J. (Ben Cook) and Buddy (Taip Oskar Ć
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: There’s one particular shot I love in this week’s Cupertino. The camera is fixed at a corner that connects two hallways in the labyrinthine San Mateo Hall of Justice. Michael and Olivia have been defending two tech bros, A.J. (Ben Cook) and Buddy (Taip Oskar Ćeman), who run a prediction-market website, WagerMode, that the state of California is trying to shut down. But because Michael has been talking to A.J. while Olivia handles Buddy — and because District Attorney Sally Clawson (Amanda Warren) has decided to offer a deal to whichever partner acts first — we get an amusing cut to Michael and Olivia flying down separate hallways, racing away from each other and off into the distance. It’s the whole theme of the episode in one snappy second: Partners zooming off in different directions.

“A.J. and Buddy” maintains that kind of energy — and visual flair — throughout most of its running time. It’s the closest Cupertino has come yet to doing a true stand-alone episode, with a story that pops up seemingly out of nowhere and then builds and builds for nearly a full 45 minutes. It’s a fantastic episode overall, harmed only by a few momentum-stalling digressions and an ending that feels a little abrupt. Not for the first time (and I’m sure not for the last), I found myself wondering how much better this show could be with another 10 to 15 minutes of running time.

The case-of-the-week begins with Christy (always a good starting point for any Cupertino). While clubbing, Christy fixates on a handsome, melancholy lad named A.J. and takes him back to her apartment without learning anything about him, which is understandable, given how many cocky Valley guys she probably encounters on a typical night out. So she’s mildly shocked the next morning when A.J. asks her to give him a ride to the airport, where a private jet is waiting. She’s even more surprised when she’s in the middle of touring the jet and it suddenly takes off for Saint Kitts.

From there, the story moves very quickly. A.J. explains that he needs Christy’s bosses to race to his house before the cops arrive to retrieve Buddy’s laptop. (They also find their retainer there, in wads of cash stashed among shelves full of shoe boxes and baking-powder cans.) When the police do arrive, what follows is a whirlwind of court appearances and client conferences, all while the DA and her officers try to move as quickly as possible to get what they need from the WagerMode boys — even if it risks violating due process.

All of this culminates in the kind of twist common to Michelle and Robert King’s legal dramas, where we often eventually discover that there are secret motivations behind what seem like simple cases. When it comes to WagerMode, Michael wants to prove that his client is a victim of selective prosecution, given that another site called PolyBetting runs an almost identical business and has a California gaming license. (It’s implied that PolyBetting does a lot of donating to politicians, including to the Trump family.) As much as DA Clawson tries to claim the moral high ground, noting that WagerMode takes bets on possible political assassinations, she eventually admits this case is really about election interference — and about the million-dollar bets from an anonymous customer: Go4Broke.

Similarly, this episode is, somewhat slyly, more about partnerships than prediction markets. It’s quite obviously about the title characters, A.J. and Buddy, who met in college and formed a symbiotic business relationship, with A.J. making bold plays while Buddy backs him up with programming genius. Yet A.J. is still a lonely little rich kid. At times he treats Christy like a playdate, offering her Pop-Tarts on a silver platter and asking her to “aisle surf” down his jet during takeoffs. And given the opportunity to betray his only real friend, the aptly named Buddy — who is actually Go4Broke — A.J. hesitates.

The other partnership examined in this episode is, of course, Michael and Olivia’s. When circumstances divide them, Olivia seizes the opportunity to show Michael that she can be more than just the sneakily sweet half of their dynamic. She defends Buddy fiercely, even getting a cut on her cheek while trying to physically prevent the police from unlocking Buddy’s computer. She also calls out Michael in front of the judge, accusing him of lying when he says he didn’t know A.J. was trying to flee the country. Michael rolls with his partner’s punches, seeing it as ordinary courtroom tussling. Olivia seems more uncertain about the parts they have to play in this case — although she’s quite good at being ruthless.

As I mentioned, this episode feels somewhat curtailed, with A.J. and Buddy’s case(s) stalling out after WagerMode starts posting odds on Clawson’s reelection. I feel like the issues this story raises — about partnerships and prediction markets — don’t get addressed as fully as they could have been. But hey, this is only episode 4 of a 20-episode season. Perhaps WagerMode will return to extract some more value from the million-dollar gold bar A.J. gave Christy as a retainer.

Part of me also wishes this episode had stuck with the WagerMode plot exclusively — although this is no knock against the scenes that keep interrupting the main story, which involve Natalia hanging around the empty PSA offices with a visiting Nichole. (A treat for Girls5Eva fans!) Some important news gets dropped during these interludes, namely that Nichole now represents Colt AI, which is suing PSA for “illegally accessing” Bo.

It’s also worth noting that as soon as Natalia wanders into the PSA backrooms, she sees the pillar where Michael and Olivia signed their partnership “contract” and adds her own name, with a new 33/33/33 split. Maybe that’s what it will take to keep Price and Siffre united: a third partner they can team up against.

Would Natalia’s power move hold up in court? Probably not. But as she herself points out, “Lawsuits are just the language of business.” In Silicon Valley, you don’t always go to court for justice. Sometimes you just want the people in your life to listen — really listen — to your complaints.
• It takes 15 minutes before the opening credits kick in this week. Good to see the Kings up to their old tricks.

• A big part of what makes this episode so fun is that for the first five minutes or so we’re just hanging out with Christy, who knows how to have a good time. We get to see the half-assed way she handles her wardrobe. (Sometimes she puts her dresses on hangers, but “then I get bored.”) And we get to see her fill her purse with all of the fancy soaps and lotions on A.J.’s PJ. (“I’m more of a Spirit Air kind of girl,” she tells him.)
• File this away for later: Olivia’s terrible sub-freeway apartment is also right above some guy running video-game servers, which make Olivia’s floor buzz all day.

• Robert King directed this episode, and one of the hallmarks of his directing style dating back to The Good Wife is his use of off-screen space and implied action, especially when it comes to the kind of technology we all use every day. Case in point: Olivia fights hard to keep the police from using Buddy’s finger to unlock his laptop, and right before the commercial break, as she falls to the floor, we hear the telltale chime of a Mac starting up.

• Another nice touch from King: the extreme close-ups on A.J. and Christy’s faces while they’re bantering and snacking on his jet. It’s unusually intimate and emphasizes how much A.J. needs close human contact.

• Another nice touch from the writers (including credited screenwriter Joey Hartstone): When the teetotaling Olivia joins her colleagues in drinking fancy Champagne to celebrate their sort-of win, her reaction to both the alcohol and the success is the same: “Bitter.”

items.title: War Recap: Stars — They’re Just Like Us
items.description: Here are some questions I asked myself as Carla Duval walked on to the set of the Jack Jeffreys Show in the opening sequence of this week’s episode: Where is Jeremy, Carla’s obnoxious co-star who appeared a few times in the season premiere and never again? Why
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Here are some questions I asked myself as Carla Duval walked on to the set of the Jack Jeffreys Show in the opening sequence of this week’s episode: Where is Jeremy, Carla’s obnoxious co-star who appeared a few times in the season premiere and never again? Why is Serena there? (Answer: To remind Carla not to mention “the D-word,” the first instruction from Serena that Carla has ever had the courage to disobey.) Shouldn’t Carla’s publicist be there? Where is Carla’s publicist?

However relevant that question may be for the rest of the episode, it was especially pressing in the beginning, given that Carla bombs her late-night appearance. She looks nervous even before starting, but making the fake-nice chitchat required of talk-show interviews while host and audience fawn over that picture of herself with Morgan — the one taken on the red carpet shortly after she was served divorce papers — proves to be impossible. Carla goes rogue. Seething through her teeth, she says that Morgan is a “bullshitter” who wants a divorce. At the suggestion of his producer, Jack Jeffreys (Danny Sapani) tries to take a commercial break, but Carla apparently wants to talk, though she doesn’t say much. She only manages to tell the audience to “shut the fuck up” when they start heckling. In the wings, Serena makes a face like she knew this was coming.

This sequence, which kicks off the rest of the episode’s events, would have been a great opportunity for Sienna Miller to invest Carla with some intensity beyond her three established registers — compliant, angry, and horny; she’ll hit them all by the end of the episode — but Carla’s meltdown isn’t convincing, especially not when television history is littered with the minds celebrities lost during late-night interviews. Later, an incredulous Bella insists the whole thing is clearly a bad PR stunt. But this theory also puzzled me. What good would it do Carla to act contemptuously toward the public, when she needs their favor as she heads to court?

Almost no good, which to a capable publicist, is good enough. Serena summons Grace Hopper (Katherine Kingsley) to mitigate the crisis, which again brings up the question of where Carla’s own publicist is hiding. I’m not a stickler for details like these. I’m not a lawyer or a celebrity or a tech mogul; I hope to never be too familiar with the proceedings of a divorce; and as long as a show builds a consistent, compelling world, I’ll believe pretty much anything. But the fact that Carla doesn’t have her own publicist undermines the world-building — who, if not a publicist, would have booked her on the Jack Jeffreys Show? — and cheapens the plot. I want to sink into this fictional world, not question it.

What I do buy is that Cathcarts is happy with Carla’s disastrous public appearance. As the Taylor & Byrne office stresses over the interview, Cathcarts surveys the several tabloid stories that have come out about it while practically licking their lips. Both teams know that the viral interview has no legal bearing, but it does have the potential to shift public opinion, which matters for litigation. Carla’s major, and perhaps only, advantage over Morgan’s wealth was the favor of the public, which she compromised when she swore at an unsuspecting audience. In the immediate aftermath, a wreath of flowers arrives for Nick and Serena, along with a card that reads, simply, “R.I.P.”

Cathcarts’ next move is to stall the litigation process as much as possible. They know, from the financial statements that Johnny sent to Schill, that Taylor & Byrne is broke, so the longer the process takes, the worse it will be for them. Beatrice calls it “the march of the snails.” When Taylor & Byrne request a statement of interests for the past six months, Cathcarts sends dozens of boxes of documents, any of which could contain the single relevant file. Except, as Schill tells Johnny over the phone, Cathcarts “forgot” to send the right box, which will only arrive the next day, via “London’s slowest courier.” It’s a dirty trick familiar to anyone who has watched a legal drama or two.

While the overworked and probably underpaid Taylor & Byrne associates sort through the boxes, Michael and Nora go over Carla’s personal assets with her while Saeed takes notes. Carla is despondent and distracted, scrolling Zephyr while they talk, but she is soon warmed by Nora and Michael’s kindness. She jokes that the only thing they’re missing is her Ferrari Testarossa, which the equally distracted Saeed puts down as an asset, right under “two horses.” He asks Molly to type up the notes for Serena, so it’s Molly who gets chewed out when Serena points out that neither Carla nor Morgan own a Ferrari. Molly retypes the list, as instructed, but when Johnny snoops around Serena’s office later that night, after everyone has left, he takes a picture of the uncorrected asset list — the one that includes the Ferrari — and sends it over to Schill. That’s how the Ferrari reappears on Cathcarts’ asset list. When they finally get a hold of it, Molly and Saeed are befuddled: How could Cathcarts possibly know about the imaginary Ferrari? Cut to Johnny looking nervous.

Meanwhile, Carla drowns in paparazzi. They mob her house and yell out cruel things about Gabe, making it “impossible” for Carla to go anywhere, including theater rehearsals. Not even Johnny’s charm can make her feel better — he offers to take her out for a drink, but she snaps at him that she’s not exactly in a position to be seen out and about.

When she enters the stage, Grace — the crisis-PR expert summoned by Serena — immediately brings up that old showbiz adage: There’s no such thing as bad publicity. It’s good that people are talking, because it means they care; and as long as they care, things can still change for Carla. And change they do, when a singer named Tamara Chong (Mei Mac) appears on a chat-cast called “Every Little Thing She Does” and encourages the public to take Carla’s anger seriously. Surely, she must have a reason. Social-media sentiment consequently shifts, and suddenly Carla’s high placement on Zephyr’s trending topics is not such a bad thing. Seizing the moment, Grace and Serena book Carla to go on the podcast that same day. Carla worries about the impact of this continued exposure on Gabe, but Serena assures her that they’ll be able to “control everything.”

Famous last words, I thought, but as it turns out, Carla is better at guesting on a podcast than on a late-night show. Looking strong and a little bit tired, as Grace advised, Carla avoids speaking too explicitly about the details of the divorce — she doesn’t bring up the cheating — and clarifies the reason for her angry outburst on the Jack Jeffreys Show: She was served divorce papers at her own premiere.

It’s the most listened-to podcast episode in the country, Smallwood tells Morgan, as well as the show’s most popular interview. Morgan resents the fact that he’s being made to look like a villain when the real villain is Smallwood. Besides, he was honey-trapped! But Cathcarts can’t use the Flora stuff because they’re not supposed to know about the honey trap, not that Morgan knows that he is not supposed to know. Thought You Can See Everything is the only thing out right now that raises questions about truth and deceit? Think again! Now I’m getting distracted imagining St. John Smallwood and Billy Evans going head to head in a court of law.

Smallwood’s advice to Morgan is that he call Gabe — who has been sending him “vicious messages” — to try to mend their relationship. For such a smart and powerful man, Morgan continues to be extremely gullible when it comes to Smallwood’s machinations. Morgan has a nice, conciliatory dinner with Gabe, which leads to a hug outside the restaurant, where Smallwood has some paparazzi strategically waiting. They snap a picture, which undoes all the healing Gabe and Morgan had just been through; Gabe immediately identifies their dinner as a PR move. The puppeteering incenses Morgan, who storms into Cathcarts to demand his lawyers quit playing games and get on with litigation already.

Then again, when has Morgan ever successfully put his foot down? Even Zephyr’s executives distrust his authority. At a meeting with seemingly every senior-plus employee of the company, Gillian and Eric address Morgan with open hostility. Guy (Olivier Sublet), a creative director who Morgan doesn’t even remember hiring, points out that the outcome of Morgan’s divorce could affect the whole company. Morgan defensively reminds the room that he is the founder, and as such, he gets to call the shots. Yet later, after he has tried to impose himself much in the same way at Cathcarts, he arrives at the Zephyr offices to discover that the board meeting he thought he was heading into is, in fact, a meeting with Michael Ancker (David Menkin), who finally comes with an offer to buy Zephyr. When Morgan says that such a transaction is impossible because of the freezing order, Michael offers to send him £2 billion through a “safe” account neither Carla nor her lawyers will be able to reach (sounds illegal). Morgan refuses Ancker’s offer outright and stops just short of spitting in the man’s face.

Whether or not the picture the Daily Mail publishes under the headline “Son Sides With Step-Father” will impact the positive sentiment toward Carla is to be determined, but it’s immediately effective in making Carla feel horrible. She was feeling better after giving in to Johnny’s “anything you need, call me X” text and inviting him to sneak into her house through the back door. They spend the whole night together, which means Johnny wakes up to several texts and missed calls from Bella. Seeing the tabloid story in the morning makes Carla reconsider the exposure litigation will bring. At the Taylor & Byrne offices, she tells Nick and Serena that she doesn’t want to go to court because of the public scrutiny it will invite into her and Gabe’s lives. Wondering how things got so vicious between her and Morgan — ahem, lady, you asked your friend to seduce him? — she remembers how at that idyllic, beloved cottage in Normandy, Morgan didn’t even know what “zephyr” meant. She is the one who named the company, after a poem she was fond of reading to Morgan. Pause: Carla came up with the name Zephyr? Nick says that if they take this simple fact to court, they could stand to win as much as half of Morgan’s money. It’ll be enough to take care of Carla and Gabe forever.

Carla immediately changes her mind and agrees to go to court after all, as she has done every time Nick and Serena have advanced their agenda, even though they have promised her this same outcome before. In War, the lawyers are more powerful than their clients, and if this makes for compelling drama, it can also lead to inconsistent characters. Morgan is wealthy and powerful, in theory, but seemingly helpless to enact any influence; Carla is “difficult,” in theory, but compliant with her lawyers. Now in the back half of its first season, War is at a loss as to how to answer a simple governing question: Who is the boss here?
Representations and Acknowledgments

• In this episode, asking for Johnny’s attention and expediency as he helps Cathcarts make the most out of chaos, David Schill quotes Keanu Reeves for the second time in the show. Loving this bit; would welcome more.
• I would also love to see a special episode that follows the theater group having to deal with Carla’s diva antics. She simply never showed up to rehearsal!

• The Ferrari Testarossa slipup is the first mistake Johnny makes as a mole, but there doesn’t seem to be much that can trace it back to him. As far as we know, he was alone in the office when he snapped the picture of the document. What it could potentially do is incriminate Serena, or at least make her look inattentive. Maybe in the end it will be Molly taking the heat, since she was the one to mistype the note, which might create some compelling drama — Molly has been watching Johnny like a hawk. I’m starting to think she’s going to be the first person to sniff him out.

• Speaking of the asset list mix-up, one thing confused me. Why is the photo Johnny sent even valuable to Cathcarts? Isn’t the whole point of the list that Taylor & Byrne would have sent it to them, anyway? Why would Cathcarts base their documents on the picture Johnny sent, rather than the list they got through Taylor & Byrne, when it doesn’t put them at any explicit advantage? It’s not like Johnny was giving them any information they weren’t guaranteed to have?

items.title: Justin Timberlake to Release Four-Part ‘Tell-All’ Docuseries, Featuring Janet Jackson, on Apple (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Justin Timberlake is set to release a four-part docuseries on Apple TV in December, described as a “tell-all,” three sources confirm to Variety.
items.author: Jem Aswad; Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: Justin Timberlake is set to release a four-part docuseries on Apple TV in December, described as a “tell-all,” three sources confirm to Variety.

One source says the series will feature Janet Jackson discussing the infamous “wardrobe malfunction” that took place during the pair’s performance at the 2004 Super Bowl. Another source says that Timberlake discusses some of former girlfriend Britney Spears’ recent comments as well.

Further details on the series, which is directed by Fisher Stevens, were not available at the time of this article’s publication; reps for Timberlake, Jackson and Apple had no comment or did not respond to Variety‘s multiple requests for comment.
Timberlake has a relationship with the streamer dating back to 2021, when he starred in the Apple Original film “Palmer.”

The news comes during a comparatively low-profile period for Timberlake, who made a guest appearance during Jay-Z’s concert in Paris last month but otherwise has been off the radar since his “Forget Tomorrow” global tour in support of his most recent album, “Everything I Thought It Was,” which was released in March of 2024.

The singer announced in July 2025 that he has been diagnosed with Lyme disease, which affected some of his performances on the tour. Fans noticed that Timberlake appeared sluggish and low-energy during performances on the international leg of the trek, which he suggested was due to the nerve damage and fatigue he experienced from Lyme disease.

“I’ve been battling some health issues, and was diagnosed with Lyme Disease–which I don’t say so you feel bad for me – but to shed some light on what I’ve been up against behind the scenes,” he wrote. “If you’ve experienced this disease or know someone who has- then you’re aware: Living with this can be relentlessly debilitating, both mentally and physically.”

The tour, which wrapped in July of 2025, was further complicated by Timberlake’s DWI conviction, stemming from his arrest in Sag Harbor, New York, the previous year. He was pulled over by police in June 2024 after running a stop sign and veering out of his lane. The incident took place shortly before the tour’s launch, and Page Six reported that Timberlake said to officers, in a much-memed comment, “This is going to ruin the tour” — however, police bodycam footage released later showed that he did not say those words, rather something like “I’m on tour.”

items.title: Druski Sets Netflix Series ‘Collect & Praise’ Based on Megachurch Sketch, Signs Multi-Year Deal With Streamer
items.description: Druski is bringing his money-hungry megachurch pastor character to Netflix.
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: Druski is bringing his money-hungry megachurch pastor character to Netflix.

The comedian will star opposite Mike Epps in a new, semi-scripted comedy series titled “Collect & Praise,” premiering on the streamer on Dec. 1. The show is based on a character made viral by Druski in an internet sketch and at the BET Awards. Epps will play the pastor’s deacon as they “scheme their way through scandal, chaos and controversy,” according to the logline.

“Collect & Praise” is the first project to be produced as part of a multi-year deal Druski signed with Netflix to create original content exclusively for the streamer through his 4Lifers Entertainment company.

The series marks the first time the 32-year-old, born Drew Desbordes, will adapt one of his popular internet personas into a longform television production. The comedian, who became famous by self-financing his content and distributing it independently on social media, now forms his first major partnership within the Hollywood studio system.

As part of the deal, Netflix will license select content from Druski’s existing catalog, including “Coulda Been Love,” “Coulda Been Daddy,” “Coulda Been Records Auditions” and his comedic skits. These series, posted directly to YouTube, have generated more than 1 billion views collectively.

“I’ve built my platform by creating characters and comedy that resonate with people,” Druski said in a statement. “This partnership with Netflix will give me the resources to build on that comedy foundation and bring my work to a new global audience. It’s a tremendous opportunity for our team at 4Lifers Entertainment to expand our reach, develop original programming for the masses and take our creativity to new heights.”

“Druski has a gift for building characters that people can’t stop talking about,” said John Derderian, who oversees Next Gen Content at Netflix. “We want the best talent in the world to bring us their most ambitious work, reach new audiences and build their brands. ‘Collect & Praise’ is just the beginning, and we welcome Druski to Netflix.”

Druski is one of comedy’s most exciting and fast-growing voices in recent years. Earlier this year, the Atlanta native became the youngest-ever host of the BET Awards, and he joined Emma Stone and Chris Pine in the cast of upcoming rom-com “The Catch.” His other credits include Prime Video’s “Livestream From Hell,” “Praise This” and the “House Party” reboot. This weekend, he will host “Saturday Night Live,” becoming the first true digital creator to do so.

items.title: ‘X-Men’: ‘Hunger Games’ Actor Ben Wang Circling Iceman Role in Marvel’s Reboot
items.description: After battling it out in the arena in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” and leading the latest “Karate Kid” installment, Ben Wang is circling another major franchise: Marvel Studios’ “X-Men” reboot.
items.author: Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: After battling it out in the arena in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” and leading the latest “Karate Kid” installment, Ben Wang is circling another major franchise: Marvel Studios’ “X-Men” reboot.
Wang is in negotiations to play Bobby Drake, aka Iceman, who was one of the founding X-Men. Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, the character first appeared in “The X-Men #1” in September 1963.

If the deal closes, Wang would join a sprawling cast that features Sadie Sink (as Jean Grey), Kit Connor (as Cyclops), Samara Weaving (as Emma Frost), Inde Navarrette (as Rogue), Maya Boyd (as Storm), Asa Germann (as Angel), Christopher Abbott (as Professor Charles Xavier) and Adam Driver (as Mr. Sinister).

Marvel Studios chief Kevin Feige revealed the new “X-Men” cast at the D23 convention in August, after Sink’s Jean Grey debuted in the blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.” The upcoming movie reboots the mutant team for the first time since the 2019 Fox film “X-Men: Dark Phoenix” and for their first outing under the Marvel Studios umbrella. Jake Schreier, who oversaw last year’s “Thunderbolts,” is directing the film from a script by Lee Sung Jin and Joanna Calo. “X-Men” is set for release on May 5, 2028.

In “Sunrise on the Reaping,” Wang plays Wyatt Callow, one of the tributes from District 12 alongside Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), who is the focus of the “Hunger Games” prequel movie.
