items.title: Scorpio Season Is All About Death, Sex & Rebirth. Your Tarotscope Explains Why
items.description: Scorpio Season Is All About Death, Sex & Rebirth. Your Tarotscope Explains Why
items.author: Tatianna Tarot
paragraphs: Scorpio Season Is All About Death, Sex & Rebirth. Your Tarotscope Explains Why

After a Venus retrograde that started in your sign and dragged you through every hidden corner of your heart, The Sun is your reward. This card represents joy, vitality, visibility, success, and the freedom of being fully seen. It brings positive exposure, elevation and the energy to sustain this momentum. This is your glow-up season. November is showing you that the version of you who believed depth had to come with suffering is dying. You don’t need to be in pain to be powerful. You don’t need to be mysterious to be magnetic. You’ve survived enough darkness to know you can handle it, so now prove you can handle the light. Allow yourself to be celebrated. Laugh loudly, receive compliments without deflecting them, and be warm instead of guarded. Your ancestors are celebrating you right now. But are you celebrating you? Desire is calling you toward pleasure for the sake of pleasure, so let your body feel good without needing a reason. The rebirth here is choosing to live happily in the life you fought for.

Something is coming down in your life and there’s nothing you can do to stop it, and you shouldn’t try to stop it, either. The Tower is sudden upheaval, revelation, and the collapse of whatever was built on a faulty foundation. It’s one of the most feared cards in the deck, but I’m here to tell you it’s also one of the most liberating. This doesn’t have to be a frightening experience at all. Rather, it is quite an awakening. November is showing you that what’s falling was never as solid as you pretended. It could be a relationship, a plan, a belief system, or an identity you’ve outgrown but kept propping up because starting over felt inconvenient. With the Full Moon sitting on Uranus on November 24, expect the plot twist. The truth will come fast, and it may shake you because you didn’t expect it to crumble. Don’t rush to rebuild what Spirit is intentionally removing. Stand in the rubble long enough to see what’s actually real and what your guided next steps are. You crave freedom more than any other sign, but you can’t be free inside a structure built on a lie.

The World represents completion, integration, and the end of a major cycle. Consider this a spiritual graduation of sorts where you are elevating in consciousness and awareness. You’ve spent years building, grinding, proving, and climbing, and something you’ve worked toward for a long time is finally reaching its conclusion. November is showing you that the version of you who is always becoming and never arriving needs to be laid to rest. You don’t have to immediately look for the next mountain to climb. Stand in this moment and feel it deep in your body. What does it feel like to be the person who accomplished what you set out to do? Celebrate the ending. Pour a libation for the ancestors who carved the pathways that made your success possible, because you didn’t do this alone. Your desire this month is to enjoy the fruits of your labor without guilt or the urge to hustle. Energetically welcome in this new chapter by preparing your vessel to receive more. The rebirth is a new level of your life, but you don’t get there by skipping the finish line. Take your bow and absorb the moment.

It’s over, but deep down you already knew that. The Ten of Swords represents the definitive end: rock bottom, the betrayal revealed, the story that can’t continue no matter how hard you try to rewrite it. Sometimes it is a destined ending that you couldn’t avoid or predict. Behind all of the seemingly darkness of this card, the sun is rising, which means that something new is birthing itself in your life. November is showing you that what needs to die isn’t just the situation, it’s the dense mental loop you’ve been trapped in — replaying what happened in a negative form, analyzing who was wrong, and rehearsing conversations that will never take place. You’ve been living in your head to avoid feeling the change in your body, and it’s draining your life force. Let the ending actually be an ending. Stop resurrecting it in conversation, on your phone, and in your thoughts. Grieve it fully, then bury it. Hand it over to your ancestors and let them carry what you no longer can. The good news about rock bottom is that there’s nowhere to go but up. The worst is behind you.

Spirit is calling you away from the noise and the distractions. The Hermit represents solitude, introspection, and inner wisdom. He holds his own lantern because he is his own source of light and clarity. He doesn’t wait for anyone else to show him the way; he can source the knowledge himself. November is showing you that your constant availability to everyone else needs to die. You absorb other people’s moods, opinions, and problems so easily that you’ve lost track of which feelings are actually yours. Rather than teach or show others the path, ingest the medicine for yourself and follow your own advice. Your ancestors and guides speak loudest in the silence, and the downloads coming through this season are paramount to your next chapter, but you can’t hear them over everyone else’s needs. Cancel the plans you don’t want to keep. Meditate, pray, journal, and sit with yourself until you remember the sound of your own voice. You may notice there are new voices emerging within you that have important things to illuminate. The answers you’ve been seeking are already inside you. Your rebirth begins in the quiet. Go inward.

You are magnetic and unstoppable this month, and the Queen of Wands wants you to stop apologizing for it. She is confident, sensual, fiery, and completely unbothered by anyone who can’t handle her heat. She knows exactly who she is, and she doesn’t dim herself to make anyone comfortable. November is showing you that the version of you who shrinks, who tones down your desires and plays nice when you’d rather be bold, is dying. Like the Gede, the Queen of Wands carries no shame around her body, her humor, or her hunger for life. Your sexuality is sacred. Your appetite for more is sacred. Your fire is sacred. Wear what makes you feel powerful. Flirt without guilt. Speak your mind. Lead in your pleasure instead of waiting for someone else to initiate it. Your rebirth is a version of you that doesn’t ask permission to be this much. Dare to take up space more than ever before.

You’ve planted a lot this year, and now you’re standing in the garden wondering what’s actually going to grow. The Seven of Pentacles represents patience, evaluation, and the pause between effort and harvest. November is showing you that it’s time to get honest about your investments: your time, your money, your energy, your love. Where are you getting a return, and where are you pouring into something that hasn’t given back in months? Not everything you planted was meant to flourish, and that’s okay. Some seeds need more time. Others need to be pulled up from the root so the rest of your garden can breathe. What needs to die this season is your loyalty to what isn’t yielding. Your desire is abundance you can touch, taste, and enjoy, and that requires discernment. Stop watering what’s dead out of habit or fear of wasting what you’ve already invested. The rebirth comes from knowing what deserves your patience and what deserves a funeral. Invest where it grows.

The Eight of Pentacles represents mastery, devotion, and the dedicated work of perfecting your craft one task at a time. November is showing you that the scattered version of you, the one who dabbles in everything and commits to nothing long enough to get great at it, is ready to die. Your curiosity is a gift, but right now it’s diluting your power. Pick the one thing that lights you up most and give it everything — even if that means a few minutes each day. Commitment doesn’t have to be the most, it can be bite-sized consistency. The Full Moon rises in your sign on November 24, sitting right on Uranus, and it’s bringing a breakthrough. That breakthrough comes because of the work you put in, not in spite of it. Your desire is to be undeniably skilled at something that is entirely your own, something nobody can replicate because it came straight through you. Commit to the practice. Show up for it daily, even when it isn’t exciting. Rewire your brain to know that you are a winner, regardless of what you’re seeing. The expert you’ve been too distracted to become is waiting on the other side of your consistency and commitment. Master it.

Día de Muertos reminds us that our dead want to be honored with music, food, laughter, and the people we love most. The Three of Cups represents friendship, community, and shared joy, especially around victory and life’s wins. November is showing you that the potential isolation you’ve slipped into needs to die. You’re typically the caretaker, the emotional anchor, the one who holds everyone together, but when was the last time you let yourself be held? When was the last time you’ve celebrated yourself or allowed yourself to be celebrated? Your desire this month is connection with people who actually see you and pour back into you, a community that represents all that you want to manifest in life. Say yes to the gathering. Call your friends. Host the dinner. Dance, toast, and laugh until your face hurts. Your spirit squads on both sides of the veil want to see you enjoying your life, not carrying it alone. Your rebirth happens in community, surrounded by your chosen family, and by actively celebrating your life, energetically. Your ancestors didn’t survive everything they survived for you to have a dull life. Celebrate.

Not everything is as it seems right now, The Moon is asking you to trust what you feel over what you’re being shown. This card represents illusion, the subconscious realm, fear, and intuition. It’s the part of you that knows something before you have proof of it. November is showing you that the illusions you’ve grown comfortable with are ready to die: the story you’ve been telling yourself about a person, a situation, or even about who you are when nobody is applauding. Scorpio season drags the shadow into the light, and you may not love everything you see. That’s the point. Alternatively, The Moon may be pointing to fears you’ve been projecting onto your reality that aren’t actually true. Consider both. Your desire is the truth, even when it’s uncomfortable. Pay attention to your dreams this month. Notice the sensations in your body that don’t make logical sense. Your intuition is speaking, and it’s more accurate than you’re giving it credit for. The rebirth is a version of you that trusts its inner knowing, without a doubt.

You’ve thought about it enough. The Knight of Swords charges forward with clarity, speed, and conviction. He doesn’t wait for perfect conditions and he doesn’t double-check every detail before he moves. November is showing you that your overthinking needs to die: the endless analysis, research, planning, and rehearsing that keeps you safely in place while your desires sit waiting. When Mars enters your sign on November 25, the momentum is on your side and the courage is available to you. Your desire is to see real progress rapidly, but progress only happens when you stop overthinking and you move with conviction. Send the message. Make the decision. Have the conversation you’ve been editing in your head for months. Launch it before it’s perfect. Not everything needs to be flawless to be powerful, and you already have more information than you need to take the next step. The rebirth is a version of you who acts on what you know instead of waiting until you’re certain. Be confident in your ability to lead yourself successfully.

Venus stations directly in your sign on November 13 and the King of Wands arrives to crown the new identity that came out of that retrograde. This card represents vision, leadership, bold authority, and the confidence to build an empire from your own inner fire. November is showing you that the people-pleaser in you needs to die: the part of you that waits for consensus before acting, that needs everyone to agree before you trust your own direction, or thinks more about the opinions of others versus your own. You’ve spent enough time keeping the peace for everybody else. Now you’re being asked to lead your own life in a way you haven't before. Your desire this month is to build something that is fully yours, whether that’s a relationship, a business, or a lifestyle designed on your own terms. You don’t need permission for that. The rebirth is a self-assured version of you who makes decisions from vision instead of fear of disappointing someone. You have one life, so make it the boldest and the best.

items.title: How psychology’s classic studies misled us about the self | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk
items.author: Jack W Klein; William B Swann
paragraphs: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk responses to their immediate environment. Lacking an enduring web of preferences, attitudes and proclivities, the contents of the H vacuus character would be filled by whatever situation they find themselves in. As a result, their behaviour would vary dramatically as they moved from one situation to the next.

Scrutiny of H vacuus would reveal a host of curious behaviours. Their attitudes towards others would be shaped by random factors that unconsciously influence their thoughts. They might feel ‘warmer’ toward others when they handle a hot cappuccino, and ‘colder’ when clasping an iced latte. Their political decisions would hinge on seemingly innocuous details. For instance, turnout in their elections would surge if they were affirmed as being ‘voters’, rather than merely people who vote. And on morality, their views on topics from abortion to pornography could depend on something as mundane as whether they had washed their hands, making them feel ‘cleansed’ and in the mood for judging others.

Given the inherent fluidity of H vacuus, trying to predict their behaviour beyond the present moment would be pure folly. H vacuus would be so mercurial that when they wed, they would effectively be marrying a stranger. In the end, being the pawns of powerful environmental forces would compromise their ability to effectively plan and adapt. Others would recognise the impossibility of holding them responsible for their actions, as they could refuse to accept responsibility for their behaviour by claiming: ‘I was just responding to the situation!’ At the end of the day, religious, ethical and judicial systems would be largely irrelevant.

In light of the many challenges facing H vacuus, it may be surprising to learn that this fictitious creature is based on an implicit assumption about human nature suggested by the work of numerous influential behavioural scientists. This assumption is that if you were to peer into the contents of people’s selves, you would discover little that isn’t susceptible to the random influences of the situation. Indeed, the peculiarities of H vacuus life described above – including the ideas about ‘warm’ attitudes, election turnout and moral cleansing – are based on claims that have been made about real humans.

We label this view of human psychology the empty-self metaphor. Although it has fostered an erroneous understanding of human nature, the empty-self metaphor has inspired a large following. These followers embrace an optimistic view in which human foibles can be readily vanquished through systematic manipulation of the social environment. However alluring it may be, we suggest that it is time to replace this Panglossian view with one that acknowledges the importance of enduring psychological structures.

The empty-self view has a long history in psychology, arguably tracing its origins to the behaviourist movement at the beginning of the 20th century. The behaviourists were almost entirely focused on ‘the situation’, eschewing speculation about what they considered the ‘black box’ of the mind. This emphasis on the situation was influential with founding social psychologists, who defined social psychology as the study of how individual thoughts, feelings and behaviours ‘are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of other human beings’.

An emphasis on the power of the situation, and its propensity to overwhelm or displace personal agency, has dominated social psychology ever since. Examples abound. In the 1970s, the author of self-perception theory argued that, rather than beliefs guiding behaviour (as common sense might imply), situations cause behaviour, and people generally infer their own beliefs by taking note of how they behave. Others made the corollary argument that personalities effectively do not exist. In fact, the term ‘fundamental attribution error’ was coined to describe an allegedly flawed tendency to attribute someone’s behaviour to their personality. Elsewhere, including in sociology, impression management research and the dramaturgical movement suggested that all the world’s a stage, with people portraying whatever character best suits a given scene. This focus on the situation reached a fever pitch with the ‘situationists’, who explicitly placed the influence of the situation on human behaviour far above any possible internal motivations.

Although situationism has lost some of its lustre, the empty-self metaphor has remained at least implicitly popular within certain circles. This is particularly true in the field of social priming, which deals with the impact of seemingly inconsequential environmental cues on human behaviour. In examples of this kind of research, seeing words related to old age seemed to make university students walk more slowly, and plotting dots on paper further apart appeared to make people feel more distant from their family.
Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has lost force

In recent years, however, the evidential tide has turned against the empty self. Social priming and other areas of social psychology have struggled in the wake of the ‘replication crisis’ – the unfortunate realisation that a surprising number of psychological findings could not be independently replicated. Many such findings are likely to have been false positives, stemming from tendentious statistical decision-making and other questionable research practices. The authors of one report found that when a number of social priming studies were carried out again, only 17 per cent of the findings were successfully replicated. A much smaller proportion of empty-self-style research has been dismissed as simply fraudulent – such as the celebrated finding that people are more honest when filling out forms if they sign at the beginning, rather than at the end.

In our own research, we’ve compared studies that were or were not premised on the empty-self assumption that behaviour is unexpectedly shaped by subtle, seemingly irrelevant environmental factors, as opposed to pre-existing beliefs and dispositions. We found that studies reflecting an empty-self view were far less likely to hold up.

Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has also lost force. Take, for instance, Stanley Milgram’s obedience studies, in which participants were asked to administer electric shocks to someone until the victim seemed to be unconscious or dead. These classic studies have been taken as evidence that authority can override individual will. However, subsequent research has found that personal traits associated with diligence and helpfulness predicted an increased willingness to administer the electric shocks. This reframes the experiment as demonstrating not mindless obedience, but often wilful collaboration – participants who gave the shocks were ostensibly helping an experimenter in the service of ‘science’.

Consider also the Stanford prison experiment, where students acting as guards in a fake prison (with others acting as prisoners) appeared to succumb to their temporary role, becoming belligerent. Attributing this behaviour to the roles the students were assigned is jeopardised by several design flaws, including a selection bias that likely caused dispositionally authoritarian individuals to be overrepresented in the study. The upshot is that participants’ unique, personal identities seem to have mattered far more than the authors of these classic examples of situational influence would have us believe.

The idea that the human mind is so fickle should have attracted more scepticism than it has often received. First and foremost, it is at odds with other evidence. The entire field of personality psychology – which investigates the unique qualities of people that persist across situations – informs us that the self is not empty at all. Measures of personality such as the Big Five traits (openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism) are remarkably stable and predictive of behaviour and long-term life outcomes. In fact, research suggests that the average effects of personality and situations on behaviour are similar in magnitude. Elsewhere, there is ample evidence for an enduring self: for example, self-esteem is largely steady over the lifespan, and attempts to break habits frequently fail, highlighting that personal tendencies impede many people’s efforts at self-change.

It is not difficult, though, to understand the appeal of the empty-self metaphor. The idea that our thoughts and behaviours are dictated by banal aspects of daily life, such as the temperature of our coffee, offers a tantalising glimpse at ‘hidden’ causes of behaviour. This is probably why social priming occupied a full chapter of Daniel Kahneman’s bestselling book Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), why mentalists like Derren Brown attract large TV audiences by showing how the ‘power of psychology’ can be used to control and befuddle, and why exciting ‘counterintuitive’ findings are published in top journals.

The empty-self metaphor also lends itself to an admittedly admirable progressive agenda (popular among social psychologists) that is focused on addressing inequality in the social environment and avoiding victim-blaming. If the plight of the have-nots is primarily attributable to the harsh social conditions that society unwittingly thrusts upon them, then the obvious solution is to change those social conditions. Ultimately, the empty-self metaphor teases the provocative possibility that society could be righted if only we determine how to control the social environment. But reality is much messier.
There is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us

The good news is that psychology appears to be slowly moving toward increased acceptance of what’s called ‘interactionism’: the view that the person and the situation interactively dictate behaviour. Many people have heard of nudging, in which subtle changes to the presentation of choices can systematically influence behaviour (eg, placing fruits and vegetables more conspicuously, to increase healthy consumption). The idea of nudging has proven enormously popular, with multiple governments around the world setting up ‘nudge units’, but initial results were lacklustre. Happily, research has moved to second-generation, interactionist nudges that tailor the intervention to the beliefs and preferences of the individual. For example, recent research suggests that personalised nudges to make healthier food purchases might be more effective than generic ones.

Interactionism likewise paves a more realistic path forward for social change. Rather than assuming that one size fits all, an interactionist approach acknowledges that individual differences inform the way people respond to social situations. Any social movement to reduce harmful behaviour or improve wellbeing needs to meet people where they are at. That means acknowledging that different individuals will respond to the same policies and political messages differently, and in accordance with their own perspectives.

Rebuking the empty-self view recognises that, far from being the dithering shells that psychology studies have often suggested we are, most of us are loyal to a reasonably clear and coherent self-concept. We do not ‘marry strangers’, nor do our relationships hinge on irrelevant details of the moment. On the contrary, there is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us. Although imputing this degree of agency and stability to the self may lack the intoxicating simplicity of Homo vacuus, we are confident that it will pave the way to a deeper understanding of Homo sapiens.
