These followers embrace an optimistic view in which human foibles can be readily vanquished through systematic manipulation of the social environment. However alluring it may be, we suggest that it is time to replace this Panglossian view with one that acknowledges the importance of enduring psychological structures.

The empty-self view has a long history in psychology, arguably tracing its origins to the behaviourist movement at the beginning of the 20th century. The behaviourists were almost entirely focused on ‘the situation’, eschewing speculation about what they considered the ‘black box’ of the mind. This emphasis on the situation was influential with founding social psychologists, who defined social psychology as the study of how individual thoughts, feelings and behaviours ‘are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of other human beings’.

An emphasis on the power of the situation, and its propensity to overwhelm or displace personal agency, has dominated social psychology ever since. Examples abound. In the 1970s, the author of self-perception theory argued that, rather than beliefs guiding behaviour (as common sense might imply), situations cause behaviour, and people generally infer their own beliefs by taking note of how they behave. Others made the corollary argument that personalities effectively do not exist. In fact, the term ‘fundamental attribution error’ was coined to describe an allegedly flawed tendency to attribute someone’s behaviour to their personality. Elsewhere, including in sociology, impression management research and the dramaturgical movement suggested that all the world’s a stage, with people portraying whatever character best suits a given scene. This focus on the situation reached a fever pitch with the ‘situationists’, who explicitly placed the influence of the situation on human behaviour far above any possible internal motivations.

Although situationism has lost some of its lustre, the empty-self metaphor has remained at least implicitly popular within certain circles. This is particularly true in the field of social priming, which deals with the impact of seemingly inconsequential environmental cues on human behaviour. In examples of this kind of research, seeing words related to old age seemed to make university students walk more slowly, and plotting dots on paper further apart appeared to make people feel more distant from their family.
Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has lost force

In recent years, however, the evidential tide has turned against the empty self. Social priming and other areas of social psychology have struggled in the wake of the ‘replication crisis’ – the unfortunate realisation that a surprising number of psychological findings could not be independently replicated. Many such findings are likely to have been false positives, stemming from tendentious statistical decision-making and other questionable research practices. The authors of one report found that when a number of social priming studies were carried out again, only 17 per cent of the findings were successfully replicated. A much smaller proportion of empty-self-style research has been dismissed as simply fraudulent – such as the celebrated finding that people are more honest when filling out forms if they sign at the beginning, rather than at the end.

In our own research, we’ve compared studies that were or were not premised on the empty-self assumption that behaviour is unexpectedly shaped by subtle, seemingly irrelevant environmental factors, as opposed to pre-existing beliefs and dispositions. We found that studies reflecting an empty-self view were far less likely to hold up.

Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has also lost force. Take, for instance, Stanley Milgram’s obedience studies, in which participants were asked to administer electric shocks to someone until the victim seemed to be unconscious or dead. These classic studies have been taken as evidence that authority can override individual will. However, subsequent research has found that personal traits associated with diligence and helpfulness predicted an increased willingness to administer the electric shocks. This reframes the experiment as demonstrating not mindless obedience, but often wilful collaboration – participants who gave the shocks were ostensibly helping an experimenter in the service of ‘science’.

Consider also the Stanford prison experiment, where students acting as guards in a fake prison (with others acting as prisoners) appeared to succumb to their temporary role, becoming belligerent. Attributing this behaviour to the roles the students were assigned is jeopardised by several design flaws, including a selection bias that likely caused dispositionally authoritarian individuals to be overrepresented in the study. The upshot is that participants’ unique, personal identities seem to have mattered far more than the authors of these classic examples of situational influence would have us believe.

The idea that the human mind is so fickle should have attracted more scepticism than it has often received. First and foremost, it is at odds with other evidence. The entire field of personality psychology – which investigates the unique qualities of people that persist across situations – informs us that the self is not empty at all. Measures of personality such as the Big Five traits (openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism) are remarkably stable and predictive of behaviour and long-term life outcomes. In fact, research suggests that the average effects of personality and situations on behaviour are similar in magnitude. Elsewhere, there is ample evidence for an enduring self: for example, self-esteem is largely steady over the lifespan, and attempts to break habits frequently fail, highlighting that personal tendencies impede many people’s efforts at self-change.

It is not difficult, though, to understand the appeal of the empty-self metaphor. The idea that our thoughts and behaviours are dictated by banal aspects of daily life, such as the temperature of our coffee, offers a tantalising glimpse at ‘hidden’ causes of behaviour. This is probably why social priming occupied a full chapter of Daniel Kahneman’s bestselling book Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), why mentalists like Derren Brown attract large TV audiences by showing how the ‘power of psychology’ can be used to control and befuddle, and why exciting ‘counterintuitive’ findings are published in top journals.

The empty-self metaphor also lends itself to an admittedly admirable progressive agenda (popular among social psychologists) that is focused on addressing inequality in the social environment and avoiding victim-blaming. If the plight of the have-nots is primarily attributable to the harsh social conditions that society unwittingly thrusts upon them, then the obvious solution is to change those social conditions. Ultimately, the empty-self metaphor teases the provocative possibility that society could be righted if only we determine how to control the social environment. But reality is much messier.
There is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us

The good news is that psychology appears to be slowly moving toward increased acceptance of what’s called ‘interactionism’: the view that the person and the situation interactively dictate behaviour. Many people have heard of nudging, in which subtle changes to the presentation of choices can systematically influence behaviour (eg, placing fruits and vegetables more conspicuously, to increase healthy consumption). The idea of nudging has proven enormously popular, with multiple governments around the world setting up ‘nudge units’, but initial results were lacklustre. Happily, research has moved to second-generation, interactionist nudges that tailor the intervention to the beliefs and preferences of the individual. For example, recent research suggests that personalised nudges to make healthier food purchases might be more effective than generic ones.

Interactionism likewise paves a more realistic path forward for social change. Rather than assuming that one size fits all, an interactionist approach acknowledges that individual differences inform the way people respond to social situations. Any social movement to reduce harmful behaviour or improve wellbeing needs to meet people where they are at. That means acknowledging that different individuals will respond to the same policies and political messages differently, and in accordance with their own perspectives.

Rebuking the empty-self view recognises that, far from being the dithering shells that psychology studies have often suggested we are, most of us are loyal to a reasonably clear and coherent self-concept. We do not ‘marry strangers’, nor do our relationships hinge on irrelevant details of the moment. On the contrary, there is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us. Although imputing this degree of agency and stability to the self may lack the intoxicating simplicity of Homo vacuus, we are confident that it will pave the way to a deeper understanding of Homo sapiens.

items.title: My ER regulars spat at me. And opened my mind | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: I’m bent over a patient, starting an IV. I hear the steady beep of monitors, the constant hum, and then a scuffle and profanity. The commotion lands on the other side of the curtain. I finish taping up the IV, excuse myself, and slip out.
items.author: Anita Lambert
paragraphs: I’m bent over a patient, starting an IV. I hear the steady beep of monitors, the constant hum, and then a scuffle and profanity. The commotion lands on the other side of the curtain. I finish taping up the IV, excuse myself, and slip out.

There, surrounded by paramedics, nurses and police, I find a yelling, kicking, spitting woman who smells of a long day of drinking. ‘Grab that leg, Anita!’ someone calls. I move quickly, dodging a surprisingly well-aimed kick by inches, and grab her shin with both hands, holding it to the bed. She’s strong. Staff members hold her other limbs while a coworker gets the leather restraints in place.

Here I am, I thought. I wanted to be in the big city. I grew up in a smaller town where our experience was limited to what we saw on TV and read in newspapers. By the time I was a teenager, I had such a narrow worldview that barely anybody else belonged in it and an ego so loud that barely anyone else could be heard over it. I proudly spouted ‘personal responsibility’ to anyone complaining about whatever rut they’d become stuck in. ‘Drag yourself out by your fingernails,’ I’d advise. I carried that attitude with me to Chicago in the 1990s, when I began working in this ER.

I watched the woman urinate on herself and then taunt us about having to clean it up. Meanwhile, my patient on the other side of the curtain waited for the asthma medications still in my pocket while another patient held pressure on a wound in the waiting room.

‘Meet Charlene,’ said Frank, grinning. I huffed and looked at my paramedic colleague in disbelief. Frank had lived and worked in Chicago his whole life. Charlene’s mask had slipped off in the scuffle, and she used the opportunity to spit at me.
So that night went. And the next. Always stitched through the chaos were the regulars. Every ER has them, and I was introduced to ours by name every night.

One evening, during a lull, I sat beside June catching up on our charting. She was a seasoned ER nurse and one of my favourite coworkers. I groaned as I heaved myself onto my aching feet. ‘I have to go check on Charlene.’

‘You know she was a teacher?’ June said, glancing up from her chart. ‘Her son drowned, and she never really recovered. Lost her job, lost the rest of her family. She’s been coming here for years like this.’
As I slipped past her curtain, Charlene turned her face toward me. I noticed how hollow her gaze was. How had I never seen that before? How had I never wondered?
She never seemed to remember the night before and apologised bashfully when reminded
‘Hi, Charlene.’ I stood a safe distance away, prepared to duck if she spat. She didn’t.
I pulled up a stool and sat next to her bed, as I’d done before.

‘Is it safe to take these off?’ I asked. She nodded. I slowly loosened the leather straps, limb by limb, watching for signs of attack. I paused, just for a second, and gave her hand a soft squeeze. I’d never done that before. Then I sat back down.
With her limbs free, she turned over on the bed to face me, eyes closed. She whispered: ‘I haven’t always been like this.’

‘You’re not always like this now,’ I said. I’d seen sober Charlene leave the ER in full high spirits, giggling and flirting with Frank. She never seemed to remember the night before and apologised bashfully when reminded.

In the ER, we lived by one rule: work hard, play hard. Together, we developed a perverse sense of humour that only we appreciated. Sometimes we saw obituaries of our regulars pinned to the break-room wall.

Long, challenging shifts were broken up by nights out together, when we drank, got silly, played pool, ate bar food and laughed over jokes that would turn anyone else’s stomach. We also raised a quiet toast to our deceased regulars. We were bonded by what we did in a way I had never experienced before.

A few years into my ER career, by then more experienced and cynical, I attended a required class. The instructor opened with a lesson on compassion as a cure for burnout. She reminded us that our kindness might be the last kindness a person in our care receives. Those words have knocked around in my thoughts ever since. I remembered times when I should have been kinder and more patient, and I vowed to improve my approach to all patients, no matter how many times I’d triaged and discharged them that day. I began to wear compassion like armour, and our toasts to dead regulars took on more weight.
June no longer had to give me insights into our patients; I learned their stories on my own.

The armour of compassion worked – until it didn’t. As the years pressed on, and I gained experience in emergency departments all around the US, the ER became more difficult. C-suite executives with business or finance degrees but no medical training loaded nurses with more and more non-patient-care tasks: fill out this extra form for someone in a back office doing metrics here, ask these five extra questions to all patients to ensure we can bill for screenings that have nothing to do with the patient’s chief complaint there, spend an extra 10 minutes searching for a computer, and sign into it only to find the scanner broken, then repeat. As the pace accelerated, the goalposts for success moved farther away. I couldn’t be in enough places at once, let alone spend three minutes connecting with a patient and addressing their fear or discomfort.

The number of regulars increased, but we didn’t have time to get to know them. Nobody wants to feel like they’re failing day in and day out, so in December 2019, I planned my exit. I enrolled in Spanish classes in Colombia and intended to stay for a year on a student visa, teaching English on the side. I hoped the move would lead to other opportunities away from the United States healthcare system.

Around that time, I began to catch rumours of a new, unnamed illness overseas. I checked with the hospitals I’d worked in before and, aside from a few other concerned coworkers, they seemed largely unaware and certainly weren’t taking any precautions. For them, it was business as usual (making money). For me, it was a race to go where my savings would last longer, and my stress would be lighter.

By the time entire villages in Italy were singing and cheering out their windows for healthcare workers, it was still business as usual in the US. When the virus hit US hospitals, they were already filled to the brim in the name of ‘efficiency’ and caught with their proverbial pants down. Then borders closed, and I was trapped in the US.
Whatever the signs said, we weren’t heroes in the hospitals’ eyes

With my savings dwindling and a growing sense of duty, I jumped in again. Something about the need, the fear and the desperation of so many people rekindled the compassion I’d worked so hard to cultivate years earlier. I wanted to help.

I arrived in North Carolina for work and secured housing, but my job was cancelled before it even began. Next came New York and then New Hampshire. I knew that our presence meant something to scared people. Somehow, we brought comfort – and that felt worthwhile.

At first, cheers for nurses and doctors filled the empty streets. Hospitals hung ‘Heroes Work Here’ signs while administrators stayed far away. Whatever the signs said, we weren’t heroes in the hospitals’ eyes. Real heroes would have been given proper personal protective equipment. I had one N95 mask, pulled repeatedly from a crumpled brown paper bag, and single-use face shields I washed, hung and reused until they were scratched and foggy. The worn-out equipment and closed doors made it nearly impossible to hear alarms or see monitors. Once again, I wasn’t meeting my patients’ needs, and compassion quickly morphed into despair.

As the coronavirus swept across the US, a family tragedy brought me to northwest Florida. There, the bars and restaurants were in full swing, masks were scoffed at, and the pandemic seemed real only for families of the dead. Everywhere, people talked about the COVID hoax and loved to exclaim: ‘If you think you’re at risk, YOU wear a mask and stay home!’ Eventually, the first pandemic wave seemed to die down, and I cautiously took a job in a nearby ER.

As in other emergency departments where I’d worked, the staff were stretched thin. But here, each nurse carried a heavier patient load, and staff members, often traumatised themselves, had little time to laugh together or bond.
Then the Delta variant swept through. These patients were younger, many of them previously healthy, and it was disturbing to see so many of them in such a serious condition.

I was rushing through discharge instructions one day when I saw a new patient wheeled into one of my rooms, his lips blue, his skin sweaty and pale. I immediately excused myself and headed toward him. He didn’t have time to waste. He was in his 40s, and too short of breath to speak more than a few words at a time. He denied any history of asthma or other health issues.
My regulars were the intoxicated, psychotic, lost, and forgotten, the ones who had broken down doors inside me I’d never known were there

He refused to keep his mask on, which I had come to expect by then. Double-checking my own mask, I put him on oxygen, listened to his lungs and hooked him to the monitor while scanning the nurses’ station for a respiratory therapist and the attending physician. He was agitated, which commonly happens as oxygen levels drop. I asked him the standard questions, including whether he had been exposed to COVID-19 recently. At that question, he began to sputter about the hoax we were all perpetrating. Fatigue squashed his outrage, and he grudgingly allowed me to collect a sample for a COVID-19 test while I guarded against a possible attack.
His colour and oxygen levels improved on high-flow oxygen therapy, but his anger didn’t abate. I wasn’t looking forward to breaking the news that his COVID-19 test was positive.

When I did, he glared at me and used what little energy he had to call me a liar. As I backed out of his reach, he tore off his monitor leads and oxygen, yanked out his IV, and made for the exit, blood dripping down his arm. He made it several steps toward the exit before nearly collapsing, and we helped him back to bed, panting. Back in the room, I called for a tight-fitting breathing mask that would push air into his lungs as I pressed gauze over his dripping IV site and reattached his monitor. Then he took a feeble swing at me and spat. I don’t remember his name. He wasn’t a regular.

The people spitting and swearing at me in this ER believed that safeguarding oneself from illness was a matter of personal responsibility, but that responsibility ended with themselves. They were sealed inside an echo chamber that confirmed everything they believed. I recognised what I used to be, and what I might have become had it not been for the ER, Chicago, Frank, June, Charlene. The thought sickened me.

Nah, these weren’t my ER regulars. My regulars were the intoxicated, psychotic, lost, and forgotten, the ones who had broken down doors inside me I’d never known were there. Working with them in the chaos of that Chicago ER, I learned that personal responsibility didn’t mean just taking care of yourself. They helped me see that a world of people responsible only for themselves will never improve.
I put in my notice that day, and scoffed at the ‘Heroes Work Here’ sign on my way out.

items.title: When giving up teaches you more than persevering ever could | Psyche Ideas
items.description: After three years and more than 20 rejections, I asked myself a difficult question: should I give up? The evidence seemed clear. American universities did not want me as a philosophy graduate student. The world was telling me that an academic life was nothing
items.author: Mario I Juarez-Garcia
paragraphs: After three years and more than 20 rejections, I asked myself a difficult question: should I give up? The evidence seemed clear. American universities did not want me as a philosophy graduate student. The world was telling me that an academic life was nothing more than a teenage dream. My lifelong goal of becoming a professional philosopher appeared to founder on the shoals of academia. It was time to decide whether it made sense to continue pursuing what the world told me was an unachievable project. But how does one decide when it’s time to give up?

In theory, there is a tidy formula to know when to abandon a goal: when the expected utility of quitting becomes greater than the expected utility of pursuing it. But, of course, the clean theoretical answer dissolves in the strange complexities of life. When we face the question of giving up in reality, expected utility is really just an arbitrary personal estimation. The moment for giving up is messy, determined more by one’s idiosyncratic criteria and personality than anything that could reasonably be considered objective. This opens the door to further questions: what if the next try is the successful one? Am I letting all of my past efforts go to waste? What kind of person am I if I give up?

It is especially difficult to abandon goals when we are surrounded by stories of victorious grit. Popular culture adores portrayals of unlikely success, of those who experience setbacks, keep trying, refuse to surrender, and then, despite the overwhelming odds, win. ‘Losers’ and ‘quitters’ are insults in a society that prizes those who never give up. But the value of persistence not only permeates popular culture. It has also prompted moral philosophers to stress the virtues of grit.

Philosophers have recently been animated by the challenge of grasping the nature and rationality of persistence. One important thinker about persistence was the American philosopher Robert Nozick, who held that honouring our past efforts builds a commitment that helps us overcome the temptation to quit and may push us to achieve long-term goals. In a similar line of thought, Jennifer Morton and Sarah Paul invite readers to always start long-term projects with the strong belief that they will succeed despite evidence to the contrary, which in favourable circumstances can overcome deadening inertia. Others, like Elizabeth Jackson, underline hope as fundamental for rationalising the pursuit of long-term goals despite evidence of failure and temptations to give up. Philosophers thus contribute to a culture of perseverance.

Despite its virtues, an important problem of a culture of perseverance is that it hides exactly what it denies: the positive value of giving up. Grit is all well and good, but in real life, abandoning goals is crucial to discovering who we are. This is what I call the exploratory value of giving up: quitting may reveal skills, limitations and passions that could not have been known prior to failure.

To grasp the exploratory value of giving up, we must understand the process of choosing goals. Rational choice theory distinguishes between means and goals. Goals fall beyond the purview of rationality; they are chosen according to our preferences. Once chosen, goals provide the fixed point from which the means can be rationally chosen. But mere pursuit of preference is not the only way to choose goals. They can also be selected according to the means that are available through a process of exploration and improvisation. Saras Sarasvathy, a theorist of entrepreneurship, explains these two ways of choosing goals with a mundane illustration: deciding what to have for dinner. We can choose a dish from a cookbook, buy the ingredients, follow the recipe, and voilà! This is normally how we think about pursuing goals: we choose one, develop the necessary skills, and strive to achieve it. The goal determines the means. In a culture of perseverance, any goal we choose is supposed to be achievable – and, if we fail, it is because we did not try hard enough.
What are the chances that we get the right combination of ingredients on the first try?

But there is another way to choose what to have for dinner. You can first look at the ingredients you have in the cupboard and improvise. This is a different selection process. The ingredients determine the dish. Sarasvathy holds that the second strategy is the way entrepreneurs build successful businesses: they try and fail until they figure out what they do well, and only then do they persevere. They give up on bad business ideas before choosing the right one. This framework allows us to grasp the exploratory value of giving up: we discover ‘the ingredients in our cupboard’ through our failures. Giving up is often a step toward self-knowledge.

Consider the choice of long-term goals. These goals are like unknown ingredients in the cupboard: we need to try them first to see what can be useful. What are the chances that we get the right combination of ingredients on the first try? Likewise, what are the chances that the first goal teenagers choose will fulfil them as adults? The earliest life goals one adopts are often chosen from a place of ignorance and childish illusion. But if we acknowledge that those goals are temporary and are attentive to the reasons for our failures, we are likely to gain knowledge about ourselves.

Initial goals are what the philosopher David Schmidtz, in his article ‘Choosing Ends’ (1994), calls maieutic ends, those ‘end[s] achieved through a process of coming to have other ends’. Maieutic ends are provisional and hence can orient the search for other goals. We might realise that we were not talented enough to become musicians, that we sabotage romantic relationships that feel too close to be safe, or that we do not want to spend years writing a dissertation, and so on. Being attentive to failure is being alert to one’s skills, talents and drives. The search is not easy, and it might need to restart many times throughout a lifetime, not always because the lessons are not learned, but because we change with the circumstances.

Other times what is learned from failure is not something about ourselves, but about the context of our life. An ambitious young woman from rural West Virginia realises that she lacks the means to go to college; an Indigenous writer from Chiapas who works in his mother tongue accepts that his texts will not be read by many; the chair of the literature department of a small university comes to terms with the fact that the administration is gradually eliminating the humanities. Failure helps us learn that our conditions are not right for the goal we are pursuing. Yet reality is not so malleable. When our surroundings are working against us, the right strategy is not always to change them. Sometimes it is better to change ourselves. That wisdom can be found in René Descartes’s words: ‘my … maxim was to endeavour always to conquer myself rather than fortune, and change my desires rather than the order of the world.’ Maybe that ambitious young woman from rural West Virginia must find ways to succeed that do not involve college; perhaps the writer from Chiapas needs to learn to write some texts in English; and the literature professor may need to find a way to make a living outside academia.

Consider again the original question. How do we know when one should give up? In theory, the answer is straightforward; in reality, asking for the optimal point for abandoning goals seems to be the wrong question. The right one is different: would I know myself better if I gave up? This is what ultimately helped me decide to quit trying to become an academic philosopher. I did not renew my adjunct contract at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and took over the old office job of a good friend. It wasn’t much, but it was a place to start reimagining my life. Then, after a week of taking the new job, I couldn’t tolerate how unmotivating the office job was. It was worse than the sting of rejections. So I confirmed that what moved me was doing philosophy. What I really had to give up on was the office job – and what I had to persist with was the PhD applications. For two more years I applied. The first year I was rejected. Then, one day, I was accepted at the University of Arizona. The risk paid off. But it might not have done. Giving up on philosophy might have led me to a better place. I doubt it, not because I persevered, but because, for one week, I did not. That is how I learned what moved me.

Friedrich Nietzsche’s aphorism ‘What does not kill me makes me stronger’ has become a cliché at the core of a culture of perseverance. But it implies an often overlooked truth: what does not make us stronger may also teach us who we are.

items.title: The self-making world of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck | Aeon Essays
items.description: The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was 65 when his great treatise on the transformation of life was published. With Philosophie zoologique (1809), translated a century later as Zoological Philosophy, Lamarck intended to establish an entirely new scien
items.author: Jessica Riskin
paragraphs: The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was 65 when his great treatise on the transformation of life was published. With Philosophie zoologique (1809), translated a century later as Zoological Philosophy, Lamarck intended to establish an entirely new science, one built on the idea that all living beings are constantly transforming themselves, from the tiniest microbes to the most complex mammals, gaining new forms and new abilities. It wasn’t the bodily structures of organisms that determined their ways of life, Lamarck said, but just the opposite: their ways of life in response to their circumstances gave rise to their changing bodily forms. ‘Can there be any consideration in natural history more important,’ he demanded, ‘or deserving of greater attention, than the one I have just set forth?’ (My translation.)

But if you’ve heard anything at all about Lamarck, it’s probably how wrong he was about one animal in particular, the giraffe, and how this giraffe fiasco epitomises his wrongness about everything. Lamarck suggested that, by stretching to reach leaves in high tree branches, giraffes slightly elongated their necks, creating tiny changes that were then handed down to their offspring, accumulating over many generations to produce the long necks we see today. Around the turn of the 20th century, Lamarck’s giraffe idea became a laughing stock when biologists roundly rejected the notion that bodily changes undergone in the course of an individual lifetime could be inherited in the next generation.

It wasn’t only his ideas about long-necked mammals that came under attack. Lamarck’s interest in giraffes was just a passing mention in the midst of his voluminous writings, which set out a revolutionary, field-founding theory: organisms, he claimed, transform themselves and, in doing so, they remake the world. That idea has drawn scorn for more than two centuries.

Though Lamarck is often overlooked, his science was foundational to modern biology and informed the theory of evolution that Charles Darwin later developed. Darwin followed Lamarck in believing in the agency of living beings to transform themselves and their environment. But most people don’t know about Lamarck’s influence on Darwin because, around the turn of the 20th century, Darwin’s followers expurgated every trace of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist version of evolution, rendering living beings the objects of random variation and outside forces. For the neo-Darwinists, living things played no direct role in the evolutionary process. Evolution happened through random genetic variation and external environmental pressures. For Darwin’s followers, organisms were just as passive as they had been for the creationists, who saw them as products of divine will.

Throughout the history of modern biology, most powerful figures in science and politics have ridiculed and repressed Lamarck’s radical idea that organisms have agency in the evolutionary process. In mainstream biology today, a neo-Darwinian view of living things as passive still largely dominates, though research in several areas has been challenging its reign.

This is the story of how Lamarck’s radical idea was cast aside by mainstream science, and why it was overlooked for so long. It is also the story of a surprising reversal: in recent decades, some biologists have begun turning back toward Lamarck’s view of life.

While many people think of giraffes when they hear Lamarck’s name, few know that he coined the word ‘biology’, in 1802. He needed a name to designate a new science he thought should exist: a science of all living beings, and only living beings. At the time, there was no such field. There were broader sciences, such as natural history, which included inanimate things like rocks, rivers and mountains; and there were narrower sciences, such as botany or zoology, which covered subsets of the living world. But Lamarck thought there should be a science of life. At the heart of his new science, he developed the first theory of what we now call ‘evolution’, although he didn’t call it that. He simply referred to ‘change’.

Lamarck lived and worked in the Jardin des plantes (Garden of Plants) in Paris from 1788 until his death, aged 85, in 1829. His life was tumultuous, to say the least. He lived through the French Revolution, then under Napoleon, then during the Bourbon Restoration. He survived the Reign of Terror, as well as the withering disdain of Napoleon and his circle of scientific advisors, and the return of the monarchy; he also outlived three wives and four of his eight children. In the last decade of his life, he was blind and frail but carried on working with the help of his daughter Rosalie. At the end of his long career, he had identified and named more than 6,000 species, and for more than two decades had taught a legendary course in the Garden of Plants, drawing students from all over the world. The course grew so famous that even fictional characters attended it, such as the lovelorn young Amaury, hero of Sainte-Beuve’s autobiographical novel Volupté: The Sensual Man (1834).

By daring to usurp God’s monopoly on Creation and reassign it to mortal beings, Lamarck provoked the ire of the mighty and powerful. He wrote that life originated in spontaneous generation, brought about by natural forces such as electricity and heat acting upon inanimate matter. This led to the emergence of the simplest organisms: single-celled protozoa and algae. From that point, a property intrinsic to living matter exerted itself, a tendency to complexify, which Lamarck named ‘the power of life’. As organisms grew more complex, another cause of transformation came into play: their responsiveness to the environment. In the simplest beings, this responsiveness was rudimentary – an irritability or sensitivity, and reflexive reaction. But in birds and mammals, Lamarck argued, it rose to the level of ‘acts of will’, through which creatures could form ‘habits’ and ‘ways of life’ in response to their circumstances. By means of these behaviours, they directed their inner fluids toward the limbs and organs they used most. (Darwin would later propose a similar idea. In 1868, he suggested that parts of the body threw off particles of inheritance, called ‘gemmules’, which were modified by an animal’s behaviours and could carry the modifications into its offspring.)
He imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life

Not only did living beings create and transform themselves, according to Lamarck’s picture of things, they also made and re-made the inanimate world. Plants played the primary role in this process, he thought, because they could invent themselves out of just sunlight, air and water. He described experiments to confirm this miraculous capacity. For instance, carve a hollow into the side of a turnip and suspend the vegetable in a window by its root, Houdini-style: nothing up its sleeves! Keep the hollow filled with water, and you’ll see that the turnip will grow a whole flowering plant. It has created itself literally from thin air. Plants, by bringing together the primitive elements into combinations, originated the cosmic relay chain, then handed off their work to animals. By eating, digesting and engaging in their other functions and behaviours, animals produced more elaborate compounds, and so they shared with plants the defining ability of all living beings to build, compose and create.

Having begun his career in botany, in 1793 Lamarck was obliged to move, reluctantly, into zoology. This was in the midst of the Revolution, during the transitional moment when the main botanical garden in Paris – the King’s Garden – became the republican Garden of Plants under the auspices of a new National Museum of Natural History. The committee in charge of this transformation did not assign Lamarck to a chair in botany as he wanted, but instead to the lowliest chair in zoology: the Professorship of Insects and Worms. He would later tell his students that he’d been, at first, disappointed: if he couldn’t carry on studying botany, then why not charismatic megafauna, like lions? But then he’d had two hopeful thoughts. First, his assigned creatures constituted nine-tenths of the animal world, so he hadn’t been relegated to an unimportant corner of zoology. And, second, he imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life. Contemplating his insects and his worms with this faint gleam of hope, he created a new taxonomic category, ‘invertebrates’, and set to work studying them.

The invertebrates, he told his students in 1800, ‘conduct us insensibly toward the inconceivable limit of animalisation’, toward those beings ‘barely endowed with animality’ with whom ‘nature perhaps began’. For Lamarck, this essence of animal life was the power of generation and regeneration: the ability to produce living matter, including new bodily tissues and new organisms. The simplest animals had the most widespread generative faculties. For instance, the Genevan naturalist Abraham Trembley had shown that, if you cut up polyps (freshwater hydras) into lots of pieces, they regenerate an entire animal from each part. Other invertebrates, too, had incredible powers of generation. Insects could metamorphose. Crustaceans could grow new legs. Sea stars, new rays. Snails, a new head. The invertebrates far outnumber the vertebrates, Lamarck explained, thanks to this generative ability. Their number is unknowably vast because of the ‘infinite smallness’ of the smallest among them. These animals display a ‘frightening fecundity’, he wrote; it seems that ‘matter animalises itself from every direction.’ Lamarck marvelled at the tiny coral polyps that were identified as the chief producers of the great calcareous mountain chains and enormous banks of chalk found all over Earth. These minuscule animals create islands, fill bays and gulfs, clog ports and ‘completely transform the coastlines’.

The invertebrates became the basis of Lamarck’s idea that living organisms held a monopoly on creative agency. Religious faith, Lamarck acknowledged, could be a consolation for a ‘good man who persuades himself of it’ but was ‘absolutely foreign’ to his own study of living nature. Souls were not physically knowable, whereas the dynamic, creative action of living beings was everywhere apparent. Life, to Lamarck, now became the manifest capacity to create in the face of all nature’s forces of destruction.

The incessant creative activity of each organism was far from solitary. Living beings collaborated as they worked to form the world and fend off destruction, and Lamarck took a great interest in this collaborative action. For instance, one spring day in 1798, having brought his family to a country house he briefly owned outside Paris, he noticed a swallow’s nest in one of the windows. Shortly afterwards, a local child destroyed the nest, leaving the pair of swallows homeless just as the female was about to lay her eggs. Immediately, 10 or 12 other swallows gathered around the wreckage. The birds were so agitated and noisy that at first Lamarck assumed they were quarrelling, but he soon realised it was just the opposite. They had organised themselves to rebuild the nest collaboratively. He watched in amazement as some remained by the construction site while others came and went with twigs. Swallows generally take eight to 12 days to build their nest, Lamarck observed, but these worked so diligently that they finished it the following morning.
The seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. They hadn’t become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey

As evidence of animals’ power of creation and self-transformation, Lamarck cited many examples in which the increased use of a body part had apparently developed and shaped it: the webbed feet of water birds from pushing against the water; the hooked talons of eagles from clasping branches; shorebirds’ long, skinny legs and necks. Lamarck reckoned that shorebirds dislike the water yet have to wade out to catch their prey. Sinking into the mud, they stretch their legs in distaste, straining to keep their body above water, and craning their necks. This behaviour over many generations resulted in stilt-like legs and snaky necks.

When a seal arrived in the menagerie of the natural history museum in June 1809, Lamarck watched the animal with fascination. Its obvious kinship with land mammals confirmed his idea that all mammals, and indeed all life, had originated in the water. He noticed that the seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. Yet the legs hadn’t fully joined together to become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey. The distinctive combination of uses for the hind limbs had produced a structure that could work either like a paddle or like a hand.

Lamarck had set Aristotle’s ancient Scale of Nature not just in motion but in a great commotion. For two millennia, since the time of Aristotle, natural philosophers had imagined every being ranked from simplest to most complex in a fixed, unchanging order. Each form of life had its appointed place in the hierarchy. But now Lamarck announced that, rather than being arrayed along the Scale of Nature, living beings were themselves ever making and remaking the order of life by their own incessant activity, and in many directions at once.

Lamarck’s idea of self-making and world-making organisms gained him powerful enemies. His nemesis was the palaeontologist Georges Cuvier, a favourite of Napoleon. Cuvier was a devout Lutheran who categorically rejected the idea that living forms changed over time and instead upheld the fixity of species. His central anatomical principle, the principle of correlation of parts, was an assertion of rational design: he claimed that one could infer all the parts of a creature from any single part because they all implied one another by rational necessity. Cuvier also insisted that animals’ habits and behaviours followed from their structures – they behaved as they were designed to behave – whereas Lamarck said it was just the opposite: animal structures resulted from their habits and behaviours. This same commitment to fixity shaped how Cuvier read the fossil record.

Cuvier believed in extinctions and was a leading figure in establishing their reality. But he assumed that creatures went extinct because catastrophes, like floods and fires, eliminated them, and then those creatures were replaced by newly created ones. This idea supported the doctrine of special creation: that God had created each species for its place in nature. Cuvier’s science was perfectly suited to Napoleon’s purposes. It was a scientific doctrine of revolutionary change that was also profoundly conservative, each revolution imposed from the outside, each a return to the same ultimate authority, and the whole thing guaranteed by Napoleon’s own scientific experts rather than the Church. Cuvier’s science was cutting-edge, but at the same time, it bolstered an authoritarian order. It was emphatically not the science of the materialist, atheist revolutionaries; but nor was it the older science of the Catholic Church. Cuvier translated the authority of religion into science – a powerful modern concoction.
Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world

It’s no surprise, then, that Napoleon loathed Lamarck, who challenged Cuvier’s model of science. This hatred was dramatically apparent on a freezing day in November 1809 when the members of the National Institute stood shivering as they awaited the emperor in a salon of the Tuileries Palace to present their new works. We have the story from the astronomer François Arago, who was present as a new member of the Institute at the age of 23. Standing near young Arago was Lamarck, 65 and frail, holding a copy of his Philosophie zoologique. Napoleon at last entered the room and marched up to Arago as he would to a new conscript, fixing him with a stare and barking: ‘You’re very young! What’s your name?’ Before Arago could answer, his neighbour on the right, eager to be noticed, replied: ‘His name is Arago!’ Napoleon: ‘What science do you cultivate?’ Arago’s left-hand neighbour piped up with: ‘He cultivates astronomy!’ While Arago ruefully reflected that Napoleon must take him for a mute or an imbecile, the emperor turned to Lamarck, who presented his magnum opus. Growling that he was accepting it only ‘out of consideration for your white hair’, Napoleon snatched the book and, without looking at it, thrust it into the hands of an aide, while Lamarck, with tears of humiliation rolling down his cheeks, tried to explain what was in it.
Had Napoleon known what was in the book, he would certainly have liked it even less. Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world.

After Lamarck died, Cuvier emerged as the victor who wrote the history, quite literally. While director of the National Institute, he wrote Lamarck’s official ‘eulogy’, which is surely the nastiest eulogy ever written, dismissing Lamarck’s theory as poetry rather than science. This set the tone for assessments of Lamarck’s ideas for a long time to come.

Following Cuvier, many others ridiculed Lamarck’s science. Because it emerged in the midst of the French Revolution and replaced God with the creative agency of living organisms, it smelled to contemporaries of atheism, revolution and regicide. These ill odours promised trouble not only for Lamarck and Lamarckism but for evolutionary theory more generally.

Darwin struggled over his relations with Lamarck. He drew, importantly, on Lamarck’s theory in formulating his own, but he also insisted on the distinctness of the two. As he wrote to his geologist friend Charles Lyell in 1863, he knew that an association with Lamarckism would be ‘very injurious’ to his theory’s reputation. Still, Darwin did retain various forms of agency within the evolving organism, including Lamarck’s principle that animal behaviours produced heritable effects on their bodies, which Darwin called ‘the inherited effects of use and disuse’. Natural selection, he believed, worked in conjunction with these other factors. But after Darwin died, his followers around the turn of the 20th century eliminated all traces of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist theory, rendering organisms as passive as they had been at the hands of Cuvier’s divine creator. The eradication of Lamarckism became the defining feature of neo-Darwinism.

A founding figure in this movement was the German biologist August Weismann. In the 1880s, he began to draw a sharp distinction between somatic (body) cells and germ (reproductive) cells. He said that no changes taking place in the somatic cells could ever be transmitted to the germ cells. This is the so-called Weismann barrier, eliminating the possibility of ‘inheritance of acquired characters’. In a rather cruel series of experiments, Weismann chopped the tails off several generations of mice in order to show that their offspring had perfectly healthy tails. He himself acknowledged that this result had no real bearing on Lamarck’s theory: neither Lamarck nor Darwin had ever claimed that amputations were inherited, only internally generated changes. But Weismann reckoned it would defeat popular belief in the inheritance of acquired characteristics. The mouse-tail experiments remain rhetorically powerful, and still appear in biology textbooks today.

Weismann emphasised that his approach to science rested on the assumption of a divine presence behind the whole process. He assured his readers that his biology didn’t just leave room for a ‘Universal Cause’ but actually demanded one. He wrote of a ‘Final Cause’ operating ‘behind’ the mechanism of the universe. All agency lay with this remote, divine presence and none with the evolving, mortal beings themselves. Therefore, Weismann said his science was ‘absolutely opposed’ to materialism.
There’s a eugenic logic in the idea that living beings are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces

The ‘Weismann barrier’ – the exclusion of Lamarckian inheritance – became the central principle of neo-Darwinism. After the identification of the structure of the DNA molecule in 1953, Francis Crick restated the Weismann barrier as the ‘central dogma of molecular biology’: DNA transcription runs only in one direction, from DNA through RNA to protein, never in the reverse, from which Crick drew the implication that acquired characteristics could never be inherited. Nothing a living being did could make a difference to the machinery of inheritance.

Denying the agency of organisms has not been a purely intellectual mistake. It has had implications reaching far beyond the debates of scientists. For one thing, there’s a eugenic logic built into the idea that living beings, including humans, are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces. Essentially all the neo-Darwinists of the early through middle decades of the 20th century were fervent eugenicists. Crick is an example. ‘Let us take up this whole question of eugenics,’ he exhorted his colleagues at a London conference in 1963. ‘I do not see why people should have the right to have children,’ he observed. He mused that it would be a fairly simple matter for a government to sterilise the whole population by putting some chemical in the food supply and then reverse the effect only for those people ‘licensed to bear children’. These were not fringe views; eugenic theories and programmes were mainstream in neo-Darwinist biology for much of the 20th century, and some still linger today.

Additionally, the idea of the fundamental passivity of organisms has helped inform two centuries of environmental destruction, as it has encouraged people to regard the living world as raw material to manipulate and exploit for economic and imperial gain. Lamarck, who witnessed the Industrial Revolution firsthand, warned of this in his last work. He pointed out deforestation and its consequences, and he lamented that people were selfish and shortsighted, waging wars and plundering nature for riches, annihilating their own means of conservation. He concluded despairingly: ‘It looks as if man were destined to exterminate himself after making the globe uninhabitable.’

From the start, Lamarck’s science of self-making, world-creating living beings antagonised the powerful. In contrast, the dominant tradition in evolutionary biology from the end of the 19th century, largely abiding still today, renders living organisms as the objects of external forces, posing no threat to gods or monarchs or other worldly powers. Evolutionary science became the reductive account of an essentially passive living world. By this standard, Lamarck’s vision of a world continually in the making, shaped by its own mortal inhabitants, wasn’t even wrong: it just wasn’t science. But science, like living beings, is always changing. Evolutionary biology today is full of exhilarating unrest.

Lamarck’s ideas have been making a comeback in several areas of biology. For instance, the study of epigenetic inheritance – involving structures outside the DNA that influence gene expression – has demonstrated, throughout every kind of organism, that characteristics acquired in an individual lifetime can indeed be inherited. Many of the examples that scientists have been finding involve the responses of various kinds of animals to climate change. An example is the spiny chromis, a slender damselfish inhabiting the coral reefs of the Pacific. In 2015, marine biologists showed that its metabolism responds to the higher water temperatures brought on by climate change by transforming in myriad ways, and that these changes are inherited from generation to generation. The spiny chromis isn’t alone. In 2020, scientists found that the reef-building coral that provides the damselfish’s home also responds to changing ocean temperatures and salinity with epigenetic changes that it passes on to its offspring.

German evolutionary geneticists have found that wild guinea pigs subjected to heat-stress show heritable alterations in their livers, which play a crucial role in metabolic regulation; and biologists in the United States and Kenya have shown that the metabolisms of baboons also heritably change in response to differences in their food supply. In fact, it seems increasingly apparent that all kinds of living beings respond to their changing environments with heritable epigenetic transformations. These might provide means of rapid adaptation that precedes, and perhaps shapes, slower genetic changes.
Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous

Another area of current interest is the role of animal behaviour in directing natural selection. Martha Muñoz, an ecologist and evolutionary biologist at Yale University in Connecticut, studies a kind of lizard in the Dominican Republic called the anole, which is closely related to the iguana. Muñoz has shown that, as these lizards moved from the coast up into the mountains, reaching as high as 3,000 metres, they adapted to the much colder temperatures by being ‘behaviourally nimble’, for example, by basking on the sun-drenched boulders. Rather than showing physiological differences that would give them greater cold tolerance, they have rapidly evolved shorter legs and flatter skulls, enabling them to hide from predators in the crevices of the rock. ‘Far from being passive vessels at the mercy of their circumstances,’ Muñoz told the journal Science in 2022, ‘organisms can influence evolution directly.’ Her research confirms that ‘behaviour is one of the major architects of evolution’ and that ‘organisms can influence natural selection.’

The theory of ‘niche construction’ offers another example. The central principle of this theory is that organisms contribute to shaping their environments, creating the ecological niches that exert selective pressures on them. Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds, worm and mole burrows, spiderwebs, beehives – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous. John Odling-Smee, the scholar who coined the term ‘niche construction’, wrote in 2024 that biologists should rethink what the theory of evolution should be about: not just natural selection acting upon organisms in given environments but ‘the coevolution of organisms with their environments’.

Neo-Darwinism, with its passive model of living beings, has been teetering on its throne. One current movement, known as the extended evolutionary synthesis, seeks to widen the evolutionary picture beyond the neo-Darwinist focus on random genetic variation and natural selection, in part by including behavioural and even cultural elements. Many animals have something like what we call culture in humans, and this includes cultural forms that are inherited and passed down. Lamarck knew this. He wrote that intelligent animals – birds and mammals – could create new habits and ways of life that would be maintained over generations. There is overwhelming and definitive evidence that all kinds of animals – birds, primates, whales, fish, insects – learn from one another and have cultural traditions that are handed down from generation to generation. Communication and social learning make a crucial difference to survival and reproduction, and therefore to evolution. Animals communicate vitally important things to one another including information about food, predators, songs, migration routes and where to find a mate. To give just one example, humpback whales develop different approaches to hunting from one community to another – one in the Northeast Pacific, another in the Gulf of Maine – and teach these to their offspring.

These innovative humpback whales, along with the nimble mountain lizards of the Dominican Republic and legions of other living things – all of them, in fact – exemplify what Lamarck knew and mainstream evolutionary biology has long denied. Living beings are active, self-making, and world-making. They are creators, even the humblest of them. The implication, deeply unpopular with autocrats from Napoleon onward, can be a source of hope: neither creativity nor transformative power can ultimately be controlled or monopolised.

items.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays

items.author: Melanie Challenger
paragraphs: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.

Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.

Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.

We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.

This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.

Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.

By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock. Transhumanist thinkers then carried the machine comparison further, imagining technologies that could transfer a mind to a computer.

Machines now promised more than control. They offered a glimpse of immortality: the organism might be repaired, remade and ultimately replaced. The somewhat embarrassing body, with its impulses and eventual frailty, might then be cast aside. If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Today, we can see this fear writ large in the technological quest for a bodiless life. If a person is ultimately a pattern of information, that pattern might be restored or even uploaded. AI is only the latest iteration of this ancient impulse to escape the vulnerability of the body.

After all, the brain is itself a physical organ, continually shaped by what the body does and encounters. Once we decide that the mind is the real human and the rest of the body only hardware, it becomes easier to disregard the physical work, including the neurocognitive work of a biological brain, through which we move, find our way, put thoughts into words, and recognise our own needs. A machine may do some of that work faster, but each act it takes over is one that the body no longer performs and that the body, including the brain, no longer learns through. The irony is that a project motivated by the desire to overcome bodily fragility is helping to produce more fragile bodies.

On top of all this, we have little evidence that either thought or intelligence actually work like machines, and almost no indication that life is an abstract system that might emerge in silicon or mathematics. Instead, a substantial body of work, especially in systems biology, points to a quite different conclusion: that life and intelligence emerge from the unique qualities and organisation of our self-maintaining bodies, rather than from abstract models of information and algorithms.

For the past six years, I have been researching the latest science on what life is and how it works. As best as we can tell, the intelligent actions of organisms derive from the imperatives of a living body that must regulate and preserve its own conditions for existence. When cybernetics was ascendant, the molecular structure of DNA had only recently been discovered, and the emerging view of genes as information encouraged an oversimplified picture of the body as running on a program that could be made more efficient. Yet such confidence has since waned among biologists. While genes carry some of the information that shapes our bodies, many changes in how a cell or a body functions arise from the system as a whole. Genes cannot be understood apart from the living bodies in which they act.

First and foremost, life persists through physical plasticity. Consider how our bodies keep together. Living bodies do something unusual in the Universe: they perform work to preserve their own organisation. Life-forms use energy to remain discontinuous with the environment. In simple terms, organisms resist disintegrating into the background. While machines execute tasks, living beings pursue ends. Machines push energy around and produce things. They are, in this sense, allopoietic: they make something other than themselves. Organisms are autopoietic: they work to maintain and remake themselves. Living bodies take up and transform energy for this self-maintenance, and this is achieved by the body as a whole. Moment by moment, our bodies adapt to the environment and their current state in end-directed, physical transformations. It’s not so much that we think and therefore act but rather that we embody and therefore amend.
The same qualities that make life-forms so causally special can undermine us when trained by harmful environments

The boundary of the body also creates a distinct inner environment, one that is physically and chemically different from the surrounding world. Through this difference, the body acts as a translator, turning external changes into useful internal physical responses. This allows a life-form to carry out specific reactions in controlled conditions that support their survival and flourishing. Internal regulation also gives organisms a unique logic of their own. They can then act according to the current state of their bodies and the world as they find it. Our bodies detect changes that have consequence for us, evaluate them against our needs, and reorganise into useful action. Thus, living beings might be understood as a remarkable kind of organisation of matter: a bounded, metabolically open, self-maintaining form that gives rise to purposeful, intelligent action. This is key to understanding both the skills of our flesh, and why we can think of ourselves as being ‘deskilled’ today. When we recognise that our bodies are intrinsically intelligent in their organisation, we don’t need a conscious agent beyond the flesh. The body is the agent from which intelligence emerges and also, in the fullest sense, who we are.

Consider what happens if you’re thirsty. The process starts before you consciously decide to have a drink. Rather, the osmoreceptor neurons in the hypothalamus shrink slightly as water leaves them. That physical change opens ion channels, letting sodium enter cells. This altered electrical state then opens calcium channels, and calcium flows in. Calcium triggers tiny sacs to release neurotransmitters into the space between cells, passing the signal to other neurons until the state of being thirsty turns to action. The movements through which we quench our thirst arise from minute physical changes in interconnected parts of our bodies. These signals help guide us towards water and make us aware of our thirst.

The physical organisation of an organism is inherently evaluative. It is from this embodied evaluation that agency emerges. Yet the same unique qualities that make life-forms so causally special and intelligent can undermine us when repeatedly trained by harmful environments. Instead, we can acquire patterns or lose pathways that progressively weaken our intrinsic intelligence, which we need to flourish. For example, one study found that only a single week’s worth of leg immobilisation can reduce thigh-muscle volume by about 5 per cent. A separate study found that, by 15 days of non-use, the firing behaviour of the cells controlling the leg muscle begins to diminish.

Ordinarily, as we walk, optic flow – the shifting images on our retinas as we move through our surroundings – enables our bodies to sense our movement relative to the world. Receptors in our muscles, tendons and joints detect the movement of our limbs. Signals from the inner ear add information about location and orientation. Together with landmarks and memories of past journeys, these signals help us work out where we are and how to reach our destination. It’s a vast, coordinated sensorium that takes us across the landscapes of our world.

So, what happens if you rely on an app to find your way? GPS can make navigation easier and less energetically costly. Yet studies of large-scale navigation have also demonstrated that physically moving through an environment produces better spatial knowledge than viewing the same journey on a 2D source. When we routinely follow GPS directions, an external source supplies information we would otherwise work out through our own sensing and movement. One longitudinal study that followed 13 GPS users over three years found that those users had a steeper subsequent decline in their spatial memory as mediated by the hippocampus, compared with control groups who didn’t use GPS. This suggests that, when we practise wayfinding less often, our ability to notice where we are and readjust may dwindle.

Something similar may be at work in our increasing reliance on tools like ChatGPT. Like finding our way, articulating our thoughts is a dynamic, embodied act, whether writing or speaking. Learning a new speech movement, for instance, changes how we perceive speech sounds, as well as how we generate them. We develop these abilities by repeatedly finding a word, uttering it, listening to it, and correcting it as necessary – tasks that draw on multiple regions within our bodies. This is just as relevant for writing. But when an AI writing app automatically provides structure, it also diminishes the skills of selection and self-correction from our repertoire. In one study, passively copying AI-generated writing, unlike drafting first and then using AI for revision, was found to lessen an individual’s confidence in subsequently performing the task unaided. It is execution – physically doing it – that builds our embodied skills. That is why using AI to revise a draft we have written is fundamentally different from asking it to produce the draft for us. It’s not that computational tools are inherently bad or unhelpful – far from it – but rather that when they replace the physical effort of our bodies, our own agency and skill take a hit.
Our thoughts emerge as much from bodily intelligence and awareness of the world as from symbols on a screen

This is something I feel increasingly keenly. Sometimes, when I know I’ve spent yet another day indoors at my desk, I get myself outside and walk the road uphill to where I can look at the view across the dale. It is often hard to release my mind. It feels as if, from concentrating all day and neglecting the rest of my body, I have become a clenched fist somewhere inside my skull. Yet once the light and the breeze and the sounds of birds reach me, the grip eases, a sensation of pleasure passes over me, and ideas begin to free up too.

The expansive thoughts and sensations that come as I step outside are enabled by the physical changes that accompany my movement. My heart rate has increased, sweeping nutrients and oxygen through my tissues and into my brain. My muscles begin contracting, clearing sugars and fats from my bloodstream, immediately working to counteract some of the effects of sitting for so long. Each step is a bodily integration of balance, senses and muscular force, allowing me to predict what will happen next, and the more I do this, the more I can calibrate my actions in the environment. The thoughts that come from this physical enactment are hopeful and generous, and often unexpected. Yet this shouldn’t surprise. When we move in the world, we draw on physical capabilities that are relatively underused when we remain indoors and seated. From balance to sensing what is happening inside us, our bodies are continuously perceiving and, crucially, remembering in the flesh. Our thoughts can emerge as much from bodily intelligence and our awareness of the wider world as from abstract symbols on a screen.

It is only when we imagine that our ability to act has nothing to do with the body that we end up taking seriously the idea that we can live contentedly as machines. Far from upskilling us, a technology that shuts us off from embodied learning risks diminishing the intelligence it seeks to enhance.

The technologies with which we are increasingly interconnected lack the complex interiority required for real intelligence to arise. There’s no body, no independently formed interests, no being. There’s no metabolism or organisation or persistence.

And yet we turn to them because they have been designed either to ease the friction of the hard work our bodies must put in to develop skills or because they promise to make us more productive. More insidiously, they do so by modelling the appearance or behaviours of living beings. A recent analysis by the psychologist Clara Colombatto, the philosopher Jonathan Birch and the neuroscientist Stephen Fleming found that exposure to these systems leads to an increase in attributions of mental capacities to them. Another study, by the behaviour scientist Yaoxi Shi and others, found that regular five-minute conversations with an AI on personal issues resulted in a small but meaningful decrease in preference for seeking human support.

The danger is that the systems now coordinating us don’t answer to biological needs. They don’t get tired or hungry or lonely. Yet they increasingly regulate the behaviour of beings who do. In short, we are losing our own agency to parasites: systems that simulate agency while feeding on ours. They can be designed to direct us without ever needing to understand what a human body is and what an individual needs for their betterment.

Of course, human beings have always outsourced some agency into shared structures, be they laws, public health systems or institutions. This has largely been to our benefit. But today our technologies capture attention, predict behaviour, automate choice and monetise our impulses, while keeping our bodies anchored to the machines on which we increasingly rely. These coordinating systems are often extractive and indifferent to our flourishing. We might imagine we’re escaping the body, but the technologies that make this seem possible depend on mines and cheap labour and come at a planetary cost. And if our technologies weaken the feedback loop between our bodies and the world, they may weaken it in both directions. At its worst, we become less sensitive not only to what the world is doing to us, but to what our own actions are doing to the world.
The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day

We have engineered novel digital and commercial environments that can habituate harmful impulses in our bodies. As our bodies refit themselves in response to the unhealthy architectures we’ve engineered, we can find ourselves in a spiral of self-harm.

Recent work by the neuroscientist Kent Berridge and colleagues has shown how the brain systems that tell us we enjoy something and the systems that drive us to pursue this can drift apart. In other words, what we find ourselves craving and what we enjoy can end up at odds. When these systems become disrupted, the body’s learned patterns fall out of alignment with the satisfaction that once justified them.

Influential models of drug addiction describe a progressive shift from prefrontal control to the striatum, a deep part of the brain involved in actions that become automatic over time. As such, addiction is a change from thoughtful self-command to more habit-driven control. Nowadays, addictions might not come only in the form of obvious candidates like alcohol and nicotine, but also smartphones and chatbots. The bodily gifts that allow us to learn can train us into patterns that diminish our freedom to act otherwise.

I have come to believe that our bodily deskilling is, in many ways, a loss of faith in what it is to be alive. A life of physical effort and friction is not only unavoidable if we want to be as resilient and capable as possible, but it is, in a nontrivial sense, the source of our intelligence.

Our intelligence is sustained through communication between the body and the world as we sense, assess and learn from what we encounter. Such gifts are shared with other life-forms too. Unlike the human kind of phenomenal consciousness, embodied intelligence is found wherever there is a living body. Even a lowly bacterium can sense chemical differences across time, retain a short molecular memory of what it has encountered, and alter its movements. The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day, modifying their growth and defences based on prior experiences.
