items.title: The 13 Governor’s Races Worth Watching on Election Night
items.description: While the battle for control of Congress has received the lion’s share of national-media midterms attention, there’s obviously a lot going on downballot, too — particularly across the governors’ races.
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: While the battle for control of Congress has received the lion’s share of national-media midterms attention, there’s obviously a lot going on downballot, too — particularly across the governors’ races.

This year, 36 gubernatorial contests will help determine the direction of many states and perhaps create future candidates for the U.S. Senate or president (25 major-party presidential nominees have been former governors, including 17 who became president). Currently, there are 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors. The governorships up for grabs this year are now split down the middle with 18 from each party.

The odds are high if not prohibitive that Democrats will hold a majority of these positions after the midterms (Silver Bulletin’s FLIPR forecasting model gives Democrats 85 percent odds of a gubernatorial majority and predicts one that would put roughly two out of three Americans in the 27 states governed by Democrats).

But there are a lot of close gubernatorial races — 13 competitive contests, according to the wizards at the Cook Political Report. Six (Alaska, Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio, and Oregon) lean Democratic, and three (Florida, Nebraska, and Texas) lean Republican. Four (Georgia, Kansas, Nevada, and Wisconsin) are rated as toss-ups. Here’s what to know about those contests.
Where Democrats are Favored

This contest is complicated by Alaska’s unique electoral system, in which the top-four finishers in a nonpartisan primary proceed to a general election that is determined via ranked-choice voting. In the primary, two Democrats finished first and second: former state legislators Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich (scion of a famous political family and uncle of Alaska’s current Republican congressman). But Begich promptly dropped out and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, which put three Republicans in the general election, including Trump endorsee and conservative ideologue Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage mayor Dave Bronson, and former attorney general Treg Taylor. The divided GOP and a united Democratic Party guaranteed Kreiss-Tomkins the lead and probably first place in the general-election balloting. According to Silver Bulletin’s polling averages, Kreiss-Tomkins has a steady 20-point lead over Wilson, the top-polling Republican, and is within striking distance of the majority that would make RCV irrelevant.

A late development in the race was the endorsement of Kreiss-Tomkins by Republican U.S. senator Lisa Murkowski, who has crossed party lines before (notably in backing Mary Peltola against Sarah Palin for the House in 2022; she’s not backing Peltola’s Senate bid this year, though). If, as appears increasingly probable, Kreiss-Tomkins wins, it will represent a Democratic gain (GOP governor Mike Dunleavy was term-limited). At the moment, both chambers of Alaska’s legislature are controlled by a bipartisan and independent coalition; that isn’t expected to change.

Incumbent Democratic governor Katie Hobbs has been expected to face a tough challenge after very narrowly defeating Kari Lake in 2022; Donald Trump carried the state by a surprisingly large margin (5+ percent) in 2024. But aside from a national Democratic wave, Hobbs caught a break when the GOP nomination was won by conservative congressional ideologue Andy Biggs. It says a lot about Biggs’s viability that the normally very aggressive Republican Governors Association hasn’t put any money into the race. Silver Bulletin polling averages show Hobbs ahead by 9.4 points.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both state legislative chambers in Arizona, but Democrats are optimistic about flipping both and giving Hobbs trifecta control of state government.

Iowa’s two-term Republican governor Kim Reynolds has been regularly labeled “America’s most unpopular governor” in the past two years, and that along with a strong anti-Trump wave in recently red Iowa has long made Democrats optimistic about a 2026 win for State Auditor Rob Sand (the only statewide elected Democrat in Iowa). Then, the Trump-endorsed favorite for the GOP nomination, congressman Randy Feenstra, was upset in the primary by “outsider” Zach Lahn, who ran an anti-Establishment but pro-Trump campaign. It was subsequently learned that Lahn had not severed his strong ties to neighboring Kansas and was still spending a lot of time in Wichita while running for governor of Iowa. This easily mocked habit gave Sand’s already strong candidacy a boost, and in the Silver Bulletin polling averages Sand leads by 7.3 points.

In contrast with the state’s red-hot U.S. Senate race, the contest to succeed term-limited Democratic governor Gretchen Whitmer has been relatively calm and steady, with two very well-known pols facing each other and the midterm blue breeze clearly giving the Democrat an edge. Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson has held a steady lead over congressman (and unsuccessful 2018 and 2020 U.S. Senate candidate) John James. Any traction James has obtained by urging a change from the status quo in Lansing has clearly been offset by unhappiness with Trump. In the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Benson leads by 7.9 percentage points, and the spotlight remains on the Senate contest.

Further downballot, both chambers of the Michigan legislature are battlegrounds, with Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball rating the fights for both the Democratic-controlled Senate and the Republican-controlled House as toss-ups. A stronger Democratic tide could not only lift Benson to an easy win but give her a trifecta.

In a close and expensive contest that has garnered immense national attention of late, Democratic gubernatorial candidate and former state health director Amy Acton is now favored over Republican billionaire (and 2024 presidential candidate) Vivek Ramaswamy in what would represent a Democratic gain in a state thought to be safely red. This contest was very close for months, with Acton benefiting from a Democratic tailwind (and perhaps some right-wing uneasiness with the GOP candidate’s race and background) and Ramaswamy outspending her massively and trying to exploit anti-vaxx unhappiness with her pandemic record in Ohio. Then Ramaswamy rolled the dice with a nasty ad featuring Acton’s disreputable mother (from whom she was long-estranged after alleging rape by her late stepfather). His campaign has now yanked the ad after internal GOP polling showed a major backlash that burnished the Republican’s already significant reputation for unlikeability. While Acton’s lead is 3.1 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, there’s a sense Ramaswamy’s campaign could be imploding.

Oregon is the odd blue state with an incumbent Democratic governor who is vulnerable thanks to generally low favorability. Tina Kotek is weathering a surprisingly strong challenge from her 2022 opponent, state senator Christine Drazan, despite outspending her and tying her to the very unpopular president. In 2022 Kotek benefited from a late surge, and her camp is hoping for that again. She leads Drazan by 1.5 points in the Silver Bulletin averages.
Where Republicans are Favored

In 2022 and 2024, the Republican advantage in what had been the close battleground of Florida blossomed, with Governor Ron DeSantis being reelected by a 19 percent margin and Trump carrying his new home state by 13 percent. Now there are signs that in this wave election the GOP edge has shrunk significantly. Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds, a Black GOP congressman and close Trump ally who had a relatively easy road to the general-election ballot, is facing a tougher than expected challenge from Republican turned Democrat David Jolly. Florida Republicans have been tripping over one another to ravage the state’s tax base, and their attention has mostly been focused on gerrymander-driven House races. But Donalds has a significant financial advantage and leads Jolly by 4.6 percentage points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages.

Nebraska is a very red state (Trump carried it by 20 percent in 2024), but GOP governor Jim Pillen isn’t very popular. He drew flak earlier in his first term for proposing sales-tax increases to pay for the elimination of property taxes. And he drew negative attention from national media reports that he has hired lots of undocumented immigrants for his family’s hog farm. He’s also on a ballot with two minor candidates, including someone claiming to represent the America First Party and a pro-marijuana-legalization advocate. All this has given Democratic legislator Lynne Walz some traction, and she actually led the incumbent in one October poll. Overall, though, Pillen leads Walz by 3.3 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, and between that and the state’s partisan character, Pillen is expected to survive.

It has been overshadowed by the insanely expensive Senate race in the state, but Republican Greg Abbott’s bid for a fourth term as Texas governor has run into unexpected trouble. Among other things, GOP gains among Hispanic voters appear to have been sharply reversed this year, and Abbott has also aligned himself pretty closely not only to an unpopular president but to his state party’s extremist MAGA wing with its abrasive views on immigration, public education, and Christian nationalism. Democratic nominee Gina Hinojosa has run a shrewd, middle-of-the-road campaign, and has hammered Abbott for his avid promotion of data centers in Texas (which he has tried hard to reverse this year with regulatory proposals). Abbott unsurprisingly has at least a two-to-one financial advantage over his opponent and is benefiting, like all other Texas Republicans, from Elon Musk’s massive last-minute spending on their behalf.

Abbott leads Hinojosa by just 2.4 percentage points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, but his past electoral record and perhaps a desire for some ticket splitting by Republicans convinced to vote against Ken Paxton in the Senate race could help him in the end.

No Democrat has won a gubernatorial race in Georgia since 1998, but the state has remained competitive in presidential races and has two Democratic U.S. senators. One of them, Jon Ossoff, is up for reelection this year and by all accounts is likely to easily win a second term. He has been campaigning jointly with Democratic gubernatorial nominee and former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, and the big question is whether he can help her win a close race over billionaire Republican nominee Rick Jackson.

Jackson came out of nowhere this year with a huge bankroll and defeated Trump’s endorsed gubernatorial candidate. But while campaigning as an “outsider,” he has managed to hang on to support from both the unpopular Trump and the very popular term-limited incumbent, Brian Kemp. Bottoms, meanwhile, easily won a majority against a large primary field and is running a moderate campaign focused on expanding Medicaid and legalizing casino gambling. But she faces a vast financial disadvantage against Jackson and perhaps some temptation among anti-Trump Republicans and independents backing Ossoff to split their tickets, particularly those put off by her race and gender (she would be the first Black or female governor of this state) or her association with an unpopular Atlanta city government. So far, though, Bottoms has held her own in the polls: She leads Jackson by an eyelash in the Silver Bulletin polling averages. It really could go either way, though the evidence of strong early voting by Black voters is a good sign for Bottoms.

Deep-red Kansas has a recent history of electing Democratic governors when Republican voters split, but current governor Laura Kelly is term limited and Republicans are united behind their nominee, state legislative leader Ty Masterson. However, the strong anti-Trump wave, which in Kansas has helped produce a very strong Senate candidate in Adam Hamilton, is also giving a late lift to Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cindy Holscher, who is running a strong campaign against data-center expansion and other corporate subsidies. Masterson leads by 4.5 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, but internal polling from the Holscher camp convinced Cook Political Report to shift this contest to a toss-up.

This very closely divided state, where 2028 presidential contestants are already spending time and money, is featuring a classic pick-’em gubernatorial race between incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo and Democratic attorney general Aaron Ford. Lombardo, whose base is in normally Democratic-leaning Las Vegas, had an early lead and has outspent Ford significantly. But the national breeze is affecting Nevada, too, and Ford seems to have caught up, though Lombardo still has a 0.5-point lead in the Silver Bulletin polling averages. Republicans have to worry about the sizable anti-Trump trend among the state’s abundant Latino population, and it’s not great to be an incumbent in the current sour public mood.

Wisconsin has long been one of the country’s most intensely competitive states, and a chaotic Democratic primary to succeed retiring two-term Democratic governor Tony Evers gave the GOP, united around congressman Tom Tiffany, some real hope. After a wild series of scandals and candidate withdrawals, Milwaukee county executive David Crowley, who had folded but then reopened his candidacy, upset democratic socialist state legislator Francesca Hong in a relatively late (August) primary. So far, Crowley has managed to keep Democrats united, but he has suffered from a more than two-to-one financial deficit against Tiffany. The Democrat has maintained a fragile lead in the polls but got some good news when the final edition of the highly regarded Marquette Law School survey showed him expanding his margin over Tiffany to 7 percentage points. Crowley now leads by 5.6 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages.

items.title: Haley Stevens’s Sabotage Mission
items.description: In the days before Haley Stevens did the unthinkable and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s fiercely contested Senate race, her staff and Democratic leaders were imploring her not to jump ship. “There have been an unbelievable amount of people who h
items.author: Daniel Strauss
paragraphs: In the days before Haley Stevens did the unthinkable and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s fiercely contested Senate race, her staff and Democratic leaders were imploring her not to jump ship. “There have been an unbelievable amount of people who have talked to her in the last 48 hours,” a top Michigan Democratic operative told me Sunday. “Everyone’s been in touch with Haley.”

One of those people was Maryland representative Jamie Raskin, whose takeaway Saturday night was that Stevens would not support the Trump-backed Republican. “I’m dumbfounded that Haley would tell me one thing last night and then change her mind today,” Raskin told me Sunday.

The reason Democrats were concerned was because Stevens, who ostensibly backed Abdul El-Sayed after August’s bitter primary, had recently ratcheted up criticism of the nominee, and some feared a defection. But in text messages to friends on Saturday, I learned, Stevens signaled that she was still supporting El-Sayed and didn’t plan to make any news on Sunday. (Similarly, Politico reported that Stevens told one Michigan official, “I am voting straight Dem!!!!”) “She’s told people different things, but all have been hogwash,” said one top Democratic strategist who has worked extensively in Michigan. “I think this was always the plan.”

On Sunday, Stevens announced her endorsement of Rogers, who she previously said would serve as a “rubber stamp” for Donald Trump. She described her decision as “personal and private” during a press conference alongside Rogers. And she said she was “not turning my back on Democrats,” a claim virtually no one in the party is buying. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who backed Stevens in the primary, called it a “despicable betrayal,” while Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin said that “anyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good.” Michigan Democratic Party chairman Curtis Hertel put it bluntly: “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”

When I asked Michigan state representative Joe Tate, a former Speaker for that chamber, if Stevens would be welcome in Democratic politics going forward, he sighed before stressing that the congresswoman is a friend. Still, he said, “this is a team sport,” and “when you do something like this and you make a decision like this you’re going to have hard feelings.” Another Michigan-based Democratic strategist suggested Stevens doesn’t have a place now in the party. “I think this is a bridge too far both in terms of the how and the when, regardless of the why,” they said. “I can’t and have no interest of getting in her head.”

While Stevens framed her decision to back the Republican candidate as a rejection of “hate” on the left, the abrupt nature of the move appears motivated more by personal pique than principle. In a New York Times interview published Saturday morning, Stevens said she would attend El-Sayed’s Sunday unity rally at a Detroit church with Representative James Clyburn. That evening, El-Sayed said he didn’t want Stevens to attend. In a video posted Sunday morning, she referenced El-Sayed telling her to stay away in her explanation of why she switched to Rogers. (Stevens also referenced controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker in the video and later, while standing alongside Rogers — not exactly a new reason to withdraw support at the 11th hour.)

The war in Gaza and U.S. military support for Israel had been a contentious issue during the Democratic primary. El-Sayed, a Muslim American and outspoken critic of Israel, called out AIPAC and its affiliated groups for spending roughly $30 million to support Stevens, a “proud pro-Israel Democrat.”

In recent days, Stevens and her fiancé, Jason Turkish, have fixated on a digital ad created by an outside group, Rebellion PAC, which suggested higher grocery prices are the result of U.S. support of Israel; they have framed the spot as antisemitic. El-Sayed’s campaign made clear nearly a week ago that it was “not affiliated in any way” with the ad, which never ran in Michigan and largely moved through national politics circles online.

Turkish, who is Jewish, announced Wednesday that he was endorsing Rogers, accused El-Sayed of acting “recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community,” and attended an event for the Republican nominee. (He’d later embark on a media blitz, appearing everywhere from TMZ to Fox News to bash El-Sayed and express support for Rogers.) People close to Stevens see Turkish as having an outsize influence over her thinking and believe he’s a driver of her erratic behavior. One Democrat close to Stevens suggested the congresswoman is “not well” and expressed hope that she could “get away from this situation and get help.” Stevens’s mother, however, told CNN that Stevens is “her own woman,” and it was “insulting” to suggest otherwise.

Stevens alarmed Democrats after putting out a rambling Friday statement in which she couched her ongoing support for El-Sayed and attendance at the Sunday unity rally with the nominee’s “expected condemnation” of the Rebellion PAC ad. She also urged El-Sayed’s campaign to take down one of their own ads featuring right-wing host and Rogers critic Tucker Carlson. Democrats were baffled by Stevens’s behavior, which had now fueled another news cycle. “I have no idea what she thinks she’s doing,” Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow, who also ran in the Senate primary, told me in a text message Friday night. “We have one job and it’s everyone lock in and win.”

Stevens’s endorsement triggered a mass exodus from her congressional staff, including Justin German, who served as her chief of staff for eight years. “This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines,” he said in a statement. “We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’s decision to support Mike Rogers.” Caitlin Legacki, a veteran Democratic operative and top communications adviser for Stevens’s failed Senate campaign, told me that “Democrats both from her official team and her campaign team are all united in helping Abdul get across the finish line.”

“There are multiple different group chats with both Abdul staff and former Stevens staff to try and help coordinate response and try and make sure that this does not sow any more division than it already has,” Legacki added. Even Democrats who have been critical of El-Sayed, like Center for American Progress CEO Neera Tanden, tweeted, “Standing with Mike Rogers is a betrayal of everything Haley Stevens has fought for her entire career.”

While Democrats are unified in their condemnation of Stevens, they’re split on the impact. One school of thought is that it’s too little, too late. Michigan is a light-blue state, and a large chunk of voters have already cast their ballots. When I asked one of the Democratic strategists if this were a game changer, he said, “No. But it entertains all the media in Detroit with nothing to do.” Another top Michigan operative added, “I think very few voters are looking to Haley Stevens. I think the impact is small.”

Still, while most Democratic voters surely made up their minds, the small sliver who haven’t, and may have been wary of El-Sayed, have now been given license to back Rogers. “I think if she had gone on the trail with Rogers two weeks ago, we would be talking about 8,000 to 10,000 votes potentially swinging,” Michigan political strategist Andrea Bitely said. “Now I think we’re talking 3,000 to 5,000 votes, which honestly could be the margin.”

If El-Sayed wins, as most polls indicate he will, Stevens will be remembered by many as a sore loser whose last-ditch attempt at sabotage failed. If El-Sayed loses, all the criticism he has gotten for tactical mistakes throughout the campaign, and questions about whether his progressive agenda could win statewide, will be eclipsed by raw fury. Stevens will be seen as responsible for the loss, especially if it’s a small margin of victory.

“These insider games feel like yesterday’s politics to me,” Raskin said, attempting to look forward. “We are in the fight of our lives for democracy and freedom against the MAGA party, and Democrats are overwhelmingly focused on winning back Congress.”

items.title: Alito’s Refusal to Retire May Haunt Republicans
items.description: Justice Samuel Alito has not retired, despite widespread speculation and an erroneous June report by NPR to the contrary. But suddenly, with Democrats increasingly likely to take control of the Senate, it seems the 76-year-old justice might have missed his win
items.author: Elie Honig
paragraphs: Justice Samuel Alito has not retired, despite widespread speculation and an erroneous June report by NPR to the contrary. But suddenly, with Democrats increasingly likely to take control of the Senate, it seems the 76-year-old justice might have missed his window to step down and let Donald Trump name his successor.

Democrats are virtually certain to win a House majority in the upcoming midterms, and recent indicators put the Senate firmly in play. Trump — not on the midterm ballot but still the driving electoral force across the country — seemingly hits a new polling low every few days, sinking to 32 percent in a recent CNN poll. Democrats have become competitive, and Republicans have invested resources in previously safe red states, including Texas, Alaska, and North Carolina. Prediction markets, which long had the Democrats around 40 percent likely to win the Senate, now put the odds over 60 percent.

Yet Alito — perhaps relying on rosier midterm scenarios that seemed more likely for Republicans just weeks ago — has declined to step down. In a recent interview with CBS News, Alito confirmed he did not intend to retire imminently but acknowledged “it’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term.” (While 78-year-old Clarence Thomas is the oldest current justice, he has suggested publicly that he will never retire; he stands to make history as the longest-serving justice in U.S. history in May 2028.)

Of course, if Democrats do flip the Senate, they’ll gain the power to reject Trump’s judicial nominations, including a replacement for Alito on the Supreme Court. And all indications are that they’d do exactly that, even if it required a blockade of a year or two.

Democrats still remember the Mitch McConnell–led Republican double cross of 2016 and 2020. When conservative Justice Antonin Scalia died in February 2016 — with 11 months left in Barack Obama’s tenure as president — McConnell, then the Republican majority leader, waited mere hours to announce that the Senate would not consider a confirmation vote on a replacement. He proceeded to block Obama’s nominee, Merrick Garland, for the next 293 days. When Trump pulled off a shocking upset, that Supreme Court seat became his to fill, and he quickly tapped the conservative Neil Gorsuch. Four years later, after Ruth Bader Ginsburg died in September 2020, Trump nominated and McConnell’s Senate quickly confirmed Amy Coney Barrett — just eight days before the 2020 election.

Now Senate Democrats are ready for payback. As Ruben Gallego put it, “We’ve got to do exactly what McConnell did to us.” Chuck Schumer said plainly, “One of the reasons that we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices, MAGA justices, on the Supreme Court.” Richard Blumenthal concurred: “I think it is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”

Notwithstanding the potential roadblock ahead, Alito claims politics will play no role in his retirement decision. He told CBS News, “It’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.”

But nobody with any sense of human nature and recent history believes that. Alito is notorious for being ideologically combative. More than any other recent justice, he has picked political fights with prominent Democrats and his liberal colleagues on the Court, and he has aimed vitriol at the media and others who question his motives or decisions. There’s no reason to conclude Alito is any less political or calculating than his recent predecessors.

In fact, the last seven Supreme Court retirements have conveniently coincided with presidencies that favored the retiring justice’s ideology. Stephen Breyer retired in 2022, clearing the way for Joe Biden to appoint Ketanji Brown Jackson. Anthony Kennedy stepped down in 2018, allowing Trump to nominate Brett Kavanaugh. John Paul Stevens (who was nominated by Gerald Ford but became a reliable liberal vote on the Court) and David Souter retired during Obama’s presidency, leaving seats open for Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor. Sandra Day O’Connor cleared the way for George W. Bush to appoint Alito in 2005. And Harry Blackmun and Byron White left the bench during Bill Clinton’s tenure, enabling the appointments of Ginsburg and Breyer.

The last justice to retire during the tenure of a president with the opposite ideology was Thurgood Marshall in 1991, which resulted in George H.W. Bush’s appointment of the arch-conservative Thomas. Marshall lived until January 24, 1993; had he remained on the bench until then, his successor would have been chosen by Bill Clinton, who was then just four days into his presidency.

We don’t know exactly why Alito has declined to retire. Perhaps he adopted the widely held assumption that Republicans would hold the Senate, which seemed a safe bet throughout the spring and summer of 2026 — prime retirement season for a justice finishing up a term in June 2026. But Republican Senate prospects began to crater in earnest this fall, after the Court’s work on a new term was already underway and retirement became a more difficult logistical and political proposition.

And perhaps Alito wants to protect and build his legacy as one of the most hard-line conservatives in the Court’s history. Over his career, Alito has authored landmark conservative majority opinions: the 2022 Dobbs decision (which reversed Roe v. Wade); a 2021 case that undermined the Voting Rights Act of 1965; and 2014’s Hobby Lobby decision, which invalidated a law requiring private corporations to provide free birth control to employees as a violation of religious liberty. Now Alito has a chance, perhaps his last one, to burnish his catalogue. The Court’s upcoming slate includes cases that could reshape Second Amendment jurisprudence, immigration policy, and LGBTQ+ rights.

Alito technically could still retire immediately after midterms if Democrats take the Senate. There’s nothing to formally prevent him from announcing his retirement in, say, mid-November, which would allow six weeks or so for Trump to choose and the lame-duck Republican Senate to confirm a replacement. But that would humiliate Alito and expose him as a craven political tactician despite his public insistence to the contrary. And a rushed, post-midterm Alito retirement would disrupt the Supreme Court’s work just as the new term hits its stride, leaving the conservative majority with one less reliable vote.

Barring a shock insta-retirement, Alito will be left with two options. He can wait out the 2028 elections — but then he’d have to bank on Republicans to both hold the White House and retake the Senate. Or he can retire in 2027 or 2028 and hope his replacement somehow sneaks through a Democratic-controlled Senate. But it’s almost impossible to imagine any Democratic Senator (other than John Fetterman) voting “yes” on any Trump nominee, even if conventionally qualified and relatively uncontroversial.

Over the past two years, Alito has had an extended opportunity to retire and ensure the nomination by Trump and confirmation by a Republican-controlled Senate of a far younger replacement, extending conservative hold on that Supreme Court seat for another generation or more. Instead, because of doctrinaire ambition, personal intransigence, or political miscalculation (or some combination of those factors), Alito has chosen to stick around.

To this day, Democrats lament Ginsburg’s decision not to retire while Obama held office, which would have ensured a liberal successor. Instead, she died toward the very end of Trump’s first term and Barrett took her seat. Republicans could similarly rue Alito’s decision for decades to come.

items.title: Juan Atkins, Techno Music Pioneer, Dead at 64
items.description: Juan Atkins, the originator of techno music and a founding member of the electronic music group Cybotron, has died at the age of 64.
items.author: Daniel Kreps
paragraphs: Juan Atkins, the originator of techno music and a founding member of the electronic music group Cybotron, has died at the age of 64.

Atkins’ talent agency Greensmith Artists confirmed the DJ and producer’s death on social media. Resident Advisor reports that Atkins was found unresponsive in his hotel room prior to his performance Saturday in Mexico City. Atkins was declared dead at the hospital soon after.

Born in the Motor City and raised in nearby Belleville, Michigan, Atkins became synonymous with techno music alongside fellow classmates Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May, the “Belleville Three” who are credited as the architects of Detroit Techno, which fused the house music playing in Chicago and the electronic music of bands like Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra.

After initially first performing as a DJ, Atkins formed the electronic music group Cybotron with college classmate Rik Davis in 1980. The duo released one album together, the influential 1983 LP Enter, before splitting up in 1985.

Atkins next formed his own record label, Metroplex, as well as began recording under the moniker Model 500. It was under that name that Atkins released his 1985 single “No UFO’s,” a track credited with bringing Detroit techno across the Atlantic when it inspired the U.K. compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit.

“Juan Atkins invented techno, full stop — he conceived it and named it — and one of its many aspects that he pioneered was the use of multiple aliases for different types of work,” Rolling Stone wrote in 2025 when “No UFO’s” landed on our list of the 200 Greatest Dance Songs of All Time.

“Lush and insistent, ‘No UFO’s,’ the first Model 500 12-inch, set the template for the Detroit approach. ‘They make these synthesizers and keyboards with functions that allow you to get as close to a human feel as they possibly can,'” Atkins said in 1997. “‘I think this is the beauty of Detroit, we were able to put that emotion into our music.'”

“The term ‘techno’ got exploited. I mean, even now, techno in Germany is different from techno in Spain. Here in Detroit everybody loved the music,” Atkins told Rolling Stone in 2024. “Nobody knew that it was techno music. Especially the Black kids in Detroit. All they knew was that this was a new sound. And whatever it was, whatever the frequency makeup was, it just pushed a button somewhere. When it got to Europe, Europe had to give it some kind of title.”

Atkins continued to record under the Model 500 moniker over the next three decades, as well as the aliases Infiniti (for his minimalist techno work, highlighted on the 1998 album Skynet), Audio Tech, and his own name.
Atkins also released albums with fellow electronic music artist like Moritz von Oswald (as Borderland) and toured with May and Saunderson as The Belleville Three in the 2010s.

“Heartbreaking news today. My brother Juan Atkins has passed away,” Saunderson wrote on social media Sunday. “Juan was the originator of Techno, a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included. I’ll never forget how he showed me how to finish my first record, Triangle of Love. That meant a lot to me then, and it still does today.”
Saunderson continued, “We shared a journey that changed music forever, and I’ll always be grateful for his friendship, guidance and everything he gave to our scene.”

“A great DJ is a leader. A mediocre DJ is a follower,” Atkins told Rolling Stone in 2024. “That’s what I try in DJ’ing and making music and presenting music. The public attention span is pretty short, and people are always interested in what’s next. Not so much what happened yesterday. Not so much what’s happening right now. But what’s next?”

items.title: BigXthaPlug Wrestles With Success on 'Better Over Time'
items.description: BigXthaPlug, a Dallas, Texas, vocalist with a deep, grainy, and authoritative mic presence, is one of the most intriguing voices in years. He’s the rare twentysomething mainstream rapper that actually raps. He doesn’t rely on an android-like croon like Don Tol
items.author: Mosi Reeves
paragraphs: BigXthaPlug, a Dallas, Texas, vocalist with a deep, grainy, and authoritative mic presence, is one of the most intriguing voices in years. He’s the rare twentysomething mainstream rapper that actually raps. He doesn’t rely on an android-like croon like Don Toliver or hearty “trap-soul” laments like Rod Wave. Instead, he spits hard and from the chest, his momentum hitting the ears like NFL linebacker Myles Garrett shoving wide receivers into gridiron grass. And happily, at least for old heads disenchanted with the state of modern rap, he frequently pays homage to OGs past and present. On 6WA, a consistently entertaining project with his 600 Entertainment crew released last March, he invited Texas-émigré-turned-West-Coast-pioneer the D.O.C. to offer a benediction, then referenced the old-school hardness of Too $hort and the late Eazy-E. On his new album, Better Over Time, producers Tony Coles and Charley Cooks sample the Notorious B.I.G.’s “Sky’s the Limit” while Leon Thomas revives 112’s classic chorus: “Sky is the limit and you know that you can have what you want, be what you want.”

Ironically, given his meteoric rise, Better Over Time often presents fame and fortune as a mirage that can’t mask lifelong pain. In an RS cover story on BigXthaPlug earlier this year, journalist Eric Diep wrote, “He’s in better spirits now, and not making sad music anymore.” Perhaps Better Over Time isn’t as persistently melancholy as I Hope You’re Happy, his Billboard Top 10-charting suite of broken-hearted collaborations with Nashville’s top country stars that helped land him a spot at the 2025 CMA Awards, where he performed “Pray Hard” with Luke Combs. Yet his frustration with seeing his friends and neighbors turn him into an object of gossip and envy after he successfully overcame poverty simmers until it nearly overwhelms what should be a glorious, Life After Death-styled victory lap. Much like on Baby Keem’s Ca$ino, another recent rap epic undone by its author’s inability to overcome lingering trauma, BigX can’t always navigate around his unnamed haters. His main instinct is to pull out a wad of bills and fling it in their faces.

Despite the peevish tone of Better Over Time, BigX remains a ferociously magnetic presence, someone who retains a listener’s focus with ease, whether it’s alone or with collaborators like GloRilla, who snaps with canny sharpness alongside him on “FAF.” Rap aesthetes have blanched at some of BigX’s arena-pop moves, like pairing with Ava Max on Better Over Time’s advance single, the airy and declamatory “Burn.” But “Burn” also underlines his expansive nature and his ability to encompass different sonic moods without cynicism. (The single even gives BigX an opportunity to celebrate his cover glow-up, as he raps, “Who from my state front-page Rolling Stone and proudly rep they city?”) Elsewhere, he blithely offers a chipmunk-soul delight reminiscent of early Kanye West on “Lite” while comparing himself to Jodeci and “Lil Wayne on Tha Carter III” and dominates a cipher with critical favorites Babyface Ray and Lil Yachty on “Believe.” Dark clouds may be slowly distorting BigX’s frame of mind, but moments of pleasure often shine through. “Been collectin’ this green/This big n—- like salad with dressin’,” he delightfully brags on “Cracced.”

BigX frequently alludes to the importance of family. The first voice on Better Over Time belongs to his mother. “It seems like just yesterday, you was fighting and getting kicked out of school and shit. Now look at your ass,” she says on “Stand on Business.” “You’re a boss, a legend.” He talks about making money to feed his two children and support his extended family and boasts on “Da Fucc” that he’s spent so much money on guns that “my grandma strapped with a stick.” “Million-dollar n—-, shit I got, you can’t afford this/Tryna stay off the Forbes list ‘cause that’s when they gon’ want shit,” he says on “Peace of Mind.” However, a few cuts later, he contradicts himself on “Give It All” when he raps, “I want the billions, the trillions, and whatever else, ‘cause the millions, I already got.” Big numbers like that will certainly put him on the IRS’s radar. It’s also proof that BigX is working out his ideas and beliefs in real time.

Better Over Time should give him an opportunity to expunge his anguish and, if not necessarily heal, then find clarity on why his preternatural talent has brought a mixture of blessings and frustration. He’s had plenty of success, from Drake and Beyoncé cosigns to Wingstop licensing his 2024 hit “The Largest” for a widely aired 2025 commercial starring NBA sharpshooter Jalen Green. So why does he feel overwhelmed like “a slave with all these chains”?

As he grinds away over the album’s 42 minutes, lucidity seems distant. “Wonder if I said fuck it and stayed in the streets sellin’ dope,” he fumes on “Lately F Rap.” “Would them n—-s still speak on my name for some clout?/Probably not, ‘cause I wouldn’t have an image.” On “Heal Me,” a cut that almost drowns in Florida singer Fridayy’s blandly Christian fervor, BigX admits that he’s riding in a “double R” Rolls-Royce: “My rug’s been damp from all these tears/But I been fightin’ how I feel for some years/I think it’s time I take this moment to heal.” Still, the final track centers on an interpolation of Harry Nilsson’s “One.” As producer Bandplay sings, “One is the loneliest number that there ever was,” BigX raps, “I’m out by myself all alone/Don’t feel welcomed in what I call home.” It’s a bit of a downer.

It’s easy to dismiss BigX’s anguish as the familiar pop trope of a rich man’s blues or, as Biggie once put it, mo’ money, mo’ problems. But he’s only 28 and clearly struggling under the glare of increased expectations from fans, his community, and the music industry. He may still be prone to youthful mistakes, as an August DWI arrest on unlawful firearm and marijuana possession charges suggested. Better Over Time implicitly promises that he’ll keep evolving in the years to come, even as it withholds the satisfaction of hearing him find closure now.

items.title: Real Housewives of Orange County Season-Finale Recap: The Skytop’s the Limit
items.description: How do you type out the sound of air being slowly let out of a balloon, then it makes a little squeal, then it kind of makes a fart sound, then the last bit of air comes flying out in a rush. Would it be like ffffsssssshhhhhhheeeEEEEEEEEEEEEEEbwfwbwfbwfbwfbwfb
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: How do you type out the sound of air being slowly let out of a balloon, then it makes a little squeal, then it kind of makes a fart sound, then the last bit of air comes flying out in a rush. Would it be like ffffsssssshhhhhhheeeEEEEEEEEEEEEEEbwfwbwfbwfbwfbwfbwfbwfpooof?That is the exact sound this final episode of the landmark 20th season of The Real Housewives of Orange County made. That is my entire review. I will not be taking questions at this time.

Strangely enough, the best part of the episode is usually my least favorite part of a Housewives season finale, when we check in with all the ladies and they close out their personal story lines. Emily goes with her daughter, Annabelle, and makes their own signature fragrances, but Annabelle rushes home immediately and pours hers on Shane because he stinks. I mean, obviously. He has like Pepé Le Pew lines coming off him at all times. Gina and Travis have pizza with Gina’s ex, Matt (yup, still would), and his new partner, Britt, and everything is right with their Eight Is Enough family. Heather sits down with her mother, Carole, and talks about how she felt left out because she is the only person in her family who ever experienced emotion and they all made fun of her. Is this how Marilyn on The Munsters felt? Tamra goes on a moving tiki boat and has drinks with Jenn and Carmella, and it was like the opening of Gilligan’s Island. Is this spon-con for Nick at Nite?

Shannon gets on a Zoom call with her three daughters and a pet psychic named Keao, which might be how you spell the sound of air getting slowly let out of a balloon. I know we’re all about to be decimated by our robot overlords, but we can do psychic readings remotely now? What vibes is she reading, and are they just the stink lines coming off Elon Musk and his Starlink internet service? They’re on the phone to find out if Shannon’s beloved dog Archie wants to have radiation therapy to get rid of his cancer. She and the girls want to know that they’re making the right decision and have Archie’s thoughts in mind —and clearly, the best way to get those thoughts is via a Microsoft Teams meeting with a woman who has more vowels than sense.

But Keao’s advice isn’t horrible. She tells Shannon and her daughters that Archie can feel them. No matter where they are in the world, he can feel their love; he can feel the vibrations of healing that they’re sending from all different countries, continents, and time zones. She tells them Archie says that, even if he gets the treatment, he might take a turn and he doesn’t want a long, drawn-out process. That’s all Shannon and the mini-Beadors need to hear. They just want to know their love is valid, their grief is real, and they’re doing the right thing. Honestly, neither decision is a bad one, but sometimes you just need someone to tell you you’re a good person and the dog you have cared for, fed, watched soak in the hot tub, and dragged around on a leash loves you back. That Keao told them that is money well spent, even if she couldn’t show up in person to collect the check.

There’s also a home scene with Jenn and her son Dominic, who apparently has been getting in trouble in school and skipped out on 88 assignments. The teachers had to call Jenn and her ex-husband, Will, to a parent-teacher conference about the situation. Oh, but Will wasn’t there. He called in on Zoom. What is he, a pet psychic? Jenn tells Dominic he needs to respect grown-ups, but he doesn’t seem to get it. Later, she’s having a conversation with Ryan and he tells her she needs to show these kids more discipline. He says that earlier in the season, when Dawson got his speeding ticket, she never punished him; nothing happened. Jenn also says Will refuses to co-parent with her, which seems insane to me. Is he not involved at all? And if he’s not spending time with them, disciplining them, or sending them money, why is he even invited to the Zoom? At that point, he’s doing less than a pet psychic, and if that is the case, she should cut him out entirely.

Jenn asks Ryan if Dominic acting out at school has anything to do with her divorce. Doy, Jenn. Of course it does. It entirely does. This is all about her and Will, them not being able to settle their differences, and the kids acting out because they feel like their parents are clearly ignoring something that needs to be addressed. Ryan suggests getting Dom a therapist, which seems like the least they can do. Jenn shoots back, “I’m just one person. I can’t be everything to these kids all the time.” Um, yes, you can, and yes, you need to be. If she can’t face reality, her children — and Jenn herself — will continue to struggle. Jenn seems very sweet and kind, but the fact that she doesn’t understand human psychology is absolutely astounding. She doesn’t seem equipped to survive in the real world. I can’t believe Ryan, a man with a jacket collection that would send Law Roach into anaphylactic shock, is the one thinking clearly in this conversation.

After we’ve checked in with everyone, Shannon goes out to some dive bars with Heather and Emily and has a nice conversation with a hot zaddy named Chad who asks for Shannon’s number. Shannon! Fuck this man! Fuck him into next Tuesday. Let him chain you up to the bed and pound you until you don’t even need a pet psychic and you have developed telepathic powers and can talk to all the pets like you’re an orgasming Dr. Dolittle. This is what Shannon needs above all else. If it’s not going to be Chad, I wish it could be Steve Guttenberg, who, sadly, did not respond to Heather’s DM that she sent to try to set up a double date with him and Shannon and her and Terry. The bar-crawl scene was sweet, funny, and necessary — I loved it.

The same cannot be said for the party Victoria D. Gunvalson Jr. throws at the Coto de Caza country club. (The D no longer stands for Denise; it now stands for Debbie Downer.) This party is a massive whiff for a number of reasons, but the biggest one has to be Tamra Judge. Just five episodes ago, Tamra threw a party and invited all the former castmates to attend the launch of her CBD line or whatever. While I was watching it, I thought, Why isn’t this the finale? This should be the finale. They just did it again, and they did it worse. Sure, Vicki has everyone in Skytops, the iconic blouses ubiquitous in the show’s early years, but this looks like the least fun, least crowded party we’ve seen on Housewives. It was flatter and faker looking than Teddi Mellencamp’s wig. (Guys, come on — she’s over the cancer and her hair has grown back. She did not need that wig, and she certainly didn’t need a wig that cheap.) Tamra stole all of Vicki’s thunder. She had more Housewives at her event and also invited Alexis Bellino, who, say what you will about Jesus Jugs, at least brought a little drama to the proceedings.

I can’t believe producers allowed Tamra to do that. RHOC had a long history of throwing a finale party where all the Housewives from past seasons were invited. They should have done that again to celebrate 20 years. They should have spared no expense and tried to get everyone there, not just Jeana Keough, Lizzie Rovsek, and Lynne Curtin. They should have paid Alexis, Gretchers, Lydia McLaughlin, Lauri Waring, and Noella Bergener. They should have gotten that girl Sarah who ate the bow off Heather’s cake; Dr. Moon; the driver of the family van, Donn Gunvalson. Get them all back, every single one of them. I would have been fine with this being a supersize episode if the last 30 minutes were everyone in the same room again going over the greatest hits, giving this once great franchise the recognition it deserves. Instead, we get gloopy-looking hors d’oeuvres on a sparse country-club veranda. This isn’t a celebration; it is a retirement party.

Tamra’s party also had some new drama thanks to Alexis showing up, Heather feeling snubbed, and Shannon upset that John Janssen was there in the shoes she bought for him. What did this party have? Carmella and Vicki have a fight that is as solid as a Twinkie soaked in root beer. Heather may or may not be mad that Tamra took selfies with Jenn and not with her. Jenn has to confront Tamra because Tamra is being too nice to her. Are any of these even arguments? The biggest confrontation is between Gina and Heather, and they’re still talking about Heather talking about Gina’s money. Heather’s mad that Tamra is the one who started the conversation, but Heather literally said the thing Gina’s mad about. What are we doing here? What is this about? It’s like the balloon has not only let its air go, it’s now all dimpled, pockmarked, and disfigured as everyone throws it around the room pretending like it’s still an inflated balloon.

As the party wraps up and all the women talk about their friendship and their powerful bonds, Lynne Curtin takes her unsold cuffs and teeters back to her Ford Focus on a pair of heels that look as rickety as a wooden roller coaster. She turns the radio to her favorite station, 93.5 KDAY, Hip-Hop Back in the Day. She rolls the windows down and pulls out of the parking lot and onto the freeway with her window still down and her arm out perilously into traffic. She can feel the wind whipping her limbs back as “Regulate” blares from the speakers. She always likes to look back; she always likes to remember the songs that made her feel like it was time to party. This is where Lynne lives every day, in those glory years when her hair was high and her husband was even higher, when the joints were thick and her eyelashes were thicker. But not this time, not after this party, where she stood around awkwardly while a group of women she didn’t know played a game she was unfamiliar with. She looks out at the sun setting into the waiting ocean and shouts along, hoping the sound of the bass, the wind, the traffic, and the dried leaves at the bottom of the palm trees making static on the breeze will drown out even these memories.

items.title: Russell Brand Is Not ‘Some Kind of Psychopath Who Rapes People and Thinks It’s Normal,’ Defense Lawyer Says in Closing Argument
items.description: Russell Brand’s lawyer has told the jury there is “no evidence” that the comedian is “some kind of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal” in his closing argument.
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: Russell Brand’s lawyer has told the jury there is “no evidence” that the comedian is “some kind of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal” in his closing argument.

“The fact he behaved normally during and after all of those ‘rapes’ tells you what you need to know. He believed they were all consenting,” said Ian Winter KC, defending Brand, per Sky News. “You would have to be a psychopath to be raping someone and asking them if they were enjoying it at the same time.”

Winter pointed out that Brand had left his email addresses and photographs and tried to kiss one of the complainants goodbye when he left. “Rapists do not leave their address,” he said. “Rapists do not leave their photographs.”
Brand has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault. The alleged incidents occurred between 1999 and 2009.
Following a three-week trial, both sides put forward their closing arguments this week, with the prosecution calling the comedian’s defense “a lot of half-truths” that were “spun into lies.”

As part of his closing statement the lawyer also rounded on the 2023 Channel 4 documentary that alleged Brand was a serial abuser as part of a joint investigation with The Sunday Times of London. The documentary featured five women who accused Brand of “rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse.” He issued a strong denial ahead of the broadcast.
One of the complainants in the current court case, who claims Brand anally raped her following consensual sex in 2009, said in her evidence she had watched the documentary.

“One wonders what her evidence would have been if she’d not seen the program,” the lawyer asked. “There is nothing random at all about these people coming forward… They have all come forward because they have been brought at the invitation of that program.”

“They are all, we say, thoroughly contaminated by the program. The very existence of them as complainants is fundamentally corrupted by that program and publicity and [that] renders it fundamentally unfair.”

In his closing statement, Brand’s defense lawyer called the Channel 4 documentary “one-sided” and “produced in a dramatic manner” and was reportedly scathing of it claiming to be a documentary. Winter said that Brand had not spoken to any of the journalists involved in the 90-minute program and had only been offered a “right of reply” – where a journalist typically contacts a subject of a story to detail the allegations being made against them and offer them a chance to respond – in order to “protect their defamation risk.”
He added that the allegations in the documentary had never been tested in court and that the journalists had “poisoned the well of justice” by prompting the plaintiffs to come forward.

Winter also accused the prosecution of “desperation” after they used Brand’s 2007 memoir “My Booky Wook” as “evidence.” Brand was cross-examined over passages in the book in which he claimed to pretend to be gay to gain women’s trust.

“In 2007 he wrote a funny book, ‘My Booky Wook,’ it contains some jokes,” the lawyer said. He then said the jury were being asked to “take what he wrote eight years after the event and somehow use it as evidence of what he was doing in 1999″.

Winter also urged the jury to disregard Brand’s “highly promiscuous” lifestyle when deciding on a verdict, saying “put out of your mind any distaste you may feel for the way he lived his life… That way of living is not criminal.”

Instead, he said: “Do what the journalists totally failed to do, put all condemnation completely out of the mind and apply pure, cold logic to the question: ‘Are we sure on the evidence we have seen [Brand] did do what is alleged?'”
“Disgusting, distasteful, immoral, who cares? It’s irrelevant to your consideration.”
He added: “Even being manipulative in the pursuit of consensual sex is completely lawful.”
“Brand is innocent,” the lawyer told the court.

items.title: Haley Stevens’ Unsettling CNN Interview Proves Why She’s Unfit for Public Office
items.description: Watching Congresswoman Haley Stevens attempt to explain her 11th-hour endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers over her fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Tuesday’s election to become the next United States Senator from Michigan, my primary feeling was one of reli
items.author: Alison Herman
paragraphs: Watching Congresswoman Haley Stevens attempt to explain her 11th-hour endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers over her fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Tuesday’s election to become the next United States Senator from Michigan, my primary feeling was one of relief. Thank God this person didn’t beat El-Sayed in the primary, despite outspending him in a landslide. Thank God this person isn’t eligible for higher office, now putting her unfitness to serve on full display. Thank God this person won’t be on our television screens much longer.

Stevens appeared on CNN Sunday night for an excruciating 15-minute conversation with Anderson Cooper, who remained calm and quietly incredulous in his line of questioning. Cooper zeroed in on an allegation by Stevens’ fellow Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, the elder stateswoman of the Michigan delegation, that Stevens had assured Dingell a cross-party endorsement was not forthcoming mere hours before appearing alongside Rogers at a Detroit church. What changed between that phone call and the next morning? What was the deciding factor in Stevens’ about-face?

Stevens proved unable to answer these simple, direct questions. (Dingell herself called the segment “one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched” mere minutes later on the very same program.) Stevens’ demeanor, all-important in television appearances since Richard Nixon’s famous debate meltdown in 1960, was the opposite of assured. Reflexively beginning each answer with “Look…” before failing to make a coherent point, Stevens blinked, scowled and furrowed her brow through a series of evasive non-answers. One of her favored talking points was a non-specific complaint about El-Sayed’s supposed anger, but it wasn’t El-Sayed whose evident ire toward their primary opponent was on full display.

Cooper largely allowed Stevens the rope with which to enthusiastically end her own political career. As Stevens repeatedly insisted how much she loves the Democratic Party, Cooper refrained from pointing out that her public refusal to vote for a Democrat was the whole premise of their conversation. As Stevens brought up the former Maine senatorial candidate Graham Platner’s Nazi tattoo and sexual assault allegations, Cooper didn’t ask what alleged actions of El-Sayed’s rose anywhere near that level. He simply bore down on the narrow, yet apparently impossible question at hand: why were Stevens’ issues with El-Sayed — like campaigning with Hasan Piker, or an ad linking Israel to high prices produced by an outside group unaffiliated with the campaign — surmountable in one moment, yet worth a public defection at a critical moment for a high-stakes midterm the next?

Stevens also sought to downplay the significance of her decision (“I’m an independent woman”), an odd posture for a woman seizing on the attention it’s won her with a national TV appearance to take. This irony Cooper could not resist calling out, since it’s too much to take. Stevens could have confined her support of Rogers to the privacy of the voting booth, a shameful yet private concession to personal animus over political principle. Instead, Stevens chose to self-immolate, then double down on her own worst instincts with an exchange that clarified nothing except the eminent wisdom of Michigan Democrats in refusing to make her their party’s chosen standard-bearer.

Then again, you can’t quite blame Stevens for basking in a highly concentrated and rapidly fading spotlight. Many of her staff has quit, as was evident in her lack of preparation for Cooper’s easily predictable queries; as Stevens herself admitted to Cooper, she’s a lame duck who won’t be serving in the House in just a few months. By throwing in her lot with Rogers and earning the public praise of Donald Trump, Stevens has guaranteed both her temporary relevance and the fact that said relevance will be vanishingly brief. The stammering, evasive person on CNN clearly wasn’t ready for primetime, ironically demonstrated in actual primetime. As disgraceful as her conduct may be, the American public can breathe a sigh of relief that we’ve dodged at least one bullet.

items.title: ‘Star Trek’ Star Gates McFadden Pays Tribute to Patrick Stewart: His Portrayal of Jean-Luc Picard Gave People Hope Around the World
items.description: On Oct. 28, Patrick Stewart died in his wife’s arms. How perfect, I thought. That is how Patrick would have wanted to die: in the arms of his beloved Sunny Ozell. Quite a beautiful, peaceful way to die. Other than his wife, Patrick loved the theater more than
items.author: Gates McFadden
paragraphs: On Oct. 28, Patrick Stewart died in his wife’s arms. How perfect, I thought. That is how Patrick would have wanted to die: in the arms of his beloved Sunny Ozell. Quite a beautiful, peaceful way to die. Other than his wife, Patrick loved the theater more than anything. I could easily envision Patrick’s final moments on planet Earth occurring while acting in a play, dying on stage in the middle of a performance.

There have been precedents. The great French playwright Molière died in front of an audience during the middle of a scene from his play, “The Imaginary Invalid.” He died doing what he loved: acting in a play. Everyone in the audience was laughing and applauding, thinking Molière’s intense coughing fit was comedic gold, until their laughter turned to horror. The audience was left reeling, but I suspect Molière went out thinking it was one of the best performances he’d ever given.

For a final performance for dear Patrick, as opposed to the beautiful and peaceful death he apparently had, I suggest it might have occurred in “A Christmas Carol,” near the beginning of his meeting the Ghost of Christmas Present. On the other hand, dying onstage as a wronged Shylock in “The Merchant of Venice” would certainly have been unforgettable. His portrayal of Shylock was perhaps my favorite onstage performance of his I ever saw.
Why do I even suggest such a thing? Because it would have allowed me to see him for a final time. How I wanted that!

Many of us would have loved to have seen him once more. Even though I knew he was very sick, somewhere in my mind, I hoped I would see him again. So imagining two magnificent dramatic death scenes helps me visualize him doing what he so loved.

One thing is for certain: Patrick’s reach across the continents was massive. After word of his death surfaced, the internet, not surprisingly, was filled with thousands of tributes of admiration and overflowing love for the Yorkshire man. He touched so many people in so many ways. Not only was he the captain of the Enterprise crew, he seems to have been everyone’s captain because of how he walked in the world.

What a breath of fresh air to have a leader who cared about the ethics of what he said! The result was eloquence. Seriousness. Intellect. The character of Jean-Luc Picard, which Patrick played brilliantly, was the antithesis of many of our leaders today.

What struck me as I scrolled through the hundreds of tributes was how much we humans desire good leaders. How, if we respect someone, we will work hard for them because of their principles. We follow them, emulate them because they enlighten us. They give us hope. Their dedication to fairness and righteousness inspires us. We begin to believe there may be solutions to seemingly impossible problems. That was Jean-Luc Picard and the modus operandi of the crew who supported him. Of course, the vision itself was the collective vision of Gene Roddenberry and all the writers and producers of “Star Trek,” but Patrick fulfilled that collective dream, our collective dream, by the way he acted the character of Picard and by how he carried himself in public. Patrick understood the need people have for heroes.

We want to believe in our leaders. Society suffers when we do not. If we fear retribution and feel there is no choice but to live in blind obedience to those in power, we lose our way. We lose belief in our institutions. Good leaders are those who urge us to step up and demand justice and truth. They spark our imaginations with their visions of a better future. They educate us. Without a belief in the basic goodness of our leaders, we lose faith in ourselves and our collective future. Our standards and principles take a dive.

A leader is also great when they understand sacrifice and responsibility. This is why, I believe, people tune into “Star Trek” or listen to Shakespeare, music or art of any kind. We are searching for hope and elevation from the daily numbness or despair. A desire to do good in the world works better with both kindness and focus — and it works better when we are surrounded by art and invention that lifts us. Jean-Luc Picard embodied that ideal. Patrick’s death means the loss of Picard, which for some hurts even more than the loss of Patrick Stewart. Jean-Luc gave us hope.

Gates McFadden played Dr. Beverly Crusher in the “Star Trek” franchise for decades opposite Stewart, including all but the second season of “Star Trek: The Next Generation”; the films “Star Trek Generations,” “Star Trek: First Contact,” “Star Trek: Insurrection” and “Star Trek: Nemesis”; the third season of “Star Trek: Picard”; and cameo appearances in “Star Trek: Prodigy.”

items.title: Simon Pegg, Mark Duplass and Haley Joel Osment Team for Dark Comedy ‘My Phone Died,’ Hyde Park Boards Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: “Mission: Impossible” star Simon Pegg is set to play a Hollywood agent in upcoming dark comedy “My Phone Died,” with Mark Duplass (“The Morning Show,” “Creep”) and Haley Joel Osment (“Sixth Sense,” “Blink Twice”) also attached to star.
items.author: Alex Ritman
paragraphs: “Mission: Impossible” star Simon Pegg is set to play a Hollywood agent in upcoming dark comedy “My Phone Died,” with Mark Duplass (“The Morning Show,” “Creep”) and Haley Joel Osment (“Sixth Sense,” “Blink Twice”) also attached to star.

Set to shoot in the spring of 2027. the film comes from filmmaking duo Hannah Leder and Alexandra Kotcheff, who will write, direct and also co-star. Ashok Amritraj’s Hyde Park International has acquired all International rights ahead of the American Film Market.

As per the synopsis for “My Phone Died,” when smart phones start exploding around the globe, it’s the end of the world as we know it. But for a few lucky survivors — a Hollywood agent, Amish woman, social media influencer, pregnant agoraphobic and her shotgun-wielding stoner mother — the apocalypse might just be a new beginning.

Pegg will play agent Gus, who narrowly escapes the phone apocalypse, while Duplass plays one of his self-obsessed clients who doesn’t. Osment plays a recovering alcoholic and social media influencer, with Kotcheff as Francis, who has abandoned her Amish community for Osment’s character, and Leder as the agoraphobic and heavily pregnant wannabe-actress Lillie.

“My Phone Died” is a Fire Tiger Films and Thank You So Much production, Kotcheff and Leder’s respective companies. The film marks the pair’s second feature together as writer/directors following 2019’s acclaimed indie comedy-drama “The Planters.”

“My Phone Died is a mad gem of a movie,” said Hyde Park International’s Carl Clifton. “It’s hilarious, smart and utterly original and there’s a genuine warmth that Hannah and Alexandra bring to their characters and every aspect of their filmmaking, that will make for a totally adorable, zeitgeisty and life-affirming movie.”.

Added Leder and Kotcheff: “We’re over the moon to be working with this extraordinary cast and Hyde Park, a company that champions original, global cinema. Our world feels like it’s teetering on the brink of mind-blowing innovation and total self-destruction. ‘My Phone Died’ is our grappling with that, and our nostalgia for simpler times.”

Simon Pegg is represented by Dawn Sedgwick Management, Haley Joel Osment is represented by John Griffin at Griffin Talent and Kristin Kong at MGMT, Mark Duplass is represented by Layne Murrow and Jessica DiBiase at CAA, Hannah Leder is represented by Mark Hartogsohn at Gersh.
