paragraphs: They were just two lucky people, in the eighth year of their marriage, living in a high-rise in a Texas city that no one back home knew anything about, and they were being discharged from the hospital that afternoon in possession of a six-pound-eleven-ounce baby girl, who had been delivered three weeks early, and of whom they were both terrified.

The C-section had been in the cards since their twenty-four-week appointment, but the preeclampsia had been a surprise—or a surprise to him, at least. His wife had been insisting for months that she knew, that she felt, something was going to go sideways. She was full of such premonitions. The worst thing about them was that she only ever remembered the ones that bore out, and failed to recall the significantly more numerous ones that did not. An hour or so before the C-section, in a lull between visits from the surgical team, she’d had another one. She had grabbed his arm and said, “Something bad is going to happen.”

For a moment, he’d believed her. He had never seen her so afraid. But his job was to keep the world at bay. “Nothing bad will happen,” he said. “I promise. Everything’s gonna be O.K.” He outlined all the things she had done right: quit drinking, eaten healthily, taken her prenatals and her low-dose aspirin, gone on long walks with the dog, and so on.
His reassurance seemed to work its usual magic. She wiped the tears from her face and began making small talk with the head nurse, who was palpating her pale, swollen arms in search of a vein.
“How long have you two been married?” the nurse wanted to know.
“Eight years,” his wife said. She pointed to the dome of her belly under the hospital gown. “We finally had sex.”

The nurse’s laughter was sincere, and he could tell his wife knew it. She sat there, pleased with herself, smiling for the first time since the doctor had sent them down to triage for blood-pressure monitoring. But then followed forty-seven minutes during which he was certain that something bad would happen—and perhaps already had. From his perch on the small stool beside the machine that periodically slurped his wife’s blood out of her body, he watched the gleaming faces of the doctors, with the red of his wife’s insides reflected in their goggles, and thought, Here it comes, the bad thing.

But he was wrong. The baby was pulled out, screaming but healthy. His wife was sewn back together and wheeled to her room. Her vitals and her blood-soaked pad were checked, then checked again. The flurry of people around her began to subside. The lactation consultant came in and explained the mechanics of the hospital breast pump. The night nurse took over and taught him how to swaddle the baby, whose name was written on the dry-erase board across from the bed.

And now here they were, three days later, and the only bad thing that had happened so far was that he couldn’t find the hat that went with the baby’s going-home outfit, a red onesie dotted with orange seeds that was meant to make her look like a tomato. The hat was green, and it represented the vine. They had bought the outfit months ago, despite themselves, when they were just beginning to believe that this baby might, in fact, stick around.

He searched for the hat while his wife staggered to the bathroom one last time. He could’ve sworn he’d brought it with him when he grabbed the go bag, had a clear memory of stuffing it into the front pocket.
His wife returned, bracing herself along the wall. “Any luck?”
He shook his head. “I must’ve left it at home.”
“Are you sure? I thought I saw it.”
“So did I, but it isn’t here.”
“We have to find it.” There was a tremor in her voice. “We can’t leave it here all alone.”
“Don’t worry,” he said, feeling the immensity of this fuckup. “It’s at home.”

He checked under the hospital bed again, so that she would see him doing it, and then started to dress the baby in the tomato part of the outfit. While he tried to pluck their daughter’s tiny hands through the sleeves, his wife went around the room picking up everything that wasn’t nailed down: the diapers and creams that the nurses had insisted were free, the enormous bladder pads from the bathroom, the unopened grippy socks, the compression stockings, and even the box of tissues, or what was left of it after three days of her trying to get her milk to come in early. “Hon,” he said, finding a teaspoon from the hospital kitchen in her pocket as he went to drape her jacket over the wheelchair handles. “Why?”
She burst into tears. “I don’t know,” she said. “To protect the baby.”

She tried to explain this better in the car as he crawled home along the back roads. “I had such an awful feeling before, and we got so lucky and everyone made it out O.K. and the milk finally came in, and I don’t know which of the things in the room was the one that made it happen, you know?”
He didn’t know, wasn’t like that, didn’t imbue Kleenex and ketchup packets with apotropaic powers.
“You made it happen,” he said. “You did.”

At home, they changed the baby, put her in the bassinet on the wife’s side of the bed, and counted her breaths together. She lay groaning in half sleep, dressed in the “AMERICAN BY BIRTH, TEXAN BY THE GRACE OF GOD” onesie they had bought to troll their parents.

While his wife stepped carefully into her pajama bottoms, he hunted around for the hat. It wasn’t where he’d thought it would be, in the pile of baby clothes, tags still on, that had been growing on the nursery chair. It wasn’t in the chest of drawers, either, or trapped in one of the dryer fins. He was a calm person, but he felt acutely the passing of each precarious second, as he waited for the baby to stir, to go from silence to noise, afraid of what she might need or do, of the possibility that the next waking would be the one that would render them helpless.
“Any sign of the hat?” his wife called.
“It fell behind the coatrack. I’ll just put it in the wash.”

He ran a deceitful load of laundry, then went into the bathroom, turned on the tub to mask the sound of his voice, and called Labor and Delivery. By this point, he knew the number by heart. The nurse they affectionately called Longshanks, the one who had walked them to the car, answered. “Oh, hi,” she said. “Is everything O.K.?”
“Yes,” he whispered. “But I think we left the baby’s hat there. Not the hospital hat, the one that we brought with us. It looks like a green stem. For a tomato.”
“Oh, no,” Nurse Longshanks said. “I’ll go check.”

His wife knocked on the bathroom door. He hung up hurriedly. The baby had pooped again, and this had to be noted in the makeshift spreadsheet he had started, freehand, on printer paper back at the hospital. He splashed water on his face and went out to update the input-output log.

When their friends brought the dog back, there was a brief scuffle over the new gate that had been set up to keep him out of the bedroom. It didn’t take the dog long to accept his exile, and he stood staring at the mysterious and fragrant bundle in the bassinet, with his big, curl-laden spaniel ears hanging ruefully over the gate.

When the wife went in to wake the baby for another feeding, the husband opened the sliding door and followed the dog out onto the balcony. It was a glorious late-October afternoon. The sun lolled drunkenly in the glazed windows of the half-built office building across the street. He could smell the smoke from the nearby barbecue joint. He had been planning to cook that night, but maybe takeout was the way to go. Didn’t they deserve a bit of indulgence, all of them, even the dog, who was tolerating this disruption rather well?

He was mentally assembling a three-meat platter when he looked down and noticed that the dog was on top of something. At first, he mistook it for some old leather chew toy. But, when it moved, he realized that it was a bat.
“Jesus,” he said, hooking the dog with his leg. “Leave it, leave it!”

The bat was lying on its back. The husband had never seen one up close before. It was bigger than he would have guessed, with a piggy, snub-nosed face and a scrawny tail and legs lying flat behind it, making it look as though its back was broken. The wings were awkward and ugly, tipped with crooked, writhing little hands, the outstretched skin loose and shivering between its fingers. The screeching he’d taken for some distant mechanical failure was actually emanating from the bat.
“Hello?” Somewhere behind him, his wife was calling his name. He looked over his shoulder. She was standing in the kitchen with the baby in her arms. “What should we do for dinner?”

When she turned to take the Frankie’s Pit flyer off the fridge, he nudged the bat to the edge of the balcony with his sneaker and pushed it over the side. It landed on the balcony below, where it continued to twitch, in what he queasily assumed were its death throes.

The dog keened after it for a while, then came inside. They ordered barbecue and tried to eat it. The baby woke, nursed, slept, and woke again. They opened a fresh box of diapers, undressed the baby together on the changing mat, and wrapped a conga line of Piglets around her tiny waist, doing their best to avoid the terrifying, necrotic plug that would, in ten to fourteen days, fall off and reveal her belly button.

His wife attempted a nap, but every time he passed by the bedroom door he could see her peering into the bassinet, and then it was time to wake the baby for another feeding. After that, miraculously, they fell asleep, the wife and the baby, and he was alone. The sun had set. He washed the pump parts and got the pumping station ready for later, then sat down for the first time in the new strangeness of their apartment. An odd, dense unknowing seemed to have followed him home from the hospital. He felt separated from language, from thought.

The dog came over and nudged his hand. Other spaniels had noble lineages and gentle dispositions. Theirs was a beautiful idiot. Neurotic and entirely without manners. Prone to despair-inducing bouts of obstinacy.

He was scratching the dog’s ears when the thought came to him. Rabies. Bats carried rabies. Why hadn’t he remembered this? Warnings were posted everywhere in their neighborhood, which was named for the bridge that housed the city’s bat colony. Hadn’t he stood on that bridge, on their first night in town, shoulder to shoulder with all the teetering bachelorettes and Midwestern grad dads, to watch the column of clicking bodies course out into the night sky?
He stared down at the dog. “Did you touch it?”
The dog went on looking at him with his faintly smiling spaniel face.

The husband washed his hands and called Animal Control. It took a while to find the number because apparently the department’s official name was Animal Protection. While he was waiting for his call to be answered in the order in which it had been received, he went out onto the balcony and looked over the railing. The bat was still down there. Even in the dark, he could tell that it was moving. Writhing on the Western-themed outdoor rug of whoever lived below them.

When the hold music cut out abruptly and a woman’s voice said, “Animal Protection, can I help you?,” every thought left his head. He stepped back inside and sat down on the plush little love seat that served as their reading nook. He needed to be able to see the bedroom door, so that he could hang up if the handle dipped to signal his wife’s emergence.
“Yes. Yes, hi, I’m wondering what the procedure is for when a bat has interacted with your dog.”
“What do you mean by ‘interacted’?”
The woman on the line took a deep breath. “Sir, did your dog get hold of a bat?”
“No,” he said. “Not exactly.”
“Please tell me what happened.”
“I came out on the balcony and found him standing over it.”
“No—it was sort of skittering around on the floor at his feet.”
“I see.” He could hear her typing. “Did your dog make contact with the bat?”

“No. I guess he could have. He was just sort of standing there, looking at it.” More typing. Why? He felt a sudden need to distance himself from the situation. “Anyway. He’s not my dog. I’m watching him for a friend.”
“I see. I need you to understand, sir: bat bites are very serious.”

“One per cent of the bats in our area carry rabies. That may not sound like a lot to you, sir, but, in a colony of one and a half million, that’s fifteen thousand bats. So, when you can’t be completely certain that no contact occurred, we have to proceed as though contact did occur.”
“Well, assuming your dog has been vaccinated against rabies—”
“—he will have to receive a booster as soon as possible, and then be quarantined in the home.”
“Yes. For a minimum of forty-five days. Unless you’re still in possession of the bat.”
He got up and headed for the balcony.
“In that case, we can collect the bat and test it. If it tests negative for rabies, the quarantine will be lifted.”
“That’s good! That’s good. Do I put it in a Tupperware or something?”
He looked over the railing. The balcony below was now empty.
“No,” the woman was saying. “Don’t touch the bat, sir. I’ll send an agent over to pick it up. Let’s start with your address. Where do you live?”

He started to tell her, then he hung up. His wife had emerged and was moving through the apartment with the room thermometer held out in front of her like a divining rod. She was trying to locate a good spot for the living-room bassinet, somewhere that registered the recommended seventy degrees. She seemed almost blissful. She noticed him looking at her and waved. For a moment, she was herself again—not worry-free, she had never been that, but free of the pulverizing new weight of imagining the baby’s demise. He could picture the arrival of the Animal Protection agent, some loud, careless government drone in huge boots who would inevitably pet the baby’s head, cleaving into his wife’s hard-won moment of peace. He couldn’t do that to her. And, anyway, he didn’t have the bat. It must have crawled to the edge of the balcony below and fallen off. He would try Animal Protection again when he found it.

He made the excuse of taking the dog outside, and went down to the fifth floor, where the twin behemoths of the gym and the pool deck blasted their relentless lights toward each other across a fake-grass bocce court. He tied the dog up, let himself through the security gate, and looked up. The balcony onto which the bat had fallen jutted out fourteen feet above him. If the bat had somehow crawled over the edge, it would have landed in the topiaries that separated the gym windows from the bocce court.

He looked around. The place was empty, as usual. People didn’t come to this pool to swim on quiet, beautiful nights, as he and his wife did. The other residents only ever used it when a booze-sponsored summer bash brought some Instagram-famous d.j. to the building.

He hopped the little fence and shouldered in among the topiaries. They were thornier than they looked and snagged his clothes as he crouched down to swing his phone flashlight over the mulch around the roots. The search yielded a pineapple-flavored vape pen and a pair of Chanel sunglasses, but no bat. He straightened up to find a woman in matching lavender workout clothes staring through the gym window at him from one of the ellipticals. He waved stupidly, pointed at the ground, pointed to his phone, mimed laughter, and waved again. Then he stumbled back out to where the dog was standing on his hind legs, looking mistrustfully over the fence at him.

Upstairs, the situation with the baby had devolved. Mother and child were sitting up in bed, stripped down to their respective diapers. Apparently, the baby had treated her mother to what had at first seemed like a smile, but instead turned out to be a prelude to the biggest blowout she’d had to date. He threw the soiled linens into the washing machine, cleaned up the baby, then held the strange, weightless furnace of her tiny body in the crook of his arm while he helped his wife climb into the shower.
“Remember,” he said, “don’t use any soap on the incision. Just let the water run over it.”

He could tell that she was trying not to cry. How was he supposed to tell her about the bat without sending her into a tailspin? Imagine bringing up rabies to somebody who had just been bisected and then stuck back together with what, at least to him, looked like packing tape?

Once his wife was finally settled—cleanly outfitted, the backs of her earrings jammed tightly into her earlobes so that they wouldn’t dislodge and fall into the baby’s open mouth—he lay down on the couch with the spare pillow and blanket and looked at the dog, who had clambered dejectedly into his usual spot, on the armchair he had destroyed in puppyhood.

The husband opened his phone and thumbed “What is rabies?” into the search bar. Throughout much of the world, it turned out, rabies was a death sentence. An ancient, slow-moving, and catastrophically dangerous virus transferred from mammal to mammal through the saliva of the infected. He was unnerved to learn that the incubation period could be as long as three months. Fatal, the internet kept saying. Once symptoms began, the disease was almost always fatal. Comment sections were filled with glib condemnations of relatives who had behaved idiotically after exposure.

On the subject of boosters, the internet said, the sooner the better. But the vet clinic was on the other side of town. He couldn’t just swing by. He would have to detour there during a grocery run, or some other plausibly lengthy errand. And, even if he could pull this off without alerting his wife, there was the matter of the dog’s sedatives. The dog was an absolute demon at the vet. Dr. Hottie, as his wife had dubbed the handsome veterinarian when she first saw him, had prescribed a mandatory “chill protocol” of several pills before all visits. Without them, the dog would start shaking in the passenger seat the second you took the exit toward the clinic. If, by some miracle, you managed to get him into the building, after wrangling him out of the car in that nightmare of a parking lot with a blind curve that yawned out onto the road, he would hurl himself repeatedly against the waiting-room door, making a spectacle of himself in front of everybody else’s mortified pets, until it was time to head to the exam area, where he would show his teeth and try for anyone who attempted to touch him (including, or perhaps especially, the husband himself).

No, the thing couldn’t be done without pills, but his wife was their usual administrator, and, when the husband checked the labels on the pill bottles, he found that they were so faded he couldn’t make out the prescribed dosage at all.
It would be so much easier if he could just get hold of the bat.

Maybe it hadn’t fallen off the balcony at all. Maybe the downstairs neighbor had noticed it and put it in a shoebox, not realizing that you weren’t supposed to do something like that. Tomorrow, first chance he got, he would go downstairs and ask.

He tried to sleep, but instead found himself studying anatomical drawings of the canine nervous system. He watched a video of a rabid dog convulsing in stark-ribbed agony. Then one of an infected man becoming unmade, wild-eyed, roaring in pain. Furious rabies, the captions said. Fatal.
At first light, he tried Labor and Delivery again.
“No sign yet,” Nurse Longshanks said. “Here’s my theory. Your hat probably got sent to the cleaners with all the other linens.”
“Oh, no,” he said. “That green’ll destroy everything around it.”
“That’s all right. Worse things happen to our sheets, believe me.” She paused. “How’s the little one? You getting any sleep?”

He lied and said that he was. It occurred to him, after he hung up, that the hat might not make it back to them after all. Its disappearance had opened something, some emotional clause, and he might need to close it himself by ordering a duplicate. But they had bought the original outfit in a wildly expensive boutique in Petaluma, and all the searches for “baby hat tomato stem” produced ugly, coarse Amazon dupes that wouldn’t fool his wife. He ordered one anyway, just in case, but it only made him feel worse.
While his wife was doing the morning feeding, he took the dog downstairs and knocked. The door swung open, and there, to his horror, stood Baby Jane.

He let go of the leash immediately and felt the dog take off in the direction of the elevator. Thankfully, Baby Jane didn’t seem to notice. Her wild white hair was up in a listing bun. Her makeup was almost done: the black eyebrows were drawn on, and she had gone around her lips with what must have been a blunt pencil, but two globs of concealer sat unblended at the corners of her eyes.

The husband hadn’t realized that she was their downstairs neighbor. He hadn’t said a word to her since their now infamous exchange in the lobby that spring, when the dog had sniffed her in passing while she was berating the concierge, and she, only half turning, had hoofed the dog right in the ribs with the heel of her turquoise-studded boot. The husband had witnessed this from about ten yards away, his dog and wife having gone ahead of him, so it was the wife who had surged back and grabbed a fistful of Baby Jane’s hair. Baby Jane had grabbed back. The two of them had been locked together, all elbows and teeth, frothing expletives into each other’s faces. By the time the baffled concierge stood up, the husband had already crossed the lobby and seized a couple of the clenched hands—he wasn’t even sure whose. He was shouting, “Take it easy, Baby Jane!,” as he tried to yank his wife free.

Because both parties received only a verbal warning once police arrived, he never got her real name. Ever since, though, even residents who hadn’t witnessed the incident had been calling her Baby Jane behind her back.
“You’re early,” she said, unfathomably failing to recognize him.

Under normal circumstances, he would have resisted being dragged into her apartment, but he wanted her to remain oblivious to the dog in the hallway. Save for the light-killing velvet drapes that hung from every window, her place was laid out exactly like his own. He bumped into one crate and then another on his way to the middle of the room, where an enormous desk that looked like the prow of a ship supported the kind of Tomorrowland-era computer he hadn’t seen since childhood. Baby Jane took a seat at the keyboard and gestured for him to choose between two mismatched armchairs. He perched on the armrest of the green velvet one, ready to sprint for the door the moment she realized who he was.
Baby Jane said, “Have you ever done this before?”

He hesitated. His mother had been scammed repeatedly by crooks disguised as authority figures when they first came to this country, and he had guardrails in place to prevent himself from giving out personal information under duress.
“October 22nd.” This, he realized, too late, was the baby’s birth date.
“Happy belated,” Baby Jane said. “Year?”
“1986.” This was the truth.
“And your time of birth?” He stared at her. Her face pooled into a sour frown. “This was all in the e-mail I sent you. The questionnaire? I can’t do anything without your time of birth.”
“Oh, yes,” he said. “Sorry. 5:47 P.M.”

This, too, belonged to the baby. She typed it into whatever form she was filling out, and asked him his birthplace. He said Belgrade—although he realized, moments later, that his parents had still been living in Sarajevo when he was born.
“Belgrade,” Baby Jane said. “That’s in Montana?”
“Sure.” Anything, at this point, to keep her eyes off his face.

A printer whirred somewhere out of sight, and she pushed a printout of a rune-like wheel of symbols across the desktop toward him. It looked like a clock that had been in a car wreck. He examined it fretfully, upside down.
“Don’t worry. You’re not supposed to know what it means. That’s my job. As you know”—she glanced up at him and frowned—“or maybe not: your sun is in Libra. Your moon’s in Gemini, and you have . . .”
“I don’t understand how any of this works.”

She tapped her fingers on the table. “I’m trying to explain it to you.” Now she was talking about ascendants and north nodes, trines and conjunctions. He wanted her to keep looking down at the star wheel so that she wouldn’t study his face. It was also too late now to tell her why he had really come. How was he supposed to introduce the subject of the bat? Here she was, with the star chart outlining the fate of a fictitious person who shared his baby’s birth date and time, and his birth year, and had come into this world in Belgrade, Montana, of all places.

“Wait,” he said. “I have a question.” He had blundered into a surprising thought. “Let’s say I was born on October 22nd. But I was actually supposed to have been born on November 10th. Would this all be different?”
“Completely,” Baby Jane said. “You’d be a Scorpio.”
“But what happens to the person I was supposed to be?”
“The person I would have been if I’d been born at the right time.”
“But you were born at the right time. You were always going to be born when and where you were born.”
There was a knock at the door, and he jumped. Here was her actual nine o’clock, right on schedule. How was he going to explain himself? Baby Jane half stood. “Come in!”
To the husband’s amazement, in came Clownpants, from way up on the nineteenth floor.
“Hey there, darlin’!” he said in his usual, megawatt way. “Did you know there’s a dog sitting outside your door?”
Baby Jane made a disgusted face. “I’m so fucking sick of this building,” she said. “This used to be a classy place. Now it’s nothing but mutts and rap music. You know?”
If the husband hadn’t been frantically nodding in agreement, Clownpants probably wouldn’t have paid enough attention to recognize him. “Well, hey there, chief!” Clownpants said.

They knew each other from the elevator and the refreshment table outside the gym, where they had bonded over their shared inability to resist cucumber water. The husband had recognized him right away as a character actor who often appeared in the late-career films of a controversial, perhaps even cancelled, director. Clownpants wasn’t leading-man material, but his work was scene-stealing. He was humble about it, too. “Every day I get to play is a blessing,” he’d say, crackling with a kind of intensity that had, at first, seemed like a performance, but was in fact just his way. The husband liked him, got a kick out of their interactions. It was the wife who had dubbed him Clownpants, for his tendency to power clash the patterns in his outfits.
Clownpants turned to Baby Jane. “Where is it?”
She gave a little shudder. “Bathroom,” she said.
Off went Clownpants in the direction of the guest bathroom. He emerged carrying a large plastic Tupperware, in which the bat was thrashing around.
“You weren’t kidding,” Clownpants said. “It’s huge.”
Baby Jane covered her eyes. “Get it out of here.”

Clownpants was holding the Tupperware at eye level. “Look at his face,” he said. “He’s perfect. He’s so angry. I guess I would be, too, if somebody put me in a box.” He grinned meaningfully at the husband, as though there were some obvious profundity to this that harked back to a previous exchange. When the husband failed to reciprocate, he raised his eyebrows at Baby Jane. “What are you dressing up as tonight, darlin’?”
“Oh, come on. It’s spooky season,” he said, opening the door to leave. “You gotta get in the spirit! Bring your dancing shoes.”

The door fell shut behind Clownpants. Baby Jane was rubbing her ears irritably. She snatched the star chart back toward herself and cracked her neck. When she looked up to resume the husband’s reading, she finally recognized him. Her face went blank.
“Excuse me,” the husband said. “I’ll be right back.”

He shot out into the hallway. Clownpants was already halfway into the elevator. The husband dived in after him. They ascended, side by side, Clownpants with the Tupperware tucked into the crook of his arm. The bat’s claws skirled weirdly against the plastic as it struggled on. There it was, within arm’s reach. All he had to do was explain, tell a few self-deprecating jokes, ask if he could borrow it.
“Hey, man,” the husband said. “You really shouldn’t be handling that.”
“Oh, don’t worry,” Clownpants said. “I’ve done this before. I get one every year for my Halloween party. You should come tonight! Bring your girl.”
“I would but, you know . . . we just had the baby.”
“No kidding! Blessings, amigo.” Clownpants absorbed him into a santal-perfumed half hug. “And your girl? Is she good?”
“She’s all right. It’s tough, you know, the recovery. It was a Cesarean,” he said.
“Oh!” Clownpants clapped him on the back. “Well, that’s good news for you, buddy.”

“We were just going in for the weekly checkup.” He was babbling, but he couldn’t seem to derail himself. “And then they told us, ‘You can’t go home—this has got to happen today.’ You know they had me just sit there while they cut her open? And when they said, ‘O.K., here comes baby,’ I stood up and looked right into her body.”
“Wow.” Clownpants shook his head.
“And then they just stitched her up and gave her Advil. You know?”
Clownpants looked at the panel of buttons. “I think we missed your floor.”
“A hundred years ago—hell, maybe even fifty—she probably wouldn’t have made it. I’d be a widower. And now it’s just Advil.”

“Well, like you said, she’s tough.” The elevator bell chimed, and Clownpants brightened. “It sounds like you got a lot on your plate, friend, but if you’re up to it: tonight, 10 P.M. till dawn, my place. Dres

items.title: Téa Obreht on Letting Your Characters Flounder
items.description: In your story “Family Lore,” a couple have just returned home from the hospital with their newborn baby. The husband notices their dog engaging with a possibly sick bat on their balcony, and this sets off a spiral of events, as he tries to figure out whether t
items.author: Deborah Treisman
paragraphs: In your story “Family Lore,” a couple have just returned home from the hospital with their newborn baby. The husband notices their dog engaging with a possibly sick bat on their balcony, and this sets off a spiral of events, as he tries to figure out whether the dog has caught rabies, without alerting his wife to the danger. How did this plotline come to you?

I rarely draw direct inspiration from my own life for my fiction—that’s what other people’s lives are for!—but, in this case, shortly after my husband and I brought our first baby home, our dog really did get hold of a bat that then tested positive for rabies. This resulted in the dog being placed in a forty-five-day home quarantine, which, compounded by the isolation of the newborn trenches and the ongoing pandemic, created the most psychologically debilitating situation I’ve ever endured. I’ve suffered from contamination O.C.D. and responsibility O.C.D. since adolescence, and my experience of that month and a half was essentially staying up all night to either nurse the baby or watch the dog for symptoms. It was horrible. Plus, no one we knew had been through anything like it, so no one could offer us any real comfort. All we had was the wildly contradictory advice we received from the vet (who was not worried), the pediatricians (who were low-to-medium worried), and animal control (who were basically telling us to pick out an urn for the dog).
You began writing this story during that quarantine period but didn’t finish it until a month after the birth of your second child, almost four years later. Why did it take so long?

I actually tried to process the incident by fictionalizing it while it was still happening. When that failed, I tried writing it several different times over the years, always from the perspective of the wife. But it was too close to home, and it kept getting tainted by reality. Then, maybe a month or two before the birth of our second baby, my husband and I were reminiscing about the rabies scare, and he said, “If I’d known how awful those forty-five days were going to be, I would have hoofed that fucking bat off the balcony, and you never would have known about it.” That changed my whole approach to the story. It gave me a new premise and orientation, and enough distance from the actual events to see the humor and the madness of it.

Arriving home with a first baby—especially after a long stretch of trying and failing to have a child—can be overwhelming. In the story, it has been the wife’s role to worry about everything and the husband’s role to reassure her. Why do you think he goes so far off the deep end now?

Because his decision to conceal the incident with the bat isolates him from his wife. New parenthood is already isolating, but at least it’s something they’ve been preparing to face as a team. Now he’s ensnared himself in the situation with the bat, and everything he does removes him further and further from the domestic bubble and the new reality on which he is supposed to be focussing.

The story is both a comedy and a thriller: each time the husband makes a seemingly logical decision it pushes him farther into comic absurdity and ratchets up the tension for the reader—who, at a certain point, can no longer imagine this guy digging himself out of the hole he’s jumped into. How challenging was it to balance plausibility and ridiculousness, fun and genuine anxiety, when writing the story?

I’m not sure why, but more and more of late I’ve found myself drawn to characters who can’t stop making mistakes. It’s challenging, but it’s also incredibly fun to refrain from protecting your characters and let them just flounder. In “Family Lore,” I also wanted to capture the vulnerability of finding yourself catapulted into total responsibility for another human being overnight. Any sense of horizon disappears. All sense of balance and proportionality is obliterated. You don’t know if something is a mild threat or a serious one. You don’t know whether something is going to last an hour or a week. For me, so much of the tension in this story came from the husband’s inability to figure out what’s freaking him out the most: the bat? The Cesarean? The fact that the baby came early? His wife’s mental state? The fact that everyone around him seems to be a little unstable?

At the beginning of “Family Lore,” the wife has a premonition that something very bad is going to happen. It’s possible to read the conclusion of the story as confirmation of that prediction. But it’s also possible to read it as a happy ending, in which no serious damage has been done. Did you want to leave it up to the reader to decide which option to believe?

Throughout this story, the husband is unwittingly chasing a sense of relief. I think all he really wants is a moment to recalibrate, a moment to gather himself for the journey ahead, which, given that he is now a parent, is really going to last the rest of his life. And I think he does get that moment in the end.
The story is set in Austin, Texas, where there is, in fact, a very large bat colony. Neither of the characters is originally from Texas. What else made this city the right backdrop for the story?

Despite its takeover by ultra-rich ghouls, Austin has remained a kind of paradise of youth. All the things that would have made it irresistible to the couple once upon a time are incompatible with the early days of parenthood: it’s bawdy, irreverent, loud, hot, fun, and unpredictable. What the husband wants is quiet and calm. Instead, he is surrounded by strangers whose names he realizes he doesn’t even know, all gearing up for a wild Halloween weekend. None of them are in the same phase of life as him, and this amplifies his panic and makes him feel even more powerless and alone. ♦

items.title: The Real Stakes of the Ilhan Omar Case
items.description: All the way back in 2015, as Donald Trump was ascending onto the political stage, he proposed a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States.” Islamophobia featured prominently in that first campaign for the Presidency. “If you have peopl
items.author: Rozina Ali
paragraphs: All the way back in 2015, as Donald Trump was ascending onto the political stage, he proposed a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States.” Islamophobia featured prominently in that first campaign for the Presidency. “If you have people coming out of mosques with hatred and death in their eyes and on their minds,” he said, on CBS News, “we’re going to have to do something.” A few months after pressing for the ban, Trump declared, simply, “I think Islam hates us.”

A complete prohibition on immigration by Muslims was blatantly unconstitutional, but that did not stop Trump, during his first week in office, from signing an executive order that banned travel from a list of Muslim-majority countries. After several legal challenges, Proclamation 9645, the third iteration of the policy, which the White House had expanded to include two non-Muslim countries—Venezuela and North Korea—was upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Roberts, in his 5–4 opinion, noted that the Court must consider not only the President’s contentious statements but also the executive’s “authority” on matters of immigration and national security.

Meanwhile, in a scathing dissent, Justice Sonia Sotomayor argued that the Court could not disregard the President’s racist intentions. “What began as a policy explicitly ‘calling for a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States’ has since morphed into a ‘Proclamation’ putatively based on national-security concerns,” she wrote. “But this new window dressing cannot conceal an unassailable fact: the words of the President and his advisers create the strong perception that the Proclamation is contaminated by impermissible discriminatory animus against Islam and its followers.”

Questions of contamination and concealment appear newly relevant in light of a raid by more than a dozen federal agents on Representative Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., earlier this month. It was six o’clock in the morning when Omar, who had just returned from a trip a few hours earlier, awoke to sounds of banging on her front and back doors. As Omar relayed in a recent interview with MS NOW, she was confused and disoriented: She and her husband were presented with a search warrant by officers with Homeland Security Investigations, an immigration-enforcement agency that typically pursues crimes such as drug or child trafficking. Over the next several hours, the agents scoured each room of Omar’s home, taking with them seventeen items, including her phones, a daughter’s old cellphone, and her husband’s camera, as well as a Somali-language phrase book.

The following day, anonymous government officials confirmed to reporters that the raid was part of an investigation into potential immigration fraud. The government was building a case to denaturalize and ultimately deport Omar, who was born in Somalia and arrived in the U.S. as a child refugee in 1995 with her family, and who obtained citizenship five years later. The Trump Administration insists that this is not a political move, but the timing of the raid—a few weeks before a heated midterm election—suggests otherwise. Trump claimed that the investigation was spearheaded by the Justice Department and had “nothing to do with me.”

This strains the imagination. For ten years, Trump and Omar, who were first elected to public office on the same night, have sparred with open disdain. Omar described her 2018 congressional victory, in Minnesota’s Fifth District, as “a rejection of Donald Trump’s way of thinking.” The following year, she began to call for his impeachment. Trump, for his part, has accused her of praising Al Qaeda; of launching “vicious antisemitic screeds”; of marrying her brother; of being an “America-hating socialist,” a “disgrace,” a “sick woman,” a jihadist, a piece of human “garbage.” She should be “sent back to Somalia,” he has said.

Perhaps these statements by the President of the United States are incidental to current efforts by the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security to tackle a possibly fraudulent immigration application from more than thirty years ago. Perhaps they are coincidences, as prosecutors build a legitimate case against a sitting congresswoman, who happens to be a Black, Muslim woman in a hijab. But it would not be the first time that Trump has issued a racist threat, and then used the levers of power to make it reality.

Trump began his first term with a clear intent to restrict immigration. It wasn’t difficult to discern his underlying motives. In a major immigration-policy speech ahead of the 2016 election, he promised to “get the right people” by calling for new screening tests—an “ideological certification to make sure that those we are admitting to our country share our values.” He has pursued this mission with furious determination in his second term, too. The number of migrants crossing the southern border has plunged. One of the first executive orders that he signed in January of 2025 effectively ended the U.S. refugee resettlement program. (Later, the Administration made an exception for white South Africans.) Although Joe Biden repealed the Muslim ban when he was in office, Trump announced more expansive restrictions; a recent analysis by the Cato Institute found that visa grants to people from Muslim-majority countries have reached nearly zero.

With the major immigration pipelines blocked off, the Administration turned its attention inward. Somali Americans became a repeated target. They “contribute nothing,” Trump told reporters, this past December, during a Cabinet meeting. “I don’t want them in our country.” Two days later, D.H.S. launched Operation Metro Surge, an aggressive and violent incursion in Minnesota, where much of the Somali diaspora lives. The official rationale was to clamp down on unauthorized immigration and to combat fraud. Greg Bovino, the former U.S. Border Patrol commander who has reportedly described undocumented immigrants as “filth,” “trash,” and “scum,” oversaw the operation; recently, he appeared at an anti-Muslim protest in Michigan alongside the far-right activist Jake Lang, where demonstrators called for the deportation of the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who was born in the United States).

The Trump Administration’s animus has not been limited to the Somali community. On the campaign trail, in 2024, then Senator J. D. Vance claimed that Haitian migrants in Ohio ate pets; this year, the Administration revoked Temporary Protected Status for about three hundred and fifty thousand Haitians. In September, D.H.S. posted (and then deleted) an A.I.-generated image of a “Transformers” character facing off against an Indian Sikh man, with the phrases “America for Americans” and “Self-deport or find out.” But many Indians, like many Somalis, are U.S. citizens, as the Administration discovered during its crackdown in Minnesota.

Even for an agency that has been accused by multiple federal judges of flagrantly violating the law, actually deporting American citizens isn’t so easy. But there is a way to do so: by revoking their citizenship.

This isn’t entirely fantastical. There is considerable precedent for such a policy. In the first half of the twentieth century, as citizenship became a defining feature of nation-states, the U.S. stripped nearly twenty-two thousand people of that privilege. According to the scholar Patrick Weil, this was the most of any democratic country in that era. Political dissent spurred these efforts, as in the case of the activist and anarchist Emma Goldman. So, too, did straightforward racism—a series of exclusionary immigration laws ushered in an official, nativist reading of citizenship. In 1923, several years after a ban on most Asian immigration, the Supreme Court ruled that an Indian man seeking citizenship was racially ineligible for naturalization, in part because of the ban: how could Indians be American citizens if they weren’t even allowed to enter the country anymore? The government went on to denaturalize dozens of Indians living in the U.S.

The Civil Rights era led to the abolition of nationality-based immigration quotas. In 1967, the Court ruled that the Constitution protects “every citizen of this Nation against a congressional forcible destruction of his citizenship, whatever his creed, color, or race.” When denaturalizations did occur, they often involved egregious offenses, such as Nazism, war crimes, or espionage. Denaturalization was a dramatic punishment, and the legal and political consensus was that it must be predicated on a dramatic crime.

The War on Terror moved away from that precedent. In 2010, the government launched a program to find people who may have misrepresented their identities to obtain permanent residency or citizenship. The program, named Operation Janus, initially uncovered three hundred and fifteen thousand instances of missing fingerprint data in immigration files, which were flagged for further investigation. Among those, only a quarter of one per cent revealed potential fraud: people who had been ordered deported and seemed to have used different identities to gain U.S. citizenship.

It was hardly a widespread problem—but it provided an opening for Trump. In 2018, his Administration expanded these efforts, announcing a task force to actively search for people who may have lied on citizenship applications; the following year, he launched his own program, calling it Operation Second Look. The move was relatively quiet, but critics voiced concerns that the effort seemed less like an attempt to protect national security than an attack on naturalization itself. A former D.O.J. attorney warned, in the Times, that “if we’re going after people who did nothing of note, or whose wrong caused no harm, it means they’re going after citizenship.” Fear pervaded immigrant communities, where naturalization was believed to offer irrevocable protection. As reported in The Nation, many immigrants reconsidered getting naturalized at all, afraid of “being targeted or tripped in a lie.” By the end of Trump’s first term, the Justice Department had filed an average of twenty-five denaturalization cases a year.

In the summer of 2025, soon after Trump settled back into Washington, senior officials at the D.O.J. directed their attorneys to make denaturalization a priority. The White House outlined target goals: no fewer than a hundred new cases per month. After a slow start, efforts are ramping up. This past May, there were fifteen cases filed. In early October, the D.O.J. announced that it was moving to strip forty people of citizenship, what it boasted was the “largest denaturalization effort in modern history.” The Attorney General, Todd Blanche, claimed that the objective was to “maintain our national security and protect the American people.”

Trump is not the first President in recent decades to have enacted discriminatory national-security policies. In the aftermath of September 11th, the Bush Administration implemented a national registry that required immigrant boys and men from twenty-four Muslim-majority countries to register with the government. The aim was to search for ties to terrorism; the government ended up funnelling thousands of Muslims into deportation proceedings on mostly minor visa infractions. Later, the Obama Administration excluded dual nationals of four Muslim-majority countries from a visa waiver program, restricting their entry to the U.S.

Cassandra Burke Robertson, a professor of law at Case Western Reserve University who studies citizenship, told me that recent denaturalization efforts are nevertheless a departure from modern Presidencies, even from the veneer of Trump’s attempt, in his first term, to ban Muslim immigrants for the ostensible reason of keeping the nation safe. There is no window dressing this time. “The Trump Administration is the first that we’ve seen using denaturalization as an end goal in and of itself, not as a means of something else,” Robertson said.

In December, 1991, Parvez Manzoor Khan, a man in his thirties who hardly spoke English, journeyed from Pakistan to the United States to visit his brother. He presented a doctored passport at the border, which he acknowledged bore a name that was not his. He was briefly detained, then released on bond. He later found work as a truck driver, in Florida; married a U.S. citizen; and became a citizen himself, in 2006. When Operation Janus revealed a discrepancy between the fingerprints in his immigration files, authorities questioned Khan, and he again admitted that he had entered through fraudulent means. In 2017, the Trump Administration brought a denaturalization suit against Khan, who by then had been living in the U.S. for nearly three decades, and had become a grandfather.

A federal court eventually sided with the government, allowing it to strip Khan of his citizenship. James LaVigne, an immigration lawyer who defended Khan in court, told me that the government was successful in part because it had such strong evidence of misconduct, including a copy of the doctored passport, which Khan confessed to using, and the fingerprint discrepancy. Khan also had been ordered deported not long after he arrived, for missing an asylum hearing. (He never got the notice to appear for it, nor was he made aware of a deportation order.)

The case of Ilhan Omar is far less clear. No evidence has yet been presented to the public that she used a false identity to enter the United States, or that she has ever been ordered deported. According to initial reports, the case hinges on the possibility that, when Omar received U.S. citizenship through her father, she was not seventeen years old, as she claimed, but eighteen, which would’ve meant that she needed to pursue a citizenship application on her own. Trump allies have dredged up another allegation, too, long peddled by the MAGA crowd: that she may have later married her brother to help him secure permanent residency. A recent Times story quotes several anonymous former and current government officials who attribute some credibility to this claim, though they did not offer any specific evidence, and Omar has denied the allegation. (How this relates to her own citizenship status, if it does at all, remains hazy.) Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin intimated, in an interview on “The Charlie Kirk Show,” that the government could bring racketeering charges against Omar and anyone who abetted her if it is found that she procured citizenship through fraud. Increasingly, the Administration appears to be hunting for a crime to punish.

Even in cases where fraud is clear, denaturalization does not automatically result in deportation. LaVigne, for example, was able to fight for Khan to retain his permanent residency and remain in the U.S. after his citizenship was stripped, in part because the government chose not to pursue deportation. As for Omar, the President and his circle have openly called for expelling her from the country. Recently, Trump suggested that she could even go to prison. “I have some serious issues with the constitutionality of what is going on,” LaVigne told me. “I say that as a registered Republican. I don’t like what I see. It’s supposed to be a nation of law, not of men.”

The government continues to expend financial resources and manpower on the case. As the writer M. Gessen noted, in The New Yorker, in 2018, “just about every naturalized citizen might look like an outlaw, or a liar,” if inspected closely enough. Still, few legal experts believe that the Administration will succeed in unearthing definitive evidence against Omar. Her father is dead. And establishing that Omar or her family deliberately lied about her age would be complicated, because birth records are practically nonexistent in Somalia.

Even if the investigation fails to result in Omar’s denaturalization, it may provide Trump a victory of a different kind. Among the President’s many allegations against Omar—that she is a jihadist, or married to her brother, or guilty of fraud—is one underlying theme: that she is not really an American. According to Trump, Omar’s disgust with him, and with Republican policies, suggests that she “hates our country.” In this view, the parameters for citizenship are not national security or public safety but loyalty.

No wonder, then, that at a recent rally in Michigan to campaign for Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Senate, Trump stood alongside David Beamer, whose son died on one of the hijacked planes on September 11th, as he excoriated Rogers’s opponent, Abdul El-Sayed. “The enemy is right here among us—local terrorists, local citizens that want to demolish our country,” Beamer said. “Abdul has a birth certificate. The birth certificate says he’s a citizen of America. You know what? A birth certificate doesn’t make you an American.” ♦

items.title: House Democrats Are Ready to Dive In on Trump-Epstein Ties
items.description: With less than a week to go until the midterm elections, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee have made it clear that in the event of a small, medium, or tsunami-size blue wave, they will be using their newfound power to go after Donald Trump for crimes
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: With less than a week to go until the midterm elections, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee have made it clear that in the event of a small, medium, or tsunami-size blue wave, they will be using their newfound power to go after Donald Trump for crimes he allegedly committed “alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history,” a.k.a. Jeffrey Epstein.

On Monday, Representative Jamie Raskin, the ranking member on the committee, called for a special counsel to be appointed to “investigate Epstein’s co-conspirators” and the administration’s “cover-up” of Trump’s involvement. He also released a 52-page report written by Democratic staffers that accuses the president of being “an active participant in Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse of young women during the mid-to-late 1990s” and alleges that “the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) are doing everything they can to keep the American people in the dark about it.”

While much of the report’s allegations were previously made public, they nevertheless paint an even more damning picture of the president of the United States than the one people had in their heads after he was heard bragging about groping women (generally), was accused of sexual misconduct by more than two dozen women (specifically), and was found liable for sexually abusing writer E. Jean Carroll. (Trump has long denied sexual-misconduct claims.)

A spokesperson for the White House told MS Now that “none” of the allegations in the report are true, and that it is “nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements.”
Here are some of the most shocking allegations in the report:
Trump accused of raping five women and girls

The report alleges that there are 11 women who “tie Donald Trump to Epstein’s sex trafficking operations,” five of whom “have directly accused Trump of raping or sexually assaulting them in Epstein’s company or direct physical presence.”

The five women are Beatrice Keul, who alleges, per the report, that “Trump violently raped her at a November 1993 pageant, at the Plaza Hotel in New York City”; Stacey Williams, who “offered a detailed and corroborated account of Trump sexually assaulting her in the early 1990s while she was alone with him and Epstein in an office at Trump Tower”; Jill Harth, who has accused Trump of “violently sexually assaulting her and another woman in 1994 at a Mar-a-Lago party where Epstein and Trump were the only men present”; Katie Johnson, who “gave FBI a detailed account of her repeated rape at the hands of Trump and Epstein in 1994 in New York City when she was a minor”; and a Jane Doe, who gave the FBI a “graphic account of Trump assaulting her when she was a minor in the mid-1980s in New York.”

In conversations with committee staffers, Keul alleged that the assault caused bleeding and bruising, and that afterward, “Trump sat her on the edge of the bed, repeated his promises to arrange for a visa and NYU admission, and made her promise she would keep quiet, saying, ‘[T]he show must go on.’” Keul also said that Epstein told her he was “Don’s best friend.”
Trump and Epstein allegedly told a 13-year-old victim they’d disappear her

The report recounts that in April 2016, a lawsuit was filed by a woman using the pseudonym “Katie Johnson,” who alleged that she was raped by both Trump and Epstein when she was 13 years old. According to an excerpt of an FBI complaint included in the report, Johnson was ordered by both men not to reveal what happened. They allegedly told her that if she didn’t comply, “we’ll make you disappear like [redacted].”
Attorney General Todd Blanche accused of cover-up, potential witness tampering

Per the report, a victim going by Jane Doe alleged that Epstein introduced her to Trump when she was 14 years old, saying, “This is a good one, huh,” to which Trump allegedly responded “yes.” Doe testified against Ghislane Maxwell during her criminal trial, describing to jurors the “abuse and sex acts that occurred at Epstein’s properties in Florida, New Mexico, and New York, sometimes involving Maxwell and groups of people.”

But according to the report, when he visited Maxwell in prison, then–Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche very pointedly did not want to discuss Doe’s claim, at one point saying, “Yeah, yeah, I don’t want to get into … he said, she said,” to which Maxwell responded, “Absolutely, not. I’m not — I don’t want to go there either” and, even more explicitly, “I’m not going to do that.”

“The whole point of the conversation,” according to the report, “was not to uncover information but to create a conspiracy of silence and strategically deter Ghislaine Maxwell from sharing information that was not public at the time regarding the relationship between Trump and Epstein.” The report continued:

Attorney General Blanche’s actions, while perhaps not surprising given his former role as Donald Trump’s defense attorney, potentially constituted witness tampering and obstruction of an official proceeding — serious felonies. At the time of this interview, the House Oversight Committee had scheduled an interview with Maxwell for August 11 — less than two weeks later. Blanche’s apparent instructions not to discuss a specific Epstein victim, and how that victim could implicate Donald Trump, could easily run afoul of 18 U.S.C. § 1512, which forbids hindering or delaying the communication of information relating to the potential commission of a federal offense to a law enforcement officer, as well as corruptly influencing the testimony of any person in an official proceeding — such as a congressional interview and investigation.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department said the report is “nothing more than a last-ditch effort by House Judiciary Democrats to mislead the public.”
Epstein allegedly introduced Trump to Melania

According to the report, a former longtime assistant to Epstein “credibly contradicted” the claim by Paolo Zampolli — who once owned a modeling agency and until recently served as an official in the Trump administration — that he introduced Melania to Trump. Instead, the former assistant has alleged, “Epstein introduced Melania Trump to Donald Trump.” (The report also notes that “Zampolli’s former partner of 19 years, the Brazilian model Amanda Ungaro … has asserted Zampolli was never “the one introducing [sic] Melania to Trump. It was Jeffrey Epstein … That’s how she met Donald Trump.”)

Last April, the First Lady put out a statement saying, “I’ve never been friends with Epstein. I never had a relationship with Epstein or his accomplice, [Ghislaine] Maxwell … Epstein did not introduce me to Donald Trump.” It was not clear at the time what prompted her to make the statement; her husband said he hadn’t known she was going to do so, and “many” White House staffers were reportedly “caught off guard.”

items.title: Trump’s Most Bizarre and Baffling Midterms Rally Rants
items.description: Both historical precedent and mountains of bad polling suggest Republicans desperately need someone to save their butts in the 2026 midterms. And one man has accepted that challenge — perhaps too literally.
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Both historical precedent and mountains of bad polling suggest Republicans desperately need someone to save their butts in the 2026 midterms. And one man has accepted that challenge — perhaps too literally.

In recent weeks, Donald Trump has held many rallies all over the country, though polls indicate the unpopular president’s presence on the campaign trail may hurt GOP candidates more than it helps. And he certainly hasn’t been playing it safe. In addition to playing his old controversial hits, from demonizing transgender people to spewing Islamophobia, he’s added a lot of strange and experimental material to his routine.

If it works, Trump will be hailed as a political visionary. If it doesn’t, Republicans may spend the next few years kicking themselves for letting Trump go with the closing midterms message Jon Husted’s got a beautiful ass, right? Here’s a rundown of Trump’s weirdest tirades from the 2026 campaign trail.
“My wife told me, ‘Sir …’”

In early October, Trump combined two longtime rally staples: the “sir, please” anecdote and the “Melania hates when I do this.” This radical move could have created something incredible, like combining peanut butter and chocolate. Unfortunately, the results of Trump’s experimental weaving were just confusing.
“You know, my wife told me, ‘Sir, do me a favor … It’s not vay-gan, it’s vegan,” he said, suggesting Melania addresses him with a formal “sir” even when they’re alone.

Moments later, Trump added another befuddling layer when he referred to his wife with both male and female pronouns. “He said, ‘It’s vegan!’” Trump recalled. “She says ‘hello’ to everybody. Melania says ‘hello.’”
[Huuuh] “He’s puking all over the place”

What Trump was trying to express with his garbled Melania vay-gan story was that James Talarico is a meat-hating pansy. (According to Republicans, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate is simultaneously too weak for Texas and a menacing boogeyman who wants to turn everyone’s kids trans.)

Though Talarico is not actually vegan, Trump has repeatedly claimed the candidate “gets sick and throws up all over the place” every time he eats meat. By late October, this evolved into the president of the United States simulating puking on stage to illustrate his point.
“Pacific Ocean, we’re gonna call it the American Ocean”

After sort of renaming two bodies of water to the “Gulf of America” and “Lake America,” respectively, Trump has set his sights on changing the name of one of the oceans bordering the U.S. But it’s unclear which one or whether the whole thing is just trolling.

At several rallies, the president told a story about pitching Sundar Pichai on renaming the Atlantic Ocean. Trump said he backed off because the Google CEO begged him not to open that can of worms, saying, “Please don’t ask us to do that.”
But maybe the Pacific is still fair game? Trump concluded one of these retellings by saying he’d “probably pass” on renaming the Atlantic but “Pacific Ocean, we’re gonna call it the American Ocean.”
“New Mexico … I want to change it to ‘New America’”
In other potential renaming developments, Trump casually referred to New Mexico as “New America,” at an October 23 rally, though it’s quite clear he does not have the power to rename the state.

Later at the same rally, Trump told a dubious story about a friend who lives in New Mexico, claiming he constantly needs to show his passport because people think he’s entering the U.S. from a foreign country.
“But I’m playing with this,” Trump acknowledged. “You know, this is tricky. It’s called New Mexico but it’s not Mexico. I want to change it to ‘New America.’”
“Most people don’t know ‘dumb’ has a b”
Trump debuted this one over the summer as he was (over) explaining the spelling of “Dumocrats,” his new nickname for Democrats. By October, it had become a regular bit:

At one point, Trump seemed to acknowledge the line was backfiring and making him look like an idiot. But he insisted most people can’t spell this extremely common four letter word. “Most people think dumb is “D-U-M,” Trump explained. “It’s “D-U-M-B.”
“We had the hurricane. We call it a ‘watercane’”

In another idiotic development, Trump said during a speech in North Carolina that 2024’s Hurricane Helene was actually referred to as a “watercane” because “it was the most — there’s never been a hurricane that anybody’s seen that threw out more water than that.”
Precipitation is a pretty well-known feature of hurricanes, so no one else is calling it that.
Solar panels “kill all the animals”

You might think Trump hates solar panel simply because they’ve picked the wrong side in his legendary feud with windmills. But on October 28, he revealed he’s actually upset because he thinks they “fry” animals on contact.
“You know, the animals jump on them and they fry because those black panels, they’re hotter than your stove,” Trump said.
“You have to go to MIT to turn on a lawnmower now”

Trump also believes you need a Ph.D. to turn on a lawnmower these days. Though it’s unclear how he’d know since the closest he’s ever gotten to operating one is that time he yelled at a kid on the White House lawn.
Kansas senator isn’t “some kind of a Shylock-type guy”
Not all of Trump’s new material is dumb. Sometimes it’s both dumb and offensive.

On October 19, Trump tried to defend Senator Roger Marshall by bringing up a damaging report about the former obstetrician aggressively suing patients for unpaid bills. The president said he’d been urged not to talk about the report, highlighted some particularly bad details, then dropped a term that’s widely considered an offensive stereotype about Jews. This pushed Marshall’s scandal as well as Trump’s use of the term back into the headlines (the president knew it’s offensive, as he was called out for saying it a year earlier). You’re welcome, senator!
“If you’re Black or you’re Jewish … you’re crazy anyway”
The generous read here is that Trump was trying to label anyone who votes for Abdul El-Sayed as “crazy anyway,” regardless of their race or religion. But that’s not how he said it.
Arnold Palmer’s penis size was “unbelievable”

This is actually one from the vault. Many people have forgotten that Arnold Palmer doesn’t get enough credit for his impressive genitalia was one of Trump’s closing messaging of the 2024 campaign. And, well, it worked. So he did an encore performance this week.

“Arnold Palmer was all man,” Trump said. “This was a guy that was all man. This man was strong and tough. And when he took showers with the other pros, they coame out there and said, ‘Oh my god. That’s unbelievable.’”
“I looked at his ass, and I’ve never done that with a man before”

Trump has been objectifying men for years now, but his praise for various men running in the 2026 midterms has become the stuff of legend. It really took off when Trump marveled about Senator Jon Husted’s physique at an October 12 rally.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Trump said. “I started examining his body. Because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked, and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass, and I looked at the whole. Then I looked at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws.”

Trump kept fawning over Husted at nearly every rally, and now we’re at the point where his ass basically needs its own Wikipedia page. The routine has grown to include hand gestures, asides about Nicki Minaj’s bottom, and claims that the newfound notoriety of Husted’s behind has given the candidate a 12-point polling boost. There is no evidence to support this, but it’s true that Trump rallygoers can’t get enough butt stuff.
Trump contemplated his now-iconic rump-related rants during a rally for Senate candidate Mike Rogers on October 25.
“I’ve been living with this whole thing about the ass,” Trump said. “Believe me, it’s of no interest to me. Other than to say Jon Husted is one hell of an athlete.”
But, Trump said, he’s “willing to sacrifice” for the good of the Republican Party. “I’d say that about your ass, too, Mike, if it gets you a guaranteed victory,” he quipped.
If Trump’s midterm strategy actually works, the GOP’s 2028 platform is going to make Heated Rivalry look prudish.
