items.title: Down and Out in the App Store
items.description: Last year, Jeremiah’s TikTok started feeding him ads for a new way to make money. The clips — some clearly made with AI, others featuring influencers — promised a payday for playing mobile games or, in some cases, simply for watching TikTok. You can “get paid
items.author: John Herrman
paragraphs: Last year, Jeremiah’s TikTok started feeding him ads for a new way to make money. The clips — some clearly made with AI, others featuring influencers — promised a payday for playing mobile games or, in some cases, simply for watching TikTok. You can “get paid to scroll,” they told an audience of people who were already scrolling. Some of the ads acknowledged this might sound too good to be true but insisted, of course, that it wasn’t.

Jeremiah tried out a few of these apps. They had names like KashKick, Swagbucks, and Mistplay. After wasting hours on games in KashKick for low payouts with too many restrictions and caveats, he switched to an app called Freecash. Most of the featured games are traps, he said — the rewards decrease as you play and give you unreachable targets — but he eventually put together a routine. At 44, he had spent years playing World of Warcraft and ’90s strategy games before it. “I can grind,” he said, “and that’s what most of these games are.” Now, he was grinding for cash by playing iPhone-era strategy games like Rise of Kingdoms, which involves building cities and battling other players for virtual resources and land. By assembling his army and succeeding in the game, he could eventually reach goals in Freecash, then redeem them for a few real dollars. Beyond his gaming background, Jeremiah had the time — he worked in farming for years in eastern North Carolina but had since gone on disability — so he professionalized his operation. He played multiple games at once: Age of Dragons, Legend of Mushroom, and countless similar ones that would pop up in Freecash’s list of offers with better terms. He set up multiple profiles on a folding Samsung phone where he could check on his progress and track his earning tasks at the same time.

Jeremiah’s fate within the games, which were themselves about the slow and precarious accumulation of virtual resources, soon had real stakes. He started setting timers so he wouldn’t miss chances to upgrade or progress. He also had to be constantly vigilant against raids, in which other players, some grinding for credit in apps like Freecash themselves, could attack and steal in-game resources, indirectly robbing Jeremiah of real earnings in the process. He defends himself by working with a clan of allied players gathered from the strange and ephemeral social environments that briefly materialize at different levels of the get-paid-to, or GPT, app ecosystem. “90 percent of the time, you get up on a server that’s full of Brazilians, but there are also a lot of people from Malaysia and the Philippines,” he said. With the arrival of automatic AI translation, these in-game chats have become somewhat more useful and less alienating. “We’ll discuss the strategy for getting higher on the game,” he added. Some are in it for the money. Others are just addicted.

For mobile-game companies, apps like Freecash are a way to buy downloads but also to filter their customers, paying out small amounts to find out which might end up spending even more. (The industry borrows a term, whales, from casinos for the big spenders who make the business model work.) Earning money by playing these games is hard. Spending it is easy. Using real money to buy in-game resources in Rise of Kingdom, for example, can speed up progress and increase your power in the game, allowing you to skip over hours of play or to dominate other players. If you’re using Freecash, this may get you closer to a real payout. But progress is often elusive and hard to track. It’s easy to overspend in pursuit of slippery goals or to become straightforwardly addicted, disengaging from the get-paid-to ecosystem entirely.

If players do eventually make enough money to withdraw, they’ll often be greeted with a string of solicitations to funnel their funds through an affiliated gambling platform like Stake, where they’ll be enticed by new and arcane promotions, rules, and fine print. Even for a grinder, it’s a grind. Since Jeremiah started keeping track and paying for some of his in-app purchases with other GPT apps like Scrambly, he has cleared $8,000 in total payouts. Still, after weeks or months of attention-draining, repetitive check-ins and resets and blurred-together earnings, wins, and losses, the notion that you’re getting paid to do things you would be doing anyway, or getting “paid to scroll,” sounds absurd. This is a common complaint in get-paid-to advice communities, which suggest that far more people wash out of these apps than stick with them. “They make gaming a grind and not fun anymore,” wrote another user on Reddit. “They are greedy af and have unrealistic timelines and crap payouts.” Jeremiah still plays mainstream games in his spare time. As for the hypermonetized slopware games that send him notifications all day and night: “It’s work.”

For Jeremiah, the get-paid-to regimen is working well enough that he hasn’t called it quits yet, even if it wears him out sometimes. “I’m on my phone all day anyway,” he said, “and it’s not the only thing I’m doing.” A few days before I spoke to him, he won a bet at cash-out and made a few hundred dollars. He was relieved, he said, and planned to take a few days off.

Apps such as Freecash have been around for more than a decade, but they’ve recently become harder to miss, appearing frequently in the App Store charts — Freecash briefly broke into the top five in September — and meeting the American public at a moment of intense economic worry and disillusionment. Hiring is low, and the entire economy is being propped up by a multitrillion-dollar bet on a general-purpose job-automating machine. Even more people than usual are worried about work, specifically and in general. The global financial crisis was followed by the rise of the gig economy. As Americans clench through the late Trump years — and inflation and high interest rates and the AI boom — it’s reasonable to wonder if a newer, harsher, and more convoluted vision of gig work is what’s waiting for us on the other side.

Mostly, though, it’s because of the advertising, which is all over social media. According to Appfigures, Freecash grew from fewer than a million downloads in October 2025 to 6 million in February 2026, boosted by a flood of ads that promised, for example, up to $35 an hour to watch TikTok, while giving users the impression that they would somehow be working for the social-media company. TikTok pulled some of these ads for being misleading, according to Wired; eventually, both Apple and Google temporarily booted the app from their stores. Now, the apps are back, and so are the ads.

Scott Sweeney, an IT and marketing professional living in Ohio, had known about this strange industry for years but had no reason to partake in it. Then, after 11 years at his tech job, he was laid off. “In my mind, I was trying to close a small gap,” he said. He had severance but also a kid. So he gave the apps a try. “The earliest experiences were pretty frustrating,” he said. Apps like Freecash are the “gateway,” he added. “You put in that first initial effort, it shows you only spent 15 minutes, and you made three dollars.” Most apps, he says, are “front loaded” — the opportunities dry up quickly and soon you’re spending “god-awful amounts of time and work to make pennies.”
My own brief experience on Freecash bore this out immediately. The first app it suggested I download was Disney Solitaire, a simple-looking game from one of America’s most wholesome conglomerates.

At first, the game ran without friction, dealing easy tableaux and offering frequent hints, bonus cards, all with a deck seemingly stacked in my favor. In the background, I was accumulating Mickey Mouse coins, a currency I had been made aware of minutes earlier, by the thousands. Things soon slowed down, and the game’s scenes stretched long, bonuses became less frequent, and my draws felt worse. Back in Freecash, my first $12 arrived within an hour. It was clear, though, that getting the rest of the way to the $25 withdrawal threshold would take thousands more taps and hundreds more small check-ins. If I wanted to skip ahead, of course, I could pay: For $5, I might get to the next milestone in Disney Solitaire, which could allow me to cash out in Freecash. (The first in-app purchase offer Disney made to me, the “BEST VALUE” package for 200,000 virtual coins, cost $49.99.) Or I could grind, like the player on Reddit who “barely even went outside” for a month, spent around $60, and then couldn’t redeem their $600 of earnings. “Probably would’ve made more money working at a random gas station in the same time,” they wrote. “At least I would’ve actually gotten paid lol.”

Sweeney didn’t have time for this. He decided, first, to focus on surveys, another available option in many get-paid-to apps. By answering market-research questions or responding to polls, he could make a few dollars during slack moments in a busy day. (A fair number of these tasks, he said, were just “asking about thermostatic opinion in American politics,” drawing a broad vibe check from a group of people who were, at least on their phones, surrounded by bad vibes.) He also got a lot of micro-tasks with pretty clear mechanics behind them. He might be asked to download an app and spend five minutes using it, which would produce a favorable engagement measurement for the developer. There were the popular data-harvesting apps, like Fetch and Receipt Hog, which offer payment for sharing receipts, with higher rates for buying specific products. There were also some newer, seemingly AI-centric get-paid-to app opportunities. “You’d get a task like ‘Take a bunch of selfies and give up your personal biometrics for $5,’” Sweeney said.

He too started treating this activity more like a job, drifting further from spare-time tasks and layered points and rewards into more explicit forms of micro-gig work. Apps like iVueit, which offers business clients “on-demand property inspections” to, for example, “verify current conditions” or “monitor retail execution remotely,” would assign him tasks nearby, where he might be able to step out during a swim class to take photos of, say, the state of the landscaping outside a Dollar General; those like Prolific offer payment for “judging AI,” ultimately feeding into models at companies like Google and OpenAI.

“A lot of people are pivoting to that sort of work,” Sweeney said. It isn’t lost on them that such work feels sort of self-eliminating, he suggested, “and it doesn’t feel great knowing that your attention is the only commodity they’re interested in.” The apps don’t let you forget it, either: To do this sort of gig work is to be confronted by endless ads, confusing promotions and sweepstakes, and a barrage of bar charts, spinning wheels, and confetti explosions, creating a feeling of constant movement and progress on the way to goals that remain just out of reach. (This may sound familiar to anyone who has used gambling apps or just browsed Shein or Temu.)

In the end, Sweeney said, this doesn’t particularly matter. “A lot of people who are doing this are just trying to find means to an end,” he said, bridging a gap as he was, stay-at-home parenting, or looking for a side hustle that isn’t too disruptive. Sure, the companies offering these tasks were coy about their various “endgames” and seemed to view users with disrespect bordering on contempt. But they were paying.

Sweeney has since rejoined the traditional workforce but still does some task work in his spare time, setting aside earnings to pay down debt or save for family vacations. He turned his research into a series of Reddit advice posts, which got a lot of attention, before identifying a better opportunity in the space: He turned those posts into an online guide to get-paid-to apps, some of which pay him affiliate commissions for new users.

AI leaders are fond of wondering aloud what work will be left for humans once their products can do much, or most, of what we consider work today. Get-paid-to apps provide an unsentimental vision of what’s left: raw attention, harvested by ads and converted into app metrics; out-of-distribution, low-context tasks meant to close gaps in machine capability; the possessions and expression of consumer preferences, which can be used to improve marketing.

But the truth behind all those TikTok ads isn’t really a novel thesis about the value of time and labor but rather something more familiar and zero-sum. After a period of trial and error, Jeremiah was cash-flow positive, and GPT apps had become a major part of his routine. His mother noticed and thought she would give them a try too. She logged onto Freecash and was also funneled into Disney Solitaire, to which she quickly became addicted. “It was a huge trap,” he said. “Before I knew it, she was dropping $200 to $300 to get $100.” Both sides of the get-paid-to model were now playing out in the same house, so he intervened and got access to her Freecash account. They were playing a lot of the same games, he noticed, but as a new player, she often got better offers and rates. She needed to step back, but Jeremiah saw an opportunity: “I use her account on an iPad now.”

items.title: 'Heat' Director Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Gun Range
items.description: Heat director Michael Mann was briefly hospitalized Saturday after accidentally shooting himself in the leg at a Los Angeles gun range.
items.author: Daniel Kreps
paragraphs: Heat director Michael Mann was briefly hospitalized Saturday after accidentally shooting himself in the leg at a Los Angeles gun range.
The incident occurred around 4 p.m. on Halloween, where police and medical responded to The Range LA following calls concerning the shooting, TMZ first reported.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann,” a rep for the director told Rolling Stone. “He was treated and is being released.”

A source close to Mann said the incident occurred while the director, an experienced target shooter for decades, was taking target practice at the licensed gun range. Though a medical team responded to the shooting, the injury was considered minor and subcutaneous.

The 83-year-old Mann, who has also helmed films like Manhunter, The Insider, and Ali, should have a few months to recover before embarking on his next project: The star-studded, long-awaited prequel/sequel to his crime epic Heat.

Heat 2 — reportedly starring Christian Bale, Leonardo DiCaprio, Adam Driver, Stephen Graham, and many more — is set to finally begin filming in January 2027, Graham recently told Today; the film, adapted from a book Mann himself co-wrote, had originally planned to start shooting earlier this year.

items.title: Tokyo’s First Animated Competition Title ‘Magic Atlas’ Was Sun Xun’s ‘All-In Moment’
items.description: Chinese artist and filmmaker Sun Xun never expected “Magic Atlas” to become the first animated feature selected for the Tokyo International Film Festival’s competition.
items.author: Lin Ying-Hsuan
paragraphs: Chinese artist and filmmaker Sun Xun never expected “Magic Atlas” to become the first animated feature selected for the Tokyo International Film Festival’s competition.

“I never thought of ‘Magic Atlas’ as an animated film. To me, it brings together many art forms. Animation is simply the label we use for its form. I’m glad people at TIFF understood the effort I put into it,” Sun tells Variety.

“Magic Atlas,” a decade in the making, is set in Luocha, a coal-mining empire where flying is forbidden. Every 60 years, a festival leaves the population unable to remember the era that came before. After a magician is arrested, he meets an orphan boy in prison and gives him the Magic Atlas. The book points the boy toward a past the empire has tried to erase.

The film moves between woodblock prints, ink painting and vivid color. Its images often do the work that a conventional plot might spell out, drawing on art and visual traditions from different periods and cultures.

Sun says the film was shaped by global events, including the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, as well as personal changes such as his conversion to Buddhism. He put all his savings into the project. When galleries shut down during the pandemic, his art sales dried up. He says he had to find buyers himself and take out loans to keep the film going.

“In my own artistic thinking, I believe every creator should have one ‘all-in’ moment in their life: to make a defining work that takes everything out of them. For me, ‘Magic Atlas’ was that all-in moment,” he says. “I hoped to finish it before my child grew up and while my parents were still alive. Sadly, my father passed away a year before the film was completed.”

Rather than comment on any one event, Sun says, he drew on different cultural and political influences to reflect the divisions he sees around the world. He also brought in images of ancient civilizations, including the pyramids, alongside mythological elements.
“Film cannot address reality directly, but it can take a wider view. It can express how we understand the world and what we are curious about,” he says.

Asked whether films need to explain their stories clearly, Sun says: “I’m actually against ‘story.’ I don’t mean that films shouldn’t have stories. I object to films that emphasize story for the sake of packaging and commercial purposes. As an art form, film should express a state of being.”

Sun names Andrei Tarkovsky, citing 1983’s “Nostalghia,” and the late Hungarian filmmaker Béla Tarr as filmmakers he admires. “They are sincere in the way they approach existence. They don’t rely only on imagined narratives. To me, that is the kind of artistic form cinema should have,” he says.

While working on “Magic Atlas,” Sun studied Dunhuang murals, Song dynasty painting and calligraphy, along with imagery from other cultures. Asked if he worries that some viewers might find the film difficult to follow, he says: “There will always be a barrier to entry. Ten years of work naturally gives the film depth. But I made this important work for myself. My goal was to realize it, not to please every viewer.”

Sun says exhibitions connected to “Magic Atlas” are planned in the U.S. and Singapore, though venues and dates have not been unveiled. He has also begun a new feature he calls “All or Nothing,” whose Mandarin title, “Fuyou,” means “Mayfly.” The film will continue the world of “Magic Atlas,” moving from the broad theme of forgetting to an individual experience of memory loss. Sun says he filmed the first shot at an exhibition space in Hangzhou and hopes to finish the feature within two years.

items.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ and ‘Clayface’ Battle for No. 1 With $10.5 Million in Sleepy Halloween Weekend
items.description: A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” and DC’s comic book adaptation “Clayface” are vying for first place at the domestic box office, with each film on track to collect around $10.5 million over the weekend.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” and DC’s comic book adaptation “Clayface” are vying for first place at the domestic box office, with each film on track to collect around $10.5 million over the weekend.

Although it’ll be a close call, “You Can See Everything” has the slight edge with $10.6 million while expanding to 3,242 venues in its third frame while “Clayface” looks just behind with $10.4 million from 3,478 theaters in its sophomore outing, according to respective studio estimates. (The final results will be tallied on Monday.) “You Can See Everything” is already a box office winner, but it would be quite a feat for the non-fiction film to ascend to No. 1 in its third weekend in theaters.
“That’s a rare achievement for any film, let alone a documentary running more than three hours,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian.

Overall, it was another painfully slow Halloween for cinema owners without any new releases, as well as the misfortune of the holiday landing on Saturday. When Halloween coincides with the weekend, families prefer to go trick-or-treating rather than visit their local multiplex. Revenues between Friday and Sunday amounted to roughly $60 million, marking one of the slowest weekends of the year, according to Rentrak. However, it’s an improvement from 2025’s Halloween weekend, which resulted in $49 million across all films, led by Colleen Hoover adaptation “Regretting You” and “Black Phone 2.”
“With costume parties, trick-or-treating and countless other Halloween activities, theaters were facing some pretty stiff competition for people’s time and attention,” Dergarabedian says.

“You Can See Everything” has been the fall season’s breakout hit with $63.88 million domestically to date. It has yet to be released at the international box office. With euphoric word-of-mouth and repeat viewings from audiences who are trying to process the stranger-than-fiction film, “You Can See Everything” is expected to leave theaters as one of the biggest documentaries in decades. And it will be very profitable for A24, which produced the nearly three-hour movie for $7 million.

“Clayface,” an R-rated origin story about the Batman villain, has generated $44.1 million in North America and $83 million globally. It’s shaping up to be a modest win for DC, having cost just $44 million to produce. That’s a much leaner price tag than DC’s other recent tentpoles, such as last year’s $225 million-budgeted “Superman” and July’s $175 million-budgeted “Supergirl.” The studio spent less on “Clayface” because the story is much darker than those family-friendly adventures, and because the character isn’t as well known compared to some of the company’s A-list superheroes. DC’s next big-screen endeavors will feature marquee names with next summer’s “Superman: Man of Tomorrow” and 2028’s “The Batman: Part II,” led by Robert Pattinson.

Laika’s stop-motion animated fantasy “Wildwood” remained at No. 3 with $7.5 million in its sophomore outing, a 39% drop. So far, the well-reviewed film has earned $25 million domestically and $35 million globally. Since “Wildwood” has a huge $100 million production budget (stop-motion animation is labor-intensive and can take several years to produce), the movie likely won’t turn a profit in its theatrical run.

Fourth place went to Black Bear’s offbeat romantic comedy “Wicker” with $4.1 million from 2,374 venues in its second weekend, a decline of just 28% from its debut. The film has earned $13.2 million domestically to date, a solid tally considering the low-budget project was acquired by Black Bear after Sundance for $2.5 million.

Paramount’s video game reboot “Street Fighter” rounded out the top five with $3.2 million in its third frame, another harsh 63% drop. The movie has grossed $53 million in North America and $91.9 million worldwide. Although “Street Fighter” is nearing the $100 million mark, it’s not close to breaking even or getting into the black. Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed “Street Fighter” for $82 million, and theater owners keep around half of ticket sales.

Elsewhere, Sony didn’t report grosses for the Jenna Ortega-led literary adaptation “Klara and the Sun” in what would have been the film’s second weekend of release. The film collapsed in its opening with $720,000 from 880 locations. The studio scaled back the theatrical footprint after critics derided the movie as “calamitous” and “confoundingly awful.” Director Taika Waititi claimed he doesn’t read reviews but, in a recent social media post, he referred to critics of his work as “sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists.” The movie cost $20 million to make and will wind up in the red for Sony. It’s the studio’s second consecutive misfire after Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” which left theaters with a paltry $9 million in North America and $17 million globally against a $30 million budget. Luckily, the studio’s losses on those films will be cushioned by two major winners, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” (the third-biggest movie ever with $2.5 billion) and Zach Cregger’s “Resident Evil” reboot ($400 million).

In limited release, Sony Pictures Classics’s crime thriller “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” cracked the top 10 with $1.7 million from 1,112 theaters. It has earned $2.1 million after one weekend in limited release. John Turturro stars in the awards hopeful, which revolves around a pickpocket master who struggles to keep up with the changing times — phones are trackable, wallets rarely have cash and guns are hiding in plain sight.

Meanwhile, Netflix’s Oscar contender “La Bola Negra” added $418,000 from 38 theaters. So far, the generation-spanning queer drama has earned $1.2 million as the streamer rolls out the film at a glacial pace. Also this weekend, Netflix released Peter Berg’s war drama “The Mosquito Bowl,” which brought back $455,000 from 349 locations — a much wider footprint than “La Bola Negra.”

items.title: Inde Navarrette Takes Swipe at Shane Gillis During ‘SNL’ Monologue
items.description: Following a Trump-centric cold open that featured the return of Tom Hanks’ David S. Pumpkins, “Saturday Night Live” host Inde Navarrette took the stage at Studio 8H for her first opening monologue. It was a fitting choice to have the star of the year’s breakou
items.author: Marlow Stern
paragraphs: Following a Trump-centric cold open that featured the return of Tom Hanks’ David S. Pumpkins, “Saturday Night Live” host Inde Navarrette took the stage at Studio 8H for her first opening monologue. It was a fitting choice to have the star of the year’s breakout horror hit “Obsession” (and the internet’s apparent obsession) make her hosting debut on Halloween night, and the 25-year-old rising star seemed more than up for the occasion, unlike a certain stand-up comedian.

“You probably know me from the movie ‘Obsession.’ And a lot of people ask me if I’m anything like my character Nikki and I’m like, ‘No… no, no, don’t do that!’” she joked, sliding into Nikki’s cadence. “But the thing is, is I’m nothing like my character in ‘Obsession.’ Like, my boyfriend is here tonight to support me and we have such a chill relationship, right?”
The camera then cut to Navarrette’s boyfriend, Nick Aiello, in the crowd bound and gagged to a chair. Then, the actress took a shot at Shane Gillis’ “SNL” monologue from earlier this month.

“I can’t believe I’m saying this, but I’m going to be in a Marvel movie,” said Navarrette, who will be playing Rogue in the new “X-Men” movie. “And I know it’s really important for Marvel that you get really fit, so I’ve been working out a lot, so every morning I put on my little whore outfit and I hit the gym.”
Gillis got a lot of flak for a lame, lazy joke about how women dress like “whores” now when they go to the gym in “neon, like, artificial bait”-colored shorts.

items.title: ‘SNL’ Cold Open Crashed by Tom Hanks as David S. Pumpkins, Nicki Minaj and Donald Trump, Who Admits He ‘Might Be Gay’
items.description: Tom Hanks returned to “Saturday Night Live” on Halloween night to revive his lounge-y David S. Pumpkins character in a cold open that skewered President Trump’s increasingly bizarre comments on the stump and his fixation with men’s physiques.
items.author: William Earl
paragraphs: Tom Hanks returned to “Saturday Night Live” on Halloween night to revive his lounge-y David S. Pumpkins character in a cold open that skewered President Trump’s increasingly bizarre comments on the stump and his fixation with men’s physiques.

The segment also featured Saidah Belo-Osagie as Nicki Minaj in a spoof of the star’s vocal support for Trump and his MAGA movement. The bit cast Minaj as Trump’s next choice for press secretary, on the heels of Katie Zacharia’s spectacularly quick flame-out in the job earlier this month.

The segment opened with Grace Reiter and Jeremy Culhane as a young couple taking a ride at a low-end amusement park Halloween celebration. Kenan Thompson then pops up in a ghoulish Grim Reaper costume to guide the couple through a series of scary scenes. Pumpkins, the character that Hanks first limned for the show in 2016, popped in with a dorky dance routine accompanied by Mikey Day and a special cameo appearance by former “SNL” trouper Bobby Moynihan. Day and Moynihan wore full-body skeleton jumpers with white face paint.

As the ride continued, James Austin Johnson turned up as President Trump, who stepped in to interrupt the ride and lament about Republicans being poised for a thumping in the Nov. 3 midterm election. The segment then went into a string of surprisingly risqué jokes about Trump’s unusual obsession with the butts of candidates that he has been endorsing as he’s hosted a string of campaign rallies in recent weeks.

“We both appeared in 2016. We’re both very loud, very orange and, frankly, very annoying,” Johnson as Trump said. “Good acting, great ass. A great ass on Hanks — something that I’ve enjoyed lately admiring. Not that there’s anything wrong with that. Just that I might be gay.”

Trump then whined that “the midterms are on Tuesday. The polls say we’re doing very badly — aww aww. They’re saying Texas is turning purple, just like my hand.” Johnson then raised his hand to show a gigantic bruise. Johnson as Trump called Texas’ GOP candidate for the U.S. Senate, Ken Paxton, “an ugly son of a bitch” but urged voters to chose him over Democrat James Talarico. Trump acknowledged that Talarico is “much better looking. What a dynamic ass.”

As Trump spoke, the other players in the scene were in freeze mode. Thompson’s Grim Reaper character broke from the scene and rushed past Johnson as Trump. Trump called out “thank you for that donation” to which Thompson replied, “Yeah, you wish, bitch.”

Belo-Osagie barreled into the segment as Minaj toward the end as Trump hails her devotion to the cause. “Trump’s out here killing it — and by it, I mean my career,” Belo-Osagie as Minaj said. Trump noted that Minaj is well-known for her curvy rear-end: “Perhaps if it was on a man, I could admire it,” Johnson as Trump remarked.
In closing, Trump brought out Zacharia who flubbed her attempt to deliver the signature “SNL” opening line, “Live from New York, it’s Saturday night.”
The Halloween installment of “SNL” is hosted by “Obsession” star Inde Navarrette, with Gracie Abrams serving as musical guest.

items.title: ‘Criminal Minds: Evolution’ to End With Season 20 at Paramount+
items.description: “Criminal Minds: Evolution” will end with its upcoming 20th season on Paramount+, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “Criminal Minds: Evolution” will end with its upcoming 20th season on Paramount+, Variety has learned.

The long-running procedural was originally revived for Season 16 at the streamer back in 2022. Season 19 aired between May and July earlier this year. Season 20 does not yet have a premiere date, but will air in 2027.

“It’s hard to put into words what ‘Criminal Minds’ has meant to all of us who have been fortunate enough to be part of this extraordinary journey, first on CBS for 15 seasons and then on Paramount+ for five,” said Erica Messer, the series’ showrunner and executive producer. While suddenly navigating the end of this chapter, I’m filled with gratitude for our remarkable cast, writers, directors and crew who have poured their hearts into this show, and for the incredible fans around the world whose unwavering loyalty has kept ‘Criminal Minds’ going for two decades. We’re looking forward to sharing Season 20 with everyone, and celebrating the legacy of this special show we’ve all built together.”

The show follows the FBI’s Behavioral Analysis Unit (BAU), who are described as “a team of profilers tasked with analyzing and capturing the country’s most dangerous criminals, before they strike again.” “Evolution” picks up after the events of the original “Criminal Minds,” which aired on CBS for 15 seasons.

“Evolution” stars franchise mainstays Joe Mantegna, A.J. Cook, Kirsten Vangsness, Aisha Tyler, and newcomer RJ Hatanaka, with Adam Rodriguez and Paget Brewster also returning. Messer serves as showrunner and executive producer, with Breen Frazier, Chris Barbour, Glenn Kershaw, Stacey Hardt, and Mark Gordon also executive producing. The series is produced by 20th Television and CBS Studios.

items.title: The NFL’s Biggest Dramas This Season Are in the Broadcast Booth
items.description: The NFL might be the undisputed king of TV content, but it is off-the-field drama that has dominated much of the conversation around the game this season so far.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: The NFL might be the undisputed king of TV content, but it is off-the-field drama that has dominated much of the conversation around the game this season so far.
In particular, it was a widely reported altercation before the Los Angeles Rams-Buffalo Bills game at SoFi Stadium this month … in the ESPN broadcast booth.

To recap: ESPN’s lead play-by-play announcer Joe Buck signed a rich new contract with the company, but his longtime analyst partner Troy Aikman has not, resulting in reported bad blood between the boothmates.

On-air, of course, viewers would have no clue (Buck and Aikman have continued to deliver a broadcast worthy of their decamillion-dollar contracts), but the dispute has become fodder, and Aikman has not been willing to shy away from discussing it.
The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback appeared on The Mike Fisher Show on Friday, where he was almost melancholy about what his future holds in media.

“I never had any interest in going into television, it was just by happenstance that I even got into it,” Aikman said, recalling the outreach from Fox Sports. “I don’t know that if they hadn’t hired me, I would have gotten an opportunity anywhere else. And here I am, 25 years later, and now as I’m into my last year at ESPN, I’m realizing that this is something that could very well be taken away from me, and so for the first time, I’m realizing how much I really do, and I’ve always enjoyed it.

“Until you risk having something taken away from you, I think sometimes you tend to maybe take things for granted,” he continued. “And so for the first time probably in my career, I’m realizing, you know, this is a great profession, it’s been a great ride for me, and I hope that it’s not over.”

As the faces of Fox and ESPN’s NFL coverage, Aikman and Buck have been staples on Sundays (and more recently Mondays) for years. The looming end of that is ripping through sports, media and the league itself. And the situation comes as Disney is set to host its first Super Bowl since 2006, with Buck and Aikman set to lead the game from the booth (they have also been a big part of its marketing). But with their rich deals, nothing can be assured, and in the TV business, any opportunity to get a better deal or sign talent that could make a difference is typically taken fast.
At a conference room in the InterContinental Barclay Hotel in Midtown Manhattan last week, NFL executive vp and chief media officer Hans Schroeder was asked about the Buck-Aikman ESPN impasse.
Schroeder, who is responsible for managing the league’s relationships with its media partners, said that it had “no concern” with the situation.

“I don’t know if you watched the game on Monday night. It was an incredible game. An incredible game, and incredible coverage by Joe and Troy, just like they always do,” Schroeder told assembled journalists in the room, adding that the league was proud of Disney’s coverage, including its numerous altcasts with the Manning brothers, Pat McAfee and Star Wars, and with all the effort going into the next Super Bowl. “I think the fans are deserving of first-class game production, which Joe and Troy have — I think going back to ’02 or something was their first year — a history of doing that as well as anyone, and I think you’ll continue to see them do that as well as anyone.”
Suffice it to say, it is not the story that the league or Disney want to be talking about right now.
And yet, the ESPN broadcast booth drama underscores what has been perhaps the most tumultuous and uncertain year ever for NFL broadcasters.

At CBS, Tony Romo’s preseason arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated (OWI) led to his ouster from the network’s broadcast booth. His replacement, J.J. Watt, was named the permanent successor last week when he was given a multiyear contract extension, with Skydance Sports chief David Berson praising him as “insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate.”

Greg Olsen is in the final year of his deal at Fox and is looking for a new home, while current NFL names like Travis Kelce and Sean McVay have bubbled up as potential TV talent in chats with agents and network execs.

A senior NFL source told THR that the league doesn’t micromanage the personnel decisions of its broadcast partners and that it isn’t involved in the calls being made when it comes to talent. But that doesn’t mean the league doesn’t have any say.

Sources at both the league and its rights partners paint the conversation around broadcasting as an ongoing conversation, with the league always interested in improving coverage of the game. More precisely, the league’s NFL deals require a quality of production from its partners that includes an A-team broadcast booth that can deliver a broadcast worthy of the league and its viewers (“first-class production,” as Schroeder said). It might be a mushy benchmark, but it does mean that more out there ideas like the Manningcast, the McAfeecase or animated altcasts remain secondary considerations, and that the main booth needs to have seasoned or otherwise A-list talent (like Tom Brady, who made his broadcast booth debut for Fox).

The drama matters, because the NFL matters. While no real fans will turn off their NFL games because of some broadcast booth drama, the entire situation is a rare speed bump for what is otherwise the most reliable bet in all of TV. And yet: The broadcast booths may change, but there’s no reason to think that the NFL will ever become less relevant, or less watched.

items.title: Michael Douglas Shares Update on Jack Nicholson: “He’s Well. He Has Disappeared”
items.description: Michael Douglas is sharing a rare update on Jack Nicholson, who has largely remained out of the spotlight in recent years.
items.author: McKinley Franklin
paragraphs: Michael Douglas is sharing a rare update on Jack Nicholson, who has largely remained out of the spotlight in recent years.
During an appearance to promote his memoir One Helluva Ride in Swansea, the Basic Instinct actor was asked about his relationship with Nicholson.
“I would have liked to have acted with Jack,” Douglas said, per The Independent. “He’s not working any more. He’s well. He has disappeared. I know that.”

He added, “I still see him, but he is fine. He is up there by his house and walking around in his slippers. It happens. He deserves it. I understand. He is a few years older than me, but I understand.”
Douglas is 82, and Nicholson is 89. The two actors only professionally collaborated on 1975’s One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, which Douglas produced and Nicholson starred in.
Nicholson’s most recent movie, How Do You Know, came out in 2010 and also starred Reese Witherspoon, Paul Rudd and Owen Wilson.

One of Nicholson’s last public appearances was in February 2025 at the Saturday Night Live 50th anniversary special. A month before that, his daughter, Lorraine Nicholson, shared a photo with her father on Instagram.
Also through Lorraine’s social media, she shared a photo of the three-time Oscar winner on her Instagram Story in April to commemorate his 89th birthday.

Douglas’ press tour for his memoir has been headline-making. He revealed in a bombshell excerpt from One Helluva Ride that he and Kathleen Turner had a secret romantic relationship while filming 1984’s Romancing the Stone.
Responding to Douglas’ admission, the actress told People, “Good heavens what a fuss about something 40 years ago! I love Michael and I look forward to enjoying the book.”

items.title: Free IP and Fresh Eyes: How Hollywood Is Reinventing the Classics
items.description: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
items.author: Lexy Perez
paragraphs: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

East of Eden showrunner Zoe Kazan has had her eye on adapting John Steinbeck’s family saga since she first read it at 15. “Somebody has to put the thing onscreen that I see in my head,” she told The Hollywood Reporter. And after “a good 20 years” of carrying that feeling, the opportunity to translate the story to screen finally came to fruition, with Kazan’s vision unfurling as an eight-episode Netflix limited series.
Hollywood has never been shy about mining the classics, with Pride and Prejudice, To Kill a Mockingbird and Little Women among the staples of film and TV’s page-to-screen catalog.

This year, Kazan’s dip into the classic canon is joined by the likes of Christopher Nolan, who has taken on Homer’s The Odyssey, Emerald Fennell’s adaptation of Emily Brontë’s Wuthering Heights, and new versions of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility and Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities. Steinbeck, Austen and Dickens come with name recognition, a built-in audience and, as Sense and Sensibility screenwriter Diana Reid puts it, “free IP.” But the prestige and name recognition only get a project so far with audiences desperate for something fresh.

This year, the writers behind Netflix’s East of Eden, Focus Features’ Sense and Sensibility and MGM+’s A Tale of Two Cities used that audience demand to do something different: leave the novels’ worlds intact and rebuild the people inside them.
For Kazan, that meant rereading Steinbeck’s Cathy. For Daniel West, it was giving Dickens’ Lucie a pulse. Reid let the Dashwood sisters Marianne and Elinor each grow into a bit of the other.

And while a famous novel might spark initial curiosity, it offers no inherent road map once development begins. So rather than reimagining these books through a modern lens, each writer chose to lean into the ways the stories already transcend time.
“You don’t need to spoon-feed the audience the modernity of it,” West says.
Why a Classic Novel Already Has Appeal

Reid is the first to admit the commercial logic of adapting a classic. “I think they are classic for a reason,” she says. But the appeal runs deeper. In an era of surface-level connection, she argues, audiences crave something that feels substantial.

“There’s nothing more satisfying as an audience than encountering someone who’s superficially very different from you — they live in another time, they have different values and customs, they dress in a bizarre way — and then realizing that emotionally you have the same inner life.”

She also knows she won’t be the last to take on Austen. “It’s nice to be part of such a big catalog. On one hand, it’s an honor and on the other, it takes pressure off, because it’ll be one of many. It doesn’t need to be definitive.”

West’s pitch for A Tale of Two Cities, a four-part series that premiered on MGM+ last month, started with what he calls a “unicorn”: a book with a huge cultural footprint that, by his account, hadn’t had a major screen adaptation in nearly 40 years. He and star and executive producer Kit Harington had been talking about adapting Dickens’ 1859 novel for roughly a decade, noting that there “hasn’t really been a seminal TV or film adaptation” of the story.

“It was done quite a lot in the first half of the 20th century, but then it petered out. So a large part of the draw was the opportunity: There was this huge built-in audience that already knew the book, or at least knew of it,” he says.

“The story itself is incredibly timely,” he adds. “It’s about a disenfranchised, broken society that is pushing back and reaching a crisis point. Within that, there’s a very personal, intimate love story.”

Kazan has a personal tie to East of Eden — her grandfather, Elia Kazan, directed the 1955 film — but part of her motivation for making a series was to tell more of the novel than that film did. Though Steinbeck’s book was published in 1952, she says, “there’s this beautiful continuum between us and the past,” which is part of what makes revisiting a classic so appealing.
Looking backward and forward at the same time, she adds, “is a profound part of what makes us human.”

“It’s the opposite of AI. It’s not regurgitation, not spitting back up what we’ve already digested,” she says. “It’s why we should read these books. They’re like a bow shot across time from one human to another.”
Rethinking the Novels’ Protagonists

Still, none of the three writers treated an established title as a safety net. Instead, their adaptations declined to modernize the novel’s setting and embraced finding new ways into the protagonists.

While developing A Tale of Two Cities, West and his producers considered a contemporary reimagining early on before dropping it. “The issues these characters are dealing with, the injustice and the way it bleeds into vengeance and cruelty, already feel very 2026,” he says.

What he changed instead was characterization. In Dickens’ novel, heroine Lucie Manette is “prone to a lot of weeping” and “quite a lot of fainting,” West says. “She’s not the most compelling heroine in large passages of it. So we made some fundamental changes. We made her much more intentional.”
He wanted Lucie to be “the central pivot of the entire story” and “the investigative force” of the opening episodes, pushing against the walls of “buttoned-up Georgian London.”

“That was a fairly big modernization from the book,” he says. Of Mirren Mack, who plays Lucie in the series, he adds: “Lucie is the central component of the whole thing, the sun at the center of the solar system, and then an actor arrives who delivers all of that and more and elevates it through her own interpretation.”

He also replaced Jarvis Lorry and Miss Pross — who he felt were “serving a similar purpose” and were too “big and colorful” for the series’ taut, volatile tone — with a new character, Hester (Sharon Duncan-Brewster). “She isn’t a proxy father figure to Lucie. She’s an inherited family member, almost an inherited stepmother. … As the story goes on, they discover that they mean a lot to each other and are more than just inherited relations. They really are family, but they come to that on their own terms. That gives them a larger emotional distance to travel.”

Thérèse Defarge (Roxane Duran) marks another departure. “We wanted to see somebody become, for want of a less anachronistic word, radicalized,” West says. “She starts as part of her community. She has a warmth and generosity. Because of what happens to her within the story, we see that crack begin to metastasize into something really sinister and ugly, and by the end, murderous. When we meet her in episode one, she’s a completely different person from what we see at the very end of the show.”

Dickens’ book centers on a couple, but West wanted to “intensify that” and “twist it slightly into much more of a triangle and make it more live and more complex” between Sydney Carton (Harington), Lucie (Mack) and Charles Darnay (François Civil). “That way we don’t really know which way Lucie is going to go until she does, toward the back end of the story. I also wanted both men to be equally attractive, equally intriguing and volatile, each speaking to a different side of her, so we really feel the pull, the tension and the dilemma she’s wrestling with.”

Kazan’s rereading centered on Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh), the character who first hooked her in Steinbeck’s story. Writing the series, which released on Netflix on Oct. 1, she realized something she hadn’t anticipated: Cathy “is almost always telling the truth.”

A fresh perspective also helped Kazan see the story as a love story between brothers Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles (Mike Faist), one that Cathy interrupts. “By watching Chris and Mike interact, I understood how much these characters loved each other,” she says.
Respecting the Literary Blueprint — and Knowing When to Change It

Creative liberties, the writers insist, aren’t changes for the sake of it. Reid describes her approach as “respect rather than reverence.” Her biggest liberty is a duel between Herbert Nordrum’s Colonel Brandon and Frank Dillane’s John Willoughby, which Austen mentions but keeps offstage. “Hearing about things secondhand in a novel is not so confusing, but onscreen, hearing a character describe it isn’t very interesting,” she says. “You need to see it to reveal the drama.”

Austen’s voice also served as a guide for balancing drama with wit. “When I read the book, I made a note of the lines that made me laugh, and a lot of those ended up verbatim in the film. Jane Austen’s just really funny,” Reid says.
Kazan’s challenge was the opposite: too much book. She was only interested in adapting it as a series because “the book is simply too big,” and even with seven episodes, “half is not in our series.”

For A Tale of Two Cities, West’s key structural decision was genre. “I always wanted it to be a thriller: a very taut, limited story,” he explains. “Four episodes felt like the perfect length to keep the pace and stakes up, and to never let any of the characters settle. I really wanted to make sure that all the characters, whether they’re in London or Paris or moving between the two, are always in a state of agitation. Their feet are never quite on solid ground, so we feel the jeopardy and the volatility of their world.”

Asked why classics keep returning, each offers their own perspective. West points to archetypes and longevity. A Tale of Two Cities, he says, “is the archetypal sacrificial story,” with “strong parallels in that act of sacrifice to the Bible and all the stories that form the basis of our narratives and our emotional map of the world.”

Classics “still feel timeless, and they still feel as resonant today,” West adds. “The key thing for us as creatives is to find a new way of telling those classic stories, an angle and something new to say about them. That doesn’t mean reinventing the wheel. It just means giving yourself the license to look at them with fresh eyes.”

Reid returns to the idea that classics are “classics for a reason.” She explains that “when an audience doesn’t feel patronized” and an adaptation allows “the classic to exist in its own time, that makes for incredibly powerful viewing.”

Kazan sees adaptations as a way to lower the barrier for new readers. “One thing these adaptations can do is make a general audience feel they have access to East of Eden, The Odyssey, Wuthering Heights.”

While they have differing ideas about what keeps the classics coming back, all three writers share the same hope: that viewers will pick up the book. Classics haven’t disappeared from school reading lists, but students are reportedly reading significantly fewer full-length books than in past decades.

“As long as we don’t ban and burn these books, everybody will continue to have access to them,” Kazan says. “There are so many books I came to as an adult that changed my life, and if I’d read them in high school, I wouldn’t have cared or understood. The most important thing is to let kids feel they can have pleasure in reading.”

There’s already evidence that these adaptations are sending people back to the page. Since the series’ Oct. 1 debut, sales of East of Eden have risen nearly 200 percent across all formats, according to publisher Penguin Classics. The novel also hit No. 1 on Amazon’s best-sellers list — 74 years after it was published. The Economist reports that U.S. sales of The Odyssey have quadrupled this year, while Wuthering Heights topped Britain’s best-seller list.

“Anything that can nudge people back toward bookshops and toward discovering those works again can only be a good thing,” West says. “The reason the work of classic storytellers like Dickens, Shakespeare and Austen still resonates is that they’re saying something about the human condition, about what we’re all struggling with, yearning for and reaching for.”

“It would be amazing if people went back to the book,” Reid says. If Sense and Sensibility “could make Austen and the classics feel less intimidating, and encourage people to see themselves in it and find emotional truth in a story they thought was too remote, that would be amazing!”
