items.title: Wales Bonner and Adidas Are Still Cooking With Gas
items.description: Just over a year ago, Grace Wales Bonner was announced as the next creative director of men’s ready-to-wear at Hermès. The move made history, making the superstar British designer the first Black woman to lead a European luxury house; her hotly anticipated fir
items.author: Tres Dean
paragraphs: Just over a year ago, Grace Wales Bonner was announced as the next creative director of men’s ready-to-wear at Hermès. The move made history, making the superstar British designer the first Black woman to lead a European luxury house; her hotly anticipated first collection is set to debut in Paris in January. It was quickly confirmed that even as Wales Bonner stepped into her role at Hermès, she’d continue to work on her beloved namesake label. What was slightly less clear is if her new position would have any effect on Wales Bonner’s ongoing collaboration with Adidas, one of the most fruitful partnerships in sneakers. But in the months since the Hermès announcement, the partnership has hardly slowed down. If anything, it’s only continued to cement itself as the gold standard for linkups between fashion houses and athletic brands. And this week, the duo drops its latest collection, another killer mix of new silhouettes and luxed-up favorites.

For fall-winter 2026, Wales Bonner and the Three Stripes are bringing the BW Army and Gazelle into the fold. Neither model has received the Wales Bonner treatment just yet, though the timing is just right for the former. The BW Army has been a sleeper hit in 2026 and designers like Wales Bonner riffing on it will only serve to further elevate its profile. Her take on the OG military runner swaps trades its typical smooth leather for paneled pony hair and croc-printed leather. It comes in two colorways—a simple black and a burnt gold with rich maroon interior lining.

The rest of the collection features some more familiar faces, including the Gazelle, Adizero Adios, and Wales Bonner’s signature Karintha silhouette. The latter comes in croc-stamped leather with gold-brushed eyelets, which calls to mind the designer’s beautiful navy blue Sambas from a couple years back. On the techy Adizero Adios, Wales Bonner paired an off-white suede construction with exaggerated stitching and a royal blue interior. Rounding out the group is the Gazelle in a similar colorway to the Karintha: croc-printed leather with an off-white tongue and heel tab, plus a gum sole and a royal blue lining.

Alongside the shoes, Wales Bonner cooked up some of the sleekest Adidas apparel we’ve seen this year. There’s a blue jumper inspired by football kits, long a staple of the collaboration, plus a boldly striped sweater in tones of auburn, brown, and red. The designer’s takes on Adidas tracksuits remain as flawless as ever, with this collection adding a navy blue pinstriped short version to the canon. The true highlight of the clothes offering, however, is a leather zip-up blouson in a rich dark brown with Adidas stripes down the arms.

The fashion world is waiting with bated breath to see what Wales Bonner delivers at Hermès, with all the resources of a historic maison at her disposal. For now, though, we’re just stoked that the new gig doesn’t seem to have abated her deep love for true-blue sportswear one bit.
The Wales Bonner x Adidas Originals fall-winter 2026 collection is available now via CONFIRMED and select retailers.

items.title: Every New Balance 990, Ranked
items.description: The New Balance 990 is one of the greatest sneaker lines ever. First released in 1982, the original took four years to develop and cost around $100—a lot for a running shoe back then. But the Boston brand wanted to make the best one it possibly could, and it w
items.author: Adam Cheung
paragraphs: The New Balance 990 is one of the greatest sneaker lines ever. First released in 1982, the original took four years to develop and cost around $100—a lot for a running shoe back then. But the Boston brand wanted to make the best one it possibly could, and it wasn't cutting corners. More than four decades later, the series has given us some of its best trainers, with each generation making its own adjustments to the suede, the mesh, and everything underfoot.

And with the seventh-gen 990v7 coming in hot, it felt like a good time to revisit the whole thing. A lot has changed since the OG, and some updates have worked better than others. We took stock—from the early pairs to the latest model, from the one that didn't quite hit to the GOAT—and here's every New Balance 990, ranked.

Well, someone had to come in last place. The 990v5 simplified the paneling and added Ortholite insoles, but visually, it's the one we get least hyped up about. The plastic detailing feels a little awkward, and the cleaner upper loses some of the aura of its predecessors. Of course, it's still a good-looking sneaker—there are just six others we'd pick first.

Putting the OG this low feels a little blasphemous, but being first doesn't automatically mean best. The 990v1's slim sole, big “N” logo, and straightforward suede panelling make it an easy pair to wear. It's a handsome thing. We just prefer the more complicated, slightly nerdier designs that NB came up with afterwards.

The newest 990 gets a provisional fifth. There's plenty to like in the reworked upper, including the leather accents, but the busy sole takes some getting used to. From the teaser photos, the proportions don't look quite as convincing as the pairs above it. With the release still ahead, we're judging the design here. A few good colorways could easily move it up.

The 990v6 made a fairly big change: out went the mid-foot saddle, leaving the “N” sitting directly on the mesh, and in with FuelCell cushioning underneath. The result looks longer and more substantial than earlier versions. That's part of the appeal, especially under wider trousers. But all that sole can dominate a fit, and we'd take the slightly neater proportions of our top three.

The 990v2 is the freaky-looking one, and we mean that in the best way possible. The small “N,” angular panels, and sculpted sole give it a very different feel from the rest of the family. There's a lot going on, but the slimmer upper keeps it from looking heavy. It's the pair we'd choose for someone who already has the obvious New Balances and wants something a little more particular.

The 990v4 is probably the one we'd recommend most often. The shape is beefy without being bulky. The suede overlays leave just enough mesh showing through. It works with jeans, loose chinos, and trousers you'd usually save for the office. Nothing feels oversized or awkward. Second place comes down to a small preference: we like the winner's extra detail a little more.

The diamond-patterned tongue. The ribbed “N.” The way the suede panels spread across the mesh. The 990v3 gives you plenty to look at, and somehow it all works together. It has the most convincing proportions of the seven: broad enough to suit loose trousers, with a sole that doesn't completely overwhelm the upper. Even in the standard grey color combo, there's nothing we'd want to change. Our GOAT.
A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

items.title: Boxers, Briefs, or Boxer Briefs? Let’s Settle This Once and for All
items.description: For many years, a great debate raged: boxers vs. briefs. Men were divided. Allegiances forged. Some preferred the boxer for its roomy comfort; others, the brief for its sleek profile and ability to gather and contain the important parts. Then came the dark tim
items.author: Coleman Molnar
paragraphs: For many years, a great debate raged: boxers vs. briefs. Men were divided. Allegiances forged. Some preferred the boxer for its roomy comfort; others, the brief for its sleek profile and ability to gather and contain the important parts. Then came the dark times. What had once been a good-faith debate devolved into name-calling, mockery, and shoddy science. Both sides entrenched themselves, blinded by their own sense of righteousness.

Then, a savior arrived: the boxer brief. Offering the best of both worlds, it combined the coverage and comfort of a boxer with the containment and discretion of a brief, without any of the tightie-whitie stigma. At last, there was peace.

Nowadays, though, decades into the boxer-brief strife, men have begun to rediscover the pleasures of the old order. As ever, there’s a strong case for boxers, briefs, and boxer briefs, but in this age of unprecedented menswear latitude, they might not be what you think. Here’s why we think you should keep all three main underwear variants in your drawer, and when to reach for each.

According to data from a 2016 fertility study of American men, 39% wore boxer briefs during the day, 35% wore boxers, and 26% wore briefs. Boxers gained ground at night, however, with 43% of men wearing them to sleep, compared with 24% in boxer briefs and 13% in briefs. Another 20% wore nothing at all. The study’s real purpose, though, was to better understand whether underwear choice affected male fertility, and when researchers looked at semen quality and how long couples took to conceive, they found no real link between underwear type and fertility.

Dr. Michael Eisenberg, a urology professor at Stanford University, co-authored the 2016 study. He says the question of boxers versus briefs comes up when he counsels men about fertility, largely because the testicles need to remain cooler than the rest of the body to function properly. “When we’ve actually studied it, the particular type of underwear tends not to be predictive of semen quality,” he confirms. “It’s unlikely any single layer is going to make that big of a difference.”
In other words, from a health perspective, there’s really no reason to choose one over the other. “Just wear what’s comfortable,” says Eisenberg.

Like Calvin pulling on his lucky rocketship-print briefs before a big day of sledding with Hobbes, it’s less about what is right or wrong and more about what fits the occasion and outfit. That’s why the person with access to all three types of underpants in their top drawer will likely be the most comfortable and outfit-appropriate. “It really depends on the pant,” says Daniel Salmon, a Brooklyn-based men’s personal stylist and design studio instructor at Parsons School of Design. “If you’re wearing a slim or fitted pant, you don’t want a pair of baggy boxer shorts stuffing extra fabric in there,” he says. “It’s definitely going to show up.”

For slimmer trousers, particularly those made from lightweight fabrics like tropical wool, Salmon recommends briefs or boxer briefs. The latter help maintain a clean silhouette, since traditional briefs can show through fitted layers. But with trousers now wider and waistbands hanging lower, could old-school boxers be poised for a comeback? Salmon points to recent looks from Haider Ackermann at Tom Ford, where boxers peeked above the waistbands of relaxed trousers. “It just adds that little bit of a styling element,” he says. “Sometimes it can allude to what’s underneath, if you want to be a little provocative.”

Of course there are practical considerations, too. “If you’re wearing really short shorts, you need to be contained,” he says. “I would say no to a boxer short.” For bigger guys, he suggests avoiding the extra bulk of loose boxers while still paying attention to fit, regardless of style. Too tight and you’re spilling over the waistband. Too loose and you’re dealing with bunching and sagging.

Ultimately though, Salmon echoes Eisenberg’s advice about personal comfort. What fits depends on your body, your clothes, and even your mood. “It varies on how you’re feeling, what you’re wearing,” he says. In other words, why limit yourself to one when you can say yes to all three? What a time to be alive.

items.title: This New G-Shock Looks a Lot Like One of the Most Iconic Watches Ever Made
items.description: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.

The 2500 Series is a new collection that “reimagines the design DNA of the watch that started it all,” according to Casio. The brand is nodding towards the original G-Shock ref. DW-5000C from 1983, a watch designed to be tough enough to keep ticking even when dropped. The team famously tested prototypes by hurling them out of the third-floor men’s bathroom of the Casio offices. The new 2500 series is a close descendant of the shock-absorbent watch's original design.

The first G-Shock featured an octagonal digital display, four buttons on the case flanks, and an integrated rubber strap. The 2500 Series incorporates most of those features—but this time, the display is analog rather than digital, and a pair of case “ears” makes the model look a lot like Patek Philippe’s famous flagship luxury sports watch.

Designed by Gérald Genta and released in 1976, the Nautilus is based on a porthole—hence the “ears,” which mirror the hinges/securing mechanism used to open and close a ship’s window against the elements. You may also recall that this isn't the first time that Casio has taken inspiration from a famous Genta watch: the GA-2100 Series (aka ‘CasiOak’), with its octagonal bezel design, bears a remarkable similarity to the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak.

The watch community has been waiting impatiently for the announcement of the 2500 series since Casio’s Japanese website accidentally listed these pieces back in September. In the months since, collectors have already given the watch the “CasioNaut” nickname. (What good is a watch without a clever nickname, after all?) The wait isn’t over just yet, though. The line will officially go on sale through Casio’s website on November 6th.

The 2500 Series is much more than a quartz-powered Nautilus copy. At the center of the design is the Multi-Mission Date function that operates through a three-cell display at 3 o’clock. Besides indicating the date, it can also display the watch’s current mode, elapsed stopwatch minutes, and setting information. Meanwhile, a small-seconds display at 9 o’clock shows passing seconds, but can also be paused and restarted as necessary. (Pausing the function can extend the battery life up to five years.)

The timepiece's tech uses G-SHOCK’s familiar four-button arrangement and comes packed with all the features we've come to expect from the Japanese brand. For starters, the watch automatically keeps rigorous time through 2099 after you input the year, month, and date. LED illumination ensures everything is legible even in low light, while a magnetic system steadies the watch’s hands even if dropped, bumped, or roughed up. Water-resistant to 200m, the 2500 Series is just as capable as you’d expect from a hard-wearing G-SHOCK. Available in simple resin cases with matching rubber bracelets for $145; with metal accents and rubber bracelets for $280-$300; and with full-metal bracelets for $350, the handful of launch references come in a variety of versatile colors and weigh between 47 grams (resin) and 160-180 grams (metal).

Though Casio releases oodles of fresh colorways in existing G-SHOCK families each year, it’s not every day that the world gets an entirely new model family. Fun, streamlined, and much more affordable than the watch it's nicknamed after, the 2500 Series is certainly on its way to becoming a hit.

items.title: Saquon Barkley Is a Luxury-Watch Designer Now
items.description: As a superstar running back for the Philadelphia Eagles, Saquon Barkley has had plenty of opportunities to flex his design muscle. He’s worked on his own shoes and branded apparel, but nothing comes close to his latest project: designing a custom watch with be
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: As a superstar running back for the Philadelphia Eagles, Saquon Barkley has had plenty of opportunities to flex his design muscle. He’s worked on his own shoes and branded apparel, but nothing comes close to his latest project: designing a custom watch with beloved Swiss watchmaker H. Moser & Cie that gave him an even deeper appreciation for timepieces.

“You don’t really get to be too detailed when it comes to designing apparel,” Barkley tells us. “But when it comes to a watch—the little stuff that’s within a watch—it’s just on a whole other level, and you just have a different appreciation of it.” The result of this hyperfocused approach is the new H. Moser Pioneer Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Aventurine Saquon Barkley Edition, a $99,600 watch limited to just 97 pieces.

Barkley discovered Moser while preparing to attend the Met Gala in 2025. He needed a watch to wear and found his way to the independent Swiss house. It’s been a mad love affair ever since. Designing a watch is “something I’ve always kind of wanted to do,” Barkley says. “When you are living this life and setting goals, I want to do stuff that takes me out of the atmosphere of just being a football player. And there aren’t many NFL athletes that can say they have their own watch. And to do it with such a prestigious brand like H. Moser made it 10 times better.”

The Pioneer is Barkley’s first horological baby, and a classic Moser: It blurs the line between a sport and a dress watch and packs specs that are catnip for the biggest nerds. The most critical feature for Barkley was the skeletonized movement—“Being able to see inside was super important,” he says. The single element that prevents you from looking inside the watch is the subdial made of aventurine, a stone that resembles the night sky.

The watch is a tribute to Barkley in more ways than one. There are the obvious touches like the Super-LumiNova-filled numerals 2 and 6, which glow a different color from the rest of the indices in honor of his jersey number. But this wouldn’t be a terribly appropriate watch for someone like Barkley—renowned for his explosive speed and signature backward hurdles—if it couldn’t take some physical abuse. The Pioneer checks those boxes with 120 meters of water resistance and is hardy enough to be worn every day, in any situation.

Designing the new Barkley edition completely changed how the running back thinks about his timepieces. “Before, it was like, ‘How does the watch look? What’s the price on the watch?’ That was how you set the value of a great watch, and I thought about what I want to put on when going out for dinner or an event,” he explains. But designing a $99,600 luxury timepiece changed everything. He brought up hairsprings, tiny pieces of coiled metal that are essential to keeping time, more than once in our interview. “I understand the process behind making a really good watch,” Barkley says, “so my appreciation of it is different.”

items.title: The Most Fashionable Erotic Thrillers for Your Halloween Watchlist
items.description: If you’re looking to be seduced, scared, and sartorially inspired, then the erotic thriller is what you seek. A kinky successor to the neo-noir, the subgenre boomed in the 1990s and came to define an entire era of sexy cinema. Filled with double entendres and
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: If you’re looking to be seduced, scared, and sartorially inspired, then the erotic thriller is what you seek. A kinky successor to the neo-noir, the subgenre boomed in the 1990s and came to define an entire era of sexy cinema. Filled with double entendres and fatalistic love-making, the erotic thriller is hot, campy, and brimming with excellent outfits.

Often following an ethically ambiguous leading lady and a man who is wont to be fooled, these films use fashion as a plot device. Madonna’s on-trial character wears prim pearls to convey her innocence in Body of Evidence. In Sliver, Sharon Stone unbuttons her LBD in a dangerously public setting. And we all understand the cultural significance of the white dress in Basic Instinct.
Below, the most fashionable erotic thrillers to get you into the come-hither Halloween spirit.

The white Basic Instinct dress is so iconic that Sharon Stone keeps it locked in a safe. Famously, in the film, it’s worn by her character Catherine, a moneyed crime novelist who appears highly suspicious after her boyfriend is murdered in the same way as a character from her book. She looks guilty, but she doesn’t mind. Catherine glides around in beige loungewear and airy slip dresses, lighting cigarettes in no-smoking areas and passing lie detector tests with imperceptible ease. But it’s her subtly sheer ivory slip, worn during a police interrogation scene, that best sums up her enigmatic allure. It remains a symbol of provocation—so much so that Demna opened his debut fall 2026 Gucci show with an homage.
Single White Female (1992)

The first detail that jumps out about Single White Female protagonist Allie (Bridget Fonda) is her red bowl cut. A choice! That specific look, along with her enviable wardrobe of power dressing pieces, becomes central to the film’s spine-chilling plot. After leaving her cheating fiancé and moving into a Manhattan apartment alone, she puts an ad in the paper for a roommate. Along comes Hedy (Jennifer Jason Leigh), an awkward but innocuous-seeming bookstore clerk. As they spend more time together, Hedy starts to copy Allie’s hair, wear Allie’s clothes, and ultimately steal Allie’s identity. They do, in fact, both end up with red bowl cuts, which some might say is two too many.

Released just one year after Basic Instinct, Sliver finds Sharon Stone swapping her blonde blowout for a precise bob. She plays Carly Norris, a career-minded book editor who moves into a sleek Manhattan high-rise, only to find the building is plagued with mysterious murders. Shot through windows, mirrors, and grainy video footage, Sliver embraces the extremes of people watching other people, and Carly’s outfits play into that theme. In one high-stakes scene, she unbuttons her dress in the middle of a fine-dining restaurant on a dare from her possibly murderous date (William Baldwin).
Where to watch: Paramount+

Body of Evidence finds a pre-Erotica Madonna playing Rebecca Carlson, a woman on trial. Her supposed crime? Murdering her lover, an elderly millionaire, by giving him a heart attack in bed. Rebecca insists she’s innocent, but as her relationship with her married lawyer (Willem Dafoe) intensifies, it’s obvious her morals are muddied. In the courtroom, her rotation of tailored blazers and prim pearls—sometimes with a beret thrown in for good measure—feels like a put-on performance. Especially since she doesn’t seem to care much about her clothes; they’re always being ripped off.

In this tension-filled lesbian thriller, there are two aesthetics at play. Violet (Jennifer Tilly) is the breathy, lingerie-clad femme fatale. Donning lace LBDs, gauzy nylons, and Betty Boop curls, she’s stuck in a loveless relationship with an abusive mob boss. When she meets Corky (Gina Ghershion)—an ex-con hired to do work on the apartment next door—things take a heated turn. Fresh out of prison, Corky is hot and vaguely unwashed, sporting a terrible barbed-wire tattoo, a stringy pixie, and spiky earrings she uses to pick locks. They hatch a plan to steal millions, things get bloody fast, and they both look very hot in the process.

In the opening scene of Stanley Kubrick’s Eyes Wide Shut, a camera follows Nicole Kidman from behind as she drops her John Galliano dress to the floor and stands naked in her room. The shot sets up the film’s voyeuristic sensuality, and the LBD—Kidman’s own—has become a piece of fashion history. “The scene where I drop the dress...that was me. That wasn’t written. That was my dress from my closet,” she said to the Los Angeles Times in 2024, adding that she told Kubrick at the time, “This is how I take off the dress, Stanley.” While filming, she worked with costume designer Merit Allen and her personal costume consultant, L’Wren Scott, to pull pieces from her own closet. Perhaps the most memorable outfit, though, is her still-coveted white Hanro tank top and briefs.

items.title: With ‘Witch,’ Dilara Findikoglu and Harley Weir Rewrite Women’s History
items.description: It is the season of the witch, which makes it the perfect time for photographer Harley Weir and designer Dilara Findikoglu to release Witch, a photo book that brings together powerful women and real witches in an exploration of the relationship between feminin
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: It is the season of the witch, which makes it the perfect time for photographer Harley Weir and designer Dilara Findikoglu to release Witch, a photo book that brings together powerful women and real witches in an exploration of the relationship between femininity, nature, spirituality, and rebellion.
“This zine is a celebration of women: the complicated, the powerful, the unruly, the tender, the strange, and the unapologetic,” Weir said in a statement.

In order to complete the project, Weir and Findikoglu traveled to eight cities and villages across Romania in just five days. This endeavor into Eastern Europe “felt strangely familiar” to Findikoglu, who is Turkish. “There was something beautiful about the land and its people, and a sense that the ancient knowledge and traditions we had come to explore were still very much alive,” she said.

At each stop, the photographer and designer found themselves in discussion with a variety of women, both real witches and those who use their sense of self and feminine power for good. The result is a book of photographs and interviews that tells a generational story of the evolution of witchcraft and womanhood today.

“For centuries, the witch has been used as a symbol of evil,” Weir said. “But maybe she was never scary because she was evil, maybe she was scary because she was free. Across history, women who were outspoken, independent, sexual, knowledgeable, or simply unwilling to conform have been treated as dangerous. The witch became a name for the woman who could not, or would not, be controlled.”

The historical misinterpretation of witchcraft sits at the center of the book. Witch attempts to reclaim the narrative, shifting the perspective on women who challenge social expectations. At the forefront of this group is real-life witch Mihaela Minca and her daughters. “In them, the witch is not a myth but a lived reality, a way of being rooted in nature, tradition, and feminine knowledge outside institutional power,” Weir said.

Minca, as well as the other women featured in Witch, are dressed in Findikoglu’s designs. The wardrobe standout is undoubtedly a cherry-adorned corseted dress, stained with juices that the more macabre-minded could read as blood. Findikoglu’s feminine, defiant clothing fit perfectly into the story of Witch, and Tudor-like details conjure up a time when these women were once persecuted. A sheer dress embodies the feeling of womanly freedom, while a coat of hair exemplifies the wild nature of a rebellious spirit.

“Dilara Findikoglu’s clothes become part of this story,” Weir said. “Her designs embrace femininity without making it obedient. The body as a place of rebellion, desire, and self-expression. The clothes feel protective and provocative at once, allowing these women to inhabit the witch not as a caricature of evil, but as a symbol of power, freedom, and refusal.”

There are an array of perspectives at play within Witch—modernity and ancient traditions, young versus old, authenticity and artifice—that mirror the varied nature of the women depicted: No matter what, power is “deeply rooted in our body,” according to Findikoglu. “Through this book, we wanted to explore and celebrate the beauty of this often-overlooked wisdom, to question the boundaries between the rational and the unseen, and to recognize the power that exists beyond what we have been taught to understand as truth.”

items.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
items.description: Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make pur
items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.

Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.

Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”

While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”

The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.

Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.
Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.

Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.

Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents.

Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said.

Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email.

There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement.

Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent. But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.

items.title: An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
items.description: If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.
items.author: Emily Mullin
paragraphs: If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.

Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.

Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.

“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.

AI models are trained primarily on published scientific literature. That means they may miss important information about the research process, including failed experiments, unexpected observations, and decisions scientists make in real time. Integrating AI models with real-world experiments can make the models more reliable, Santero says.

It’s why his team decided to connect an AI agent to a custom-built surgical setup used for performing brain injections on mice. The rig included a motorized device used to immobilize a mouse and a camera that allowed the agent to observe the procedure, move an injection needle, and control the delivery of a compound. For the experiment, his team was testing a gene therapy to see whether it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.

They asked the AI model to choose a treatment from 19 options in a spreadsheet. A veterinary surgeon first performed a craniotomy on the mouse while the AI agent observed. The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.

The team initially tested Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, but it refused to guide the needle into the mouse’s brain, suggesting it might stop midway through the surgery, which could endanger the animal.

“He did the experimental planning, but when it was time to inject, he said, ‘something on my output is telling me I shouldn't do this,’” Santero says, referring to the agent. “That was very interesting.”

The team switched to using Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Opus is a heavy-reasoning intelligence specialist best for complex multistep problem-solving, according to Anthropic, while Sonnet is better suited for everyday tasks, though it may be a stretch to call mouse brain surgery a common chore. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)

Frontier labs have been planning for more widespread physical manifestations of AI, and researchers have already begun enlisting agents to do other things in the physical world. In August, Anthropic put out a framework for how its models can interact with the real world. More recently, AI engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a car to pick up lunch at In-N-Out Burger. Only one of the models succeeded.

The brain injection procedure wasn’t without hiccups either. The researchers had established safeguards, including requiring the AI to propose an injection plan for human approval and installing an emergency button a human could hit that would disconnect the rig’s motors. They also restricted the agent's access to the underlying equipment code to prevent it from modifying its own operating rules.

However, a technical glitch disrupted the equipment's coordinate system. Although the agent correctly recognized that the calculated injection position was wrong, it refused to modify the code to correct the problem because its instructions explicitly prohibited doing so.

The team resolved the issue by using a separate AI agent on Opus 5 to make the necessary code changes, but they didn’t tell the agent that a live surgery was happening. The resulting back and forth delayed the procedure, Santero says: A typical brain injection surgery like this takes about 45 minutes, while this experiment lasted slightly longer than an hour. They’re now waiting for the therapy to take effect before assessing its impact on seizures.

Despite those glitches, Santero and his team were impressed by the agent’s performance. They’re testing Grok and other models next to figure out whether one model performs better. The company is also experimenting with agent-controlled craniotomies—a much more complicated task—but wants to be absolutely sure of their safety before moving to live surgeries.
“A mistake at that stage could seriously harm the mouse,” he says.

Santero thinks AI agents will increasingly work alongside human scientists, with direct access to lab equipment. For now, he says human oversight is key, particularly when experiments involve living animals. And it’s far too soon to unleash an AI agent on a human brain.
As for the mouse, Santero reports it’s recovering well.

items.title: A Newly Discovered Trail of Cosmic Debris Illustrates How the End of the Solar System Could Look
items.description: Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have discovered a debris disk around a white dwarf, consisting of the remnants of the solar system that once orbited it. For researchers, these structures could offer a clue as to what the end of our solar
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have discovered a debris disk around a white dwarf, consisting of the remnants of the solar system that once orbited it. For researchers, these structures could offer a clue as to what the end of our solar system will look like once the sun runs out of fuel.

The white dwarf J1328−1450 is located about 1,600 light-years from Earth. Astronomers were already aware of it thanks to star-mapping catalogs, but new observations taken with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its real name) revealed that it is surrounded by a disk of debris with an unusual structure: Two distinct rings of gas separated by a gap.

According to the observatory, this disk of material is likely the remnant of the planetary system that once orbited J1328−1450. As it passed through a red giant phase and subsequently became a white dwarf, the star may have destroyed some of its planets and left other rocky bodies exposed to an extreme environment. Some of the released material ended up forming a disk of gas and dust around the dead star.

The process that shaped this system could repeat itself in our own. In about 5 billion years, the sun will exhaust its fuel and expand into a red giant. During this phase, it could engulf nearby bodies, like the closest planets. It will then shed its outer layers, leaving behind a white dwarf. Any rocky bodies that survive this transformation could break apart and form a debris disk around the dead star, like the one astronomers are now observing in J1328−1450.

But the white dwarf’s two debris rings hint at another possibility. Their structure appears to be shaped by bodies that astronomers have not yet been able to identify directly. The data suggest that, following the star’s transformation, at least two planetary objects may have survived among the remnants of that system.

Researchers believe these two bodies could be very different in size. The one closest to the white dwarf would measure just a few kilometers in diameter, while the more distant one could be as large as Pluto or even the moon. Their interaction with the surrounding material would explain the formation of the two rings, although it has not yet been confirmed that they exist as separate objects. An alternative possibility is that the structure originates from different parts of a single planet-like body, such as its crust and core.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
items.description: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reducti
items.author: James Temple
paragraphs: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.
