items.author: Zahaan Bharmal
paragraphs: The senior partner didn’t waste any time. ‘I’m sorry, Zahaan,’ he said, ‘your services are no longer required at the firm.’ We sometimes called him the Burger King behind his back, because he ate a Whopper Meal at his desk every day. I’d never spoken to him before, and now I never would again.

It was the summer of 2001. I was fresh out of university and nine months into my first job as a management consultant in London. My parents had allowed me to move back into my old room, where I routinely collapsed after getting home from the office well after midnight. Professional life was punishing, but I gave it my all. For a brief time, I felt like I was flying: at my first performance review, I was told I had ‘partner potential’.

But then I got a phone call, telling me that one of the senior American partners wanted to meet me. That was unusual; but then again, I’d been working so hard and getting such good feedback, I figured it couldn’t be anything too bad. I was directed to an office on the first floor, several levels below where I usually sat.

After he fired me, my ears buzzed and my chest tightened; I don’t remember much else, except being told that I shouldn’t even return to my desk. It became apparent that the location of the meeting had been chosen because it would allow me to take a single flight of stairs down to the ground floor. No one would need to see me, and I wouldn’t need to speak to anyone.

The decision felt cruel and unfair. But more than anything, it seemed to violate the laws that for many years had been my way of making sense of the world: the laws of physics. Cause and effect, action and reaction. What followed was an unlikely journey – one in which the equations I thought I’d left behind at university became, unexpectedly, a companion through the messiest parts of life.

Before work, before university, I attended a competitive and prestigious all-boys school in London. While I’ll be forever grateful for the opportunities my education afforded me, life still felt tough for me as a lonely and anxious teenager. The school’s social currency was confidence, quick comebacks, and an effortless cool I never quite mastered. I often felt like I was watching from the edges, trying to decode the rules of a game that everyone else grasped intuitively.

The only thing that got me through was physics. The most fundamental of the sciences, physics represented a world that was perfectly ordered. It offered structure, rules and predictability. There was no social speculation; I could just work hard and try to figure things out. Problems and solutions, equations and outcomes. It didn’t matter how popular I was – what mattered was whether I understood the system. Slowly, the chaos of the world developed a sense of form and structure.

That clarity stayed with me, through school and into university. I read physics at Oxford, convinced for a long time that I wanted to become a scientist. It wasn’t always easy; there were late nights, bitter struggles with problem sets, moments I wondered if I’d ever get it. But when it clicked, it was wonderful: entropy, quantum mechanics, cosmology, all those deep, strange laws that govern the Universe. Physics seemed like it had a purpose, and I thought we’d go the distance.

But at some point in my final year at university, things started to change. Physics still fascinated me, but I found myself drawn to other subjects too – politics, economics, business. I wanted to understand not just how the Universe worked, but how people did. So after graduating, I decided to leave physics behind and see where those other interests would take me.
For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist

As it turns out, when I stepped away from physics, many others did too. In the years after I left university at the turn of the millennium, physics began to fade from view in the English classroom. In 2006, physics A-level entries (post-16 qualifications in the UK) were down 37 per cent from where they were in 1991. The absolute numbers have since rebounded – but not for everyone. Today, the gender gap remains stark: only 23 per cent of A-level physics entries in 2026 came from girls, a figure that hasn’t budged much in decades. And more than half of GCSE physics classes in England (taken by 14- to 16-year-olds) are taught by a non-specialist, with a shortage of some 3,500 physics teachers nationally.

Research looking at why students choose or reject physics has found that it’s seen as abstract, difficult, and disconnected from real life – a perception that’s remained steady, even as enrolment has recovered. Meanwhile, newer fields – computer science, behavioural economics, even data journalism – have felt more immediate, more applicable. They speak the language of now.
What’s strange is that this perception problem has happened at the same historical moment in which physics has begun popping up in other surprising places.

Dominic Cummings, the strategist behind Brexit and later Boris Johnson’s chief adviser, gave physics a fair share of the credit for the success of his campaigns. In one of his highly popular newsletters, he paraphrased the theoretical physicist Richard Feynman: ‘The most important thing is not to fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.’ Then there’s Elon Musk, who credits the success of his many business ventures to physics and ‘first-principles thinking’: discard convention, start from fundamental truths. And for decades, the legendary investor Charlie Munger made the same case in finance, saying that the ‘logic and power’ of physics had helped him enormously.

For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist, praised by public figures whose decisions affect millions of lives. But look closer, and the picture is more complicated.

In the first instance, billionaires and political operatives make for awkward ambassadors; Cummings, Musk and Munger might be brilliant, but they’re also extremely divisive. But more than who they are, what interests me is how they’re putting physics to work – whether they’re truly thinking with the discipline, or just brandishing it for rhetorical effect. Is ‘physics’ simply a shorthand for cutting through complexity, for stripping down problems to their most basic parts? Or does it genuinely offer something distinctive that other sciences and ways of thinking cannot?

Philosophers call the first approach ‘reductionism’: the idea that if you break any system into small enough components and trace them far enough, you eventually arrive at physics. That view can be powerful, and explains why so many people find it attractive.

It’s also been spectacularly successful. When 19th-century physicists showed that heat was simply the motion of atoms – that temperature, seemingly its own phenomenon, was actually just particles bouncing faster – an entire science collapsed into physics. Years later, that same approach helped particle physicists break matter into smaller and smaller pieces until arriving at something apparently irreducible. From the reductionist instinct came quarks, leptons and the Higgs boson. Their catalogue blueprint, the Standard Model, remains one of the greatest intellectual achievements in human history.

But reductionism has its limits. Take politics: a radical reductionist might say that this too comes down to physics, because politics is about the behaviour of groups of people; groups are made of individual people; people are made of atoms; atoms are governed by physics. But does this mean that we could predict the outcome of, say, a national election by studying the behaviour of individual atoms inside the brains of every registered voter? Unlikely. Putting aside issues of practicality, what would be the point? Economists already have economics. Psychologists already have psychology. Politicians have political theory. Physics has value only if it’s additive and illuminating.

For me, the real value of physics had never been as a cudgel for smashing things up into their smallest bits, but as a framework for navigating systems – for recognising patterns, probing assumptions, and testing whether the models we rely on actually work as they’re meant to. We see this way of thinking throughout the history of science. When cholera swept through Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow didn’t know its cause. But he mapped the cases, identified the pattern, and traced the outbreak to a single water pump on Broad Street. The founder of what we now know as epidemiology, Snow worked by constructing and interrogating mental models of the world, probing their assumptions, and following the data wherever they led.

The question, then, is not simply whether physics can be borrowed as rhetoric, but whether it really helps us to see the world more clearly, in ways that complement and benefit other disciplines. That, at least, was what stayed with me after I stopped studying it formally. Not equations or textbooks, but a way of thinking that I found myself reaching for when my world was falling apart.

Getting fired was one of those moments. I had worked so hard, yet somehow I’d still failed. Everything I understood about cause and effect told me this shouldn’t have happened. But here I was, after months of working flat out, with nothing to show for it.
An infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance

While some might have turned to therapy or career counselling, I turned back to physics to try to move on. The immediate cause was clear enough. The dot-com bubble had burst, sending ripples across the global economy that eventually reached my desk. Belts tightened, and the harsh rule in such circumstances tends to be last in, first out.

The dot-com bust was not the first nor last time something like this would happen. In 2008 came the subprime mortgage crisis; in 2011, the eurozone crashed; in 2013, the rupee tanked; in 2015, there was turbulence on the Chinese stock market; and in 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic. All these crises had two things in common. First, almost no one saw them coming – at least not precisely when or where or how. Second, they weren’t triggered by some enormous dramatic collapse, but by small, seemingly innocuous failures that cascaded into something far larger. For example, it just took a few small incidents that might otherwise have passed unnoticed – like the failure of a local mortgage lender in Southern California – to precipitate the subprime mortgage crisis.

All these events are examples of what physicists might call chaotic systems – deterministic in theory, but in practice so sensitive to initial conditions that tiny variations can spiral into radically different outcomes. A well-known example is the ‘three-body problem’, popularised by Liu Cixin’s 2008 novel of the same name and a 2024 Netflix adaptation. If you have two planets orbiting each other, you can write down neat equations to predict their paths forever. But add a third planet, and suddenly the maths explodes into unpredictability. The three bodies are still governed by clear laws, but an infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance.

The mathematician Edward Lorenz discovered something similar in 1961 when running weather simulations. His first attempt entered starting values rounded to six decimal places. His second try was rounded only to three. Yet the results diverged so dramatically that he initially suspected it was a computer fault. In fact, tiny differences in initial conditions had cascaded into entirely different weather systems. The atmosphere, like the economy, like a career, was deterministic in principle and unpredictable in practice.
As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do

Understanding the crash was one thing, but physics also helped me think about what came next. I had believed that inputs led to proportional outcomes; logically, in that world, the way to get ahead was to work as hard as possible. But physics teaches that chaotic systems play by different rules. They call instead for surge capacity, an extra buffer that allows them to absorb shocks. Without it, even small failures can lead to total collapse.

Think of a power grid. Most of the time it hums along without problem. But during an unexpected surge, such as a heatwave when millions of air conditioners are switched on at once, the system can overload and shut down. To prevent this, engineers design grids with slack in the system and extra capacity to handle unexpected spikes. Without it, a minor disruption can cascade into a blackout.

That was my mistake. As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do. We optimise everything from our schedules to our to-do lists – convinced that if we just push a bit harder, we’ll be fine. But the more we operate at our limits, the more fragile we become.

Physics provides a different lesson. Rather than relentlessly maximising, resilience is about building the capacity to withstand outlier events when they come. That might mean time slack, leaving space in our lives to recover rather than scheduling every minute. It might mean career slack, developing new skills, side projects and networks, rather than relying on a single path. Surge capacity might not prevent a crisis, but it sure helps survive one.

After my brief and bruising spell in consulting, I joined the civil service and spent most of the rest of my 20s working in government. I loved the sense of purpose, the colleagues and the privilege of shaping policy. Yet, if I’m honest, I still carried a small canker of resentment and jealousy towards my former consulting colleagues.

Compared with the UK national average, I know I was paid well as a civil servant. But with friends on six-figure salaries, it felt like I was failing at something. They could afford nicer clothes, cars and apartments. And then there was the magic trick of turning money into more money by buying assets, further widening the gap between their bank balances and mine. What stung wasn’t the inequality itself, but the perceived unfairness of the circumstances. I felt like I’d worked just as hard and still fallen behind. That distinction between inequality and unfairness became important to me.

Psychologists have shown that we’re wired to make this distinction from a very young age. In one Yale study, children were asked to split 10 coins between two people based on their performance on a task. When the two people performed equally, the children split the coins five-five – equal and fair. When one person did better, the children split the coins six-four – unequal but still fair. The interesting result happened when the children were told that both people had performed equally, but they now had to split 11 coins. With no way to maintain fairness, what could the children do? They decided to simply throw away one coin. Time and again, the children prioritised fairness.
People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged

This distinction is also evident in physics. Inequality, in the literal sense of unevenness, is built into the fabric of the Universe. In the very beginning, the cosmos was smooth and equal, a uniform fog. Only when tiny imperfections appeared – quantum fluctuations that allowed matter to clump in some places more than others – did galaxies, stars and planets emerge. Without that inequality, there would have been no structure, no possibility of life. In that sense, inequality is not always a flaw. Sometimes it is the condition for growth and diversity.

We see the same principle in natural systems. Rivers branch into unequal tributaries. Lungs and blood vessels evolve into networks with a few large arteries feeding many smaller ones. That inequality of size isn’t corruption or greed, but a kind of efficiency. It allows flow. Yet when the flow is blocked, like when a river silts up or a vessel clogs, the system fails. The problem, in other words, is not inequality itself, but unfairness: the obstruction of flow, the stacking of rules, the blocking of opportunity.

I think this is true in human systems, too. A society where some are richer than others may be tolerable, even healthy, so long as opportunities and resources can still move freely. But a society where opportunity is blocked, where the rules are stacked, where unfairness rules – people reject that instinctively. Just as I did when I looked at my friends’ consulting careers and wondered why I’d been cast out. Physics, then, suggests that a lack of justice is the real problem, rather than inequality per se. People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged.

Suddenly I saw this dynamic about fairness everywhere I looked. The financial crisis of 2007-08 wasn’t just about banks making risky bets, but about the perception that ordinary people paid the price while bankers walked away with bonuses intact. The eurozone crisis wasn’t just about debt, but about southern European countries being squeezed by rules they hadn’t set. The Occupy protests, the Arab Spring, Brexit, Donald Trump – all, in their different ways, were rebellions against unfairness.

Looking at the world through a physicist’s lens, these moments resemble phase transitions. You can heat water gradually and nothing seems to change – until you reach a critical threshold, a boiling point, and suddenly the whole system transforms from liquid to gas. Human societies, too, can bear strain for a while. But once unfairness feels systemic, the pressure builds until the system flips.

Small wonder, then, that in an age of tumult and transition, physics has found new admirers – especially among those who want to catalyse radical change, for better or worse. Musk speaks of first principles, Cummings of complexity. Their examples show how the tools of physics can shape thinking far beyond the laboratory. But in their hands, physics can feel more like a weapon than a framework, a way of bulldozing nuance in the name of clarity. For the rest of us, the challenge is not simply to borrow the garb and glamour of physics, but to carry forward its mindset – one that values humility as much as boldness, and curiosity as much as certainty.

That, I think, is where physics can still make its greatest contribution. Not by giving us ready-made answers or comforting illusions of inevitability, but by training us to question ourselves and live with the resulting uncertainty. Public discourse is saturated with physics, yet we need a deeper grounding in what it really teaches us about how to ask better questions, to test our own blind spots, and to admit what we don’t know. That need feels more urgent as new technologies only increase the temptation to reach for shortcuts.
We need artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both

So what would it take to embed this shift? My journey with physics began when I was a teenager, and that’s where I believe we need to start now. Too often, we present physics to young people as dry and technical. We teach them equations but not frameworks, facts without wonder. We rarely tell them that physics can help with the messiest parts of life, bound up as they are with uncertainty, resilience, decision-making.

In the UK, we make things worse by forcing students to choose just three or four subjects to study for the final two years of school. In practice, this often forces a split between being on the ‘science’ track or the ‘arts’ track. That false binary deprives us of exactly the kind of multidisciplinary thinkers we need: artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both.

When I visit schools now, I try to show physics as a kind of superpower. I want young people to feel that physics is something they can use, not something that excludes them. More than anything, I want them to feel it’s theirs.

I started this essay as a young man being shown the door by a superior. I ended it somewhere else entirely, with physics as a way of making sense of the messiest parts of life. But, really, what I’ve been edging up to is a story about how certain hardwon habits of mind can help us find meaning in the messiness and unpredictability of reality. For those of us who are not professional scientists, maybe the real task isn’t to love physics uncritically, or wield it carelessly, but to use it wisely. Physics shouldn’t be a shortcut to rock-solid certainty, so much as a way to live more humanely without it.

items.title: Brilliant Things to Eat and Drink This November
items.description: From tantalising new restaurant openings to one-off feasts and a taste of Christmas come early, here’s our round-up of November’s culinary highlights across London
items.author: Daisy Woodward
paragraphs: From tantalising new restaurant openings to one-off feasts and a taste of Christmas come early, here’s our round-up of November’s culinary highlights across London

At Carmelina’s, the newly opened Italian restaurant at The Webster hotel near Covent Garden, guests can drop in for a quick bite or settle in for a long, leisurely evening. The space comprises a 100-cover restaurant, an upstairs café-bar and covered terrace, and Carla’s, a late-night cocktail den. In the low-lit, forest-green dining room, designed by Red Deer, frosted-glass chandeliers hang above tables where chef Simone Serafini presents everything from fresh pasta to Sicilian red prawns and porchetta with sautéed bitter greens. Upstairs, the green-and-pink striped terrace is primed for spritzes, while downstairs, Carla’s channels the spirit of an Italian disco bar, complete with negronis and a shimmering mirror ball. Come for dinner, stay for another drink – or three.

The family-run team behind Barrafina and El Pastor is bringing a taste of Spain’s bustling neighbourhood beer bars to Borough Yards this November. At Cervecería Los Primos, cold beers will be poured straight from the tap into frosty glasses, with tapas served throughout the day and no reservations required. On the menu: crispy fried pig’s ears, golden bombas stuffed with txistorra sausage and silky aioli, flaky tuna empanadas and, for pud, freshly fried churros with chocolate sauce.
Moro Alumni Series: Tim Siadatan

Moro, the much-loved Exmouth Market restaurant famous for its Spanish and North African fare, has been feeling nostalgic of late. Ahead of its 30th birthday next year, the eatery launched its Alumni Series, inviting former chefs back into the kitchen to cook convivial Sunday lunches. The series concludes on 15 November with a special homecoming feast by Tim Siadatan, who spent three formative years at Moro before going on to co-found London favourites Trullo and Padella. Among the dishes on offer are agnolotti stuffed with delica pumpkin, mizithra and cinnamon, topped with sage butter, and a panna cotta take on Moro’s yoghurt cake with pistachios and pomegranates.

Two years after leaving Sessions Arts Club, British chef Florence Knight is back on the London dining scene with Lunette, her first solo restaurant, opening this November. Perched on the 11th floor of Nick Jones’s St Clement hotel near the Strand, the intimate, 30-seat space will serve sweeping Thames views alongside Knight’s quietly inventive, seasonal cooking. Four courses at lunch will become eight at dinner, with trial dishes ranging from crisp pomme soufflé filled with smoked eel and nasturtium to milk custard with Cévennes onion and caviar, and pork loin with figs and anchovy sauce. A sneak preview of handblown glassware and feather-shaped steak knives suggests the table setting will be every bit as refined as the menu.

For those craving the Mediterranean sun, Zylia, the new Greek-Cypriot taverna in Covent Garden, offers a delicious consolation prize. Co-founded by chef Nick Molyviatis, formerly of Kiln, Oma and Singburi, and Barry Karacostas, the restaurant has won over critics in a few short months and just earned a place in the Michelin Guide’s October selections. Its charcoal grill is the main attraction, turning out Cypriot sheftalia – pork parcels wrapped in caul fat – alongside souvlaki and Ibaiama pork chops with fennel and olive relish. For something heartier, there’s suckling lamb shoulder kleftiko, slow-roasted with potatoes, peppers and onions.

London is hardly short of pizza joints, but a forthcoming arrival in Bermondsey is squaring up to the competition. Slated to open in late November on Tanner Street, Five Feet is the brainchild of Legare’s Jay Patel, WatchHouse founder Roland Horne and former Dusty Knuckle chef Jack Ellingham. Here, dough is serious business: inside a dedicated, glass-walled room, a French stone mill will be used to grind British heritage grains into flour on site – the basis of thick, airy, square-shaped pizzas, baked in black iron pans. Toppings will range from fennel sausage, ricotta and Calabrian chilli honey to potato, caramelised onions and aged cheddar. Save room for cinnamon-crunch bomboloni with Jersey milk gelato.

On the third Thursday in November, France celebrates the first wine of the year’s harvest, Beaujolais Nouveau – a young, fruity red made from Gamay grapes that’s released just weeks after picking. Happily, Londoners can get in on the Fête du Beaujolais celebrations too. Among the restaurants and wine bars raising a glass to the occasion this year is Toklas, one of our favourite Mediterranean restaurants on Surrey Street, replete with its own adjoining (and highly acclaimed) bakery. On 19 November, chef Chris Shaw will prepare a special Beaujolais-inspired menu, accompanied by a glass of Château Thivin Nouveau for £80 per person. The restaurant’s wine team has also compiled a list exploring the region’s more complex crus for further red-wine revelry.
Colonel Saab’s Christmas Feast

Get a head start on festive feasting at Colonel Saab, whose Christmas menu, served from 24 November to 24 December, offers a welcome departure from the usual turkey and trimmings. Filled with art and antiques collected by founder Roop Partap Choudhary and his family on their travels across India, the restaurant’s two decadent outposts, in Holborn and Trafalgar Square, will be adorned with crackers, pine fronds and baubles for the occasion. The three-course affair begins with dishes such as stuffed paneer tikka and coriander chutney, followed by confit duck curry or the First-Class Officer’s Choice Railway Mutton Curry (Wes Anderson, eat your heart out), simmered with coconut milk and a splash of vinegar. To finish, take your pick of sticky toffee pudding or chocolate cake with vanilla ice cream.

Ten years after opening Three Sheets in Dalston, brothers Max and Noel Venning are returning to their old stomping ground with Berryman’s, a tiny martini, wine and oyster bar opening on Kingsland Road on 13 November. The 20-capacity, standing-room-only spot takes its cues from old-fashioned European coastal bars, with dark oak panelling, low lighting and a curved marble counter. Expect Cornish oysters served with inventive accompaniments, from gherkin granita to strawberry mignonette. To drink, there are vespers and gooseberry-spiked white cosmopolitans, while dirty martini crisps and a jamón, ’nduja and cheese-filled bikini sandwich round out the snack options. It’s walk-ins only – simply turn up and slurp up.

After making his name as the youngest-ever head chef at The Dorchester’s Grill, Tom Booton is going it alone this November with his first solo restaurant. Named after Booton’s beloved pup, Ralphie’s promises a playful take on British comfort food in an elegant setting – all dark walnut, antique furnishings and brass accents. Diners can anticipate dishes such as crispy cod cheeks with warm tartare sauce, and pork and mushroom pie with charcuterie sauce, plus the rather spectacular-sounding vanilla soft-serve sandwich, finished with warm hazelnut and fudge sauce which will be poured tableside. Four-legged diners haven’t been forgotten either: there’s a dedicated dog menu, complete with bespoke bowls.

items.title: Craig Ellwood’s mid-century modern Kubly House is for sale in California
items.description: Craig Ellwood (1922 to 1992) was a charismatic and self-made architectural superstar, adept at whipping up mid-century modern confections throughout the hills and canyons of California for a coterie stylish, artistic, and creative clients.
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Craig Ellwood (1922 to 1992) was a charismatic and self-made architectural superstar, adept at whipping up mid-century modern confections throughout the hills and canyons of California for a coterie stylish, artistic, and creative clients.

Born in Texas as Jon Nelson Burke, Ellwood never formally qualified as an architect yet, remarkably, his name is now attached to some of the most iconic houses of the last century, including Case Study House #22, the Stahl House, the meticulous precision of Case Study House #16, the Salzman House, as well as houses 17B and 18.
Sliding panels conceal the kitchen from the den
Sliding panels conceal the kitchen from the den

Although the 1950 Ellwood-Zimmerman House in Brentwood was needlessly demolished in 2024, there are a still a notable number of surviving projects that bear his signature style, including the 1976 campus for the ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, designed with James Tyler, and the renewed and restored Moore House, also from 1965.
Primary bedroom seen from the outside

Now Ellwood fans have another opportunity to buy into the legend, this time with slightly less of the cultural burden borne by the Stahl House. The Kubly House is located in Pasadena and has a close connection to ArtCenter. Completed in 1965 for the princely sum of $45,000, the three-bedroom, two-bathroom house covers a modest 2,277 sq ft.

The clients were Don and Sally Kubly, both ArtCenter alumni and educators; Don went on to become its second president. The process of building the house kickstarted the creative partnership that eventually led to Ellwood’s involvement on the new campus buildings a decade later.

The structure is simplicity itself, a glass and timber box with a clear Miesian inspiration (allegedly sketched on a napkin by Ellwood during a client lunch). All utility spaces sit within the glazed envelope, with a galley kitchen at the heart of the property, flanked by a living room and dining/family room. The corners of the rectangular plan are given over to bedrooms, with the primary ensuite bedroom on one side and two children’s bedrooms on the other, sharing a bathroom.

Steps and terraces, aligned with the centre of the house, lead down to the landscaped 0.6-acre garden and pool. The post and beam pavilion is raised up on short pilotis above the gently curving site, with mature trees along the perimeter providing framed views from every room.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The Kubly family retained the house until 2022. The subsequent owners undertook a sympathetic restoration of what is believed to be the architect’s only residential project in Pasadena. This included updating all the house’s major systems and restoring the surfaces, structure and glazing, readying the Kubly House for the next phase of its history.
The Kubly House, 215 La Vereda Road, Pasadena, for sale via Chris Suarez and Kimberly Benz of Suarez + Benz at Compass, TheKublyHouse.com, priced at $3,250,000

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: JORDAN FIRSTMAN - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut
paragraphs: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut

Jordan Firstman (American, 35 years old, completely fabulous) might be familiar to readers from his brassy internet memes, or his brilliant leading role in ‘Rotting in the Sun’, 2023’s crime thriller set in sexy Mexico. Or from the news that his debut as a director ‘Club Kid’ (which he also wrote and plays the lead in) was heralded with a seven-minute standing ovation at Cannes earlier this year and triggered a fierce bidding war between the biggest studios in Hollywood. A star was born.

Because he does so much, Jordan often struggles with knowing what to call himself. Luckily, help is at hand from Luca Guadagnino, Jordan’s friend of close to ten years and the director of ‘I Am Love’, ‘Call Me by Your Name’, ‘Queer’, ‘Challengers’ and so many other cinema highs. Here, Jordan gets some handy life advice from his fellow multi-tasking director, who also photographed and interviewed him for this story. The following Q&A has been edited for maximum readability and pleasure. Ready?
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Text and photography by LUCA GUADAGNINO
JORDAN — Did I get too sunburnt?

L — A little bit. You’re a bit red, like a lobster. One second, baby, that’s not the beginning of the interview. It should start this way: Okay, Jordan Firstman has always been at the forefront of the most up-to-date things: the most up-to-date behaviour, the most up-to-date public persona. You have been directly and indirectly commenting on the state of the world and making fun of it and finding a way to showcase your personality and individuality. Eventually this has allowed you to be perceived as who you actually are. Not many people succeed in that. How do you see that in the face of the way the world works right now, the way in which authority expresses itself, the way in which parts of the world are in flames but not for the right reason?

J — Well, thank you. That’s a compliment, I think. I’ve always just tried to go from the inside out, and I’ve always known I’ve had a problem with saying everything that was on my mind, and I think it took, from high school, about a decade to figure out how to say that in a way that worked for me and didn’t hinder me. I remember my high school theatre teacher told me that I had special powers, and he said, “But you have to use your powers for good and not evil,” because I think he saw me. He saw that I was capable of both.
L — What kind of evil were you capable of at that stage in your life?

J — I’m able and have since I was a kid been able to see through things and speak honestly about them. He saw that I’ve always felt a strong sense of justice, and when people weren’t treating me or my peers right, I would be outlandish.
L — Is this something that comes out when you deal with power, or people in positions of power?

J — Until very recently this is how I have felt with a lot of people, where I think there is something hidden in their actions. Maybe they feel like I’m going to corrupt the system they have made, so they want to take my voice or my thing away from me, and I often respond very strongly to that.

L — I don’t know anyone, or at least haven’t met anyone in the last ten years, who has been able to express themselves through so many different mediums and through so many different types of performance in the way that you do. Whether that’s movies, or YouTube videos, or TV, or acting as an actor or writing as a writer or directing as a director. Is it possible that it’s a sort of victimisation of the self that helps propel you?
J — I believe I have been very, very lucky, but also, you know, I had to go to the internet because I had eight years of trying to develop ideas for TV that I just kept hitting walls with.
L — But do you agree with me, Jordan, that if you’d had fame and success, let’s say at the age of 22, 23, 24, just after theatre school, you would have become a horrible person?
J — I think it wouldn’t have been great for me. I don’t know if I would have become a horrible person, but I think I would have potentially self-destructed.
L — It’s so important to understand that maturity and success are better allies than success and youth.
J — Well, they say youth is wasted on the young, do they not?
L — I agree. Do you like younger men, men your age, or older men?
J — I usually like my age or older. Young people just end up annoying you in some way or another.
L — Do you despise people that are not fit, particularly men?
J — Of course. I envy you for many, many reasons.
L — No, no, I think the only reason you envy me is my belly and my lack of muscles.
J — I like your belly. I mean, I like a belly. I think it’s a classic gay thing, too, where we like to feel a body with some fluff on it, but we don’t want it for ourselves. I like a bigger guy.

L — One day, many, many years ago – I was very young – I met David LaChapelle, and I shot a tiny little documentary about him that I never edited. It must have been 1994, something like that, and David was super fit, and I was, like, 23 and he said to me, “Listen, as a gay man, I make sure that I’m very fit, because I have to offer something that someone else will recognise as attractive to them.” Do you think these politics are still valid?

J — I think so. It’s not only gay men, though. I mean, maybe it’s not straight men, but I don’t know. I feel we’re at a place in culture where everyone is being objectified. Male movie stars are being objectified purely for their appearance in ways they never have been, which I guess is a good thing. It’s great for women to kind of reclaim that gaze, but then it’s also got some sides that are not so positive. Every- where you look in Hollywood, everyone is bone thin, or every guy is on steroids.
L — What happened to body positivity?
J — I think it ebbs and flows. Everything that was cool in 2019 became not cool in 2022 and then whatever was cool then became not cool in 2025. Things just move very fast now.
L — How many categories of men are there? If you had to take me on a journey through the labyrinth…

J — I’ve never subscribed to the whole “gay animal” thing. I think it’s very weird that we compare ourselves to animals. I don’t really understand that. A lot of people fall in between categories. I’ve always thought of myself as just a normal-looking gay guy.

L — When I met you, I thought you looked like a straight-acting gay guy. For a moment, I actually thought you were straight. Now I would say, first of all, you’re very handsome and very attractive, and it’s interesting because you’ve kept being so throughout the ten years that I’ve known you, which is great, so congratulations.
L — But I have to ask, would you see yourself in the otter category?
J — No! I don’t think I’m an otter, because I think of otters as a little thinner framed than I am. I think I’m a little bit bulky. I think I’m supposed to be… God wants me to be fat.
L — God wants you to be a bear.
J — Yes, God wants me to be a bear. Honestly, I hate these categories. It actually makes me feel sick.

L — One of the things that comes to mind when I think about you is your very emotional investment in autobiography. Everything is autobiographical: even in Rachel Sennott’s show, you appear as a version of yourself, which I think is a great thing, because, as you know, I love Bernardo Bertolucci, and Bertolucci always said movies should be documentaries about the actors playing the characters. Do you think this will always be the case for you, or do you think that – after these long apprenticeship years of expressing yourself through movies, through acting, through performing, through writing and directing – you will try to test yourself with a more transformative way of presenting yourself?

J — But you know, in ‘Club Kid’, there’s a lot of me in it but it’s not me or my story. With my favourite artists and film-makers I get this sense that I can tell what they are going through in their personal lives when I see their work. I think you are like that, even if you maybe don’t agree. I feel like Paul Thomas Anderson is the same way. Stephen Sondheim, not to be a total faggot about it, but, you can tell he wrote ‘Sweeney Todd’ when he hated the world, he wrote ‘Company’ when he was a single man and in his forties. So, I would like to be the type of artist that finds different stories to tell, based on where I’m at in my life.
L — You are already there. You know that, right? Even the movie that you did as an actor with the director whose name I constantly forget…
L — ‘Rotting in the Sun’, by…?

L — Exactly, Sebastián Silva. Sebastián Silva is a mega cult director, he has an incredible following, he’s beloved by the most sophisticated critics, and he has a very, very strong personal voice as a film-maker.
L — And then the movie ‘Rotting in the Sun’: it’s as much yours as it is his.
J — I couldn’t tell if you liked it when I sent it to you.

L — I think the movie pushed buttons in me that made me feel that I hated it, and then I watched it a few years later, because people kept saying how great the movie was, and I can see the greatness now. Sometimes you need to hate things in order to understand them.
L — Okay, so you are now thinking, maybe next time I’ll put on a mask to cover myself, but I will still try to express the inside of myself, the inner emotions.

J — Yes. I’m interested in doing projects without me appearing in them. I think maybe for the next one I would still like to be in it, but then with the one after that I would like to explore something else. You know, what would my emotions and POV look like from a 60-year-old woman? I’d like to put my filter through different types of characters, and see how that lands.
L — ‘Club Kid’, a tear-jerker story of a father and a son, truthfully starts from an anguish-filled and tear-jerking experience in your life with a man, correct?
L — Why did you feel that a father-and-son relationship was the best metaphor to tell the story of this lost love?

J — The movie really started from the very simple thought that me next to a kid is funny. I wanted to take my life – the way I live, the way I talk – and see what happened when there’s a ten-year-old boy suddenly there. But then I went through a break-up in the middle of writing it, and it became about something else, and when I watch it now, I can really see the metaphors of being both the parent and the child to someone you’re dating, and vice versa. There’s a lot of transference happening. I think it happened in a really natural way: just the more I worked on it, the deeper it got.
L — I think every character is you, particularly the two main characters. Or let’s say the main character, Peter.

J — I really love Peter, and there’s so many parts of Peter that I wish I was more like. I definitely pushed back on myself a couple times, wondering whether the characters in my movie were too good or too idealised. And I came to a place where I kind of wanted the characters to be good people. I feel that right now you don’t really see that so much. I feel like we’re in the anti-hero movement. It’s very in vogue.
L — What is the anti-hero movement?

J — In a lot of films currently every character needs to be a bit of a shitty person for it to be palatable, or to create a bit of distance between the audience and the character. I don’t want to name movies, but I think it’s very millennial, and very, very my generation to have this detached distance from the characters – almost as a protective shield.
L — I want you to name these movies.
J — I’m not… Luca, I told you, I’m growing up and learning how to keep my mouth shut in interviews, unlike some people… ‘F1’, is that the movie you shit-talked?
L — That was Jodie Foster. Jodie’s amazing. Do you know her?
J — But didn’t you say something about ‘F1’ too?
L — No. Jodie Foster made remarks about ‘F1’. She said that ‘F1’ seems to be a movie made with AI. What do you think of Jodie Foster?
L — Have you ever met Jodie Foster?

J — I have never met her. She’s the aunt of one of my dear friends and I’m scared to meet her because either she’s gonna love me or hate me, which is often the case with lesbians. But I think she’s a legend and amazing, and I hope she would like me.
L — But don’t you think the liking or the not liking will depend on how you present yourself?
J — Yes, but as you know, maybe I would get nervous and say something off-putting.
L — It seems to me that Jodie Foster is one of the brightest people you can meet in Hollywood. What would be off-putting to say to Jodie?

J — I don’t know, I would probably end up being, like, “Oh, you know, lesbians sometimes are like this or don’t like me,” and then she would be, like, “Oh, you think all lesbians are like that?” and I’d be, like, “No, no, not all lesbians, I’m sorry,” and then I would just put my foot in my mouth.
L — Next question. Do you have children?
J — I do. I have a child, and I have to be a little bit careful. I just can’t say any proper names.
L — Okay? Do you think you’re the father?
J — No, I’m the…uncle. Right now, I’m the uncle who gave my cum away.

L — Wait, I just realised you have already told me this story and how personal it was, and it’s my bad that I asked you about it. It was unconscious because I was thinking of the character in ‘Club Kid’ – this gay man who discovers one day that he has a ten-year-old child. I was wondering if you think you could have a kid of around ten somewhere in the world that you are not aware of?

J — Sometimes I think I would be such a great dad, and I would love to have a kid to hang out with, and then sometimes I think I would be a horrible parent and ignore my kid and go off and eat at Erewhon by myself. One of the questions at the core of ‘Club Kid’ is: “What makes a kid?” Is love enough, or do you need to raise them in a traditional way for them to be all right? I think a lot of parents have kids when they are a bit stuck and they use the kid as a way to move to the next thing and hope that they will figure out, or learn, who they are through that, but often that doesn’t work. So I wanted to give Peter, the dad, the gift of time to not have drugs in his life, to not have partying, to have some form of stability.
L — That is your conservative side coming out.

J — I knew you were going to say this, because we’ve talked about it before together, and I’ve thought about it a lot since you said it. You said to me: “You’re a very conservative person,” but I think, no tea no shade, Luca, I’ve been in it, and when you’re in this hyper specific scene that I am just now kind of exiting, I think anyone who sees this movie that has experienced the G and the drugs and the state of it now knows it is not sustainable, you can’t end up there.
L — What were Jordan Firstman’s first five years of life like? Do you remember them? Where do you come from, what’s your hometown?

J — I’m from Long Island, a nice Jewish family with some bubblings of darkness underneath. It seemed nice to me at the time, and then, you know, you find out things. I guess, like any family, mine had their secrets.
L — What’s the dark secret of your family that you want to disclose?

J — I really can’t say at this juncture, but hopefully I will be able to, I don’t know, make something about it one day. But just a lot of lies, a lot of financial stuff that was being lied about and some familial generational trauma kind of stuff. But I can’t really talk about it.
L — You grew up in the ’80s, right, or in the ’90s?

J — In the ’90s. I was born in ’91. I do remember it being very, very nice, very, very peaceful. I was very shy, I was very sweet, I was smiling a lot. I started to be kind of funny around, like, five. I would watch ‘Seinfeld’ with my parents and do Kramer impressions, so I think that’s when that started. I think people are surprised when they meet me, and I can sometimes be a little shy. I’ve learned how to be an extrovert, but I think my true self is a bit shy.
L — Like pretty much all the comedians and, I would say, all the talented people.

J — I think creative people often have a lot going on in their minds, and it can be very overwhelming or overstimulating when they meet people. Especially as a somewhat public person, people come up to me all the time, and they have some sort of perception of me, so they want to have a certain vibe.
L — Do they all want to have sex with you?

J — No, the ones who want to have sex with me talk shit about me on Twitter and don’t come up to me in real life, and the ones who do come up to me are, like, usually very, very nice, but they want to banter. I think, through the nature of my work, I’ve created that lack of boundary, maybe, especially when I was doing this stuff online. People just come up and want to immediately have a rapport with me, joke around, and most of the time I’m not in the place to want to do that.
J — I don’t know. I think joking is such a personal thing; you have to be with someone that you trust. For me, I can’t just joke around.
L — So at the age of five, you started to exhibit some comedic tendencies. But when would you say you started to realise it was something really fundamental about yourself?
J — I would say I honestly started getting what comedy was when I started watching Woody Allen in high school.
L — You know Woody Allen is not mentionable as an artist.
J — But I was in high school! I didn’t know the things that I know now.
L — You are gonna be in trouble quoting Woody Allen in an interview.
J — You can’t say you watched Woody Allen as a high schooler?
L — I already had a lot of shit with making my movie ‘After the Hunt’, having the title sequence paying homage to his movies. How do we get off of the Woody Allen?
J — Okay, okay, I’m gonna think of something else…
L — No no, Woody Allen is now within the interview; we can’t remove him. But how do we reassure the readers that we are good people?

J — I do not condone anything that ever happened in his personal life. I think he genuinely is a sick person and I genuinely do think that he became disturbed at some point. But when I was in high school and was someone who didn’t know anything about his personal life, the way he wrote characters was very new to me, and I found it very interesting. When I was in high school all I wanted to be was affluent.
L — Did you like Brian De Palma when you were growing up?
J — I didn’t watch any De Palma until my early twenties.
L — Okay, so that didn’t have any power or influence on your upbringing?

J — No, but when I discovered Paul Mazursky, that was the real wake-up call for me as an artist. Because even Woody Allen, his dialogue is very arch in a lot of ways; it’s very pointed, it’s very sharp. But Paul Mazursky, when I saw that, I was, like, “Oh my god,” because it had a naturalism that not many funny movies I loved had, but it still had this edge of observation and humour. But the edges were really soft. The dialogue felt very soft to me, and when I saw ‘Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice’ I just fucking lost my shit. That really shaped the way I’ve written. That and ‘Enlightened’, the Mike White show. Those were the two things I saw in my early twenties where I was, like, “Okay, this is the type of writing I would love to do.”

L — I think that the idea that you quote Paul Mazursky is fantastic. I love that director. There was another Paul that I love, which was Paul Bartel, and there is one movie called ‘Scenes from the Class Struggle in Beverly Hills’ that I think you’ll love very much.
L — I’m offering you an idea to watch the movie, love the movie, and maybe remake the movie, because it’s one of the great movies of the late ’80s, and it’s very Jordan Firstman, so watch that.
J — Okay, I want to watch.

L — Now that you’ve done ‘Club Kid’, and since I saw the movie, I don’t think of you as an actor or as a comedian anymore. I think of you as a director, and I think that will be forever. Did you want to be a director forever?
J — No, I think I would say a film-maker. I hate to say it, but film-maker feels like the right term to me.

L — No darling, that’s wrong. “Directed by” is the most noble thing you can think of when you go to the cinema. “Directed by John Ford.” He’s a director, and the director is the quintessential personality of cinema.
J — The person that gets all the autonomy is the director, but I think the writing is so important, and they very rarely write.
L — How do we deal with the fact that many of the greatest directors of all time, and many of the greatest movies, have been directed by directors who didn’t write?
J — I don’t know how to deal with that.
L — Would you work with a script that you’ve been handed but didn’t write yourself?
J — It’s tough for me. I’m new right now. It doesn’t feel so appealing to me. I’m definitely getting scripts sent to me but they just don’t do it for me.

L — I think the fact that you aren’t getting any good scripts is normal, because 90 percent of scripts are not good, or not good enough: they are too formulaic, they don’t have a real point of view, they are derivative, and so on. But that has been the same since forever. When you meet a great writer with a great script, that’s the moment in which you, as a director, are completely freed. So, I want Jordan Firstman to consider the possibility of working with a writer in the future, and to be a director: “Directed by Jordan Firstman.”
J — I’m open to it right now.
L — I don’t think you’re open to it.
J — I’m open to a world where I’m open to it.
L — When you were in Cannes, did you think, “Damn it. Why didn’t they put me in the competition?”
J — No, I promise you. Not for one second. How could I feel anything but, “What the fuck is happening?”
L — Were you upset that you didn’t win Un Certain Regard?
J — I think I was upset for three hours.

J — Genuinely, I was bummed for three hours. But you know, I understood the decision. You know, you can never really be sad about losing something. I’ll probably say this 20 more times in the course of the next year, but this is the first time I’m saying it: genuinely, when we wrapped production on ‘Club Kid’, I felt so lucky for the experience and what it opened up in me and for getting to not only do it but do it my way, that everything else feels like a bonus.
L — How will you prepare yourself for the award season?

J — Stay in the gym. Try not to drink. I want to figure out how to be myself, but not say anything too outlandish. I want to stay on people’s good sides. I don’t know, it’s gonna be my first release, so I just…I want to stay present, I want to stay alert, I want to be able to do this again, so I want to do everything I can to ensure that I’m able to, you know, make another movie the way I want to make it.
L — Can I give you a tiny little bit of advice? I don’t want it to sound paternalistic, or like I’m patronising you, though.
L — Shoot your next movie within the next ten months.
J — Can you give me an extension…
L — Twelve months, 14 max.
J — Okay, 14 months from now.
L — It means basically you being on set in March. Can you do that?
L — Are you writing something?
J — I am. I have the idea, but I don’t want to give a timeline.
L — All the people who are reading this interview are completely rooting for you and want you to keep going without the industry timelines. Make a movie in a year.
J — I am going to try to go as fast as I can. But I want it to be good. I want to have time to rewrite it and work on it. You know what I mean.
L — I do, absolutely. Jordan, have you ever used your smile as a weapon?
L — When did you realise your smile was a weapon?
J — I think honestly pretty young, and I definitely used it romantically a lot in my twenties.
L — Have you ghosted lovers that you charmed with your smile?
J — I’m not a ghoster, believe it or not. I’m pretty open, and I think I’m very clear with what I’m looking for in people.
L — Let’s enact a scenario where you break up with me.
J — I have had so much fun spending time with you, and I hope we can keep spending time. I think romantically I’m not really looking for this right now, but I think you’re amazing.
L — What are you looking for?

J — I don’t know, I don’t know, but I think I just need to keep my options open right now, and I hope we can still hang out. I’m a huge fan of everything you do. I think you’re so handsome and beautiful, and I know I really believe that. I swear, Luca, I really believe this.
L — Jordan, you are full of shit. And you’re using the smile. This is on the record: he’s using the smile to kill me!
J — That is how I would do it. Don’t you think that was a very kind way to break up with someone?
L — No, I think it’s formulaic. It’s a bad script.
J — I believed it, though.
L — It was a very good improvisation. I think the people will love it.

Photographic assistance by Jacopo Vimercati and Nicolò Rampazzo. Digital operation by Emanuele de Rossi. Styling assistance by Ilaria Taccini. Hair by Alessandro Rebecchi at Artlist Paris. Tailoring by Camilla Masi. Set design by Flavia Manacorda. Production by Frenesy.

items.title: Palace and Burberry’s Surprise Collab Is Peak British Banger
items.description: If you had any lingering doubts about whether Burberry is back, leave them at the door. Britain’s most storied British brand just dropped a banger of a surprise collaboration with fellow UK label Palace Skateboards that is so bloke, so beautifully British, it
items.author: Chris Erik Thomas
paragraphs: If you had any lingering doubts about whether Burberry is back, leave them at the door. Britain’s most storied British brand just dropped a banger of a surprise collaboration with fellow UK label Palace Skateboards that is so bloke, so beautifully British, it almost feels illegal. As an English colleague translated into his native tongue: “I need to splash my wonga on this clobber.”
Put simply, Palace x Burberry goes hard-hard. Partly because it’s one of those rare link-ups that feels like a no-brainer in hindsight, yet it came out of nowhere.

The 10-piece capsule features the requisite skateboards, baseball caps, scarves, and shirts with Burb’s check pattern and co-branding. But the big cheese of the bunch is an update on Burberry’s iconic Camden car coat, which has been covered in screen-printed illustrations of the British countryside and topped off with its OG Equestrian Knight mascot vaulting out of the Palace Tri-Ferg.

Chalk this up as yet another win for the label’s current creative director, Daniel Lee. Burberry works best when it remembers its Britishness, which is exactly the brand strategy that Lee has put into place since taking the helm in 2022. That’s translated into collaborations with iconic UK-based artists like textile designer Celia Birtwell, illustrator Sir Quentin Blake, and Young British Artist figurehead Gary Hume.

Even with Palace, it doesn’t feel like course-correcting after a rocky few misfires (the less said about its price hike to Chanel-level luxury, the better). Instead, it feels like a brand that’s got its confidence back.

Sure, Burberry has done the streetwear route before with its 2022 Supreme collab during the Riccardo Tisci era. But that was transatlantic. This hits different because it’s homegrown. A god-tier meal deal, if you will. Good news for Anglophiles, bad news for that rent check: the collection releases on November 5 at the new Palace London flagship.
