items.title: Judge Dismisses Trump’s Wall Street Journal Defamation Lawsuit Over Published Epstein ‘Birthday Book’ for a Second Time
items.description: A federal judge has once again dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation claims against the Wall Street Journal over a 2025 report by the paper that a 2003 birthday letter to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein was purportedly written by Trump.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: A federal judge has once again dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation claims against the Wall Street Journal over a 2025 report by the paper that a 2003 birthday letter to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein was purportedly written by Trump.

Trump’s lawsuit “falls short of pleading actual malice,” wrote U.S. District Judge Darrin P. Gayles in his opinion on Saturday. “Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.” Judge Gayles dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot refile the claim.

In April, Judge Gayles ruled that the lawsuit “fails to adequately allege actual malice,” a legal standard in the U.S. for proving defamation. At the time, the court dismissed the complaint “without prejudice,” since he had only made one attempt to state his claims.

Trump sought at least $20 billion in damages on two counts of defamation in the initial suit, filed in July 2025. He sued the WSJ, its parent companies Dow Jones & Co. and News Corp, the reporters on the story and Rupert Murdoch.

“We have just filed a POWERHOUSE Lawsuit against everyone involved in publishing the false, malicious, defamatory, FAKE NEWS ‘article’ in the useless ‘rag’ that is, The Wall Street Journal,” Trump wrote at the time on Truth Social. “I hope Rupert and his ‘friends’ are looking forward to the many hours of depositions and testimonies they will have to provide in this case.”

items.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Fends Off ‘Clayface’ for Top Spot on Friday With $3.56 Million
items.description: A24’s “You Can See Everything” narrowly beat Warner Bros. and DC’s “Clayface” at the Friday box office, cementing its status as the must-watch documentary — or film, for that matter — of the moment.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: A24’s “You Can See Everything” narrowly beat Warner Bros. and DC’s “Clayface” at the Friday box office, cementing its status as the must-watch documentary — or film, for that matter — of the moment.

The buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc generated $3.56 million on its third Friday from an expanded 3,243 North American theaters and should earn $10.65 million by Sunday, per rival estimates. That’s on top of the cumulative $56.85 million it’s already pulled in across North America since it opened in theaters on Oct. 16.

Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

Just behind the doc, “Clayface” landed at No. 2 on its second Friday, making $3.3 million from 3,478 North American theaters. The gory DC film has made $36.9 million domestically so far, with rival estimates suggesting the film will gross another $10.25 million by Sunday.

Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star. Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.”

Laika’s “Wildwood” landed in third place on Friday, grossing $2.39 million from 3,100 North American theaters. Featuring a voice cast that includes Carey Mulligan, Jacob Tremblay and others, the stop-motion film looks to add another $7 to $8 million to its cumulative domestic gross of $25.2 million through its second weekend in theaters.

Directed by Travis Knight, “Wildwood” revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted. Strong reviews should continue to propel the lavish film at the box office, which carries a substantial $100 million price tag.

Black Bear’s “Wicker” followed with $1.43 million in its second Friday from 2,374 North American theaters, landing in fifth place behind the concert film “BTS World Tour ‘ARIRANG’ in South America,” which brought in $2 million from 1,010 North American theaters. Described as an “audacious comedic fable,” “Wicker” is targeting another $4.1 million in its sophomore weekend, adding to its $13 million cumulative domestic gross.
“Wicker” tells the love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband (Alexander Skarsgård) from the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Elizabeth Debicki also stars.

items.title: Maya Jama on That Shocking ‘Celebrity Traitors’ Finale, [SPOILER]’s Betrayal and ‘Heated’ Last Roundtable: ‘My Heart Was Jumping Out of My Chest’
items.description: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for the finale of “Celebrity Traitors” Season 2, now streaming on BBC iPlayer.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for the finale of “Celebrity Traitors” Season 2, now streaming on BBC iPlayer.
There’s no question Maya Jama carried this season of “The Celebrity Traitors.”

As the only original Traitor to make it to the final episode, the “Love Island” host successfully went undetected for five weeks and recruited three hooded accomplices in comedian James Acaster, professor Hannah Fry and YouTuber King Kenny. Not a single Faithful even threw a hint of suspicion her way until “Good Omens” star Michael Sheen zoned in on her at the last roundtable, leading to her banishment just before endgame.

“It was actually quite shocking for me too, I’m not gonna lie,” Jama tells Variety the day after the finale as she preps for her annual Halloween party. “After every day I was like, ‘How the fuck did I get away with that one? And why are you not looking at me?'”

Ultimately, the remaining Faithfuls — comedian Romesh Ranganathan and actor-singer Sebastian Croft — were victorious after voting out Traitor Kenny, donating £41,500 ($55,600) each to the charity of their choice. And although Jama didn’t prevail, she’s decided to also give what she would have won to the charity she was supporting, Action for Children, which provides foster care and residential support for children and young people seeking asylum in the U.K.
“Obviously, I would have loved to get to the [endgame], but the whole point is money going to charity at the end of the day,” she says.

Jama is also walking away from “The Celebrity Traitors” with a whole new crop of close friends — Kenny, Ranganathan, Croft and Fry are among the attendees of her Halloween party. “We’re the most unlikely group ever, but it’s a bond that you can’t have with anybody else because we’re the only ones who went through this exact experience,” Jama says.
Below, Jama tells Variety more about her “Celebrity Traitors” experience, including Kenny’s big betrayal, Acaster’s dramatic exit and where she thinks the Traitors went wrong in their gameplay.
Happy Halloween! What’s your costume this year?

I can actually reveal what I’m being: Mo Farah, the Olympic champion. I’m going to be in a bald cap and he sent me his actual Olympic outfit. I think people are expecting me to be sexy, but they’re just gonna see like, a bald man.
That’s incredible. You know, the last time we talked you told me you really wanted to play a villain. Look at you now!
Yeah, I know! I manifested it a bit too hard, I think.
How are you feeling after the finale? Did you watch it live?

I had loads of people over and we watched it last night. Honestly, it’s super scary watching back because we filmed in May, and you know bits of what happened but you just have no idea what’s going to be included. [I was] just nervous like, how did I defend myself [at the last roundtable]? I remember feeling my heart jumping out of my chest at every moment, so I was like, please let me have kept composure. But I was actually really proud of myself. It felt a lot more heated in the moment, even more than it showed on the TV.
It was amazing that your snarky comment after you got banished — “Good luck, you’re going to need it” — ended up playing a part in James Blunt’s banishment from the endgame.
A little sprinkle sprinkle at the end. I just thought, to be honest, the game’s wide open now so go fend for yourselves, everybody.
Going back to the beginning for a moment, did you always want to be a Traitor?

No! I was like, 50-50. Once I sat down with Claudia [Winkleman], I was like, “I actually don’t mind because there’s benefits to both.” If I’m a faithful then I can just be myself and try to do my best investigating job, and then if I was a villain, what you saw was me being like, “Well, I never get to play a villain and I’d actually like to be a cheeky little evil killer.” But I was more leaning towards wanting to be a Traitor because I just felt like, I might as well get the full experience. And I knew that it would definitely challenge different sides of me. I haven’t used many manipulation skills recently, so I wanted to put them to play.
And poor Richard E. Grant, who was an original Traitor with you but mistakenly said it out loud and became the first person to be banished.

I know, Richard would have been so great to just have around and laugh and get up to mischief with. I think he got too excited and panicked. I don’t know if he thought that he could get away with it, or maybe he thought it was allowed? I’m not really sure.
How did you get yourself into the Traitor mindset?

My plan always was like, “OK, you know these people a little bit, but barely.” I wasn’t super close with anyone [before] — I knew Kenny, Romesh, Rob [Beckett] and Leigh-Anne [Pinnock]. But I didn’t know them well enough for them to know if I was lying. So I think my whole mindset was like, “If you just be yourself and get on with everyone… No one thinks that someone that they get on with is going to lie to them.” And we spent so much time together — we really, really bonded and had the best time. Unfortunately, you didn’t see much of it because obviously it’s game focused, but everyone really bonded on a deeper level. And it’s hard to think that somebody would lie to you after that.

You took to being a Traitor really well, but others not so much — James Acaster was very reluctantly recruited and ended up outing himself at the penultimate roundtable. What was your reaction to that?

I know, bless him. Never in a game would you expect that you’re going to be put in a situation where you absolutely hate being a Traitor. And I obviously had no idea beforehand that he didn’t want to be a Traitor, I just thought everyone’s kind of up for it. But yeah, it was hard. I don’t think anybody knows how it would feel once you’re in the situation, and that’s going to impact everyone completely differently. As he said, for him it was a lot. You’re like, “OK, this is a game, we’re playing for charity.” But then these people have real feelings, and trying to find the balance between it is tougher than it looks.
I can imagine, being in a castle in Scotland for three and a half weeks playing this game, you can get really immersed in it.

Oh, 100%. I came in there like, “Oh, this is just fun and we’ll have a laugh, silly silly.” But there’s definitely days where you’re like, “Jesus, this feels really real.” And you can’t escape the bubble of being in the castle and everyone’s emotions and feelings. It definitely gets heavy at times. Everybody has a five-minute phone call everyday, but with the producers in the room. But because I was so tired from coming back to the turret late every night, and obviously being a Traitor from day one, I didn’t call anyone the whole time because I just wanted to be in bed longer. So I was really just immersed in the Traitor lifestyle the whole time. It’s a mind trip.
After James’ departure, you and Kenny decided to murder Michael Sheen, who was starting to suspect you. Talk me through that decision, because it feels like that’s where things unraveled a bit.

I’m not gonna lie, after James left I just thought, “OK, I’m fucked. I’m going to have to clutch at every straw available at this point.” And Michael was obviously the most on my case, and there was no persuading him otherwise. I thought, this is kind of a kamikaze mission, but it’s my only hope right now. So I’ve gotta get rid of him and hope for the best. In our defense, that murder in plain sight — there was no way out of it. It was like, all three of us in the room.
What was the murder in plain sight like in real time? That seemed so stressful just watching it.

We were in that room for at least half an hour trying to make them yawn. And there were not yawning, even though it was late at night. Usually, if you yawn at someone, they yawn back. I was focused on Jerry [Hall] trying to make her yawn, and [Acaster] was focused on Ross [Kemp] and it was just like, whoever gets there first. But it was hectic, and we were running out of time. Honestly, I didn’t even think we were going to get it.
Jerry Hall, what an icon! What was it like getting to know her?

I absolutely love her. She was just hilarious the whole time. I actually think she invited all of us to her birthday party after [filming], but I was away and I’ve been trying to get in touch with her. So if Jerry reads this, can you call me? I wanna hang out.
That final challenge, where you’re rappelling off the side of a helicopter, was wild. What was that like and did they prep you on that stunt beforehand?

I am a bit of a thrill seeker — I’ve sky dived, I enjoy those kind of things — so I was raring to go. But they gave us a five to 10 minute, “This is what you do,” and then we were off. Of course, with that production company they’re going to have the best of the best, so I trusted that they weren’t going to let me die on TV. So I probably had more confidence in doing it than I would if i just did it on a normal day. I kind of just went for it, and it was one of my highlights actually. I was lowkey trying to appeal for a Bond role. Like, you know what, maybe if the right person sees that I can hang out of helicopters, I might get an acting gig.
From “Traitors” villain to Bond villain, perhaps?
They can see I can do a poker face, so hopefully that adds to the CV.
And then you were banished at the final roundtable and betrayed by Kenny when he voted for you. How do you feel about that now?

You know what, I obviously love Kenny to bits. I think he’s amazing. And he didn’t really have much of a choice, so it didn’t hurt as much. In hindsight actually, watching back, I’m like, maybe we could have wrangled it. But in the moment, it just felt like everyone was going for me. And if Kenny did protect me, then he was going to be finished — even though he did end up being finished anyway. It felt like the only option, so I didn’t hate him for it.
Have you been keeping in touch with everyone?

Yeah! Literally as soon as I left, there was already a group chat. As different people were leaving, everybody just joined the group chat and we were all debriefing on the wild-ass experience we all had. Obviously, we were all NDA-ed up, so that was kind of the only place that we could actually discuss everything.
From your view, where did things go wrong for the Traitors?

Getting to the end, they had to start looking at the quieter ones. And I think that me and James weren’t necessarily quiet, but we just weren’t as outspoken as some of the other guys and we didn’t have heat on us. And where else do you look when you’ve been getting it wrong the whole series, other than at us? If I could go back in time, I probably would have thrown a few more theories out or maybe spoken a bit louder, but that could have backfired also. So you can’t really have too many regrets.
Was there something that surprised you about filming the show that viewers may not know?

The roundtables definitely felt way more intense than I’d imagined and go on for a lot longer. And everyone speaks at the roundtables, so you’re only seeing a few conversations, but everybody does have an input.
They were different each time, but they were supposed to be an hour and some days they went on for an hour and a half. I think there was one that was two hours.
I also have to ask about your looks on the show. How did you put them together?

I was working with my stylist, Rhea Francois, and we literally packed seven suitcases and I was just praying the whole time that I at least got to get some of them out. I didn’t realize how cold the castle was going to be, so there were a lot of dresses and skirts I never got to wear because I was absolutely freezing most of the time. Usually I’m in the sun with “Love Island,” so I wear more revealing, summer looks. So I really wanted to make a point of doing the opposite of that and showing a different side to me, that it’s not always crop tops and mini skirts.
Overall, what did you take away from this experience? Did you learn anything about yourself?

I was reminded about how resilient I am. You don’t really know what you’re capable of in some situations until it actually happens. And I’m really proud of myself for just holding it down despite the stress all around. Also being able to thrive off minimal sleep from day one. Because everybody was tired, but the Faithfuls had a lot more sleep than the Traitors. So the party girl era really helped me on that one.
How much sleep were you getting each night?
I’d say like three hours, four maybe? Near the end, I was like, “OK, you’re delirious.” But she kept going.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Surprise Halloween Episode Drops on HBO Max
items.description: Just in time for the spooky holiday, HBO has released a surprise episode of “It: Welcome to Derry” on the streaming platform. Titled “A Story of Derry,” the special comes in at 30 minutes and is set hundreds of years before the show’s events and the introducti
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Just in time for the spooky holiday, HBO has released a surprise episode of “It: Welcome to Derry” on the streaming platform. Titled “A Story of Derry,” the special comes in at 30 minutes and is set hundreds of years before the show’s events and the introduction of Pennywise.

The timing is perfect for a surprise release of the supernatural horror, which HBO renewed for a second season in August. “It: Welcome to Derry” originally premiered on HBO Max on Oct. 26, 2025. It is based on Stephen King’s novel “It” and builds on the two-part “It” film reboot from 2017 and 2019. The show serves as a prequel to the films.

That month, before the show’s official renewal was announced, co-creator Andy Muschietti told Variety that the writers’ room had opened for Season 2. “There’s gonna be a lot of that depression-era hustling in the air in our characters. Everybody’s trying to get by and survive the circumstances. They are gonna do crazy things,” Muschietti said. “And of course, the social, cultural, horrible things that were happening in the era, too. We’re not going to skip those. [They are the] very center and the heart of our story.”
He also clarified that Season 2 will have a different aesthetic than Season 1.

“In this case, on the surface, Derry is a graveyard almost. It’s a carcass of something because people are depleted, poor, tired, jobless, homeless. The kids don’t have a suburban, comforting life,” Muschietti said. “They’re in a very different situation. Some of them are orphans or runaways, and so the environment is pretty bleak. But there’s always the aspect of hope that is always there, burning, and it’s what keeps our new group going.”

Season 1 is set in 1962 in the fictional town of Derry, Maine, and details the town’s residents’ earlier experiences with the evil, shape-shifting clown, Pennywise. Season 2 will do back in time to 1935 and takes place during the Great Depression. Per the logline, the story “centers on the bloody massacre of the Bradley Gang, a group of bank robbers who stop in Derry to buy ammo and end up facing unimaginable horror.” (The Bradley Gang Massacre is one of the interludes in King’s original novel.)

items.title: ‘SNL’: Inde Navarrette Digs at Shane Gillis’ Joke About Women Dressing Like “Whores” at the Gym as Tom Hanks Crashes Cold Open
items.description: Inde Navarrette made her Saturday Night Live hosting debut on the show’s Halloween episode, and kicked things off with a dig at the most recent host of the late night series.
items.author: McKinley Franklin
paragraphs: Inde Navarrette made her Saturday Night Live hosting debut on the show’s Halloween episode, and kicked things off with a dig at the most recent host of the late night series.

The actress began her monologue by referencing her star-making role in Obsession: “You probably know me from the movie Obsession. People ask me if I’m anything like my character Nikki, and I’m like, no. No, no, don’t do that.”

“But the thing is, I’m nothing like my character in Obsession. Like, my boyfriend is here tonight to support me,” she said, as the camera panned over to her boyfriend, Nick Aiello, duck-taped in the audience. “We have such a chill relationship, right?”

Navarrette went on to discuss how she’ll be next portraying Rogue in Marvel Studios’ X-Men reboot. The character preps requires a lot of working out, she noted. “I can’t believe I’m saying this, but I’m gonna be in a Marvel movie. I know it’s really important for Marvel that you get really fit, so I’ve been working out a lot.”
“So every morning, I put on my little whore outfit, and I hit the gym,” she said, in a callback to Shane Gillis’ controversial monologue on the most recent episode of SNL on Oct. 10.

During his SNL appearance, he said at the top of the episode, “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now. Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial vape-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look!”

Continuing with her monologue, Navarrette invited the SNL cast to the stage to show off their Halloween costumes “since none of the cast could go out tonight.” Marcello Hernandez appeared as “a sexy TSA agent,” as Kam Patterson portrayed Elizabeth Holmes.
Jeremy Culhane also joined, using his time during Navarrette’s monologue as an audition for Jake Schreier’s upcoming X-Men movie.

“I know you were cast as Rogue in the new X-Men movie, and I randomly heard they, like, I guess they haven’t even cast Wolverine yet,” Culhane said, to which Navarrette replied, “Oh, I’m so sorry. I can’t comment on that.”

“Well, I can, and I’d love to be in the movie with you,” Culhane, dressed as Wolverine, said. Grace Reiter then joined dressed up as none other than the bird at the center of the viral Kelly Clarkson, Art of Play controversy.
“It’s actually a group costume,” Reiter said, as Veronika Slowikowska popped in dressed like American Idol winner. “I want to buy the bird,” she said. “Sell me the damn bird!”
“I am not for sale!” Reiter as the bird said.
Tom Hanks’ classic Halloween character David S. Pumpkins made a surprise appearance in the cold open, opened by Reiter and Culhane as they embarked on a spooky ride.
James Austin Johnson’s Trump, of course, crashed the party to discuss the upcoming midterms.

“Are you sad you don’t get to see your third David Pumpkins scene? I’ll send you four minutes. He keeps popping up and confusing the people on the ride. ‘But you don’t actually have a lot in common with Mr. Pumpkins.’ We both appeared in 2016. We’re both very loud, very orange, and very frankly annoying,” Johnson’s Trump said.
“Good acting, great ass. A great ass on Hanks — something that I’ve enjoyed lately admiring,” he added. “Not that there’s anything wrong with that. Just that I might be gay.”

He was joined by Nicki Minaj (“my friend and future press secretary”), portrayed by Saidah Belo-Osagie, who showed her support for the president. “Trump’s out here killing it — and by it, I mean my career,” Belo-Osagie said.

“I’m Nicki, the Trumpy. Like, I don’t even know why you Democrats bother at this point. Like, give it up. It’s me,” she added before exiting the stage. “Thank you, Nicki. She’s got quite an ass. If only it were on a man, perhaps then I could admire it,” Johnson’s Trump said.
And Slowikowska also appeared as Katie Zacharia, Trump’s brief, former White House Press Secretary, to butcher SNL’s opening catchphrase, “Live from New York, it’s Saturday Night!”
She instead said, “With confidence. Live from New York. And from so many cities,” before she was cut off.

Pumpkins wasn’t the only character of SNL‘s past to pop up, as Bobby Moynihan’s Drunk Uncle appeared during the Weekend Update segment. He was even joined by the Milwaukee Brewers, the 2026 World Series champions. Christian Yelich, Brice Turang and team manager Pat Murphy were on hand to rep for the winning team. Moynihan even joked that Yelich was Pete Davidson.

Navarrette rose to acclaim this summer for her starring turn in Curry Barker’s new horror hit. She plays Nikki Freeman, a woman who is cursed after Bear (Michael Johnston) wishes that she’d love him more than anyone else in the world.

The low-budget film grossed over $522 million worldwide, breaking a plethora of records along the way: Obsession is Focus Features‘ biggest movie of all time; is the top-grossing festival acquisition (hailing from TIFF); and earned the biggest second-weekend box office spike in modern times outside of the Christmas holiday.
She’ll next star in Marvel Studios’ X-Men reboot, Apple Original Films’ sci-fi thriller The Waffle House Index, which she will also executive produce.
Saturday night marked Navarrette’s SNL debut, and she was joined by Gracie Abrams as musical guest. Elsewhere on season 52, Jalen Brunson, Dakota Johnson and Gillis have hosted.
After the Obsession actress, Druski will host on Nov. 7; he is the first social media influencer to ever host SNL. The Strokes will be the musical guest.
John Mulaney will host the Nov. 14 episode, and he’ll be joined by Phoebe Bridgers.
Before Saturday night’s episode, SNL shared a tribute for Patrick Stewart, featuring a clip from his 1994 appearance on the show.

items.title: Eric Bauza Remembered as a “Once-in-a-Generation” Talent Who Gave Looney Tunes a New Voice
items.description: At the 2024 Annie Awards, the Oscars for the animation industry, Eric Bauza stepped up to the podium and, in the lispy-spitty tones of Daffy Duck, pleaded with Warner Bros. to release Coyote vs. Acme. Bauza would later explain that Daffy, as the cartoon world’
items.author: Scott Roxborough
paragraphs: At the 2024 Annie Awards, the Oscars for the animation industry, Eric Bauza stepped up to the podium and, in the lispy-spitty tones of Daffy Duck, pleaded with Warner Bros. to release Coyote vs. Acme. Bauza would later explain that Daffy, as the cartoon world’s go-to character for begging and pleading, seemed an appropriate choice. The room roared.
Bauza died suddenly on Oct. 25, of natural causes. He was 46.

“This week, this entire tower [Warner Bros. headquarters in Burbank] is in mourning,” says Susan Rogers, a producer at Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, who worked with Bauza on the upcoming animated short Daffy Season. “Everyone is grieving, because I think everybody felt a personal connection with him.”

The animation world is remembering him as the artist who revived the Looney Tunes characters for a new generation, as the man widely regarded as the new Mel Blanc. Voice actors, directors, showrunners and studio executives describe a performer who inherited one of Hollywood’s most protected legacies and made it his own.

“Other people can do Looney Tunes voices, but you can’t replace Eric Bauza,” says Alex Kirwan, producer of Cartoon Network’s Looney Tunes Cartoons, which features Bauza in multiple roles, including Bugs, Daffy and Marvin the Martian. “He did all these voices, but he was also part of the community. Every single person who works in animation knows him, and every single voice actor knew him and loved him.”

Bauza’s route to Bugs Bunny ran through the animation trenches. Born in Scarborough, Toronto, he started out as an animator, character designer and layout artist at Spümcø, the company behind Ren & Stimpy. His voice-over breakthrough came playing Stimpy in Spümcø’s Ren & Stimpy revival Adult Party Cartoon. The series bombed, but Bauza’s performance caught the attention of the animation community.

Kirwan’s wife started at Spümcø the same day as Bauza, so Kirwan had heard about “the animation guy who does voices” long before he ever heard him audition. When Bauza auditioned in 2018 for the Bugs Bunny role on Looney Tunes Cartoons, he stood out from the pack. “We listened to like 50 people going, ‘What’s up, doc?’ over and over again,” Kirwan recalls. “His jumped out right away.”

Many actors could match the pitch and timbre of Mel Blanc’s original Looney Tunes performances, but only Bauza, says Kirwan, had the same frenetic, high-energy spirit. “He had this very loony energy,” Kirwan says. “There were little line reads in there that were very specific references to very specific shorts. I could tell when he screams here, he’s doing the Bugs Bunny scream from [original Looney Tunes short] Hair-Raising Hare. And I’m like, ‘oh, this guy’s like us. He’s a super fan.’”

Rogers says that enthusiasm was rooted in an almost obsessive knowledge of the characters and their history: “He would spend an hour or so every day watching Looney Tunes, he considered that his gym workout. He was just such a fan.”

“Just his enthusiasm and joy around the characters,” adds Rogers, who says Bauza played a huge role in the revival of the franchise for a new generation, “and his encyclopedic knowledge and insight into the history. There wasn’t a single short he couldn’t quote or couldn’t reference.”

Pete Browngardt met Bauza years earlier, casting him as Belly Bag, the title character’s fanny pack, on his Cartoon Network show Uncle Grandpa. (The name was changed for U.K. audiences, who wouldn’t have tolerated a cartoon character saying “fanny.”) Over more than 150 episodes, the two became friends and between takes Bauza would try out the Looney Tunes voices.

“The guy could do anything. It was fucking unbelievable,” Browngardt says. “He could do Homer Simpson and Trump and everybody. And I remember thinking to myself, if I ever did Looney Tunes, this is the guy.”

Years later, when Warner Bros. offered Browngardt a chance to work on Looney Tunes Cartoons as a writer, he knew who he wanted in the booth. “When you’re doing Looney Tunes, more than half of it is the voices,” he says. “So much of it is Mel Blanc and his legacy, and to find the sort of next Mel Blanc was like, we could pull this off. We could do it justice.”

But Bauza, both men say, was more than a mimic. Kirwan points to the range of Warner Bros. projects Bauza took on and how he reinvented the iconic characters for each performance. On Bugs Bunny Builders, a preschool series, Bauza’s Bugs is cuddly and sweet. His Daffy on The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie, which Browngardt directed, is a crazed conspiracy theorist.

“In Coyote vs. Acme he did Foghorn Leghorn as a scary, evil villain,” says Kirwan. “In Space Jam: A New Legacy he does Porky Pig in a rap battle. You could throw anything at him. He didn’t just do the voice of Daffy Duck. He did the voice of 10 different Daffy Ducks that were all completely unique. I am hard-pressed to think of any other modern actor who’s done anything like that.”

Coyote vs. Acme was arguably the ultimate showcase for Bauza’s vocal talents. Will Forte, John Cena and Lana Condor might be the live-action leads, but Bauza, who voices Bugs, Daffy, Porky, Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn and the beep-beeping Road Runner, is the star. At first, however, it looked like his performance would never be heard. Then-Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav decided the $30 million to $40 million marketing spend needed to release the film wasn’t worth it. He shelved the movie as a tax write-off.

Bauza pushed the hashtag #ReleaseCoyoteVsACME and released imagery from the film on social media long before he took the cause to the stage at the Annies. His Daffy appeal went viral and likely contributed to the studio’s decision to sell the film to Ketchup Entertainment for a reported $50 million. Coyote vs. Acme has since grossed more than $100 million worldwide. Ketchup confirmed it is submitting the film for best animated feature consideration at the 2027 Oscars.
Browngardt says that kind of public advocacy was classic Bauza. “He was a great spokesperson. He was the real deal. Pure authenticity was Eric Bauza.”

The response from the industry to Bauza’s death has been as much about the man as the work. Posting on Instagram, Jack Quaid called him “one of the kindest people I’ve ever met.” “One of the most kind, generous and talented people,” wrote voice actor Matthew Mercer. Hazbin Hotel creator Vivienne Medrano, noting she had seen Bauza just a week before his death, wrote that she was struck by how someone “so joyous and talented” could be gone so soon.

Others spoke to his stature in the industry. Voice actor Vincent Martella described “a giant. A titan in our industry.” Director Jorge R. Gutierrez, who worked with Bauza on projects including The Book of Life, wrote that he used to design and write characters “giddy, thinking how he would bring them to life.” Adam Rosette, co-director of GOAT, who shared a desk with Bauza at a small animation studio in 2010, recalled that the last thing he texted his friend was that he was “the voice of our generation.” Warner Bros. Television Group chair Channing Dungey said Bauza “followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc” and called carrying on the Looney Tunes legacy “among the greatest honors of his life.”

Bauza had recently been recognized by The Hollywood Reporter, appearing in the inaugural Animation Power list, celebrating the industry’s most influential figures. He attended THR‘s accompanying Most Powerful People in Animation breakfast in Beverly Hills on Oct. 16, just nine days before his death.

One tribute landed with particular force. Mike Myers posted on Instagram, first with a short note calling Bauza “a great talent” and a day later with a line about how he “made Scarborough proud.” Like Bauza, Myers grew up in Scarborough, a suburb of Toronto.

“If Bauza knew that Mike Myers knew who he was, he would have just fainted,” says Browngardt. “Mike Myers was his hero. Eric dressed as Wayne from Wayne’s World like 20 years ago. Maybe it’s because they’re both from Scarborough, but I even think they sound similar. And, like Myers, Eric was a multiple performer, he could play all these roles, wear all the hats.”
“He was the Mike Myers of animation,” Kirwan adds.

Browngardt believes the entertainer in Bauza was only beginning to emerge. He remembers watching him work a New York audience on the Day the Earth Blew Up press tour, doing a Trump impression that won over an initially skeptical Big Apple crowd. “He was funny, he was witty, he was sharp. He knew how to entertain a room. He could be a game show host. I think his career was going on a trajectory of breaking out of just being in a booth behind a mic. I think he could be in front of the camera a million times over.”

Rogers remembers a similar ability to connect with people and to use his characters to bring a room together. “I don’t think he ever met anybody he didn’t like. He was brilliant at walking into a room, and if there was any kind of tension in the room when he walked in, he immediately dispelled it as a character. If he was gonna comment on something, it was as a character; it was never Eric. Eric never complained about anything.”

Both Browngardt and Kirwan return to the same point: Bauza gave his time to everyone, whatever the size of the project. “It didn’t matter if you were the biggest celebrity in the world, if you were working with LeBron James on Space Jam 2, or if you were just trying to make a little indie short,” Browngardt says. “He’d give everyone the same amount of time and effort. How many people can you say that about?”

Kirwan notes that Bauza took on many smaller projects he had no need to do, and that students making films could reach out to him and get a reply. With his fiancée, Caro Beurmann, he co-founded Saturday Morning Cartoons United, a nonprofit screening series of vintage cartoons that raises money for the animation community, including industry members affected by the L.A. wildfires.

Kirwan has his own memories. Bauza got his family seats at the Hollywood Bowl for a Looney Tunes symphony night, where he performed What’s Opera, Doc? as both Bugs and Elmer Fudd. Another came during the recording of the Day the Earth Blew Up score, when the orchestra was wrapping up and nobody knew Bauza was in the room. “He just started speaking as Porky Pig, giving compliments to the musicians. You just see everybody’s heads whip around and this huge smile come onto their face. It just warms your heart.”
“I never saw a dark side. I never saw Eric get angry,” Browngardt says. “Maybe it was a Canadian thing.”

Work Bauza completed is still on the way. His Looney Tunes short, Daffy Season, will play ahead of Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat, opening Nov. 6. Warner Bros. will include an in-loving-memory card for Bauza in all Academy screeners of the short. And on Nov. 15 he will be heard voicing two different characters on The Simpsons, fulfilling a longstanding dream of appearing on the iconic show.

Bauza did voice work and several musical numbers on the planned feature Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical, but the future of project, which was in pre-production at the time of his death, remains uncertain.
Browngardt says finding a successor will be hard. “It’s gonna be sort of huge shoes to fill.”
“I don’t think you replace Eric Bauza,” says Rogers. “The hole he leaves is huge. There are many talented people out there, and the franchise will move on. But there’s only one Eric Bauza.”
Kirwan is more hopeful. “There are other people who love these characters, and I hope there are other people who can step forward and bring that love.”
Bauza was always conscious of the legacy he had inherited. Whenever he spoke about his chracters in public, notes Kirwan, he made a point of naming every actor who had voiced them before him.

“Talking about the Looney Tunes characters, he would always say: Mel Blanc’s let me borrow his Cadillac to take for a spin,” remembers Browngardt. “He’d say he was just trying to return it without a scratch. He knew someone else was going to use it at some point, but he was just trying to take care of it while he was in it.”

items.title: Jaalen Best Wanted to Be a Pro Athlete. Now He’s Playing ‘The Greatest’ Boxer Onscreen
items.description: This story might sound familiar: a rising student discovering who he is as he juggles his love for both the court and the stage.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: This story might sound familiar: a rising student discovering who he is as he juggles his love for both the court and the stage.

However, this isn’t High School Musical. It’s the beginning of Jaalen Best’s trek to Hollywood, which started his junior year at East Carolina University in 2019 and led him to his breakout role, portraying legendary boxer Muhammad Ali.

After stumbling into an intro to acting class, the 28-year-old quickly caught the professor’s attention. “She would tell me how great I was at improv and how I had a face for television and I should consider moving out to a bigger city or state and pursuing acting,” Best recalls.
But he wasn’t ready to hear that yet. “I’m like, ‘I’m a basketball player. This ain’t happening.'”

Best later got another acting push from his then-girlfriend, who convinced him to audition for his hometown production of Pocahontas in Clinton, North Carolina. Though skeptical at first, he decided to give it a real shot, landing the role of Pocahontas’ father, Chief Powhatan.

“I would wake up early at 5 a.m., and I would do basketball practice for the first three hours of my day, finish classes, and then I would drive an hour and a half to my hometown and do two-hour rehearsal,” he says. Despite the chaotic schedule, Best eventually came to a realization while on stage: “I was having more fun than basketball.”

While recounting this period of his life with The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom earlier in October, Best playfully acknowledges the similarities to the beloved Zac Efron-led Disney movie, with one exception: “I wasn’t the star player. I was riding the bench and just getting my opportunity,” he quips.
Much like how Troy Bolton moved away to college to pursue his dreams, Best made the decision to move to Los Angeles post-college to follow his own.

The first few years in Tinseltown proved challenging, as Best was one of thousands who came to the city with the same goals. But after years of background work, occasional guest roles and finding new talent representation, he finally got the audition he had been longing for in 2023.

“There were maybe seven or eight auditions,” he recalls, referring to the months-long audition process for the role of Muhammad Ali in Prime Video‘s The Greatest, which premieres Nov. 4. “It also was during the [actors] strike as well, so a lot of it was completely delayed and being pushed back.”

As months drew by between auditions and no confirmed offers, Best sought other roles. He later got offered a six-month contract with Days of Our Lives, but admits he was still holding out hope for The Greatest. That’s when his team flagged producers on the biopic of his pending soap opera booking and “instantly they’re like, ‘OK, we’re sending him to L.A. to do a network test,'” the actor recalls.

A day after the test, as he headed back to the airport, Best receives a call that The Greatest creator Ben Watkins wants to meet at his office. “I walk in and I shake his hand, and he’s just telling me, ‘Hey, there’s a couple of executives that don’t think you can hold up the voice, and they think you just practiced really well, and you just wowed us at these auditions.'”

In that moment, a confused Best was willing to do whatever’s necessary to prove he’s meant for the role. “[Watkins’] like, ‘I’m going to put you on camera and I’m going to ask you some things, and I just want you to talk back,'” the actor says. “We do that, and then he wants me to repeat some phrases, like Muhammad Ali’s favorite line, ‘I am the greatest.'”
After repeating a variety of phrases, the showrunner gives Best one final line: “Jaalen, you got the role.”

“I’m so locked into repeating the phrases and making sure I’m giving, I’m like, ‘Jaalen, you got the role.’ And I say it in [Muhammad’s] dialect,” he recalls. “And [Watkins’] like, ‘No, Jaalen. You got the role.’ I started to say it again, and I’m like, ‘Wait, what?’ And then they bust in, and it’s like this moment.”

Before Best could fully celebrate, he had to get one more blessing from Muhammad’s wife, Lonnie Ali, before officially stepping into the ring. After meeting her in Louisville, Kentucky, a nervous Best was on the flight home when he “got a text from Ben basically saying, Lonnie sent a message saying, ‘He’s the one in more ways than you know.'”
Below, Best opens up to THR about honoring Ali with his performance; the advice he got from Michael B. Jordan, who served as an executive producer on The Greatest; and what he can’t live without.
Playing such an iconic figure, how did you navigate honoring him with your performance, but also bringing your own portrayal to the screen?

When I got the role, I started going down this deep dive on him, and I tried to gather my own perspective of what I believe he displayed to not just me but to the people. And people would tell me so many stories as well. Every time someone has an Ali story, I stop everything I’m doing and I listen in because I think it’s important to see how he affected people just off of one meeting, whether he just put his fist up or whether he just threw air punches at them or whatever the case is. It’s very beautiful to be able to rely on real connections that he made with people.

I can’t ever be Ali, but I needed to get as close as possible to him. And it’s great because I feel like the look that I had, I’ve always grown up being told, “Hey, you remind us of a young Muhammad Ali,” and that never registered to me until I got in the training process. My body was naturally kind of shaped like his in a way. … And sometimes, I would just wear these white boots every single time I would train because he always wore his white boots. And my trainer would also give me footage to break down at night for homework. So on top of me doing all my studying, I broke down every punch and every movement and the rhythm of his bounces in the ring, and then I would be able to show up the next day and replicate all of that. So all of these things just allowed me to truly get to a place where I felt like I was embodying him and just really just showing up as him. And I started to rely on my own instincts and I would just say, “You know what? No more watching the movies, no more watching this.”
With Michael B. Jordan serving as an executive producer on the show, how much did you get to chat and learn from him?

He’s a mentor for me. I call him Big Bro. He calls himself Big Bro. So it’s definitely something that has allowed me to feel much more of a personal connection to him as opposed to just business. Him looking out for me in terms of trying to make sure that I have a great, long career with incredible success. You hear him all the time say he wants the younger generation to be better than him, and he’s always coming with that energy when he comes to me, and I think that’s incredible.

He’s somebody I can constantly look up to and see the greatness that he’s doing. I tell him, “Thank you for the blueprint and for showing us the way and continuing to lead us, especially as Black men who just want to be successful and help our community and just be a face of the world and the industry in a positive way and lead with great influence.”
For those who are just getting to know you with your role in The Greatest, what do they need to know?

I’m just a regular guy. I love just being inside, watching TV. Sometimes it’s hard to get me out of this room. I love going to parks and I love riding horses. I love doing just anything that people would say is boring. And then I just picked up tennis, so I’m learning tennis. I’m just trying to have fun.
What’s something you absolutely cannot live without?

I’m learning to relax a little bit on the coffee. I’ve been going a little crazy lately. I just love the taste of it so much. Sometimes I was literally, it’s so wild, two o’clock in the morning, I’m waking up and I’m processing, oh, should I chill off the coffee for tomorrow? Should I try to go the day without coffee? But I’m just constantly in this battle with myself because I feel like I sometimes would just order two different cups because I want to try a different coffee, but I don’t want to sacrifice to not get my favorite.
The Greatest premieres Nov. 4 on Prime Video.

items.title: 53 Classic Halloween Costume Ideas Inspired by the Pages of W
items.description: Halloween is only a week away, and even though you promised you wouldn’t put your costume off again this year, life gets in the way, and coming up with a creative and chic look can feel like an impossible task. Really, though, there’s no need to reinvent the w
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: Halloween is only a week away, and even though you promised you wouldn’t put your costume off again this year, life gets in the way, and coming up with a creative and chic look can feel like an impossible task. Really, though, there’s no need to reinvent the wheel, the classics are there for a reason. A cowgirl, a bride, a sexy nurse—you can’t go wrong with any of those, but you can also kick them up a notch, and add a bit of a high fashion twist to these tried-and-true costumes. Below, we’ve compiled some luxe takes on classic Halloween costumes inspired by W photoshoots, so you can look great with minimal effort, and stand out no matter your Halloween plans.
Cowboy Harry (aka Cowboyrry)
What’s Halloween without Harryween? As the singer wraps his 2026 residency at Madison Square Garden, pay tribute with a little cowboy homage.

There’s nothing stopping you from building a whole backstory around your costume. Or, you can just steal the one Timothée Chalamet created for his recent W cover: A 30-something dreamer-schemer living with his mom and making money off his pimped-out controllers and Yu-Gi-Oh! skills.
Timothée Chalamet directed by Josh Safdie for W Magazine Volume 2, 2026.
No beak? No problem. Plumage is all you need to transform into a high-fashion bird à la Rihanna (though the talons will help).
Rihanna photographed by Tim Walker for W Magazine Volume 3, 2026.

OK, so you have a pair of bunny ears lying around; they’re easy enough to throw on for a last-minute costume. But take things to the next level with some inspiration from Jeremy Strong and add some fake blood. Now, you’re an evil bunny.
Jeremy Strong photographed by Tyrone Lebon for W Magazine Volume 1, 2026.
All you need is a handful of friends and just as many blonde wigs to dress as a group of Kate Hudsons for your Halloween party this year.
Kate Hudson photographed by Tyrone Lebon for W Magazine Volume 1, 2026.
Embrace your inner Nurse Ratched (or Elle Fanning for her Best Performances cover) and dress up like a nurse with an ulterior motive this spooky season.
Elle Fanning photographed by Tyrone Lebon for W Magazine Volume 1, 2026.
All you need is a mic, and you've got a great excuse to interrogate your friends all night.
Harry Styles photographed by David Sims for W Magazine Volume 4, 2026.
Just because you bought the elaborate, fur-covered costume doesn’t mean you need to suffocate under the mask all night. Take a note from Rocky and ditch the top. Now, you’re a mascot off-duty.
A$AP Rocky photographed by Tyrone Lebon for W Magazine Volume 1, 2026.
Little Red Riding Hood, a roller derby skater, a flower child—Sydney Sweeney’s cover shoot for W has more Halloween costume inspiration than Party City.
Sydney Sweeney photographed by Carlijn Jacobs for W Magazine, Special Summer Issue, 2025.
Let’s be honest, the devil is extremely brat, and Charli XCX would definitely approve of dressing up like a high fashion devil in a chic red look this Halloween.
Charli XCX photographed by Hedi Slimane for W Magazine, January 2025.

Not all fairies wear wings, and Chappell Roan proved that in her cover shoot for W, declaring “I’m a fucking fairy,” in an array or eclectic looks, which can absolutely be recreated with items already in your closet (and a whole lot of makeup).
Chappell Roan photographed by Tim Walker for W Magazine, Volume 3, 2025.
Did she murder her husband? Maybe. Did she look great while doing it? Most definitely.
Ayo Edebiri photographed by Luca Guadagnino for W Magazine, February 2025.
Embrace the burlesque revival with over-the-top bouffant hair and layers of chic pieces that can be removed without revealing too much.
Mikey Madison photographed by Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott for W Magazine, January 2025.
Natasha Lyonne is proof that you don’t need to dress up like a baby to nail a cupid costume.
Natasha Lyonne photographed by Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott for W Magazine, January 2025.
Skip the green face paint, and grab your favorite black dress and boots, add a little eyeliner and a pointy hat and you’re all good to go.
Jennifer Lawrence photographed by Jamie Hawkesworth for W Magazine, Volume 1, 2023.
Yeah, everyone’s going to be doing it, but that’s just because it’s a great costume. All you need is a whole lot of pink and a Ken to follow you around all night.
Margot Robbie photographed by Tim Walker for W Magazine, Volume One 2019.
The perfect costume if you don’t want to make small talk at the party.
Scarlett Johansson photographed by Tim Walker for W Magazine, June 2011.
Look good while still staying warm during your late October night out.
Seth Rogen photographed by Jamie Hawkesworth for W Magazine, Volume 1, 2023.
Okay, you may not have access to Schiaparelli couture, but you can definitely still pull this interplanetary look off.
Zendaya photographed by Jack Davison for W Magazine, Volume 2, 2022.
Pair some angel wings with an etheral white gown for a more mature take on this classic costume.
Jennifer Lawrence photographed by Jamie Hawkesworth for W Magazine, Volume 1, 2023.
Wear your favorite dress and all-white makeup for a chic take on the classic Halloween costume.
Tilda Swinton photographed by Tim Walker for W Magazine, May 2013.
A simple outfit with black with white spots is reminiscent of the young version of the dreaded spotted lanternfly. Add red wings for the full effect.
Janelle Monae photographed by Jamie Hawkesworth for W magazine Volume 1 2023.
Break out all the feathers and prepare to molt all night long.
Jennifer Lawrence photographed by Tim Walker for W Magazine, October 2012.
If the devil can wear Prada, why not the pumpkin?
Photograph by Willy Vanderperre for W Magazine, Volume 5, 2021.
Level up your simple bunny ears by wrapping yourself in some faux fur.
Photograph by Willy Vanderperre for W Magazine, Volume 5, 2022.
Make like Beauty and the Beast’s Belle in a golden yellow gown—this one just so happens to be from Alexander McQueen but any sweet yellow frock will do.
Ruth Negga photographed by Tim Walker for W magazine Volume 1 2022.
It’s all about the theatrics with this one.
Cate Blanchett photographed by Shirin Neshat for W Magazine, 2018.
While everyone else may be dressing like Barbie, try a creepier version of the costume by throwing on your best baby doll dress, a bow in your hair, and a dead-eyed look on your face.
Amelia Gray photographed by Willy Vanderperre for W Magazine, Volume 6, 2022.
Put on a colorful dress, strap on some wings, and poof: You’re a butterfly! Bonus points if both items match your hair color. Even more points if they match your home, as well.
Florence Welch photographed by Tina Barney for W magazine, Volume 2, 2018.
Every Halloween party needs a nurse on standby.
Kate Moss photographed by Richard Prince for W magazine, 2003.
The anthurium flower has captured fashion’s attention thanks to its prominence on the dresses and accessories at Loewe. But it also makes for a striking costume when recreated at home.
Model Mona Tougaard photographed by Rafael Pavarotti for W Magazine, Volume 1 2023.
Get your Joker costume in this year before Folie à Deux comes out and the party is crawling with them.
Will Ferrell photographed by Mario Sorrenti for W Magazine, February 2012.
A fuzzy bear costume is perfect for a cold Halloween night.
Photograph by Tim Walker for W magazine, Volume 4 2018.
Once you have the jacket, the hat, and a riding crop–you won’t even need pants.
Madonna photographed by Steven Klein for W magazine, June 2006.
Gather all the tulle you can find, and go as a couture bride.
Anya Taylor Joy photographed by Paolo Roversi for W Magazine, April 2017.
Most ballerinas don’t wear heels with their tutus, but you can make an exception for Halloween.
Photograph by Craig McDean for W magazine, December 2006.
Unless you’re Rihanna, it’s unlikely that makeup master Pat McGrath will do your makeup for Halloween. But, you can always take a stab at imitating her work.
Photo by Mert and Marcus for W magazine, September 2014.
No birds were harmed in the making of this costume.
Scarlett Johansson photographed by Tim Walker for W magazine, June 2011.
Skip the tricky fins, just add a snorkle.
Unknown T photographed by Tim Walker, W Magazine 2021.
Find someone who is willing to commit to being Batman, and then wear whatever you like as their sexy sidekick.
Photograph by Inez and Vinoodh for W magazine, December 2008.
You probably already own something with cheetah print. Pick up a matching mask for an especially ferocious evening.
Photograph by Craig McDean for W magazine, December 2007.
Okay, this one is a little bit trickier. But once you have the tail, and someone to carry you around, it’s easy.
Kristen McMenamy photographed by Tim Walker for W magazine, December 2013.
A more abstract option, but a cool one, nonetheless.
Brie Larson photographed by Juergen Teller for W Magazine, February 2014.
Simply imagine your version of what may or may not be flying those UFOS.
Julia Nobis photographed by Steven Meisel for W Magazine, March 2014.
Every Halloween party could use a David Bowie moment.
Tilda Swinton photographed by Tim Walker for W Magazine, August 2011.
It’s not 2024 yet, but a politician costume is definitely still in style.
Justin Timberlake and Amanda Seyfried photographed by Michael Thompson for W Magazine, October 2011.
