Then I also said, just shamelessly, “Can I be in it? Or can I be in anything that you write?”
Scott: So you gave money for the original Edinburgh show? Wow! I never knew that. You must feel so proud of that.
Colman: I’m pretty thrilled with myself, yes. But also just trying to buy Phoebe's friendship.
Scott: A perfect way to buy friendship. That's how you got mine and I'm still getting those direct deposits every month.
Colman: It works, doesn’t it?

Scott: Phoebe and I had done a play at the Soho Theatre about 10 years before Fleabag. And so the first [season] had come out and everybody loved it. And then she called me and said, "I'm thinking of writing this other character. Can we have a sort of talk about it?" We hadn't seen each other in a few years, and we ended up having this incredible walk around Soho and talking about love. And she had this idea of this priest and we talked about religion and what that means. And I remember bringing her into this place in Soho and it's on St. Martin’s Lane, which is the Quaker meeting hall. Have you ever been in there?

Scott: You know that scene where we go into the Quaker meeting hall? Anyway, I brought her into this place and I said, "This is where I come to sort of chill out sometimes and you can go into some really silent room in the middle of St. Martin's Lane." And so we sat in there for about two hours and we just talked about love and life. And then she incorporated it into the story. I sort of signed up to it with no script. So the day before the read-through I was like, "Oh my God, this is incredible." She's so brilliant that she just incorporates things and that amazing mind is always at work.
Olivia, when the “hot priest” situation happened, what was it like seeing Andrew, your friend, suddenly catapulted into this sensational online narrative?

Colman: Well, I remember my girlfriends just going, "Oh my God, the hot priest! I'm having awful thoughts about him!” And I loved it. I thought it was hilarious. All my women friends, just thinking filthy thoughts about you.
Scott: People do get very feral. It's the priest thing. It's the collar.
Colman: It's the taboo. It's the transgression of it.
Scott: Who would have thunk it? I knew that it was kind of funny and sexy and actually very soulful, that relationship between those two characters, but you never think it's going to be…
Colman: I was so cross with Phoebe when I first read it though, and the ending that they weren't together. Why can't you make a happy ending? I want to re-watch it all now.
Scott: We should have a little Fleabag party. That would be so fun.
Colman: Fleabag holiday. Oh my God, let's get a nice big house in a countryside. I want to have dogs and just watch Fleabag every night.
What do you remember about shooting that dinner scene together?
Colman: It took two days to film that scene. And it felt like, “I can imagine film students are going to study this one day.” It's so brilliantly written.
Scott: And I remember at the time I had a 103-degree temperature. I was so sick. But it's that amazing thing about when you're acting, you sort of forget about it.
Colman: I don't want to make this about me, but I had pneumonia when filming Wicker.
Scott: Did you really? How long did you have it for?

Colman: I can't remember. I started to sort of get better as they sort of fell in love, weirdly. Otherwise, I don't think I could have done the marriage dance thing. But it is amazing how you just—and maybe we're sort of a bit old-school, but maybe it's silly.
Scott: Probably it is a little bit silly. You just do those things…
Colman: The fear that you're going to get replaced. Still in the back of my head that someone else will take the job.

Scott: Absolutely. And in a way, it might be a little bit foolish. I had to have a sort of affect having a weird panic attack in [his one-man stage adaptation of Uncle] Vanya, and towards the last two weeks, I was like, "This isn't really stopping." Because I think your brain knows, but your body doesn't know and you sort of continue. It is a sort of corny, nuts thing to do for your life.
Colman: This rather beautifully ties in with Elsinore, doesn't it?

Scott: You're acting and you sort of forget about it for a little while. And in some ways, on a much, much more serious scale, Ian Charleson was really suffering with illness, and he went on and he did this heroic, Olympian part. And then he would just collapse at the end.
Colman: He died six weeks after?

Scott: Yeah, six weeks later. I suppose it's about quality and quantity, right? Dr. Johnson basically said, "You can have more time. If you just give yourself a bit more time, then there might be some developments in the treatment. But if you play this part, it's going to mess up your immune system and it's going to mess you up. It could be fatal." And that's their big conflict. And then bit by bit, it's about art and what it means and how we use our time. And eventually—
Colman: They had come to an understanding.
Andrew, how did performing Hamlet onstage back in 2017 inform your performance as Ian Charleson playing Hamlet?
Scott: It was kind of difficult because all the scripts leave my head almost immediately. So I had to relearn Hamlet.
Colman: Do you find, when you're auditioning, the audition scene is the hardest one to film if you get the job?

Scott: Oh my God, totally. Because you're like, “You liked that. Can I do it again?” Because you feel like that must have been what they liked because otherwise I wouldn't be here. You're so right. Did you like auditioning?

Colman: Partly because I really enjoyed forcing them to like me. I'd go in and they'd go, "What the fuck? She's not right for this." I go, "I'm going to win you over. I'm going to do it." And so there was a job where I was playing a mom to some really tough lads and I really enjoyed it and they went, "Oh." Now with everyone taping, I wouldn't get the work I got if I had to do tape. I had to be in the room to win people over.

Scott: And also, I think what's difficult is that if you're putting yourself on tape, you present what you think that your instinct is. But if someone goes, "Oh, actually no, I think a person is much less friendly or more generous or whatever." You go, “ok,” because acting is so much about going, “I can do it a different way.”
Colman: It’s great for people who are far away and can't afford to get the train fare, but I think it's tough for actors now.

Scott: I remember auditioning for Sherlock and exactly the same experience as you had where I think they were like, "Who is this tiny little fella that's coming in?” And I remember thinking, "I'm going to frighten you. I'm going to frighten you." I remember I sort of shouted in the audition and I could tell they were like, "He's a bit creepy actually."
Do you always know when you’ve gotten the part?
Scott: No, you never know after an audition, do you? You sort of have an instinct.

Colman: Occasionally I knew that I didn't get it. I used to do a little thing: I'd go, "Do you want me to leave the script?" And if they went, "Yes, that'd be great. Thank you," I knew I hadn't got it.
Do you prefer dramatic parts or comedic ones, or is there even a difference in your approach?

Scott: If we were to meet for dinner, I don't think we'd go, “We'll do the sad bit. We'll do the funny bit.” I think you've got to be prepared for all the colors. You know what I mean? That is why you are truly exceptional. I don't think you can be a really great, great actor to my mind without having a terrific sense of humor. And that's just what you have. You just have that interest in the lightness of human beings. I don't love overly serious acting, just because I don't think it's real to human beings.
Colman: I think the funny has to be based in realism and if you're trying to lay on funny, play funny. It's not funny. But you are naturally funny and you're naturally feeling and giving.

Scott: I think that's why even though we had some serious scenes to do, but also we should say that the screenplay was just massively funny. And they have a sort of antagonistic relationship and I always think antagonism is a funny thing to play. It's a great fun thing to do. And then they gradually sort of warm to each other.

Olivia, what’s your approach to awards acceptance speeches? Because some have gone viral, like your shoutouts to Lady Gaga, or calling your Favourite costars Emma Stone and Rachel Weisz “my bitches.” What goes through your head in those moments?

Colman: No idea. I can't remember any of it. The Oscars, it's like a wedding day. I remember my dad saying, "There'll be moments, just stop and just look at it. Take it all in. Look at all the faces. Who's there?" And that was amazing advice. And on my wedding day I remembered it. And it was before phones and things—that magic of theater— when it's gone, it's gone. And so that was rather beautiful. But the Oscars was such a head fuck because it’s such a huge occasion. You just sort of can't believe that's happened, and you wake up the next day and go, can't remember any of it.

Scott: I think it's a testament to you because you come on and you're just completely yourself and what's completely yourself is just completely adorable and sincere. That speech is just so incredibly sincere and it's fun and it's also ridiculous, but also meaningful.

Colman: It means so much. And that's why in the buildup when people talk about it, I really understand how it's, “Please don't, please don't” because you can't help but sort of dream about it. And then it happens and then you wish you'd paid more attention.
What role of each other’s would you have loved to try to take on?
Scott: I don't want to do anything that you've done. I'd just be shitter.
Colman: I want to be in more of the stuff that you've done. I want to be in scenes with you.
Scott: Would you do a play? Do you feel you just don't really want to do a play?
Colman: I think until my youngest [child] has left home, I find going out to work just as everyone's getting cozy heartbreaking.
Scott: It's so hard. Or even in the summer when everyone's like, “Oh, we might go to a beer garden,” you think—
Scott: I'm going in the dark. I’m going to scream in the dark.
Colman: The camaraderie is extraordinary. I love that. I miss that. I miss rehearsals, but I might not go back to it until I know my kids are all grown.
Is this something that you’d want to see each other do in the future?
Colman: Well, we talk about doing a little thing together about houses.
Scott: We think we should have a reality show about houses and beach walks. We might not have a huge viewership.
Colman: We walk around and we go, “I wouldn’t put that there.” We'd be a bit bitchy going around people's houses. We thought that'd be fun. Probably no one will see it.
Scott: Nobody would watch that. They’d think, “What awful, horrible people.”

items.title: Darializa Avila Chevalier Explains the DSA
items.description: In June, Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic nominee for Congress in the 13th District of New York, burst onto the national stage when she won her primary against five-term incumbent Representative Adriano Espaillat. Along with several other candidates t
items.author: Mark Guiducci
paragraphs: In June, Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic nominee for Congress in the 13th District of New York, burst onto the national stage when she won her primary against five-term incumbent Representative Adriano Espaillat. Along with several other candidates this cycle, Chevalier became emblematic of a new swell of progressivism in America. Almost immediately, she came under fire for inflammatory posts she had made on the internet—about defunding the police, abolishing prisons, and Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank. She has what many would characterize as some pretty radical views.

Chevalier comes from the world of academia—she’s a PhD candidate, a longtime grassroots organizer, and a member of the New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. But we don’t live in a theoretical world, and it seems to me that ideological purism often gets in the way of getting real things done. So, ahead of next week’s midterms, I wanted to know whether she stands by some of her most divisive statements and how she plans to govern once the race is over and she (presumably) takes office. And I really wanted to know who Chevalier is as a person. I sat down with her on October 26 for a conversation about how she views protests, being recruited to run for office, being compared to AOC, why President Donald Trump likes Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and more.
Mark Guiducci: Candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier, welcome to the show.
Darializa Avila Chevalier: Thanks so much for having me.

Thanks for being here. Darializa, you are the Democratic candidate and presumptive winner for Congress in the 13th District of New York. You’re also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, one of many candidates this election cycle who represents a swelling progressive movement. Your national profile is growing.

You were photographed by Annie Leibovitz for our New Establishment Issue, and today I wanna talk to you about how you situate yourself in the political landscape and the leftist surge that we’re seeing right now. And I also wanna talk to you about you. So let’s start a little bit with your background.

New York is your home now, of course, but you were born in Florida and briefly lived in the Dominican Republic and in Venezuela before settling in Tallahassee, I think, as a teenager. And, you know, looking back at your childhood, I wanna know, what was the moment that you had your first political inkling?

Yeah. I mean, I moved around so much as a kid—not only around all those different places, but also within those different places, right? Because my mom was a working-class single mom. My dad wasn’t very involved, but he was also very working-class and, you know, he’s a truck driver. My mom’s a caseworker, worked multiple jobs, and it was not always easy.

And I think my first moment where I realized, Oh, we’re, like, very working-class, if not working-poor, was when I was driving to school with my mom one morning and we had to stop for gas, and my mom said to me, “Crouch down and look for coins,” because we weren’t sure whether we had enough to get gas to get to school.

And we crouched down; I think we barely got to a dollar, and I went into the, the gas station and I gave the man at the counter the dollar, and he looked at me, looked at my mom—who was waiting and looking into the gas station, watching me—and looked back down and said, “I put $5 on the pump.” And I think that was the first time, and I was small. I was still in elementary school at this point that I realized, Oh, this is not something that people normally experience, right? And we were literally relying on the kindness of a stranger that day.
When would you say that you were able to start putting language to that? You know, a five-year-old or a six-year-old probably doesn’t know that they’re working-class.
They know the situation, they know the emotions, but when were you able to start putting the language to it? ’Cause I think that’s an important piece to the politics, you know?
Yeah, I think, you know, as I got older, I was definitely aware that class was a thing.

I think I didn’t call it class, right, until I started reading more about, you know, people’s experiences. I think even in our society, we confuse what working-class means often, right? And we think about ourselves; everyone wants to be middle-class, right? And even folks who are really struggling, like they’re one paycheck away from losing everything, seeing themselves as middle-class [is] a point of dignity, right?

No one wants to see themselves as struggling so much that they could lose everything, but that is the reality for most Americans in this country. And once I was reading more, you know, just progressive, leftist, socialist literature, right, that was talking about these things in a very concrete way and giving language to it—I was reading folks like Baldwin and Du Bois and Angela Davis, right?
And they were really talking about these experiences in ways that really resonated.
Is this, like, high school?

Yeah, high school I was reading Baldwin; I was reading, you know, more class-conscious literature. And college, I guess, it was really where, like, things started to get a concrete definition for me, right?
I realized I just really wanted language for my experience, for the experience of my community, and, you know, I really felt really immersed in that world of literature and theory.

So you went to college at Columbia. You’re a New York transplant. How do you think your experience as a non-native New Yorker—I also didn’t grow up here—how do you think it influences your relationship to the city that you’re about to represent?

Yeah, I mean, I love the city so much because it made me the woman that I am. You know, I came and I was 18, but I also grew up coming here often because my mom’s side of the family was here, and New York always felt like the place where I could be all parts of myself. And having lived here since I was, you know, a teenager and 18 and growing into myself, I learned that I love organizing here, right?
I became politically active, and I became active in my community here. And, you know, if you ask me where my roots are, it’s here at this point, because this is where most of the people I love are.
I understand that. I moved here the day after college, and—
I get it. You were just saying your organizing started here.

And that really started when you were an undergraduate at Columbia as part of the Students for Justice in Palestine. I’m curious what you thought that movement was missing when you came across it and what you thought you could bring to it.
Yeah. Well, I actually started organizing earlier than that.

I was—well, in college, but before I joined Students for Justice in Palestine. I was organizing around ending sexual violence on campus. Emma Sulkowicz’s name is coming up a lot now because of the case at Cornell, but I was at school at the same time as her. And this was something that we, on campus, were really starting to build around and organize around to get the university to make meaningful change.

And I think, you know, unfortunately, clearly from what we’ve seen in the last few months, a lot has not changed on college campuses for a lot of people. But that was the work that we were already doing. And I was also organizing with the Black Students Organization, which takes its name because it was an organizing organization, whereas, you know, at other universities, it’s usually the Black Student Union.

We were actually invested in organizing Black students on our campus. And I joined SJP after having gone to Palestine. I’d spent a summer there in the West Bank. And having firsthand experience for, you know, just witnessing the apartheid system there, and—
That was 2014. And I was there as tensions were rising in the West Bank.

And the day after, or within a few days of getting home to the US, you know, Israel began bombing Gaza, and it was a very dark experience. I don’t have another word for it. I just felt so disempowered to be at home scrolling through the names and images of the people who had been slaughtered in Gaza, and people who look so much like the people I had just left behind in the West Bank.
And I think that was where I first started to really take an interest in the notion of power.
Because I’d never felt so powerless in my life.
You attended the pro-Palestine rally on October 8, 2023. What was your thinking in attending that event, and how do you think about it now? Do you regret that?

You know, I have always believed that protests are about power. Again, like, I think power itself is a morally neutral thing. It is about whether or not you can change the conditions around you, right? And so empowering communities to be able to change those circumstances is something I think about all the time.
But what conditions on October 8?
Like, what are the conditions that you’re thinking, That’s the day to go?

Yes, and so, you know, as someone who’s an American citizen, as someone who pays my taxpayer money, the thing that I have power over in this cycle of violence is where my government uses my tax dollar in this cycle, and the party that we pay our tax dollars to and that we support and arm is the Israeli government, right?

And, you know, are there folks who say things you disagree with at any protest? Yes, of course. The same is true for many elected officials who attended the Israel Day Parade with Israeli officials who have openly called for the genocide of Palestinians, right? And I would hope that they have vehemently disavowed that, right?

But when it comes to advocating for the human rights and human dignity of Palestinians, there seems to be a double standard, right? Where we can’t express our outrage at our tax dollars being used in a way that denies people their human rights and their dignity, particularly when so many people in our communities are being denied those resources, right? Whether it’s in funding schools, whether it’s in addressing childhood poverty.
And I really deeply believe that we are responsible for having a power analysis when we engage in any kind of protest, right?
I think the people that you mentioned, especially public officials, should have to answer the question that you just posed to them.
But specifically on the October 8, you would do it—like, you would go back again on October 8, 2023, to that protest?

I would, because that same day, what I was thinking about was my experience in 2014, where I had sat in my bed and felt powerless, right? And knew in 2023 what was coming was Israel’s response would lead to more and more death.
And that same day, hundreds of people had already been killed, right, in Gaza. And to me, when we mourn human life, we have to mourn human life and prevent more loss of life.

I’m thinking about, on October 7, 2023, people who have done Birthright trips to Israel or have visited in some way and are scrolling through faces and names of people they knew. How do you feel your experience differs from theirs?

I think where, again, asking a question of, where are we positioned to interrupt cycles of violence? I think losing someone you care about is something that, universally, we can all empathize with, right? It is something that is tragic and heartbreaking and is hard to wrap our heads around. If in that moment I could’ve called up the president to yell at Netanyahu, to tell him to stop dropping the bombs, or if I could have, you know, called whoever at any point in the cycle of violence, of course you’d wanna do that.
That’s not a power I have. The power I have is to organize my community into creating that societal shift.
But do you see how those experiences are similar?
Again, the experience of losing somebody, I think that is a universal, like, experience of loss and trauma and pain and grief. Where I see things are different is, again, around a question of power.

Do you have the power to create a world where there is less grief, right? And I think if we look at things institutionally, our government currently is investing in continuing grief for a certain group of people.
Today you are no longer just an organizer. You are poised to be an elected official. When you were younger, did you ever think that you’d be running for office?
Did you see that for yourself?
Can you describe the moment that you decided to run?
I don’t know that it was a moment.

I was recruited to run by Justice Democrats, and I—you know, it’s an organization that takes community nominations, and they told me that someone from the community had nominated me, and that they had spoken to other members of the community and really were excited about this idea.

And I was like, All right, well, I’m just gonna take some time to think about it, ’cause this wasn’t something that I’d thought to do. And I had many conversations with other organizers, with members of my community, with folks who I was like, Oh, they’ll definitely tell me this is a bad idea. And to my surprise, everyone was like, “No, this is a great idea, but it really is up to you.”
This is the same organization that found AOC. How did they find you, and how did you start that relationship?

Yeah, I mean, I’ve been organizing for a really, really long time. And we actually had spoken with them about running somebody else, and a few months later, I get an email, and they told me that folks had reached out to them about me.
And the first question I asked was, “Why me?” And I was like, “And do you know—”

Well, I was like, “And do you know that, like, I have been very vocal,” right, “on a lot of issues?” And they said that’s why. Because they really just wanted someone who felt firm in their convictions and on their view of what this country can and should be for working people across this country.
And I had to really sit with that because it was not an easy decision to make, and so that’s why it took me so long to give them a yes.
So I wanna know, in your mind—
How did you win? Because beyond grassroots organizing, moving out an incumbent like Adriano Espaillat in Harlem is no mean feat.
In the clearest possible terms, how do you think you did it?

And it was bringing groups together and building a coalition that knocked over 155,000 doors, that talked to their neighbors even when it was not an easy conversation. And it was, you know, organizing all of the members of our coalition into this larger vision, because not everyone was sold at first.
You have been using this word organizing. What is organizing?

So organizing is coming together with others in your community or who share your same understanding of what the problem is, right? And coming together to address that issue. It is about fundamentally shifting power away from the concentrated few toward the many, right?
So when we think about, for example, housing organizing or tenant organizing, right?

It is about tenants coming together, right, to build power among themselves to change the conditions in their building, whether that is because the tiles on the floor are actually dangerous for the grandma who might trip on them, right?
Or the leaks that are making it so that you are having to endure black mold and just deeply undignified conditions.
And coming together to build the power to have these repairs actually happen.
In the campaign, for instance—

What does that look like on the day-to-day? Like, what are some things that I might not understand is organizing that you—you know, things that you did in your campaign that I might not understand as organizing, but that were effective?

I think a lot of people, they think there’s, like, this wow or flashy thing that happens in organizing that is what makes it like all of a sudden the power has shifted, but really, it is deeply unsexy work. It is the boring phone calls. It is the meetings that could’ve been an email.
It is the thing that, you know, just brings people together and [makes them] feel connected on a human level to build the trust necessary to move toward something else.
And what’s the role of the DSA in that? In that organizing and in that coalition, how did the DSA influence, impact, your race specifically?
Yeah. Well, I mean, DSA is such an incredible organization.

It is a member-based organization, so if you’re part of the DSA, it’s because you love organizing and you love being in that work, and you share this vision of a socialist, or democratic socialist, country. And once they were excited about this race, right, we knew we could win because we all of a sudden had an army of folks who were ready to knock on doors, were ready to talk about a politic that works for working people.
When you say “they” about the DSA, who’s they? I mean, because is it, like, Megan Romer, the co-chair of the national chapter? Is this the mayor?
Well, I’m a member of the New York City chapter of DSA, which is, you know, affiliated but separate from the national DSA. And I think maybe we take a step back and explain what DSA even is.
That’s perfect. Yes. Let’s do that. I had Ta-Nehisi Coates in this chair a few weeks ago, and the conversation went there, and even he was asking, “What is the DSA?”
Well, to Comrade Coates, I can explain that a little bit more.
It is a member-based organization that is focused on building people power in a democratic way.

And so if you share the values of a socialist, which, to us, is making sure that the wealth that working people produce is also wealth that working people can benefit from and enjoy in our society, then, you know, you can come organize with us to make sure that we’re building that world. And when I talk about socialism, I think sometimes people get stuck in the theory of it and don’t understand what that concretely means.
Sure. It’s a tough brand in America sometimes.

Yeah. And I think most of the most popular policies we’ve ever had in this country’s history, including now, are themselves socialist policies. So thinking, for example, of Social Security or Medicare, right? These are incredibly popular policies, to the point where we’re always fighting to defend them, right?
And we should be fighting to expand them. We should be fighting for more socialist policies that make the lives of working people better.
But is the DSA—is it a party?
It is not a party. It is an organization.
Okay. It is an organization.
It is a member-based organization.
So is it a wing of the Democratic Party?
I mean, many of us are members or are part of the Democratic Party, right? We’re registered as Democrats, but it is—

Yes. And I’m the Democratic nominee. But the DSA is just an organization. It is an organizing organization, right? And organizing, again, is really about shifting power away from a concentrated few toward the many.
The national chapter of the DSA has a published platform that includes aims like abolishing the presidency—
Abolishing the Senate, replacing the Supreme Court, open borders. How do you—do you agree with that? Or how do you address that with people who read that and are frightened?
Mm-hmm. I mean, again, I’m a member of the New York City chapter.

There are some of those things that I really just don’t agree with, like I don’t agree with abolishing the presidency, for example. But I do think that the beautiful thing about DSA is that it is truly a democratic organization. So as a New York City chapter member, right, I can participate in all of the democratic decisions that happen within our chapter.

And anytime we make a decision as a chapter, we are voting on it, right? And the beautiful thing is, if you have an idea for how to shift politics or policies to work for working people, inside the chapter, you can introduce that, right? You can introduce a resolution. And so—
So what I’m hearing is that it’s not—it’s more of an approach.
It’s not one specific policy or goal in mind, or even one specific worldview; that it’s flexible depending on—
Yeah. I mean, there is a huge diversity of thought within DSA, right? And even between national and the New York City chapter, there’s diversity. There’s, like, sometimes disagreement, right?
And that is what democracy is, right? And I think democracy is a practice, it’s an exercise, and it’s something we have to do often, right?
You have often been compared to AOC, also a New York DSA member. You’ve been called the next AOC; AOC but to the left. She recently endorsed you. What’s your relationship like?

It’s a positive relationship. She is someone who has really laid a path for so many people to be able to come into Congress as a working person. And, you know, I have a lot of respect for the congresswoman, and I’m really excited to see what she might do next.
What do you think are the key differences between the two of you?
Yeah. And, again, I think I’m my own person, right? So—

I think, as someone who comes from a different area of organizing but largely agrees with, you know, the vision that she came into Congress with, I think it’s exciting to be able to come in with a new perspective of where we can grow things even further, right?

President Trump has been recently praising AOC. He said—sort of begrudgingly, he said he doesn’t mind her so much, which is funny coming from the leader of the MAGA movement. And, of course, Mayor Mamdani and Trump have had very public meetings, cordial meetings at the White House and then Gracie Mansion.
Why do you think he likes them?

I am also very fascinated by this. And I think part of it is that he’s a New Yorker, right? And I think that’s something for New Yorkers to also contend with, right? But I think he just also is someone who understands popularity, right? And I don’t mean popularity as like—
Yeah, he likes a winner, and I think he likes it when people are actually willing to stand on what they believe and not just, you know, kiss up to him.
Who do you think gets more from that relationship, him or them? That’s interesting. Specifically Mamdani.
You know, I think it has been really fascinating to watch the way that they’re cognizant of the power disparity.

He’s the president of the United States. That is just the political reality, unfortunately, for all of us, right? But to watch, you know, the mayor and to watch the congresswoman in the way that they interact and really move strategically to make sure that New Yorkers benefit from every interaction that they have with the president has been…
Honestly, I’m taking notes. Because I’m like, eventually, right, that will be something that I’ll have to do.
Yeah. It makes me think of something else too, which is, like, you know, so much of campaigning, certainly organizing, is about principles and ideology, and there’s a purity to that.

When you’re governing, you have to work with people, whether it’s centrist Democrats or even Republicans, and that often means compromise. How do you think about that? Are you prepared to compromise, or do you sort of—are you prepared to compromise?

I think that juxtaposition is funny and interesting because, even in a campaign, you’re organizing with people who you might not always agree with on everything, and that doesn’t mean that you compromise your ideology, that you compromise your vision of the world, that you compromise your principles, right?

I deeply believe that we have to be uncompromising in our principles and willing to move on strategy. Because if we are set on strategy, then what does that mean for our principles? Where are we bending there?
Can you give an example of where you’d compromise, or an example of AOC or someone else who has had to make compromise that you’d be okay with?

You know, I’ll actually point to myself, and that is that I’m running for office. I never thought that I would run for office. I’ve always seen myself as a grassroots organizer, and when I realized we had a strategic opening to meaningfully transform politics in this country, I said, Okay, let’s do this.
Let’s use this vehicle that I had for many years not really—like, that was not my world of organizing, right?

As much as I saw it as valuable, it just wasn’t where I was. But I stepped into it because I saw it as a really important vehicle for how we shift our politics more largely. And after winning, right, people told us that that could only happen in New York, and a week later, Melat Kiros won in Denver.
And then after that, 103 Democrats voted to stop sending arms to Israel. So we’ve already transformed the politics of what’s considered acceptable politics within the electoral world.

Sure. I was gonna say, when you get to Congress, do you see your role as someone that is there to make laws or to move the Overton window to the left so that the laws that are made are closer to what you and your compatriots are after?

Yeah. I think it’s both and. I mean, I think, like, if we are only ever talking about our values, but we’re not shifting the policies, then the world around us doesn’t actually change. And I think about—I mean, we’ll just continue down this example of the issue of the genocide, right?

We can talk about our values.We can convince an entire country of people. We’ve convinced the entire Democratic base on this issue, and yet we still have elected officials who are voting against the interests of their base, right? The material conditions have not changed, right? And that’s only going to happen when we have policy that also shifts with it.

And so that’s why it’s important that we are being, you know, good colleagues, right? And we’re talking to folks, finding those points where we do have something in common, and organizing our colleagues to see reason as well, right? Because it’s—yes, sometimes we have to, like, see reason of why something is difficult for them.
That’s what I was gonna say. Are you ready to see reason?
Yeah. And they have to also see that, like, their Democratic base wants them to move on these issues.
How much time have you spent with your future Republican colleagues?
Well, actually, I haven’t spoken to many, but I’ve spoken to, you know, folks across the spectrum on the Democratic Party at this point.
Have you met any Republican congresspeople?
Not actual members, but I’ve met plenty of Republicans.
Just normal people who are Republicans?
Oh, plenty. I mean, I grew up also in Florida.
So there are plenty of Republicans there.
I know, you know, that there are—
Who’s the Republican that you’ll reach out to first when you get to Congress?
I haven’t thought that far, actually.
But I, you know, I’ll say—
Yeah. No, I mean, I’ll say this. I think that there are no two people who agree on every single issue, even as aligned as you might be, right?
And you’d be surprised how people who think very differently can still find a point of commonality and can build trust.
That’s the point of this whole thing.
Exactly, and so that is what organizing is.
Earlier this month, ICE agents attempted to arrest 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the Bronx.

They shot him in the neck while he was in the car with his five-year-old son in the back seat. As you pointed out in the aftermath of this incident, the shooter, an ICE agent, hasn’t been identified or charged with a crime. Can you talk me through what you think should happen now?
Yeah. I think there should be a full investigation into what happened.

I think Oscar should be released and returned to his family, and so that he could get medical care. He still has the bullet in his body and is losing hearing and feeling in his face. And, you know, I think we need to abolish ICE. I don’t see a world in which an institution that is a rogue militia, that is walking around in crowded streets with no uniform, no identification, masked, and shooting into cars—seven bullets into a car that had a five-year-old child in it—while people were returning home from school and work, is an agency that has any business operating in our country.
We’ve seen so many instances of communities and families being torn apart because of ICE’s actions, and the only reason that it exists at this point is to serve as Trump’s cudgel for fascism.
If the shooter in question was apprehended, what should happen to them?
I mean, they should be prosecuted, obviously.
But I also think—I don’t have faith in that because what we’re looking at is the institution that would oversee that is Trump’s, right? It’s Trump’s DOJ. And so I think what the solution here—
Yeah, I mean, this is attempted manslaughter at best.
It’s attempted murder, right? This was, like, ICE shooting at somebody in broad daylight.
I see a bit of a contradiction between wanting the shooter apprehended and your stance on prison abolition, and where’s the shooter going, if not to jail?
Mm-hmm. You know, abolition is a process and a vision, right?

It is the idea that we are constructing a world where a shooting like that doesn’t happen to begin with. And so when I talk about abolishing ICE, the point is that we are taking away the condition for this to ever happen again. We are taking these arms off the street. We are taking these people away from the power to do that to our communities, right?

And we are reinvesting those resources into things that actually make our communities more safe. Abolition is also the view that we should be proactive in safety and not reactive. Because right now we’re talking about an incident that already happened, where a man was shot, right? The world that we’re trying to build is one where that isn’t something that can come to pass.
I understand that, and I think that is a worthy vision, and to advocate for

items.title: Drake’s Stylist Juliet Charlotte Has Seen All Your Memes
items.description: Stylist Sessions is a series of conversations in which Vanity Fair’s style correspondent, José Criales-Unzueta, unpacks the details, strategies, and Easter eggs on red carpets with the leading stylists. Up next, Juliet Charlotte tells VF about dressing Drake a
items.author: José Criales-Unzueta
paragraphs: Stylist Sessions is a series of conversations in which Vanity Fair’s style correspondent, José Criales-Unzueta, unpacks the details, strategies, and Easter eggs on red carpets with the leading stylists. Up next, Juliet Charlotte tells VF about dressing Drake and, yes, reading all your comments about his looks

If you have access to the internet, it’s likely that you’ve seen what Drake wore to celebrate his 40th birthday last weekend in New York City. The rapper opted for a pair of red Versace leather pants and a cheetah jacket, a customized Chrome Hearts jeans and a suede vest, and an archival Chanel scarf paired with gray sweats. But it was an Hermès by Martin Margiela fringed shawl from 1997—a bonafide fashion vintage holy grail—that launched a thousand memes. Drake stepped out, and the jokes poured in: he was dubbed “pumpkin spice papi,” a nod to his nickname and Instagram handle @champagnepapi, described as a Real Housewife on a girls trip to Aspen, and as someone ready for “Christian girl autumn,” another viral trend.

Drake has been the punchline in culture many times, but—online trolls be damned—he’s been dressing better than ever. Chalk that up to his new-ish stylist, New Jersey native Juliet Charlotte. The 27-year-old started her career working with Ye and his fashion brand, Yeezy, as part of his wider styling team. Now that she’s a year into working with Drake, she’s based in Toronto. She also styles the up-and-coming Canadian singer-songwriter Chxrry, whose debut album U, Me & My Ego was released earlier this year.

Charlotte is a singular kind of stylist, particularly in that she prefers to buy pieces—some new, most archival—to build archives for her clients instead of borrowing clothes that any other celebrity could wear. In her first-ever interview, she tells VF about dressing Drake, and addresses the many memes. Spoiler alert: She’s seen them and remains unfazed—she even found some of them funny.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

Juliet Charlotte: I started styling five years ago now. I had just turned 21. Kanye’s team reached out to me, his GM [general manager] at the time, this guy named Laurence Chandler. They were like, “Are you a stylist? Can you come in and do some fittings with us?” I was literally a college student working a retail job, and I was like, Yes, I am a stylist. Of course I can [laughs]. It was around the time of the pandemic, when Ye was at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium and working with Demna. I walked into this room and there’s Demna and all these Balenciaga clothes and Ye. I just wanted to work. I was excited, and I just pretended that I knew what I was doing. I ended up working with him up until maybe two years ago now. I learned a lot from that experience, and then I took on new clients. I worked with [rapper and singer] Molly Santana, and now Chxrry and Drake.
Why do you think they thought you were a stylist?

I was going to school for fashion in New Jersey, and I didn’t actually know which area of fashion I wanted to enter. I just knew that I always loved clothes. When the pandemic happened, all the stores closed, so I had to find a new way to make money. I started to make angel number necklaces, and it just blew up and it was really profitable for me. Looking back, it’s kind of embarrassing, but I was young and it allowed me to buy clothes that I wanted. I would take pictures and post on my Instagram just casually. It wasn’t like I wanted to be an influencer or anything, I just wanted people to see the way I dress. It was a very casual thing, but Yeezy is very reference-based, and I guess I kept showing up on mood boards at that time. So Ye was like, let’s just get this girl in here.

I was part of a bigger team, and Ye would throw me into different roles. So it wasn’t always just styling. Sometimes I was working on e-commerce or doing campaigns, or sometimes it was Bianca [Censori]’s wardrobe. It’s really collaborative at Yeezy. There’s so many talented people that work on everything together.
I was wondering if there was a Ye or Yeezy connection, because I noticed an aesthetic throughline with your personal style. What would you say is your aesthetic, your “thing,” as a stylist?

The Yeezy background definitely helped make me this way, because I want to simplify everything and strip down everything and just be like, let’s just do the absolute best version of whatever you want to do. I’m always trying to declutter. And I really think that came from working with Ye, because he just wants to strip everything back and make it just simple but beautiful and effective.

Drake is a maximalist when it comes to his style, and I appreciate that. I don’t want to just throw my personal style on anybody that I work with. I really want to take what they love and be like, “Okay, let’s do the best version of this.” Working with him, I really just try and keep it in his world and keep it to things that excite him.
Have you always been into vintage fashion? Or is it something that you’ve developed with Drake to build that into his wardrobe?

Obviously we just had that Hermès by [Martin] Margiela moment, which I really enjoyed and I thought it was fun. But I’m really interested in taking pieces, just random vintage pieces that didn’t get such a moment in the past, because that Hermès piece already had its moment on the runway. It’s fun to bring it back, but the way that I like to shop is finding vintage pieces that didn’t get a moment and reinventing them. Obviously there’s a lot of amazing designers right now, but I’m also not so into over-consumption, and just what we’ve turned into. I’d really rather shop vintage as much as I can.

Drake is someone who has such a wide range of influences and sounds. When you work on looks for him, are you trying to pull from this really wide range of inspirations and aesthetics, or are you trying to be a little more focused? Do you try to speak back to the music or do you just try to be a little more focused on just the look?

Sometimes we’re pulling inspiration from Michael Jackson or Liberace, or another artist. But, for example, we’re in Texas right now. He just bought a ranch in Texas. It’s so beautiful. When I first started working with him and I came to the ranch, I’m like, “You are a ranch owner. You’re not larping this aesthetic. You literally live it.” I was really inspired by the saddle shop that’s nearby and all these different stores because it’s two hours away from Houston. He was already wearing [Western clothing] when I met him. This is just a different variation of it. The Western stuff is heavily in his style now, loves vests. I take what I see in his everyday life and see what we lean on more. Like even this mob boss type of thing—he’s really interested in Italian culture, and I’m Italian, so that influence comes in as well.
He has had such a long and prolific career, and he is often self-referential. Do you ever reference early moments in his career?

We did just pull back in his “FOMO” video. We did a variation of the “Hotline Bling” outfit that he wore. But we really don’t draw back too much, I think because he’s just evolved so much as a person. I’ll still send him some looks and be like, “Oh, you ate this,” [laughs]. I have met him as the person that he is now and I’m like, “Okay, he just turned 40. Let’s just be elevated and grown.”
Chxrry is building something really strong. What’s it like to work with both an artist that has been working in the industry for so long while also with someone who’s so green?

Chxrry and I have become best friends in the process, so we’re just figuring it out together. We’re the same age. She’s so early in her career that I’m sure she’ll have many evolutions, but for now it’s just about having fun.
With Drake, he just loves clothes and is pretty easygoing, but there’s obviously a lot more pressure that’s involved because he’s so established. It’s very different, but equally as rewarding.
I have to ask about the birthday outfits. I thought they were great, but I’m curious if you planned a birthday weekend wardrobe or if you are more casual about it?

Well, October’s a crazy month, so there’s so much stuff going on so I did a lot of preparation. We knew that we wanted to do a beautiful suit, but we actually had three other suits that fell through before that one. Last minute, our atelier had just made that tux for him, and then I got the brooch, we put on a bow tie. It all came together at the last minute, and that Chanel scarf I had just bought that morning in New York. The Hermès shawl I bought the day before we left for the trip in Canada. Everything is really just down to what he’s feeling like that night. We can do all this preparation, but that night if he’s like, “Actually, I just feel like being more chill or I just want to do this,” we just pivot, and we always figure it out.
I like that he seems to wear only things he owns, when many celebrities wear borrowed clothing. Do you also do that, or do you prefer to just buy things?

On the record [laughs], I hate pulling. I hate loaning. I hate all of that. It gives me anxiety. I hate if it was my stuff and it was out in the world and you just never know what happens. It could get messed up in travel, and there’s just wear and tear. Things just happen. I know it’s a huge part of styling, but for me, I’d rather just source the pieces myself and have them be a part of our archive and a part of our collection.

With someone like Drake, who is so big, you want there to be an archive of what he’s done and worn, otherwise it’s all lost in brands’ sample closets. I have to ask about the memes. People had so much to say about the Hermès by Margiela. As the stylist, what do you think of that?

I love a joke. I love a joke we can laugh about, but I still love the look. I don’t feel less than or like, “Oh God, it’s a meme.” I still love the look. I think it was amazing. Even when we did “FOMO” and he was wearing that leather jacket with the fur on one side, that was a women’s Saint Laurent piece. I love when men do things that are out of the box, or that isn’t just pants and a shirt. Why not wear a fringed shawl? I was into it, but I could appreciate the joke and I did think some of them were funny.
Pumpkin Spice Papi was really funny. If anything, becoming a meme nowadays adds to the look. It’s already a Halloween costume.

Yes [laughs], I’ve seen that. I was too young, but I always think that if we had the internet the way that we do now, what would people say about Michael Jackson or what would they say about Prince? I’m sure there would be so many memes. There would have to be.

You mentioned the Saint Laurent women’s jacket. Something that I always really liked about Drake’s style is his willingness to just go there and have fun with fashion. There’s something really cool and really refreshing about that.

It’s really just fun and it’s really just down to what we’re both happy with. And as a man, if you’re really comfortable with yourself and comfortable, and you know who you are... He gets so many opinions projected on him all the time and he just doesn’t care. He still chooses what he likes. It doesn’t change his mind. I think it’s just because he’s so confident and comfortable with who he is. It’s really refreshing to work with somebody who’s not like, “Oh no, I can’t wear that. That’s crazy,” or whatever. If anything, he’s just like, “Oh yeah, fuck it. Let’s do it.” He’s really just excited to try new things. And even the fringe shawl, we spoke about it afterwards and he was like, “Yeah, it was sick. I loved it.” There’s nothing that can change his mind.

People may not think I’m the best [stylist] or whatever, but I like it. I don’t trust anyone else’s opinion because you’re not in my shoes, so you can’t really tell me how I should do it. Drake as a person has so much fun with his life. He had a blast for his birthday weekend. He doesn’t care about comments and neither do I. We don’t sit there and read them. We’ll give a chuckle if it’s funny or share a meme, but keep it pushing. We have fun.

items.title: Heat From Cremations Is Being Used to Warm Homes and Swimming Pools
items.description: In 2011, Redditch Borough Council in England tried something that hardly anyone in the UK had heard of before. Staff announced they were going to warm the local swimming pool with heat from a nearby crematorium.
items.author: Chris Baraniuk
paragraphs: In 2011, Redditch Borough Council in England tried something that hardly anyone in the UK had heard of before. Staff announced they were going to warm the local swimming pool with heat from a nearby crematorium.

A public firestorm ensued. The plans were met with international headlines, and a labor union official branded them “sick and an insult to residents.” (A spokesman for the union, Unison, says this was not—and is not currently—the organization’s official position.)

“All you’re doing is basically heating a radiator and sending the heat down a tube,” says Guy Revans, of Redditch and Bromsgrove Councils, just south of Birmingham. “But death is always an emotive subject, isn’t it?”
Eventually, the relentless press coverage faded away. The project won a green award, and the crematorium has warmed Redditch’s swimming pool since 2013.

Although extremely rare in North America, European countries have been harvesting warmth from crematoria for years. The total volume of heat available from crematoria is modest, but as people search for ways of reducing the environmental impact of funeral rites, utilizing crematoria waste heat provides a way to lower their carbon intensity.

Roughly 1,200 cremations are carried out every year in Redditch. A heat exchanger captures heat from flue gases emitted by the facility’s two gas-fired ovens as part of a process to remove vaporized mercury from dental fillings, before venting the remaining gas into the atmosphere.

That’s a common process at many crematoria. In other words, excess heat is often captured by default, meaning the next question is, does it make sense to waste the heat—or use it? In Redditch, the heat exchanger connects to a water loop that travels 200 meters underground, eventually reaching another heat exchanger supplying the swimming pool.

Helpfully, such a sizable body of water “acts as a heat sink”, adds Revans. “You put heat into it during the day, it retains that heat for a considerable length of time.” The recreation center also has gas-fired boilers that can provide more heat when necessary. Overall, the system has saved the council tens of thousands of pounds per year in fuel costs.

Similar projects have emerged elsewhere recently. A school currently under construction in Aberdeen, Scotland, will receive excess heat from the city’s crematorium. The crematorium already relies on waste heat to warm its own premises.

“They were only utilizing a tiny amount of the heat available; the rest was going to the atmosphere,” says Ian Davidson, chief executive of Aberdeen Heat & Power, who says that the system now has full planning permission. The crematorium will provide just under 1 gigawatt-hour of heat annually, roughly half the school’s total requirement. A heat pump will cover the rest of the facility’s needs, and the entire system should be fully operational by February 2027.

Some crematoria are going even further in their pursuit of green credentials. The crematorium that will open in Kangasala, Finland, in 2028 will be connected to the town’s district heat network, a system of pipes that supplies more than 6,500 homes with hot water for heating. The crematorium will be fully electric, powered partly by solar panels on its roof.
“It’s a special thing,” says Timo Heikkilä, an energy and building systems consultant at Thenco Oy, who is working on the project. “I’m really glad I get to be a part of this.”

Winter temperatures in Kangasala can remain below 0 degrees Celsius for weeks on end. In Finland, there is a push to use less natural gas for heating, says Heikkilä. Although once cheaply available from neighbouring Russia, that country’s invasion of Ukraine and concerns over climate change have prompted Finland to seek alternatives. In some locations, this means utilizing waste heat from unusual sources, including crematoria.
“Finns,” says Heikkilä, “are quite practical.”

Ian Rudkin, who has managed multiple crematoria in the UK and is currently a board member of the Cremation Society of Great Britain, says many crematoria are becoming more eco-conscious. Today, software can schedule the firing of gas ovens to align with funeral services, ensuring they don’t waste energy and are only turned on when needed, for example. And some crematoria hold coffins for up to 72 hours, so that several may be cremated in a sequence, which is more efficient.

“When we first brought that in, [families] seemed a little bit shocked,” says Rudkin. Soon, however, people became more accepting. “They’d make comments like, ‘Dad always used to turn the light off at home to save energy.’”

But implementing heat recovery tech at crematoria in the US is more difficult, says Paul Seyler, director of strategy at Matthews Environmental Solutions. There, district heat networks are rare, and crematoria tend to be privately owned. That means the investment needed for heat exchangers and pipework necessary to link buildings together is higher.

“We’re studying this and watching it closely because, when the economics align, we’d like to be in a position to offer a solution,” says Seyler. Wasted heat is, after all, just a waste of resources, he adds. Besides a few small-scale experiments, Seyler says he isn’t aware of any fully operational systems in the US that utilize heat from crematoria.

The closest example is in Canada at a funeral complex in Sainte-Thérèse, Quebec. This 3,255-square-meter building houses family rooms, a large chapel, a crematorium, and a kitchen, among other facilities. Heat exchangers installed just over a decade ago soak up heat from cremation flue gases and distribute it around the complex, including the sidewalks to melt snow in the winter.

“The owner was not immediately on board as he thought it may have posed an ethical dilemma,” recall design engineers Martin Roy and Lianne Cockerton in an article about the project, published in the ASHRAE Journal.

Now, visitors pass an LED screen in the reception area that displays the energy performance of the building, based partly on the heat exchanger’s operation. While gas is still used for some of the building’s heating needs, as well as for cremations, the new system saves an estimated 29 metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually.

Recovering heat from cremations is one way of attempting to counter the “devastating impact” that humans have had on the environment, says Hannah Rumble, an associate at the University of Bath’s Centre for Death and Society. “I can see that would be a reason why people might choose to be cremated at a particular crematorium.”

Most crematoria contacted by WIRED say they do not emphasize the presence of heat recovery technology to families or mourners, though a spokeswoman for Aberdeen City Council adds that the council there will “undertake some public awareness-raising on the new system before it is operational to ensure transparency.”

Gaynor Doherty, an independent humanist funeral and wedding celebrant in the UK, says using waste heat from crematoria is “sensible,” though she suggests a natural burial, where bodies are simply shrouded or placed in biodegradable coffins and allowed to decompose in the environment, might be preferable to many eco-minded people. The carbon intensity of cremation varies from facility to facility, but could be around 250 kilograms of carbon per gas-fired cremation. Recovering heat from the process offsets some of those emissions (one company claims savings of 100 kilograms) but not all.

A study published in 2024 estimated that, if all crematoria in the UK were tapped for waste heat, they might only meet 1 percent of the county’s total heating needs. This sounds small, but decarbonizing heat is notoriously difficult, so any interventions to achieve that can be valuable. Plus, some people may feel that sharing the heat from their cremation could carry a lot of meaning.

In Finland, the all-electric crematorium in Kangasala will not produce as much heat as a gas-fired equivalent, though it will run 24/7 because it’s more efficient to operate by using electricity to gently top up heat retained in ceramic materials within the ovens. The connection to the district heat network means that, when mourners return home from funeral services at the new crematorium, it is conceivable that at least a small portion of that warmth they feel after stepping through their front doors will come from the cremation of the person they loved.

Heikkilä says working on the project has prompted some big questions for him. “I have thought about it, and once my time is up, I would like to be cremated, and I would like my waste heat to be recycled,” he says. “It’s the sensible thing. The last favor you can do for the world.”

items.title: Polymarket Halted International Trading After Hackers Drained Accounts
items.description: Trading has resumed on Polymarket’s flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders.
items.author: Kate Knibbs
paragraphs: Trading has resumed on Polymarket’s flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders.

A third-party vendor based in the United Kingdom was breached, not the prediction market’s website itself. Law enforcement in the UK have been notified of the incident, the company said. Trading was initially paused while the company investigated for several hours.

On X, prominent traders complained that they had lost money; blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps reported that around 700 users appeared to have been affected, with approximately $2.7 million stolen. Polymarket declined to comment when WIRED asked how many traders were impacted by the breach and how much money was lost, but the company said it will refund impacted traders.

The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company’s newer platform for people within the United States. Polymarket runs two separate prediction markets; Polymarket US operates as a federally regulated financial exchange within the country, while the flagship Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based platform that is banned in the United States and a number of other countries.

This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced security woes. In June 2026, Polymarket experienced another breach, which resulted in over $2 million in losses for impacted traders.

The company has been a lightning rod for controversy since its 2020 launch. In the past few years, it has been the center of several high-profile alleged insider trading incidents resulting in arrests. One case involved a Special Forces soldier accused of wagering on the capture of Venezuela’s former leader; another involved a Google employee who allegedly used confidential information to make millions. In both cases, the suspects have pleaded not guilty.
Polymarket recently raised $1 billion in August 2026, with a fundraising round led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. It is now valued at $21 billion.

items.title: The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself
items.description: Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually.
items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.

For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.

Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.

“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”

&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.

And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.

The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.

The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.

Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.

Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.

Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.

Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.

But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.

Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.

Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.

Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.

Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.

Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”

Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.

But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

items.title: Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
items.description: A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now
items.author: Joel Khalili
paragraphs: A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.

The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.

“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”

The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.

The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)

Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.

Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.

“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.

“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

items.title: This App Brutally Shames You by Tracking How Many Hours You’ve Lost to Scrolling
items.description: You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a health
items.author: David Nield
paragraphs: You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.

One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.

It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.

You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.

Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”

The main interface shows each day as a straightforward series of circles representing hours. Every circle that’s filled in black is an hour you’ve lost to an app that has pulled you away from something more worthwhile.

It’s quite a brutal and minimalist approach, but I like it. It really brings home how much time you can spend on apps that aren’t really all that good for you, especially when you start looking at your progress (or lack of it) over entire weeks or months. However, I did find that once I’d lost a particular hour, my brain wanted to cram in as much absent-minded scrolling as possible during the rest of that hour.

By default, an hour is marked as lost if only if you spend seconds inside a distracting app. It's quite a harsh approach, but it needs to be—otherwise I think there would be the temptation to use up any allotted free time after every hour resets. You can extend this threshold period through settings, if you pay for the app.

Another handy feature here is the ability to set designated quiet hours. These are times when you really, absolutely do not want to look at your phone unnecessarily: Any use of a distracting app here blackens the boxes for all the hours in the quiet zone, not just one.
