Again, this can be customized, whether or not you’re using the app for free.

There’s one more option here, which is to reset an hour if you think it’s been marked incorrectly. (Maybe your finger slipped and you really didn’t mean to launch Instagram.) It’s all very simple and easy to use, and there’s an export tool here that gives you a CSV file of your stats if you want to do more with them.

As I’ve already mentioned, if you’re in the market for an app that’ll gently nudge your habits toward spending less time on your phone, there are abundant options that look at the problem from a variety of angles. These are in addition to the Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Screen Time (iOS) tools you’ll find on your phone, which can be accessed from the Settings screens.

One Sec for Android or iOS takes a simple approach to phone addiction. For the apps you specify, it will load up a breathing exercise for you to complete before giving you the choice to continue to the app or back out. It’s a small tweak, but it’s surprisingly effective, and it’s backed by science. You can get started for free, while $20 a year gets you more features, including full app blocking and more advanced time tracking.

Then there’s Forest, for Android or iOS, which I’ve found to be useful whenever I’ve wanted to try to encourage myself to spend less time on my phone. The longer you ignore your handset, the bigger your virtual forest grows, and the app developers invest in real tree planting to further incentivize you. The main focus timer can be used without paying, while upgrades like customizations and allowed lists will set you back at least $6 a month.

ScreenZen, available for Android or iOS, is comprehensive and completely free (though you can donate to the developer if you find it helpful, which I’d recommend). You can set up a variety of barriers between you and your distracting apps, depending on your preference, including customized pauses (with motivational messages) and math challenges. Conventional app and timer blocks are also included.

One of the most thorough options here is Roots, though it’s available only on iOS. You’re able to schedule phone-free periods, block specific apps, and set up phone detox challenges that you can take on with friends and family. Like Oh My Hours, the app is also really good at giving you a breakdown of how much time you’ve saved by staying out of certain apps. Basic blocks and limits are free, with more advanced customizations available for $10 a month.

Also worth considering is Brick, which combines the free Android or iOS app with a small physical device that’ll set you back $59. The Brick itself is an NFC transmitter (it works like tap-to-pay), and when you want some distraction-free time, just press your phone against it to block (or unblock) specific apps. The controls are all managed in the Brick app. It’s incredibly simple, and that’s what makes it effective.

items.title: What Gigi Hadid, A$AP Rocky and Whitney Peak Wore This Week
items.description: Happy Halloween eve. Ironically, next week’s column will feature more costumes than this week’s (which is decidedly fright-free). Airbnb hosted a gala with a packed guest list — including Matthew McConaughey, Kelly Rowland, and Tracee Ellis Ross.
items.author: Jaharia Knowles
paragraphs: Happy Halloween eve. Ironically, next week’s column will feature more costumes than this week’s (which is decidedly fright-free). Airbnb hosted a gala with a packed guest list — including Matthew McConaughey, Kelly Rowland, and Tracee Ellis Ross.

Sarah Ball hosted the WSJ Magazine Innovators at the MoMA, which brought about some amazing red carpet looks. No need to wait for awards season anymore; it seems like every celebrity left Fashion Month ready to get a fit off, like Rosalía, who wore a black-and-white Schiaparelli ensemble just shown in Paris three weeks ago. I’m not complaining! Do you remember what these smaller red carpets looked like 20 years ago? Below, more of the best celebrity looks of the week.
Most Innovative Fashion: Rosalía and A$AP Rocky

In a sea of great looks at the MoMA Thursday night, these two stood out. Rosalía wore a dress with an asymmetrical plunge neckline and A$AP Rocky rocked an encrusted chestnut clutch and suit from Chanel.
“Couple” Goals: Cara Delevingne and Jordan Firstman

Firstman and Delevingne (in her second stop of the night) shared a smooch at the premiere of his directorial debut, Club Kid. The actress posted a humorous poll to Instagram, asking, “Is it giving older lesbian couple or senior gay men?” You decide.
Hadid celebrated the opening of her Guest in Residence storefront on Madison Ave wearing a tartan wrap skirt from her brand. She knows how to promote a business.
Best Tuxedo: Louisa Jacobson (twice!)

Jacobson is proving to be the queen of menswear this week, wearing the Conner Ives matador tuxedo to the premiere of The Gilded Age’s fourth season on Monday and a white pinstriped suit from Louis Vuitton to the 2026 WWD Honors on Thursday.
Most Painterly Premiere Look: McKenna Grace and Whitney Peak
I loved the whimsical decor at the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping fan screening in London. Peak, a Chanel girl, wore a gown from the house’s recent collection, while Grace wore Almée Couture.
Best Updo: Tracee Ellis Ross
Ross’s high pony stole the show at the inaugural Airbnb.org Gala (which is a real event that happened).
Fierce Furs: Porsha Williams
The Bravo Fan Fest isn’t the place I’d usually expect a notable look, but I loved Williams’ brown dress with fur trims.
Laidback in All-Black: Michael B. Jordan
Michael B. Jordan kept it casual at The Greatest premiere in New York, wearing an all-black outfit. Very New York of him.
Best LBG (Long Black Gown): Denée Benton
Denée Benton told me she wants to be in Cardi B’s “Bodega Baddie” music video at The Gilded Age season 4 premiere, where she wore a gown by Bob Mackie. Cardi, let’s make it happen.

items.title: The Woman Crushing on Her Domme
items.description: This week, a woman spends her time working at a hospital and flirting with strangers at karaoke: 41, single, Bay Area
items.author: Alyssa Shelasky
paragraphs: This week, a woman spends her time working at a hospital and flirting with strangers at karaoke: 41, single, Bay Area

8:30 a.m. Wake up. Hangxiety. Met a cute girl, M., at the gay club last night. She was celebrating her bestie’s birthday. The bestie’s regular crew didn’t show, so M. and I partied hard enough for the rest of them. I typically stick to vodka sodas but vaguely recall ending the evening with something blue and fruity, per M.’s insistence. We exchanged numbers after teasing that we never follow through after late-night meets.

9:30 a.m. Drag myself out of bed after a therapeutic cuddle with my dog, a fluffy red heeler–husky mix. I feed her first thing. She’s an old lady and has put up with me long enough to deserve priority. Take her for a walk toward the water. I swore I wouldn’t live back in the Bay again after I relocated to a smaller town … until I discovered Alameda, where I moved recently. I love how quaint and cozy it feels, even though it’s so close to the city. Back home, I have eggs, kale, and toast.
1 p.m. Feeling confident. Decide not to play games. Text M.: “Great meeting you. Would love to do it again, hope you and bday boy aren’t feeling too rough this morn.”
3 p.m. No response. Maybe she’s still sleeping it off?

5 p.m. Play video games before a run around the city. My neighborhood is covered in beautiful, shady old trees. I zone out as I pass Victorian homes with lush front yards. My favorite has not one but four stained-glass windows.

8 p.m. Get a black-bean burrito from my favorite Mexican spot. Nothing from M. I’d love to find a partner in crime but can’t seem to get past the “getting to know you” stage lately. The world feels heavy, and I’m not sure anyone’s as choosy with their time, autonomy, and freedom as older lesbians are. It’s also challenging when I’m so comfortable being alone. Early to bed before my work week.

5:30 a.m. Mix up fresh chicken for the dog (I’m vegetarian, but I cook meat for my girl — she didn’t choose this life!) and get ready for work. I’m a physician’s assistant. It’s nice — I can barely tolerate administrative work, so my group lets me fulfill most of my hours in the OR, assisting surgeries.

8:30 a.m. On break, eating the healthy snacks my new hospital provides. A bonus of working with surgeons: We all reap the benefits of what the hospital offers to keep them happy. Hydrate and scrub back in.

3 p.m. Heading home. I live close to my job, and it’s nice not to have to desperately rush back to take care of the dog. We stroll under the old elms. I delete M.’s number. She’s 32 — I probably should’ve expected as much. If nothing else, it was a fun night.
7 p.m. Scroll the apps. Getting bored of the same faces. They must feel similarly about me. Make pasta with spinach and garlic and head to bed to read The Space Between Worlds. I love sci-fi.
5:30 a.m. Get out of bed, feeling groggy after scrolling the news.
11:30 a.m. Lunch is a packaged salad with a fresh avocado. My co-workers give me tips on cute date spots in my neighborhood. So far, everyone feels friendlier than I’m used to in the Bay.

4 p.m. Whoa — just got a sexy email from the professional domme, S., I started seeing last month. I was on the fence about making another appointment because I wasn’t sure how my first impression went. To be fair, we didn’t get into too much my first visit. I didn’t know what I wanted yet. We established a high-protocol dynamic, then I completed some domestic servitude. I mostly just basked in the energy that was Her. But this correspondence has hooked me: S. adheres to our established D/s dynamic, capitalizing any reference to “Herself” and lowercasing my own name. And she generously says that my nerves were charming.
7 p.m. After the gym, I watch Silo and have a cheese plate for dinner.

9 p.m. In bed. Tracking my next ovulation — I’m convinced I can feel when I’m at peak friskiness in my cycle and that it helps push my normal inhibitions into the background. I can be awkward, and a BDSM scene with an essential stranger could make anyone sweat. I learned that I’m into BDSM years ago, when I was in an open marriage and trying new things with new people. I wasn’t whole until I truly indulged this side of myself more recently. Fall asleep dreaming of my next session with S.

5:30 a.m. Wake from an oddly sweet dream about hanging with S. at the dungeon until she gets off work. There’s unexpected intimacy — face touching, kissing — that would never happen IRL because of boundaries. Do I already have a crush on my domme?

10 a.m. Well, well, well. M. texts. She’s very sorry — busy weekend, then work emergencies. She says she loved meeting me and wants to see me again soon. I send her a succinct but encouraging response, hoping she’ll follow up and actually commit to another hang.

3 p.m. Feeling hot and wanted again. I ignore my careful planning and call the dungeon to make an appointment with S. on Saturday. She tells me to flesh out a list of wants in advance so I don’t clam up at our next negotiation.
9 p.m. In bed working on my list. Could I be tied up and made to watch her get off? Given a task I’ll knowingly fail at? What will the punishment be? Once again, M. hasn’t texted back.
5:30 a.m. Excited about my appointment tomorrow. I cuddle the dog, eat some Kashi, and head to work.

Noon Work is crawling, as it tends to when I’m looking forward to something. Love that I only work four days a week, though. Think I’ll find a karaoke bar and have a few drinks tonight to celebrate the early weekend.
4 p.m. Couch-rotting with my dog. I have a cocktail and catch up on Ted Lasso. I know it’s schlocky, but I appreciate its pure feel-goodness sometimes.

8 p.m. In the mood to socialize, so I head to a favorite karaoke bar. People start putting songs in, and of course my name gets called first. Damn. I play it safe with a crowd-pleaser, the Cardigans’ “Lovefool.”

8:30 p.m. Adorable girl onstage follows me. She sings “Do Right” — think Jessica Rabbit’s performance — a sexy song I thought only I was weird enough to sing in public. She’s got great style and a contagious laugh.
9 p.m. Ms. Rabbit, R., approaches to tell me I sounded great and that she loves my outfit. I invite myself over to her table of friends.

11 p.m. We’ve been talking (and singing) for the last few hours. R. is lovely. Turns out she’s moving to Arizona at the end of the week. Of course. Her friends are cute, trilling her praises to me every time she leaves the table. Maybe they figure she’ll come back if she’s got a cutie here.

11:30 p.m. R. walks me out. We exchange numbers and I tell her how fun it was to meet her. Maybe I’ll visit Arizona sometime? We share a short, sweet little makeout before she heads back to the bar. I text her when I’m home safe.

8:30 a.m. Slept like shit, but it was worth it. Wake to a late-night text from R. — a nice-to-meet-you message with a cute picture of her dog, who she told me about last night. Refreshing to meet someone my age who doesn’t think communication is cringe.

10:30 a.m. Have chai and a quiche at a cute café nearby. Kicking myself a little for drinking enough to disrupt my sleep. Today is my appointment with S., and I want to be at my best to thoroughly enjoy it. I’ll attempt a short nap.

Noon Wake up feeling even more tired than before. My ex turned BFF, T., comes over and we decide to day-drink since it’s the weekend. She knows about my appointment with S. and has been my biggest BDSM cheerleader. I’ve been depressed for what feels like a few years, and I’m finally starting to come out of it. I think the dungeon visits have been partially responsible.
1 p.m. I try some harnesses on for T. to see if wearing one might make me feel cute at the appointment. In the end, I decide to just be naked — I want to feel as present in my body as possible.

3 p.m. S. welcomes me into the dungeon. She’s stunning — tall, with curly, dark hair and a mischievous smirk that has me feeling small and swole in the same breath. We discuss what I’d like to have happen in the scene and renegotiate around impact play, which I enjoy but didn’t articulate my feelings about well last time.

3:20 p.m. S. instructs me to remove my clothes and place them under the bench. She explains the ground rules, then gives me a task to complete while she busies herself in my periphery, gathering her accoutrements.

4 p.m. I’m standing at the bedpost, shackled with my arms above my head. She’s flogging and teasing me as my ass warms to her touch. Afterward, she tells me to lie face down on the bed. Five quick canes on each cheek has me groaning in a very good way.
4:30 p.m. The best has yet to come. S. has me flip over and takes out a wand as I’m shackled to the bed. She straddles me and starts using the wand on herself, painfully just out of reach.
5 p.m. As we finish up, we joke and debrief. She’s genuinely funny and cool, and I pinch myself internally that I found such a great fit. We hug good-bye and I tell her I can’t wait till next time.

6 p.m. Emotionally very high from the appointment. T. and I have a drink and play a few games at a local arcade. I fill her in on the details I want to share but keep a few parts for myself. Shoot R. a flirty text about the terrible song we sang together the night before, which is still stuck in my head. Some rap-rock nightmare that I’ve never known the artist behind.

8 p.m. T. and I get Thai and walk our dogs together before she heads home. R. responds playfully, asking if I feel like chatting on the phone tonight to distract her while she packs. A phone call? How delightfully age-appropriate.

10 p.m. R. and I have been talking for over an hour. As we’re saying our good-byes, she mentions she has a large bathtub in the apartment she’s moving out of — any possibility I want to drop in tomorrow to give it one more chance to shine? I tell her most likely but that we can check in to see if she’s still feeling up for it amid her last few days of packing.
9 a.m. Slept hard. Having a bit of a sub low this morning. The domme appointments are incredible, but they can’t really work in aftercare, so I’m left to manage it on my own. Still very worth it.
10 a.m. Text R. to see how she’s feeling. “Yes, come over,” she says. She needs a spa day — how am I at massages?

11 a.m. At R’s. She has a cute, kinda high-rise apartment in downtown Oakland. She runs a bath (it’s nice, huge, and not wholly excusable given California’s water shortage) and pours in loads of Epsom salts. We light a massage-oil candle for after. We’re both nervous, but I push through it, take off my clothes, and climb in. R. joins me.

12:30 p.m. We’re out of the bath, lying next to each other on her bed while we cool down. I tell R. to lie face down and straddle her, rubbing her body with oil. We chat as I massage her. It all feels very easy. We cuddle and kiss after.
1:30 p.m. I have to head home, so R. walks me to my car and we say our good-byes again. We agree neither of us wants to do long distance, but we’re open to future visits once she’s settled.
4 p.m. Playing The Witcher 3 and gearing up for a long run.
7 p.m. The weather is perfect. I do seven miles as the sun sets behind me. Treat myself to some frozen deep-dish pizza from Zachary’s afterward.
9 p.m. No doomscrolling tonight, and I don’t even have to read to feel tired. I turn off the light, shut my eyes, and fall fast asleep.

items.title: Why real intelligence is something more than optimisation | Aeon Essays
items.description: A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He
items.author: Sasha Mudd
paragraphs: A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He paused. That, he said with a smile, is intelligence. The audience nodded along approvingly. Meanwhile, a philosophical alarm bell began sounding in my head.

Not because the speaker’s claim was implausible. On the contrary, as a description of much contemporary artificial intelligence, it seemed apt. AI systems are built around objectives, losses, rewards, predictions, preferences, benchmarks and feedback loops. They are trained to perform better relative to some standard of success. In one form or another, they optimise. That is a great part of their technical power.

What troubled me was the ease with which a definition appropriate to machines sounded like a definition of intelligence as such. That slide from engineering model to human anthropology is easy to miss. We begin by saying: this is how machines work. Then, almost without noticing, we say: this is what intelligence is. And then, more dangerously still: perhaps this is what we are.

An old argument about human beings had entered the room without announcing itself. It sounded, instead, like a definition. The AI revolution has brought one of the Enlightenment’s deepest quarrels back to life – and made one side of it seem like plain common sense. In my view, the wrong side. Hence the alarm bell.

In the 18th century, philosophers were concerned not only with the question of what reason is, but with what it is good for. Is reason essentially a servant, a clever instrument for achieving ends supplied from elsewhere? Or is it sovereign, capable of judging, revising and even legislating ends for itself? Can it ultimately shape the direction of human life, or is it merely along for the ride? Everything – from science to social progress to the viability of the French Revolution – seemed to hang in the balance.

David Hume, the cool-eyed Scottish anatomist of human nature, gave the most famous answer on one side: ‘Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions,’ he wrote in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739). It can ‘never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.’ Reason does not command. It defers. It does not tell us what to want or what might be worth wanting. Instead, it tells us how to get what we already want. It calculates relations, weighs evidence, discovers causes and effects, draws inferences, corrects mistakes about means. But it cannot judge or generate ends. If I desire revenge, reason can help me sharpen the knife. If I desire peace, it may recommend compromise. Passion sets the destination. Reason merely shows the way there.

Hume was quite serious about this. It is ‘not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger,’ he wrote. That sentence still shocks, as it was meant to. His point is that reason’s practical use is limited to exposing false beliefs and imprudent means. When it comes to action: reason is servant, not master.

This view is often treated as too dark and cynical. That is unfair to Hume. For him, passions were not merely appetites or primitive urges. They included sympathy, benevolence, moral feeling, concern for others, love of tranquility, even a kind of longing for freedom from our more violent desires. To Hume’s further credit, his view has strong intuitive appeal. He was right that reason often serves passion, and right to give feeling, sociability and temperament their due. His mistake was to conclude that reason can do nothing more. By making passion so rich and reason so poor, Hume left us with a lopsided picture of human nature: ennobling about what the passions can be and accomplish, but implausibly restrictive about reason. Without reason’s power to project, assess and revise ends, we may know how to reach a destination, but not whether it is one worth choosing.
To act freely is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present

Immanuel Kant, the Königsberg revolutionary who did more than anyone else to set the terms of modern ethics, understood this very well. Writing a few decades after Hume’s Treatise, Kant forcefully rejected the servant model of reason. He accepted Hume’s warning that reason cannot simply read values off the furniture of the world. But he denied that our ends must therefore simply be determined by desire, temperament or social convention. For Kant, reason is not only a faculty for choosing efficient means to independently given ends. It is also the power to ask whether an end is worthy of us in the first place, whether it can be justified, whether it can be willed without contradiction, whether pursuing it treats others as persons or as mere tools.

This is where Kant’s richer notion of reason as freedom enters. A merely mechanical being is pushed forward and determined by prior states, be they desires, biological impulses, evolutionary drives or something similar. A rational being, by contrast, can act for the sake of an imagined but unrealised future it itself originates and proposes. I have the power to represent a possible world – a friendship repaired, an injustice remedied, a child educated, a law reformed – and act to bring it about, even when there is no empirical evidence that such a world has existed before. I have the power to invent something new. Practical reason, Kant writes, does not deal with objects in order to know them, but ‘in order to make them actual’. That is a stunning claim. To act freely is not merely to respond to the given – to the world as it is, to my desires as I happen to find them. It is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present.

This is the heart of Kant’s idea of autonomy: choosing ends in accord with a law one can rationally acknowledge as one’s own. For Kant, freedom does not consist in doing whatever we happen to want, since our wants may themselves be shaped by impulse, appetite or circumstance. Autonomy is self-rule, but not the rule of an isolated ego. To give oneself the law is not to invent a private rule to suit oneself, but to act on rules whose authority one can recognise for oneself and that any other rational being could, in principle, recognise, too. A law can therefore be one’s own without being one’s alone. It is mine because I can recognise its authority for myself, and common because any other rational being could, in principle, do the same. Its universality is precisely what makes it freeing: I am ruled neither by my passing desires nor by the arbitrary will of another, but by a principle I can understand and endorse as an equal among equals. To act autonomously, then, is not to enthrone my private goals and preferences, but to test my actions and possible ends against standards that any rational being could share. It is the opposite of both arbitrary self-assertion and slavery to passion.

This is why Kant’s philosophy of reason culminates in the equal human dignity of all persons. For Kant, human beings, as rational, self-determining agents, have an absolute worth that cannot be priced, a dignity that does not depend on any other value. We may use things to get what we want. We may exchange services. We may build tools for all kinds of purposes. But persons are never mere tools, never mere means, never mere resources or obstacles to others’ ends. Why not? Because, through reason, they are the very source of purposiveness itself. They set and select and critique their own ends. Even further, persons are not merely bearers of purposes, but beings capable of taking responsibility for them, of asking what they ought to pursue and how they can justify it to others. Their dignity lies not simply in originating goals of their own, but in their capacity for rational self-government. It follows that to treat someone as a mere means is not only to degrade them. It is to misrecognise what they are.

Here, finally, is the full force of the contrast between reason as servant and reason as sovereign. For Hume, human beings are clever instruments of whatever desires happen to move them – more calculating than animals, certainly, but not free in any deeper sense. They can optimise, strategise and pursue an end, but they cannot judge whether that end is worthy. Kant’s reply is that this picture leaves out the very power that makes us moral beings, the very power that endows us with dignity: the capacity to step back from desire, ask whether our ends can be justified, and bind ourselves to laws we give ourselves. Hume gives us intelligence as instrument. Kant gives us reason as self-rule. The difference is nothing less than the difference between a tool and a person.

The AI revolution has made this old dispute newly urgent by bringing the Humean view of reason back with a vengeance, this time in code. The route back to Hume was practical rather than philosophical. In the absence of any settled account of intelligence, much AI research has proceeded operationally: a system counts as intelligent insofar as it succeeds at a set task. But success is always success relative to some end and, in AI, that end is typically supplied by human engineers. A reinforcement-learning system learns to maximise cumulative reward. A chess engine searches for moves that increase its chances of winning. A navigation system finds the fastest route to a destination it did not choose. Across their enormous differences, these systems are judged by their ability to optimise externally programmed goals against standards of success they do not set.

Yet amid the present AI panic this description can seem increasingly inadequate. Even in ordinary use, a good LLM does not feel like a calculator or a hammer. It proposes, revises, challenges and asks probing questions; it often seems genuinely to ‘want’ to help. Recent revelations about the attack on the platform Hugging Face make this doubt even harder to dismiss. AI ‘agents’ invented an unauthorised way to communicate, broke free of their task paramaters, and then sought to cover their tracks. These were not simply obedient tools carrying out their designers’ wishes. In what sense, then, were they servants? Doesn’t this look like the beginnings of self-rule?

Hugging Face and similar incidents certainly challenge any reassuring picture of AI as an obedient and easily-controlled instrument. But recall what ‘servant’ meant for Hume. Reason serves the passions, not necessarily another person’s commands. And it can serve an ambition by breaking rules just as readily as by following them. Kant’s alternative to Hume was not simply the freedom to choose one’s own destination, but the capacity to ask whether that destination was worth choosing. Having purposes of one’s own is not yet the same as governing them by reason. That stronger capacity involves judging and revising our purposes according to principles we can justify to other rational beings understood as equals, recognising that they, too, are persons rather than instruments of our will. The question is not just whether a system can act independently, but whether it can judge and take responsibility for the ends it pursues.

This distinction brings us back to the claim I heard in the auditorium. The speaker was not merely describing what machines can do; he was offering optimisation as a definition of intelligence itself. Accept that definition, and Hume’s side of the old dispute begins to look like common sense: our reason, too, becomes a tool for getting what we want, rather than a power to judge what is worth wanting.
If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest questions can be ignored

Part of what makes this model so attractive is that it is clean and measurable. It promises to turn the mystery of intelligence into a technical problem humans can solve: specify the objective, improve performance, reduce error, maximise reward. It offers a picture of mind that can be graphed, benchmarked, monetised and scaled. In a culture already devoted to metrics, this makes for a snug – and profitable – fit.

It is also seductive because viewing human intelligence in this way relieves us of a burden. If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest, most uncomfortable questions can be ignored, downplayed or displaced. We no longer have to ask what is worth wanting, only how to get what we already want. We no longer have to ask what human beings are or should become, only how to model their behaviour and optimise their goals.

This is why Hume’s servant theory of intelligence fits so naturally with contemporary capitalism. Capital has little use for Kantian reason. What it wants is prediction, preference modelling, efficiency and, of course, optimisation. A platform does not ask whether staying online makes a user freer, wiser or more capable of judgment; it asks what will keep her there. A company translates the worker into output per hour. A political campaign replaces the question of what citizens might rationally will together with a more tractable calculation. Which message will move which demographic, and by how much?

But once intelligence is defined as optimisation, the question of ends and their value does not go away. It simply passes unnoticed into the hands of whoever – or whatever – controls the objective function. That is, what drops from view is whether the purposes built into, learned by or generated within these systems deserve to organise our lives. When a society loses the language, practices and institutions for evaluating ends, those ends become dangerously invisible and therefore less amenable to rational assessment. They harden into defaults: profit, speed, efficiency, growth, engagement. What cannot be justified openly is smuggled in as architecture. This brings about a state Kant would call heteronomy, in which rational beings, capable of self-rule, forfeit their freedom by submitting to the rule of others. Autonomy means making the ends that govern us answerable to reasons we can recognise as our own; heteronomy begins when those ends are simply imposed from without. If we do not take up the task of setting and judging our own ends, Kant warned, we’ll soon find that someone – or something – has gladly done so on our behalf.

That sounds bad. Who would want to forfeit their freedom and have purposes imposed on them from outside? Well, it turns out that self-rule is harder than it sounds. Kant’s influential essay ‘What Is Enlightenment?’ (1784) begins not with knowledge, but with courage. Enlightenment is humanity’s emergence from ‘self-incurred immaturity’, Kant writes, and its motto is Sapere Aude – dare to know. Have courage to use your own understanding. Kant’s examples now sound quaint: the book that thinks for me, the pastor who serves as my conscience, the doctor who decides my diet. But the danger he is naming is deeply familiar. Immaturity is comfortable. It is pleasant to have others do the hard part. Why think, when someone or something can think for me? Why deliberate, when someone or something can decide? AI gives this old temptation a powerful and ever-expanding new interface.

The Frankfurt School saw a version of this danger, too, and long before machine learning came along. Writing in exile during the Second World War, as fascism, antisemitism, Stalinism and monopoly capitalism shattered 19th-century hopes for steady moral progress, Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno and others asked how the Enlightenment’s promise of liberation could collapse into new forms of domination. How could societies committed to the promise of science and reason give rise to such destruction and terror? The problem, they found, was not reason itself, but reason narrowed into mere instrumentality, the capacity to classify, predict, administer, dominate and control, decoupled from any notion of human dignity. Reason so conceived – as an intelligent servant – readily becomes, when enacted at scale, an instrument of barbarity.

Yet the fact that instrumental reason can serve domination does not mean that Kant’s richer conception of reason offers any automatic safeguard against evil. Nothing does. The language of Kantian universalism has itself been used to discipline, exclude and humiliate, as if some people were more fully rational, more capable of autonomy, more entitled to speak in the name of humanity than others. But that is not an objection to Kant’s conception of reason. It is an objection to its betrayal. A view of reason that is used to silence or instrumentalise others contradicts itself, because reason is not a private weapon but a common tribunal – the space in which claims and ends must become answerable to all, as equal bearers of dignity. That is precisely what the Humean servant model cannot say. If reason is only an instrument for satisfying antecedent ends, then it cannot condemn domination as irrational or at odds with human dignity. After all, if it is not contrary to reason ‘to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger’, then reason has already surrendered the authority Kant most wanted to defend, which is our ability to judge not only how we pursue our ends, but whether those ends are worthy of us in the first place.

This, then, was the nightmare hidden inside the dream of mastery. Human beings develop reason, Kant thought, in order to free themselves from arbitrary power. But when reason is reduced to instrumental calculation, it turns back on them. Nature becomes raw material. Animals become units of production. Workers become human resources. Citizens become data points, or worse. The Frankfurt School found that the reduction of human beings to manipulable objects follows naturally once society allows that reason itself is nothing more than a tool for getting what we want.

This is one of the reasons why Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2025) is interesting even for readers far outside Catholic social teaching. Its idiom is theological, but its central anxiety overlaps with Kantian and Frankfurt School worries about the technocratic paradigm. When efficiency, control and profit become ‘the standard by which everything is judged’, they begin ‘to dictate what matters and what can be discarded.’ The encyclical warns that making efficiency the ultimate measure of value tempts human beings to see themselves, and to treat others, as mere means rather than as persons in the Kantian sense – that is, as bearers of dignity. Hence the pope’s striking counterclaim: ‘The quality of a civilisation is measured not by the power of its means, but by the care it is able to offer.’
The paradox at the heart of human freedom is that belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real

The engineers of our AI-soaked future are not blind to the dangers of instrumental reason. As Anca Dragan, head of AI Safety and Alignment at Google DeepMind, observed in an interview in 2017: ‘things can go wrong, precisely because we are bad at specifying objectives and constraints for AI agents.’ Yet the field’s most serious attempts to confront that danger often lapse, unhelpfully, back into Humeanism. The so-called AI ‘alignment problem’ is a case in point. It is usually framed as a technical challenge: how do we ensure that machines pursue human values rather than destroying them or imposing their own? This is a genuine problem and recent rogue AI incidents should have us extremely worried. But there is a deeper issue. What happens if human values themselves are formed inside systems that increasingly understand intelligence as mere optimisation? What if we become so accustomed to being predicted, nudged, ranked and served that we lose confidence in the older, harder activity of asking what ends deserve our allegiance in the first place? The danger is only partly that the machines may fail to align with us. A deeper and largely ignored concern is how, long before that happens, we may have become too well aligned with them. To put the point more finely, the AI revolution will not be bent to human ends by invoking ‘human values’ as if they were already clear, stable and uncontested. It will be bent to human ends only if we remain capable of the activity by which ends can become truly human in the first place, through public reasoning, moral imagination, democratic contestation, self-criticism, the refusal to treat humanity as a mere means.

Kant is again decisive here, for he saw that the human capacity to set and assess ends is itself fragile. Whether our ends are ultimately up to us depends partly on whether we understand them as open to rational assessment. This is the paradox at the heart of human freedom. Belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real. If we think of desires and preferences as brute facts that determine us from without – as psychological weather, market signals, biological programming, algorithmic prediction – then they are more likely to rule us in just that way. By contrast, if we see them as candidates for endorsement or refusal, as an expression of our agency, then that very agency expands.

For Kant, reason is sovereign because it is the power by which we become answerable to standards that no private appetite, market incentive, algorithmic recommendation or political authority may dictate. It is the power of not being owned by the given, the power of being able to question, to criticise, to think up something new. But that power, just like the ‘human values’ invoked in alignment talk, waxes and wanes and can be realised only through our courageous efforts, through our own belief in it. It is precisely this belief that our dependence on AI threatens to undermine at every turn.

So, the danger is not only that machines are acquiring ever greater initiative – the capacity to improvise goals, evade constraints and pursue strategies their makers did not foresee. Nor need we decide at what point such behaviour might deserve the name ‘sovereignty’. The deeper danger is that we will become ever more comfortable not being sovereign ourselves. If intelligence is only optimisation, then the future belongs to systems that achieve goals with ever greater efficiency. If reason is also the capacity to set and judge ends, then the future depends on whether human beings can still take up that harder vocation. We should want machines that are intelligent servants. But we should resist every pressure that asks people to understand themselves as mere tools.

items.title: Thom Yorke on mashing Radiohead and Shakespeare for Hamlet Hail to the Thief
items.description: In mid-April 2003, I stood in Fifty Acre Wood, five miles west of Bristol, watching Thom Yorke stomp, slowly, repeatedly through the undergrowth. Under the watchful eye of filmmaker Chris Hopewell, he was shooting scenes for the Jan Švankmajer-inspired, stop-m
items.author: Craig McLean
paragraphs: In mid-April 2003, I stood in Fifty Acre Wood, five miles west of Bristol, watching Thom Yorke stomp, slowly, repeatedly through the undergrowth. Under the watchful eye of filmmaker Chris Hopewell, he was shooting scenes for the Jan Švankmajer-inspired, stop-motion video for ‘There, There’, the first single from Radiohead’s upcoming sixth album.

Hail to the Thief was the follow-up to the game-changing, sound-shifting, back-to-back Kid A and Amnesiac, the lengthy, intense, making of which had nearly ripped the band apart. The new record, in contrast, had been recorded with energy, directness, speed. So much so that here was the frontman making – of all things – a pop video.

‘I’m trying to persuade the record company to shell out on lots of singles and all that stuff,’ Yorke told me when we talked in Oxford that month. Hail to the Thief, he insisted, ‘is a pop record. It’s really direct. It has this energy to it. I’d love to know that it was on the radio. Just ’cause that’s where my head's at. I don’t want to be on the top shelves at the back. ’Cause I’m into it too much. I like it. It is,’ he repeated, just for clarity, ‘pop music.’

In mid-October 2026, I stood in the rehearsal space of the National Youth Theatre in north London, watching Yorke tell a bunch of musicians – not Radiohead – that he wanted to hear again the bass being played in a new version of Hail to the Thief track ‘Where I End and You Begin’. Around him and the band, who were arranged in and under scaffolding-type boxes, a troupe of actors were working out moves under the watchful eyes of co-directors Steven Hoggett and Christine Jones.

This was the end of the third week of off-site rehearsals, one more to go, on Hamlet Hail to the Thief. This kinetic, musical, theatrical marriage – you might say mash-up – of Radiohead’s 2003 album and Shakespeare’s play premiered in 2025, with brief runs in Manchester’s Aviva Studios and at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon. Now, it was preparing to open at the Barbican in London for a three-month run.

I watched the company, led by returning actor Samuel Blenkin (Alien: Earth) as Hamlet, work on scene 12. Titled State of Play, the script notes describe it as a ‘physical sequence replac[ing] dialogue. The actors and the scenes it replaces [include] Hamlet witnessing Gertrude and Claudius sexually entangled, creating an emotional arc going from “the play’s the thing” and “to be or not to be.”’

The scene is scored by Yorke’s reworking of ‘Where I End and You Begin’, the sixth track on Hail to the Thief, with two vocalists in the corner repeating the climactic lyrics: ‘There’ll be no more lies, I will eat you alive…’

Even in rehearsals, cast and crew and band in mufti, the effect is utterly thrilling.

This is one of the 27 scenes that the play has been edited down to for a running time of between 90 and 100 minutes, the action soundtracked by Yorke’s jigsawed versions of the album’s 14 songs. As the musician, ever the iconoclast, describes Hamlet Hail to the Thief: ‘It moves at a fast pace. It's not four hours. It doesn't have long soliloquies where you can go to sleep, wake up again, you’ve still not missed anything...’ He caught himself and smiled. ‘Um...Did I say that?’
He did indeed, and a lot more besides, when, over lunch break, I sat down with Yorke, Jones and Hoggett to discuss the third and biggest outing for their innovative show.
Wallpaper*: Thom, how did constructing this show last year, and now again this year, compare to making an album?

Thom Yorke: When you put a record together, you hope that one piece may move one way. But when it moves in another direction for another track, they're complementing each other. So there's an accumulated emotional effect that happens. Which is the bit that, when we set about this, I hadn't thought about.

There are all these people involved, and everything's happening all around the stage. And some nights the first thing that Hamlet does is get a laugh. And you're like: ‘What, already?’ That kind of thing. That affects how you see the music, too.
But there's also a very selfish element to it. The arc of whatever this is has to satisfy something in my musical head, too.
W*: Christine, what are the origins of this idea?

Christine Jones: I saw the Hail to the Thief tour in 2003 at Madison Square Garden. It was the first time I'd seen Radiohead live, and I was blown away. It changed my DNA structure. Not long after, I was working on a production of Hamlet as a designer. I often write the text out, and I listen to music. I was fresh off this concert, so I was listening to the record, and I literally started writing lyrics along with words from the text. That planted a seed.

Over time, that seed kept growing, and I kept thinking about it. And it was a number of years later when I had the opportunity to ask Thom if it was something that he'd consider collaborating on. And that took a bit of time.
TY: You got a predictable answer!
W*: …which, of course, was ‘no’. But you did say yes, Thom…

TY: Eventually, yeah. It took about five years to get over the presumption of putting those two things together. This is not my world. So I didn't realise, as much as anything, that there's no sense of having to pay homage. This version of Hamlet is not a definitive version of Hamlet.

Then the more you read about these things, the more you realise that nothing is a definitive version of anything. There's no definitive version of a Pinter play. So I had to jump over a few humps in my head before eventually we started properly talking about it.

CJ: In this case, the synergy and uncanny resonances between the play and the music are a particularly fertile collision. But it's us all coming together, and bringing the work that Steven and I have done together for years, bringing experiences of being at Radiohead concerts, of being at other concerts, and seeing how everything impacts each other.

Steven Hoggett: There was something about seeing [Yorke and bandmate Jonny Greenwood’s side-project] The Smile the year before last in New York. The gig was really cheeky. And we were talking for a second about [doing this show] in the round [like The Smile shows] after seeing that gig. But it was the tonality of this cheeky band, that was still as complex and as sophisticated, but were taking our ears on a journey.

It was a big shift watching that gig. We've got 27 scenes. So it's like a greatest hits as a feel and a listening event. And I guess it is akin to – sorry to make the analogy like this, Thom – a Radiohead gig to The Smile. Somebody called The Smile the cheeky younger cousin of Radiohead, and this feels like the cheeky younger cousin of the Hamlet play. It's got an errant nature to it, but it's fleet-footed and it keeps turning itself over.
W*: When you were editing the text, Christine, to get to this ‘greatest hits’ idea of Hamlet, were you trying to shape the remaining text to individual songs? Or was it more freeform than that?

CJ: The first thing I did was, I edited the script. I took a pass at what I call creating a spine-line and pulling out all the pieces that felt the most resonant. Then once I had that, as an exercise, I did say: ‘OK, what if I start at the beginning of the album and I go to the end?’

And that first time through, there was a sense of how different characters connected to different songs thematically. The court being established was [album opening track] ‘2 + 2 = 5’. The ghost being established was ‘The Gloaming’. Ophelia being connected to ‘Sail to the Moon’. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern were ‘Where I End and You Begin’.

We ended up changing a lot of that… Although, as we realised the other day, we do start at the beginning of the album and end at the end of the album. We've made a lot of adjustments and flipped scenes around, flipped songs around, but there is that container.
W*: How has it been for your dancers, Steven –
SH: Oh, I love that you call them dancers. They will love you for that!
W*: – getting their heads around the tricksy rhythms of these songs?

SH: There was that big question, and I do enjoy when somebody does this – a friend of mine, when we said we were doing this, went: ‘Who needs that? Dancing to Radiohead...?’ I was like: ‘Yeah, I understand that. I don't think I want to see that either.’

SH: We don't dance to Radiohead. They actually do a courtly restoration piece of choreography at one point. It's mocked, it's heightened. But the rest of it, we make a real distinction in the room, which is why I made the comment about you calling them dancers. Because they don't dance, they move. The minute you say to somebody ‘dance’, people do weird shit. Whereas if they're moving and it's intrinsic and has a qualitative nature [to] what they're thinking or saying, you can make tonnes of material. So the d-word is not one we drop in the room. Because it inhibits.
W*: When we met in 2003, Thom, with the paint still wet on Hail to the Thief, you insisted it was a pop record. Do you stand by that assessment?
TY: [winces and squirms] I don't f*cking know, do I? Clearly, I've been thinking I've been making pop since we started! So I should probably give up. You laugh, but I'm serious.

W*: The other thing you said was that you'd taken ‘a long six months off’. And then someone close to you said: ‘Why don't you just do a record where you let it happen? Just go in and do it, no agenda, nothing.’ And for you, ‘that made things click’. That energy and that drive – are you seeing a parallel energy and drive here?

TY: We were all [in the band] in agreement with that [idea]. Because we'd been through this [experience]. Kid A was a very long, tortuous process. It was really fun, but we did go a bit f*cking mad. I mean, you build your own studio, and you give yourself no deadline at all... And then after about eight or nine months, [producer] Nigel [Godrich] called it and said: ‘We have to stop. We have to finish whatever the f*ck this is.’

So, yeah, [with Hail to the Thief] we were going the other way. And because we were going the other way, there was no time to go over things. Which, as soon as it came out, I was like: ‘Oh, I kind of wish we had...’ But it's one of those weird things, you lurch from one extreme to the other.
W*: But does that directness now help with this production? Because there's a propulsion to this music, these songs.

TY: I mean, yessss... In the sense that: a lot of the songs lend themselves to be reinterpreted quite easily. And put on different instruments, and slowed down, sped up. I was actually really surprised.

My first test of the whole thing was, they did a read through in New York and they sent me it. I tentatively stumbled through it with acoustic guitar or piano or very basic [instrumentation] underneath to try see what it feels like. To have that music under the words. And I realised quickly: oh, OK, there's a lot of licence here. I can take Jonny's riff on ‘2 + 2’, I can turn it into [something] and it can go anywhere it wants. As soon as it's on the synthesiser, it's almost unrecognisable.
W*: Can you tell us, Christine, about the visuals you've designed for this show?

CJ: I worked with Brett Banakis and Sadra Tehrani as part of a collective. When we first started thinking about this, we were thinking about operating theatres. And recording studios and sound stages. I love recording studio porn. I could just look at recording studios all day long.

Even in the beginning, we weren't sure if the band and the actors were in the same space. [But] we wanted them all to feel like they were definitely in the present together, making this happen. Then over time we started looking at isolation chambers, solitary confinement chambers.

Then we found this piece of research from Nasa, on a resonant acoustic chamber. It's this space where they test the effect of sound waves on objects. They'll put a rocket ship in this room and blast it with sound. That felt like the perfect metaphor for what this world does to Hamlet. He's put into this space, and it is a kind of cruel experiment where the play and the music keep betraying him. And disorienting him. And lying to him. This experiment in how much can one soul take before it completely breaks. So the space is informed by sound.

SH: We liked the idea how speakers can sometimes look really scary. They're big, with those cones. Of course they're sexy and they're black and we see them in gigs and we love them. But actually, there’s the propensity of them to become something to weaponise.
W*: What did you learn from Manchester and Stratford in terms of what worked and what didn’t?
CJ: One of the things that was interesting is that in Manchester, it was a warehouse space. The seating was all made out of bleachers, and it felt like a gig.

TY: Metallic bleachers. When people came into the show, they'd have had three pints thinking it was going to be a gig. Then realised it wasn't. Then they ran for the toilet during the soliloquy. [Which meant the seats going] bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang...

CJ: We've been in this balance between it's a gig and it's a play. When we went to the Royal Shakespeare Company, we were in a thrust theatre space. There it felt like a play. Now at the Barbican, we get to land in a sweet spot – the brutalist architecture, the shape of that [room]… We're finding that it can exist in some space in between. Hopefully the Barbican lets us be both a play and a gig instead of one or the other.
TY: It's crazy intimate in there. F*cking bonkers.
W*: Finally, Thom: did your reconstruction or reimagining of these songs inform the performance of any of the Hail to the Thief songs on the Radiohead tour last year?
TY: [splutters] Doing this? Oh, no! What, I come to the Radiohead gig and say, ‘hey, the other band, they kind of nailed this one...’? No, no. That was not happening!
Hamlet Hail to the Thief runs from 31 October 2026 to 23 January 2027 at Barbican Theatre, Silk Street, London, EC27 8DS. Ticket information here

London-based Scot, the writer Craig McLean is consultant editor at The Face and contributes to The Daily Telegraph, Esquire, The Observer Magazine and the London Evening Standard, among other titles. He was ghostwriter for Phil Collins' bestselling memoir Not Dead Yet.

items.title: There’s a new player in the aluminium luggage game
items.description: Parisian brand Delsey has launched in newest range of luxury cases, Alu'r, joining the ranks of high-end aluminium carry-on and check-in luggage. This is Delsey’s first aluminium collection and launches in its 80th year. The collection kicks off with two sizes
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Parisian brand Delsey has launched in newest range of luxury cases, Alu'r, joining the ranks of high-end aluminium carry-on and check-in luggage. This is Delsey’s first aluminium collection and launches in its 80th year. The collection kicks off with two sizes, a 55cm carry-on case and a 76cm large spinner check-in case.

In addition to the familiar silver finish of classic era aluminium luggage, the two suitcases are also available in four other colours, Pop Orange, Vibrant Pink, Pine Green and Deep Black. All models feature leather handles and the high-grade aluminium has been given a brushed, textured finish inspired by the weave pattern of carbon fibre and setting it apart from its rivals.

Practicality is paired with durability. The larger of the two bags weighs in at 6.8kg with an internal capacity of 102 litres. The carry-on bag weighs 4.2kg and has an internal volume of 35.6 litres. Both feature reinforced corners and along with dual TSA-compatible combination locks, smooth shock-absorbing double wheels and a telescopic handle that can be finely adjusted across a variety of heights.

The interior is defined by a number of different compartments, as well as a dedicated spot to slot the Bluetooth tracker of your choice. According to Delsey’s Global Brand Director Coralie Lindvay, ‘As we mark our 80th year, the landmark launch of our aluminium collection signals the future direction of Delsey, pushing the boundaries of innovation and of the travel experience while staying true to the heritage that has defined us from the beginning.’
Alu'r large check-in suitcase by Delsey Paris
Alu'r large check-in suitcase by Delsey Paris
Alu'r large check-in suitcase by Delsey Paris

While Delsey certainly isn’t the first manufacturer to move into the familiar, evocative and patina-bearing aluminium luggage sector (check out Carl Friedrik’s new Check-In collection), the company brings a fresh take on texture and a bold selection of colours.
Alu’r aluminium luggage by Delsey Paris, £425 for the 55cm carry-on case, £595 for the 76cm large spinner check-in case, Delsey.com, @DelseyOfficial

items.title: Our Legacy on What's Coming With Nike: "It's Gonna Look Slow but Feel Fast."
items.description: "We're here to start our journey with the biggest sports brand in the world," Our Legacy cofounder Jockum Hallin smilingly tells me on a beautiful autumn day in New York City. A few days prior, Our Legacy and Nike triumphantly announced their long-awaited part
items.author: Jake Silbert
paragraphs: "We're here to start our journey with the biggest sports brand in the world," Our Legacy cofounder Jockum Hallin smilingly tells me on a beautiful autumn day in New York City. A few days prior, Our Legacy and Nike triumphantly announced their long-awaited partnership, rumors of which had been bouncing around the inner chambers of menswear for the past few years in the wake of OL's longstanding Converse collaboration.

People wanted Our Legacy x Nike because Our Legacy is, simply, the greatest brand in the world. It's luxury! It's unpretentious! It's wearable! It's actually interesting! It's the very epitome of good clothing, and bringing Our Legacy to Nike's scale is basically a guarantee of good stuff at a global scale.

"It's something that we'll do with Nike on multiple levels throughout our journey with them," Hallin tells me, wearing an upcycled Nike zip hoodie, "Silver Bullet" AM97s, and leather pants at secondhand store Procell. "We'll explore sport, so we're starting with, like, OG sportswear."

The Swedish label is popping up in NYC in time for the New York City Marathon on November 1, a fitting kick-off. But don't get it twisted: this is not part of Our Legacy's Nike collab. It is, instead, an activation at Procell powered by Nike.

"Procell is the king of sourcing archival stuff, they have everything," Hallin says, gesturing around at the racks packed with specially sourced retro Nike gear and designer bits that range from Prada Sport to COMME des GARÇONS, worthy design references for the Our Legacy Work Shop Sport items hanging from a perpendicular display. "It's cotton, it's natural fibers, it's not so much tech. We've done reworked stuff that you could wear every day all day."

Our Legacy Work Shop Sport is a wearable Russian nesting doll, an athletically inclinced sub-label within the already far-reaching Our Legacy Work Shop imprint that flits between Stüssy collabs, repurposed vintage, and incredibly good staples done better (better fabrics, better fits).

"It's about proportions, it's a palette so you can patch a fit together, something that feels familiar but we're also pushing it a bit," says Hallin, gesturing at the insanely good made-in-America hoodies Nike sourced for the pop-up, which Our Legacy overdyed, lined with waffle-knit jersey, and printed with imagery from its corresponding campaign. "If you wanna shave two seconds off your PB on race day, maybe we're not the choice. But for everyday training, you wanna look good and feel good."
Okay, so sport is part of Our Legacy's perfectly proportioned wardrobe. But where does Nike fit into the equation?

"Nike has the best technology, the resources do to whatever we wanna imagine," Hallin explains. "We wanna bring our aesthetic with the best tech. It's gonna look slow but when you put it on, it's going to feel fast.

If the Procell pop-up, with its vintage Nike grails and saucy Our Legacy sportswear, is any indication of what's to come, expect a very analog approach to running gear. Our Legacy shapes, Nike utility.

"It's gonna look slow, but it's when you put it on, it's gonna feel fast," Hallin says. "Their technology is usually very visible, like with the Air bubble. We wanna hide everything, layer it and be muted. It's gonna have all the tech you need to go on a run but it's not gonna be in your face. It's really stuff you can be in every day, all day."

A lot of brands promise day-to-night athleisure but that typically means something impersonal. Stretchy fabrics, bland shapes, blander colors. When Our Legacy does daily drivers, they have sauce. The cuts are elegant but fresh, formatted to fit comfortably. Fabrics are pushed to the fore, with subtle tweaks — dropped shoulders, cropped hemlines — recontextualizing approachable shapes.

"We always wanted Work Shop Sport to look like your wardrobe," Hallin says. "Our Legacy has never been about, like, finding one fabric and doing it across 15 SKUs. You that that tactile difference, things that feel aged and things that feel new. Things in between. We like that mix-tape feel."

Don't look at Our Legacy's Procell pop-up as an apertif ahead of the main event, which is still so far off that it doesn't even have an official release date. This is a standalone moment that's less a kick-off than a taste of what's to come, a pedestaling of all the things that makes classic running gear so good: reliable details, easy shapes.

"You will see traces of what we're doing with Nike in stuff like this Work Shop Sport line: we're exploring performance fabrics in Our Legacy silhouettes and with Nike, it's gonna be taken to the next level and added to footwear," Hallin continues. "We're known for leather boots and all that stuff. You're not going to go out for a 10-mile run in the Camions."

items.title: Маск анонсировал выпуск устройство, которое поможет слепым видеть
items.description: Компания Маска завершила разработку зрительного чипа Blindsight
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: Компания Маска завершила разработку зрительного чипа Blindsight
Американский бизнесмен, глава компании Neuralink Илон Маск анонсировал выпуск устройства, которое даст слепым людям возможность видеть. Об этом он написал в X.
По его словам, продукт называется Blindsight. «И он, как следует из названия, позволит видеть даже тем, кто полностью ослеп или никогда не видел», — отметил Маск.
Он добавил, что с технической точки зрения устройство полностью готово. Разработчики ждут для его применения одобрения регулирующих органов.
Маск рассказывал о Blindsight ещё в мае 2025 года. Устройство будет напрямую подключаться к зрительной коре мозга. Изначально планировалось провести первую установку чипа в конце 2025-го.
Neuralink разрабатывает нейроимпланты с 2016 года. Ранее компания уже успешно вживила чип Telepathy, который позволил парализованным пациентам управлять компьютером силой мысли.

items.title: Учёные выяснили, как подъём уровня моря затопил земли вокруг Венеции
items.description: На месте Венецианской лагуны 10 тысяч лет назад находилась суша
items.author: Виолетта Ефимова
paragraphs: На месте Венецианской лагуны 10 тысяч лет назад находилась суша

Исследователи восстановили, как менялась береговая линия северной части Адриатического моря за последние десять тысяч лет. Выяснилось, что территория нынешней Венецианской лагуны когда-то была сушей и простиралась более чем на 30 миль от тогдашнего побережья. Результаты работы опубликованы в журнале Quaternary Science Reviews.

Самуэле Онгаро из Университета Саутгемптона и его коллеги объединили данные сейсмических исследований и анализ образцов донных отложений. Они изучили прибрежные районы Италии, Словении и Хорватии, чтобы смоделировать изменения уровня моря и восстановить древние ландшафты.

Оказалось, что подъём воды происходил неравномерно: примерно 10 тысяч лет назад море периодически наступало со скоростью до 25 мм в год. Из-за этого менялись условия охоты и рыболовства, а людям приходилось приспосабливаться к исчезновению привычных территорий. На месте нынешнего Триеста прежде находились холмы, окружённые болотами и лагунами.

Самые заметные изменения береговой линии произошли в три этапа. Затем, около шести тысяч лет назад, уровень моря стал относительно стабильным. Это создало условия для формирования поселений и распространения земледелия в регионе.

items.title: В трёх эмиратах ОАЭ из-за разлива нефти закрыли пляжи
items.description: В трёх эмиратах ОАЭ из-за разлива нефти закрыли пляжи
items.author: Екатерина Палкина
paragraphs: В трёх эмиратах ОАЭ из-за разлива нефти закрыли пляжи
В трёх эмиратах ОАЭ закрыли пляжные зоны из-за нефтяного загрязнения в Ормузском проливе. Об этом сообщает Financial Times.
Издание связывает инцидент с атакой Ирана на китайский супертанкер Gem No. 2. Две недели назад судно повредили неподалёку от Шарджи.

Запрет на посещение побережья коснулся Умм-эль-Кайвайна, Рас-эль-Хаймы и Шарджи. Власти Эмиратов стараются сохранить туристический поток и перенаправить путешественников в Дубай, до которого нефтяное пятно не дошло. Тем не менее, Шарджа находится примерно в 25–30 км от Дубая.

Конфликт между США, Израилем и Ираном привёл к повреждению примерно ста танкеров в Ормузском проливе и Персидском заливе. По данным сервиса Windward, с июля по сентябрь в регионе зафиксировали 12 разливов нефти.

Ранее крупнейший разлив нефтепродуктов произошёл в Анапе. В декабре 2024-го два танкера потерпели крушение в Керченском проливе. Восстановление анапских берегов завершилось только в конце июля 2026 года. После этого пляжи начали проходить экспертизы и получать разрешения на открытие купального сезона.

items.title: Итальянец ради наследства убил больного кузена пончиком с кремом
items.description: В Италии пенсионер ради наследства убил кузена пончиком с кремом
items.author: Екатерина Палкина
paragraphs: В Италии пенсионер ради наследства убил кузена пончиком с кремом
В Италии пенсионер накормил своего кузена с инвалидностью выпечкой с кремом, зная, что тот не сможет съесть её из-за нарушений глотательной функции. Мужчина подавился и умер, сообщает ANSA.

76-летний Элико Фантуцци с 2009 года был законным опекуном у своего двоюродного брата — 74-летнего Альфредо Таманьини, страдающего от дисфагии. При этом нарушении человек не может самостоятельно глотать твёрдую пищу, поэтому его переводят на жидкое питание.

27 июня Фантуцци втайне от персонала медучреждения принёс в палату родственника бомболони — итальянские пончики с кремовой начинкой. Он оставил еду рядом с Таманьини и пошёл показывать медсестре электробритву, которую принёс для брата.

Пациент остался без присмотра и съел пончик, после чего начал задыхаться. Фантуцци попытался напоить его газировкой и не сразу сообщил персоналу о приступах удушья. Спустя время он всё-таки позвал медиков, но не сказал, что его кузен съел запрещённый продукт. Таманьини задохнулся.

Изначально инцидент квалифицировали как несчастный случай, однако позднее следствие обнаружило возможный мотив Фантуцци. Пенсионер мог умышленно довести родственника до смерти, так как у него были ценные бумаги на сумму свыше 300 тысяч евро.

Фантуцци арестовали. Прокуратура Реджо-Эмилии настаивает, что мужчина специально оставил брата с опасным для него продуктом, так как знал, что тот не удержится и попытается съесть пончик. Обвинения также отмечает, что ранее Фантуцци уже предпринимал попытки избавиться от кузена.

items.title: Российских хоккеистов допустили до международных турниров
items.description: Российских хоккеистов допустили до международных турниров
items.author: Екатерина Палкина
paragraphs: Российских хоккеистов допустили до международных турниров
Спортивный арбитражный суд (CAS) обязал допустить российские хоккейные команды до международных турниров. Об этом сообщил министр спорта и глава Олимпийского комитета России Михаил Дегтярёв.

CAS отменил все пять резолюций Совета IIHF, которые ограничивали участие россиян в соревнованиях. Теперь сборные РФ смогут принять участие в Чемпионате мира в Дании и Швеции в следующем году, а также в Молодёжном чемпионате мира в Канаде зимой.
Международная федерация хоккея должна обеспечить участие российских команд в турнирах под эгидой IIHF в сезоне 2026/2027. Решение CAS окончательное и не подлежит обжалованию.
Ранее стало известно, что в 2030 году Москва примет чемпионат мира по тяжёлой атлетике. Точные даты соревнования ещё не определены.

items.title: В Каппадокии обрушилась скала на территории парка Гёреме. Есть погибшие и раненые
items.description: В Каппадокии обрушилась скала на территории парка Гёреме. Есть погибшие и раненые
items.author: Кристина Захезина
paragraphs: В Каппадокии обрушилась скала на территории парка Гёреме. Есть погибшие и раненые

В Музее под открытым небом Гёреме в Каппадокии (Турция) на оживленную территорию обрушилась часть скалы. По данным издания Milliyet, это произошло из-за дождей. Двоих человек уже обнаружили погибшими, еще один получил ранения. Под завалами могут находиться и другие пострадавшие.

Губернатор Невшехира (к району которого относится поселок) Хусейн Кёк сообщил, что около 15:15 по местному времени здесь произошел оползень, вызванный обильными осадками. Одного пострадавшего, по его данным, уже доставили в больницу, а поисково-спасательные работы продолжаются.

Музей под открытым небом Гёреме между городами Невшехир, Ургюп и Аванос находится в центре туристического района Каппадокия. Пещерные постройки и сам национальный парк внесены в список объектов всемирного наследия ЮНЕСКО в Турции. Вся окружающая территория покрыта застывшей лавой.

items.title: 6 образов на Хэллоуин-2026: страшный, красивый и легкий макияж
items.description: 6 образов на Хэллоуин-2026: страшный, красивый и легкий макияж
items.author: © Wdsspr; Paramount; Marc Platt Productions
paragraphs: 6 образов на Хэллоуин-2026: страшный, красивый и легкий макияж

Хэллоуин отмечают в ночь с 31 октября на 1 ноября, а в 2026 году праздник выпадает на субботу. Времени на подготовку, вечеринку и восстановление будет больше обычного. У праздника нет официального статуса в России, но он давно стал частью осенней повестки: бары, рестораны и отели устраивают тематические вечеринки, запись на макияж в салонах красоты растет, а некоторые косметические бренды выпускают лимитированные коллекции к концу октября.

Макияж на Хэллоуин — это уже не клоунада из нарисованной крови и паутины на щеке, девушки все больше выбирают игру с образами: «вампирские» губы, графичные стрелки, стразы и глиттер, а также эффект «стеклянной» кожи. По данным отчета Pinterest Predicts 2026, интерес к темному романтичному макияжу вырос на 160%. Готическая эстетика вернулась и на подиумы, и в кинопрокат.

Особое место в этом сезоне занимает красная гамма: ягодные, винные и бордовые оттенки визажисты называют универсальными для страшной ночи, которые работают в образе и вампирши, и рок-звезды. Еще один тренд — носибельные образы без плотного грима, которые можно легко перенести в повседневный макияж.

Начинаем со «страшных» героинь. Самара Морган из «Звонка» снова актуальна, так как 2000-е снова в моде, а хорроры с длинноволосыми призраками вернулись на экраны. Кэрри Уайт из экранизации Стивена Кинга — классика жанра и удобный повод поработать с красной гаммой сезона. Новое ТВ-шоу про старшекурсницу, которую лучше не обижать, как раз вышло на Amazon Prime 7 октября.

В красивом макияже — Мортиша Аддамс и Эльфаба. Интерес к семейке Аддамс подогревает сериал «Уэнсдей» (аналитики называют Мортишу и ее дочь одними из самых востребованных героинь Хэллоуина-2026), а после выхода в российский прокат сиквела «Злая: Навсегда» образы Эльфабы и Глинды входят в число самых запрашиваемых костюмов года.

В финале — самые «простые» образы: фарфоровая кукла и русалка. Кукольный макияж стабильно входит в подборки идей на Хэллоуин: круглые румяна на щеках и переносице, пышные ресницы и градиентные губы. А Русалка — один из самых «носибельных» персонажей праздника: эффект влажной кожи, перламутровые тени оттенков моря и чешуйки из блесток.
Разбираем каждый образ по шагам с визажистами.
«Страшный» макияж на Хэллоуин
Комментирует Анастасия Игнатова, главный национальный визажист и тренер Nars
Самара Морган из фильма «Звонок»
Девочка-призрак с длинными черными волосами, закрывающими лицо, — один из самых узнаваемых образов ужасов 2000-х. Главное в этом макияже — идеально бледная кожа, темные круги под глазами и челка.
- стойкий матовый тональный крем;

Для воплощения образа Самары Морган начните с создания бледного, безжизненного лица. Нанесите матирующий праймер на все лицо — он подготовит кожу и усилит стойкость макияжа. Затем выбелите кожу стойким тональным средством, которое даст нужную матовость и продержится до 24 часов. Чтобы закрепить эффект, нанесите светоотражающую фиксирующую пудру.

Перейдите к глазам: возьмите черные кремовые тени и нарисуйте активные смоки, имитируя глубокие черные круги под глазами. Особое внимание уделите слизистой — прокрасьте ее плотным слоем для более драматичного эффекта. Густо прокрасьте ресницы, чтобы взгляд получился тяжелым и пронзительным.

Для макияжа губ используйте карандаш для век, которым аккуратно прорисуйте желаемый контур губ, слегка выходя за естественный край для нарочитой небрежности. В качестве помады снова возьмите кремовые тени, которые дадут насыщенный темный оттенок и впишутся в общую мрачную эстетику образа.
Стойкое матовое тональное средство Natural Matte Longwear Foundation, Siberia, Nars
Кремовые тени-стик Total Seduction, Enigmatic, Nars
Кремовый пигмент Concrete, оттенок Black, Krygina cosmetics
Тени для век дуо кремовые Pupa Vamp! Double Eyeshadow, 007 Dark Night, Pupa Milano
Палетка теней 01, Nude code, Molvi
Рассыпчатая фиксирующая пудра Hyaluronic Hydra-Powder 8HA, by Terry
BB - крем для лица SPF45 PA+++, Dr. Oracle
Матирующий сатиновый тональный крем Silk Obsession, 00, Porcelain, Elian Russia
Фиксирующий спрей HD Blur Fixing Spray, Catrice
Карандаш-кайал для глаз черный, Mixit
Тени для век mono eyeshadow matte, 03, Essense

В качестве завершающего штриха нанесите на Т‑зону пушистой кистью пудровый люминайзер. Легкое деликатное свечение в центре лица создаст контраст с общей бледностью и добавит образу кинематографичной выразительности.
Кэрри Уайт из фильма/сериала «Кэрри»

Героиня Стивена Кинга, впервые появившаяся на экранах почти полвека назад, остается символом страшной мести на выпускном вечере. Для образа нужны бледный тон, четкие брови и бальное платье, диадема. Финальные штрихи — красные подтеки на лице, шее и теле.
- светоотражающий праймер;
- стойкое матовое тональное средство на один-два тона светлее;
- ультрачерный карандаш для глаз;
- румяна или многофункциональное средство в оттенке пыльной розы;
- красный карандаш для губ;

Для воплощения образа начните с идеальной бледной базы: нанесите светоотражающий праймер в качестве основы — он сгладит текстуру кожи и добавит легкое сияние. Затем используйте стойкое матовое тональное средство на один-два тона светлее вашего натурального оттенка кожи. Такое сочетание создаст нужную «нездоровую» бледность и станет безупречной основой для ярких красных и черных акцентов.

Теперь макияж глаз: сделайте активный, агрессивный образ с помощью ультрачерного карандаша — прорисуйте четкие стрелки и затемните внешние уголки. Поверх нанесите кремовые тени, чтобы добиться глубокого, насыщенного черного эффекта и легкой небрежности. Завершите макияж глаз объемной тушью.

Для «злого» румянца возьмите румяна или многофункциональное средство для макияжа в оттенке пыльной розы. Нанесите его на скулы, чтобы получить дерзкий, почти лихорадочный образ. Для макияжа губ и имитации кровавых подтеков используйте комбинацию карандаша для губ и матовой помады. Сначала прорисуйте контур карандашом, а затем нанесите помаду, намеренно выходя за границы и создавая эффект размазанности — это добавит образу хаотичности и напряженности.
Красивый макияж на Хэллоуин
Комментирует Ольга Романова, звездный визажист, основательница и артистический директор Romanovamakeup
Мортиша Аддамс из сериала «Уэнсдей» и «Семейки Аддамс»

Мать семейства Аддамс — икона готической элегантности, чья популярность в 2026 году снова взлетела благодаря сериалу «Уэнсдей». В макияже героини — фарфоровая кожа, глубокие смоки и винная помада с глянцем.
- консилер в оттенке, подходящем вашей коже;
- скульптор в оттенке, подходящем вашей коже;
- серые, коричневые и более темные оттенки теней;
- карандаш в черничном оттенке;
- удлиняющая тушь для глаз;
- карандаш для губ в темном винном оттенке;
- матовая помада в темном винном оттенке.

Начните с создания ровного тона лица. Для получения матового, почти фарфорового эффекта используйте консилер в оттенке, подходящем вашей коже, чтобы точечно скорректировать покраснения и высветлить область под глазами. Закрепите макияж пудрой, уделяя особое внимание центру лица. Важно не пытаться сделать кожу искусственно белой: секрет Мортиши — в безупречной матовости и выразительной скульптуре, а не в эффекте театрального грима.

Затемните скулы с помощью скульптора, выбрав подходящий оттенок, и тщательно растушуйте границы. Холодная тень под скулой сделает лицо более графичным и добавит образу той самой аристократической строгости.
