Для глаз подойдут серые, коричневые и более темные оттенки теней, чтобы создать дымчатую растушевку с акцентом на внешние уголки глаз. Дополните ее карандашом в черничном оттенке: он поможет усилить глубину вдоль ресничного края и подчеркнуть контур. Завершите макияж глаз черной тушью.
Брови сделайте четкими и выразительными с помощью карандаша. Не нужно рисовать новую форму поверх естественной: достаточно аккуратно заполнить пробелы и подчеркнуть изгиб.

Финальный акцент — губы. Карандаш поможет обозначить контур, а матовая помада добавит насыщенный красный акцент. Если хочется более темного винного настроения, смешайте оттенок с подходящим темным карандашом для губ и растушуйте цвет к центру. Для глянцевого финиша нанесите немного блеска.
Результат — не костюмная маска, а эффектный вечерний макияж с характером: матовая кожа, глубокий взгляд и губы, которые не нуждаются в дополнительных украшениях.
Эльфаба из фильма «Злая: Навсегда»

Эльфаба — зеленокожая ведьма из мюзикла Wicked, чья история продолжилась в фильме «Злая: Навсегда», вышедшем в российский прокат в ноябре 2025 года. Интерес к ее образу не спадает. Макияж героини — изумрудный тон лица, графичные брови, темные смоки и длинные волосы под остроконечной шляпой.
- зеленая краска для грима (по желанию);
- палетка теней с изумрудными и графитовыми оттенками;
- черная подводка и кайал для глаз;
- карандаш и гель для бровей;
- накладные ресницы (по желанию);
- карандаш для губ в темном оттенке;
- помада в темном и красном оттенках.

Если Мортиша — это готическая классика, то Эльфаба — ее фантастическая, смелая и совершенно непредсказуемая родственница. Здесь главное — решить, насколько буквально вы хотите воплотить образ. Для полноценного перевоплощения понадобится специальный зеленый грим, предназначенный для лица. А вот глаза, брови, скульптуру и губы вполне можно выполнить обычными средствами.

Если вы выбираете версию с зеленым лицом, сначала нанесите специальный грим тонкими слоями и дождитесь его фиксации. После этого можно переходить к макияжу глаз. Для дымчатого эффекта используйте темные оттенки теней и карандаш. С его помощью подчеркните линию ресниц, чтобы усилить глубину взгляда. Нанесите его вдоль верхних ресниц, растушуйте к внешнему уголку и добавьте немного теней на нижнее веко. Брови должны выглядеть графично и выразительно. Карандаш позволит заполнить пробелы и подчеркнуть форму. Не бойтесь четкого изгиба: на фоне зеленой кожи он добавит образу драматичности.
Зафиксируйте результат при помощи туши для бровей. Для ресниц используйте черную тушь, сделав акцент на внешние уголки. Если хочется усилить театральный эффект, дополните макияж накладными ресницами.

Губы можно оставить темными, но контур должен быть очень четким (немного выходящим за границы). Для более мрачного результата нанесите красный оттенок тонким слоем и затемните контур подходящим карандашом.

Если же вы предпочитаете современную интерпретацию Эльфабы без зеленого грима, сделайте акцент на изумрудных и графитовых тенях, оставив кожу естественного оттенка.

Завершат образ длинные косы или темный парик и остроконечная шляпа. И помните: выразительность Эльфабы строится не только на цвете, но и на контрастах, поэтому не стоит перегружать все зоны лица одновременно.
Комментирует Ольга Комракова, международный визажист Clarins в России

Фарфоровая кукла — образ из разряда «легко и красиво». Здесь бал правят ровный фарфоровый тон, круглые румяна на щеках и переносице, пышные ресницы и пухлые губы. Все средства найдутся в обычной косметичке, а образ легко усилить веснушками и бантами в волосах.
- устойчивый тональный крем с матовым эффектом;
- черный карандаш для губ;
- светло-коричневый карандаш для бровей;
- матовая помада для губ в оттенке пепельной розы.

Для создания фарфорового тона кожи я рекомендую использовать устойчивый тональный крем с матовым эффектом. Чтобы утрировать милые припухлости под глазами, на самую выпуклую часть нижнего века (прямо под ресницами) нанесите светлые тени для век. Чуть ниже этой припухлости проведите тонкую линию светло-коричневым карандашом для бровей, создавая иллюзию естественной тени. Слегка растушуйте линии.

Для повторения кукольного эффекта на ресницах я советую выбрать объемную тушь для ресниц. Наносите ее в несколько слоев, работая кончиком кисти, — так проще слепить ресницы в акцентные пучки.

Губы и скулы можно подчеркнуть одной текстурой, например, можно воспользоваться помадой с матовым эффектом в оттенке пепельной розы. Центр губ можно дополнительно утрировать черным карандашом. Нанесите его с грифеля пальцем похлопывающими движениями.

Русалка — это эффект влажной кожи, перламутровые тени в оттенках моря и чешуйки из блесток. Основной макияж собирается из обычной косметички, а сложность добавляют детали и аксессуары, от заколок-ракушек до жемчужин, наклеенных на скулах.
- база под макияж, придающая сияние коже;
- тональный крем с сияющим эффектом;
- тени для век в оттенке шампанского;
- палетка теней в розовых оттенках;
- черный/темно-синий карандаш кайял для глаз;
- карандаш для бровей в холодном оттенке;
- блеск для губ в розовом оттенке;
- трафарет с чешуей (по желанию).

Чтобы создать эффект влажной кожи, нанесите на лицо, шею и область декольте базу под макияж, придающую сияние. Дополните ее тональным кремом с таким же эффектом. Вместо пудры можно завершить макияж тенями для век в оттенке шампанского.

Макияж глаз в тенденции Siren Eyes акцентирует миндалевидный разрез глаз и приподнимает скулы. Очертите форму черным или темно-синим карандашом, стараясь вытягивать внешние углы глаз горизонтально. На веки нанесите те же тени, просто более насыщенно. Для этого можно распылить на кисть для теней фиксатор для макияжа.
Губы оттените холодным светлым оттенком карандаша для бровей и дополните розовым блеском для губ.

items.title: New Rules from Corporate for Ghosts
items.description: Your shift begins when a human sees you, not when you arrive in their home.
items.author: Brian Frazer
paragraphs: Your shift begins when a human sees you, not when you arrive in their home.
When you scare somebody, you can no longer say, “Boo.” Our trademark for that expired. Instead, try “Woo-hoo!” or “Yowza!”
No more groaning. It makes you seem old.
All horrifying sounds must be executed in the correct order. From now on, it’s creaky floors then slamming doors.
Henceforth, you will need a vaccine passport to go between earth and the netherworld.
Sheeted ghosts, please keep the thread count under two hundred. Our budget is tight this year.
After walking through a closet door to frighten a person, please refrain from criticizing their wardrobe.
No up-close magic. We’ve been getting way too many complaints.
If you are contacted by a medium, you need to enter the encounter in the Google Doc.
Promotions will no longer be contingent on seniority, and will now be allocated on a “how much did you scare the shit out of people” basis.
No more selling ghost merch. No Hamlet doublets, no Patrick Swayze ceramics, no Ghost of Christmas Past bike chains. We’ve realized that it dilutes our brand.
If you are exorcised, you will receive only forty per cent of your annual salary.
No selfies with the person you’re trying to frighten the bejesus out of.
Sick days on Halloween will no longer be permitted. Sorry, but that’s our peak scary time, so suck it up and “be sick” in November.
No more aftershave or perfume. It seriously minimizes the element of surprise.
Vaping pens will no longer be reimbursed on your expense accounts.
No more telecommuting. The haunting-via-Zoom experiment was a dud.
Failure to adhere to new mandates will result in a trip to H.R. And it’s scary up there.

items.title: Christa Pike’s Execution Doctor Speaks
items.description: Dr. Mark Fowler knew something was wrong after 45 minutes passed without word from the warden. In most cases, executions take no more than ten minutes. When he was summoned from his waiting room to the chamber next door, he saw 50-year-old Christa Pike, who’d
items.author: Rachel Corbett
paragraphs: Dr. Mark Fowler knew something was wrong after 45 minutes passed without word from the warden. In most cases, executions take no more than ten minutes. When he was summoned from his waiting room to the chamber next door, he saw 50-year-old Christa Pike, who’d received two lethal doses of pentobarbital that night, strapped to a gurney, gasping for air. “She’s not dead,” Fowler recalls the warden saying. “I thought, Well, in human beings there’s a spectrum of responses to medications and we’ll give it a few more minutes,” he says. Another half-hour passed. Fowler worried she might survive with irreversible brain damage. “She’s going to be in a permanent vegetative state with a quarter-million dollars in medical expenses.” He came back in and diagnosed her as comatose. The deputy commissioner ordered the execution to stop. Now, instead of taking part in Pike’s death, Fowler’s job was to bring her back to life.

He ordered an oxygen tank and an ambulance arrived to take Pike to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, where she was put on a ventilator and treated for severe burns and blistering in her arms. Later, it would become clear that the IV hadn’t been properly inserted into her veins. Sometimes the thin plastic sheath can clog or dislodge, or the push of medication can cause it to fold, Fowler says. Whatever happened in this case, “it was delivering medicine to the subcutaneous tissue” of her arms, he says, rather than her bloodstream. After ten days, she regained the ability to walk and talk before returning to the Tennessee women’s prison.

In the machinery of an execution, each participant is a cog performing a compartmentalized task, diffusing responsibility and obscuring their individual complicity. The paramedics who set the line wouldn’t have known that something went wrong with it because protocol instructs them to leave the room before the injection team enters. In turn, the Department of Corrections employees who inject the drug leave before the physician comes in. (A similar psychological ritual takes place among firing squads, where one randomly assigned gunman shoots blanks, shielding each from knowing if he delivered the fatal bullet.) Fowler’s role on the execution team that day was to pronounce Pike’s death, though in more complex cases, he is sometimes called on to place IV lines himself.

Tennessee’s lethal-injection protocol may help absolve culpability, but it can make executions faultier. Participants may be EMTs with limited medical training, or they may be prison guards with none at all. Physicians almost never agree to take part, and when they do Tennessee prohibits them from observing the full procedure. Pike’s attorneys have cited more than a half-dozen other cases in recent years of excruciating, drawn-out executions caused by failed IVs as well as the use of untested chemicals from unnamed suppliers.

It is extremely unusual that Fowler, a 69-year-old grandfather and Sunday-school teacher in Union City, Tennessee, is known to us at all. He was publicly outed, accidentally, by a warden last year. The identities of execution participants are meant to be kept secret to protect them from social stigma, legal liability, and professional consequences. “Doctors are not lining up to do this,” says Fowler, who otherwise spends his days monitoring opioid prescriptions for chronic-pain patients and writing conservative op-eds for the Union City Daily Messenger. The American Medical Association prohibits physicians from taking any part in executions, including monitoring vital signs, inserting IVs, and declaring death, on the grounds that it violates the oath to “do no harm.” Fowler, who receives $3,000 per execution according to a deposition he gave last year, doesn’t see a contradiction between that pledge and the seven or so lethal injections he’s participated in over the past decade. For him, the work is about the fulfillment of a solemn obligation. “How can you morally say, ‘I’m for the death penalty so long as somebody else does the work?’” he says. “I do things that nobody wants to do.”

It is even more unusual that he’s providing a glimpse into the extraordinarily secretive world of American executions and the bizarre logic that perpetuates their cruelty. Fowler agreed to speak to me, he said, because I was familiar with his writing — polemics in support of ICE, Israel, and traditional masculinity among other subjects. “I’d like to be remembered as a Renaissance man,” he tells me. “Someone who has an advanced appreciation of life.” He is inspired by Epictetus, the Stoic philosopher, and Saint Paul, who helped execute Christians before converting to the faith and then being executed himself by the anti-Christian Roman emperor. “Paul, who went through real hardship, said, ‘I have learned to become content in whatever circumstances I find myself,’” Fowler says. That included imprisonment “back in the day where there was nobody inspecting prisons for humane conditions.” In a “fallen world” of freeloaders, criminal migrants, weak men, and “race hustlers,” as Fowler has put it, he is an enforcer of tradition and individual responsibility. “There are times when you have to draw a line and say, ‘You have traversed socially acceptable norms and we must extract from you the ultimate penalty.’”

Fowler sees his career as an example of doing the “dirty work.” His father couldn’t afford to send him to college, so he worked and paid his way through law school in the early 1980s. Then he took a job as a public defender, a role few of his peers wanted. “History is replete with examples of the government pushing around and persecuting people without due process,” he says, mentioning the false rape accusations against Duke lacrosse players in 2006 as an example of why he values the constitutional right to a defense. But he didn’t like many of his fellow attorneys — they were “every bit as vile as the literature portrays them to be” — and says most of his clients were guilty. A couple of them even deserved the death penalty and didn’t get it, he adds. There were rewarding moments, such as a case involving a man who had been charged with harassing his ex-girlfriend. Fowler convinced the man to stop contacting her, got the case heard in a lower local court that doesn’t keep formal records, “and it saved that man’s job and his reputation.”

Over time Fowler’s caseload became increasingly filled with low-level domestic disputes and car accidents, and, by the 1990s, he was looking for more meaningful work. He saw an ad in the newspaper offering free tuition for physicians training in underserved areas, including his hometown, and decided to pursue a new career in family medicine. Since graduating from the University of Tennessee at Martin, he has held a string of jobs in nursing homes, jails, and hospice wards. For a while, he was a medical examiner. “I did the kinds of things where people are sick and suffering and dying that nobody wants to do because they don’t pay well,” he says. Along the way he befriended a surgeon who worked with the Tennessee Department of Corrections to oversee executions. When the man retired a decade ago, the department asked Fowler to take his place. He accepted.

On his first day shadowing an execution as a trainee, he recalls feeling nothing. “I was there to learn and observe and I went and I learned and observed. That’s the end of that,” he says. There’s “no doubt” in his mind that the inmates he has personally helped put to death deserved their punishment. “I usually research their records and take a look at what it is they’ve done and so forth.” Over most of the next decade, he says, his work was limited to declaring deaths and the procedures went smoothly. But everything changed in the past year as Fowler became the public face of the death penalty’s most egregious failures. First he was identified as the physician in the 2025 execution of Byron Black, whose lethal injection his attorney described as “torture.” Then, in May, he was involved in the botched execution of death-row inmate Tony Carruthers. After paramedics failed to establish traditional IV lines, Fowler attempted a semi-surgical procedure to place one in a vein near Carruthers’s clavicle, which would deliver the drug directly to his heart. Carruthers’s attorney reported seeing “a lot of blood” and hearing her client groaning in pain over the course of an hour. “There was a bit of theater in that,” Fowler says. But he ultimately stopped (“of my own volition”), not because he couldn’t do it, he says, but because he didn’t have adequate anesthetic and it was becoming too painful for Carruthers — “not to mention the fact that there are lawyers standing there taking notes and scribbling furiously.”

Fowler was roundly accused of incompetence, partly for admitting he hadn’t inserted a subclavian IV in 12 years. Carruthers’s sister sued him for malpractice, claiming her brother suffered a stroke during the procedure that led to paralysis. (He is now back in a Nashville prison on a one-year reprieve.) Fowler denies that he lacked the necessary expertise. “I have gotten it successfully several times,” he says of placing subclavian IVs at hospitals in the past. “It’s like riding a bicycle, and, frankly, the motor skills and neurological skills required to ride a bicycle are far more complex than placing an IV line.” (He called the stroke allegation “completely false.”) Now, he and the state are facing the possibility of malpractice or negligence lawsuits from Pike’s family, which one of her lawyers argues is likely. Fowler says he’s not worried — his conscience is clear.

He does not see a contradiction between his work and his evangelical Christian beliefs. He starts his mornings with devotional readings from the Book of Common Prayer and strives to be kind to others. “I like to think that I tip generously. I like to think I treat waitstaff generously. I have a housekeeper, and I have traditionally paid her more than she asked,” he says. But he has his own interpretation of the Sixth Commandment. “‘Thou shalt not kill’ does not have any application to the legitimate actions of the government in terms of executing murderers, nor does it have any application in self-defense, and it does not have any application morally in war,” he says. “When the state says, ‘We think there are some things so heinous that we should effectuate the ultimate punishment,’ I think that’s legitimate.” (The same applies when the state says those punishments should be nationally televised, he believes — as Pete Hegseth initially suggested for the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan in December. When it comes to “Muslim radicals,” he says, “it’s time they understand that we mean business.”)

The power of the state, Fowler continues, trumps the power of religious redemption. “Anybody, and I mean anybody, could find God and accept Christ’s redemption,” he says, including Pike (though, he thinks as a Buddhist, “she’s on the wrong track”). As he sees it, his role is to enforce the death penalty as determined by the state, regardless of its moral legitimacy: “Is it unfairly administered? Probably. Is it always deserved? Not necessarily. My job is not to say ‘yay’ or ‘nay.’” In Pike’s case, he has no doubt the punishment is fair. “I lament that I am having to deal with Christa Pike, who bludgeoned another woman to death,” he says, but that’s the extent of his regret. “She is what she is.”

In 1996, Pike, then 18, became the youngest woman ever sentenced to the death penalty. She and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, had lured into the woods their 19-year-old Knoxville Job Corps classmate Colleen Slemmer, who Pike claimed had bullied her and tried to seduce Shipp. Over the course of an hour, she and Shipp tortured the young woman and fatally crushed her skull with a rock.

Attorneys and anti–death penalty advocates have argued in the years since that the court should have given more consideration to Pike’s psychiatric conditions and history of severe childhood trauma. Pike was born with brain damage because of her mother’s alcohol use during pregnancy, and she was raped and beaten repeatedly between her toddler and teenage years. At 12, she attempted suicide. When it came to the murder, Pike couldn’t control her impulses, psychologist Bethany Brand wrote in a 2023 evaluation. “Unmedicated and untreated, she was not able to put the ‘brakes on’ her bipolar- and trauma-triggered emotions.” (Shipp, who was 17 at the time, received life in prison. He is up for parole in 2031.)

None of Pike’s appeals or clemency requests succeeded and she spent 28 years in solitary confinement. In January, her attorneys alleged that the state’s execution protocol would amount to cruel and unusual punishment. Pike has a blood-clotting disorder and small veins, which would make placing an IV difficult, if not impossible, and the effects of pentobarbital torturous. At one point she asked to be hanged instead. A judge denied Pike’s requests and her execution was scheduled for September 30. By that morning, she was ready to die.

Since then, Governor Bill Lee has halted all executions in the state for the rest of the year. Pike’s attorneys are now amending their case from earlier this year to prevent the state from attempting to lethally inject her again. Fowler agrees on one point: The lethal-injection protocol ought to change. Instead of pentobarbital, he prefers the older three-drug cocktail involving potassium chloride, which some states banned for being too painful but he believes is more effective. And the process should be simplified, he says, with fewer handoffs between team members and more oversight: Instead of leaving the room, “the people who place the IV lines should thereafter be observant about what’s happening with them as the medicine goes in.” Pike “complained of pain in her arm. They should have stopped and reassessed, and they didn’t.”

Fowler hopes the state will follow through on Pike’s execution, partly to provide “a sense of justice” for Slemmer’s mother, who was present at the initial attempt. He imagined how she might have questioned God — “Why couldn’t God direct a policeman to save their daughter?” These are concepts Fowler has been thinking about a lot lately, since he completed his second semester of seminary. He recalled what Job said in the bible after losing his children: “The Lord gives and the Lord takes away. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

“People will say, ‘Why don’t you just walk away from this?’ And the answer is, that’s exactly what the advocates against the death penalty want,” he says. “They felt that if they could humiliate me I would step back from it — because I promise you, there ain’t anybody else in Tennessee going to sign up for it now — and the answer is, I cannot be pushed off a course that I find correct. I refuse to compromise.” What seems to bother Fowler is the feeling of being misunderstood. “I’m not an evil, vicious person. I’m not unscrupulous. I’m not uncaring, and I’m not incompetent,” he says. He shut down his Facebook account and tries to ignore the news. “It’s not like I’m ashamed” of the work, he says, but he is disturbed by the “calumny” he’s facing. Then again, he adds, “people said bad things about Jesus, didn’t they?”

items.title: A Magazine That’s Actually a Shop
items.description: Type in shop-magazine.com and you will enter the world of Magazine, an online “destination for divas everywhere” and love letter to wallet-draining excess. It’s a shop, but also a magazine, founded by shopaholic soulmates Coumba Samba and Sylvie Makower. Born
items.author: Marley Wendt
paragraphs: Type in shop-magazine.com and you will enter the world of Magazine, an online “destination for divas everywhere” and love letter to wallet-draining excess. It’s a shop, but also a magazine, founded by shopaholic soulmates Coumba Samba and Sylvie Makower. Born from a friendship stretched between New York and London, Magazine turns a shared fascination with fashionista-dom into a website. It’s a transatlantic affair for a medium that is, fittingly, both nowhere and everywhere: an online space that feels positively physical, practically begging you to swipe your credit card.

From a lime-green 1940s showgirl dress to a pink-and-white Betsey Johnson confection, the colors pop with an almost suspicious perfection. It’s clear that Samba and Makower have a knack for knowing what a girl wants, embracing the fun that comes with acquiring clothes.

But Magazine is not just a place to empty your wallet; it is somewhere to fill your brain, too. Every drop arrives with an online magazine, ranging from essays on a pair of Fall 2011 Lanvin heels, to the quest for the perfect black mannequin. It’s a pink-painted corner of the web where reading becomes wanting, and wanting is very much the point. If you like your money pixelated on a screen, you’ve found your destination, darling!
MARLEY WENDT: What are three colors that capture the spirit of this project?
SYLVIE MAKOWER: Bubblegum pink.

SM: I also love tangerine. Magazine has a very girly, diva-abundance vibe. Neither of us are minimalists by any measure, nor are we into the monochromatic stuff. So, exuberant bright colors, heavy on the pink.
How did Magazine come about?

SM: A year ago while we were having breakfast and drinking coffee Upstate, I was thinking “Oh, Coumba’s being awfully quiet.” She was just on her phone, and seemed to be working. Then I noticed the reflection in her big glasses: Vinted, scrolling by. It was such a beautiful image. It suddenly dawned on me that we are twin flames in being massive shopaholics.

CS: We kind of floated the idea, and I was like, yes, we need that. Especially here in New York, there’s lots of nice vintage places, but sometimes the curation doesn’t really fit with what I’m seeking, so I’ve resorted to online shopping.
The website has a slightly DIY early internet quality to it. Has your relationship to the internet shaped the way you think about Magazine?
CS: It does have this “blog vibe” to it. At least for me, I kind of grew up on Tumblr, so that has a part to play in it.

SM: We like the idea of having this slightly low-stakes, immediate form of online publication where nothing’s too overdone. The actual visual language of the website had a lot to do with our web designer, Alec Mapes-Frances, and also Coumba.

It was quite an organic process. We just kept adding elements. For instance, there’s a sticker of Coumba in a margarita glass in the corner of the website. This links to her many years of writing a personal margarita review. And we also have an agony aunt, Miss Chlo, who you can submit questions to. We wanted to bring many worlds and portals together on the site.
Coumba, what makes a great margarita?

CS: Honestly, I’m a simple girl at heart. I also don’t really like alcohol. The whole reason I started it was because I was looking for a classic cocktail, and wanted to keep tabs on it. I’m just looking for something straightforward, no riff-raff or weird orange juice in it.
On the website, for the listings of the items, there are GIFs of you guys that emulate self-tape videos. Tell me about that.

SM: We thought it would be funny to do a spoof on the walking video that your modelling agency requests, because it’s such a humiliating medium. I modeled for a long time as a teenager, and Coumba still does.
What makes a piece of clothing right for Magazine?

SM: A philosophy that I’ve begun to incorporate is “shop for yourself.” If I Iove something, I’ll buy it. We want to have a mixture of well-constructed, fancy designer pieces, and weird, accessible items. To me, there’s nothing worse than being dressed too well…
CS: You’re spot on. Everything is unique, special, and bright.
Describe your perfect day of shopping together.
CS: We once went to this vintage fair in London called Frock Me!, and just spent the whole day there. I put in my earbuds, walked around for five hours, and spent all of my money. It was beautiful.
SM: Coumba sent me these crazy messages a few hours in telling me I had to come. And when I came, I found her racing around as if she was possessed. I love those fairs so much.
Why did you want Magazine to be an actual magazine as well?

SM: We wanted to print out images of the clothes, like the books of images of counterfeit bags on Canal Street. We thought we could call the shop Magazine because it’s like a magazine. And then Coumba suggested that we make an actual magazine.
CS: It all just clicked. I was also doing zines while I was in uni, so it’s always been an interest of mine.

SM: We wanted somewhere to explore what’s going on in the shop and beyond in greater depth. The magazine is by no means just about the stock though. For our current feature, Fiona Alison Duncan has written a pseudo fictional essay about personal effects.
And if Magazine was an actual shop, what would it look like?

SM: There’s not a moment in my day when I’m not thinking about it! It’ll be very pink. My hypothetical dog, which I intend to own within the next calendar year, will be running around. It’ll be a watering hole for divas, where people can come to shop, but also to congregate and have tea.
What type of music is playing as you walk in?
CS: Probably some classic ’80s dance tracks.
What are your favourite shopping-diva words of wisdom?
SM: I would like to quote our agony aunt, Miss Chlo: “You don’t need to find yourself before getting dressed. Sometimes getting dressed is how you find yourself.”

items.title: Gisele Bundchen Interview: Motherhood, Happiness, Modeling Career
items.description: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
items.author: Steff Yotka
paragraphs: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
photography COLLIER SCHORR

When she was 15 years old, Gisele Bündchen left Horizontina, Brazil, and moved to Tokyo to become a model. It was 1995. She didn’t speak Japanese or English. To reach her parents, grandparents, and five sisters, she used an international calling card on a landline phone. She would speak to them every 15 days, exactly.

“It was, in a way, liberating because I felt like I was living life,” Gisele says, thinking back to getting lost on the subway, navigating teenage growing pains, and learning how to integrate into a foreign reality. “I was experiencing life.”

Thirty-one years later, there is little of life Gisele hasn’t experienced. She walked her first major runway show for Alexander McQueen in 1998, and for the next decade was a regular on the catwalk for Gucci, Dolce & Gabbana, Versace, Valentino, and Marc Jacobs. She signed an advertising contract with Dior, posing for Nick Knight amongst bubbles and saddle bags, then another with Dolce & Gabbana for its glittering perfume The One, and then another with Victoria’s Secret. She routinely wore the brand’s Red Hot Fantasy Bra—estimated to be worth $15 million in 2000.

Gisele was the Forbes highest-paid model for 12 years in a row, from 2005 to 2016. Her own website estimates she has appeared on an unprecedented 1,200 magazine covers (this issue will be her seventh for i-D). She walked the runway during the 2016 Olympic Opening Ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, released multiple singles, and has appeared in a handful of movies, from Taxi (2004) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006). Gisele has fundraised for Lotus House, Save the Children, The Red Cross, and more. In 2016, Taschen published a book commemorating her 20 years of modelling, retailing for $700 and selling out in one day. The cover shot is by Irving Penn of a nude Gisele. (“I still have the note from him saying that it was wonderful. ‘You did great.’”) Inside are now-legendary photographs by Steven Meisel, David LaChapelle, Inez and Vinoodh, and Juergen Teller. Gisele has published one autobiography and one cookbook, which is to say nothing of the digests she posts on Instagram to her 22 million followers. She is so famous and so known, from Brazil to Tokyo to New York to Mars, that it would be impossible for any one of us to calculate exactly where we know her from or how many times we’ve seen her face.

And yet, for Gisele, who turned 46 in July, those wandering Tokyo days are among her most special. “My whole thing is going back to that,” she tells me, tucked into an armchair in a white tank and jean shorts. “How can I create more of that reality in my life?”

You see, despite being the object of so many gazes, Gisele prefers to set hers on the sun, the sea, the sky. She was born on a farm in Brazil, surrounded by her grandparents, parents, sisters, and pets. Now, 6,900 kilometres away, she’s recreated that paradise in Northern Miami with her children Benjamin (16), Vivian (13), and a baby boy (16 months), her husband Joaquim, and a pair of dogs.

“Life is a gift,” she says. “I think I have so much joy in my life because I really see the ordinary as the extraordinary… The sun rises every day. You can walk around and be grateful for it, or you can just be disconnected from all these incredible things. You can be robbed of your life if you think life is this”—she mimics looking down at her phone—“and you forget life is so much more.”
She smiles, sipping from her room-temperature water. “Anyway, I’m sure you have more questions for me.”
Because we got into the meaning of life and Gisele’s very philosophy of being so quickly into our first meeting, here’s what happened in the lead-up—minutes one through seven:
1. I enter Gisele’s small ranch home a couple blocks from her larger, beachfront estate. I am promptly served her homemade granola and her proprietary tea (warming, like dark chocolate and honey).
2. Alfie, her gigantic German Shepherd, comes in first and gives me the once-over. “He’s my protector,” Gisele smiles, kicking off her sandals and wrapping me up in a hug.

3. “You smell amazing,” she says, and I just give her the bottle of perfume in my purse. She asks if it has parabens, and I say I don’t know, and she tells me never to use anything with parabens, especially on your wrists or neck. It’s been three months and I am still too embarrassed to research: Does Maison Louis Marie’s scent Aboukir have parabens?
4. She checks my astrological vibe to make sure this interview will go well: “What’s your sign?” she asks squarely.
“Cancer. I knew we’d talk about it. I read you’re a Cancer, Scorpio Moon. What’s your rising?”

“Oh, go girl! I don’t even know how I ended up doing this job. If you let me, I would just never leave my house, because I’m a crab. And with the Scorpio Moon, for me, if it’s not deep, I don’t want to talk about it.”

That’s the guiding premise of being Gisele: Always searching for depth, connection, and meaning. In some way, modelling was the perfect job for her—homey, crablike tendencies notwithstanding—because it allowed her to find connections the world over. The high-low of the industry, which led to anxiety attacks in her mid-20s, was the impetus for Gisele’s soul searching. “Shit happens to all of us, but I think I don’t stay there,” she says of the down days. “I learned how to meditate. It’s like you can take a step back: You can be having an experience and observing yourself having that experience at the same time.”

Meditation led her to yoga, which she practises routinely, and then to Pilates and then to jujitsu. Recently, she has added weight training. “I do weights three times a week. I do Pilates once or twice a week. I do yoga two or three times a week. I work out every day because, for me, working out—I don’t see it as something I have to do. I see it as something I get to do,” she says. “It doesn’t matter if I’m surfing, if I’m playing volleyball with my daughter, if I’m paddleboarding. Whatever it is, I feel like it’s a moment of being.” She bares a bicep. “Now for the first time in my life, I can do pull-ups.”

Early this summer morning, she took her baby to the park. Much like his older half-siblings, he has picked up on Gisele’s connectivity and generosity. “I have to show you this video.” For the first time, she whips out her phone and opens her camera roll. As she scrolls through—I promise I’m not trying to peek!—I realise almost every photo is of her kids. “He’s so funny,” she says of her son, captured waddling around the park with a paper towel. “I mean, he’s 16 months and he saw that I was cleaning the park—because Miami, it’s so damp all the time!—and he wanted to participate and he felt really good about it,” Gisele beams, watching her tiny son dry off the slide, the seesaw, the swing.

“Kids give us this opportunity to live again, to be more present and to experience life again. To do it maybe differently than we’ve done it before.” She pauses. “I don’t know. I find every little thing so amazing.” Gisele goes on to show me videos of Benny DJing in his bedroom, his baby brother dancing by his side. She has pictures of Vivi playing volleyball (“She’s amazing!”) and dancing with friends. She scrolls to a dancing video. “I mean, what is better than this? This is my daughter and she’s like, ‘Mum, let’s do a dance class.’ So this is us doing a dance class. I’m not so great,” Gisele laughs, “but look at her and her friend—and that’s her mum’s friend.”

She quickly scrolls through about 20 more videos before she chucks her phone away. “By the way, I don’t know if you noticed, my phone doesn’t ring. There’s no alarms. It never rings. It’s liberating.”

A silenced iPhone and spending all day with her family is a far cry from the past 30 years of Gisele’s life. To briefly summarise the lore: Her mother enrolled her, her twin sister Patí, and younger sister Gabriela in modelling classes in Brazil. Gisele was later scouted to participate in the Elite Model Look competition, and in 1995, she placed second. From 1996 to 2016, life didn’t stop—she spent the better part of her 20s and 30s at the white-hot centre of it all: Fashion, fame, celebrity, paparazzi, and money. She was signing bigger contracts than other models, getting bigger media attention, becoming an entity bigger than Gisele Bündchen from Horizontina, Brazil. She was, by 2004, a supermodel, capital S. Everything about her sparkled.

“I’ve experienced the rat race. I was on the hamster wheel in my early 20s,” she says. “I won Model of the Year at 19. I worked so hard from 14 to get to that place, I felt like I couldn’t say no [to major jobs].” And sure, Gisele encountered so much of the bullshit so many models of the ’90s and ’00s did. She tried not to let her industry’s lack of protection faze her. “Even though I wasn’t going to the parties, I was doing 360 days [of work a year]. I wanted to be the best that I could be every day. I wanted to bring my best.”

We start to look through some of her runway fits from her catwalk days and she sparks up with delight. “Girl, it was very tight inside. You couldn’t really move so much—but, I mean, look how he made you look!” she cheers of a supersized Fall 2004 Christian Dior look by John Galliano. “I’m forever grateful to McQueen, I’m forever grateful to John. I was always so excited to do the Dior shows because I never knew what I was going to look like.”

She singles out a Galliano show for Dior held at Versailles. “This was 60 years of Dior and I wasn’t even doing shows anymore. John was like, ‘Please, Gisele. This is all my muses and it’s going to be the 60 years, it’s to be in Versailles.’ I was like, ‘I must do it,’” she remembers. “Look at these shoes. It was like a platform without a heel. I was walking on cement, like bricks. It was crazy. I was like, ‘Am I going to fall and break my ankle?’”

But that’s the thing about Gisele: Even if she’s struggling to walk or struggling to feel beautiful—as she often recounts of that first-ever McQueen show, where she hit the runway topless with a trompe l’oeil white tank painted on by Val Garland, rain falling and her lashes dripping into her eyes—she is always going to do her best. “I didn’t say no or complain because people were giving me the opportunity,” she reflects. “I came in, I did my job, I went home… and I think what I really appreciate and really enjoyed about fashion is that it got me to access and experience different sides of me. I really wanted to be the best canvas for the creatives. I felt like it was my way of contributing.”

But working in the oil-slick glossy world of new millennium modelling meant that few people saw Gisele as a full person—because of her beauty, her chameleonic qualities, and her prowess, she was quickly regarded as an idol. Nice to look at, nothing to say. The first time she appeared in i-D, on the cover in December 1998, she wasn’t interviewed. Instead, the photographer who took the picture was, and here’s what he had to say about the smart and vibrant Gisele: “She’s certainly gorgeous. I’d marry her.”

Her “godfather” in the turbulent fashion industry was Steven Meisel. (Are you surprised that the greatest model of her generation would find kinship with the greatest photographer of his?) In one of the earliest pieces of press about Gisele, a New York Magazine article from 1999, Meisel already saw her as more than a body to stand in front of his lens. He felt her spirit. “Gisele is able to change because she wants to—it’s not in her looks; it’s in her mental process. She is malleable and is willing to be a silent screen star because she understands that modelling is acting,” he told the mag. He later wrote the foreword for her Taschen book, and she still speaks of him as her guardian angel. “I’m grateful for him. I don’t think I would have been the model that I was if it wasn’t for him, for real. We got to play together. I shot with him every week.”

And yet, after weekly Meisel shoots, over 130 Vogue covers, and decades on billboards and TV ad spots, Gisele wanted more. Well—maybe not more in the way you and I might think of it. She wanted to actually enjoy what she’d accomplished, and that meant leaving the fracas behind. After a decade in Boston, she relocated here, to Florida, to co-parent her older children and set up a new world of sea and sun and sand. Being mum, practising gratitude, taking care of herself and her community have become more valuable than any seven-figure ad job: “I say no to 99 percent of the jobs I’m offered because, when I put it on the scale, I’m like, ‘Am I going to miss my daughter’s volleyball game? Am I going to miss going to the park with my son? Am I going to miss my son DJing?’”

That’s why, with the exception of a few trips to her home in Costa Rica, to see family in Brazil, and recently, to Tahiti, Gisele rarely leaves Florida. “Having a baby at this moment of my life is such a gift, because I’m in a different place. I don’t have anything to prove. I don’t feel like I really, quite frankly, care.”
“I’m not defined by other people’s opinions,” she continues, firmly. “I feel like I get to choose how I want to live my life.”

Being alive today can feel like a quest for more: Make more money. Diversify your portfolio. Get PRP+ to be more beautiful and then Ozempic to be more svelte. Become a brand and use that brand to become more famous. Every day of your life can be used to sell something or say something or self-improve. I don’t think I have ever encountered a person more satisfied with exactly how her life is than Gisele. She has a lot, sure, but it’s long been enough. She’s done a lot, sure, but she’s not looking back. She’s been everywhere, yeah, but she isn’t driven by getting in your face.

She’s not a brand. She’s not an entrepreneur. She’s not a self-help guru—even though I tell her she should have a podcast. She’s not forcing Gisele-dom down our throats and, in some way, it seems like she doesn’t really want to be famous at all. That she’s financially well-off, she tells me, is just an opportunity to take care of her sisters and her family. She doesn’t want fancy clothes. She hasn’t been to New York in over two years and she’s not eager to come back.

“At the end of the day, this is your temple, this is your life, this is your journey. How do you want it to look? What do you want it to be? Who defines success?” she asks, as concerned in that moment with my well-being as with her own. “What is success? Some people say success is power, money, fame, more. Some people say success is being able to spend time with your kids, to have food on your table, to have a home to live in, to have great relationships and actually enjoy every day. I find that, quite frankly, much more successful than…” she trails off, not eager to point a finger. “It’s up to each person to define, because when I was in my 20s, success was different than what I feel today.”
“What do you want your legacy to be?” I ask as we’re wrapping up our conversation.

“In the end, I ended up having the best time. I ended up enjoying it all, staying in it, learning from it, and growing up in it. It’s been a blessing. However people see me, that’s okay with me. I want to look back and think, ‘I really enjoyed this journey. I really loved fully. I really experienced every emotion. I really had meaningful relationships. I tried to make the world a better place, and I made my surroundings more harmonious and loving and beautiful.’ I want my kids to feel like I was a great mum and that I helped them become the best version of themselves. I want to feel like I lived striving to be the best version of myself. Hopefully, I can look back and say I did it.”

Today, after I pack up my things and head for Miami International Airport, she’ll go to a birthday dinner. It’s a rare night out for Gisele, and after decades of no carbs and no dairy, she might have some of her friend’s homemade sourdough. “What’s better than bread and cheese? Oh my god, I don’t know!” she laughs. Tomorrow, she’ll wake up early to paddleboard. She’s worried about me not seeing the sea one last time before I get on a plane back to New York, but she’s calmed when I tell her I spent two hours on the beach this morning. As I wheel away my little suitcase and say goodbye, she pops her head out the front door with a final blessing. “Live the life you want to live! Everything else is going to shake out.”
