paragraphs: Late October officially lands us at the start of the holiday season, a typically chaotic period I have never been very effective at managing. There are costumes to plan, parties to throw and attend, and between it all, many end-of-year deadlines to meet. A little push and pull between my full calendar and the routine that keeps me steady is inevitable. But there’s no reason to white-knuckle through it without some help. The products that spoke to me this month are all stopgaps in some way or another—handy ways to fortify against, or work with, the busy stretch ahead.

While I’m still working my way through the stash of sunscreens I bought in Europe and Asia during recent travels, I am nonetheless stoked that US formulas are finally catching up to their superior foreign counterparts. A quick recap for context: This past June, the Food and Drug Administration approved its first new sunscreen ingredient in over 25 years, a chemical filter called Bemotrizinol, or BEMT for short. It’s a standard part of most SPFs abroad, valued for its stability when exposed to UVA and UVB rays, its gentleness on sensitive skin, and its low potential for skin penetration—meaning, it’s less likely to be absorbed into the bloodstream in comparison to other chemical UV filters. As of September, a few sunscreens with the ingredient have begun trickling out into the marketplace—and more are surely on the way. I got my hands on the version from La Roche Posay, the brand I usually search for in European drugstores, earlier this month. I’m happy to report that it’s extremely lightweight. It rubs in easily and leaves no white cast or excessive grease behind—just a punch of hydration, thanks to some welcome glycerin. Also, for those of you with facial hair, La Roche-Posay’s (notably bearded!) head of brand engagement Justin Ollivierre assures me it plays nice with scruff, and doesn’t create the flaking effect common with other formulas. Wearing it while walking or gardening under the strong, persistent Los Angeles sunshine, my skin hasn’t experienced even a hint of redness. And given my dear city’s reputation for polluted air, I’m also grateful for the concoction’s Litchiderm and Exo-P extracts, which are meant to protect the skin barrier from oxidative stress. It’s not quite the next-level skin care product that sunscreens are abroad, but it’s a significant step up. Go get a bottle immediately.

Extremely caffeinated energy drinks are becoming the norm at the office and in the gym, but I personally can’t handle a cold brew without getting the jitters. If I drank a Celcius Heat, packed with an eye-popping 300 mg of caffeine, I think I might implode. But I still lean on caffeine to focus at work and lift better, like everyone else. I just prefer to get it from various types of green tea, both to protect my sleep and sensitive stomach. I make an Ippodo matcha in the morning, buy jugs of jasmine Tea’s Tea to portion out throughout my workweek, and when I really need a pick-me-up, I down an Ito En Sencha Shot. While an espresso shot contains approximately 60 mg of caffeine, these only have about 40 mg. It’s a tamer, more refreshing option to put a little pep in my step. Not to mention each one is infused with a healthy helping of vitamin C. One of these, in fact, may have had a hand in helping me write this column.

Whenever I travel, I always seem to either forget my razor at home or leave it behind in a hotel. Over the years, this bad habit has left me buying flimsy, plastic razors as replacements—not ideal! Schick’s new limited-edition Hydro Razor is a nice in-between travel option—not quite the quality of your at-home shaving setup, but also far more elevated than what any hotel toiletry kit has to offer. It has a weighty metal handle with some grip to it, and comes with a sturdy magnetic stand to place on a countertop. And it delivers a precise shave without irritating the skin. A nice little upgrade for your Dopp kit during a chaotic holiday season.

If you follow skin care as closely as I do, you probably already know that PDRN stands for polydeoxyribonucleotide, which—gasp!—is a small DNA fragment of salmon sperm. Over the past few years, it’s become a popular ingredient across Korean skin care brands eager to capitalize on the fascination over the more invasive, painful, and, I must say, very effective salmon sperm injections or microneedling, which center around polynucleotides (PN), also found in salmon sperm. Funny enough, many brands are now developing plant-based versions of PDRN, all but stripping it of the original reason it earned so much attention in the first place. But that doesn’t mean it’s not effective. Case in point: Dior’s new silky smooth PDRN shot. This patented formula combines a plant-derived PDRN with vitamin Cg and niacinamide to plump, brighten, and smooth skin. I can dab this at my elevens, crow's feet, and dark spots before bed, and no matter how little sleep I get, I emerge in the morning with fortified, radiant skin.

As long as I’ve exercised, I’ve been locked in a never-ending endeavor to prevent post-workout breakouts. The reality is, if I go for a long hike, or catch an evening yoga session, I’m not always able to shower off my sweat immediately afterward. When I finally am able to spritz off, I find it can be helpful to counteract the dirt and sweat seeping into my skin with a little extra exfoliation on my back, neck, and chest. I loathe a harsh “peel” wipe, but these exfoliating sheets from Prequel are gently effective. They use a mix of different acids to lift dead skin cells without sacrificing any moisture, thanks to an infusion of squalane. Since using them I’ve noticed fewer exercise-induced blemishes. They’re a nice, light option to tuck into a backpack, Dopp kit, or gym bag.

items.title: 'Backrooms' Director Kane Parsons on What Scares Him the Most
items.description: Backrooms, your anxiety-inducing horror film about a man trapped in an endless world of portals leading to disturbing environments, earned a staggering $118 million globally on its opening weekend. You are 21 now, and were a teenager in 2022 when you started t
items.author: Lynn Hirschberg
paragraphs: Backrooms, your anxiety-inducing horror film about a man trapped in an endless world of portals leading to disturbing environments, earned a staggering $118 million globally on its opening weekend. You are 21 now, and were a teenager in 2022 when you started the project as a series on YouTube; after it went viral, A24 signed you to develop it into a feature film. You’re the youngest director ever hired at A24, and Backrooms is the biggest hit in the company’s history. And yet you’re back at home in your childhood bedroom in Petaluma, California. Do you still have posters on the wall?
No posters. My childhood bedroom looks like a CIA agent lives here—there’s film equipment everywhere in an empty white room.
You made your first film in eighth grade, and it won an award.
It was called Late for School, and it was kind of sci-fi. It won the Five Minute Film Festival award here in Petaluma. I later extended the film to 30 minutes— I wanted to increase the quality.
Backrooms has the feeling of found footage, like The Blair Witch Project. Were you influenced by that film?

I watched Blair Witch only one time. I was more influenced by body-cam footage on YouTube. You can find video content of dynamic situations in people’s lives. As creepy as that sounds, there’s nonfiction footage of emotional moments; environmental footage where people are alone in a room. I would watch 30 minutes of people walking in dead malls or empty parking lots. Spatial anxiety fascinates me.
Although your bedroom walls are white, you seem to be intrigued by the color yellow—Backrooms is suffused with that shade.

When I was growing up, my walls were yellow. The yellow in the film was influenced by the short story “The Yellow Wallpaper,” by Charlotte Perkins Gilman. [“The Yellow Wallpaper” is a horror fiction story from 1892, about a woman confined to a room; obsessed with the yellow wallpaper, she descends into madness.] I spent a lot of time fixating on creating a sickly, suffocating, gross yellow. Interestingly, when we’d post thumbnails on YouTube of “Backrooms” videos, if they didn’t have yellow in the background, they would get much less traffic. There’s an efficacy in yellow.

Most horror directors your age work with young, relatively unknown actors in their films. Instead, you cast Academy Award nominees such as Renate Reinsve and Chiwetel Ejiofor. Was there a reason you chose them?

In terms of characters, I prefer people with more life experience. If an external idea hits a young person, they are immediately vulnerable. But when a person has a history and a set of beliefs and views, banging up against something new and unsettling causes a tectonic change. An older person evaluates an obstacle in a different way than a young person does—they have to weigh what they are seeing against their life experience. You couldn’t tell the same story with younger individuals.
I’ve experienced things that people might call ghostlike, but I prefer to think the ghost is in my own brain.

I’m most frightened of violence against consciousness. And, of course, that fascinates me also. I don’t like the idea of brains being grown in petri dishes. And I can be afraid of darkness. But isn’t everybody?
You have said that you often prefer television to films. Which shows do you love?
My brain goes to Mr. Robot, Better Call Saul, and Barry. I love Bill Hader.
Barry is a dark comedy. Would you ever direct a comedy?
I think I could! I’m not a funny person, but I think I could navigate that world.
Did you watch Backrooms with an audience in a theater on the opening weekend?

Yes. I watched it in the one theater in Petaluma where I saw films as a kid. It was great to see the poster in front. They were selling Backrooms merchandise in the lobby. It was quite wonderful, and also surreal.
You’re an original! Who is an original to you?

The musician Gary Wilson. My director of photography and I carpooled to set every day on Backrooms, and we’d play Gary Wilson in the car. On the days that we didn’t play a Gary Wilson song, we’d have a bad shoot day. So that became our superstition. Without Gary Wilson, there would be no Backrooms.
Grooming by Michael Moreno for Oribe at The Only Agency; Photo Assistant: Jordan Zuppa.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried Is Ready to Ring in the Holiday Season With Tiffany & Co.
items.description: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality, you’ll just be saving your future self a lot of stress. And luckily, the brands are, once again, ahead of schedule, already rolling out their holiday content for our benefit. Ferragamo, Dior, Chanel, and more have released their 2026 holiday campaigns, and the images are getting us in the yuletide mood. So while the leaves may just now be falling off the trees, soon they’ll be on the ground, covered in snow—and there’s no time like the present to dive into the 2026 holiday campaigns.

Fresh off her buzzy turn in You Can See Everything, Amanda Seyfried has returned to New York from Texas, just in time for the holiday season. The actor is Tiffany & Co.’s newest House ambassador and the star of its holiday campaign, “Love Is a Gift.”

As part of the campaign, Seyfried acts in a short film, “You & Me,” which tells the story of two different Christmas celebrations: one taking place in the present day, and one in 1992. Between these two moments passes a Bird on a Rock ornament, originally gifted decades ago and still a prized possession all these years later. It’s a story of tradition, holiday memories, and the connection between generations.

“I’m thrilled to join the Tiffany & Co. family as their newest House ambassador and to be part of a campaign that celebrates love, family, and the traditions we carry with us through generations,” Seyfried said in a statement. “‘You & Me’ captures beautifully how a meaningful gift can hold memories and become part of a family’s story. It was incredibly special to bring that idea to life with Tiffany this holiday season.”

The holidays are all about family, so it makes sense that Kim Kardashian enlisted her very famous sisters to star in the Skims Holiday campaign. Shot by frequent Kardashian collaborator Nadia Lee Cohen, the campaign takes inspiration from nostalgic holiday portraits, placing Kim, Kourtney, Kylie, Khloe, and Kendall in scenes you may recall from your own home videos.

The sisters are styled in pieces from the Skims holiday shop, wearing outfits with varying degrees of coziness. Khloe and Kourtney are covered head-to-toe in their respective patterned onesie and red long johns. Kylie and Kendall, meanwhile, show off more skin in bras boasting classic holiday prints. All the girls don retro glam—bouffants and old-school glasses. The result is a vintage scene with no clear time stamp. But it doesn’t matter, because Santa still clearly approves.

Gigi Hadid, Louisa Jacobson, and more gather in a grand townhouse to celebrate the holidays. The polished wood walls are covered in wreaths, the tree is bedecked with ornaments, and everyone is dressed in Miu Miu.

The wardrobe highlights contrasts between lifestyle archetypes and seasonal themes. Silk dresses are paired with upcycled knits and sportswear-inspired zip-front blousons. Cropped sweaters reveal button-down shirts, and utilitarian cotton canvas separates are layered over sequined bralettes.

But the models are not alone in this uptown space. They are joined by plush toy bears, rabbits, geese, and more. Treated like treasured guests, these additions provide whimsy to the scene, a composed portrait of bourgeois behavior subverted by humor and play.

Friendly furry creatures are not unique to the Miu Miu campaign this season—they pop up in the Prada world as well. This time, though, the woodland pals are hand-drawn by a team of artists led by cinematic animator John Pomeroy.

Sadie Sink gets down on the ground with a trio of mice to admire a patterned, calf-hair loafer. Maya Hawke faces off against a sly fox as she braves the elements of a frozen setting. There is a whimsy to these wintertime scenes, which emphasizes Prada’s humanity and a connection to craft that lies at the heart of the brand’s approach to creation.

Kris Jenner is the matriarch of the Ferragamo family in the brand’s 2026 holiday campaign, The Joy of Loving. “Ferragamo is all about family,” says creative director Maximilian Davis. “And when I design, I am always thinking about that, too: how a collection can be worn by different generations, but also how pieces you love will be held onto and passed down through them.”

The momager stars as the director of a fictional film, leading screen tests featuring the campaign’s various faces. There’s Paloma Elsesser and her brother, Sage; girl group The Womack Sisters; and Sofia Testino with her dog, Syko. Actress Joan Chen is joined by her daughter, Audrey Hui, while acting coach Nancy Banks poses with her son, actor Benny Buckley.

The campaign connects back to the roots of Ferragamo, and founder Salvatore Ferragamo’s original desire to build a better life for his family through his love of invention and creativity. “One of the founding values of Ferragamo has always been of beauty that develops from craftsmanship, humanity, and joy,” says Salvatore’s son, Leonardo Ferragamo. “This campaign is telling that story.”

Loro Piana invites you to a weekend at the cabin, where the elegantly falling snow outside matches the chic inhabitants’ wardrobes. Models are dressed in the brand’s holiday collection, an expression of style that plays out across textures, hand-finished prints, exclusive patterns, and elaborate stitches.
Loro Piana’s usually muted color palette is realized once again, this time in the form of dark greens and earthy browns. They are highlighted with pops of winter-white and marigold.

Warm jersey tops and trousers form the foundations of these après-ski looks. On top, classic Loro Piana outerwear like the Spagna jacket and Konny vest are crafted in wool and finely detailed with needlework; the wearer stays warm while also making an enviable sartorial impression.

Chanel is hitting the slopes for its 2026 Coco Neige collection. Bright-red knits and colorblocked puffers stand out against snow-capped mountains. The images have a retro flair, but the clothing is distinctly modern.
A snowball fight adds even more joy to this already playful campaign, while penguin and polar bear-shaped purses and earrings provide the perfect amount of whimsy.
Shearling caps keep ears warm, while winter whites are embraced with aplomb. It’s a reminder that dressing for warmth does not mean sacrificing style or charm.

Indulge in your sweet tooth with Dior’s 2026 holiday campaign, which sees the brand’s famous 30 Montaigne store reimagined as a sugar-dusted gingerbread house. Anya Taylor-Joy and Deva Cassel star in a joyous musical video. The house’s ambassadors prance around the store, snacking on Dior cookies, spritzing the brand’s famed fragrances, and trimming the icing-lined cookie Christmas tree.

items.title: I Did Push-Ups With Snap’s Chunky AR Glasses
items.description: I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.
items.author: Boone Ashworth
paragraphs: I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.

The Lens (what Snap calls apps on its augmented reality headset) is called Thirty Ups. It is in Halloween mode now, so when I look down, a virtual cartoon Jack-o’-lantern sits right next to where I’m supposed to start working out. I’m not trying to get jacked right now, but my goal is to see if these gigantic smart glasses will fall off when I’m staring straight down and moving up and down.

I get into position and start my workout. When I go down and back up, a little virtual circle on the ground below me starts counting up. I don’t get to 30 push-ups. I’m surrounded by people, many of whom are now staring at me, and it feels too hot outside to keep going without feeling gross. I get in 12 reps before giving up. The glasses only count 11 because it tells me I “skipped” one. Great.
The nearby Snap representative is thrilled. “You’re the first person who’s tried that one,” he says. I’m also pleasantly surprised. These glasses seem huge, but they stayed on my face just fine.
Snap announced its Specs in June. They cost $2,195 and will start to ship in the coming weeks. It took a few months for Snap to share what actual features would be available on the glasses

WIRED’s Julian Chokkattu and I both tried out Snap’s Specs last week. He got a dedicated demo with the company. I was offered one, too, but instead I happened to stumble upon the Specs First Look demo at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. The space has been here for just a couple of weeks.

It was a warm Sunday afternoon, and a steady stream of people came through the mall’s demo zone. Snap reps handed out Specs to anyone curious enough to register and hang out. Kids were running around, and the glasses looked especially large on their faces. When people left the demo, they got a free cup of ice cream with a small, Specs-shaped chocolate cookie.

The Specs had a dozen or so Lenses available for testing. Aside from the push-ups, the Specs let you finger paint in midair, see navigation directions overlaid on the real world, or engage with the physical environment by drawing on a notepad or analyzing text in a print book. They also have some sporty features, like one that allegedly helps with golf and another through a partnership with the NBA that guides you through shooting hoops.

You may have noticed that the glasses look pretty chunky. That’s true, but I was pleasantly surprised by how lightweight they felt and how well they stayed put. (The glasses come in two sizes, so if the small is too tight, try the larger model.) Another surprise was how well the virtual digital elements held up in bright light. I made a point of walking into direct sunlight to test out the screen. With the brightness turned all the way up, the onscreen elements were still visible. The glasses had automatically switched into “sunglasses mode” and dimmed to block the sun. The Snap rep said the lenses protect the eyes from UV rays at all times.

The problem, though, is that Snap is really trying to make the case that these glasses—or at least future, smaller iterations—are the holy grail of consumer tech. But I still don’t care to wear them in public. Walking around with the AR elements on can be distracting. Even if you turn it all off, the waveguides on the lenses still have a rainbow shimmer in your vision as you move. I wouldn’t want to wear these while driving or even walking when I really need to see where I'm going. At one point in the demo, I had to dodge a kid wearing a pair of Specs who was wildly swinging punches at something on the screen only he could see.

Most of the device features are controlled with your hands, like pinching two fingers together to open a lens or move something around. You can play Beat Saber-esque games by moving your hands around. But the controls can be finicky, and I found myself clawing at the air repeatedly to move or open something. Chokkattu tried writing in Google Docs—a demo showing the Specs as a computer you can work with anywhere—but the connected Bluetooth keyboard had a severe input lag, making typing a chore.

It also feels odd that some Specs features really just feel like advertising. A Harry Potter spell-casting experience is a fun idea, but really it just comes across as an ad for the upcoming HBO show. The Specs also have a shopping feature which lets you browse stores online. It’s a reminder that one day your augmented vision will be bombarded with pop-up ads.

I have a hard time imagining who these glasses are for. Given the price, it’s clearly aimed at developers and early adopters. But I tried the developer version of the Specs in 2024. The new glasses are much more comfortable and slightly less chonky, but the software hasn't changed much since then. Snap has shown off the same finger painting demo every time I’ve tried them, and every time it works until it doesn’t. The Specs are interesting but lack a killer feature, and Meta and Xreal both have more polished mixed-reality glasses that cost less. That’s going to make Specs a hard sell.

“We see consumer adoption as a process—the hardware, software, available experiences and price all need to develop together,” a Snap representative wrote in a statement to WIRED. “Specs bring computing into the world without pulling you out of it.”
For now, Snap’s most compelling pitch might be the free ice cream.

items.title: Liquid Glass Finally Makes Sense on the iPhone Duo
items.description: Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.
items.author: Craig Grannell
paragraphs: Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.

“With all major design updates, there’s a natural process where we take a bold leap forward, and then we continue to iterate,” said Apple's human interface designer, Shubham Kedia, during a predictably sleek keynote video. “Our team really appreciates your feedback, and we considered it deeply as we refined the new design.”

Not quite “Sorry, everyone, we messed up,” but for Apple, practically an apology tour. The subject was Liquid Glass, Apple’s most divisive interface design since at least iOS 7. Apple's Vision Pro mixed-reality headset (which itself flopped) inspired the translucent design language, and the company brought it to millions of other Apple devices.

The result was a mess—at odds with Steve Jobs’ famous line, “Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.” Liquid Glass started obsessed with gloss and effects, despite promises it would bring your content to the foreground. Yet Apple’s own press release showed interfaces with illegible text. Worse, users found constant reflections and flickering color shifts distracting, and a lack of clarity across devices hurt accessibility.

But iOS 27, alongside updates to Apple's other software platforms, signaled a shift in priorities after Kedia’s mea culpa. Kedia spoke of reincorporating design cornerstones in what was, if not quite a U-turn, then at least a rediscovery of a core principle: how it works. Instantly, interface elements across Apple devices gained greater clarity and structure, making it easier to tell apps' components from content. The most obvious change, though, was a slider.

Apple said it tuned Liquid Glass to diffuse complex content more effectively, keeping elements legible when above imagery and text. But it also acknowledged that not everyone wants the same thing—some users might prefer a more tinted look, and others “would like Liquid Glass to be even more clear.” You can now decide for yourself with the Liquid Design slider in Settings. For a company known for being opinionated, such bet-hedging was surprising but not unwelcome. Choice isn’t a bad thing, and now users had more of it.

“I immediately pushed that slider all the way to the most tinted setting, and pretty much all the legibility issues vanished,” Ben Rice McCarthy, an indie developer behind popular apps like Obscura and Indigo, tells WIRED. McCarthy has long criticized Liquid Glass. Now? Not so much.

“Liquid Glass introduced a lot of issues without adequate solutions, but this year’s operating systems solved or improved a lot of them,” McCarthy says. “There’s the adaptiveness of the interface. Buttons can grow into menus. Controls merge and divide like cells as you transition between views. Toolbars can expand and contract smoothly as the view changes size.”

Flexibility matters when resizing windows across any device. But while announcing its updates, Apple also dropped major hints that all but confirmed new hardware—it showed iPhone apps running on an iPad or a Mac could resize to a suspiciously specific shape that matched the rumored inner display dimensions of Apple’s upcoming folding phone.

When Apple showed off the iPhone Duo, everything clicked. Its passport-shaped display bucks the trend of iPhones and their rivals growing taller over the years. The Duo is wider and almost squat, and when opened, it naturally defaults to landscape, echoing the iPad Mini display.

Apple being Apple, it wanted to avoid the jarring jolt between displays that’s often evident on rival foldables, so it made content appear to move seamlessly from one screen to the other. That begins with the hardware. As Molly Anderson, Apple's vice president of Industrial Design, said at the September keynote: “To achieve this continuity, we designed iPhone Duo around a consistent aspect ratio that is the same across both displays.” But it’s the software—rooted in Liquid Glass—that sells the illusion.

The most arresting element is a fancy animation, which various folks in the Android space are now busy being “inspired” by. It reinforces the idea of a flowing interface. Meanwhile, Liquid Glass freed Apple from being prescriptive about where essential controls live. On the Duo, they sit at the side. When the phone’s closed, that frees up space for content. When it’s open, the controls stay in a consistent spot, so you never have to hunt for them. Reorient the device, and everything settles into the most appropriate place.

That’s form following function, not function being subservient to form. This device and its flexible interface don’t strictly need the Liquid Glass design language, but the two feel made for each other. Liquid Glass finally makes sense on the iPhone Duo—and with Apple’s other refinements, it’s starting to make sense elsewhere, too.
How much of this is happenstance is hard to say. Given Apple’s lead times, pure coincidence seems unlikely. And even if Liquid Glass wasn’t made with the Duo in mind, it adapts to it.

Liquid Glass feels more considered. It’s increasingly tuned for individual devices rather than governed by a “universal” aesthetic forced onto them all. The result is operating systems that feel solid rather than fragile, with interfaces less likely to fight content for your attention. On Macs and iPads, the Liquid Glass revamp now looks more like a love letter to Aqua—Apple's water-themed interface introduced in 2000. On the iPhone, it’s usable again. On the Duo, it’s a delight.

That’s not to say it’s perfect. “There’s some weirdness that hasn’t been fully resolved, and there needs to be a consistency to all these materials or the metaphors break down,” McCarthy says. “But overall, Liquid Glass is vastly improved.”

And it’s worth remembering that while the Duo is new, Liquid Glass is relatively young, too. As developer Steve Troughton-Smith wrote, “For some iPhone apps, even with keen developers, it will take six months to a year of work to properly support iPhone Duo. A lot of developers are still trying to finish the Liquid Glass transition they started last year.”
A useful reminder that transitions take time. But at least now, Apple’s vision looks clear.

items.title: Hillsong’s Former Pastor Is Rehashing His Beef With the Biebers
items.description: Remember Carl Lentz, the former Hillsong NYC pastor whose infidelity rocked the celebrity-megachurch community in 2020? Well, he and his wife are back with a new book, in which they revisit some old beef with their former congregants Hailey and Justin Bieber.
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: Remember Carl Lentz, the former Hillsong NYC pastor whose infidelity rocked the celebrity-megachurch community in 2020? Well, he and his wife are back with a new book, in which they revisit some old beef with their former congregants Hailey and Justin Bieber.

Lentz became a big name for anyone keeping track of the extended megachurch universe in the late 2010s, when he emerged as Bieber’s swaggy spiritual adviser. (He was also the lead pastor and co-founder of Hillsong NYC, the East Coast branch of Bieber’s beloved church, which was frequented by Chris Pratt, Selena Gomez, and NBA star Kevin Durant as well.) Lentz and Bieber seemed to have fallen out in 2020 after Hillsong’s then–global senior pastor Brian Houston wrote in a newsletter that Lentz had been dismissed from the church due to “leadership issues and breaches of trust, plus a recent revelation of moral failures.” Houston, another founder of Hillsong, resigned in 2022 after two women accused him of misconduct. Lentz admitted to both an affair with his family’s nanny and an Adderall addiction in the 2023 FX documentary The Secrets of Hillsong.

The Biebers unfollowed the Lentzes on social media in the wake of the scandal, fueling speculation that they wanted to distance themselves from their pastor and his transgressions. Now, Carl and Laura Lentz have co-authored a book about it all — it’s called Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations to Help Heal the Hurt, naturally — that offers more details about what happened between them and the Biebers. According to the Lentzes, once Carl’s infidelity began making headlines, Hailey and Justin forced them to move out of the NYC apartment the Biebers had lent them.

Per “Page Six,” Laura wrote that the family had been planning a move to Brooklyn “for months” when the Biebers stepped in with an offer to let them stay at their place in New York while they looked for their new home. The couple allegedly told the Lentz family to “use their place as long as needed” and to “take [their] time.” After Carl’s extramarital affair surfaced, however, the Lentzes claim the Biebers rescinded their hospitality with a righteous quickness.
“Somebody on Justin’s team [called] to say we needed to be out of his and Hailey’s apartment in the next 24 hours,” Laura wrote. “We hastily packed our things and loaded them into a rented U-Haul.”

Per “Page Six,” Carl felt the Biebers’ decision was unfair to his wife and kids. “I deserved to be kicked to the curb,” he wrote, “but I felt Laura and the kids were just innocent bystanders suffering once again for my sins.” Carl and Laura share three children, the youngest of whom was 11 at the time. The Biebers haven’t yet commented on the Lentzes’ fickle-landlord accusations.

Meanwhile, Carl and Laura are busy promoting their book, which was published last week. The 208-page book, which is marketed as an “unfiltered” look at the couple’s journey to “rekindle their love,” appears to be the Lentzes’ attempt to get back into the good graces of the megachurch community after both were fired from Hillsong in the aftermath of Carl’s affair. They also want the Biebers to know they’re not harboring any bad feelings.

Carl wrote that he totally understands now that he put the couple “in a precarious place on multiple levels” following the scandal, and that their relationship with the Lentzes dragged them into a “publicity nightmare they never asked for.” But you know who wasn’t afraid of the PR maelstrom? (Whoever you guess is going to be wrong.) It was Tyler Perry.

Apparently, Perry offered the Lentz family a port in the storm, allowing all five of them to move into his Manhattan Beach mansion after the Biebers kicked them out. That same year, Perry also lent one of his residences to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle after they stepped down as working royals and left the U.K. He was also recording Paw Patrol: The Movie at the time — you can’t accuse him of slowing down during the pandemic. (And if you’re wondering, Perry loves the Lentzes’ new book.)

These days, Hailey and Justin Bieber attend Churchome, another celebrity-loved megachurch with a Beverly Hills congregation that happens to have ties to Hillsong. But I’m sure everything there is fine!

items.title: 11 Hair Icons To Know, From Zendaya’s Hairstylist To TikTok’s Fave Trichologist
items.description: There’s a reason so many people reach for the kitchen scissors after a breakup: Hair is one of the most personal ways to change how you look — and how you feel. But it’s also a space for some of beauty’s most exciting experimentation, from gravity-defying updo
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: There’s a reason so many people reach for the kitchen scissors after a breakup: Hair is one of the most personal ways to change how you look — and how you feel. But it’s also a space for some of beauty’s most exciting experimentation, from gravity-defying updos and intricate braiding designs to colorists challenging our ideas about aging.

The pros behind those transformations don’t all work the same way. Some create the celebrity looks that take over your FYP; others are rethinking the products, techniques, and traditions that shape how we wear our hair. From wigmakers to scalp specialists, lash and brow artists, and entrepreneurs, the honorees of Bustle’s 2026 Beauty Icon Awards are pushing their respective crafts forward.
Ahead, meet the 11 experts helping shape the future of hair and beyond.
The Internet’s Trichologist: Abbey Yung

Dealing with dry ends, an oily scalp, or hair that just won’t grow? Abbey Yung has a routine for that. The certified trichologist and social-media star, who’s amassed nearly 5 million followers across TikTok and Instagram, shares tips and product recommendations for just about every hair concern. (And many of her favorites are drugstore finds.) Her recommendations come with something more useful than hype: an explanation of the science behind them.
The Celebrity Lash Queen: Alanah Sahaba

The hair on your head isn’t the only thing worth thinking about — at least, according to Los Angeles-based lash artist Alanah Sahaba. After leaving college in 2020, she started doing lashes full time, quickly building a celebrity clientele that includes Kehlani, Quen Blackwell, and Megan Thee Stallion. From barely-there fox eye sets to colorful, anime-inspired designs, her work is about more than just adding length and volume. She treats lashes like another form of self-expression, creating looks that feel like an extension of each client’s personal style.
The Red-Carpet Trendsetter: Coree Moreno

If you’ve found yourself obsessing over Zendaya’s hair lately, Coree Moreno may be the reason. The goddess braid that sparked countless TikTok tutorials? He was behind it. He also created her piecey pixie cut. But Zendaya isn’t the only star who trusts him with her hair: His client list includes Hollywood names like Chase Infiniti and Madison Bailey. With a knack for working with natural texture, Moreno isn’t just following trends — he’s helping set them.
The Ayurveda Advocate: Diipa Buller-Khosla

Most people pick up a beauty trick or two from their mom, but Diipa Büller-Khosla got a whole brand’s worth. Raised by an ayurvedic doctor and dermatologist, she grew up surrounded by traditional Indian beauty rituals — and in 2021, turned those childhood lessons into Indē Wild, a hair and skin care brand that combines ancient wisdom with modern science. Five years later, it’s landed on Sephora shelves, introducing those 5,000-year-old traditions to a whole new audience.
The Editorial Architect: Guido Palau

Cher, Madonna, Beyoncé — some people are so iconic they don't need a last name, and in the fashion world, hairstylist Guido Palau is one of them. He got his start at London’s legendary Vidal Sassoon salon in the early ’80s, before a gig with George Michael put him on the map. Since then, he’s become a defining force in editorial and runway hair, creating everything from architectural updos for Schiaparelli to old Hollywood waves for Lana Del Rey’s W Magazine cover. With bombshell blowouts among his recent credits, Palau continues to shape the looks that define beauty's biggest moments.
The Gray Hair Guru: Jack Martin
Follow: @jackmartincolorist

Gray hair isn’t something to hide — just ask Jack Martin. The Arizona-based colorist has built a career out of helping women embrace their silver strands, counting Andie MacDowell and Sharon Osbourne among his celebrity clients. Using his signature French blending technique, he weaves together shades of silver, gray, and white for results that look every bit as dimensional as any good blond or brunette dye job. In an industry that often treats aging as something to disguise, Martin offers a different vision — one that doesn’t begin with covering up.
The A-List Brow Artist: Kelley Baker

Even if you don’t know Kelley Baker by name, you’ve almost certainly seen her work. Based in Beverly Hills, she got her start as a makeup artist before finding her niche in brows. Now, she’s responsible for some of Hollywood’s most recognizable arches, working with everyone from Kim Kardashian and Megan Fox to Drake. Whether she’s carving out a bold brow or a softer, more natural frame, her work is proof that a few strategically plucked hairs can do a lot of heavy lifting.
The Hollywood Hairstylist: Mara Roszak

For hairstylist Mara Roszak, inspiration has always been close to home. Growing up in L.A.’s Laurel Canyon, hairstylist Mara Roszak developed an appreciation for the laid-back, California-cool aesthetic that’s since become her signature. Her clients include Emma Stone, Zoe Saldaña, and Sandra Bullock, but there’s more to her perfectly undone looks than meets the eye. Roszak has been honing her craft since her teens, landing her first celebrity client, Sarah Michelle Gellar, before she even got her license. More than two decades later, she’s channeled that experience into her own hair care brand, Roz, with a simple premise: Effortless hair should actually be effortless.
The Wig Whisperer: Noah Scott

The Internet loves a wig allegation — but when Noah Scott is behind the hair, good luck spotting the lace front. After teaching himself how to make wigs through YouTube tutorials at just 8 years old, he got his big break creating Ariana Grande’s signature extra-long ponytail for her 2019 Coachella performance. Since then, his celebrity clientele has grown to include everyone from Lindsay Lohan to Zara Larsson, all turning to him for custom hairpieces. But you don’t need to be an A-lister to get in on the fun. Through his online store, WhatWigs, he’s making red-carpet-worthy hair transformations available to anyone who feels like switching up their style.
The Braid Specialist: Tashana Miles
Follow: @tasha_worldofstyles

Tashana Miles isn’t just a stylist — she’s an artist whose medium is braiding. Whether she’s creating sculptural Bantu knots or geometric cornrows, she approaches each style as an opportunity to experiment with shape and design. That creativity, paired with meticulous technique, has made her a favorite of A$AP Rocky and Beyoncé. For anyone looking for inspiration for their next protective style, Miles offers a reminder that braids can be as individual as the person wearing them.
The Extension Innovator: Tendai Moyo

Tendai Moyo thinks synthetic braiding hair is overdue for an upgrade. As co-founder and CEO of Ruka Hair, she’s challenging the industry’s reliance on conventional plastic-based fibers with Synths 2, a collagen-based alternative designed to look and feel like human hair. The patent-pending material is also designed to be biodegradable and withstand heat styling. With Ruka expanding its retail presence, Moyo is pushing the conversation beyond how braiding hair looks to how it’s made.

items.title: Exclusive: Joe Amabile Shares His Thoughts On That 'Bachelor' Casting Rumor
items.description: Bachelor Nation’s Joe Amabile Is Sprinting To The Finish Line
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Bachelor Nation’s Joe Amabile Is Sprinting To The Finish Line
The reality TV star opens up about recovering from brain surgery, marrying Serena Pitt, and a Bachelor casting rumor.

Joe Amabile has had quite the eventful summer, to say the least. The Bachelor Nation alum (aka Grocery Store Joe) had to undergo brain surgery after doctors found a “blueberry-sized” tumor. However, through his recovery, the 40-year-old refused to lose sight of one of his goals: running the New York Marathon on Nov. 1.

“When I got my unexpected diagnosis of having a brain tumor and having to go through brain surgery, it was a goal that I set for myself to just keep me motivated and keep my mindset positive,” he tells Bustle. “Brain surgery is out of your control. I’m not going in my own head like the doctors are, so it was just nice to give myself that control.”

Naturally, Amabile’s medical crisis made him reflect on many aspects of his life, from friendships to his financial situation. He partnered with Northwestern Mutual to share why getting your finances in order is essential. “It’s so important to be flexible and able to switch things when something unexpected happens,” he says. “That’s what Northwestern Mutual does so well.”

Marrying his Bachelor in Paradise costar Serena Pitt gave him a new outlook on saving. “Before getting married, I don’t think I had any financial goals,” he says. “It’s just so important to save money and put it away for a family. You’re trying to build a life together, and regardless of what people wanna say, money is very important.”

After a gradual but successful recovery, Amabile looks forward to reconnecting with some of his fellow reality TV star runners. “I run it with Zac Clark every year, and Matt James is running it again,” he says. “I’m friends with Dylan Efron, and he’s running it.”
Below, Amabile opens up about his marathon journey, his wife’s support, and his thoughts on Bachelor Nation’s future.
After your recovery, what has become a bigger priority in your life, and what new goals have you set for yourself?

Being vulnerable is one. I wasn’t really vulnerable on social media at all, and once I decided to share, it’s honestly helped me so much. It’s comforting to hear other people’s stories about going through something similar and having good outcomes. Right now my goal is not to do too much, because I tend to overdo it.
Tell me how Serena’s been supporting you during this marathon journey.

[Laughs] Uh... I don’t know if she is so happy that I’m running the marathon. She is OK with it and will support me, but she’d rather I didn’t run it, if I’m gonna be completely honest. But she’s been wonderful. I’ve never been through [a major health scare], and neither has she, but she’s always been by my side. Her resilience and strength are a testament to who she is as a person.
You two are one of the few couples who are still standing from Bachelor Nation. What do you see for the future of the Bachelor franchise?

Oh, that’s an interesting question. It depends on who they choose as the Bachelor and the way they cast the women. There’s a lot of competition out there, but there’s still only one Bachelor and Bachelorette, so I think the show will be OK.
What do you think of the rumor that producers are eyeing Dr. Mike to be the next Bachelor?

That would be a great pick. He doesn’t need it financially, and his social following is already massive, so I’m sure that’ll help. If you’re looking for someone who is there for the right reasons, I think it’s him.
How has Bachelor Nation supported you during this health journey, whether it’s the fans or your fellow contestants?
So many people have just showered me with love and support. So many Bachelor alumni have reached out and sent me Uber Eats and DoorDash. Honestly, it’s almost been too gracious.
Your fellow Bachelor Nation star Joey Graziadei just returned from filming The Traitors. Would you ever consider doing that one day?
If they asked, I would be lying if I said no.
Do you want to be a Faithful or a Traitor?
I don’t have a preference. The way the show’s set up right now, it takes a lot of luck at the beginning, no matter if you’re a Traitor or a Faithful. It’s a little bit of a popularity contest.
How do you hope you’ll come out of the marathon, and what message do you hope to send?

I hope to finish. I don’t think I’ll beat my last two scores, but I want people to get that you can do anything. As long as you set that goal, something unexpected happening doesn’t necessarily have to change the outcome. It just changes the path.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Sophia Bush Has Gifted Cheryl Strayed’s ‘Tiny Beautiful Things’ More Than 30 Times
items.description: One Nightstand With Sophia Bush
items.author: Charlotte Owen
paragraphs: One Nightstand With Sophia Bush
The actor and activist, who’s just released a new memoir, shares four books that have shaped her worldview, including works by Gloria Steinem and Cheryl Strayed.
In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.

For activist and actor Sophia Bush, writing her memoir, And I Will Tell You Mine: Notes from a Life in Progress, proved a surprisingly challenging experience. “When you are a thinker, a writer, when you’re privileged enough to have regular therapy, you really think you know your sh*t and then your book drags you,” she says. “It’s horrible. I called a few friends who are writers and I was like, ‘Why do we do this? Who let us do this?’”

Bush has been in the public eye since being cast as Brooke Davis in One Tree Hill in 2003, bringing the added complication of fame. “If you are a gorgeous writer, like a personal hero of mine, Cheryl Strayed, and you write the bone marrow of your life and that book becomes famous, you’re allowed to do that,” she says. “If you are someone the world perceives as famous in whatever way they do, you don’t get the same carte blanche to talk about your life.”

For that reason, Bush returned to the fundamentals she learned while studying journalism at the University of Southern California. “I wrote the New York Times piece, the investigative reporting of some of my life experiences to get them out, and then I had to decide what to reduce,” she says, nodding to intimate chapters that cover her divorces and what she describes as workplace sexual harassment. “Over a hundred pages of my book I pulled out and literally burned. I had a little ritual all to myself and I burned them. It didn’t feel like something I owed to everyone else. I don’t think you have to give someone your whole heart.”

For the chapters about her experience shooting One Tree Hill, she also sought consent from those involved before moving forward. “We’ve got an incredible group chat, but I chose to have individual conversations with every single person and individual dissemination of pages and things because I didn’t want anybody to feel swayed by the group,” she recalls, adding that she even anonymized two people who she “smushed into one.”

The goal was to protect the relationships they’d built with each other, despite the odds. “When I started working on TV in the early aughts, the machinery loved to input women and chew them up and spit them out,” she says. “The benefit to the machine itself is to cast you, the woman, in a role that they can then clickbait to death, but that’s not who you are. The hours are crazy. If you have a not particularly great boss, like we all didn’t, you’ll be taught to compete instead of collaborate. You’ll be pitted against each other and then won’t understand why suddenly everything feels weird. And you can’t talk about it because you can’t have a fight with your friends at work. So then it buries and it festers and it just cements.”

Bush, stepmother to the two children of her wife, former US soccer goalkeeper Ashlyn Harris, compares the craft of writing to raising a child. “Everyone I know who’s a parent has thoughts about what parenting will be, and then they meet the person their child is in every stage and they are that person,” she says. “Nothing you do is going to change who they intrinsically are. You hope to raise them well, you hope to make them feel confident, you hope to love them enough that the world doesn’t break them, but they are who they are.” Her book proved to be similar.
“The book is going to be what it wants to be,” she says. “You think you know the book you’re going to write, and then it pulls you on a journey.”
Keep reading to discover four of Bush’s favorite reads.

Bush’s first selection is Gloria Steinem’s 2015 memoir My Life on the Road, tracing the activist’s life from childhood through the 2010s. The morning Bush joins One Nightstand, she’d learned of Steinem’s passing at 92. “It was just such a surreal thing to sit and read over these gorgeous articles. I knew she hadn’t been feeling well,” she says. “Strangely, some friends of ours were talking about the next talking circle we wanted to host with her. And I said, ‘I know she’s not well, but she’s Gloria.’ I think we really thought she would just be with us forever.”

Steinem’s memoir made an impression on Bush when it came out, but it became a true North Star while writing her own. “It’s very surreal and it’s an interesting thing having just finished my first memoir to think about the memoirs and the life stories like hers, like this book that truly shaped me,” she says. “I think about the fact that I grew up a fan of hers and she became a friend. She became a person I could text. I will never not be so grateful that I got to be in her orbit.”

Steinem’s work also informed Bush’s own activism. “One of the things I learned from her was that I’ll show up for the small organization that’s working in one town on a border in Texas to protect migrant children in the same way that I’ll show up for a federal election,” she says. “It’s so clear for me how the political is, in fact, personal. And that’s her whole thesis. I think when you know it, it doesn’t have to feel overwhelming. It actually is so empowering. You realize that each of us has a hand on a lever of change, and that makes me feel optimistic rather than pessimistic.”

One of the last conversations she had with Steinem was on FaceTime. “She held a talking circle on women’s health, and I was working in Los Angeles and I couldn’t be there, but my partner was there and a group of our best friends were there,” she says. “It was so lovely just to see her, and she grabbed my partner and was like, ‘I love her.’ I said, ‘I know, right?’ She was like, ‘I’m just so happy for you two.’”
Her second choice is Tiny Beautiful Things, a collection of responses from Cheryl Strayed’s advice column “Dear Sugar.”

Bush has purchased and gifted the book more than 30 times. “There are things from running the gamut of Eastern and Western tradition that I understand to be universally true about humanity,” she says. “I believe Cheryl’s book to be one of the most spiritually sacred texts that any of our peers has ever written, because what she’s doing is modeling love out loud and in the hardest moments and in some of the most beautiful, and it is so exacting and yet so gentle.”

Some of Strayed’s advice has had an enduring effect on her. “We are all so much more than the worst mistake we’ve ever made or the greatest success we’ve ever had. We’re human beings in the center of all of that,” she says. “I think especially for women, the world encourages us to just self-obsess about our failures, or to wonder what everyone thinks of us, or to be so ashamed for existing or speaking, God forbid. We have to figure out how to divest from that, and I think we do that in community.”

That said, she’s judicious about giving advice. “I'm a little on the spectrum,” she says. “I've had to learn that my neuro-spiciness that goes like, ‘You're not alone. I have a thing.’ Calm down. Slow down. Like a Cheryl, I want to make people feel seen and know they're not alone. I also know that the immediate, ‘You're not alone. I can also offer you a terrible thing or a hard thing or a bad boss or whatever.’ It’s not always helpful.”

She continues: “As a person who has crazy pattern recognition because of the way my brain is wired, I can go big 30,000 feet: ‘Well, this is the system and this is what's going on with you and this is what women are dealing with in the workplace,’” she explains. “Also not always helpful. I love the data. Not everybody needs it.”

Her third pick is The Bitter Southerner, a triannual magazine coming out of the American South. Although Bush is California born and raised, she feels a strong connection to the region. “I spent 10 years in North Carolina. I’ve lived in Texas, and I’m madly in love with a woman from Florida,” she says.

It’s also been at the center of much of her activism. “The South is so culturally rich and has also been so historically under-resourced and taken from,” she says. “In all of my travels everywhere, some of my favorite fellow organizers, some of the most hilarious radical minds I know, come from my Southern friends that are like, ‘It’s f*ck this sh*t o’clock, and we're going to fix America.’ And, I’m like, ‘OK!’”

Bush says living in North Carolina while filming One Tree Hill was an enlightening experience. “It was very strange to move somewhere and be walking down a sidewalk downtown next to my neighbors of color and have to pass Confederate statues,” she says. “Interestingly enough, moving there enabled me to begin on the journey of having conversations about disparity in real time, not talking about what happened historically, but about: What were the patterns of our history that still exist today?”

Her final pick is Parable of the Sower by Octavia E. Butler. Written in 1993 and set in 2024, the novel follows a California on the brink of collapse due to climate change and social decay. “In the year 2026, it’s weird to revisit it because you realize she’s a gorgeous writer and perhaps a psychic,” she says. “One of the things that inspires me most about her is she wrote her lead female to be someone who is willing to ask the questions that most people are too scared to answer, that most people want to ignore because they are on the precipice of something scary and they're trying to cling to what was, but what was will never exist.”

Strangely, Bush says Butler’s dystopian world has a hint of optimism. “What I think it encourages is readers to be bold enough to envision something we can build together,” she says. “We only survive in community. The only way through is to build together and everyone’s experience — the diversity of race, generation, economic status, all of it — is actually what gives a community the amount of thought and the different experience levels to be able to build something together.”

items.title: I'm 29, I Make $110K & I'm Deep Into The Wedding Season Of My Life
items.description: A Week In Denver, CO On A $110,000 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In Denver, CO On A $110,000 Salary
This week: a data scientist working in politics who makes $110,000 per year and spends some of it on a ginger stick-on moustache and eyebrows that she ordered for her sheriff costume. YEEEEHAWWWW!

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Editor's note: This is a follow-up diary. You can read the previous one here.
Location: Denver, Colorado

Joint Income/Financial Setup: My boyfriend and I moved in together about a year ago and are working towards combining our finances in a way that feels right for us. We have a joint RocketMoney account where we create a monthly budget and can generally monitor whether we are spending more than we take in. We split things proportionally to our income (he has been laid off twice in the last year #journalism and cobbles together several recurring freelance jobs while job searching for a full-time role in the brand content space), so I pay more in rent, I pay for his healthcare and I help subsidize his therapy (it's his first time going and I wanted to make sure he had as few barriers as possible!). I cover more of the dinners, entertainment, and such, but we split groceries equally. Given that we don't have any joint accounts or anything, I'll report on just my spending!
IRA (old 401k rolled over): $72,951
Various investments (managed by Merrill Lynch): $280,004
Paycheck Amount (2x month): $2,938.32

Housing Costs: $1,100 (my boyfriend and I have a sweet deal on a two-bed in Denver. He pays $575 and I pay $1,100, not including utilities. It's not our dream apartment by any means, but it's amazing for the price and allows us a great lifestyle).
NYT subscription: ~$10 (news, games and food).
Local mutual aid organization: $17
Colorado abortion fund: $20
Phone: $0 (yes, I continue to mooch off my parents).
Fox One: $21.82 (going to cancel this as soon as the World Cup is over!)
Health insurance: $0 (luckily my company pays).
Health insurance for my boyfriend: $~230 (pre tax, my company covers 70% as he is listed as domestic partner).
Therapy: $400-600 (I pay out of pocket $200 a session, which is steep, but I've been working with this therapist for years and I love her).
Therapy for my boyfriend: $75-100 (his copay is $50 per session so I split with him).
401(k): $231 (pre-tax, employer matched 75%)
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

Yes! I grew up between Brooklyn and Westchester, New York — both affluent communities in which everyone I knew was on the college track. My parents and stepparents and grandparents and everyone else had attended college, and many had master's or PhDs. When I was a senior in high school, I learned that my grandparents and parents had been saving for my college education since my birth but that I would still have to take out student loans. In my affluent community, no one talked about needing to take out loans, only “dream schools” and “following your heart,” so I was really ashamed (which I now know is stupid. Financial transparency is empowering!). However, my mom worked at NYU at the time so if I went there I got a 90% discount. I was on the fence but ultimately decided to go to NYU over other private and public schools and it was the best decision my 18-year-old self ever made. Graduating without any debt, and with money that my parents had left over, has changed my life and I'm incredibly lucky to have had that option.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

Going to school in Westchester, I often felt less privileged and a bit different than my peers. My mom was the breadwinner in the family and got on the train to NYC early every day with the dads, while many of my friends' mothers were stay-at-home moms who played tennis and were involved in PTA. My friends took international vacations every year and had multiple Juicy tracksuits (tbt to 2006) but we had to ask my grandparents to help out with my flute lessons, and I only ever got one Juicy tracksuit because it was on major discount at Filene's Basement (lol). That being said, I never wanted for anything serious and am so grateful that my mom instilled the value of budgeting in me early. Starting in high school, I got a sizeable allowance ($100!) every month for doing chores but that was it; there was no asking for movie tickets or pizza money. This taught me to save for the things I wanted and I do feel like I have a better grasp on money now than many of my friends who were raised more privileged than me. My dad is a documentary filmmaker who had his own production company, but had to close it when my stepmom got sick in my early high school years. He then did odd jobs (filmmaking-related), while always pursuing 3-4 personal projects at a time. When I was <12 he told me he was in $70K+ debt, but between an inheritance from his parents and help from my stepmom's very affluent parents, they were able to provide for my brothers and me. His lack of job stability (and my stepdad's, who is also in the film business) always made me want to get a steady job and definitely shaped my relationship to money and career.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

When I was 12, I got a summer job as a counselor at a day camp in the Hamptons. I was paid $100 a week under the table but I was SO excited. My older cousin worked there and we spent the following five summers chasing after other cute counselors, going to the beach and engaging in standard teenage mischief. Although I wasn't paid great, I was able to charge an outrageous amount for babysitting ($25 an hour as a 15-year-old in 2011?!) because of the wealth in the Hamptons and therefore had plenty of money for groceries, eating out and even saving. Over the five summers I saved a few thousand dollars, which helped immensely in college.
Did you worry about money growing up?

Not really. I always had food on the table, lots of clothes, and a new gadget at Hanukkah. As mentioned above, growing up affluent in a VERY affluent community definitely made me feel less than sometimes, but I never seriously worried.
Do you worry about money now?

Yes and no. A few years ago (during my previous Money Diary!) I went on medical leave from my job due to depression and burnout and ended up working for over a year doing odds jobs: front of house at a local bakery, babysitting/dog walking, and data collector at a museum. My salary during that time went from ~$115K to ~$30K and I learned A LOT about myself and how to be happy with way less. I worked harder than I ever had before (4:30 a.m. wake-up calls!!), and met incredible people who were grinding to put themselves through college, etc. It really put my privilege into major perspective and made me realize how much of a bubble I had been living in. Last summer, when my boyfriend got laid off, I kicked my "white collar" job search back into high gear and ended up back working as a data scientist (similar work to what I had been doing before I burned out). Though I initially took the job because we needed it and was apprehensive about going into politics, I have come to really really enjoy the day-to-day and my team. I have much better appreciation for my salary, and save ~$800-1000 a month easily, while treating myself and my loved ones (in large part because of my low rent). That being said, I do worry about my future goals and how to get them to come to fruition financially. I really really really want to own a small house or townhome, and even with a down payment ready to go (and I am SO lucky for that) the month-to-month costs seem forever out of reach. I look at 2-bed, 2-bath listings near me in the $450-550K range and see that the monthly expenses would be over double what I pay now, which does not feel justifiable. I also want a child or children and simply don't know how it would be possible with my boyfriend and I's current earning potential. (My boyfriend works in a field where lay offs happen A LOT, especially with AI, and he believes he won't ever make $100K+ a year). He wants to get married and have a wedding and I can't see how we'd justify 10s of thousands of dollars on a party — let alone how he would afford a ring. I'm incredibly financially lucky and I do not worry about our day to day in the slightest, which is such a blessing, but as an everlasting worrywort and pragmatist, I do worry about our future goals and how to make them achievable.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

Six months after college, I moved in with a roommate in NYC and became responsible for everything except healthcare and phone bills. I had a decent paying job and could cover all my expenses fairly easily. My financial safety net is primarily myself and I have a few months of expenses saved and much more in stocks. When I was making less than my boyfriend he treated me to dinners and paid more in rent, so we do lean on each other financially in that way, which I love, it feels great to have that mutual support. That being said, I could always move back in with either of my parents if I really needed to. While I love living in Denver and definitely do not want to move back to NY any time soon, it wouldn't be the worst option and I would likely do that over liquidating my investments.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.

Yes, quite a bit and I'm incredibly privileged. In college, my step-grandpa passed away, and since my stepmom had passed as well, $80,000 of his life insurance payout went to me. In addition, post-college my mom and dad gave me the remainder of their college funds for me ($40,000 and $20,000, respectively). All of this has gone into investments and remains untouched. And of course, my parents paid for my college tuition, books and housing. Last year when I was working odd jobs my parents paid for my plane tickets home, and when I faced a particularly tough string of job rejections my mom sent me ~$200 bucks to cheer me up. After many years of feeling less privileged than my peers, I realized just how privileged I am and how rare of a situation I am in! I want to fight for others to have safety nets (at the very least lets get medicare for all) and have dignified lives in the way I've been able to.
10:00 p.m. — Take my dog out again and head to bed by 11:30 p.m.

I usually track my spending pretty closely through the Rocket Money app, but I enjoyed the experience of thoroughly journaling about my day, and I hope to do that part a bit more consistently. Adding up my bills and net worth and such at the beginning also helped to reinforce just how lucky I am, and how much of a safety net I (and to a lesser extent E.) have. Helped alleviate some of the anxiety and rumination I experience around our long term financial future. Sure — we might not be as well off as my friends who have a $300K+ joint income, we might not own a house or have money for a wedding, but we're doing alright, and for that I'm very grateful.
The first step to getting your financial life in order is tracking what you spend — to try on your own, check out our guide to managing your money every day. For more Money Diaries, click here.
