items.title: Monica Veloz Wants You to Grieve Out Loud
items.description: I consider myself a pretty private person. I’m a journalist. My job, as my j-school professors drilled into my head, is to tell other people’s stories, not mine. On social media, I mostly post career highlights, leaving my romantic relationships and other inti
items.author: Raquel Reichard
paragraphs: I consider myself a pretty private person. I’m a journalist. My job, as my j-school professors drilled into my head, is to tell other people’s stories, not mine. On social media, I mostly post career highlights, leaving my romantic relationships and other intimate details of my life a mystery. It’s intentional. It’s protective. It’s how I want it. And maybe some of it is cultural. After all, Latinas are often taught not to air our dirty laundry in public. And yet, come July 2027, some of the darkest and hardest moments of my life will be sitting on a bookstore shelf near you.

My debut memoir, The Best Love Stories Are Between Friends, will be out in the world, and in its pages, strangers and relatives will read about experiences I never shared with anyone. Why? Because the grief of losing my best friend, Angelica Alvarez, to stage 4 small-cell carcinoma lung cancer four years ago nearly killed me, too. And talking about her, our friendship, and the life-affirming power of girlfriends that sustain us, even in their death, is what helped pull me back to life.

Sometimes, shamelessly allowing our grief to be seen, even in a culture that tells us to suffer in silence and move on, is what helps us carry it, and what allows those around us to carry theirs, too.

Monica Veloz, aka Monicastylemuse, understands this, too. The beloved Dominican-American content creator and beauty influencer is used to being honest about the challenges she faces as an Afro-Latina or her journey through motherhood. So when her own mother, Mama Muse, died of stage four gastric cancer, she mourned publicly, out loud, as her community of more than 400,000 followers on Instagram and Youtube (respectively) bore witness.

In this episode, we speak with Monica about losing her favorite person, the loneliness of grief, and what it means to mourn out loud and in public without shame or fear of judgment. We explore the power of grieving on your own terms, honoring your loved ones unapologetically, and finding ways to keep those relationships alive long after death.

items.title: I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s
items.description: I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s
items.author: Raquel Reichard
paragraphs: I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s
"I wanted so desperately to go away to camp for myself, to play tug-of-war, toast marshmallows, and then whisper under covers to a group of girlfriends I only saw a couple weeks every summer."

"I stood amid the towering trees, taking it all in, grateful for the younger body that carried me up the trail and the older, more mature mind that knew to pause and appreciate the beauty around me. "

"I remember watching the sunset that last night and how my campmates and I ended our trip by singing Camp Rock’s “This Is Me” — just as we would have if it was 2008, when the Disney Channel classic dropped, when we were all still teens just imagining camp days like this one."

items.title: Drew Starkey’s Disappearing Tricks
items.description: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:
items.author: Emma Madden
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:

At 3am, the insomniac is most awake. His mind raves, his heart thumps against the pillow, and the rest of the world falls silent somewhere else. “In a real dark night of the soul, it is always three o’clock in the morning, day after day,” wrote F. Scott Fitzgerald in a 1936 essay. Drew Starkey posted that quote to his Facebook, among others about sleeplessness from Walt Whitman and Albert Einstein, when he was 17. In his own dark-souled hour, Starkey would smoke some weed, read Tolkien, and say to himself over and over: “I can’t sleep.”

Starkey was plagued by several ailments as a teenager. He’d lie awake at night, seething with extreme stomach pain from a hiatal hernia. His doctor advised him to stick to a paleo diet. Starkey has never publicly discussed either the stomach pain or the insomnia. “I don’t know how you found out about this. It’s so wild to me. I haven’t thought about it in ages, but I know exactly what you’re talking about,” he says. He is referring in particular to a piece he wrote for his university’s literary anthology about his sleeplessness. I read it and immediately felt I understood him better. “Years of difficulty sleeping sent me out in to (sic) a black sea without any direction. The distinction between me and the world outside of my thoughts became blurred during the night. In this process, I lost myself,” he wrote.
“I’ve been an insomniac since I was 13,” he tells me today. “I still have a lot of trouble sleeping. I become much more creative and alive at night, and maybe I do lose something of myself at night.”

There is something about this loss of self that resembles his understanding of acting. He views his work, ultimately, as an act of sublimation: “In every way, you have to submit yourself,” he says, paraphrasing a Kristen Stewart quote. In the long, wide night, he fantasised about putting himself somewhere else. He became obsessed with the slow drip of time.
“I still ruminate on it quite a bit. I have a weird skill of guessing what time it is.”
Without looking, I ask him to tell me the time.
“3:38pm,” he says, cold as a clock.

So: it is 3:38pm in New York City. Starkey has just wrapped a day of press for the final season of Outer Banks. For hours, he has been subject to the glamorous indignities of today’s press junket. “Yeah, it was a lot of playing games with my castmates,” he says. All day long, he has been playing the role of “Drew Starkey.” He goes to places he wouldn’t ordinarily go, wearing clothes that aren’t his. Usually, that means head-to-toe Dior; Médaillon loafers, which he tries to wear as often as he can get away with. (“I just love those buckles.”)

He has gone from the teenager who wore beige chinos to the best-looking version of himself: groomed and styled by professionals. His sandy-blond hair is spiked at the back of his head; he has a closely shaved beard. His lips are pinkish memory foam, his husky-dog eyes forever sparkling and limpid. Physically, he is absurdly suited to male superstardom. Temperamentally, he appears resistant to it.

As Starkey climbs higher up the Hollywood food chain, this might be the last time we speak before he reaches the loftiest echelons of fame. “The trick is to treat it all like you’re playing a character, because you are,” he says. And, to ensure he “stays sane,” he says, “there are things about myself that I want to keep for myself. So while I’m presenting myself, I’m also protecting a version of myself. It feels like an unnatural process to let millions of people know your actual nature.”

Starkey understands that all of us perform ourselves for one another; he’s just doing it on a much larger and more literal stage. The character “Drew Starkey” that exists onscreen transfers to parties, red carpets, fancy rooms where he might not otherwise go. “You have to lean into a specific version of yourself,” he says, “as opposed to, say, the person you are at home.” Today, back in his hotel room, he seems closer to that back-home self. His voice is low and largely unemotional, but warm. His energy has a low-key gravity to it, a kind of inwardness that seems remote without quite becoming aloof. If he took one of those aura photos, I’d imagine the colour around him would be a soft duck-egg blue.

After a long day as Drew Starkey, he has changed into a blue-striped shirt and dark-blue jeans. Nearby, his publicist wears a pair of sunglasses jewelled with Claire’s gems, the letters R A F E spelled out in friendship-bracelet beads. It was gifted to him by an Outer Banks fan. Hundreds have been following Starkey all day. They still wait outside his hotel room as we speak.

For seven years, Starkey played Rafe Cameron in Outer Banks, a character he says he knew “inside and out. I could defend him, make cases for him.” The last scene he ever filmed as Rafe was a pickup shot of him walking through the woods and breaking through a treeline. “Then I heard, okay, Drew, that’s a wrap,” he says, “and then I walked about 20 yards away and just started crying.”
He describes it as grief. “It was the last time that I was gonna get to play this person. It felt like losing someone.” I wonder if some of that grief was also for the loss of home.

The show was filmed in Charleston, South Carolina, close enough to his hometown that he could spend his summers back at his family home. “I didn’t know if I’d get that time again,” he says. “It’s where I’ve spent most of my time these past seven years.”

Starkey grew up in Asheville, North Carolina. His first memory is trailing through the apple orchards near his Appalachian home. His first word was “apple.” His first, and perhaps most enduring, dream was to own a little piece of land in Asheville and tend his own orchard.

For years, Outer Banks allowed him to remain relatively close to that life. Now, the farther he gets from home and into Hollywood, the farther he reaches for roles that take him outside himself. In his breakout film role as Eugene Allerton in Luca Guadagnino’s Queer, he played an American expatriate in Mexico City who becomes the fixation of William Lee, played by Daniel Craig. The performance required a vanishing act from him: Eugene is self-effacing and withholding to the point of opacity. Starkey played him with great restraint, not allowing any of the character’s interiority to peek through onto the surface. It was the inverse of Rafe, whose every feeling overpowers the characters around him.

In every role, Starkey appears an actor of great charm, imagination, surrender, and command. He can play good and evil. He can play both top and bottom. He is drawn to characters who fuck, or, as he puts it, “Characters who have their own kinks about life.” Since he has played characters who are both submissive and dominant, I ask whether he sees acting as a kind of power play – not only sexually, but in the more fundamental sense of determining who controls a scene and who yields to it.
“Absolutely. There’s a sub and dom in every scene,” he says. “And I think the more you lean into who has control in the room, the closer you can get to the truth of what a scene and what a story is.”

In his latest role as Cyrus in Adam Wingard’s A24 slasher-action movie Onslaught, he plays a government agent who leans a little leather daddy: bleach-blond hair, dyed eyebrows, almost unrecognisable as Drew Starkey. Starkey relished the transformation. “I wanted to take it as far as he could,” he says. “I would like to seek things out that are as far removed from myself as possible.”

His recent roles have carried him farther and farther away from the YA version of himself that made him famous. As he was wrapping the last season of Outer Banks, he quickly started learning how to play guitar and piano and sing for Deep Cuts, A24’s adaptation of Holly Brickley’s novel about a music-obsessed couple. Now, he can play four or five songs “really well,” he says. He studied with Blake Mills, the virtuoso guitarist and producer, while director Sean Durkin made Starkey and castmate Cailee Spaeny a playlist to get them into the 2000s of it all, filled with Wilco, the Strokes, and Red House Painters.

Then there was King Snake, Jeff Nichols’ Southern Gothic film, which he wrapped in July in Arkansas alongside Margaret Qualley. They play a young couple who inherit a haunted farm. The material brought him back to the old folk tales his Appalachian relatives told around campfires – the stories that made the mountains feel eerily mythical and thick with lore.

Qualley, who also grew up in Asheville, North Carolina, turned out to belong to that world, too. “Acting with her felt like cosmic intervention,” he says. Starkey had first met her when he was nine, when he spent time at her mother’s house, a family friend. Years later, they found themselves in the same orbit again.
“I went up to her at a party and was like, I met you when we were nine,” he says.
“Our parents were friends,” he told her, before eventually getting the recognition he was waiting for: “Ohhhh.”
It sounds like the sort of anecdote that will eventually calcify into a story Starkey tells over and over during the film’s press run.

For now, Starkey comes without the Hollywood lacquer. He is forthcoming and gracious in conversation, but contractually faithful. Can he address the rumours that he’ll play Cyclops in the upcoming X-Men reboot? “Can’t do that,” he says. American Psycho? “Nope.” What about the film he wrapped in early October? “Nope” again.

Every topic besides those is a concession. He says he still gets nervous in the days leading up to a press appearance or a day on set. But once the cameras are rolling, something else happens. “Disappearing into characters feels like a protective layer,” he says.

In every single role, just like in the grief he felt when he finally had to let go of Rafe after several years, there is “a sacrifice.” “I view the work like I’m some kind of martyr. I use the work to lose myself,” he says.

He says he’s been this way his entire life, a martyr to his passions. “If I didn’t do well at a basketball game in school the world would literally feel like it’s ending,” he says. “For me, I have to perform at the highest level, or it’s nothing to me.” Now, approaching 33, he says he feels like he’s “maturing.” “Like I’m realising my old way of thinking isn’t sustainable.”

He is also now trying to figure out what is left when he is not working. “For the past few years, I’ve been in a constant rotation of projects,” he says, “and I feel like the only thing I’m able to pull from now is my work experience, and not from life. I’m in need of a psychological break.”

When it comes to maintaining a sense of self off set, he says, “that’s still a skill I’m having to learn.” Now, with projects coming one after another, the problem is beginning to look less like how to lose himself and more like how to keep something in reserve. It all reminds me of what he wrote about his insomnia while he was in college: “In this process, I lost myself.”

But near the end of that piece, after thousands of words describing himself caught between the white consciousness of waking and sleep, he wrote how he’d finally “found myself in those shipwrecked hours.” He had spent the night trying to lose himself, and take the world away with him – “the distinction between me and the world outside of my thoughts became blurred during the night” – and then on the page, he found a way back to himself. “I knew I’d find land. I just didn’t know how long it would take for me to get there.”

In trying to regain himself and reach landfall, he’s remembering how much he loved to write, something he struggles to do while acting. As a student, he learned from the masters of minimalism and elision, Raymond Carver and Ted Chiang. “I always thought that’s what I’d end up doing, writing,” he says.
He dreams of picking it up again, maybe writing under that tree in his future orchard. “One day I’ll take writing seriously,” he says.
“What would you write?” I ask.
“I don’t know,” he says. “I love short story fiction and short story creative nonfiction… But I don’t know what I’d write. I need to start so I can find out.”

items.title: Naomi Ackie on Female Friendship, Hollywood and I Love Boosters
items.description: As she stars alongside Keke Palmer, Taylour Paige and Poppy Liu in Boots Riley’s anarchic new film I Love Boosters, Ackie talks finding her feet in Hollywood and the thrill of taking on a new challenge
items.author: Hester Underhill
paragraphs: As she stars alongside Keke Palmer, Taylour Paige and Poppy Liu in Boots Riley’s anarchic new film I Love Boosters, Ackie talks finding her feet in Hollywood and the thrill of taking on a new challenge

With every new film, Naomi Ackie finds herself wondering the same thing: will she click with her fellow castmates? “It’s a gamble every time you get a job. You’re like, am I gonna like everyone? Are they gonna like me?”

With her latest film, I Love Boosters, Ackie struck gold. Cast by rapper-turned-director Boots Riley as part of a shoplifting girl gang – alongside Keke Palmer, Taylour Paige and Poppy Liu – the chemistry between the actresses extended well beyond the set. “Boots knows how to pick them. I felt so bad for him sometimes because we would just be chatting and chatting. It was like herding cats. But he was just like, ‘Let the women do what they need to do.’”

A follow-up to Riley’s 2018 debut Sorry to Bother You, the film stars Palmer as Corvette, the ringleader of a crew of shoplifters (or ‘boosters’) who become hellbent on taking down an evil fashion corporation run by designer Christie Smith (played by Demi Moore). The film sees Riley take his playful visual style into hyperdrive to create a psychedelic vision of the Bay Area, with candy-coloured costuming by Shirley Kurata – the stylist behind Everything Everywhere All at Once – and an equally zany soundtrack from Oakland band Tune-Yards. “He’s an auteur; no one can do what Boots does,” says Ackie, who plays Sade, Corvette’s straight-talking best friend who gets sucked into a mysterious pyramid scheme. “He’s a director who has such a strong vision, and yet he also sits back and really allows you to explore it the way you want to.”
“I don’t really look for scripts in terms of whether they pass the Bechdel test, but I think that because I’m a feminist I naturally gravitate to things that speak to me” – Naomi Ackie

When it comes to the Bechdel test (a measure of female representation in film, based on whether two female characters have a conversation that isn’t about a man), I Love Boosters passes with flying colours. So do two other of Ackie’s recent films, Eva Victor’s Sorry, Baby and Zoë Kravitz’s directorial debut Blink Twice, both of which place female friendship at the heart of their stories. “It’s rare to find a film where men aren’t centre stage,” says Ackie. “I don’t really look for scripts in terms of whether they pass the Bechdel test, but I think that because I’m a feminist I naturally gravitate to things that speak to me.”

Growing up in Walthamstow, north London, Ackie attended an all-girls school, an experience that taught her a lot about the complexities of female friendship. “There’s so much school politics. And there is nothing like a girl bully. They get into your mind, man. So I experienced both sides – incredible friendships and also very difficult ones.”

After leaving school, Ackie attended London’s Royal Central School of Speech & Drama. She graduated in 2012, landing a string of theatre roles and television bit parts before making her 2016 film debut in Lady Macbeth. Playing the maid to Florence Pugh’s titular character, the role earned Ackie a British Independent Film Award (BIFA) for most promising newcomer. But it wasn’t plain sailing from there. A steady trickle of film and television work came Ackie’s way after her win, but by the age of 26 she was still living at home with her dad in Walthamstow and working part-time at the West End’s immersive Crystal Maze experience. She was seriously considering giving up acting when she was cast as former stormtrooper Jannah in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker (2019), JJ Abrams’ closing chapter of the sci-fi sequel trilogy. The role thrust Ackie into the Hollywood limelight, opening the door to a string of high-profile projects. In 2022, she played Whitney Houston in the biopic I Wanna Dance With Somebody, and in 2025 starred as heroine Nasha in Bong Joon Ho’s sci-fi comedy Mickey 17.

Despite making a name for herself in Hollywood, Ackie still lives in the UK. “LA is fun, but I’ve always associated it with work. London is just a vibe, isn’t it?” On set, though, she sticks to an American accent as a way of remaining in character between takes. “I’m not trying to fool anyone; it’s just so I can stay in that part of the brain. But I’m not method by any means.”

But as with Mickey 17, where she played opposite Robert Pattinson, and The Rise of Skywalker – which starred Daisy Ridley and John Boyega – Ackie often finds that she’s not the only Londoner on set. “The cultures are very, very different, so sometimes you do feel slightly homesick. So I think whenever I get the chance to work with a fellow Brit, I'm a happy girl.”

It’s been a busy year for Ackie, who has other high-profile releases coming up, including DC body horror Clayface and They Follow, David Robert Mitchell’s eagerly awaited sequel to his cult horror It Follows. She’s also just finished shooting Sugar Raye, a British indie drama in which she plays a former boxing champion attempting a comeback. For the role, Ackie spent eight months training in the sport. Taking on a new skill has become something of a theme in her career; in preparation to play Whitney Houston, Ackie spent around six months in vocal training, and for Star Wars she had to master archery and horse-riding. When it comes to what’s next, she’s already cooking up some ideas. “My new thing is dancing. I want to find a film that’s about burlesque or ballroom dancing. Something where I have to learn something new. Because it’s a really fun way of upping the challenge.”
I Love Boosters will release in UK and Ireland cinemas on 30 October

items.title: Is LA's new Olympic identity a design triumph or a missed opportunity?
items.description: Los Angeles was awarded the 2028 Summer Olympics and Paralympics back in September 2017, which will make it only the third city to have hosted the games three times (after London and Paris, which was the last Olympic city in 2024). LA last hosted back in 1984
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Los Angeles was awarded the 2028 Summer Olympics and Paralympics back in September 2017, which will make it only the third city to have hosted the games three times (after London and Paris, which was the last Olympic city in 2024). LA last hosted back in 1984 (and before that 1932); in theory the city is well versed in the art of the spectacle. A little bit more of the aesthetic and artistic approach to the games was unveiled today, as the slogan – ‘Stars Align’ – and a short brand film and logo were revealed.

It’s no exaggeration to say that Olympic design is freighted with cultural significance and expectation. London 2012 famously fell foul of the taste police, while Rio 2016 was a little cartoonish and Tokyo 2020 (held the following year due to the pandemic) felt understandably muted. Paris 2024, overseeing by director of design Joachim Roncin, raised the bar, walking a stylish tightrope between bold graphics and cultural sensitivities.

Ric Edwards, VP of Brand Design and Look for LA 2028, has described the brand as ‘platform of infinite expression to reflect the diversity of LA stories’. One of the key jumping off points for the ‘Look of the Games’ was the colourful floral display put on by Southern Californian superblooms, when the desert bursts into life. Colour is therefore a key part of the identity, which is further broken down into 13 patterns, or ‘blooms’, each tied in to an integral community and cultural component of the city.

On top of this, there are four unique typefaces developed for the identity, each one taken from elements of urban typographic design like the strip mall and hand painted signage. For the first time, the LA28 Olympic emblem emblem will be a dynamic one, cycling through the first dynamic Olympic emblem, with the ‘L’, ‘2’ and ‘8’ represented by three different typefaces and the ‘A’ cycling through graphical representations drawn from the cityscape.

There’ll be naysayers, inevitably, but it’s a valid attempt at creating a visual identity that embraces the massive scale and complexity of LA, one of America’s most diverse cities. It also acknowledges the huge contribution made by the Games workers, both during the events themselves and the period leading up to the opening ceremony. ‘No one makes the Games alone.

It's an athlete's years of early mornings, a volunteer's first shift, a small business getting ready for the world, a fan's voice in the stands. Each of those matters on its own,’ says LA28’s Chief Marketing Officer Alex Merchán, ‘'Stars Align' is what happens when they all come together at the same moment, and that's where the extraordinary comes from.’

The ‘Stars Align’ reveal film is soundtracked by the Red Hot Chili Peppers ‘Can’t Stop’, a rather obvious choice given the sheer scope of options that must have been available. Nevertheless, it’ll certainly help with brand recognition. As the Games draw closer, expect to see the LA28 burst forth just like those desert superblooms, garlanding the city in a colourful celebration of the competition to come.

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: Bjarke Ingels wants to rethink the refugee camp
items.description: Short-term aid cycles have long been the traditional way to address human displacement. However, this is not necessarily a long-term, sustainable solution, as the global population of refugees is projected to reach 1.2 billion by 2050. In response to this urge
items.author: Tianna Williams
paragraphs: Short-term aid cycles have long been the traditional way to address human displacement. However, this is not necessarily a long-term, sustainable solution, as the global population of refugees is projected to reach 1.2 billion by 2050. In response to this urgent issue, today (29 October 2026), a group of global architects, humanitarian leaders, and financial strategists has announced the launch of ‘Refugee Cities’, a decadal infrastructure project designed to provide permits and a self-sustaining ‘city’ design, funded by institutional investment rather than relying on finite philanthropy.
Discover BIG's 'Refugee Cities' project

Architecture juggernaut BIG (Bjarke Ingels Group) partnered with to.org, a platform that delivers infrastructure projects within refugee settlements, including the Bidi Bidi Performing Arts Centre in Uganda, to work together on the project and redefine the economics of human displacement.

The collaboration aims to rethink refugee settlements and turn them into urban economic hubs. So far, the first building prototype comprises a modular structure designed as a ‘single-family base unit’.

‘If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be said to suffice. If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for. We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,’ says Bjarke Ingels, founder and creative director of BIG.

The city is focused on ten design principles. Its foundation is the family unit, clustering homes into neighbourhoods, which evolve into districts that can eventually expand over time. At the core will be shared infrastructure, logistics, and production facilities, such as a food market, a co-working centre, an arts and crafts hall, a football field, technical workshops, a fitness rooftop, a healing garden, a health centre, and training spaces to support the city as it evolves.

The project’s financial modelling is designed to acquire land and develop infrastructure that helps provide sustainable commercial returns over several decades. Named ‘Opportunity Zones,’ these buildings will span manufacturing and agriculture. The project also requires host-nation governments willing to grant regulatory flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

The first phase of the plan begins immediately, starting with the construction of a single-family base prototype, which will be located at the Bidi Bidi Performing Arts Centre and will present a tangible look at the project's long-term durability. To launch full-scale execution, there is an active call for both host governments to designate land and regulatory zones, and funders to commit early-stage capital.

Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. When she isn’t writing extensively across varying content pillars, ranging from design and architecture to travel and art, she also helps put together the daily newsletter. She enjoys speaking to emerging artists, designers and architects, writing about gorgeously designed houses and restaurants, and day-dreaming about her next travel destination.

items.title: Beauty Freak: Good Head Is Beauty’s Next Obsession
items.description: In Beauty Freak, a column for Highsnobiety, Sable Yong explores how the culture of beauty impacts our lives.
items.author: Sable Yong
paragraphs: In Beauty Freak, a column for Highsnobiety, Sable Yong explores how the culture of beauty impacts our lives.

Sometime in 2023, I had an appointment with a hairstylist who also happened to be a trichologist — a specialist who studies hair and scalp health. As she was sectioning my hair, she asked, “If you don’t mind me asking, did you have COVID about eight months ago?”

She pointed to a weft of fine, downy hairs sprouting a few inches underneath my middle part. “See, this is all new growth. Hair grows about an average of half an inch a month, and there’s about four inches here,” she said.
I actually did have COVID about six months ago, I told her. “Oh, well, you’re lucky then; your hair grows fast.”

This type of hair loss is called telogen effluvium, and while the shedding can begin around two to three months after recovery, it can go on for about six to nine. It’s temporary, and regrowth can and will follow, inshallah. But two to nine months is more than enough time to develop balding paranoia.

Things like this used to be cause for embarrassment. But our obsession with transparency when it comes to personal maintenance has done a lot to destigmatize certain taboo topics: acne, stretch marks, cellulite, scars. Now, the beauty-and-wellness industry is coming for our scalps. Virtually every subway car and bus stop is flanked by ads for hair-loss solutions: plump, serifed fonts marketing DTC subscription-based treatments in tones of faded hunter green or mauve. I recently spotted a truck idling on Spring Street, emblazoned with, “Honk if you want 19,000 more hairs.”

It’s certainly the best time in history to be fussing around with the top of your dome; the scalp-care market is currently valued at $15 billion. I’ve attended so many scalp-care brand events this year alone, many of which hail from South Korea, the global beauty wellspring. The idea is pretty simple: if you want nice, healthy hair, start with your scalp. Most of these events feature some kinda of scalp analysis, a quick education on how the scalp works and what it needs, and a demo of whatever product promises to do just that. I also experienced my first head spa, a treatment originating in Japan that has spread worldwide. Imagine a shampoo and a blowout, but you’re laid out on a table with your head resting in a sink. A halo of water around your head gently rinses your hair while your scalp, neck, and back are massaged for an hour or more. It’s heaven.

I’ve always thought that the scalp massage is the best part of getting your hair washed when you go to the salon for a cut; I’d certainly pay to make it the main event. And lots of people seem to agree, with head spas featuring widely on the “Come with me to…” algorithm. It’s a visual scroll-stopper because it’s something familiar (a shampoo sink) but enhanced (a mini water park around your head).

More recently, at another such brand event, I had the terrifying pleasure of getting my scalp assessed with one of those microscope-like camera devices that zoom in until your head looks like alien terrain. My results placed me in the good-to-above-average percentile for hair health. But, as always, there was room for improvement…with Omi’s patented IFP-131™ peptide, which anchors and strengthens hair to the follicle so that it sheds less.

It seems that everywhere you look, there are new products, supplements, and protocols designed to address what’s going on with your head. Omi’s gummies and capsules are $86 for one month’s supply — and clinicians recommend a three-month course for best results. The K18 Future IQ Biomimetic Hair Longevity Serum claims to prevent shedding, premature graying, and something called scalp aging — and it’s $120 a month.

Scalp massagers, which can help with blood circulation if you use them diligently, range in price from less than $10 on Amazon for what looks like the business end of a salad-mixing fork, to $198 for a 24-karat-gold-plated comb from premium Japanese hair brand Lovechrome. Feel like leveling up? There’s a whole spate of modern tech-y interventions, including red-light hats, microneedling rollers, and PRP injections (for in-clinic treatment), all of which will run you several hundred dollars. (I haven’t tried any, but I have friends who have, to varying results.)

I’m not surprised that the scalp has become beauty’s next frontier. After all, it’s directly tied to one of our most prized physical attributes: our hair. What does slightly shock me is the sudden and sheer abundance of solution marketing to what has historically been a men’s grooming issue. Anyone would start to suspect that we’re experiencing some kind of wholesale follicular anxiety.

It’s true that millennials, the consumer class of the aughts, are finally aging into their balding years. They happen to be doing this at a time of peak aesthetic scrutiny thanks to social media. They want to look good compared to the Kardashians and Bachelorettes of the world (most of whom are wearing weaves or wigs). And, perhaps more than any generation to come before them, they carry a lot of anxiety around aging; it’s no coincidence that this is the generation glomming onto the longevity movement. If we can put a wellness spin on getting older — something like “scalp care” — it doesn’t feel quite so daunting. What is daunting is the task of weeding out misinformation from a vast landscape of affiliate links that promise to solve your scalp insecurities.

If you’ve been suspecting that things are feeling a bit breezier up there, I’d first recommend using something free: your hands. When I asked the tech who analyzed my scalp what treatments were clinically proven to promote hair growth, she shrugged and suggested that anyone could just routinely massage their scalp to get the blood flowing. “It’s the only thing I’ve known that works as long as people make it a habit,” she told me. “But no one really mentions it because it’s free.”

items.title: NFL Touched Down in Paris Last Week, Here’s What Happened
items.description: Last Sunday, the first-ever NFL game in France took place at Stade de France. A landmark moment for American football, the league made sure to mark its arrival with a jam-packed schedule of events, retail pop-ups, and fan-zone activations around Paris.
items.author: Angelee Kholia
paragraphs: Last Sunday, the first-ever NFL game in France took place at Stade de France. A landmark moment for American football, the league made sure to mark its arrival with a jam-packed schedule of events, retail pop-ups, and fan-zone activations around Paris.

The week kicked off with the opening of a dedicated NFL Shop presented by American Express in Galerie Joseph. As a temporary home for all things NFL, the pop-up brought Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints team merch to the central Marais district, as well as limited-edition collaborations from Fear of God, Peace Collective, and other streetwear labels.

For those looking to explore more American football-inspired fashion, Citadium transformed its space with a New Era activation, where New Orleans Saints star Cameron Jordan popped by for a meet-and-greet. Elsewhere at Galeries Lafayette Haussmann, Sweet Pants unveiled its NFL-focused streetwear, while Casablanca and PSG also brought their French heritage to collections displayed at their flagship stores.

Later in the week, the league teamed up with Adobe to launch the NFL House. Taking over Pavillon Cambon-Caulines, the 1,600 m² space was curated with exhibits of memorabilia, including the Super Bowl rings and the Vince Lombardi Trophy, while hands-on workshops set out to immerse fans in the cultural side of American football.

Continuing to wave the NFL flag across Paris, several iconic locations played host to special activations. The Eiffel Tower, for example, welcomed a new installation by Louisiana-born artist Jammie Holmes. As part of the “COLOR FIELD” project, the piece framed a football field at the foot of the monument with hand-painted end zones. At Seine, a Hail Mary contest caught the attention of onlookers as players attempted to get the ball over the river in excitement for the long-awaited game.

The celebrations culminated on Sunday with the Steelers vs. Saints face-off. Over 78,000 fans were in attendance, and thousands more tuned in, turning the debut NFL game in France into a global moment for the sport. After the first half, Burna Boy took the field for a headline show, performing hits “Ye,” “On the Low,” and “4 Kampe.” As the second half kicked off, the Saints hoped to flip the lead but fell short as the Steelers took the victory.
Take a look back at a week of NFL in France via the gallery above.
You can find out more about NFL fixtures on the league’s website.

items.title: Инна Чумакова: Спектакль «Пиковая дама» на льду
items.description: 24 октября на Навка Арене в Москве состоялась премьера первого в мире ледового спектакля «Пиковая дама» по мотивам повести А. С. Пушкина и оперы П. И. Чайковского. Невероятное масштабное и драматическое действо, где лед становится живой сценой, переплетая теат
items.author: Инна Чумакова
paragraphs: 24 октября на Навка Арене в Москве состоялась премьера первого в мире ледового спектакля «Пиковая дама» по мотивам повести А. С. Пушкина и оперы П. И. Чайковского. Невероятное масштабное и драматическое действо, где лед становится живой сценой, переплетая театр, музыку и олимпийское мастерство фигурного катания.

Над созданием спектакля работала звездная команда: режиссёром постановки выступил Юрий Квятковский, хореографию поставила лауреат «Золотой маски» Ксения Михеева, костюмы создал Игорь Чапурин, художником-постановщиком выступил Николай Симонов – главный художник МХТ имени Чехова, а оригинальную музыку, вдохновлённую Чайковским и Шнитке, написал композитор Никола Мельников.

Сюжет «Пиковой дамы» не оставляет равнодушным ни одно поколение. Главный посыл произведения: разрушительная страсть и одержимость неизменно приведут человека к потере личности и печальным последствиям.
Татьяна Навка и ее команда предлагают зрителю собственное прочтение и соединяют на льду язык драматического театра и пластику фигурного катания.

Оформление постановки просто завораживает: лед окрашен в черный цвет, затемнена атмосфера арены – все это создает впечатление мистики и тайны, а грандиозные декорации хочется разглядывать и изучать. Более 100 костюмов, специально снятый немой фильм и элементы кукольного театра – все внимание мгновенно поглощают эмоции и мастерство героев, их страсть и уникальное искусство владения телом.

В главных ролях выступают олимпийские чемпионы и призёры международных соревнований: Татьяна Навка (Графиня), Никита Кацалапов (Герман), Виктория Синицина (Лиза), Алексей Ягудин (Томский), Петр Чернышев (Граф Сен-Жермен), Повилас Ванагас/Владимир Морозов (князь Елецкий), Маргарита Дробязко (Графиня) и другие именитые фигуристы.

«Смысл и проблемы, о которых хотел рассказать Пушкин, остаются. Но это будет совершенно другая "Пиковая дама"», – подчеркнула генеральный продюсер и художественный руководитель постановки Татьяна Навка.
Отмечу, что для команды Navka Show этот проект стал первым спектаклем, предназначенным для взрослой аудитории, и, на мой взгляд, он будет интересен как старшему поколению, так и подросткам.
Еще один смелый шаг к созданию ледового театра: сотрудничество с Юрием Квятковским обогатило спектакль, положив начало творческим экспериментам.

«Жанр этой постановки по-настоящему сложно определить. Фигурное катание дает свои акценты и динамику, отличную от, например, хореографических партитур. Здесь «тонкий лед», граница между разными жанрами. Получилась фантасмагорическая драма», – поделился режиссер Юрий Квятковский.

Продолжительность шоу - 2 часа с антрактом, возрастное ограничение 12+. Сложные трюки, особые визуальные решения, мистика пушкинской повести – грандиозное музыкально-спортивное шоу, уникальное действие, которое доставляет эстетическое удовольствие и вызывает сильный эмоциональный отклик.

items.title: В России могут расширить перечень документов для покупки табака
items.description: В России могут расширить перечень документов для покупки табака
items.author: Екатерина Палкина
paragraphs: В России могут расширить перечень документов для покупки табака

Минздрав России предложил расширить перечень документов для подтверждения возраста при покупке табачной и никотиносодержащей продукции. Документ опубликован на Федеральном портале проектов и нормативных правовых актов.

Согласно проекту, продавцы смогут принимать временные удостоверения личности. Это коснётся как граждан РФ, так и лиц без гражданства. Всего обновлённый перечень будет включать 14 позиций. Сейчас покупатели используют 12 видов документов, среди которых паспорт, загранпаспорт, водительское удостоверение, вид на жительство и удостоверение беженца.
Новые правила затронут не только сигареты, но также кальяны, вейпы и прочие устройства с никотином. Если ведомство утвердит изменения, обновлённый порядок вступит в силу 1 сентября 2027 года.

Ранее Минздрав сократил список медицинских должностей. Из него убрали миколога, диабетолога, протезиста, сексолога и ещё несколько специальностей. Вместе с тем в перечень включили новые профессии, такие как нейропсихолог, нутрициолог, медицинский логопед и другие.

items.title: «Новая газета»* заявила о прекращении работы
items.description: «Новая газета»** заявила о прекращении работы
items.author: Екатерина Палкина
paragraphs: «Новая газета»** заявила о прекращении работы
Российское издание «Новая газета»* прекратит свою работу спустя 33 года с момента основания. Об этом говорится в заявлении редакции, опубликованном на сайте газеты.
«9 ноября мы погасим свет в нашем доме, где прожили 30 лет, выключим сервера и уйдем. Газеты больше нет», — сказано в обращении к читателям.

4 сентября 2026 года Минюст внёс «Новую газету»* в реестр иноагентов. Решение обосновали тем, что издание распространяло «недостоверную информацию» о действиях органов власти и избирательной системе РФ. С 2022 года у «Новой газеты»* по иску РКН была аннулирована лицензия СМИ.

29 октября портал РБК сообщил, что редакцию «Новой газеты»* выселяют из здания в Потаповском переулке в центре Москвы. Также закрылся музей Анны Политковской, который находился в её бывшем рабочем кабинете. По данным The Economist, после того, как «Новую газету»* внесли в реестр иностранных агентов, финансовые счета издания оказались под угрозой блокировки.
* Интернет-издание «Новая газета». Внесен Минюстом России в реестр иностранных агентов.

items.title: Встреча с Екатериной Глинкиной «Ешь, люби, худей»
items.description: Встреча с Екатериной Глинкиной «Ешь, люби, худей»
items.author: Анна Данилина
paragraphs: Встреча с Екатериной Глинкиной «Ешь, люби, худей»

В редакции «Сноба» состоится встреча с Екатериной Глинкиной — специалистом в области клинической и функциональной биохимии, метаболистом, нутрициологом и психологом. Екатерина расскажет о прочной связи питания с женским здоровьем, иммунитетом и весом, о том, что побеждает — генетика или эпигенетика, о рационе, который поддерживает здоровье, и о принципах питания здоровой женщины.

Отдельный блок будет посвящён мифам про еду, суперфудам для женщин разного возраста и тому, как сделать «осень» в жизни женщины красивой и благополучной. Екатерина ответит на вопросы участников о продуктах, витаминах и диетах. Встречу проведёт комьюнити-менеджер проекта «Сноб» Татьяна Санькова.
