Then came innings of quiet. Both pitchers settled into the game, and the offenses stalled. Strikeouts, pop-ups, and, yes, a few sacrifice bunts. The Brewers and the Rays play an attritional brand of baseball. They grind out at-bats, put the ball in play, and hustle hard down the line. (“I wish we played like them,” one rival general manager told ESPN, referring to the Brewers.) Still, this was, in part, what all those pundits were worried about. Would the average viewer want to watch a bloodbath of small-ball hermeneutics? Caminero, finally, gave the crowd something to watch. In the top of the fourth, he belted a double over the outstretched glove of Garrett Mitchell, the Brewers’ center fielder; a batter later, the Rays scratched across their first run. It would be their only score until the top of the ninth, when a Brewers’ game-ending double play was overturned on a coach’s challenge, and the Rays plated a run on the miscue: 3–2 ballgame, two outs in the ninth, runners on second and third. The Milwaukee reliever Trevor Megill was unphased; he struck out Jonny DeLuca on a diving knuckle curve, shouting in joy as fireworks skittered into the domed sky.

What do we want from a World Series? Or, maybe more existentially, what do we want from baseball? The sport has seemed to be in a perpetual state of crisis for as long as I’ve been alive: labor disputes, performance-enhancing-drug and sign-stealing scandals, widening payroll disparities, the complicated intrusion of sabermetrics, declining television ratings, games that take five hours to finish. Somewhere along the line, the national pastime, as it were, lost its grip on the American imagination. And what, or who, was to blame? The M.L.B. cracked down on steroid use, punished teams accused of cheating, and added measures to speed up the pace of play, instituting a pitch clock and limiting mound visits and pickoff attempts. Perhaps because of these interventions, baseball has enjoyed a recent surge of renewed enthusiasm. The past two World Series—between the Dodgers and the Yankees, in 2024, and, last year, between the Dodgers and the Toronto Blue Jays—saw a spike in ratings, and a more inspired cultural reception. I’m prone to thinking it’s the stars: tuning into a Dodgers game means watching Shohei Ohtani, the greatest ballplayer to ever live, play alongside future Hall of Famers Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, and Clayton Kershaw. The Yankees’ run to the World Series, in 2024, saw them trot out a revamped murderers’ row of Aaron Judge, Juan Soto, and Giancarlo Stanton. These were titans of the home run, outlandish talents whose bats looked like toothpicks in their hands. Maybe it was the cities they played for, too, the major metropolitan areas that made the pageantry feel that much more grandiose. You didn’t need to understand what OPS or WHIP meant when you watched last year’s Game Seven masterpiece between the Dodgers and the Blue Jays. You just needed to behold the go-ahead home runs and diving grabs from the stars whose names even your co-workers knew.

But this concentration of top-level talent in the league’s biggest markets has beget another apparent crisis for baseball. Unlike the other major American sports, the M.L.B. imposes no cap on team spending, making it so that monoliths like the Los Angeles clubs can shell out several times as much for their players than smaller budget teams like, say, the Brewers or the Rays. Ohtani, of the Dodgers, earns about three times as much annually as the entire Rays starting lineup; Juan Soto, of the Mets, makes roughly the same as the Brewers’ nine-man group. Mark Attanasio, the Brewers owner, is one of the many team governors who believes a salary cap “not only will help us compete, but more importantly all of the teams with lower payrolls, too,” as he argued at a recent press conference. With the league’s collective-bargaining agreement set to expire in December, owners like Attanasio will contend that a revised revenue-sharing system will promote parity and level the playing field, whereas the players, represented by their union, are willing to strike—even for an entire season—if their billionaire bosses continue to insist on a salary cap. “The opportunity for players to get paid is what this is all about,” Bryce Harper, of the Philadelphia Phillies, said in July. Cody Bellinger, of the Yankees, put it more pointedly: “If the billionaires are wanting it, they’re billionaires for a reason.” He went on, “They want to continue to enhance their portfolio as much as possible. Us players understand that.”

It can certainly be argued that the Dodgers are bastardizing baseball’s competitive balance, gleefully outbidding every team during free agency because, well, they can afford to. (This was once the domain of the Yankees, who, compared with the Dodgers, now seem thrifty.) Their big-money strategy has undoubtedly worked: they have won three of the past six World Series, and will likely be contenders for years to come. But spending money is not a surefire path to success. The Los Angeles Angels have repeatedly lapsed into losing seasons despite doling out huge contracts to big-name free agents, and the San Francisco Giants have suffered several consecutive below-five-hundred seasons after investing in a slurry of high-priced talent. (I’ll spare you, Mets fans—finishing last in the N.L. East, with the highest payroll in baseball, surely hurts enough.) Baseball rosters are large and unwieldy; the margins between success and failure are slim and hard to control for. There is no equivalent to a LeBron James shaping every possession of an N.B.A. Finals game, or a Tom Brady dictating his team’s every offensive drive. Baseball is an ensemble game, a wildly erratic sport to predict. As Roger Angell wrote, for The New Yorker, in 2011, the sport “always remains a fraction beyond our reach.” An extra left-hander in the bullpen might determine whether a team advances in the playoffs; a scrawny kid taken in the twenty-fifth round of the M.L.B. draft, earning the league-minimum salary, might make a game-saving play in the World Series. After the Brewers swept the Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, the Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said, in a postgame interview, that the Dodgers “may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we have a bunch of gamers.” Because that’s how baseball goes, doesn’t it? Slumps and funks come for everyone, and a five-foot-nine right fielder for the Brewers named Sal Frelick might launch a home run in Game Two of the World Series to cap off a thrilling late-game comeback. Sometimes a sacrifice bunt and a sturdy bullpen can make up for hundreds of millions of dollars in salary disparity. Sometimes the money only takes you so far.

The Brewers and the Rays aren’t all scrappy have-nots, however. Their rosters are the products of shrewd trades and rigorous international scouting, wise draft picks that paid dividends years after they were made. The Brewers had begun scouting their best offensive player, Jackson Chourio, by the time he was a fourteen-year-old living in Venezuela, signing him to an eight-year, eighty-two-million-dollar contract before he even reached the majors. That now looks like a sweetheart deal—a coup for the Brewers. Or take Caminero, whom the Rays acquired in an afterthought of a trade with the Cleveland Guardians a few years back. Call it luck that he became one of the best hitters in the sport, or call it astonishing scouting; probably both, but I’ll prioritize the latter. The Rays have the third-most wins in the American League since 2017, despite consistently operating with one of its lowest payrolls. About half their current roster was new to the team at the start of this season. It’s no surprise that their scouting department has developed a reputation as being soothsayers, almost mystical in their ability to spot a no-name prospect’s potential long before anyone else does.

Maybe one day in the not-so-distant future, Caminero and Chourio will play for the Dodgers or Yankees. By that point, the Rays and the Brewers will have likely developed a new crop of prospects to replace them, guys who make pennies compared with the game’s highest-paid players. Or maybe not. Maybe talents like Misiorowski and Caminero and Chourio only come around once every couple decades. Enjoy them while you have them, I guess, and win with them while you can—they may not be around for long, and World Series rings don’t come easy.

Milwaukee is making the most of the opportunity. On Saturday night, during Game Two, the Rays looked poised to even the series, taking an early 4–0 lead in the top half of the first inning, but the Brewers clawed and elbowed their way back into the game, one run at a time, as they had all season. They’d trailed in every game against the Dodgers, in the N.L.C.S., and still swept them. When they finally took the lead against the Rays, in the seventh, on the twenty-two-year-old Cooper Pratt’s single, it felt like a knockout punch; their closer, Aaron Ashby, hadn’t allowed a run all post-season, and that didn’t change on Saturday night. Perhaps these Brewers aren’t some small-market darling, after all. Two games away from their first World Series title, they seem about as fearsome as any team could possibly hope to be. ♦

items.title: Who Will Be the Next James Bond?
items.description: How was your weekend? Did you find an unexpected person in your bed? Did you slay a couple of heavies with your bare hands, then do it again, with extra venom? Did you save the world? If not, I have bad news: you are not the next James Bond. The quest for a ne
items.author: Anthony Lane
paragraphs: How was your weekend? Did you find an unexpected person in your bed? Did you slay a couple of heavies with your bare hands, then do it again, with extra venom? Did you save the world? If not, I have bad news: you are not the next James Bond. The quest for a new occupant of what remains, despite everything, the hottest seat in cinema—the role of 007—reached its latest climax on October 23rd to 25th, in London. Thither, “according to several sources,” in the words of The Hollywood Reporter, a chosen few were summoned to butch it out for the ultimate honor. Talk about a Bonding exercise.

Who those sources were cannot, of course, be revealed. Like purveyors of royal gossip, Bond whisperers never identify themselves; to do so would be to court the fate of Professor Dent, in “Dr. No,” who is shot after attempting—the fool!—to kill Bond with a mere tarantula. (The actor playing Dent, Anthony Dawson, had already tried to do away with Grace Kelly, in “Dial M for Murder,” and been stabbed for his pains. How epic can fails be?) Anyway, we are now informed, reliably or not, that the final contestants for the part of 007 include Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor. Otherwise known, as any TV addict will tell you, as that guy from “Slow Horses,” that guy from “Masters of the Air,” and that guy with the ears who played Prince Charles in “The Crown.” Also allegedly in the running: Jack O’Connell, who, in “Sinners,” became one of the first vampires to dance an Irish jig. In a solemn aside, the Reporter adds, “It is unclear who else may be testing.”

In short, we haven’t a clue. In recent years, all too many names have drifted in and out of the frame: Idris Elba, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Henry Cavill, Jacob Elordi, Richard Madden, Tom Hardy, Theo James, and Paul Mescal, although, given how miserable Mescal looked when he had to fight someone who was riding a rhino, in “Gladiator 2,” his odds may have lengthened. Age is another disqualifier. Elba, now fifty-four, was touted as a possible Bond for so long that his chance has come and gone, whereas Lowden, Turner, and O’Connor are thirty-six. A decade ago, the Irish actor Aidan Turner (you may have seen him in “Poldark,” on PBS) was all the rage, and his compound of intensity and levity, like that of his countryman Pierce Brosnan, appeared to fit the bill—one of Bond’s defining knacks, after all, is for orchestrating the victory of good over evil without taking either of them too seriously. But Aidan Turner is forty-three, and, like most of us, he will surely recall the crowning exchange, between hero and villain, that lends “The Spy Who Loved Me” its philosophical weight:

One man whose mortal time ran out this year, to the understandable dismay of his admirers, was Sam Neill. Born in Northern Ireland, he grew up in New Zealand before relocating to Australia, and that cultural backdrop, fronted by his other virtues, might have made him an excellent Bond. He was dashing, effortlessly amused, and quite unassuming in his command of our attention—so much so, indeed, that he specified how badly he did not wish to play 007. “I wouldn’t have been any good and I wouldn’t have enjoyed it,” he once said. In 1986, nonetheless, he went to Pinewood Studios, outside London, for a screen test. It survives online, enabling lunatics like me, who treasure films that never came to pass, to watch Neill intone the sacred liturgy of Bond. Entering his bedroom, he discovers that he is not alone:

There is almost too much to unpack here. First, the intruder, lying in wait and in bed, is gamely played for the purposes of the audition by Fiona Fullerton, who only the year before had been in “A View to a Kill,” Roger Moore’s last movie as Bond. Second, where is the choker? The sequence is lifted from the second Bond film, “From Russia with Love,” in which, as Tatiana, Daniela Bianchi—lest we forget, a former Miss Universo Italia—wears a black choker and barely anything else. Details matter, as they did for Ian Fleming, who, in the original novel of “From Russia with Love,” not only bedecks Tatiana with “a quarter-inch black velvet ribbon round her neck” but also saddles her with an awkward, if well-meaning, gaffe:

One wonders if this repartee, which was wisely omitted from the script, rang in the ears of James Brolin, who reënacted the same scene, with a British accent and a touch of aplomb, for his screen test, in 1982. He was up for the role of Bond in “Octopussy,” and his Tatiana, for the test, was played by Maud Adams. (No Bondian needs reminding that she had earned her spurs as Scaramanga’s doomed girlfriend in “The Man with the Golden Gun.” Do keep up.) In the event, although Brolin believed that the part was his, and even had orders to “prepare certain muscles for certain things I wasn’t adept at yet,” Moore returned for his sixth excursion as Bond in “Octopussy,” opposite Adams. The state of Moore’s muscles is unrecorded.

There is another snippet of Bond that has been used to challenge contenders for the throne. It comes from “GoldenEye,” and it consists of Bond introducing himself to Xenia Onatopp, one of his nemeses, and smirking maturely as he hears her name. In 2005, with “Casino Royale” on the cards, actors such as Sam Worthington, Antony Starr, Rupert Friend, and Henry Cavill (then a stripling of twenty-two) were invited to pronounce the words “Bond—James Bond” for the camera. Casual clips display their halting efforts. Eventually, all the young dudes lost out to Daniel Craig, who, in the course of five films, went on to make the role his own—and, it must be said, to demonstrate the toll that it took. Craig’s appeal was undimmed to the end, yet the joy slowly faded from his gaze, and maybe the question we ought to be asking is not “Who will be the next Bond?” but “Who in his right mind would want to be Bond?” Also, “Why do we still care who Bond is or isn’t?” Oh, and one last complicating factor: Bond is dead.

Critics who reviewed “No Time to Die,” Craig’s final Bond film, were cautioned against spoilers. It was made plain that anyone disclosing the destruction of 007, in a missile attack on a remote island, would earn a visit from a tarantula, or worse. Yet die he did, and his end signalled that of a long-standing deal; in 2025, the Bond franchise passed from the grasp of Eon to that of Amazon M-G-M. One was tempted to ask: Who’s the spoiler now? It was like SMERSH giving way to SPECTRE.

Fans feared the worst. Would Bond be chopped up and parcelled out in pieces: a spinoff series titled “Moneypenny,” perhaps, on Amazon Prime? Or a period peek at Bond the teen-aged Etonian, with pimples and a tailcoat? Consider the grievous damage done to “The Day of the Jackal,” when, in 2024, it was rehashed by Peacock and stretched to ten episodes, with all the twists undone. Imagine 007 unmanned by a comparable tedium—slumped in a greasy London flat, counting his nicotine patches and waiting for M to call.

Thus far, to be fair, a certain continuity has been established. There will be a full-length film, rather than a Bond-flavored show. The director will be Denis Villeneuve, fresh from “Dune: Part Three.” (The transition could be tricky; we may find Q pottering around with a tube coming out of his nose.) The screenplay will be written by Steven Knight, who created “Peaky Blinders.” Like his predecessors, he will be stuck with the standard problems. What does a criminal mastermind look like these days, for instance? Is he a trillionaire who designs a flying car? An algorithm? Or a devious Russian, jerking the chain of the free world? No fiction is needed to furnish those. By custom, we like a squeeze of reality with our 007, like lemon on an oyster, but no more than that. Remember the confusion of “Die Another Day,” which demanded that Bond be tortured by North Koreans and drive an invisible car?

James Bond, in truth, was never much of a character. He was a name with a dream attached—an expensively tailored suit, into which a succession of actors could slip. Minor adjustments were made to the inside leg. Such stylish emptiness is daunting, and one doesn’t envy those who are now being encouraged to try it on for size. Lowden has lingered so long in the dishevelled shadow of Gary Oldman, in “Slow Horses,” that we have yet to inspect him in the light. Turner I have barely observed, though his visage, carved and mean, suggests that he might obey my private rule for Bond: he should, in theory, be able to trade places with the villain. O’Connor, conversely, may be hampered by his sympathetic warmth. As a priest, in “Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery,” he took a phone call from a troubled parishioner (Bridget Everett), and what ensued was, to my eyes, the most affecting scene in recent American cinema. The irony is that it meant physically shutting the door on his co-star, none other than Daniel Craig. Could it do the same to O’Connor’s prospects for Bond?

Who wins the race, and when the winner will be announced, none of us can say. Even then, the fuss will persist. It’s hard to forget the spectacle of Craig at his public launch, in 2005, when he was unveiled as the latest Bond. The poor guy had to travel up the Thames on a speedboat accompanied by Royal Marines but clad, laughably, in a life jacket, like a kid on an inflatable-donut ride. Suddenly, the in-joke that is uttered by George Lazenby, the harassed successor to Sean Connery as 007, near the start of “On His Majesty’s Secret Service”—“This never happened to the other fellow”—acquired a new and haunting significance. For Craig, it was not until the opening scenes of “Casino Royale,” when he shot one miscreant and butchered another in a bathroom, deploying the basin as an offensive weapon, that all the charges of wussiness were dismissed.

Is it too late to bring back Lazenby? He’s merely eighty-seven years old, and he seems in passable shape, though he may now require a bathroom for reasons other than homicide. Beyond that, I can nominate only one performer who meets all the criteria for Bond. The name’s Blunt. Emily Blunt. A verifiable grownup, she is also a proper film star, not a face you half recognize from TV. She can carry both a firearm, as she proved in Villeneuve’s “Sicario,” and an entire movie—see Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” in which she acted opposite O’Connor and spoke Russian. Blunt is quick-witted, languorous, panic-free, as funny as hell, and as English as strawberries and cream. In one swoop, she would take the hoary old trope of “Bond girl” and toss it in the trash. Needless to say, she won’t get the part of 007 (it only ever happens to another fellow), yet she merits it more thoroughly than any of the gang who gathered in London this past weekend. Here’s my plan: by way of a consolation prize, Lowden, Turner, O’Connor, and any other ex-hopefuls could drape themselves around Blunt on the poster for the next James Bond film, wearing brave smiles and tiny swimming trunks. Gentleman, here is your mission. You will be Bond boys. Good luck. ♦

items.title: The Founder of Arab Americans for Trump Has Some Regrets
items.description: The Michigan Senate race between the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and the Republican Mike Rogers has been subsumed in recent days by an endless stream of bigoted, Islamophobic attacks. A Rogers surrogate—Senator John Kennedy, of Louisiana—stated at a rally that El-
items.author: Isaac Chotiner
paragraphs: The Michigan Senate race between the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and the Republican Mike Rogers has been subsumed in recent days by an endless stream of bigoted, Islamophobic attacks. A Rogers surrogate—Senator John Kennedy, of Louisiana—stated at a rally that El-Sayed sleeps in a “Bin Laden jersey.” Rogers himself has been saying that El-Sayed would be loyal to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Rogers agreed when the sports podcaster Dave Portnoy called El-Sayed a “terrorist.” President Trump, in the course of trying to get Rogers elected, has said that El-Sayed would bring jihadists to America and referred to him as “Muhammed.”

These attacks have been criticized by Arab and Muslim leaders in Michigan, including Bishara Bahbah, who launched the group Arab Americans for Trump in 2024. That year, he campaigned for the then former President alongside Massad Boulos, the Lebanese businessman who happens to be Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law. I interviewed Bahbah back in August of 2024; we spoke again by phone this week. Our conversation, edited for length and clarity, is below.
Is there anything I should mention to readers about your bio?
I am the chairman of Arab Americans for Peace, and I am still a member of the Republican Party. And I am involved in the current midterm elections.
So, did Arab Americans for Trump become Arab Americans for Peace?

We changed the name last year to Arab Americans for Peace when the President started talking about Gaza as the property of the United States. I believe that Gaza belongs to the Palestinians and no one else, and therefore that kind of talk really was very upsetting and out of line. Therefore, we changed the name.
Didn’t Trump say that Biden has “become like a Palestinian” at the debate in 2024?
He said that about Chuck Schumer.
O.K. He said it about Biden, too.

I released a press release that year saying that the word “Palestinian” is not a slur and it should not be used as such. And it just doesn’t seem to have had an effect because he also recently called Schumer a Palestinian.

You need to keep putting out more statements. Hopefully at some point he’ll understand that it’s offensive. But I want to talk about what’s happening in the Michigan Senate race right now, because you said you’re still a Republican, and what’s happening, as far as I can tell, is that Abdul El-Sayed is running against Mike Rogers and is facing a tremendous amount of bigotry and Islamophobia from the Rogers campaign and its surrogates and from President Trump. How bad has it gotten?

I’m going to Michigan on Wednesday, and I’m a Christian. I’m not even a Muslim, but the fact that Muslims are being targeted in such a demeaning, racist fashion is just crossing a red line, like calling him “Muhammad.” We know that Muhammad is widely considered the most popular name in the world. Would the President like to be called something other than Mr. President or Donald J. Trump? Is it acceptable for somebody else to come up with a different name and call him that just because they would like to do so? It’s not. So Islam and Islamophobia is going to only have a counter-effect with regard to the Arab and Muslim voters in the United States and also voters who are levelheaded because bigotry is just not acceptable.
And I think the fact that the President is escalating his attacks along those lines is a sign of desperation.

But even when Trump has not been desperate—and it seems like he might be a little desperate now, since Republicans seem like they’re about to have a bad election—Trump’s bigotry and attacks on minority groups, including Muslims, have been constant. This is not just that his party’s behind in the Michigan Senate race, so he’s going to launch a few broadsides against Muslims. This is his entire political career, no?
Well, in 2024, the President seemed to have behaved.
Sir, I just said to you that he called Joe Biden a Palestinian during the debate.

I understand that. I understand that. I’m not questioning that either. All I’m saying is that his tone during the elections in 2024 was very different than what it is right now. He said something at one point in 2024 that offended the Yemenis in Michigan, and he immediately apologized.

He apologized at the time, yes. [Amer Ghalib, the mayor of Hamtramck, Michigan, who supported Trump in 2024, claims that Trump apologised privately for calling Yemenis “terrorists” but added that Trump declined to do so publicly.] But it seems like in 2024 the President was desperate to get the Arab and Muslim vote.
He made lots of racist comments during 2024. He talked about Haitians eating pets.
So when you said that he behaved during 2024, I just wasn’t sure what you meant.
I mean, it was not to the extent that it is right now. And he attacked the Somalis, he attacked the Haitians, and that’s not acceptable.
O.K. But it’s gotten worse now, you’re saying?
It’s gotten a lot worse, yes.
So it’s like if there was a list, the Muhammad thing would be at the top of the list, and then the Haitian stuff and the Somali stuff would be a little lower down the list.

Well, I mean, they’re all offensive. And I wouldn’t say that, because I’m Arab American, I’m more offended by the Muhammad issue. It is just all equally offensive. I feel bad for the Haitians, for the Somalis, for the Palestinians, for the Muslims. It is just not acceptable.

A number of Muslim Americans either voted for Trump or did not vote for Kamala Harris. And one of the main reasons was the devastation that was going on in Gaza, that the Biden Administration had supported. And I think a lot of liberal people were angry when people didn’t vote for Kamala, but a lot of people also felt that what was happening in Gaza was unconscionable. That was part of what you were thinking, correct?

Absolutely. I mean, our priority in 2024 was to end the war in Gaza, and our pleas with the Democrats at the time went nowhere. And President Trump, at the time, promised that he would end the war in Gaza. [During the debate with Biden in June of 2024, Trump also urged Biden to let Israel “finish the job” in Gaza.]

I think your critique of the Democratic Party is one that a lot of people have become more and more sympathetic to over the past few years. But when I talked to you last time it wasn’t your critique of the Democratic Party on Gaza that I found so surprising. It was that you seemed to be putting personal and political trust in Donald Trump, and I think that’s the part that people find a little hard to wrap their minds around.

You’re right. You’re right. I had faith. I believed his words. And now, on the Gaza situation, well, we were able to get a ceasefire in Gaza, and you might have heard or read that I was personally involved in the negotiations leading up to the ceasefire in Gaza, beginning with my intervention on behalf of the White House as a background negotiator between Hamas and the White House. [Asked for comment about Bahbah’s claims, a Trump Administration official told The New Yorker, “None of this is accurate. This individual was not involved in peace negotiations between Israel and Hamas.”]
The ceasefire that happened in January of 2025, or the ceasefire in October of 2025?

Well, both. There was a ceasefire that was forced upon Netanyahu by Trump in January of 2025. Then, in March of 2025, Netanyahu was able to convince the President that he had to finish the job, meaning finish Hamas, and broke his word with regard to the ceasefire.
And then proceeded to cut off aid to Gaza for months.

Let me tell you the way things have transpired from my perspective. So, in March of 2025, Netanyahu was able to convince Trump to allow him to break the ceasefire and resume the fighting, which led to famine in Gaza during the summer of 2025. After that, I was asked by [the United States special envoy to the Middle East Steve] Witkoff to get involved in the negotiations with regard to the ceasefire in Gaza. And the initial Witkoff proposal that was made public then was a proposal that I had written for Witkoff. So we got engaged in the ceasefire negotiations, which really took a very long time and ended up in another ceasefire in October of 2025. So there were two ceasefires at the time, and now, of course, the ceasefire of October 2025 was supposed to go into phases, and it led to the release of the Israeli hostages, and it led to the release of the Palestinian hostages in return.

You said earlier that you changed the name of the organization when he said that Gaza belonged to the United States, correct? That happened in February of 2025. But you were still working with the Trump Administration well after this, correct?
Yes. I was asked by Witkoff to mediate between Hamas and the White House.

You were communicating with Witkoff, and you also campaigned with Massad Boulos, who is Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law. And these are people that you have real relationships with, I assume. What do they say now? Are you still in touch with them?
No, I’m not in touch with Massad Boulos. Our relationship ended right after the elections.

After the Presidential elections. He just cut off communication, and all the promises that were made with regard to what the President would do for the Arab American community were never really fulfilled. And Massad Boulos essentially cut off the relationship with me.
He just didn’t respond to messages, that type of thing?

No. One of the things that Massad Boulos reportedly did was meet with the head of the Regional Council of Judea and Samaria. And he called him Governor. Governor of what? A governor of the West Bank, which is an occupied territory. That, to me, was a reason to sever ties with Massad Boulos because—
Oh, so you’re the one who severed ties?
You say you’re still a Republican. Does that mean you’re still hoping for Republican success, but not in Michigan? How are you thinking about what you’re rooting for in these elections?
Well, as far as I’m concerned, community comes first before the Party, and the country comes before the Party and community. So this is where I stand right now.
Community comes first before the Party.
So you’re not hoping Republicans win in 2026?
Well, all I’m saying is that the rhetoric that has been lobbed against our community has turned off the community, and I don’t see the community voting Republican this time around.
But what about you? How are you going to vote?
I’m not going to answer that question.

O.K. Do you think that some people might think that the stand you’re taking against Trump and his bigotry now is slightly undermined by not even saying that you believe people should vote for the opponents of Trump and that bigotry?

People can interpret what I’m saying any way they want, and that’s fine with me. All I’m saying is our support of Trump in 2024 was for the primary and sole reason of ending the war in Gaza. That was it. It was not necessarily . . . I mean, a lot of the values of the Republican Party match with the values of the Arab and Muslim American voters, which is fine, but sometimes there is a breaking point because when there is no respect for the community, how is the community going to behave? I mean, the community is not dumb. They expect to vote for people who support them. They’re not to be expected to vote for people who attack them.

When I look back at our previous interview, it’s a lot of me asking you questions about things Trump said, and you essentially denying them or saying that he’s been misunderstood, or essentially that it won’t be that bad, or it was so great because you got on a phone call with Trump.

And do you feel like you were vying for influence, and so you had to say them? Do you feel like you were a little bit brainwashed and you actually thought that Trump was a different person? How do you understand looking back?
Well, I was counting on his commitment to end the war in Gaza. That was my primary reason.
Right. And I’m asking why you believed it.
He told me that in person multiple times. I mean, he told the whole country that he demanded—
Sir, you must know Donald Trump saying something, whether it’s to you in person or to the country, has no meaning, right? You know that.

Well, he told the entire country that he’s a man of peace, that he has not waged any wars during his time, and that he wants to bring about peace in the world. And, honestly, I believed him at the time.

Right. I believe that you said something about him being a President who ends wars, and I had to remind you that Joe Biden had ended the war in Afghanistan. Trump actually increased drone strikes. You seemed to be of the opinion that Trump was much more of a man of peace than perhaps the record suggested. That’s why I’m asking these questions.

If you’re asking that I had put too much faith in President Trump at the time, I did. If you’re asking me if I had believed his words at the time with regard to the ceasefire in Gaza, I did. If I was misled, I was misled along with the entire country.

I guess there were also a lot of people in the country who were horrified by what was happening in Gaza and were angry about it, but also never put any faith in Donald Trump. And it seems like that position has been somewhat vindicated.

We’re all different in terms of how we react to people and statements, but at the same time the fact that I knew that in his first term he imposed the Muslim ban, and then when we asked him about it during 2024, he said, “No, no, no, there’s not going to be a Muslim ban, and there’s not going to be wars.” Unfortunately, it seems to me that maybe I was too naïve at the time.

I know I’ve asked you a version of this before, but just to try to reflect on it, when you do think back to those days when you were campaigning with Massad Boulos, campaigning for Trump, talking to him on the phone, what do you think about that now? What pops into your mind?
I did what I did for Gaza, and Biden did not listen to us, and a wise individual should make a choice between a bad situation and a worse situation, and I was forced to make that type of a choice.
And do you think you made the right choice?

Well, we ended the war in Gaza. It’s not a perfect ceasefire right now because there are people who are getting killed by the Israelis on a daily basis, and the United States is not saying a word about those violations. And, also, you look at what’s happening in the West Bank, which is being literally overtaken by extremist Jewish settlers who are doing whatever they want to do with the acquiescence of the Israeli Army and the Israeli government, and without any objection from the U.S. government. So I am terribly disappointed in what has transpired, and given that I’m that disappointed, I don’t really hold much hope for the coming two years as far as anything happening with regard to Gaza. ♦

items.title: Did Substack Fix the Internet?
items.description: The question of how to survive as a writer is only slightly older than the impulse to be one in the first place. How to express yourself freely but also to be valued for said expression? Historically, strategies for making ends meet have included seeking relig
items.author: Kyle Chayka
paragraphs: The question of how to survive as a writer is only slightly older than the impulse to be one in the first place. How to express yourself freely but also to be valued for said expression? Historically, strategies for making ends meet have included seeking religious or royal patronage; producing printed books; serializing your work in publications; and hustling to sell your own subscriptions, as Alexander Pope did when he funded his eighteenth-century translation of the Iliad. The investigative journalist I. F. Stone had his own printed-and-mailed newsletter I.F. Stone’s Weekly, which cost five dollars a year and ran from 1953 to 1971, reaching some seventy thousand subscribers. In more recent years, the go-to option for an aspiring writer has been starting a newsletter of her own, often on Substack, a digital platform that launched in 2017 to allow writers to charge money for their writing. Hamish McKenzie, Substack’s co-founder, argues in a new book (that venerable format!), “How to Save the Media,” that Substack’s ecosystem of individual authors behind personal paywalls has solved the problem of cutting through the social-media cacophony and fulfilled writers’ quest for a livelihood. In McKenzie’s estimation, Substack represents “a better system design that distributes rather than concentrates both power and responsibility.”

McKenzie is a journalist by trade, who spent much of his career covering tech startups. With “How to Save the Media,” he has published something between a memoir and a manifesto, delivered in the quippy tone of twenty-tens blogging. He breezily recounts his life in the media industry, which began when he escaped his youth in small-town New Zealand to study journalism in Canada. After finding fecund ground in the Hong Kong tech scene, he landed in San Francisco during Silicon Valley boom times. He endured stints at such niche publications as PandoDaily before working at Tesla (and, after leaving, wrote a book about the company, leading to clashes with Elon Musk). While working at the messaging app Kik, he met Chris Best, Kik’s chief technology officer and his future Substack co-founder. The two saw that media companies were overly reliant on social media for distribution, and that profits were flowing to the likes of Facebook rather than to the creators of content. They wanted to build “a game where people would happily pay for good media,” scaling up the preëxisting achievements of writers such as Andrew Sullivan and Ben Thompson, whose small digital publications thrived on a subscription model. Substack would help writers publish their content and charge their readers while managing the messy back-end business, in exchange for ten per cent of writers’ revenue.

McKenzie courts for Substack such writerly talents as Bill Bishop, Matthew Yglesias, and Bari Weiss, whose publication The Free Press remains among the most popular and best-earning offerings on the platform. He recounts a boozy literary party sponsored by his company and quotes liberally, and redundantly, from his own old speeches and blog posts. The Substack team fends off acquisition offers from Jack Dorsey’s Twitter and Musk’s X, choosing to prioritize their independence. They also navigate debates over free speech from critics who complain that Substack hosts, and thus profits from, hateful content including pro-Nazi newsletters. McKenzie’s justification is ultimately the same as that of the social networks that he argues against: Substack is a neutral platform empowering its users, not an arbiter of truth. He writes, “When a platform decides what its uses are and aren’t allowed to see, it effectively positions itself as a centralized police force with the moral authority to decide what’s good and what’s bad.”

Such big-tent branding has helped Substack to become an unqualified success, at least in the eyes of its investors, and has made “Substacking” a cultural buzzword, much as “tweeting” dominated the early twenty-tens. It’s not just reporters who have Substacks now; celebrities (Pamela Anderson), musicians (Patti Smith), and traditional publications (including The New Yorker) do, too. (I, full disclosure, have my own accounts.) The rescued “media” of McKenzie’s title encompasses not just journalism but a broader realm of entertainment, with Substack providing a monetizable layer between creators and their fans. The company is, in essence, a crowdfunding e-commerce site, belonging to the same category as Kickstarter, Patreon, Gumroad, and OnlyFans. But it has out-evolved its ancestors and bested its competitors in its relevance to public discourse and in its direct commodification of online parasocial relationships. McKenzie predicts that “new companies will emerge” from such subscription platforms, but thus far Substack has only encouraged further atomization as audiences gravitate toward the loudest, most charismatic voices. The result is not a revived traditional media industry—few Substacks employ editors, for example—so much as a new form of public square in which anyone can shout.

“How to Save the Media” belongs to the genre of instructive founder’s autobiography, in which the heroic entrepreneur inevitably endures some brief trials on his path to power and riches, and offers the business lessons learned along the way. If mass social platforms driven by advertising are what’s wrong with the internet, McKenzie argues, then a platform driven by subscriptions can save it. Substack does allow thousands more writers (and podcasters and miscellaneous creators) to sustain careers in an otherwise barren industry landscape; it is now considered normal to charge your followers’ credit cards the cost of a fancy caffeinated beverage each month for the privilege of receiving your reporting, recipes, or ramblings. Yet as the company has grown, Substack has also come to look more like its stated enemies: it added a Twitter-esque feed of algorithmically recommended short posts, called Notes; its app has become a multimedia hub. McKenzie criticizes social media for how it “turns publishers into digital characters who compete for attention on crowded feeds,” but aspiring writers now hustle to make themselves known as characters on Substack, too. The writer Emily Sundberg, whose newsletter “Feed Me” is one of McKenzie’s highlighted triumphs, observed, in an influential 2024 essay, that “if you blacked out the names of many of the writers I come across on Substack today, I wouldn’t be able to tell them apart.” She went on to pinpoint the Substack generic style: “lists, random thoughts, and (easy to write) roundups of ‘what I’ve been doing’ do really well on this site.”

Another new book, “Content Machines,” by the Carleton University professor Sarah Brouillette, is less optimistic than McKenzie’s about digital platforms’ influence on publishing. In the online marketplace, Brouillette argues that writers have become mercenaries, “a node in a network of needy users” who must “invest their own time and money in design and sales if they want to succeed.” The book proceeds through chapters on such phenomena as the user-generated fiction platform Wattpad, BookTok and the popularity of the romance genre, Audible’s many algorithm-gaming offerings, self-publishing advice gurus, and autofiction’s relationship to social media. In each case, she analyzes how the structures and forces of the various internet platforms shape the style of the writing hosted on them. A roving analyst in addition to a well-read academic, Brouillette pays close attention to the trappings of Wattpad conventions (known as WattCon) and to such textual specimens as “How to Write a Book in 48 Hours,” by the self-publishing coach Dale L. Roberts, which suggests such hacks as using talk-to-text programs or “outsourcing” work to others. She concludes that writing on the internet, particularly in spaces where it’s simple to charge money for it, tends to push writers toward the confessional, the self-helpy, and the soothing.

Though Substack is not one of Brouillette’s subjects, much of what she describes applies equally to the platform—like, say, “a new kind of labor regime that turns people’s daily online creativity into an agglomerated mass of possibly monetizable material.” As content creators struggle to compete for attention and subscription dollars, they end up finding their way to the same solutions, relying on “established patterns,” Brouillette writes, echoing Sundberg’s observation; the goal is less to produce great writing than to “maximize your work’s efficiency.” Social media is blamed for raising a generation of self-promoting narcissists and fuelling a precipitous decline in attention spans and intellectual engagement. But in the new writer economy a “desperation for attention” is practically “an industry command,” Brouillette writes. The platform may not save journalism as a whole, but it certainly helps prolong the careers of those willing to play the “game,” as McKenzie put it, of cultivating their personal brands. ♦

items.title: The Cheesecake Factory War Continues: All the Absurd Updates
items.description: All year, Republicans have struggled to find a message that would resonate with American voters and turn back the rising blue tide ahead of what look likely to be brutal midterm elections. They’ve tried everything, from transphobia to Islamophobia to redemoniz
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: All year, Republicans have struggled to find a message that would resonate with American voters and turn back the rising blue tide ahead of what look likely to be brutal midterm elections. They’ve tried everything, from transphobia to Islamophobia to redemonizing immigrants to rebooting the Red Scare to blaming Joe Biden for President Trump’s economic malaise, but none of it clicked. Then inspiration struck. A little over a week before Election Day, Barack Obama quipped that the gold- and renovation-obsessed Donald Trump has “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

You might think Trump’s allies would be upset about Obama comparing the president to a notorious palace-dwelling despot who ran his country into the ground. But Trump officials and MAGA influencers aren’t defending Trump against that slight. Instead, they are accusing Democrats of elitism (another old classic) and making standing with the Cheesecake Factory a closing midterms message. And they’re not the only ones still talking about Obama’s most disastrous gaffe since the tan suit. Below, the latest and hottest takes about this vital new American discourse, which may — or, more likely, may not — be studied by political scientists for generations.
Barack Obama is perfectly happy to reiterate
At a campaign rally in Georgia on Wednesday night, the former president had some fun reacting to the reaction, and professed that he had a spent a lot of time dining at Cheesecake Factory:
And then he made fun of how Trump and his administration “mobilized” a “government response” to his joke:
Hannity bemoans the demonization of gourmet meals

The Fox News host also defended Bessent, suggesting the treasury secretary was not, as Obama said, ordered to go to the Cheesecake Factory by the White House, but did so out of his own free will (while Tomi Lahren argued that Cheesecake Factorygate shows that Trump is a relatable billionaire):
Prompting a White House slop back
After Obama doubled down, the White House war room aimed its AI image generator and fired:
“It’s time for Trump to work a shift at the Cheesecake Factory”

The Washington Examiner’s Christopher Tremoglie thinks Trump should reenact his 2024 McDonald’s working-class cosplay and “make Obama eat his words and serve them with a delicious piece of cheesecake from the restaurant”:
Consider the possibilities.

For example, say a restaurant guest orders the Cheesecake Factory’s Tex-Mex egg rolls. Trump comes out, delivering their food and reminding them that he has stood up to China and implemented strong border security along the Texas-Mexico border.

Someone orders the chocolate tuxedo cream cheesecake? After delivering dessert to the patrons, Trump reminds them that tuxedos are worn by the corporate executives who have committed to new investments in the U.S. totaling $11 trillion.
The Slop Factory on the Cheesecake Factory

The White House social-media team, after celebrating the Cheesecake Factory as a “great American institution,” teased a Tuesday afternoon “surprise” on X — which ended up being a low-energy troll with a live loop of an AI-generated cartoon Trump waving to people in front of a Cheesecake Factory, set to down-tempo music and accompanied by what looks like a Google doc of anti-DEI talking points:
On Monday, the team made a different piggybacking attempt:
“This is about the Democrats not being able to appreciate beauty”
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt tried to change the subject Tuesday:
Obama wishes his Oval Office looked as gold as Trump’s
See for yourself, this Trump-endorsed author says:
Longtime Cheesecake Factory designer rejects comparison to gold-covered White House
CNN spoke with the chain restaurant’s former vice-president of design, Rick McCormack:
“I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that sound bite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today …”

“Cheesecake wasn’t covered with gold appliqués and things like that. It really is two different environments,” McCormack said. “It’s easy to say, ‘Oh, this has shiny things on the wall. Cheesecake has shiny things in it. Let’s compare the two,’ but that’s to someone who really is not knowing what they’re talking about.”
“Middle America’s cup of tea”
Washington Examiner columnist and veteran Trump-country-diner correspondent Salena Zito defended the idea of Cheesecake Factory luxury during a appearance on Monday’s Hugh Hewitt Show:

You walk into the Cheesecake Factory, and it is pretty much Middle America’s cup of tea. It’s decorated lovely. There’s, you know, ornate, there’s lighting, there’s a menu the size of the old yellow pages, and it’s just like a big treat to go to the Cheesecake Factory.
The Cheesecake Factory is “literally a melting pot”
Monday night on Fox News, Greg Gutfeld symbolized the many flavors of Cheesecake Factory’s massive menu:
Trump’s self-defense on the campaign trail: “I fix things good”

He barely mentioned the Cheesecake Factory at a Mississippi rally Monday, but he did reiterate at length why he loves renovating the White House. “It relaxes me,” he told the crowd before detailing all the work he’s had done.
Trump: “Stupid” Obama doesn’t understand filth or columns

Trump more directly attacked Obama while speaking with reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Monday, declaring that “for you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory — that just shows why you were a lousy president”:

We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly. Guys like Obama don’t see it. You don’t see dirt. He doesn’t see filth. He doesn’t see broken ornaments on a building.
It has to be clean. The columns can’t be broken. The bricks can’t be falling off from under the plaster. And for you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.
The Wall Street Journal editorial board mails it in

The editorial board tried to seize on the Cheesecake Factory news cycle in a Monday op-ed titled “Obama Goes Socialist, Scorns Cheesecake.” The board members took the issue so seriously they even visited the restaurant chain’s website:

Making fun of chain restaurants is quite an angle for Democrats, who keep insisting that they haven’t forgotten the working man in Middle America. The Cheesecake Factory has a couple of hundred locations, the company says, so it must be doing something deliciously right. But to all of those diners in Cleveland, Grand Rapids, and beyond, here’s Mr. Obama’s message: How déclassé.
Meantime, instead of resisting the socialist takeover of the Democratic Party, Mr. Obama is throwing in with it.
“I would just tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try,” says Everyman Scott Bessent
The ultrawealthy former hedge-fund manager had lunch at the Cheesecake Factory in downtown D.C. on Monday, then “slammed” Obama to reporters, as CNBC notes:

“This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader’s tomb,” Bessent told a Fox Business reporter who asked about Obama’s remark as he left the restaurant near the White House. Bessent was apparently referring to the Obama Presidential Center, a monolithic structure that opened in June.

“I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try,” Bessent said. Obama vacationed on Martha’s Vineyard as president, and he and his wife Michelle now own an estate on the exclusive island.
Bessent said he ordered “what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger.”
Bessent wasn’t the only Republican rushing out to a Cheesecake Factory:
Real Americans cling to the Cheesecake Factory
The Cheesecake Factory is an aspirational place

Chain-restaurant lover Clay Travis got in on the outrage, too, saying he remembered how, when he was growing up, the Cheesecake Factory was once “the most expensive place we could go to for a fancy dinner”:
Some pushback on that aspiration:
Manifest Cheesecake Factory
Fox News personality Tomi Lahren seemed to say she once dreamed about eating in a Cheesecake Factory:
The Cheesecake Factory exists above politics!
At The Atlantic, Elaine Godfrey decries inserting the beloved restaurant into America’s culture wars:

Enough! I wanted to scream. Leave the Cheesecake Factory out of your culture wars! Like any number of kitschy, charming American chain restaurants—Rainforest Cafe, Johnny Rockets, and even, God love it, Applebee’s—the Factory can obviously be mocked. But it must be mocked from a place of love. It should exist above partisan politics as a sacred third space, one of the few we Americans have left.
“It is America at its utmost—all decadence, performance, and fun,” she concluded. “The Cheesecake Factory is for all of us.”
Democratic speechwriters need to go on dates at the Cheesecake Factory
The Cheesecake Factory is elitist
Some of the pushback on Monday was about the incorrect assumptions that the Cheesecake Factory was some product of the American heartland:

The Washington Sun did its own analysis and concluded that “the Cheesecake Factory isn’t quite what Republicans are describing — or at the very least, its faux-marble gates are more likely to be in wealthier areas than working-class ones”:

Home values in ZIP codes within 3 miles of a Cheesecake Factory are about 27% higher than comparable areas without an industrial cheesecake outlet, according to The Washington Sun’s analysis of data from Overture Maps, Zillow and the Census Bureau. That puts it in the same class as Lululemon, P.F. Chang’s and The UPS Store.

Much of the Cheesecake Real Estate Premium comes from the fact that these restaurants tend to be located in upscale malls, which we define as those with upscale outlets such as the Apple Store. Though, the Cheesecake Factories outside of malls also still tend to be in more expensive areas.
The Cheesecake Factory debate represents “a constant tension between the Brooks Brothers patrician and the Kid Rock populist”
Again, everyone seems to have missed the point of the actual joke
This post has been updated.

items.title: Poll Suggests the Unimaginable: A Democratic Senator in South Carolina
items.description: During this last week of a high-stakes midterm-election campaign, polling data is flying around with ever-increasing velocity, and the big mystery is whether a Democratic wave can flip the United States Senate (control of the House is generally being conceded
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: During this last week of a high-stakes midterm-election campaign, polling data is flying around with ever-increasing velocity, and the big mystery is whether a Democratic wave can flip the United States Senate (control of the House is generally being conceded to Democrats). Indeed, there are a lot of close Senate races in states ranging from Maine to Alaska. And another venue is on everyone’s watch list after today’s release of a new high-quality New York Times–Siena survey: deep-red South Carolina, where appointed GOP senator Darline Graham is in the fight of her brief and sudden political life against Democrat Annie Andrews.

Among likely voters, Andrews and Graham are tied at 48 percent of the vote, per Times-Siena. The survey shows a modestly more Democratic-leaning electorate than is customary in the Palmetto State, where President Trump’s job-approval ratings are not great. It also indicates that Andrews is getting a small but crucial slice of Trump 2024 voters and is doing very well among 2024 nonvoters (including new voters: She is capturing 70 percent of under-30 voters in this poll). Andrews also seems to have made a good personal impression on voters: Her favorable-to-unfavorable ratio in the poll is 44 percent to 29 percent with 25 percent “very favorable,” compared to Graham’s 44 percent to 41 percent ratio with 26 percent registering a “very unfavorable” opinion of her. Andrews’s professional background as a pediatrician feeds a campaign message focused on reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and restoring access to Obamacare subsidies. Meanwhile, Graham’s backers mostly seem inclined to vote for her out of a sense of partisan duty, which isn’t exactly the best reason to get off the couch on Election Day.

The poll cannot be dismissed as an outlier: Graham had only a small lead (1.5 percent, according to the Silver Bulletin averages) in earlier polls. She is also likely suffering from cumulative unhappiness among some Republicans toward her always-controversial late brother, her sparse experience in politics and government, and the big advantage she had in the primary and runoff elections thanks to her vocal backing from President Trump and the man who appointed her to Lindsey’s seat, Governor Henry McMaster. The candidate she narrowly defeated in the runoff, Representative Ralph Norman, is refusing to campaign with her, calling her “a fraud of a candidate.” There’s also an effort among some Norman backers (which he has not endorsed) to encourage voters to write in his name. Another sign of GOP erosion is an Andrews endorsement from former Republican governor David Beasley, who cut an ad with his Democratic successor, Jim Hodges, supporting the Charleston doctor.

To be sure, most of the South Carolina GOP Establishment is kicking out the jams for Graham, and as part of his red-state rescue effort for Senate candidates, Donald Trump will hold his second general-election rally in the state later this week. Republicans remind observers that there have been false reports of a 21st-century Democratic breakthrough in South Carolina, most notably in 2020, when Graham’s big brother needed a late surge to put away Jaime Harrison, who had raised a small fortune for the race. Still, the climate for Republicans this year could be significantly worse than it was in 2020, and few would contend that Darline is a political talent quite like Lindsey. At present, South Carolina seems to have joined Kansas as red states where weak GOP Senate candidates are in trouble. Trump carried the former state by 16 percent in 2024 and the latter by 17 percent. This edge may be enough to keep Adam Hamilton and Annie Andrews out of the Senate. But don’t bet the farm on it.
- Final Pre-Midterms Polls Show Depth of Trump Slump
- Senate Control Could Hinge on Alaska’s Weird Politics
- Every Way Trump Might Mess With the Midterms

items.title: What would you bring to the afterlife? Sometimes the strangest things form the most moving picture
items.description: On Tuesday I walked over to Soho to see a preview screening of Spanish-language film La Bola Negra, directed by “Los Javis” (Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo). It’s a story set during the Spanish Civil War and the present day. It’s about love and desire. It’s
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: On Tuesday I walked over to Soho to see a preview screening of Spanish-language film La Bola Negra, directed by “Los Javis” (Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo). It’s a story set during the Spanish Civil War and the present day. It’s about love and desire. It’s about secrets and telling the truth. It’s about being gay. The film could be an Oscar contender for Best Picture: a campaign that will be aided by the shimmering, mesmerising presence of Penélope Cruz and a poised performance from Glenn Close.

Now, press screenings are not the most intimate of settings. The room is usually packed with seen-it-all critics who make their living from finding fault, taking things apart, spending the duration of the film scribbling big thoughts in little notepads. But in this velvet-chaired cocoon, I found myself lost in this epic, weaving and sometimes fantastical tale. The directors deliberately take their time to stitch all the narratives together (at one point I wondered if I should ask my jotting-away neighbour if he knew what the hell was happening). But even this pacing keeps you transfixed.

Towards the end of the film – when all is finally clear – there’s a fleeting moment when a young man stoops to kiss the head of his boyfriend. It’s just an “I’m here for you” kiss but I felt a tear jog down my face, and then another. I brushed them away. Why was I crying? For them, for me, for us? I need to see the film again because there’s something buried there. A little bit of me? A little bit of you too?

There’s something that I forgot to tell you about my brother-in-law’s funeral. Phil had been partial to a Starbucks, so his granddaughter arrived at the funeral service carrying a venti latte. She placed this next to the coffin. I was desperate to see if, for once, a Starbucks employee had managed to spell a name correctly but I was too far away.

Anyway, this last order for Phil sat there throughout the entire service. It was even there as the curtains closed and the coffin was dispatched to the flames. I have mentioned this Starbucks detail to a few people and it seems that, just as the ancient Egyptians entombed their dear departed pharaohs with all sorts of crap for the afterlife – mummified cats, cooking utensils, electric barbecues – modern grievers are keeping the tradition alive. I have been told of a Sunday roast being brought to a church and numerous pints of beer (even, in one case, to the funeral of a gentleman who had died an alcoholic).

Just so you know, I think that I will be happy to go to the next world free of pizza or pies – even if, finally, the carbs don’t matter. Though if you order one final cheeky margarita, I might be up for that.

On Monday, London will discover that a 1km stretch of the famous retail strip Oxford Street has been pedestrianised overnight. I wrote about this news for the Monocle Minute yesterday. I am sure that the project will be a success but I grew up in a new, postwar town with a fully pedestrianised centre and it was rubbish. It would have been so much nicer with cars. To keep the retail streets pedestrian only, the town was ringed by ugly multi-storey car parks. And, at night, once the shops had closed, it was desolate. People preferred to drive to pubs and restaurants in nearby villages. Over the years the town centre became edgy at night; the walkways stank of wee. Meanwhile, neighbouring towns with traffic, movement and activity thrived.
The plans for Oxford Street seem full of potential. But just getting rid of cars is not enough. I will watch and wait a while before getting too giddy about this change.

items.title: Susan Collins’s Biggest Problem? Donald Trump
items.description: Susan Collins was concerned. Not in the publicly hand-wringing way for which the Maine Republican senator has been repeatedly mocked, most notoriously for trusting then Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh’s statement that Roe v. Wade was “settled law.” No, t
items.author: Chris Smith
paragraphs: Susan Collins was concerned. Not in the publicly hand-wringing way for which the Maine Republican senator has been repeatedly mocked, most notoriously for trusting then Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh’s statement that Roe v. Wade was “settled law.” No, this was a serious political concern.

In late September, ProPublica published a story alleging that Donald Trump’s Department of Justice killed an investigation into whether Collins had given a military contractor favorable treatment in exchange for campaign money. The bombshell dropped just as Collins was heading into the final weeks of her toughest reelection race ever, a contest that could decide whether Republicans retain a Senate majority. The corruption accusations threatened to damage Collins’s strongest appeal to voters: her ability to deliver jobs and funding to Maine. Should she issue a statement denying any wrongdoing and then ignore the ProPublica story as much as possible, trying to cut off its oxygen? Or should Collins punch back hard?

Those strategic choices were the immediate, high-stakes priority. Yet even as her camp calculated, an absurdity hovered in the background: After years of Trump bluntly insulting Collins, could he really have gone out of his way to try to do her a favor? “I don’t know whether that notion,” a Collins insider says, “is ironic or comic.”

Troy Jackson is the Democratic nominee, a late replacement for the disgraced Graham Platner. The former logger and state legislator can be a stiff speaker, but in four contentious debates, Jackson has effectively blamed Collins for the soaring cost of everything from home heating oil to blueberry processing—by tying Collins to Trump’s tariffs and the president’s war with Iran. Because no matter who the Democrat on the ballot is this November, in many respects, the greatest obstacle to Collins winning a sixth term has long been the leader of her own party.

The two tangled frequently during Trump’s first term as president, peaking with Collins voting in favor of his second impeachment after the January 6 insurrection. The invective resumed when Trump returned to the White House. Along the way, he has castigated Collins as a “disaster,” a “loser,” and “absolutely atrocious,” and declared that she should “never be elected to office again.” Those are just some of the public attacks. In private, the president reportedly tore into the senator in a “profanity-laced rant” over the phone, after she voted in January in favor of curbing Trump’s war powers.

“Like most things with the president, he says exactly what he thinks,” a senior Republican strategist says. Steve Bannon, the on-again, off-again Trump adviser, sees something in Trump’s antagonism that goes beyond the political. “She’s the kind of person he has no time for—the mousy personality,” Bannon tells me. “She’s just a non-event. Even when she’s against something, she’s not really against it. And it’s not like she’s calling him and explaining why she’s not on board. It irks him.” Collins has sidestepped questions about whether she would campaign alongside Trump if he turns up in Maine this fall, but she pointed to a scheduling conflict to explain her absence from an appearance by Vice President J.D. Vance in Brewster in August.

Yet Trump has lately bitten his tongue about Collins, even as she strenuously tries to distance herself from him on everything from July’s fatal ICE shooting in Maine to Trump’s recent imposition of punitive tariffs on Canadian goods. Insiders say the president’s silence is strategic: He needs Collins to win if the Republicans are going to hold their Senate majority. “He’s pragmatic, a practical guy, always has been,” says the senior Republican strategist, who knows Trump well. “Is there any other Republican who could win in Maine?”

Mike DuHaime, a national Republican strategist who directed Senate campaign spending in previous cycles, believes Collins’s familiarity to Mainers will insulate her from the corruption allegations. “The biggest factor in that race,” he says, “is whether voters who still like Susan Collins are going to try to send a message to Trump at her expense.”

You may have heard Maine’s Democrats have had an exciting year. First came the meteoric rise of Platner, an Iraq veteran turned oyster farmer who seemed to be the next great populist hope until he was undone by an unceasing run of scandals, from the Nazi tattoo on his chest to accusations of sexual assault. (Platner has said he wasn’t aware the tattoo was recognized as a Nazi symbol and has since covered it. He has denied the sexual assault allegations.)

Platner’s noisy ascension and implosion didn’t just leave the Democrats looking untrustworthy. For months the saga consumed nearly all the media coverage in the Maine race, turning Collins, the five-term incumbent, into an afterthought. Whenever she did enter the conversation, Collins was commonly reduced to a caricature: the disingenuously naïve, dithering swing vote.

The people in Maine and DC who know her best, though, describe Collins as far tougher than she looks. “People always expect her to break,” a senior Democratic senator says. “She is more savvy and has more integrity than most people give her credit for.” Even a national Republican strategist with ties to the White House offers grudging respect: “She knows exactly what she’s doing and why she’s doing it. She is a damn good politician.”

Indeed. Collins made some mistakes during four debates with Jackson in the past month, including garbling the name of a Maine man shot and killed by ICE. But in the final showdown she also nimbly improvised a response to a protestor, provoking Jackson into telling Collins to “shut up,” a moment that generated helpful headlines.

Collins grew up just about as far north as you can get on the East Coast and still be in the United States, roughly 15 miles from Canada, in the town of Caribou, Maine, population 7,396. In a region known for its poor potato farmers, Collins’s family, as owners of a hardware store and a lumber mill, were relative royalty. “They had serious money,” says Gerry Conley Jr., a former second-generation Democratic Maine state legislator. “And she had a lot of connections.”

Still, Collins’s talents seemed, initially, best suited to working behind the scenes. Her first political job was as a staffer for 12 years to Maine Republican senator William Cohen. She returned north to serve as Governor John “Jock” McKernan’s commissioner of the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation, a role that put Collins at the center of a 16-day state government shutdown that was prompted by a dispute over workers’ compensation rates. “She was by far the smartest person in that administration,” Conley says. “She was dangerous, a tough negotiator.”

Bookish and bespectacled, Collins didn’t seem like an obvious candidate for office herself. It was something of a surprise, then, when Collins ran for governor of Maine in 1994; it was little surprise that she finished a weak third to Angus King, an independent, who won.

But Collins has always been a driven student. While working for Cohen, she met his chief of staff, Thomas Daffron. Daffron—who has shifted between jobs as a lobbyist and a congressional staffer—became Collins’s political mentor and, in 2012, her husband. In 1996, she returned as a more polished campaigner and won the Republican nomination to replace Cohen, whom president Bill Clinton appointed secretary of defense. Collins effectively styled herself a moderate in the vein of Maine senatorial predecessors Cohen, Olympia Snowe, and Margaret Chase Smith. She also demonstrated, not for the last time, a knack for facing an underwhelming opponent. Collins dispatched Joe Brennan, a retread Democrat, by slightly more than five points. In the three decades since, she hasn’t had a genuinely close race.

The battle against Jackson, though, looks like it will go down to the wire: a Washington Post poll, released October 9, showed the Democrat edging to a four-point lead. Bannon, interestingly, believes the Republicans’ intense focus on saving Collins could very well backfire for the GOP, not just in Maine, but across the country. “Iowa is in play, Kansas is in play, Nebraska is in play—because of Susan Collins,” he says. “The Senate majority didn’t move MAGA legislation, like the Save America Act, because John Thune was adamant about protecting his weakest members. And Collins is always number one on that list. If you don’t give the grassroots, low-propensity voters some reasons to show up in a midterm, they just don’t.”

In Maine, Collins’s problem isn’t the MAGA faithful. It’s independents, who make up nearly 33% of the state’s registered voters, and who have soured on Trump. So Jackson and Democrats are relentlessly trying to lash Collins tightly to the president. “Donald Trump owns Susan Collins,” Jackson told reporters recently. With independents, Collins is counting on the thing that has sustained her all these years: Whether you agree with her policy choices or not, she’s stable, sane, and at heart a “county girl,” a humble local, a true Mainer. Platner is gone from the race, but the turmoil he generated still resonates and makes Collins look dependable compared to the Democrats. The crescendo of outsider spending and criticisms could help bolster her appeal. “There’s a cultural norm, deeply rooted in Maine, that she’s one of ours and we’re going to stick with her,” says Tom Connolly, a Portland lawyer and longtime Democratic activist. “She has remarkable survival skills.”

Collins frequently walks through the Senate hallways carrying a large stack of briefing books. This isn’t an affectation. “She’s the hardest working person I have ever experienced in my life,” says Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist and Maine native who was a senior aide on three Collins Senate campaigns and also worked in her Washington office. “She has not gotten to where she is on charisma. She has gotten there on diligence. In some ways, she still thinks like a staffer.”

Collins travels from Washington to her home in Bangor nearly every weekend. In mid-July she marched, to a mix of cheers and boos from the 10,000 spectators, in the 42nd edition of the Moxie Festival Parade, an annual event in Lisbon, Maine. “She didn’t hang out or anything afterwards,” says Angie D’Amours, the event’s cochair. “Angus King [now Maine’s other senator] does, typically. She was out of there fairly quickly.”

Collins’s team did not return requests for comment for this story. The senator has energetically crisscrossed the state this fall, though a local reporter has been struck by how tightly controlled Collins’s camp keeps her appearances. “Platner was making himself available for hours in breweries and pizza places, and it stoked this enormous hunger for town halls,” the journalist says. “Susan hasn’t had one. When she does go to events, they tend to be way up north in the reddest, safest, most provincial towns, where she gets a warm welcome and knows enough people personally to feel insulated from any public negativity, of which there’s plenty.”

Maintaining a sense of normalcy and a human connection with her constituents has become increasingly difficult as opponents have dialed up their ire—most recently, flocking to Collins’s Maine office to loudly protest July’s ICE shooting. Even the sidewalk outside her home has become a flashpoint: When someone chalked a pro-choice message on the cement in 2022, Collins called the cops.

“The money she delivers, it really matters to small towns, and she and her staff are really masterful at letting people know that she was instrumental in bringing this funding home to Maine,” says Susan Young, the opinion page editor at the Bangor Daily News, who has known the senator for more than 25 years. “Susan Collins is a fabulous technocrat. But if you want someone who is a visionary, who will speak truth to power—there are more times she needs to buck the administration.”

Indeed, one payoff for Collins sweating the legislative and bureaucratic details has been a literal payoff for Maine. The senator, now chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has steered nearly $1.5 billion to the state in just the past five years, funding everything from hospitals to the Bath Iron Works. Over her career, Collins has made an art form of leveraging her votes, and the possibility that she might cross partisan lines, to support Maine projects, often to the frustration of Democrats. “Harry Reid used to say, ‘Susan Collins is always there when you don’t need her,’” says Jim Manley, a longtime top aide to the late Democratic Senate majority leader.

Trump’s arrival, though, blew up Collins’s preference for precision and process. The Capitol Hill game shifted from conventional horse-trading to a cult of personality, and Collins seemed out of her depth. But as long as she could occasionally appear to distance herself from Trump and maintain her image as a tortured, well-meaning moderate—while ultimately voting with Republicans 95% of the time—she could protect herself with enough Maine voters.

Now, however, Collins’s talent for funneling money home has collided with Trump’s destruction of governing norms. There’s no indication the president knew about the DOJ pulling the plug on its investigation of Collins in 2025—but the Trump administration has, more broadly, dialed back the pursuit of white-collar crime.

When the ProPublica story broke, an FBI spokesman said the bureau had “found nothing” to show that Collins or her campaign had broken any laws. Of course, that hasn’t stopped Jackson’s campaign and its allies from hammering Collins over the allegations. The senator’s team has chosen to respond aggressively. Annie Clark, a top aide, called the accusations “categorically false.” Shortly after Maine Democrats staged a press conference outside Collins’s office in Portland to trumpet the issue, Collins’s campaign manager Steve Abbott held his own, dismissing ProPublica’s reporting as relying on “allegations from a guy who was…trying to get his sentence reduced, as the article states directly.” Collins herself went on a Wall Street Journal podcast to label the story “a disgraceful smear job.”

The forceful counterattack makes sense in such a close race. And the controversy, the Collins insider says, may turn out to be perversely beneficial. “I have no question about the senator’s integrity,” he says. “But this whole thing could end up reminding people she’s relentless in pursuing money and jobs for Maine.” The state’s Democrats had their own scandal, and it drove their first nominee out of the race. Collins may not be corrupt. But at least her mess is on brand.

items.title: Little Shop of Horrors: An Oral History
items.description: Like an unassuming plant from outer space, Little Shop of Horrors had humble beginnings—but managed to blossom at a surprising rate. The musical is performed numerous times each year across the globe; the current Off Broadway production has been running for se
items.author: Andrew Buss
paragraphs: Like an unassuming plant from outer space, Little Shop of Horrors had humble beginnings—but managed to blossom at a surprising rate.
