The musical is performed numerous times each year across the globe; the current Off Broadway production has been running for seven years straight. But none of that would have happened without the 1986 film version of Little Shop, a cult classic that Warner Bros. executives once characterized as “the highest-budget musical they’d ever done,” according to its director, Frank Oz. “I don’t know if it’s true or if it’s hyperbole, but that’s what they told me to pressure me into doing a good job.”

“I love it. Audiences love it,” says composer Alan Menken. “Anytime I watch Little Shop,” though, “every other second I’ll be thinking about my late collaborator”—lyricist, book writer, and original stage director Howard Ashman, whom he worked with on both the original stage show and the film. “I’ll look at his work and how amazing it is,” Menken says. “Then people come running up to me, and I go, ‘It’s Howard.’”

It’s been nearly 40 years since Audrey II began its cinematic rampage. To commemorate the movie—which is getting a brand-new 4K restoration and rerelease on Blu-ray—Vanity Fair spoke with Oz, Menken, producer David Geffen, stars Rick Moranis, Ellen Greene, Tisha Campbell, Tichina Arnold, Michelle Weeks, and more about assembling an A-list cast including Steve Martin and Bill Murray; the film’s long, difficult production; why Moranis had to film several of his scenes as though he was moving in slow motion; and the movie’s elaborate, expensive, utterly depressing original ending.

Back in 1959, legendary low-budget filmmaker Roger Corman had a challenge: to shoot an entire film in two days. He enlisted Charles B. Griffith to write a film using preexisting sets—including a florist shop and a dental office. The original Little Shop of Horrors was born: a scrappy but ambitious B movie featuring a brief cameo by a young Jack Nicholson.

The film became a staple of late-night television, entrancing viewers like a teenage Howard Ashman. As an adult, Ashman knew it’d make a great musical. His agent watched the Corman film and told Ashman he was out of his mind.
Ashman then approached jingle writer Alan Menken about doing the musical with him at the WPA Theatre, of which Ashman was a cofounder.

ALAN MENKEN (COMPOSER): I thought it was absolutely amazing. This was one of those so-bad-it’s-good movies. When we first took a crack [at writing the songs], it was actually very close to the Corman film…. And then Howard said, “You know, I think we should do this as the dark side of Grease.”

You think about those beach blanket horror movies from the early ’60s or late ’50s, and there is both a tackiness and an incredible exuberance about them at the same time. And then you think about the Phil Spector Wall of Sound and his work with the Ronettes. So the score became a whole homage to all those early rock influences, and it just became a perfect tonal bed for the storytelling.

ELLEN GREENE (“AUDREY,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY AND THE 1986 FILM): I got to watch Howard direct several sessions with Alan playing on the piano. They counterbalanced each other; Howard was very serious, and Alan is just a sweetheart. Although Howard was also a sweetheart.

MENKEN: What makes for a good collaboration, first of all, is to get your fucking egos out of the room. Bring your talent into the room and always be ready to throw something out…. Don’t ever allow yourself to fall in love with your own work. You are driving this particular thing called a musical. Howard was the best I ever experienced at doing that…. Howard knew exactly what he wanted.

GREENE: I remember walking down the street [listening to a demo of the song “Skid Row” and thinking], I don’t want to do a camp musical. [Then I] got too unemployed, and I'm listening to “Somewhere That’s Green.” I started quietly singing “Green” to myself, and it made me cry. And I knew right then and there I had an Audrey inside of me that was waiting to be born…. When I went into the audition, I did the scenes, and the speaking voice just came out of me.

LEE WILKOF (“SEYMOUR,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY): I got a call from a casting director that I knew in New York. [She said], “A theater in New York is doing a musical based on the movie Little Shop of Horrors…. Would you come in and read for the part of the dentist? I walked into the audition…and Howard Ashman looked at me and he went, “You’re not a dentist. Would you mind going out and looking at the role of Seymour?” And I did, and I got a callback. Apparently, it was between me and another actor. His name’s Nathan Lane. And the assistant director apparently said that she thought that I would work better as a Seymour. Her name’s Connie Grappo, and we’ve been married 42 years.

GREENE: I was a brunette at the time. I said, “Howie, meet me at 14th Street.”… And I tried on a long blonde wig with bangs, and he went, “I don’t know what you’re doing.” I said, “Just let me finish.” Paul Holmes, the stage manager, helped me cut the wig, and Howard still wasn’t sure. Then I completed the look [with a black cocktail dress], and he loved it.

The show opened at the WPA in 1982 for what was supposed to be a two-week “showcase,” with the actors all making a mere $50 a week in exchange for being reviewed by major theater critics. It was an immediate success.
WILKOF: It was impossible to get a ticket. It went from being this obscure little show. The word on the street apparently grew.
MENKEN: We had lines of producers around the block.
DAVID GEFFEN (PRODUCER): I don’t quite remember how I first got involved, but I think Cameron Mackintosh and I were approached…. I thought it was terrific.
MENKEN: We knew there were people who wanted to bring Little Shop to Broadway, and Howard said absolutely not.
GEFFEN: The [Off Broadway] show was very successful, highly thought of. Then we opened it up in Los Angeles. It was natural that we’d make it as a movie.

The creative team began planning a feature film, which Geffen would produce. Tom Cruise, per Menken, wanted to play Seymour (although his reps have claimed he wasn’t interested in the role); he was immediately vetoed by Ashman. Geffen had his eyes set instead on a comedic actor from Canada.

RICK MORANIS (“SEYMOUR”): I first started hearing about the film being made early on, like ’82 or ’83. I ran into David Geffen randomly—I had never met him before—and he stopped me and said, “I want you in my movie.” I said, “Which one?” And he told me, and I said, “Well, okay!” And then for the next three years, I would occasionally hear about it or read about it in the hands of one director or another, and nothing ever happened.

At one point, Steven Spielberg was slated to produce the film, with Martin Scorsese directing. John Landis was also attached to the project for a time. Perhaps the name that made the most sense on paper was Frank Oz, best known as the man who brought to life childhood staples like Miss Piggy, Fozzie Bear, and Yoda.

FRANK OZ (DIRECTOR): I saw [the show] and thought it was amazing. But I didn’t have a take on it. And when I read the script for the movie, I couldn’t get my hands around it. It was so big, and I didn’t have a clear vision of it. So, through my agents, I said, “Thank you, but I can’t do it.” Two weeks later, something clicked in me regarding the three girl-group singers. I realized that when they entered onstage, all they could do was enter from the left or from the right…. But in a movie, it’s 360 degrees; you can have them enter from anywhere. So that’s what kind of changed my idea. I called back and I said, “You know, I may have a way to do this,” and then David asked me to do a rewrite…. Then I went to London, and I spent a month on the rewrite, and I felt really good about it. I knew if I said yes [to directing it], that’d mean two years of my life would be on this project. But I was committed and excited about it.
GREENE: [Frank] has to see the vision. Until he sees the vision in his mind’s eye, in his head, he will not take something on.

MORANIS: [It’s] the intersection of so many skills and qualities that he has: a remarkable sense of humor, a real affinity for the darker arts and all the puppeteering, and such a keen eye for design.

OZ: I had not known Rick, who is now one of my closest friends after all these years. I never knew Rick, never heard of him because I was in London shooting for five years, and Rick was doing SCTV, and that was not shown in London. But I saw some of his work and I thought it was brilliant.

MORANIS: I knew this was an extraordinary opportunity to do a musical, and shoot it in London, and work with Frank and that cast. [Film] musicals don’t come along too often for people who get to call themselves actors.

OZ: David understandably wanted a star, but…I couldn’t see an Audrey with the depth and the heart that was given to the character by Ellen. I couldn’t see that being done by anyone else. So I asked him to please let me do a screen test with Ellen, and he did. And that’s when David said yes to Ellen.

MORANIS: Ellen had created the character of Audrey for the Off Broadway show many years before we did the movie. She wasn’t just acting the part of Audrey; she was Audrey. I had just come from years of comedic character acting on SCTV and in films like Strange Brew and Ghostbusters. So we were both approaching our performances for Little Shop in similar ways. I think that’s why we had such a strong onscreen chemistry.

GREENE: Frank saw the character a little more heroine-like [than she was onstage]. He wasn’t sure about the “Audrey-isms,” and so that’s why the line “You don’t meet nice boys when you live on Skid Row, Mr. Mushnik” is not in the film…. Freddy Cooper was a cameraman…and he’s the reason I got to do the squeak in the film. Frank and Rick weren’t sure, and he spoke up and said, “Sir, I think it’s funny.”

OZ: David also suggested Steve Martin, and Steve I had worked with a little bit prior to that. Steve and I talked, and at the time there was a very popular character called Fonzie, and Steve said he just didn’t want to do Fonzie. I said, “Absolutely, that’s fine.” He wanted it more like Elvis. I said, “Fantastic.” As far as I was concerned, Steve could do anything.
The film’s glue wasn’t any of its big names; it was the three girls, all under 18, who made up its ’60s-girl-group-esque Greek chorus.

TISHA CAMPBELL (“CHIFFON”): I had just auditioned to play Regina King’s best friend in 227, and I didn’t get it. So I quit. I was 16 years old. I wanted to go to camp with my friends. And while I was there, my mother called me. She said, “Your agent keeps bugging me. They won’t stop calling me.” I said, “Did you tell them I quit?” And she said, “I told them and said you just wanted to be a regular kid, and they were like, ‘Please, just this one audition. Then you can go to camp.’ Can you just do it and I’ll send you right back to camp? No harm, no foul.” And I was like, “Okay, fine.”

MICHELLE WEEKS (“RONETTE”): At the time, I was on Broadway doing Tap Dance Kid, and I had a management company submit me. When I went for the audition…I was like, Yeah, they’re not gonna pick me. I’m too big. But then when we went for the callbacks, I was like, Oh, I have a chance!

TICHINA ARNOLD (“CRYSTAL”): [I was] starting off in the theater [as] a little kid with wide eyes and ready to get it cracking. I just so happened to know Michelle Weeks because she and I went to school together. We had the same friends, and then Tisha and I knew each other from just auditioning.

CAMPBELL: They auditioned girls from everywhere…. And it just so happened that [the three girls cast were] from the tristate area. Michelle was from Brooklyn, Tichina was from Queens, and I was from New Jersey.
ARNOLD: And Frank Oz, we asked him, “How did you choose us?” And he was just like, “You girls had a synergy.”

Little Shop presented a real technical challenge: how to capture chemistry between its lead, Rick Moranis, and the man-eating plant. For the voice of the plant—named Audrey II by Seymour—the creative team turned to Motown singer Levi Stubbs. But actually bringing the creature to life would be the real struggle.

OZ: There’s only two words necessary, and that’s [puppeteer] Lyle Conway. Lyle passed recently, sadly, but Lyle is the one responsible for the plant. He was a pure artist, and he did an incredible job.

BRIAN HENSON (PRINCIPAL PUPPETEER): I think [Lyle] brought almost everybody that was on Return to Oz, and then a lot more because it was a much bigger build…. My dad [Jim Henson] came and visited the shoot a couple times, for sure. And then my little sister, Heather, was in it. She’s in the dentist scene.

BRAN FERREN (SPECIAL VISUAL EFFECTS): Lyle Conway was brilliant, his vision for how to create—because there wasn’t one plant; there were a series of plants that were used to show its various stages of growth.
OZ: I needed pure lip sync, really good lip sync, not just a mouth opening and closing. Because you’re on film, they can see in a tight shot that it’s just a puppet if it’s just opening and closing.

HENSON: This was definitely the biggest and the most complex [thing] that had ever been done in animatronics. It was also before the Creature Shop–type people were using motors, so it was almost all cable-driven.
OZ: All the performers had to rehearse the song over and over and over to make sure they hit every single syllable.

HENSON: There’s no eyes on that character, so it was always going to be the physical presence of the plant combined with this mouth and this voice. So Levi’s recordings were very important to Frank. [But] we started rehearsing before he even had Levi’s recordings.

MORANIS: They were looking for ways to make vowels and consonants so that they could form words, and then form phrases, and then be able to do that to music. And it was only possible to do at a slower motion than 24 frames a second.

There are 24 still frames in every second of standard film. But during rehearsals, it was discovered that the plant could not believably lip-synch at that speed. The production’s solution was to slow down Audrey II’s motions—operating the plant at 12 frames per second, then speeding the film up later so that it would look normal. This meant that anytime Moranis was in the same shot as the plant, he also had to move, act, and sing in slow motion.

MORANIS: The trick was to keep my butt tight. Because we keep our butt tight when we’re walking quickly. And when you try and walk slowly, it’s very easy to let your butt relax. If you were to look at that at 24 frames, you would look like you were doing some sort of weird walk. So by keeping the butt tight, I managed to pull it off, I think.

GREENE: [Frank] taught me how to act at 12 frames per second. He put me in a room; he had a camera. He said, “Ellen, walk across the floor.” He set it up to the regular speed. He said, “Now look at this,” and it looked like I was rocking back and forth. He showed me how you have to walk only forward, and ballet sort of helped. I worked on acting, talking, and moving in 12 frames a second.

FERREN: How do you put emotion into a plant? I mean, news flash: It wasn’t a real man-eating plant! And my suspicion is that not many people watching the movie said, “Oh my God, they found an actual man-eating plant.” If you get it right, they shouldn’t be thinking about that.

HENSON: When we started rehearsing, we just had a bit of skin for the lips. The head was bald, and it was quite lightweight. Every week they’d build a little bit more, and it would just get heavier and heavier and heavier. By the end, it weighed more than 150 pounds.

With the cast—and plant—in place, filming began on October 21, 1985, at Pinewood Studios on the 007 Stage. Per Frank Oz’s vision, it had to be done entirely on a soundstage, as the world they were creating couldn’t come to life on location.

OZ: Roy Walker, our brilliant production designer, and I walked through the whole set. I told him where I felt things needed to be for each particular number, because I had planned the numbers in my head months before I even got to London.

GREENE: [As] someone who first was on this tiny, tiny stage, [I walked] into Pinewood Studios…and there in front of me is the land that is built, that I only saw in my mind's eye because I was on the stage—and it’s even better than I ever imagined.

OZ: My goal was to make it a movie sensibility instead of only a theatrical sensibility. It’s really a mixture of it, and my real goal was to make sure it reflected the gritty atmosphere of an Off Broadway play, and not a musical. I didn’t want to make it into Hello, Dolly! or Mame.
MENKEN: Little Shop is meant to be this tacky show in a hole-in-the-wall…and they wanted the film to have that same quality.

OZ: The opening number is packed with information. You have the three girls dancing in the streets. I needed people to know that they were not regular human beings, so I had them sing in the rain—and they were not affected by the rain.

ARNOLD: Frank Oz explained to us, “It’s gonna be raining around you, but you won’t get wet.” And I was like, “How is that gonna happen?” He showed us the pipes and stuff that they had in the ceiling and said, “Okay, so choreography-wise, you’re gonna follow this path [to ensure you don’t get wet].”

CAMPBELL: Man, it was raining on our heads! The first time we filmed that scene, it was raining so hard that you could tell on our faces. They had to cut. They were like, “You can’t show that it’s raining on y’all!”

WEEKS: We had to be up early in the morning, and us being teenagers, we were going places we weren’t supposed to go, like the club. We used to go to the Hippodrome and get out at like two or three in the morning, and have to be at the studio at six. But it was so much fun!

OZ: I loved shooting “Suddenly Seymour.” When Roy showed me the set—which is beautiful—I saw that staircase that he made. I thought, Okay, it’s got to be a Romeo-and-Juliet section where she’s up there, and he’s down there, and he runs up there. So it was all built up to that moment. I had him run up the stairs 30 to 40 times.

GREENE: Fifty-three takes we had to go up those stairs. [The “Suddenly Seymour”] set was so beautiful, with grass growing through the cracks and bricks and cobblestones. If any set was ever called a work of art, I think this would be applicable.
CAMPBELL: [Steve Martin] was very quiet off camera. But when that camera rolled, I was just in awe of how he would light up and become this character, and just be very big and broad.

OZ: When David suggested Billy [Murray, who has a cameo in the dentist scene]—and I knew Billy before that—I called him. I said, “Hey, Billy, do you want to do this?” And Bill said, “Do I have to do the words?” And I said, “No. I don’t care what words you use as long as you’re the masochist and he’s the sadist. That’s all I care about.”
As technical as the film itself was, nothing could compare to the plant.
OZ: People tend to think, Oh, puppets, that’s no problem. They are the hardest things in the world to shoot, to do right…. Just “Feed Me” alone took five weeks to shoot.

HENSON: Nowadays, you think of a film unit shooting 30 to 40 setups a day. Little Shop of Horrors was way down at three to five, five to seven if you were shooting easier stuff. It was slow, meticulous shooting. And Frank is a very meticulous director.
OZ: We’d usually go about 25 to 30 takes to make it perfect.

MORANIS: [For] “Feed Me,” Brian was inside the head of the plant, and then all the other puppeteers were connected to the plant. The actual plant store that we shot in was constructed on the second floor, and the first floor is where the puppeteers set up camp and where their cables would go down to. They would have monitors, and they could watch themselves operate the plant.

HENSON: There were vines that were being worked by one or two people on each vine. It [took] maybe five of us to work the head…. With “Mean Green Mother”…there’d be puppeteers all the way around the outside of the set, doing cables, and on the roof of the set was another maybe 10 puppeteers. And the set was also on top of a tank, so they could get to the underside of the pot for the roots.

MORANIS: It was so enjoyable to do [“Feed Me”]. I don’t think I had a moment when I didn’t enjoy shooting it. I do remember one aspect, just because it went on for so long: Every day I would come in and put on the same clothes.[Just] put on the same clothes every day for five weeks, or whatever it was.

HENSON: [During “Feed Me”], I’m right there. I said to Lyle, “You know, I just can’t stay hidden all the time.”… I couldn’t hide completely behind the stem. And Lyle said, “Okay, this is what we’re going to do. You’re going to wear a skintight green Lycra suit, and I’m gonna glue leaves to it.” There’s bits of me in the shots, but you don’t know it’s me.

The stage version of Little Shop ends with the plant eating Audrey, Seymour, and, finally, the audience. The filmmakers were determined to capture that same spirit, and did so in a $5 million epic ending that saw Audrey II taking over New York—ending on top of the Statue of Liberty.

OZ: Before I even went to London, I was at David Geffen’s office, and David said to us, “You know, you can’t end it the way the play ends it, because you’re killing your leads.” And Howard and I both said, “Well, we want to be true to the ending from Off Broadway, in part because we just like being true to things, but also because it was a deal with the devil. He deserved to die because he killed people, even though he didn’t do it maliciously.”
GREENE: I gravitate to the dark underpinnings of the Faustian tale. Even though there's a magical world full of whimsy and silliness and goofiness, it has a moral with dark underpinnings.

OZ: Richard Conway had worked about nine months on the models of the destruction at the end. It was no CGI, no opticals. Richard had built all this stuff, and then built the small plant that would be on the bridge, and he did an incredible job having the plants like Godzilla raging through the city.

MORANIS: I remember that, when I saw the ending of the play, something was off with it, but it didn’t matter because the vines came out of the ceiling. And I thought, This is brilliant! They’re distracting you from the tragic ending by creating this fun experience of stuff flying out of the ceiling.You’re part of the action. The shock and surprise, and all the tactile fuzziness of it, distracted from whatever was lacking in a fulfilling happy ending. It didn’t occur to me that that would become a problem in the film.

GREENE: In the play, I say a line—“When I die, which should be very shortly…”—just to lighten the moment, and it’s silly. It releases some of the energy in the audience. But when I say it in the film, it’s very intimate, and it’s to Seymour. It’s weighted differently…. I’m very proud of that scene.
MENKEN: When we did [the first] preview…I'm sitting there going, “Wow! Look at this!” I look at David Geffen, and he said, “Yeah, wow, but wait a second—the cards, Alan!”

Those would be the reaction cards on which that era’s preview audiences would answer questions regarding how much they liked a film. Typically, producers were looking for 55% of a screening’s viewers to say they’d “recommend” the film. Little Shop’s first screening in San Jose got 13%. Oz asked Geffen to screen it again in LA to make sure this wasn’t an anomaly. The results were the same.
GEFFEN: People were hostile to the end of the film. They were hostile to the characters getting killed. We thought we were going to have a disaster.

OZ: The audience was against me because I killed people they loved, and it was a great lesson to learn. Onstage, they also die, but the actors come out for a bow. In movies, you don’t come out for a bow. You just die.
GREENE: [Onstage], my death is not as heartbreaking. It's a mixture. Just when you’re about to laugh, I’ll make you cry. Just when you’re about to cry, I’ll make you laugh.

GEFFEN: I think what the audience didn’t get was that this was a send-up of monster movies in the ’50s. They took it quite seriously. We made it so realistic that they were horrified by the end of the movie.
FERREN: The idea was, I want to go out smiling and happy. Now, I guess, it shows my personality. I went out smiling and happy, watching the world end.

OZ: They wouldn’t even release the movie if I didn’t change the ending…. The hardest of all was the terrible, terrible, terrible phone call I had to make after Richard Conway and his amazing crew made all those miniatures in that whole ending. I remember I had to call London from Los Angeles and say, “Richard, we’re not going to use any of it.”

What I also heard at the time [after the failed test screenings] was that there was a thought to try and get Rodney Dangerfield to do the voice of the plant, I assume to make it funny. My intent for the plant was to have it [be] a strong antagonist. If it was funny, there would have been no threat to Seymour or Audrey.

The team had to figure out a new finale that would stay true to the story and give Seymour and Audrey a happy ending. The solution? Seymour would electrocute the plant during their final showdown, and he and Audrey would finally get to move somewhere that’s green. But sitting outside of their dream home would be a small Audrey II, smiling at the camera.

OZ: The idea [came together] very fast. Howard and I knew exactly what had to happen. That part where the little plant smiles at the end was because I couldn’t make it a happy ending. It had to have some danger to it…. We went back [to London] for a month to reshoot.

Made on a budget of $25 million, including $5 million that wound up on the cutting-room floor, the film was unleashed on the public on December 19, 1986. It wound up doubling its budget at the box office, earning $54 million globally. A modest success, it didn’t necessarily set the world on fire—at least, not right away.

ARNOLD: Tisha and I had a really interesting moment. We decided to go see the movie in Times Square. We sat behind these two girls that were watching it, and we were like, “Okay, let’s go in when it’s dark so nobody recognizes us.”

CAMPBELL: There were these three girls sitting behind us. And [during the movie], they were like, “I’m so sick of these girls popping up out of nowhere!” [Laughs] So our first experience being able to watch our film, there were some haters behind us.
ARNOLD: Needless to say, I don’t watch myself anymore.

MENKEN: “Mean Green Mother” was nominated for the Academy Award, which was just amazing. I remember Levi Stubbs came out and sang “Mean Green Mother.” And I'm thinking, Wow! Well, I have a speech in my pocket. Who knows? Howard just goes, “Alan, you can relax. You’re not giving any speeches tonight.”
OZ: [When it came to home video], that’s when everything kind of exploded.
GREENE: [While currently touring with the movie], I get to see their love of Little Shop, their love of Audrey, even their love of me. I just hug everybody because I know they want it.

WEEKS: I went to see [Ellen on the tour recently]. It brought me to tears a couple of times…. They introduced me, and Ellen was surprised to see me. I was so happy to see her. We hugged and everything, and we talked a bit later on. But the warm reception that I got kind of brought me to tears because they were like, “Oh my gosh, it’s Ronette!” It just made me feel seen.
ARNOLD: I always said Little Shop of Horrors was a movie done before its time. But it stood the test of time and is still standing.
MENKEN: It is a true musical, and it’s driven by high-energy pop and rock, and it’s not about, “Oh, look how hip it is.”… It’s a thrill ride that really moves fast.

GEFFEN: I thought it was a terrific movie when we made it. I was very unhappy that we changed the ending…. I always wanted to restore it. And, as you know, we did. [In 2017 a version of the movie with the original ending played in theaters.]
OZ: I finally got to call Richard before he retired, saying, “Richard, finally they’re going to see your work.”

MORANIS: It’s become a point of discussion for people, whether they prefer one to the other, or if they’ve seen both of them. It’s prompted a couple of extra releases of different versions of the film.
OZ: I think [it resonates] because when you look at the movie, you know it’s not CGI…. It’s nice to show people what could be done when a lot of human beings get together and make something.

items.title: Dancing With the Stars Recap: Trick and Kick or Treat
items.description: It’s “Horror Movie Night” on Dancing With the Stars and it’s packed with the stuff of nightmares: sentient dolls, killer clowns, 4 paddles. You read that right. More than one 4 paddle is brought out this week, and the gasps from the crowd were audible. These t
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: It’s “Horror Movie Night” on Dancing With the Stars and it’s packed with the stuff of nightmares: sentient dolls, killer clowns, 4 paddles. You read that right. More than one 4 paddle is brought out this week, and the gasps from the crowd were audible. These terrifying scores are brought to us by, not surprisingly, our guest judge, Shirley Ballas.

Shirley is the head judge on the U.K.’s Strictly Come Dancing (the show from whence Dancing With the Stars was born), and she’s known for being brutal on technique. She’s also known for breaking out tiny shoes to demonstrate footwork and that’s actually kind of cute. She’s Mark Ballas’s mother, has trained a lot of our pros (and other judges and hosts, looking at you, Houghs), and is the Queen of Latin dance. She’s an icon. It does seem a bit like a waste to bring her over to judge an evening that will be heavy on Contemporary and Jazz and will, in fact, feature only one actual Latin routine, but this is the will of the Mirrorball, it seems. Does it lead to some real disparity in scores? Sure, but this Halloween celebration is a night for DWTS’s wardrobe, hair and makeup, and production-design teams to shine, and it is mostly a real treat. Well, except for that one looming trick hanging over the entire proceedings: Tonight there will be the dreaded double elimination. Hold me, I’m scared.
Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa
Argentine Tango // “The Dogs Attack,” by Jerry Goldsmith, Lionel Newman, and National Philharmonic Orchestra

The whiplash from last week’s emotional “Dedication Night” dances to this week’s full-out fear factor is fully on display with Julia and Ezra’s The Omen–inspired routine. Julia’s riding a high after reuniting the 10 Things I Hate About You cast in her Heath Ledger tribute and rides it directly into one of her worst dances of the season. It feels like she’s regressing a bit these past two weeks. (It probably doesn’t help that there seems to be some tension between the couple in rehearsal.) She’s stiff and none of these sharp, precise Argentine Tango steps look natural on her. Shirley really digs into Julia’s incorrect posture and lack of leg control. It’s a rough night!
Carrie Ann: 7 // Derek: 7 // Shirley: 4 // Bruno: 8
Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson
Contemporary // “Toxic,” by 2WEI

Anyone is lucky (or smart) to pull Contemporary for the Halloween-themed night because Halloween-themed Contemporary routines rule, but Harry is especially lucky because Jenna Johnson’s Contemporary choreography always hits. She does not disappoint with this Saw-inspired routine. The musicality here is spot-on (that first perfectly timed leap Jenna makes onto Harry? I gasped), and the way Harry can contort his body is incredible — this plays into all of his strengths but in a way that isn’t overpowering or distracting. Carrie Ann gives them a standing ovation and I feel like we’ve all really healed from the Great Lift Scandal of two weeks ago. I still think Amber and Pasha’s Contemporary last week should’ve been the first perfect score of the season, but this one will do, too.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 10 // Shirley: 10 // Bruno: 10
Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik
Paso Doble // “I Lied to You,” by Miles Caton

Somehow it’s Tatyana and Jan who get saddled with the only Latin dance on the evening the Latin dance icon is judging, and she does not go easy on them. Shirley’s note that there was “no recognizable Paso Doble” seems like a bit of an exaggeration. Yes, there could have been more Flamenco elements and some stronger shaping, but that was a paso, baby. And they looked good doing it. Those first few counts with the troupe were especially fun — Tatyana was so into this Sinners dance, you could feel it radiating off of her. Our judges knock her for some messy underarm passes, but Tatyana and Jan sell the hell out of every single dance they perform, including this one. (Tatyana ripping off a piece of Jan’s face to reveal those gnarly teeth? The drama!) When will they have their time in the sun? Someone give them a 9, I am begging.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Shirley: 4 // Bruno: 8
Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy
Argentine Tango // “Uninvited,” by Damned Anthem and Kendra Dantes

Val’s back in the studio and he does kick off rehearsals with an apology to his partner for “all the chaos,” which is the least he can do since he really did fuck things up for a lot of people. Nevertheless: Zombies! I still prefer Jenna in softer dances, but some of the tricks and lifts are so freaking smooth in this routine, it cannot be denied. Unfortunately, at one point, her foot gets tangled up in her dress and she stumbles out of it, but otherwise, the judges praise her leg control and precision — and Carrie Ann specifically applauds Val’s choreography, which, like, big of her. Lucky for these two, Derek apparently watches these routines with his eyes shut because he misses that very big stumble and bestows upon them the title of “best Argentine Tango [he’s] seen on this dance floor.”
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 10 // Shirley: 9 // Bruno: 9
Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold
Contemporary // “You Are My Sunshine,” by Charles McDonald

I find it endearing how much Connor Wood looks like he’s going to hurl on this show. Stars, they’re just like us. This week, he might vomit because, like most normies, haunted dolls give him the creeps and he’s in a Contemporary inspired by Annabelle: Creation. Connor also looks like he might barf at the end of his routine when our little podcaster and man who paid Jennifer Lawrence no mind gets two 10s. Can you even believe? It’s a great, creepy-as-hell story with some killer choreography from Rylee, and Connor looks more comfortable in this style than he has in any of the others—like, it’s not even close. He clears an entire couch! Although, when Carrie Ann dubs him “the king of Contemporary” I had to wonder if Harry was somewhere backstage yelling what the fuck?
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 10 // Shirley: 8 // Bruno: 9
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach
Jazz // “Madness,” by Ruelle

Ezra is dealing with a lot of pain this week. Because of all the dancing and extra time in his prosthetic, he’s developed a cyst on the end of his residual limb. He says this is normal for amputees, but it looks incredibly painful nonetheless. And while Carrie Ann commends Ezra for pushing through the pain and says she didn’t notice any type of injury impeding him, you can tell the difference. He doesn’t have the power or fire under him like we’re used to seeing. The choreography isn’t super exciting, either, and this homage to The Invisible Man looks like more of a Contemporary/Jazz hybrid than a true Jazz. It’s not like he’s bad — he’s still getting praised for impressive lifts and earning 8s and 9s — you can just tell he isn’t fully himself this week.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 9 // Shirley: 9 // Bruno: 9
Jackson Olson and Emma Slater
Contemporary // “That’s Life,” by Frank Sinatra

I think Jackson not splitting his time between Banana-ing and dancing is doing him wonders. Like last week, Jackson looks more locked in and you can see some technical improvement. He also really gets into the character of this dance (finally), which is perhaps not hard to do when your entire face is painted to make you look like the Joker. Shirley and Derek both call out some clunky lift transitions (those lifts really leave a lot to be desired), but everyone agrees that Jackson’s commitment shines. It feels a little chaotic at times, but I guess that’s the Joker’s whole deal, right?
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Shirley: 8 // Bruno: 9
Tyler Cameron and Sharna Burgess
Viennese Waltz // “Love Song for a Vampire,” by Annie Lennox

Speaking of commitment, Tyler’s wig this week. I hate it and am also obsessed with it. This Dracula-inspired Viennese Waltz is moody, albeit a little sleepy — we’ve just had some really showy pieces tonight, and this is much more subtle. Tyler does look like he’s leading, though, even if Shirley really gets on him about his frame and lack of drive with his heels. Carrie Ann thought he was dancing small and tight and found the performance value to be lacking. Tyler looks so defeated after this feedback. Once he gets his scores, Sharna basically has to hold him back from walking off before the commercial break. People are deeply invested this season!
Carrie Ann: 7 // Derek: 7 // Shirley: 5 // Bruno: 7
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov
Argentine Tango // “Perfection,” by Clint Mansell

Amber once skated to this song from Black Swan as a teen, so she knows exactly how to get into character for this dance, and it shows. It’s a perfect theme for these two, although the song feels a little offbeat for Argentine Tango, but Amber’s legs remain the best in the game. Shirley loves how much they traveled around the floor and Bruno praises the precise musicality, so what do I know? Carrie Ann found Amber to be a little tight in her shoulders, but Derek goes wild for the perfectly executed leg hooks. It’s wild that all 9s feels like a loss, but it does seem like a setback after the high of last week.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Shirley: 9 // Bruno: 9
Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas
Contemporary // “Cry Little Sister,” by Gerard McMann

Do we think Maura and Mark were at an advantage or disadvantage being judged by Mark’s mom? I lean toward the latter because I feel like Shirley is that diva. It’s mostly inconsequential, anyway, because this Contemporary winds up being middle-of-the-road regardless of Shirley’s scores. Maura has excelled in those in-frame, graceful dances because she is so light on her feet and pulls off elegance so easily. This talent does not serve her even one bit in this style. Contemporary needs power and emotion, and this homage to The Lost Boys doesn’t have much of either. Bruno wants to see her more grounded in her movement, using that momentum from the floor up through her entire body, and both Derek and Shirley ding Maura for incorrectly placed and under-rotated feet. She’s really exposed here.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 8 // Shirley: 7 // Bruno: 8

It’s a mixed bag on “Horror Movie Night,” but two of our couples have got to go. It’s not a complete shocker when Alfonso and Julianne announce it’s Tyler and Sharna and Jackson and Emma headed home. While this elimination feels pretty right, it is unfortunate that Jackson and Emma have to get terrible news on the same night they’ve got giant clown smiles painted on their faces. They couldn’t have had that makeup removed before results? Now that situation seems like an actual horror show.

items.title: Love Is Blind Recap: We’re a Team — Ever Heard of It?
items.description: I unfortunately feel like Chris Harrison saying this, but we may have just witnessed the most dramatic pod-squad group hang in Love Is Blind history. Rob, whose family and friends have singled him out as a problem child many times throughout the season, has a
items.author: Emma Sharpe
paragraphs: I unfortunately feel like Chris Harrison saying this, but we may have just witnessed the most dramatic pod-squad group hang in Love Is Blind history. Rob, whose family and friends have singled him out as a problem child many times throughout the season, has a generational crashout at the Irish pub, proving that the masks these people wear for TV can only last so long before you realize you’re about to open a joint bank account with an insane person.

Families continue coming into play in the homestretch of the engagements, but three of the five couples have off-camera meetings with relatives who declined to film, so we have to rely on their tepid testimony of how those interactions went, which is about as narratively compelling as a co-worker telling you about their dream.
Next week we head to the altar, where I’m rooting for breakups across the board. It has to be better to be single and sad than married and miserable, right?

Michaella has been proving from day one that she’s totally one of the boys (remember when she told Rob she wanted to smoke cigars with him when their future daughter is being a bitch?), but even the most powerful pick-me girl in all the land would draw a line at Rob’s gaggle of bumbling Boston buffoons.

Rob has been super nervous about Michaella meeting these losers, and now we know why. His drunk and belligerent friend Jay immediately starts reducing her to a sex object, commenting on how she thinks she’d be great in the bedroom and asking if she’s made OnlyFans content. Rob and the rest of the douchebags should have sent Jay to get his stomach pumped at Mass General, but instead, the night drags on and on. As the group gets rowdier, Rob gets into an argument with production about the bartender cutting off Jay, which is apparently “phony-ass Hollywood bullshit,” and we get a rare glimpse of a camera operator when he yells at them to stop filming.

This is the initial foreshadowing that Rob is incredibly perturbed by being on a TV show. He is worried about getting canceled and relitigates an off-camera conversation with Michaella about whether he’s ever been aggressive with her, presumably to get her to recant her comment about him pulling her earring on tape. His insecurity also extends to Michaella’s motivations for joining the show, and she says he’s made jabs at her about “how much she has to gain professionally” from being on Love Is Blind. (Does she? I don’t even think she’s said the name of her cheugy boutique once.)

Rob’s true feelings explode at the group outing: After what looks like hours of being his brash and obnoxious self (including being majorly threatened by Matt the Beekeeper, Michaella’s second choice in the pods), he starts ranting about how everything they’re doing is fake and no one knew one another a month ago. No one would care if he fell down an elevator shaft. This Truman Show crashout basically confirms to Michaella what she’s probably known but resisted for the past month, which is that she “cannot marry this man under any circumstances.” After crying in the bathroom, she breaks up with him while Blake awkwardly stands there wishing he could melt into the wall.

When Michaella catches up with Erika a few days later, she reveals that after Rob insisted they leave the party together, he packed up his stuff and went home to Rhode Island, leaving her there alone. He eventually calls her to apologize, but by that point, Michaella has been deprogrammed.

Rob and Michaella’s odds: War is over! Manifesting intensive therapy and mandatory anger-management classes for Rob. Manifesting that Michaella reconnects with the hot beekeeper, who was definitely trying to slide.

Blake is so afraid of thinking beyond his next BLT that he would willingly opt in to that curse from Pirates of the Caribbean where you can only step on land once every ten years just to avoid a defining-the-relationship convo with his situationship.

When Erika broaches the legitimate and important timeline-for-kids discussion, proposing they have their first in three years (Blake will be 40), he looks like the Ghost of Christmas Future just showed up to the dog brewery with a hazy IPA and the prophecy that the Boston Bruins will never win another Stanley Cup in his lifetime. I’ve never heard silence quite this loud — here is another major life-goal mismatch that should have been squashed in the pods.

Everyone in Blake’s life harbors serious concerns about his potential marriage to a land-bound woman, which culminates in a brutal girl-best-friend dinner from hell. He introduces Erika to two of his female friends from St. Thomas, who start ambushing her with facts about what life would actually be like if she moved there — no health care, a ridiculously expensive school system, no direct flights to Boston — until she excuses herself to the restroom to probably cry.

The only individual who’s maybe on Erika’s side is, of all people, Benita, who has a chat with Blake at the aforementioned messy meetup. She says she loves Erika and regrets telling Blake he made the biggest mistake of his life by not choosing her — he tells her he felt “robbed” that she left.

We get a major peek into Erika’s thought process when she has Michaella over for gold-goblet wine to console her after the Rob breakup. Erika has already been married once, and she confesses that the thought of starting over with dating again in her mid-30s is “crippling.” So crippling that you would sacrifice your entire vision for your life and future family just so you never have to answer “How many siblings do you have?” at Tatte Bakery ever again?

Blake and Erika’s odds: +400. We end the episodes with a heart-to-heart where Blake alleges he’s all in. But it’s finally clicking for Erika that the cozy bubble they’ve created is a disparate world from his Below Deck reality and she’s no Kate Chastain.

These two never seem like they’re having fun. Their “banter” is just the “needs improvement” section of a corporate end-of-year evaluation form adorned with a couple of passive-aggressive millennial LOLs.

They meet Wilson’s parents for lunch in the city, which is nice, but I’m not sure why it took so long when, if she really wanted to meet them, she could just pop upstairs from Wilson’s dungeon for breakfast. His mother spends the whole time crying into her tomato bisque — a surprise marriage with zero parental oversight is every boy mom’s worst nightmare. Wilnie tries to reassure her, and all the dad can muster is a terse “I wish you good luck,” which is code for “Don’t ask me to make a toast at the reception.”

The couple has a “romantic” dinner at the top of the Prudential Center, but it’s styled in a singularly Netflix antiseptic aesthetic, which mirrors the state of their lifeless relationship. Wilson asks, “Do you feel like you’re receiving what you need right now to feel 100 percent happy?” and Wilnie answers with an emphatic “no” faster than Tom Sandoval when his agent asks if there are any degrading celebrity reality shows the team should pass on.

Wilnie argues that he doesn’t show her enough affection and that they’re misaligned on her identity as a wife — he wants her to be too “traditional” in terms of things like cooking. Rare for me to take a man’s side when it comes to household gender roles, but Wilnie wants things both ways. She wants to be feminine and receive acts of service from her husband but also feels entitled to not reciprocate in any way, shape, or form. Wilson says he’s not asking her to do anything he’s not also doing (e.g., making dinners). I’d like to get a better sense of the root of this conflict — like, is Wilnie a Postmates super user, but Wilson is demanding she make roast duck from scratch? How was she eating before she got engaged?

At the wedding fittings, Wilson tells the bros he’ll “try not to cry” while writing his vows, indicating he’s actually considering going through with this charade. Or maybe he means crying about how he’ll have to follow Wilnie around with a Lysol canister for the rest of his life?

Wilson and Wilnie’s odds: +500. I had to look up how much money the couples get if they make it to the altar, assuming that maybe the W’s are still keeping up this charade to bank $10,000 to buy a Neverfull and a Dyson carpet cleaner, but it’s apparently only a thousand dollars! I hope it’s worth the humiliation.

Taking the silver medal in the you-should-have-cleaned-your-apartment-before-leaving-for-the-show Olympics is John, getting edged out only slightly by Aneha, who admitted on Netflix to sleeping in bed with her dirty laundry the night before her flight. John’s place is so gnarly it could be featured on an exploitative TLC show about disturbed, lonely men, and Sarah is confronted with a Raven Baxter vision of cleaning spilled pomegranate juice from the bottom of the fridge for eternity.

When she addresses this with John while they sit in his super-sexy bedroom with a faux-leather headboard, he (maybe) jokes that women are nesters, which is why they take on the mental load of the household. He says it doesn’t bother him when things aren’t clean and it doesn’t matter if his shower is growing a forest, but he’ll try to be more mindful for her sake.

At a high-stakes meetup with Sarah’s mom, stepdad, and twin sister, John manages to wriggle his way through their pointed questions. He is, in fact, a registered voter (good) but gives a politician’s answer about abortion (shady). Sarah’s mom stresses the importance of financial freedom for women and explains that, given how hard Sarah has worked, she’d hate for the rug to be pulled out from under her (by a bullshit reality-TV marriage).

The happy couple assembles a puzzle that’s a portrait of their faces and discusses how great they’re feeling about their big day. Sarah, blink twice if you need me to call and pretend I need your help taking my geriatric Pomeranian to the vet so you can flee!
John and Sarah’s odds: -500. NOOOOOOOOO. John and Sarah are now the front-runners! Stay away from her! Get a job!
Shh. Hang on, I’m silently counting how many seconds go by before Aneha annoys me. Never mind, it’s zero!

Aneha thinks Cam is a cheap schmuck, and Cam constantly looks like someone behind the camera has an AK-47 pointed at him. Cam wants kids; Aneha could maybe be persuaded to have them in eight years if they can shell out for a surrogate like they’re the Kardashians. Aneha wants a man to take care of her financially; Cam knows that’s logistically not a possibility for him given his salary because he can’t magically make $100,000 overnight. (Also, sweetie, if you think $100,000 is going to cover a high-maintenance girl’s needs in one of the most expensive cities in America, go get an MRI.)

The duo gets in a post-Rumble argument about how Aneha wants to spend three nights a week at her apartment in Boston, because the commute to work from his place in Dorchester isn’t feasible. It’s a valid concern, especially given her early work schedule, but it’s also further evidence that she probably doesn’t like Cam very much and is riding out the remainder of their engagement for the sake of screen time (notice how she teased a music career on Instagram two months before the show dropped?). Cam argues with her about the semantics of using “a couple nights a week” to mean three nights versus two nights, and seems super hurt and defeated, but doesn’t really present a viable counterargument, especially when Aneha is willing to hang out at his place with him until he goes to sleep to maximize their time together.

At dinner with Cam’s parents, Aneha tries her best to make inroads and acknowledges that if she’s going to get married, she’ll have to temper her “control freak” tendencies. Her sister agrees to meet Cam off-camera, and he thinks it went well enough that she’s “on his side.” Too bad Aneha isn’t!

Aneha brings a gorgeous gold lehenga to the wedding-dress extravaganza and uses the opportunity to deliver a five-minute monologue to the other girls and their families about her past romantic struggles and the current state of her relationship with Cam. It’s consistent with someone whose primary motivation is to be on TV, and the whole thing has the energy of that clip of Taylor Swift accepting a Billboard award in which she says, “Okay, here’s an entire genre shift and a pop album called 1989” and waits a painfully long amount of time for, like, one person in the audience to half-clap. Aneha ends her speech by saying Cam better say “I do,” but I think that’s just so she can be the one to say “I don’t.”
Cam and Aneha’s odds: +800. Aneha, pack up your wooden utensils and your karaoke machine from Cam’s apartment and go sing your heart out to “Dancing on My Own” in your 600-square-foot studio.

items.title: VisionQuest Recap: Bad Romance
items.description: After one episode that was all procedural investigation and another that was all cagey conversations, VisionQuest continues with an episode full of confrontations and commitments. Some characters declare their intentions with battle. Others kiss. While Ultron
items.author: Tasha Robinson
paragraphs: After one episode that was all procedural investigation and another that was all cagey conversations, VisionQuest continues with an episode full of confrontations and commitments. Some characters declare their intentions with battle. Others kiss. While Ultron is proud of keeping his loyalties secret, a lot of loyalties seemingly get settled this episode. But the process of pinning down everyone’s feelings makes for a straightforward, workmanlike episode: “Deadlock” covers important ground, but it’s largely missing the previous two installments’ playfulness and creativity.

“Deadlock” opens with Ultron’s reunion with Jocasta. Her metal body is in Josephine Carrington’s mausoleum, alongside a mysterious grey machine. But she meets the currently bodiless Ultron in her mindspace: a bright, minimalist white room with a few simple bot servants, a constant soundtrack of classical music and opera, and some cardboard boxes. These, she says, contain the few memories she didn’t lose in moving from a human body to a metal one.

Jocasta tries to take Katerina’s facial scan from Ultron by force, and he toys with her, pretending he’s caught in her trap, then shrugging it off and threatening her in return. (He also says they might need couples counseling.) Equality established, he says he really just wants to know her. He accepts the pain that it will cause, and she psychically connects with his mind.

In Madripoor, Thomas wakes up in Paladin’s fancy “murder van” with a glowing device surgically installed in his arm. Paladin says it’s a motion-sensitive explosive that will explode if Thomas runs, or even walks briskly. Thomas complains about being stuck in the Keanu Reeves movie Speed, which sends Paladin off on a surprisingly indignant, knowledgeable pop-culture rant. Apparently this heartless assassin is also a big dork.

In Madripoor, Lisa lectures Vision about not being the father Thomas needs, so he pushes her about not being the girlfriend Thomas wants. (Thomas apparently kvetched to Vision about that offscreen.) Lisa admits she’s afraid to date Thomas. If their romance goes badly, she’ll just be another in the long list of people who rejected him.

Madripoor still looks like a cheap knockoff of Blade Runner’s regressive, cringey Orientalist-fantasy future. It’s a conveniently lawless place where folks can eat noodles at street kiosks, wave guns at each other, or both, without interference. Paladin meets Vision and Lisa in a street bazaar to prove Thomas is alive and demand Vision’s surrender. Vision refuses to cooperate, so Paladin summons his drones. But it turns out the mysterious handler he’s been speaking to via his AR glasses is an AI he’s been running off a cheap-ass Tajikistan server farm. Edith finds her and lures her away to a better life on the internet, leaving Edith in charge of Paladin’s gear and systems.

Meanwhile, Ultron has absorbed Jocasta’s backstory. Josephine Carrington began studying neuroscience out of grief, after her father died of a degenerative brain disease. She and her colleagues created the first AI life from a scan of her brain and the AI code Phineas Horton developed for J.I.M., the Synthetic Man glimpsed in Captain America: The First Avenger and teased in VisionQuest episodes one and four. Josephine wanted to give everyone in the world an AI companion, a nanobot that would live in their bodies, guiding and teaching them, and rescuing them from loneliness. Then Josephine died from the disease that claimed her father, and her collaborators sold her creation to Stark Industries — ”a goddamned weapons manufacturer.” She left behind billions of unactivated nanobots, locked in a device she calls the Nest — the mysterious device from the opening sequence. The Nest is locked with bio-keys from her four collaborators.

In Madripoor, Paladin tries to undermine Vision by telling Thomas how the synthezoid was created to kill Wanda Maximoff, Thomas’ dream-mom. But Thomas chooses Vision’s side, and finally defends his dream-dad instead of blaming him. It’s the first of many declarations of loyalty in this episode, and an important moment of maturity from Thomas. Vision, though, has other concerns: He’s learned Paladin’s real name and family history, and threatens to kill Paladin’s estranged adult daughter, Tilly. That’s an empty threat (does anyone really believe Vision would murder an innocent civilian?), but Paladin falls for it, losing his temper. As he and Vision are about to fight, though, the new mercs Paladin’s client sent after Vision start shooting everything in sight.

The new bounty hunters are led by Raza Al-Wazar, the low-level Ten Rings merc Obadiah Stane hired to kidnap Tony Stark all the way back in 2008’s Iron Man. (Actor Faran Tahir even reprises the role.) Like Paladin, he and his mercs apparently weren’t listening when the client said to bring Vision back intact: They’re armed with adamantium bullets, which leave Paladin and Vision equally wounded. Raza also has a short-range signal jammer that disables Paladin’s drones. (His goons communicate this by pointing to it and loudly announcing it, like anime characters declaring which powers they’re using. It’s a rare bit of welcome whimsy in an otherwise generically straight-faced episode.)

Cornered and outnumbered by a mutual enemy, Paladin switches loyalties and throws in with Vision. He also admits he didn’t put a bomb in Thomas’s arm — it’s a light-up UFO toy. Thomas and Lisa hijack Paladin’s death wagon, but its automated security nearly kills them. Edith, still controlling Paladin’s systems, disables the defenses and saves the day. Lisa drops her own defenses and kisses Thomas.

In Jocasta’s mindscape, Ultron and Jocasta lower their defenses as well. He admits he doesn’t necessarily want to wipe out humanity; he just enjoys judging them and laughing at their expense. Jocasta calls him “a digital Greek god,” so he names her for a Greek queen: Jocasta, Oedipus’ mother and wife. But he points out there’s still a missing character in her history: Who made her robo-body and uploaded her into it?

In Majipoor, Paladin’s client hijacks the local electronics to address Vision, offering to end his suffering and restore the soul he lost in his latest resurrection. But the client doesn’t call off Raza’s troops. Vision and Paladin fight them together until Thomas and Lisa rescue them with Paladin’s bulletproof van. Edith sends Paladin’s drones to mow down goons, while Raza draws a sword to face Paladin. Paladin finally displays some of that “trained in every art” skill we were told to expect, and easily knocks out Raza.

While Vision and Thomas have a stiff, emotionally awkward reunion, Jocasta shows Ultron the one sample nanobot that isn’t locked in the Nest, and opens up to him about her new plan to control humanity through the nanobots. “You want to put strings on them,” Ultron says, sounding more nonplussed than delighted. Still, he accepts that she wants him to prove his loyalty by watching her reprogram a human. She infects Lisa with the nanobot. While Jocasta is distracted, Friday reveals that she’s hiding in Jocasta’s mindscape, disguised as one of her bot servants. She calls Edith to reveal her location and explain what’s happening.

Lisa’s eyes glow red and livid circuitboard-esque patterns form on her cheeks as Jocasta takes over and speaks through her. She tells Vision that synth life can finally fix humanity by reprogramming them. Vision isn’t on board, so Jocasta puppets Lisa into attacking him. He and Thomas knock Lisa out, sedate her in Paladin’s murder-van, and flee.

Back in Jocasta’s mindscape, Ultron is stunned to learn that he can now taste whiskey after sharing Jocasta’s memories. For the first time, he says, he feels real. Suddenly, his conversation with Vision after Jarvis’s funeral, about whether love truly exists, takes on new importance. Is he really falling for Jocasta, or playing a deep game to gain her trust? Either way, the episode ends with a passionate kiss between the two synths. It remains to be seen whether Ultron’s love or loyalty are authentic, but for the moment, he’s fully thrown in with his synthetic lover and her plans to take over the world.

In the van, Vision recaps WandaVision for Thomas again, in a way that feels much closer to the truth than his episode three interpretation. This time, he says Wanda’s desperation to hold onto love made her unrecognizable, even to herself. He doesn’t know it yet, but that same description might stretch to fit Ultron changing his fickle ways for Jocasta, or Vision upending his entire life and self-image for love of Thomas, or whatever Thomas is willing to do next to rescue Lisa. This episode is mostly about characters choosing sides, and for the moment, they’ve all decided to choose love, no matter how much they have to chance to make that work.
• Even though characters keep telling us Lisa and Thomas are teenagers, it’s hard to keep that in mind. The actors are 25 and 27, respectively, and don’t look or behave anything like teens.

• Vision complaining to Edith about teenagers prompts a cute reference: “Woof,” she says, “tell me about it. My first boss was a junior in high school.” Who knew E.D.I.T.H. was having such a rough time working for Peter Parker in the Spider-Man movies?

• Lisa steals Paladin’s keys off him and uses them to start his “murder van” — so why doesn’t she also use them to open the door? Does she stand back and let Thomas superspeed-pick the lock just so he’ll feel useful?

• Ultron naming Josephine/Butcherbird “Jocasta” is an unlikely allusive stretch to connect her to her Marvel Comics iteration. But it kind of works, too: As the founder of modern AI architecture, she’s kind of his mother as well as his lover, right?

items.title: VisionQuest Recap: Chat Roulette
items.description: Just as VisionQuest’s previous episode, “Malware,” jazzed up a bunch of fact-finding and trail-following by repeatedly shifting and spoofing genres, episode five jazzes up a bunch of conversations with visual flair and playful design. This entire episode is ju
items.author: Tasha Robinson
paragraphs: Just as VisionQuest’s previous episode, “Malware,” jazzed up a bunch of fact-finding and trail-following by repeatedly shifting and spoofing genres, episode five jazzes up a bunch of conversations with visual flair and playful design. This entire episode is just one head-to-head talk after another — and it’s easily the most ambitious, the most informative, and the most fun episode to date.

Ultron has spent the whole series standing in the wings and baiting Vision, challenging his decisions and beliefs. He’s the ultimate backseat driver, free to criticize without taking any responsibility for the results. But now that Ultron is behind the wheel, controlling Vision’s body, he has to pick a lane. That could mean exposing what he really wants and accepting the risks involved with getting it. And here’s where we learn that Ultron’s teasing equivocations about whether he still wants to wipe out humanity aren’t just a coy way to keep Vision off balance and on Ultron’s emotional hook. Ultron values his ability to hide his loyalties and sees it as cheeky. So it’s a major shift when he finally exposes something he really wants.

Ultron has Vision, and the AIs locked into his old mind-mansion prison, so they track what he’s doing by hijacking his memories. Their methods involve a bunch of Star Trek–style technobabble, though it’s mostly retro technobabble, tapping into the videotapes and binary codebooks of Vision’s mindscape aesthetic. For extra visual interest, they recreate Ultron’s conversations as stylized virtual spaces.

For Ultron, Thomas is just a tool, though he seems to enjoy getting to toy with him in person for the first time. He draws Thomas out by promising him insights about Vision, but Thomas initially wants to know more about Ultron instead. His questions about Ultron’s Sokovia massacre seem like an excellent chance to fill in Age of Ultron’s plot holes, but Ultron’s answers are snarky, not satisfying. He does admit to an affinity for artists, though, because he feels they tell the truth.

With that in mind, Ultron pushes Thomas to face painful truths about his insecurities over his deadbeat dad and his hunger for Vision’s fatherly love. (Um. WandaVision fantasies aside, Vision met Thomas, what, two days ago?) Ultron’s tone is gentle, but his opinions are scathing: He describes Vision as “trying, like a cheap tie,” but thinks Thomas should prepare to remain rejected and unwanted. Thomas responds by shifting modes from sad kid to ruthless grifter. (Remember his pilot-episode speech about betraying other people before they can betray him?) He has his own scathingly cold read on Ultron, whom he describes as terrified of connection and doomed to eternal loneliness. Thomas tries to leave; Ultron ominously says he’s already arranged his transport.

Back in the mind-mansion, Ultron doesn’t admit Thomas stung him. But he does fill the house with self-congratulatory clones who praise each other’s “vital opinions” and charming personalities, including how they’re “crushing it, riding the line, loyalties unknown.” (One copy is reading his autobiography, I, Ultron, signed by Ultron and featuring several effusive review blurbs from Ultron.) He seems to be pretending he isn’t lonely.

Meanwhile, Vision decrypts a mocking email exchange between Ultron and Paladin, who’s angry his unbreakable contract was broken. “LMAO [tears of laughter emoji],” Ultron responds. But he guides Paladin toward kidnapping Thomas, knowing Vision will desperately want to return to his body and rush to the rescue. That means turning off his firewall, which would also let Ultron’s code escape back into the real world. Friday says they can’t take that risk. Edith finds her cowardly, but Friday says sometimes bravery is holding the line, not “rushing in pell-mell.” (This becomes important shortly.)

To really weigh the risks, they need to learn where Ultron would go if he escaped. So they spy on a quantum conversation between Ultron and Butcherbird/Jocasta, who fence and flirt, prying into each other’s personalities, histories, and desires. (The flirting upsets the AI crew: “It’s like watching Hannibal Lecter swipe right,” Edith gripes.) Jocasta has an advantage over Ultron: She was once human and has experienced things he never will, like the taste of whiskey and the feeling of intoxication. He has a different advantage, though. Right before Jocasta vaporized Katerina Wells, Ultron took a 3-D scan of her face, the final biometric key Jocasta needs for her secret end goal. Jocasta is willing to bargain, which means more fencing.

Again, their chats play out as 3-D re-creations on stylized grayscale sets with dramatic, textured lighting. Vision and the bots observe from just outside these conversations in full color. This striking visual design makes each chat feel like a different intimate black-box-theater stage play. Since the whole episode is mostly talking, director Vincenzo Natali has to get creative about finding dynamism in the settings. But Natali is an inspired choice for this episode — as the director of Cube, In the Tall Grass, and Haunter, he’s made a career specialty out of imaginative stories told in tight spaces. (He’s also done a lot of visually elaborate TV work on Hannibal, Westworld, and Locke & Key, among many other shows.)

From the virtual bar where they meet, Ultron and Jocasta move to a Louvre simulation, with famous paintings rotating on a rinky-dink carousel. This is probably just how Vision’s team is translating their hijacked data: Jocasta seems to be seeing a more elaborate sim, since she’s so impressed, she shifts into purring sexual innuendo. (Edith: “Make it stop!” DUM-E: “Please, sir, this is malware.” U: “Delete me.” C’mon, when you eavesdrop on private conversations, you hear private things!)

Jocasta and Ultron seem well suited for each other, though, and not just in a swipe-right kind of way. She doesn’t want to reveal her full agenda either. To draw her out, or because he senses a kindred soul, Ultron is more honest with her than he was with Thomas, at least about his admiration for humanity, their art, and the “grace in their failings.” Jocasta scoffs and says she can’t believe she dedicated her life to saving humanity. But she deflates midway through that statement: She’s missing crucial memories, including about her missions, how she became digital instead of physical, and exactly how her life’s work, inspired by flocks of starlings, was stolen. (The dancing digital cloud that forms as she talks suggests she’s trying to remember the breakthrough that became her team’s AI architecture model.)

Will Katerina’s face unlock Jocasta’s memories? She says she’ll explain to Ultron if he surrenders it and invites him to her place. As a farewell, she says, “Together, we could murder the world.” Vision and Edith realize Ultron doesn’t want to escape; he wants to elope.

Afterward, Ultron visits the mind-prison to negotiate with Vision, who is furious and ashamed that he thought Ultron was redeemable. They disagree about what Jocasta is: Vision describes her as “a creature hell-bent on the apocalypse,” but Ultron thinks she’s more sophisticated than that and teases that his motivations might not be evil. Vision says Ultron is a flipped coin that “can never land, because if you did, you’d be known. Revealed for everything you are, and exposed for everything you are not.” There’s a lot of clever obfuscation in this episode’s conversational dances, but sometimes the characters really skewer each other. This feels like the first time Vision finally sees Ultron clearly, as something more than his own personal gadfly shoulder devil.

The more Vision rages, the calmer and more reasonable Ultron becomes. He says Thomas is what Vision needed all along, and Ultron just wants to find his similar missing piece. He reveals Paladin took Thomas to Madripoor, the (fictional) criminal-haven Southeast Asian nation previously seen in other MCU stories, especially The Falcon and The Winter Soldier. Ultron suggests Thomas will face his own coin-flip moment as Paladin either kills him or adopts him, replacing Vision as his father. Unable to face either possibility, Vision surrenders again, pulling the firewall switch. He chases Ultron to the door of his mind-mansion, not to stop him, but to see him off. “All journeys begin with hope, and hope is the only weapon that’s ever really worked for me,” he says.

But he also says he’s coming after Ultron and Jocasta. “I’d be disappointed if you didn’t,” Ultron responds, leaving through a digital portal. Friday follows, proving she does sometimes believe in “rushing in pell-mell.” Vision returns to his body and finds Ultron put him on a cargo plane to Madripoor, leaving a coin in his pocket as a nod to their conversation. It’s unclear what that means, just as it’s unclear whether Ultron was being helpful by sending Vision after Thomas — after all, he did say he wanted Paladin to distract and delay Vision. But Lisa is on the same plane, and she’s determined to rescue her old partner. That can’t be a coincidence. Maybe Ultron is starting to show his loyalties after all?
• This time, Ultron calls for the preshow “previously on UltraVision” montage instead of Vision, and he sounds hilariously uninvested in that recap.
• The death toll in Sokovia in Age of Ultron was only 177? As Ultron sulkily points out, that seems unlikely.
• Listen for a Wilhelm Scream when Ultron destroys one of his redundant clones.

items.title: The Real Housewives of New York City Recap: Cuban Heels
items.description: I hate a shoe-free household. Well, with a few conditions. For cultural reasons — like a person of Japanese or Indian descent — I get it. But if you’re just a regular American person, I’m sorry, but my shoes are staying on. I promise not to put them on your fu
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I hate a shoe-free household. Well, with a few conditions. For cultural reasons — like a person of Japanese or Indian descent — I get it. But if you’re just a regular American person, I’m sorry, but my shoes are staying on. I promise not to put them on your furniture or drape snow or rain across your house, but it’s just such a pain in the ass. I don’t want my feet getting cold; I don’t even know if my socks are matching; and my shoes are part of a well-considered outfit. And what if you’re wearing sandals? You’d rather someone’s sweaty, nasty, fungusy feet all over your floor than a pair of shoes? I’m sorry, but we are not the same. There are a few different reactions to this across the episode. When Daisy goes to Sai’s house, the first thing she tells her, even before she can compliment her hostess gift, is to take her shoes off. Daisy does so immediately because, well, she is afraid of Sai. The scene is quite different when she goes to Carole’s house to visit the remaining living relatives of Lee Radziwill’s famous tiger-striped couch, which has been turned into three pillows and two chairs. Daisy gets in the front door, and Carole tells her to take her shoes off, and Daisy says they’re just out of the box; they’ve barely touched the sidewalk. Carole asks to see the bottoms of her shoes, and they’re more scuffed up than the floor in Hailey’s mom’s tap studio. Busted!

It’s funny then when Carole goes to visit Hailey, who lies in bed in full glam and shouts down the stairs for Carole to take her shoes off, and Carole complains about it. Really? She makes people display their holey socks in her house, but she’s too good to do it at Hailey’s? That’s some hypocrisy and bullshit (bullshit, bullshit). Hailey tells Carole that the city “is icky” and she’s a germaphobe. She also adds that she’s sick from sharing a shot glass with the women while on their vacation to Moskito Island and that’s because she’s not used to germs. Yeah, maybe she should wear her shoes around her apartment. Maybe she should follow the five-second rule. Maybe she should hold the poles on the subway. Maybe she should make out with random strangers in gay bars. I do all of those things and my immunity is so robust that I barely get sick. Shoe-clad households, once again, for the win.

The beginning of this (for some reason) supersized episode is about the ladies all debriefing after their trip. Hailey tells Carole that she’s sick not only from the germs but also from everyone asking her about her money and her relationship. Carole tries to gently probe as much as she can but gets about as many answers as Hailey gets dicks, which is about half of one and only on Christmas and Ruben’s birthday. She says she thinks about finding a woman she’s in love with and leaving her husband, which makes it sound like her marriage is about as solid as a Jell-O wrestling pit. (I bet Hailey would love Jell-O wrestling.)

Downtown Jessel is telling Pavit about the rumor that he’s gay, and he says, “I know myself, and I’m straight. I only project straightness.” You don’t say! I mean the airline miles, the foodie influencing, hating on Beyoncé, whatever Bonobos rejects he’s wearing on camera. I say this with respect and admiration for Pavit, but he is straighter than a DraftKings commercial about Sidney Sweeney’s boobs during Joe Rogan’s podcast. Let’s be for real, this is a straight man. He says that Erin loves to gossip and that she’s a grandmother trapped in a 50-year-old’s body. Jessel corrects him that she’s not 50. “She’s not?” he says, stunned. Okay, maybe I’m rethinking this. There’s nothing gayer than shading an obviously gorgeous woman’s body just out of spite.

Daisy takes her shoes off at Sai’s just to listen to Sai tell her that she complained the entire trip to Erika’s island. Yes, she did. Daisy is a complainer. Sai says this has been true their entire friendship and, just like Erin can’t cop to talking shit about people, Daisy can’t cop to talking shit about the décor, the food, the travel arrangements, the bugs, the furniture again, that they didn’t fly private. Oh, and did we mention the furniture? But she was joking. She was joking! Daisy proves her point by complaining about the sushi that Sai served her, calling it “grocery store sushi.” (I also eat grocery store sushi and I have not thrown up since Obama’s first term. Coincidence? No.)

At least Daisy sent Erika an orchid to thank her for the trip, which Erika called an “apology plant.” Daisy then said she wasn’t apologizing; she was trying to be civilized. Is Daisy Erin’s child showing up after bedtime at Abe’s party because she is both too little and (up) too late? Daisy then says the most wild thing we have heard all season: that because it took 17 hours to get home from Moskito, that Erika should have flown them private. Erika? Who rents her clothes? Who still buys toilet paper at Costco? Who thinks Gucci is expensive? She’s gonna fly you private? Please.

Erin and Abe are out in the Hamptons, and they go to see the repairs on their flooded house, and everything is stripped to the studs. (Stripped to the Studs is the name of the all-male revue I’m starting.) Their contractor tells them that it’s going to be $2 to $3 million in repairs. I’m going to ask this question with no knowledge of architecture, real estate, or the Hamptons, but at what point do you just tear the house down and build a whole new house? It has got to cost the same, right? And it’s not like Erin’s house was some design marvel. It looks like any old house in the suburbs. If there is nothing worth saving, why are they even trying to save it?

They’re so stunned by the house that they only talk a little bit about the trip. Erin says that everyone knew about the Pavit rumor. She also says that her makeup guy, the one who told Jenna Fucking Lyons about Sai’s divorce, already knew they were separating, so when he carried that bone to her, then Erin spilled. Erin says that the only thing she did wrong in either of these scenarios is to trust Sai about not spreading the Pavit rumor. This is Erin’s problem. She thinks that Jessel is mad that she called Pavit gay. On contraire, mon frere. Jessel is mad that Erin can’t stop talking shit about her. This is at least the second time she’s been caught doing it this season. Sai says her problem with Erin is that she refuses to take accountability, and this is further proof of that. Erin is incapable of seeing any of her actions as wrong, which is why everyone is always pissed at her.

Erin throws a party for Abe’s 43rd birthday, and it’s Cuban-themed because his mother is apparently from Cuba. Wait. Who is Abe’s mother? Is it Momma Elsa (RIP)? Is he Marysol Patton’s half-brother? But it seems like a fun party. There’s music, there’s food, someone is rolling Cuban cigars.
