items.title: The Things We ‘Stole’ From Our Roommates
items.description: “I am not sure that I exist, actually,” said the Argentine author Jorge Luis Borges in the 1980s. “I am all the writers that I have read, all the people that I have met, all the women that I have loved; all the cities I have visited.” And in this economy, wher
items.author: Bianca Nieves
paragraphs: “I am not sure that I exist, actually,” said the Argentine author Jorge Luis Borges in the 1980s. “I am all the writers that I have read, all the people that I have met, all the women that I have loved; all the cities I have visited.” And in this economy, where high housing costs favor shared living arrangements and many adults are moving back in with their parents, I would add: I’m every roommate I’ve ever lived with.

Roommates get a bad rap, but not all of them are like Leighton Meester’s character in The Roommate (2011). As someone who’s shared my living space with a handful of strangers, best friends, and lovers, I can gratefully say I’ve collected more positive memories over the years than nightmare stories. What I’m perhaps most thankful for — beyond the relationships themselves — are the ways my roommates have influenced me through their routines, their advice, and even their products. I’ve “stolen” more than a few items from the people I’ve shared a home with: Once I tried my roomie’s ginger-tea honey when I was sick, and now I keep a stockpile of the jars for flu season. When I’m lazy and I don’t want to follow my grandma’s extensive refried-beans recipe, I use a recipe my ex found that tastes almost as good and requires half the prep time. And after my first roommate in New York introduced me to these small porcelain toothbrush holders, I convinced my whole family to use them, too. Their influence!

The more I asked my friends and colleagues, the more I realized how many of us have picked up lifelong rituals and treasured items like these from the people we’ve split rent with. So, in honor of Our Place, The Cut’s series about roommates, we decided to share the wealth by highlighting a handful of helpful hacks, practices, products, and beliefs that roomies have pilfered from one another — not in a creepy, kleptomaniac way but in a “humanity is not lost” sort of way. Hopecore, if you will.
The Roommate Who Took Hydration Seriously

“I used to be one of those girls with a huge water bottle, filled to the brim with ice, which I would chug at all times of the day. However, my roommate (and best friend) is really tapped into health and wellness and changed how I drink water. One time she mentioned that it’s healthier not to chug but instead to take smaller sips, and always drink the water at room temperature. The practice stuck. I feel like it helps with bloating and aids digestion. She also introduced me to the cutest water-bottle brand on the planet, Bink. The bottle is made of glass, so it sweats a little bit, which makes me not want to use ice at all.” —Julia Jergens, PR and brand communications specialist
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate Who Solved Every Stain Problem

“A couple of months into living together, I was scrubbing a bedsheet like a hunched-over old woman, and my roommate said, ‘What are you doing? Just use this Japanese lingerie spray!’ and the stain disappeared almost instantly. Since then, I have used it on literally any stain you can think of, and it still works.” —Steffi Cao, columnist at Slate
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate Who Made a Case for Acupressure Sandals

“My roommate let me borrow her acupuncture sandals a lot during my senior year of college. They hurt like hell, but my feet would feel amazing afterward. Since then, I swear by them.” —Danielle Cohen, senior news editor at The Cut
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate Who Cooked With Fancy Salt

“My college roommate introduced me to flaky salt in a salt crock. I was used to keeping salt in its usual container, but she switched me to Maldon salt, specifically in a Le Creuset salt crock. At the time it felt extra, but now it’s the only way I’ll store and use my salt.” —Daniela Bao, founder of Chévere Means Cool
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate With the Knitting Needles

“The year after COVID was my final year of college, and I lived with three roommates: my best friend, my sister, and my sister’s best friend. During that time, when the world still felt a little scary, my best friend taught all of us how to knit. We would watch Glee reruns and knit every night. I still knit now — though I’m not very good.” —Brooke LaMantia, writer at The Cut
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate With the Perfect Coffee Order

“My roomie changed my caffeinated life. I used to be a black-coffee type of girl until she introduced me to her order: a large rockaccino (iced cappuccino) with soy milk, an extra shot of espresso, one shot of cinnamon, and one shot of Svetia sweetener. Sadly, they only make it at Caffenio, a coffee shop in Mexico, so it’s my sweet treat whenever I’m there. When I moved to New York, another roommate introduced me to drinking beer in Rona wineglasses, but it strictly has to be a Modelo. Classy!” —Maria Margot, producer and designer
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate With a Statement Necklace for Every Occasion

“When I moved into my freshman dorm with a friend from high school, I wasn’t much of a jewelry person. But this was the fall of 2013, the peak era for those bright, pastel-colored statement necklaces that women in my year wore with peplum blouses and skinny jeans. My roommate kept an entire shoe box full of these necklaces on a shelf in her closet, and she let me borrow whichever pieces I wanted whenever I wanted them. I loved them. Those specific resin designs aren’t really my style anymore, but they were definitely my gateway into a lifelong love of fun jewelry. Whenever I find myself on the hunt for an eye-catching collar or bib necklace now, I know I have my roommate (one of my best friends to this day) to thank for the influence.” —Lauren Puckett-Pope, senior editor at The Cut
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate Who Knew Her Way Around the Kitchen

“My former roomie told me the correct way to salt pasta water was to make it as salty as the sea, and she taught me to finish cooking the pasta in the sauce. We’re still friends, and we heavily influenced each other’s interior decorating. She got me into using textiles as wall hangings, and I got her into vintage mirrors.” —Carina del Valle Schorske, writer
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate Who Loved French Skin Care

“In 2012, Instagram was barely a thing, TikTok skin care didn’t exist, and I was studying abroad in Paris, trying to figure out which cleanser to buy. That’s when my roommate introduced me to the magic of French pharmacy skin care, especially Avène and La Roche-Posay. Over a decade later, I’m still using them and have never looked back.” —Kisai Ponce, audience development director
The “Evil” Roommate With Good Detergent

“I found the Zum laundry detergent, specifically the frankincense one, through an evil roommate I once had. At least I got something out of the friendship/housemate breakup. She got the detergent from a college dorm roomie about five years ago, and now I’ve introduced it to my current roomie and another friend.” —Eimy Figueroa, creative and founder of Gentler Day
New! You can now save this product for later.
The Roommate Who Bartered Clothing Rentals

“My roommate put me on Nuuly. Before I converted to the clothing rental service, she would bestow me with one surprise Nuuly item of her monthly box in exchange for space in my storage unit. Now, with my current (new) roommate, we share our Nuuly items each month. Sharing is caring!” —Grace Klara Marshall, intern at The Cut

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 29, 2026
items.description: The moon spends most of the day in sociable Gemini. Thanks to lucky energy from Jupiter around noon, then relaxed and pleasant vibes from Venus in the early evening, everyone’s likely to be in a good mood today. If you’ve been stressed out and overworked latel
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: The moon spends most of the day in sociable Gemini. Thanks to lucky energy from Jupiter around noon, then relaxed and pleasant vibes from Venus in the early evening, everyone’s likely to be in a good mood today. If you’ve been stressed out and overworked lately, you could finally get a much-needed reprieve. This is also a good time to charm new people, get started on exciting projects, or take big swings at work. Still, if all you really want to do is relax and enjoy the atmosphere at the moment, don’t feel guilty. You deserve it.

You know your time is finite, so you care about making the most of it. You want to spend your days meaningfully, whether that means making progress toward your goals or improving the world around you. But try not to worry about being “productive” today. The best way to use your time right now is simply to get out into the world and have interesting experiences. Even if you can’t yet see what those experiences mean or how they’ll matter in the long term, trust that they’re valuable in their own way.

You understand that conflict is necessary in any relationship. Real human connection will always involve misunderstandings and disagreements, and if you want deep and long-lasting friendships, you need to be willing to navigate the difficult times as well as the enjoyable ones. However, you shouldn’t always feel stressed out by your relationships. Today, spend time with the friends who consistently make you feel good about yourself, who make the world seem like a happier, more interesting place. Any confrontations or difficult talks can wait until later.

In general, you try to pace yourself, allocating your time and resources effectively and efficiently. Ideally, you always want to have some energy remaining at the end of every day. But today, don’t hold back. It’ll be invigorating to go all out and live completely in the moment. You can rest and recharge later; for now, it’s better to err on the side of exuberance rather than caution.

Sometimes, you feel forced to work against your natural moods and feelings. You might want solitude and quiet, but if your schedule is packed with social events, you feel you have to put on a smile and get out there anyway. Maybe you want to rest, but you’ve got deadlines coming up, so you need to push through. As much as possible today, let your desires and instincts guide you. This might require rescheduling plans or disappointing some people, but trusting your own intuition will be worth it.

Make it your mission to talk to new people today — ideally ones you wouldn’t normally spend time with. The goal isn’t to network with those who might benefit you in some tangible way. Nor do you need to worry about forming long-lasting relationships with everyone you meet. But simply expanding your horizons (and having fun doing it!) will prove a worthwhile endeavor. The more people you interact with right now, the more likely you are to be surprised, to see the world in new ways, and to hear something that inspires you.

Give yourself permission not to overanalyze things right now. You might fear that if you’re not constantly on high alert, carefully analyzing everything around you, you’ll miss something important. But while there’s a lot to be said for paying attention, it’s impossible to keep up that level of vigilance all the time. Today, take a break. Deal with any tasks that need your immediate attention, but don’t go looking for deeper problems to unpack.

Sometimes you’re vaguely embarrassed by your own desires. It seems presumptuous to want anything beyond what you already have. Plenty of people’s lives are far worse than yours, and you imagine you should focus your energies on being grateful rather than ambitious. But today, stop convincing yourself it’s somehow wrong to want more. If you’re dissatisfied, you’re allowed to seek out something better; if your life feels boring, give yourself permission to explore different options. Even if things are objectively fine, that doesn’t mean you have to settle.

Right now, you’re craving reassurance that you’re on the right track — that you’re making good decisions, steadily progressing toward your goals, or simply living a meaningful life. But sometimes your desire to do everything right ends up overwhelming you, preventing you from thinking clearly. So today, allow yourself to tackle the hours ahead one task at a time. Don’t focus so much on the bigger picture; don’t try to be perfect. If you simply give your best in each moment, it’ll all add up to something good in the end.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You try to be thoughtful and generous with the people around you — not because you expect anything in return but because it’s the right thing to do. But today, the generosity you show others likely will end up working to your benefit. Trust that your good deeds will be rewarded, even if not immediately. If you go out of your way to be good to the people around you right now, you won’t regret it.

Today, you’re likely to notice issues others might have missed — and when you do, you may struggle to decide what to do about it. Is it better to call attention to these problems, ultimately saving everyone trouble? Or is it better not to bother people in case you come off fussy and hypercritical? Today, the best course of action is to speak up. Even if people don’t appreciate your help in the moment, they will in the long run.

You have a habit of refusing people the benefit of the doubt until they’ve demonstrated they’ll do the same for you. You don’t want to make an effort to help people only for them to turn around and be rude or unappreciative; you’d rather assess their behavior before deciding how you’ll act. But today, don’t be so calculating. You’ll be happier and sleep better at night if you behave according to your own values — regardless of what anyone else does.

The people around you might seem unusually nosy today. They’ll likely have all kinds of questions about your life, your relationships, your hopes and dreams. Their curiosity could easily start to feel intrusive. But try not to get defensive. These are people who care about you and want to understand you better. And you don’t have to answer their questions — you can appreciate their good intentions while still honoring your own boundaries.

Nécessaire has mastered the art of caring for skin below the neck, and this all-in-one body set is proof. From body wash to lotion to deodorant, this woody olibanum set is scent synergy in body form.

items.title: Ellah Wakatama, the godmother of African books | Psyche Portraits
items.description: Not long ago, a group of East African writers gathered at my house in Nairobi for a writing weekend. We were all working on manuscripts – novels set in Kenya and in Kazakhstan, histories of people in Ethiopia and Uganda, works we each imagined would be our mag
items.author: Carey Baraka
paragraphs: Not long ago, a group of East African writers gathered at my house in Nairobi for a writing weekend. We were all working on manuscripts – novels set in Kenya and in Kazakhstan, histories of people in Ethiopia and Uganda, works we each imagined would be our magnum opus – but the problem, invariably, was how we might turn these into published books. Over beers and pizza, we brainstormed. Maybe what we needed was to be agented in London or in New York. Maybe what we needed was to move to London or New York. Maybe we simply needed to support each other, edit one another’s manuscripts. (But how would that help us get published?) Then, a Somali author who’d won some of Africa’s most important literary prizes for shorter work, chimed in. What we needed, he said, was to be adopted by Ellah Wakatama.

To be an African writer today – especially one writing in English, especially one younger than 40 – is to reckon with the idea of Ellah. Born in Zimbabwe when it was still under the Rhodesian flag, and now based in Britain, she is an editor-at-large at Canongate, an independent publishing firm. But it is more accurate to describe her as the most powerful woman – person – in Anglophone African literature today. From friends whose books she has touched, one hears of the fury of her red pen, of what they describe as the best editing they’ve ever experienced. From those who’ve worked with her, one hears of a person who doesn’t suffer fools, nor clichés like ‘suffer fools’. No other individual has so influenced the 21st-century African canon, if there is such a thing. Wakatama calls it ‘the bookshelf that my grandchildren will refer to’. Her lifelong project is to shape that bookshelf, to turn it into a library unto itself.
The night went on, as did the weekend. We’d all laughed when he said it, but beneath our laughter were three uneasy truths:
- There were no publishers in East Africa who would put out our work.
- We were doomed to try and find our own way into publishing networks in the West.
- Having a literary godparent was what had worked for generations of African writers.

In the beginning was Chinua Achebe. It is a rule of African literature that any exegesis has to begin with him. Achebe is famous as a novelist – Things Fall Apart (1958) really is one of those great books that everyone should read before they die – but he was more important as an editor of Heinemann’s African Writers Series (AWS), which introduced Western readers to an array of African authors, fledgling and established alike. Novels by African writers had existed before Achebe but, for writers of a certain generation, the AWS was arguably the only publishing vehicle for their work. The great Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, for instance, had his first book published because he gave his manuscript to Achebe. Now we needed to give our manuscripts to Wakatama. She was editor, agent, publisher and godparent, all rolled into one.
But how had she become this person? How did a kid from Harare grow up to wield such influence? I, a kid from Kisumu, a city in Kenya, was determined to track how this had come to be.

The idea of Ellah is different from Ellah in person. In June 2025, I met Wakatama in Accra where she was leading a writing workshop for Pfumo, a Pan-African literary collective she’d recently co-founded. Who was this person in front of me, smoking a cigarette she’s rolled herself? So giggly, so cheery, a bit frilly. She squealed when we passed the store of her favourite Ghanaian designer. I wanted to gossip with her. She exuded fun.

I put to her my Achebe comparison, although I could already see holes: Wakatama’s hair is far more glorious and, unlike the grand old man of African letters, she’d never been a novelist, though she’d briefly tried to be a poet, and co-authored a book of short stories when she was 21. Wakatama, laughing, wouldn’t agree with the Achebe analogy – we both knew that would be in bad taste – but said she could see the throughline of my logic. She was, after all, a child of the age that the AWS represented and sought to shape: Africa after empire.

The second child of Winnie Ndoro and Pius Wakatama, Ellah spent her first four years in a village south of Harare with her grandparents. Winnie and Pius had met at work: she, educated, was a secretary; he, a township boy who sold newspapers, had, Ellah told me, very much ‘married up’. Pius didn’t finish high school but he could write in English; he’d read the short fiction in DRUM, a South African magazine he sold, and thought to himself: I can do that! He could, and did, and then became a novelist in the Shona language, well-known enough that he was invited for a residency at the University of Iowa.
‘I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia’

This time, the whole family went. In Iowa, little Ellah struggled to make friends, partly because she barely spoke English. Once, she saw a group of Black girls playing outside but they wouldn’t speak to her since all she spoke was Shona. That people who looked like her couldn’t understand her was deeply unsettling; soon after, Ellah stopped talking altogether for six months. When she resumed, she stuttered badly in English. Her mother, Winnie, enlisted a speech therapist who used C S Lewis’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe to help her. If you can read this word w-a-r-d-r-o-b-e without stuttering, the therapist once told her, we will have a peach melba. Ellah thought and thought, said the word without tripping over it, then snarfed down her reward.

Perhaps that’s where it started – the belief that books could be a salve against the world. A few years later, when her class went on a field trip to see a wardrobe that had once belonged to C S Lewis, Ellah packed spare socks, a sandwich and a flashlight because she was going to Narnia and not coming back. But when they opened it, it was just an empty wardrobe. ‘I was really disappointed,’ she told me. ‘And I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia.’

In 1976, the family moved back to Zimbabwe, where a war of liberation was being waged. A year before Ellah was born, the white minority in Rhodesia had seized power, declaring independence from Britain. Consequently, two liberation groups – ZANU and ZAPU – had started a resistance war, rejecting rule by a clique of white settlers. Pius and Winnie wanted to be home when it was won. Ten-year-old Ellah, no longer mute, had forgotten how to speak in Shona. Winnie enrolled her in the best private elementary school in Zimbabwe at the time. Only white girls were students at Bishopslea but Winnie saw no reason why her daughters shouldn’t get the best education. Neither did the school’s British headmistress. But the Rhodesian government was angry this had happened, and they deported the headmistress.

All the while, the war continued. Some of Ellah’s relatives were either fighting or living in villages fenced off because of the war. Her classmates were told to support their soldiers; one year, they had to knit balaclavas for the prime minister Ian Smith’s forces, so Ellah went home and asked her mother for green yarn. Winnie was furious; no daughter of hers was going to make balaclavas for the Rhodesians. Ellah cried and cried; all she wanted was to fit in with the other girls. As a compromise, Winnie bought her brown wool – nothing but the green of the Rhodesian flag would fit the Rhodesians.
‘It had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world’

This is one part of what shaped Wakatama. The memories of the war. The race laws in Zimbabwe. The fury with which her mother disregarded them while ensuring that her children were equipped to navigate them. The other part is books. Ellah moved from Nancy Drew and The Hardy Boys to Hermann Hesse and Taban Lo Liyong, working through her father’s library. She wrote Liyong a fan letter; to her delight, he responded. She and her best friend forged their mothers’ signatures so that they could borrow Georgette Heyer paperbacks from the adult library. Then, in 1980 – the year of the first free elections, of Zimbabwe’s independence, of the start of high school – she was assigned to read Doris Lessing in class.

Lessing’s The Grass Is Singing (1950) – the story of the relationship between Mary, a poor white farmer’s wife, and Moses, a Black servant on the homestead – was the first book Wakatama read that was set in Zimbabwe. She found it shocking – and confusing. ‘As a girl, I wanted to become a woman who stood at the vanguard of the battlelines that Lessing had set out, the questions she asked about selfhood and a woman’s place in the world,’ she would later say. ‘But Moses was the one who was my relative.’ It was a challenge in newly independent Zimbabwe to hold both those stories: ‘Lessing, on the one hand, speaking for my gender, and her boldly imagined Moses, on the other hand, bearing witness to my people’s dispossession.’

Enflamed by Lessing, she started writing fiction. A magazine called Moto had a monthly short-story competition, top prize $100, which she entered and won. Her story was about a prison inmate suffering an existential crisis – full of ‘deep emotion, injustice and pretty sentences’. With her prize money, she bought a pair of shoes, grey snakeskin. ‘My brother was at school with a Kenyan boy I really liked,’ she added. ‘So I took him and his friends out to lunch.’ When her father read the story, he said: ‘Yes, Miss Ellah, it’s very good.’ But he was a traditional writer; he believed stories should have a beginning, middle and end, and a moral lesson. Hers didn’t have any of that. ‘The next month, he sent in a story and he won,’ Wakatama told me. ‘It’s something a therapist would have a field day with but, in our house, it was a massive joke.’

Pius Wakatama was a man of strong opinions and believed all his children should have opinions, too. He would argue with them and expect them to argue back. ‘Are you a man or a mouse?’ he once asked Nhamu, Ellah’s younger brother, when he refused to engage. ‘Dad, I’m a mouse,’ Nhamu responded. (Ellah laughed at the memory.) Pius was also extraordinarily large-hearted, often bringing home people who were in a tight spot: struggling relatives, street families, hitchhikers. ‘I grew up with that kind of thing,’ Wakatama said. ‘I think it had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world.’ Once, at the school where he taught, he heard a student crying in the girls’ bathroom because her parents wanted to marry her off. ‘Don’t worry,’ Pius told the young woman. ‘Bring your suitcase with you tomorrow.’ He went home and told Winnie he was bringing her a new daughter. The next day, he knocked on Ellah’s bedroom door and said: ‘This is Florence, she’s your sister.’

Wakatama went to the same college as her mother, a small Mennonite school in rural Indiana. There, in her final year, she declared that she would not read. Specifically – and ‘with all the irritating self-riotousness of youth,’ as she once put it – she announced that she would not be reading any dead white males. Craft your own reading list, her professor told her. This was a turning point. ‘Even though it would be years later that I started working as a publisher, it defined how I approached publishing,’ she told me. ‘The bookshelf was wrong; I knew there was more to it. My professor challenged me to find that “more” – and I did.’
She put James Baldwin on her list, and Alice Walker. Then she discovered Tsitsi Dangarembga.

Dangarembga’s Nervous Conditions (1988) was the first book published in English by a Black Zimbabwean woman. It follows 13-year-old Tambu at a mission school and confronts the ‘nervous conditions’ – a phrase taken from Jean-Paul Sartre – of being caught between traditional African culture and Western colonial influence. The novel’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – jolted Wakatama, not least because Tambu’s brother had almost the same name as Wakatama’s brother, Nhamu. It felt as if, in exploring the dissonance of social mobility in Zimbabwe, Dangarembga was writing about Wakatama and her peers: she ‘felt that the author had peeked inside our most secret diaries and written us into being.’

More than a decade would pass before Wakatama found her way back to books. After college, she married Richard Allfrey, a British boy she’d met in the US, and, while in grad school, decided to have a child because she was ‘curious about motherhood’. She wrote her dissertation with little Gabrielle on her lap. (‘I’d breastfeed and type, breastfeed and type.’) Afterwards, the family moved to England, where she worked a series of jobs in the education sector. ‘I hated every single one,’ she said. The racism in England rankled her but, more than that, she was bored. One day, on holiday in Zimbabwe, her parents sat her down. Pius asked what she was doing with her life. Her mother added: ‘You’ve been sitting on your brain so long you’re going to forget to use it.’
‘They didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out with the guys in the post room because they were Black’

Ellah cried after that intervention. She felt she was letting down her family, letting down Zimbabwe – in those early postcolonial years, the feeling was that your education was meant to improve things. Then her daughter unwittingly spearheaded another intervention. ‘We can’t live with you because you’re so unhappy,’ Gabrielle, seven at the time, told her after she returned from work one day. ‘You spend all your time and money on books,’ Richard chimed in. ‘Why don’t you just work in books?’

Gabrielle, now 34 years old, doesn’t remember giving her mother this advice, though she told me it must have been very good advice for a seven-year-old. She and her sister Rujeko, born 10 years after Gabrielle, were also in Accra. She was enjoying seeing her mother work with writers. Wakatama knew how to talk with writers in a way she hadn’t instinctively known how to talk to babies. When Gabrielle was born, Wakatama – unsure of how to interact with an infant – would read her the paper. This was the 1990s and the Soviet Union had crumbled, so she read Gabrielle stories about Boris Yeltsin. What Gabrielle remembers is struggling with dyslexia
and her mother encouraging her to read, being patient, open and supportive.

After that second intervention, Wakatama worked for a year as a temp at Penguin’s offices in London, before being hired as an assistant to both the editor of the Ancient Classics series and the editor of the Modern Classics series. She was 30. There were books everywhere, piles on the floor, spilling out of cabinets, teetering stacks on desks. I’m home, she thought to herself. But the trouble with being home is that sometimes not everyone there accepts that it is your home. ‘I knew I was with my tribe of people,’ she told me. ‘But they didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out quite a bit with the guys in the post room because they were Black. Nobody was cruel to me – it just never occurred to them at the time.’
She paused. ‘I didn’t look like an editor because none of the editors looked like me.’

She’d sit at the desk looking at the Modern Classics: there were Russian writers, and Japanese writers, and French writers. She began to wonder where the African writers were. ‘How can you say you have a Modern Classics list, and you don’t have Achebe? You don’t have Ngũgĩ? It made absolutely no sense to me.’ Encouraged by her boss, she reached out to people who’d worked at the African Writers Series, and licensed some of those authors: Dambudzo Marechera from Zimbabwe, Bessie Head from Botswana, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o from Kenya. She became interested in Black writers from elsewhere, for instance championing the work of the Jamaican-born Linton Kwesi Johnson, who became the first Black poet, and the second living poet, to be included in the Penguin Modern Classics series.

‘I wasn’t at this point thinking I’m out to change literature,’ she told me. ‘I just thought this bookshelf is wrong. As a child of independence, you know you’re supposed to be changing the world, you don’t just submit and do your job. Plus, I was ambitious as fuck.’

It’s hard to write about editors. Who profiles editors? Writers are easier, at least published ones. Why did you say this 40 years ago, you might ask them; Why does the structure of your novel resemble Flaubert? While talking to Wakatama – we were discussing Wole Soyinka’s hair (‘like a cloud!’) and that time in 2010 she interviewed him – my own early obsessions returned to me: Peter Abrahams and the world of 1940s Johannesburg he created in Mine Boy (1946), Gustave Flaubert’s Parisian aristocrats in Sentimental Education (1869). I knew from an early age that I was going to be a writer; I’d been trapped by literature, deriving pleasure ever since from moments when I could do what those writers did: bring an idea in my head to life on the page, turn a half-formed thought or image into a sparkling sentence.

None of these moments would have been possible without an editor. Only a specific kind of obsessive understands Andy Elisburg’s role in the Miami Heat’s NBA championships, or Elvira Nabiullina’s in Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine, and it’s the same with editors. Writers know. Without an editor who ‘gets it’, we have little chance of succeeding – a sentence my editor most certainly did not force me to write. Or, think of musicians and their producers: there was no Michael Jackson without Berry Gordy, or Kendrick Lamar without Dr Dre. I mentioned Dre to Wakatama, specifically the way she stopped trying to be a poet and began publishing other writers, just as he killed his own rap career, and she cackled.
‘No one’s ever compared me to Dr Dre before!’

The books she is drawn to are ones ‘that feel like they had to be written’, she tells me later, when I ask about the bookshelf she is building, the one her grandchildren will refer to. ‘There has to be a message, a question, an exploration. This works best when filtered through character and place – so the story is equally important.’ In this, she has come to agree with Pius: a story needs a message and a plot. But she remains drawn to beauty. ‘It’s the layers underneath that will keep me reading and re-reading,’ she added. ‘I remain obsessed with beautiful sentences, that delicate crafting of the thought until it becomes poetry.’
Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done

After Penguin, Wakatama moved to Jonathan Cape, an imprint of Random House. Among the first big writers whose books she worked on were Julian Barnes and Ian McEwan. She said: ‘I copyedited On Chesil Beach, which has one mistake in it.’
I said I would read the book to try to find it.
She laughed and said: ‘You won’t know the mistake. If you find it, tell me. Ian said it was his fault, not mine, but I still blame myself.’

Although she now had more room to commission books, her acquisitions budget was still tiny. She scoured the list of writers awarded grants by the Arts Council of England, reaching out to them to see if they had anything to publish. That’s how she published Biyi Bandele’s Burma Boy (2007), about African soldiers in the Second World War, and Nii Ayikwei Parkes’s debut novel Tail of the Blue Bird (2009), a thriller that blends forensic science and Ghanaian folklore. Both challenged the way she thought about editing. In a multi-lingual book, for instance, the non-English parts are usually italicised. But Ayikwei Parkes refused to submit to this; in Blue Bird, this convention is flipped. Typically, ‘English is the standard and the rest of us are deviations,’ she told me. But in Blue Bird, a lot of the narration is by a man who doesn’t speak English: only when he uses a non-Akan word (particular to English) do italics appear. Ayikwei Parkes’s insistence on italicising these individual words of English, rather than those of Twi or Ga, was an assertion that the centre of the world was where the writer said it was, that Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done.
‘That was really, for me, political,’ she said.

Ayikwei Parkes told me how unexpected it had been to find an editor willing to change her mind about editorial style. ‘For most conventional editors, it might be baffling to accommodate such a conceit,’ he said. ‘But she fully grasped the political thrust of my stylistic choice and supported its use, protecting me from the clutches of standard copyeditors.’ When I mentioned the Achebe-Wakatama comparison to him, he disagreed. ‘I sort of resist the idea of godparents for African writing, a notion that doesn’t exist for Western writing. What I will say is that Ellah is, like Achebe, certainly interested in the dignity and autonomy of the African personality and perspective. She believes and understands that Africa is a continent from which the world can be observed, made sense of, influenced and remade.’

Growing up in Zimbabwe, Wakatama says, made her a better editor. ‘Because as an African, for my generation at least, you grow up in an education system that doesn’t include you in the literature; therefore, you have to fill in the gaps yourself. So almost any African, if they were a reader anyway, is going to be a better reader than an English person – because we’re always reading outside ourselves, as well as within ourselves.’ She paused. ‘Which I don’t think we acknowledge enough. I think, now that I’m older, especially post-menopause, and also senior enough not to care what anyone thinks, I can just say it out loud.’

It has taken decades of being dismissed for her to speak so freely: of working under bosses who paid lip-service to diversity, of going to award ceremonies and realising the only other Black people in the room were waiters, of having smaller purchasing and marketing budgets than her colleagues. She recalls trying to acquire a book once, championing it fiercely, but being turned down – mere months later, it was bought by another editor in a different division for five times the price. ‘I told them: This is nonsense – you could have had this book for five grand six months ago when I found it, but because someone else says that it’s good, you’re now going to take it. What the fuck?’

Above her desk at Random House, she’d put up a picture of Toni Morrison, previously an editor at the company. ‘I used to look at that picture and think: She survived and I can too.’ But it was after the death of Nhamu, her younger brother, that she decided things could not go on as they had. Nhamu had suffered a series of strokes, and his death a decade later catapulted Wakatama into a deep depression, a depression that would be matched in depth only by the one triggered by her later divorce from her husband. ‘[Nhamu] was one of the true loves of my life,’ she told me, dabbing her eyes. ‘I was a completely different person after he died … his dying made me think: If he’s gone and I’m left behind – if his life has ended, what am I gonna do with mine?’
‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long’

Shortly after, she joined Granta as deputy editor of the literary magazine. She loved its international scope and finally had what she’d always wanted: a proper budget for commissioning writers. She also began to commission authors for Granta Books. She said: ‘I am driven by a mission, I really am. I’m not a religious person, but I grew up in a religious family. Part of that is about what are you here on earth for? The most important thing to me is books. My daughters will absolutely tell you that they had to fight for my attention. And I want others to have the chance to experience what I’ve experienced. Granta finally gave me that opportunity to do that level of commissioning.’

She started doing workshops – in Nigeria, China, Sri Lanka – to train other editors, as well as more public talks and radio. Her first big interview was with Wole Soyinka. She read him a poem on stage; it was a poem he had written when younger about what he’d be like when his hair was silver. Ellah told him: ‘Look at you now, you’re pretty much all silver. You know, what do you think about the poem?’ The great man laughed.

In 2011, she was awarded an Order of the British Empire for her services to the publishing industry. Somebody noticed, she thought to herself, somebody noticed the work I’m doing. Meanwhile, some colleagues asked: Well, what are you getting that for? ‘We now call these microaggressions, which are never microaggressions,’ she said. ‘My answer was always, for surviving this.’

What does it mean to be the only person of your kind in a room, constantly having to prove you belong? For Wakatama, the cost was psychological. ‘I wish someone had said to me: This life that you’re living is really fulfilling your soul but beware of the damage it will do to you,’ she said. It is tempting to buy into the hoopla of being the first this-or-that, of having a seat at the table, ‘to get sucked into that sense of, Oh, I’m special,’ she warns. ‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long.’

Part of her mission, therefore, is to continue to facilitate the entry of gifted writers into the global publishing infrastructure. In this regard, the English writer Max Porter, who worked alongside Wakatama at Granta, describes her as ‘a proper writer’s editor, deeply committed to and connected to her writers, not necessarily just the one book she is working on.’ As someone new at the time to the publishing world and ‘a little suspicious of it already’, Porter was inspired by how Wakatama nurtured and protected the writers she worked with ‘in the line and on the page and in the world.’

In 2020, after the murder of George Floyd forced a new racial reckoning in the United States and beyond, Wakatama watched white agents rush to sign Black writers. ‘I was like, you’ve got to be kidding me,’ she recalled. ‘After 20 years of saying: Publish Black writers now, you have this.’ Young writers were suddenly being offered massive advances. ‘On one level, that’s great – I’m thinking: Baby, take the money and run! But when you pay half a million for a book and the book sells 10,000 copies, it’s a failure. Remember, it’s an advance against your royalties. So, the next time, you’re starting off in debt.’ The result is that the publisher thinks these books don’t sell and ‘you’ve made it impossible for those authors to be successful.’

In Accra, I sat in on some of the Pfumo sessions. One reason Wakatama co-founded the collective was her concern about how few African nonfiction writers were published internationally. As the participants discussed writing craft, she listened closely, her head tilted towards the speaker, her legs crossed. When she talked, she leaned back, her hands a vital part of her speech. Books surrounded us. (‘It’s overwhelming to realise how many of these I edited,’ she told me.)
When a participant read out her work softly, Wakatama told her to read it again because she wanted ‘a big voice’. Here are other things she said to the writers presenting their work:
‘How do you feel about that?’
‘You’re not being brave enough. I need you to be brave.’
‘Greener pastures, no. That’s a cliché. We don’t use them.’
‘I don’t want you to run away. I want you to try. I think you’ll get it.’
‘I know I said lean into the poetry, but maybe you leaned too much.’

One evening in 2017, Wakatama saw a post on Facebook by Dangarembga, the author of Nervous Conditions. That book’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – had shocked Ellah, but when her own Nhamu died, she returned to the novel in her sorrow. How astutely Dangarembga had written of what Ellah herself had to grapple with: ‘the psychic trauma of fitting into a world that seems to demand an erasure, a forgetting of the self before.’ Dangarembga’s second novel, The Book of Not, had come out in 2006. She was now seeking an editor for her third, which she would self-publish.

That Dangarembga would struggle to find a publisher despite her success was an indictment of an industry that still struggled to recognise African writers. Wakatama didn’t know Dangarembga personally but she reached out anyway. ‘Your writing is so important to so many of us, why are you self-publishing?’ she asked. ‘If you do self-publish, please can I offer my services for free as your editor?’

The new book – This Mournable Body (2018) – was remarkable, Wakatama thought, and she offered to introduce Dangarembga to a friend who ran Graywolf Press, an American indie publisher. Wakatama flew to Harare; Dangarembga came to the family house for lunch. When she was younger, Dangarembga recalled, she often corresponded with a Zimbabwean writer called Pius Wakatama. Was he a relative, Dangarembga wondered. Pius laughed. It was him.

Graywolf bought the book. Wakatama was then still editing it for free, but she added a clause in the contract stipulating that the publisher would pay her an extra (hefty) fee if the book made it to the Booker shortlist. ‘Everyone was fine with it because it was never going to happen,’ she recalled, smiling. But by now Wakatama knew to bet on herself. ‘When she got shortlisted and the money hit my account, I was, like, Yeah. I told you all.’

items.title: We need a language to name the grief that comes without death | Aeon Essays
items.description: I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say
items.author: Derek van Zoonen
paragraphs: I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say goodnight, her cheeks covered in thick layers of night cream. Then, out of nowhere, the image would flip into the raging woman who was so entangled in her own suffering that she turned her frustration on us. Over the years, that second woman slowly swallowed the first, as she got pulled into my brother’s addiction. It’s hard to say where her own unhappiness ended and my brother’s suffering began, but together they drifted into a parallel reality, cut off from the world beyond their heads. There was no funeral for this. No condolence cards. No flowers. No phone calls. No leave of absence. What was I supposed to mourn?

And yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning. Can there be grief without death? I have come to think that we grieve much more often than we realise, and that death is grief’s most visible occasion rather than its essence. If that doesn’t match your experience, it may be because we rarely call these other losses by their name. Most of our losses arrive without a funeral. That is the human predicament: we are creatures built to attach, living in a world where nothing stays. Sooner or later, we lose the things we care about. And since we are complex beings with a body, a mind, a community and an environment – beings who love many different things – there is a great deal we can lose, from our physical health to our sense of who we are, from relationships to homelands to the natural world we share with other species. For creatures like us, there is no way around heartbreak: to live is to lose. Grief is what love does when its object is gone. It is love with nowhere to go.

Over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses. There is the psychological loss of my father as I knew and loved him: a brutal stroke rendered him incapable of walking and cycling, and cycling was the only thing that could ‘make his thoughts liquid’, as he used to say. There is the loss of old friendships. First you are no longer part of each other’s lives – you just update one another about your life – and then, one day, it becomes awkward to reach out at all. There is the gradual softening of an academic identity I’d spent the most vital years of my life constructing. It was a genuine vocation, a life of the mind that taught me to think slowly and carefully. But it was also, as I came to realise, a way of living safely at one remove from where actual life takes place. What is slipping away is a future in which being an academic philosopher would be the whole answer to the question of who I am.

There was the woman whose calmness, clarity and silence embodied the qualities I have come to like so much about the Nordics since moving to Norway. Like a magical stranger, she entered my life unexpectedly, but at the same time her arrival felt so natural, her presence so obvious, that it was as if she had always been there. After our first meeting, which lasted almost 24 hours, I wrote in my journal: Ze is gekomen om te blijven. ‘She had come to stay.’ And she did, for nine intense months. She tried to teach me to ski. We listened to the music of Nils Frahm, which reminded her of melting snow. And she made me see that the deepest form of intimacy happens in the space between the words.

But despite the depth of our bond, she left, abruptly, as if she had never been there. She had fallen in love with another man. I was left behind, dazed and disoriented, and although my heart was broken, this kind of loss did not have a name that matched how shattered I felt. It was ‘just a breakup’, and it didn’t even deserve that name: we had been dating, but it never technically became a relationship. It was also a romantic connection that ran alongside another one, a long partnership that was open by mutual agreement and conscious design. Much about it wasn’t legible to most people around me. I faced the grief largely by myself. No scripts, no rituals, no recognised form, no legitimacy, no shared language, no way to make sense of what had happened to me.

Part of what made the experience so disorienting was a narrow idea of what grief is. In psychology, in philosophy and in our Western culture at large, grief has been treated almost exclusively as a response to the death of someone we love. It’s a neat, tidy understanding. The most celebrated grief memoirs – think of The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) by Joan Didion and A Grief Observed (1961) by C S Lewis – are concerned with the loss of a life partner. And Michael Cholbi’s Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) – one of the most extensive philosophical treatments of the emotion – focuses mostly on the grief we experience at the death of someone we love or who otherwise matters to us.
Restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches

Death is visible and final: it has a body, a date, a medical certificate. The other losses are blurrier: they have no physical object, no clear beginning or end, no tangible proof they happened. We also have an infrastructure for death: funerals, condolence cards, flowers, casseroles, bereavement leave – a whole social script. Perhaps the infrastructure defines what counts: if there is no social and cultural scaffolding to digest the experience, it must not be real grief.

The prime reason for the single-minded focus on death loss, however, must be that bereavement is simply the most striking instance of a broader emotional phenomenon that comes in degrees. But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.

If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.

Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.

What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):

Grief is thus distinctive insofar as it involves recognising and comprehending the implications of lost possibilities for the structure of one’s life or world, and – over time – coming to reorganise one’s life accordingly.

This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).
‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’

My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.

The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.

The case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.
They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience

‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.

Those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’

The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.

The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.

Sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.
If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves

But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):

Grief and love are sisters, woven together from the beginning. Their kinship reminds us that there is no love that does not contain loss and no loss that is not a reminder of the love we carry for what we once held close.

Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.

The tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.

Behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.

Christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.
The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder

Arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.

What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.

But the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.

Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.

I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting said what neither of us could.

items.title: Lucy Bridge Wants To Bring Colour Back to Beauty
items.description: As her debut book Colour Mode is released, the make-up artist talks us through her technicolour world
items.author: Dominic Cadogan
paragraphs: As her debut book Colour Mode is released, the make-up artist talks us through her technicolour world

Lucy Bridge has always lived her life in full colour. When she was at school, the make-up artist dyed her hair a new shade every week, much to the despair of her teachers, and after moving to London in 2008, it was her affinity for popping to the shops with neon pink blusher and green glitter eyebrows that turned the head of famed photographer Tim Walker – who scouted her for a shoot in i-D after spotting her on the 55 bus.

Today, she is one of fashion’s most prominent talents, known for colouring outside the lines and a roster that includes Jean Paul Gaultier, Mugler, Dries Van Noten and Tom Ford, where she is now global make-up artist for the brand under Haider Ackermann. A scroll through her kaleidoscopic oeuvre reveals crimson lacquered lips that deepen to merlot at the edges, acid green eyeshadow and licks of molten silver and gold. It’s an urgent antidote to the neutral tones of the minimalist ‘clean girl’ who currently reigns in beauty.

It comes as no surprise, then, that her debut book Colour Mode, created over three and a half years in collaboration with creative director Veronica Ditting, is a smorgasbord of shades. A trip down the rabbit hole into the make-up artist’s mind, alongside ten commissioned shoots – featuring photographers Paolo Roversi, Oliver Hadlee Pearch and Thurstan Redding – ‘Looks in Process’ captured by Jean Marques offers a glimpse into the fantastical creations as they come together.
Here, Bridge talks us through the inspiration behind three of the stories in Colour Mode and her collaborative process with each photographer.

“This shoot really represents my head as a make-up artist and what goes on in my brain. It’s totally bonkers, so abstract and very out there. I must admit it’s my favourite one out of the whole book, all the wacky colours. We started with beads on the face and we needed another beaded element somewhere. I tried them on the eyes; it wasn’t quite working. We tried the hands, it didn’t work. I was like, ‘Right, one of these models needs to give me one of their feet’ and honestly it was incredible. After I did the foot, Lauren Michelle Pires tested out a few different colours and then actually put fake toenails on. On the day, Carlijn was like ‘I didn’t really understand the foot when you were doing it, but my agent is obsessed’ and anyone I’ve shown this shoot to has been mesmerised by the foot. I don’t really know where it came from, it just sprang from my imagination. I need it blown up one day and put up in my house.”

“I’ve been working with Tim on and off for the past 15 years. He’s been so nurturing. He’s really helped me throughout my whole career and given me a platform. He was inspired by the psychedelic hippie group from 1970s San Francisco, The Cockettes and I did some wacky make-up inspired by them. There’s a lot of trust between me and Tim, so we didn’t have too much back and forth before the shoot – we had a cup of tea in the morning and a little discussion and then we cracked on. I knew I wanted a simple white background so the make-up was the focus and then we worked with Gerry O’Kane to create these characters. Tim has been in the game for a long time and he knows what he wants to do, so I knew we were going to get something incredible.”

“Jack was actually the last photographer to shoot for the book, it took us about two years to get together. I’d only worked with Jack once previously, but Veronica had a long-standing relationship with him – she calls him the magician. I always go into a shoot with a very methodical and clear idea of what I’m going to do, whereas with Jack, it was much looser because I don’t even think he knows what he’s getting on the day. I love his world, it’s so surrealist. We wanted the shoot to look really timeless and you can’t quite place it, it could have been shot in the 1920s, but it also feels so modern. We were shooting and all of a sudden he started projecting my make-up palettes onto the model. I didn’t know Jack had taken a picture of them when I was doing the make-up and it was genius and that’s what made the cover. It’s not technically make-up, but it’s showing my practice as a make-up artist and it’s nice that Jack brought it into the shoot so elegantly.”
Lucy Bridge Colour Mode is published by Thames & Hudson and out now

items.title: Lance Oppenheim on His Feature Fiction Debut, Primetime
items.description: The 30-year-old Floridian’s feature fiction debut Primetime, with an “operatic” performance from Robert Pattinson, taps into a culture war that’s still raging and at times, he says, felt more like making a documentary than some of his documentaries
items.author: Miriam Balanescu
paragraphs: The 30-year-old Floridian’s feature fiction debut Primetime, with an “operatic” performance from Robert Pattinson, taps into a culture war that’s still raging and at times, he says, felt more like making a documentary than some of his documentaries

Between his fiction feature debut Primetime and his Nathan Fielder collaboration You Can See Everything, Lance Oppenheim, a 30-year-old from Florida, is behind two of the buzziest films of the year. The day I talk to him over Zoom, his three-hour Elizabeth Holmes doc has been slapped with an R rating for “graphic nudity” – fanning the flames of online speculation about a film Oppenheim insists should be experienced with “no context”.

What he will say about the enigmatic doc is that, together with Primetime, this is a new stylistic chapter for his filmmaking. Oppenheim rose through the ranks of Hollywood with the documentaries Some Kind of Heaven (about America’s largest retirement village) and Spermworld (following unregulated online sperm donors). Oppenheim’s Robert Flaherty-inspired “docu-fantasias” would involve spending sometimes years with his subjects and using “the tools of narrative filmmaking” to recreate subjective experiences.

“Primetime was different. And I would say [so was] You Can See Everything. That was made in a completely new style [...] very rigorously vérité documentary. With Primetime, by saying that in some cases it felt more like making a documentary than my documentaries themselves, I mean [in terms of] the process. On a documentary, because the crew is so small, normally I’m able to control the image, to wait and see how I want to shoot something. If I don’t get it right, I’ll go back and do it the next day.”

By contrast, Primetime was a sprawling shoot: 780 people were involved, 20 different camera formats were used, and shot listing and rehearsing were avoided. At the epicentre of Primetime and You Can See Everything are two slippery subjects. The former follows Chris Hansen, the television host who spearheaded To Catch a Predator, played by an exquisitely slimy Robert Pattinson. The NBC show would document sting operations baiting would-be child predators to a stage house, and turn Hansen’s confrontation with them (and their arrests) into peak viewing entertainment. Like Hansen, Oppenheim calls Holmes a “cipher”. The Theranos fraudster invited Oppenheim’s documentary crew into her home days before her prison sentence in a seeming bid to outsmart Fielder and his team.

Primetime begins as Hansen’s flagship show is programmed in competition with Lost, upping the pressure for Hansen and his producer Andie (a brilliantly nihilistic Merritt Wever). A new “decoy” is recruited – Daniel (Skyler Gisondo), a Rent-singing adult actor posing as a minor. And Hansen’s marriage (to Anna Faris) starts to unravel once his affair is discovered by the press. These personal dramas unfold amid the carnivalesque television set, inhabited on and off camera by Oppenheim’s own crew. “I liked that we were living a parallel existence as the characters were in the movie,” he muses.

It is Pattinson’s exacting, “operatic” embodiment of Hansen – as Oppenheim puts it – that brings the film truly into a hyperreal dimension, however. The actor, who also produced Primetime, approached Oppenheim with Ajon Singh’s script for the film but didn’t initially plan on starring. “[Robert and I] talked so much ad nauseum about the script,” says Oppenheim. “My wife gave birth to our son five days before production started, and he was in the delivery room with me on FaceTime, calling mid-delivery with ideas for the script.

“We spent Christmas together, staying up until three in the morning, drinking beers and talking about the character, watching Hansen vs Predator together.” He adds: “This is more of a media collage than anything else. He’s essentially playing every version of Chris Hansen that’s ever existed [...] stitching all that stuff together with something very vulnerable and human, which I think comes from Rob’s experience dealing with essentially becoming an overnight celebrity. He was struggling to make sense of how to be himself, but also give people what they wanted.”

Amid QAnon paedophile ring conspiracy theories and the rise of “predator hunters” in the manosphere, Primetime taps into a culture war that’s still raging. “There was still so much anger and confusion post-9/11 that the regimented concept of being a Democrat or Republican, this binary, started to exist,” reflects Oppenheim. “Because of all the anger and fear and anxiety, it almost felt like the show, when it arrived in the early 2000s, was the perfect receptacle for all of this stuff. It’s to me a very Bush-era concept of politics of ‘if you’re not with us, then you’re against us.’”

Despite Hansen’s dubious methods – and his threats to sue Oppenheim for making the film – the director maintains that he is still a fan of the TV show personality. “Chris’s reaction to the film itself, in a lot of ways, feels exactly like the sort of behaviour we were trying to trace. It’s actually proving the thesis of the movie,” he urges. “When the movie was first announced, [Hansen] was at the Crime Con convention, and I think he said something to the tune of you may have thought that Robert Pattinson was going to be here, but it’s me. He’s gone from journalist to crusader, and then from crusader to vigilante [...] an almost messianic person cleansing the world of an ancient evil” – all the while hijacking the film’s publicity to nail a book deal and an autobiographical series.

“He kind of reminds me of Batman or something,” says Oppenheim. “He’s doomed to living a lifestyle where he has to fight crime for the rest of his life. Like in The Dark Knight Rises, Bruce Wayne, you see that it’s taking a toll on his body physically and spiritually.” Oppenheim says he eagerly awaits Hansen’s reaction to actually seeing Primetime: “I want to go on his podcast with Rob. Ideally I’d even love to do the A24 podcast with him and talk about the movie and have a seat together.”
Previews for Primetime start from 28 October, before arriving in UK cinemas on 30 October

items.title: When Is a Monastery Like a Calvin Klein Store? When John Pawson Gets to it
items.description: How should we live? What is space? How minimal can a building or room be? These are some of the questions architectural designer John Pawson brings up in his book The Minimal Home, and which come up in his commissions. The designer behind the Calvin Klein Coll
items.author: Sami Reiss
paragraphs: How should we live? What is space? How minimal can a building or room be? These are some of the questions architectural designer John Pawson brings up in his book The Minimal Home, and which come up in his commissions. The designer behind the Calvin Klein Collections Store in Manhattan, London’s Design Museum, and a number of monasteries, he is minimalism’s ambassador if there ever was one. A Pawson building tends to be stripped down to its essence and spacious. Even his apartments are cavernous; work is both demanding and light.

Such simplicity and directness of purpose didn’t happen overnight. Pawson, raised in Yorkshire, and who worked formatively under Shiro Kuramata, the generationally important Japanese designer, and founding member of Memphis Group, entered the Architectural Association School of Architecture in his late 20s already converted to minimalism, then opened his practice in 1981.
